Preliminary Note
In this and later volumes I have ignored the underlining of the dates, or parts of dates, in Locke's letters, and generally, in vol. v and later volumes, the underlining of names and dates in his endorsements. The underlining was intended, not for emphasis or distinction, but to catch the eye; adequate representation would require leaded type; marking of the kind is scarcely necessary in print.

Letters Nos. 849-1241
Locke's Life: Principal Dates for this Volume
This table is planned to provide dates that should be serviceable to readers of the correspondence. It is not a chronological framework for Locke's life.
The principal difficulty in its compilation is that for many incidents in his life precise dates do not exist. Thus, if the mention is accurate, Locke was acquainted with Robert Boyle on 20 May 1660; there is nothing to show how much earlier the acquaintance was made. Unsatisfactory as many of them are, the dates are the best available.
In the dates a. (for ante) is to be taken to imply shortly before. In the dates for books when a precise date accompanies the word 'published' it is to be taken as the date of the earliest notice that the book had been, was, or was about to be, published, and not necessarily as the day of publication.
        
1686 	a. 24 April/4 May. Locke sends Clarke transcripts of part of the Essay (probably Books I and II). 
	17/27 August. Locke sends Clarke a transcript of Book III of the Essay. 
	Early September? Locke's 'Méthode nouvelle de dresser des recueuils' published. 
	a. 22 September/2 October. Locke goes to Utrecht. 
	28 September/8 October. Locke mentions Benjamin Furly for the first time. 
	October/November. Skelton attempts to seize English fugitives. Locke went to Rotterdam about the end of November and to Amsterdam late in December. 
	14 December. Peter Locke dies. 
	21/31 December. Locke sends Clarke a transcript of Book IV of the Essay. 
 
1687 	Early February. Locke goes to lodge with Furly in Rotterdam. Locke resided usually in Rotterdam until he sailed for England on 10/20 February 1689. 
 
1687-8 	Winter. The supposed pardon for Locke. 
 
1688 	c. 27 January/6 February. The Abregé of Locke's Essay printed (the 'Extrait' was published probably about April). 
      
1689 	12 February. Locke returns to London. He resided in London until July 1690, when he went to Oates. 
	April. The Epistola de Tolerantia published at Gouda. 
	29 May. Locke is appointed a Commissioner of Appeals in Excise. 
	3 October. A Letter concerning Toleration licensed for publication. 
	18 November. Two Treatises of Government advertised. 
	Mid-December. The Essay published.

1686
April
849. Locke to Edward Clarke, 24 April/4 May 1686 (846, 863)
Rand, pp. 162-5. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The transcription is unreliable.
Amsterdam, 4th May, 1686.
Sir,
The manner wherewith you continue to speak of the advice I have ventured to send you concerning your son, makes me fear that in perusing it you more regard the intention and friendship of the author, than the meanness of the thing itself; since you so far mistake it as to think that it has laid the debt on your side, and such an one as you imagine you can never get out of; which, when I on the other side consider your favours, I conclude I have all the reason in the world [to say] in your own words, that I must forever remain your debtor. But to enter into a dispute with you, wherein an excess of friendship makes you obstinate, I have another reason to suspect that your consideration for the person that gave it makes you overlook many things in the advice itself, since that I receive not from you any objections about any part of it. For though I must own it is according to the best of my skill, and though I know the affection I writ it with to be very sincere, yet I can by no means fancy my opinion infallible, or that it should in all things so exactly jump with yours and madam's, that you should find nothing (in what is already put in practice) to be added, omitted, or altered, whereof however you say nothing at all. For I doubt not but when I revise the foul copy,†1 which I keep by me on purpose, I shall myself find occasion for additions or alterations.
I do not at all wonder that you have not yet found a tutor to your mind, and I confess the truth somewhat pleased with it. Not that you are hitherto disappointed, but that I perceive that you are more curious in your choice than to take up a venture with the first or second that comes in your way. 'Tis of great consequence to your son, and therefore you cannot be too nice in it. If you could get your cousin†2 to Chipley, a sober, well conditioned young man with moderate learning would do the business, but you know his humour and how averse to trouble especially of some kind.
― 2 ―

But as to the law suit I mentioned in my last, I conclude upon second thoughts that it is best to let it perfectly alone without meddling at all in it, any farther than E P†1 himself shall of his own accord discourse of his own concerns and give his advice about it, and then it would perhaps be not amiss to enquire and reason with him for your own satisfaction of the grounds he proceeds on.
 
As to your Carolina affair, I remember the owner told me it was a Landgraveship of forty-eight thousand acres of land, and the privileges thereunto belonging, which are to be seen in the Fundamental Constitutions.†2 This is enough for your Scotch friend to know to see to what terms he will come, which, when they are judged reasonable or near the matter, the patent now in the executors' hands will be forthcoming time enough, if the mice have not eaten it, as I believe not, in a strong wooden chest where he was wont to keep it, and which Adrian†3 had the direction to open, which I remember was this: You must turn the key with the sun once round and a quarter, and then turn it back again half a round and so let it stand. For example, the key put in at the keyhole amust be turned by b-c-d quite to b again, and from b be turned back again to d, and there let stand, and then the lid of the chest may be lifted up. [This] I am sure is the just quantity of the motion that the key must have, and I think for making it you must begin the motion with the sun; but this I do not perfectly remember, and therefore nothing must be forced in the case, for if the contrary motion from a to d and so round be the way to open it, you must do the quite contrary in all things. When it is open you will find one turn to lock it as it does other locks. This much I remember of the lock itself, but where the chest itself is, that the executors know, I for my part know not. This I only know, that if you can persuade my cousin Somerton and his wife to make use of it and remove thither (which I should advise him to if the plantation
― 3 ―

flourishes and promises any good), he may have this interest for acceptance.
As you are content your pictures should remain in the hands of the merchant here†1 that bought them for you, till you have informed yourself concerning that sort of merchandise, and to what port either London or Exeter you were best have them, so I find he is not in haste for the <state>†a of the account between you, which therefore you need not be at the pains to send till he demand it. He hopes, as I perceive, that this shall not be the last business he shall have with you, and therefore expects not to have the just balance returned, but an entire sum, something near it may serve the turn. The rest, I perceive, he is not troubled should remain as a nest egg till a farther occasion: as much as I know of him he is a very fair conditioned man, and knows very well your character.
I am glad to hear my Lady King's son†2 thrives so very well, but the Lady I meant is a relation of the Lady that did me the honour to remember to me in your last.†3 Pray present my humble service to her, and let her know I should be glad if there were anything here for her service. My service also to my Valentine,†b Susan, and her man Thomas,†4 and to all you mention in your last letter.
Sutton business dissatisfies me mightily. If that estate will yield nothing by the year, I am of opinion you should sell it and make present money of it; at least the very proposition will quicken the man that deceived you and your aunt†5 so scurvily.
My most humble service to your Lady and little ones.
I am, Sir,
your most humble servant,
J. L.
I hope you will talk at large and fully with Adrian. He that copied my last long letter mistook in the names of some books which I much desire you to correct, and for Bacon to set down Chillingworth, and for Tacitus, Tully.†6 I sent you lately a part of my
― 4 ―

reasonings de intellectu humano,†1 which I hope came safe, for you know we are all concerned for our own conceptions how idle soever.
850. Locke to Nicolas Toinard, 29 April/9 May 1686 (818, 853)
B.M., Add. MS. 28,728, ff. 28-9. Printed in Ollion, p. 118.
(English) 
Amsterdam 9o May 86
Suspicaberis forte tam diu silentem a silentibus rediisse, sed bono sis animo, non cum spectris res est, tenue illud quod olim noveras corpus nondum in pulverem solutum, animusque qui semper fuit in te idem. Sed quorsum tam taciturnus? nec hoc meæ sed aliorum culpæ tribuendum, quamvis si ita res ferret te majora mihi condonaturum non desperarem. Quamprimum huc accessi Wetstenium adii ut de te certior fierem. de sanitate gavisus sum et quod de harmonicis adhuc cogitas. Vidi folium impressum, sed Matthæum mallem quam Josephum.†2 Schedas complica et te cum illis Veredario trade et ad nos advola de hospitio ne sis solicitus cubiculum et lectum apud me tibi paratum scias. Fac tandem ut aliquot tecum
― 5 ―

fæces transigam dies antequam nox longa veniat. Triumviratum officiosissime saluto. Vale et ama tui amantissimum
JL
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Toinard chez Madame la Presidant à Orleans
Endorsed by Toinard: 9. May, 86.
(Latin) 
Amsterdam 9 May 86
You will perhaps suspect that one who has been silent so long is a revenant from the silent world; but be of good cheer; you do not have to deal with phantoms; the attenuated body that you knew of old is not yet resolved into dust, and the spirit is the same that it always was towards you. But why so speechless, you may ask? Well, you must lay the blame on others, not on me, though I would not despair of your forgiveness for greater offences, if the need should arise. The moment I arrived here I went to see Wetstein to get news of you; I am delighted to know you are well and are still thinking about things harmonical. I saw a printed sheet, but I would have preferred Matthew to Josephus.†2 Make a bundle of the sheets, entrust yourself to the post with them and fly to us; you need not be concerned about lodgings; there is a room and a bed for you in mine, you may be sure. Do manage at least to let me [p. 5] spend a few happy days with you before the long night comes! I send my best wishes to the Triumvirate. Good-bye, and love your most affectionate
JL
May
851. Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 29 May/8 June 1686 (854)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 144-5.
Walter Yonge, 1653-1731, of Colyton, Devon; third baronet 1670; M.P. for Honiton 1679-81; for Ashburton 1689-90; for Honiton 1690-1710; a commissioner of the Customs 1694-1701, 1714-31; married (1) in 1677 Gertrude, d. 1679, daughter of Sir William Morrice of Werrington, bart. (p. 296); (2) at St. James, Clerkenwell, 18 June 1691, Gwen, d. 1729?, daughter of Sir Robert Williams of Penrhyn, bart. His sisters included Isabella, wife of Richard Duke (p. 13 n., etc.), and Elizabeth, who married Bartholomew Beale in 1692 (p. 16, n. 1, etc.). In 1680 he acquired an estate at Escot in Talaton and rebuilt the house at once: J. L. Vivian, The Visitations of the County of Devon, [1895], p. 841; G.E.C., Baronetage, iii. 232; R. Polwhele, The History of Devonshire, 1793-1806, ii. 271-2.
Yonge probably came into political life as an adherent of Shaftesbury. He entertained Monmouth at Colyton in 1680 when Monmouth was making his western progress: G. Roberts, Life of ... Monmouth, 1844, i. 101-2. He is mentioned several times by Forde Grey, Lord Grey of Warke (no. 422), in The Secret History of the Rye-House Plot, 1754 (see pp. 16, 17-18, 104, 122*). On 19 May 1685, when Argyle was in Scotland and Monmouth's invasion was imminent, he was ordered to be taken into custody; by 28 August he was at liberty, and was at Tunbridge Wells with John Freke (p. 58 n.) and Richard Duke, probably his brother-in-law: Cal. S.P., Dom.,1685, no. 689; H.M.C., Portland MSS. iii. 387. Letters and notices below.
Locke mentions Yonge on 12 June 1683 in his Journal, and Mrs. Duke as far back as 1679: pp. 165-6. This year he was with Yonge probably in Amsterdam on 22 May, N.S. He and Freke were together in Haarlem on 5 18th: June. On 14 June he went to Rotterdam, and was with Yonge there on the ibid. Yonge's date for the letter is evidently new style.
Rotterdam 8 June 1686
Dear Sir
Though you were justly punished for leaving your friends so unnecessarily, yet we could not but be troubled to find by the letter
― 6 ―

that followed you from Amsterdam, that you were dissappointed in the very business that caried you from us, we doubted not but you would be much in pain for want of it, and therefore Mr Freke†1 took care to send it back to Amsterdam Thursday night†2 directed as you desired to your lodgings, which we take to be the true reason why you did not receive it the next day, and we are confirmed in that opinion by the miscariage of a letter Mr Freke wrote you before we went to Amsterdam, and sent by the same direction, so that I design to enclose this to your bookseller. We take it for granted your letter is from our friend whome you expect,†3 and presume you have it before this time, if not you can not faile of recovering it from the post office; We flatter our selves that it may informe you that the Doctor purposes to come over with my Sisters,†4 and consequently that you will hasten hither to meet him; however we can not but wish you here to goe with us to morrow morning to the Brill, for by the last post I had an account that my Sister had taken places in the Harwich coach in order to her coming over in the packet boat which is to come away from England this night, so that if the wind continues good we promise our selves that we shall embrace our friends to morrow in the evening, and so return hither again on monday morning, and that night hope to meet you here, or a better reason to the contrary, then you gave for going from us. I am much obliged to you for getting me the Novelles des lettres†5 and Sir William Temples book,†6 pray compleat the favor by bringing them and any other book you pick up for me with you. As to Sueurs history,†7 I think I am obliged to take it of Van Someren†8 because he bought it purposely for me, but if he has two Editions of it, pray chuse the best (as of all other books where the difference of the price is not more considerable.) As I remember I have met with
― 7 ―

a precept in a good Author against Vain Philosophie,†1 and therefore a little of that will serve my turn; but if you please at your leisure to make me a note of the best Italien and Latin authors which you would recommend to me, I may furnish my selfe hereafter with such of them as I have not already in my library; in which I must informe my selfe from England, having no Catalogue with me of those books. I have ordered Varillas' Education of a prince†2 to be bound up for me here. As to Cardinal d'Ossat's letters,†3 Mr Freke saies he is unwilling to buy gold too dear, but if you think the edition in quarto to be true, and not a very ill character and a reasonable penyworth, he desires to have it. My paper minds me of concluding, yet you must give me leave first to assure you that I am (without a complement) unalterably
Your most obliged friend and faithfull servant
WALTER YONGE
My fatt brother†4 desires me to tell you, that with all his ill nature he had forgot both the quarrell and occasion of it as soon as you were out of sight, a quality few lean men can brag of; and he and your other friends kiss your hands. Adieu.
Address: Aen Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Jacob Van de Velde Boeckvercooper op de Hoeck van de Korte Niesel t'Amsterdam
On an inside page: For Mr John Locke.
Endorsed by Locke: Sir W. Yonge 8 Jun. 86

852. Dr. Caspar Sibelius to Locke, 3/13 June 1686 (785, 858)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, f. 106. In the address Deventer is suspect; Locke's only recorded visit was in September 1684: Journal.
(English) Vir Nobilissime, Fautor pl. honorande,
Nuperas Tuas humanissimas unà cum donario pro fæminâ meâ addito è manu Amicorum ritè accepi, gratias Tibi dico ingentes. Harum præcipua ratio est Casus quidam, cujus historiam hîc vides annexam, idque eâ de causâ egi non solùm cùm sperem inde manifestum Ægri commodum sed etiam propriam in Re Medicâ utilitatem: nec enim confiteri piget Tua Consilia et Responsa Medica ante hac ad me missa Mercurios†1 mihi fuisse quæ palpantem et devium in viam reduxerint, quin et maximo honori duco Magni Æneæ dextrâ cadere.†2
(English) Vir honestus, Lapicida et Cæmentarius civicus, ætat. 38. annorum, constitutionis à Naturâ macilentæ, abhinc quarto anno retro ex Febre Continuâ ardenti et gravi decubuit, quae etiam biennio post ipsum rursus afflixit. Posteà à primâ Febri illâ disparente percepit dolorem gravativum et nonnihil lancinantem juxta regionem sinistram Lumborum prope Renem sinistrum eo in loco ubi costæ nothae sunt, qui dolor ab attactu digiti exasperatur et singulâ vesperâ horâ
― 9 ―

7. maximoperè intenditur cum insequente siti, linguâ albicante, Calore quodam p.n. totius corporis et maximè volarum manuum exasperato, pulsuque celeri, frequenti, duro, vehementi. Tussis adfligit eum nocte dieque tùm inanis tùm cum screatu sputi antehac sanguinei, jam verò plurimi, viscidi, tenacis, globosi, non fætidi, fusci: dicitque æger se statim Hæmoptoen passum quamprimum corpus fortiter moverit vel plurimum frigidi unico haustu assumpserit. Lassitudo spontanea totius cum imbecillitate summâ pedum maximè molesta est, imprimis vesperi cum Calor exacerbatur cum Respiratione difficili quæ de die satis libera eo tempore excepto quo Tussire cogitur, tùm enim dolorem percipit sub sterno. In summâ Totum corpus q. sceleton est et Facies propemodùm Hippocratica. Urina intensiùs tincta, clara, fulgida mingitur, post horulæ quietem turbatur et postea sedimentum copiosum, crassum, fuscum deponit. Alvi excrementa adhucdum sunt naturalia quoad colorem, quamvis substantiâ, sicciora et duriora. Hypochondria et Abdomen molle, non tensum, vel durum. Quantum Ego conjicio, Febris est ex genere Lentarum Febrium, propriè Hectica dicta unà cum Pulmonum Ulcere.
(English) 1. Quæritur, An Cura Lactis sit instituenda? Quale Lac an
― 10 ―

Caprillum vel Bovinum? Quâ Methodo sit porrigendum, ne grumescat vel bilescat in Stomacho, vel obstructiones in glandulis et visceribus pariat?
(English) 2. An insuper nonnulla Aperientia sint Lacteæ Curæ adjungenda pro deobstruendis glandulis quò Lympha nutrititia eò melius per corpus distribuatur?
(English) 3. An non et Opiata ad Effervescentiam illam et acrimoniam Massæ sanguineæ interdiù sub accisâ dosi exhibenda, præsertim cùm Æger aliquando totâ nocte non dormiat, et si dormit semper turbulenta somnia habeat?
(English) 4. Denique quâ Diætâ restaurante et <quâ>†a methodo uti debeat æger?
(English) De quibus et singulis obnixè rogo, ut quantocyùs me edoceas, cùm propriâ Experientiâ de hoc Affectu edoctus sis: Æger enim se omnia à Te præscripta ad amussim se servaturum promisit, sique alio modo quàm per Lac possit curari Æger, quæso perscribe quoniam Cura Lactea aliquomodo <difficilis>†b nostro Cæmentario erit observata. Plura adderem, nisi Tabellarius ad discessum se præpararet. Hisce Vale, Vir Nobilissime, et fave
T. Fautori et Amico
C. SIBELIO
Daventriæ d. 13. Jun. 86.
― 11 ―

(English) 
Address: A Monsieur, Monsieur J Lock Mon tres cher Amÿ presentement à Deventer. Citò, citò. par Couvert.
(Latin) Excellent Sir, and most honoured helper,
Your recent very kind letter together with the gift which you added for my wife were duly handed to me by my friends; I give you my warmest thanks. The principal subject of my present letter is a certain case which you see described in what follows; my reason for acting thus is not only that I hope for some clear advantage to the patient therefrom, but also for what may be useful to me in medical practice; for I am not ashamed to confess that the counsels and replies on medical matters which you have sent me in the past have been Mercuries†1 for me, leading my groping and devious steps back into the right path; indeed, I count it the highest honour to 'fall by great Aeneas's hand.'†2
(Latin) A worthy man, a municipal stone-mason and builder, aged thirty-eight, of a naturally meagre physique, fell ill four years ago with a burning and severe continual fever, which attacked him again two years later. After that first fever passed off he began to feel an oppressive and rather acute pain on the left side of his loins, near the left kidney, in the place where the floating ribs are situated; this pain becomes sharper when touched with the finger, and reaches its greatest intensity for an hour at 7 o'clock in the evening; this [p. 9] is followed by thirst, a white tongue, and a certain amount of heat throughout the body during the night, which is most severe in the palms of the hands; the pulse becomes rapid, frequent, hard, and violent. He is troubled by a cough night and day; this is sometimes dry and sometimes accompanied by hawking of saliva, which was previously bloody but is now abundant, viscid, clinging, in lumps, not malodorous, and brown-coloured; the patient says that he has had fits of blood-spitting immediately after any violent movement of the body, or after taking any considerable amount of a cold drink at one draught. He is troubled by lassitude of the whole body without any external cause together with extreme weakness, especially in the feet; this happens chiefly in the evening when his temperature rises, accompanied by difficulty in breathing, which is free enough in the daytime except when he is obliged to cough, for then he feels a pain in his chest. In short, his whole body is like a skeleton, and his face is almost Hippocratic. His urine is deeply coloured; it is clear and bright when passed, but after standing a short time it becomes clouded and then deposits a copious, thick, brown sediment. His motions up to now have been natural in colour, though in substance rather dry and hard. The hypochondria and abdomen are soft, not tense or hard. As far as I can guess, it is a fever of the slow kind properly called hectic, accompanied by ulceration of the lungs.
(Latin) 1. The question is, should he be put on a milk-cure, and on what sort of [p. 10] milk, goat's or cow's? How should it be given, so as not to clot or produce acidity in the stomach or obstructions in the glands and intestines?
(Latin) 2. Should the milk-cure be supplemented by some aperients, in order to free the glands from obstructions, so that the nutritive lymph may be better distributed throughout the body?
(Latin) 3. Should not some opiates too be given by day in restricted doses, to counteract that fermentation and irritation of the mass of blood, especially as the patient sometimes gets no sleep all night, and if he does sleep always has troubled dreams?
(Latin) 4. Finally, what should he take in the way of a restorative diet, and on what system?
(Latin) I beg you most earnestly to inform me on all these points as soon as possible, since you yourself are fully informed on this complaint by your own experience; the patient has promised to observe all your instructions to the letter; and if there should be any possible treatment for him other than that with milk, please write and tell me of it, since a milk-cure will be somewhat difficult for our builder to observe. I would have added more, only that the post-boy is preparing to go. With this much, then, good-bye, excellent Sir, and believe me to be
Your well-wisher and friend
C. SIBELIUS
Deventer 13 Jun. 86.
(Latin) 
Address: To Mr. Locke, my very dear friend presently at Deventer. Haste! Haste! Under cover.
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Sibelius 13 Jun. 86
853. Locke to Nicolas Toinard, 25 June/5 July 1686 (850, 862)
B.M., Add. MS. 28,835, ff. 9-10. Printed in Ollion, pp. 118-19.
(English) 
Amstel: 5 Jul. 86
Sero jam ultimis tuis sed quam primum post iter huc reversus sum respondeo.†1 Nescio quando visurus sum harmoniam Evangelicam tam lentè enim procedit prodromus Josephianus ut incipiam et tuos et meos numerare annos ut videam an isti spei aliquis relictus sit locus. Etiamsi certo scias me nihil tibi negaturum, nullam tamen ausim tibi hac in re meam promittere operam, non quod nolim tuæ per omnia obsequi voluntati, et quantum in me est istud promovere opus, sed quod prævideo, nisi ipse adsis et editioni præsis, per tabularios uti jam cœptum est, res peragi non potest et harmonia non perficietur nisi post octavæ sphæræ revolutionem, et tum tandem mundus tuam videbit quando illam audiet harmoniam.†2 cogita
― 12 ―

quæso an non hæc nimis longa erit periodus, interim plurimi avidè expectant et ego inprimis opto, etsi eo thesauro te donante jam dives sed a te didici aliis bene velle, fac quæso ne tam utile tam exoptatum opus tuâ vel tarditate vel incuriâ intercidat. De M:S. Viennensi Wetstenius se solicitum promittit. eâ de re quamprimum a te monitus fuerat se scripsisse aiit. sed hæc ut audio chronologica sunt. ego vero eandem semper canto cantilenam nec inconcinne ut mihi videtur quandoquidem harmoniâ sit. Triumviratum veneror, et expecto ut de eo me certiorem facias. Ante annum adversariorum methodum Latio sermone donatum ad Te obsequii mei tesseram transmisi†1nescio an ad manus tuas pervenerit. Siquid amplius eâ in re velis jubeas modo, paratum me habebis et obtemperantem. Vale et me ut facis ama tui amantissimum JL
C'estoit par grand hazard que l'honeur de vostre derniere est tombèe entre mes maines faute d'adresse qu il falut. c'est pour quoy Je vous prie d'avoire la bontè d'adressèr vos lettres pour moy
Aen Mijn Heer Jacob Vande Velde
Boekverkooper op de hoeck van de Korte Niesel
tot Amsterdam
(Latin) 
Amsterdam 5 July 86
I am late in answering your last letter but am writing this as soon as possible after returning here from a journey.†1 I do not know when I am to see the Harmony of the Gospels; its Josephian forerunner is proceeding so slowly that I am beginning to count your years and my own, to see if there is any room left for that hope. You may be sure I would deny you nothing; still, I would not dare to promise you any help of mine in this business, not that I would hesitate to obey your wishes in all things and to do everything in my power to push the work on; but from what I can foresee, unless you are present yourself to superintend the production the thing cannot be put through by post in the way it has begun; in fact the harmony will not be completed until after the revolution of the Eighth Sphere; when the world hears that harmony it will at last see yours;†2 so consider, please, whether that [p. 12] is not too long to wait. Meanwhile a great number of people are eagerly expecting it, and especially myself; true, I have already been enriched with that treasure by your gift, but you have taught me benevolence to others; please see to it, then, that such a useful and desirable work is not lost, whether through slowness or through negligence on your part. Wetstein promises to do his best about the Vienna manuscript: he wrote about it, he says, immediately on hearing from you. But this, I hear, is concerned with chronology; whereas I am always singing the same old song, and not untunefully either, it seems to me, seeing that it is in harmony. My best respects to the Triumvirate; I expect news of them from you. A year ago I sent you my method of keeping notes translated into Latin, as a token of my obedience to you;†1 I do not know whether it reached you. If you have any further wishes about it you have only to command me; you will find me ready to obey you. Good-bye, and continue to love me your most affectionate J.L.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Toinard Chez monsieur des Noiers devant l'Espèe roiale dans la rüe Mazarine au Fauxbourg st Germain à Paris
Endorsed by Toinard: Amstelodami. 5. Julii 86.

854. Mrs. Isabella Duke and Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, [9/19 July 1686] (855; 851, 857)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 1. Isabella, 1650-1705; sister of Sir Walter Yonge; married Richard Duke in 1673: Vivian, Visitations of Devon, pp. 312, 841, 863. There is a note about her constitution and her miscarriages in Locke's journal, 20 October 1679 (pp. 165-6); she consulted Dr. S—, presumably Sydenham; it is not clear whether or not she became acquainted with Locke at that time.
The date of the letter appears to be old style. Mrs. Duke left Locke at Utrecht: p. 20. She took three days to travel from Utrecht to Maastricht, and one day from Maastricht to Spa; and stayed several days at Maastricht. Locke's only recorded visit to Utrecht about this time was between 8 and 11 July, N.S.; Journal; hence the date 9/19 July for the letter.
[Mrs. Duke:]
Spaw†1 July 9th 1686
Sir
I ought to begin this with the highest acknowledgments of my many and great obligations to you, of which I have a deep sence, though I want words to express it as I would doe, and time too, having been all this day so much indis-posed that I could not use a pen; but I cannot think that, or any thing else a sufficient excuse to delay one post thanking you in the best manner I am able for all your favours, for the great tenderness and concern you have expressed for me, and the Friendship you have promised me, which I esteem the greatest good fortune, an advantage as much above my hopes, as my deserts; but I shall entertain it with all the respect and gratitude imaginable, and be ever returning it by all the services, and expressions of kindness, that I am capable of. and in obedience to the obliging command you laid on me to give you an account of my Journey, I must tell you that I endured it much better then I could have imagined, for though the Utrecht Chariots†2 made us all weary enough, and is without dispute the worst Carriage in the World, yet I was much better at the end of the Journey, then when I sate out in the morning, and had the Courage to leave Bois le Duc†3 the next day after dinner in a large Brabant Waggon which held us all, and our Baggage, and undertook to bring us into Mastricht the next day in good season; but we suffered many
― 14 ―

hardships before we got thither, for we were wretchedly lodged the first Night in a German Town call'd Enthoven,†1 whither we came extream late, and could get nothing good or wholsome to eat or drink, beds we had, such as they were, but our Waggoner allowed us but little time in them, but called us up at two a Clock that we might reach Mastricht in good season; but after a hard dayes Journey we were forced to lye upon straw a Mile short of it, the Rogue pretending to be sick stopt at noon two or three hours, so that 'twas nine a Clock before we got thither and then the gates had been shut an hour, that Town being kept very strictly by a Garison of about 8000 men.†2However we were told that our Inn was the best in all that country, we met with good Milk and Eggs, and a room tolerably clean, Just large enough to hold us, where we lay all together till sun rising, and then got into the Town and went to bed; and tarried several days till we were well recruited; and then came hither in one day in a Brabant Waggon, which is a way of travelling that we are very well pleased with, and I beleive you would have endured very well; but when any cross accidents occurr'd we drank your health, and reJoyced that you were at your ease in Amsterdam, and that our importunity's had not exposed you to those inconveniencies; though we want your company extreamly; this is the dullest place that ever I came into; I was never so disappointed in my expectations of which it fals infinitely short. 'tis a poor Village that lyes at the foot of 2. or 3. great hills that surround it somewhat like Bath, but 'tis a little contemptible place that bears no proportion to it, where we have no walk nor conveniencyes of any sort; and very little company. Mr Forester†3 his Lady and Family came this after noon, and I beleave will make a much greater figure then any of the company here, and I beleeve will quickly be weary of the place, as I shall be, unless the waters do wonders for us; but I cannot yet say any thing of their nature, or use, having only tasted them, but had neither time, or opportunity of informing my self concerning them. Mr Duke took 21. of his Pils at Mastricht which wrought about 6. times, he has begun his Waters
― 15 ―

this day, and is much pleased with them; and confident of good success. he and all the rest of your Friends tender you their best services, and hope for the favour of a letter from you sometimes. be pleased to direct it chez Monsieur Berinsen ala Ville d'Anvers, a Spaw. pardon me if I abruptly bid you adieu, and hasten to subscribe my self what I am with much affection Sir
Your Most Obliged and most Obedient Servant
ISABELLA DUKE
[Yonge:]
Sir
Though you were very positive in declaring you would credit no account of our Journey but what came under my Sister's hand, yet you must give me leave (by way of Advertisement to any friend of yours that may be desirous to see the Spaw) to informe you that the Utrecht wagon is the same with the rest of the wagons in Holland; that the post-wagon is a very good conveyance from Bois le Duc to Maestricht in one day without hazard of lying by the way, and from Maestricht it is but one dayes Journey hither either in a Charret†1 (or Cart) or on horseback, but some goe by water to Liege which shortens the Journey by land. Pray favor us with an account of what news you meet with for I fear we shall otherwise live in ignorance of the English Affaires. I am unalterably
Yours W.Y.
The only walk we have here is the Capucins garden which is indeed very pleasant.
My service to Dr. Thomas if he be with you
Address (written by Yonge?): For Mr John Lock.
Endorsed by Locke: Mrs Duke 9o Jul 86
855. Mrs. Isabella Duke and Richard Duke to Locke, 19/29 July 1686 (854, 857; 859)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 2. The date of Locke's letter indicates that Mrs. Duke's date is new style.
[Mrs. Duke:]
Spa July 29th. 1686
Sir
This morning I was made happy by the receipt of Yours of the 26th from Amsterdam, which came very Seasonably to releive me,
― 16 ―

for I was then in a very ill humour, which could not have been cured by a remedy less extraordinary; not but that we have good Bread, and good Wine, and Pottage and Mutton enough; and every one a bed, and good ones too; but we have such Violent and Perpetual Rains, that we are beaten of from the use of the Waters, and lose our time here; all that's past goes for little or nothing with me, who have not tasted them this three days, though they agree very well with me when the Weather gives me leave to drink them. I once reach'd eight Glasses, and several dayes seven, but I do not yet find that keen Appetite, which Tunbridge Waters use to give me, neither do they pass so well, but I beleive all would be well if we had dry hot Weather, which I pray for on many considerations, but principally that we may return the sooner to you, whose Excellent Conversation can even at this distance charm all discontents, and make me forget all the inconveniencyes I am exposed to. there never was so much good Nature, so much Witt, so much Friendship, and so much Flattery, put together in one letter before; but the three first atone for the last, and render it as it is, most acceptable to me. I admire it extreamly, and can never read it often enough, or thank you sufficiently for it; every new Reading of it entertains me with something new, and withal so ingenious, and so soft and kind, that it gives me a new pleasure, and such gratfull resentments, as I want words to express; believe them such as you design'd to excite, and that I can never want a due sence of my many and great Obligations to you; and particularly of this last Favour. my Sister Betty†1 also thinks herself very happy in your tender affection, and kind remembrances of her; and sends you her humble Thanks by my hand, but the Men will speak for themselves in the bottom of my letter, which therfore must not be to long; but I cannot have done till I have told you how glad I am that Dr Taffee†2 is already come to you, not only for your sake, but for my own; for by the time we return to you I hope his Stories and Newes will be pretty well over, so that he will not ingross you wholly to himself, but will allow us our share of you, who have the greatest vallue imaginable for you, and the Truest Friendship. I am much pleas'd with your way of correction, and do hope that in this hasty scribble you will find faults enough to procure
― 17 ―

me another letter, which will be much desired, and Thankfully acknowledged by
Your most Obliged Friend and Faithfull humble servant
ISABELLA DUKE
[Duke:]
Had I been to answer your letter I should have begun with Intellectuall complections,†1 which I believe are as good words to begin a letter with, as a book, but I shall onely make a return to what concerns my self. I can assure you that though I say it my self I have been a very orderly fellow. I seldom sleep but when I cannot help it, drink as much water as I can let down, and take my electuary when I don't forgett it. I doubt whether all lean men can give so good an account of themselves, but if you are for a hearty peace send us all your news by the next, and you may expect hence all we can learn from Monsieur Spanheim who is just arrived from Paris where he has been Envoy from Brandenbourg.†2 Sir W.Y. and mr F.†3 are your servants, but none with greater gratitude and respect then
Yours to command
R <DUKE>†a
I am so desirous to send this by this daies post that I can onely add my desire to give our best services to our Welch friend.†4
Address (written by Duke): Aen Mijn Heer Mijn heer Jan Lock ten huys van Mijn Heer Jacob Van de Velde Boeckverkoper op de Hoeck van de Korte Niesel t'Amsterdam

856. William Charleton to Locke, 20 July 1686 (843, 864)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 64-5.

Deare Sir
Though it could not stand with the Doctors†5 Conveniency to take with him all the things which I mention'd in mine of the 9th
― 18 ―

June, yet was he pleased to charge himself with the Booke you desired, and a small Box of some of the naturall curiosities your freind would have, the rest I shall keep by me till an opportunity presents. Nothing that is curious either of birds, Insects, or East India plants, can come amisse so they be not common, but the things I am most desirous of are a branch of the nutmeg tree with the fruite on, a branch of the cinamon tree with its fruit, I having already been favoured with it by yourself in flower, a large Phalangium a sort of Indian spider, The Tarantula of the Kingdome of Naples and the Cochinele fly.†1 Sir I thanke you verry kindly for the concern you have for my health which I blesse God is much better then formerly, nor have I been wanting in using remydy's when occasion required, though I am naturally verry averse to Physick, that you are so well as I have been Informed is great satisfaction to me, with my humble service to your self and the Doctor I take my leave and am
Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
W C.

857. Mrs. Isabella Duke, Sir Walter Yonge, and Elizabeth Yonge, to Locke, 31 July/10 August 1686 (855, 860; 854, 876; 1334)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 134-5. The date is probably new style.
[Mrs. Duke:]
Spa August: 10th. 86.
Sir
Your Obliging letter of the 6th. of August came to my hands this morning, whilest I were in Bed, drinking my Waters; and is the very best entertainment I have met with since that I received, and read, those two which you first bestowed on me; for which I must be ever paying you my Thanks, since I can never sufficiently acknowledge the greatness of that favour, or of my other innumerable obligations to you. to which you have made no small addition by this last demonstration of your Friendship, in which I esteem my self extreamly happy, and shall alwayes cherish it, and be ever returning it in the best manner I am able. and since you press me to do it by my frequent letters, I will shew my obedience, though I have nothing new, or any way diverting to entertain you with; and I want that excellent faculty which you possess in perfection, of talking ingeniously upon every subject, and inventing new ones (and those infinitely beyond any that could be offered you from abroad) whenever the dulness of your Friends sets your charity, or your good nature on work to relieve them. if my conceptions were like yours, and could I so elegantly express them, I should be alwayes best pleased when I had my pen in my hand, and should not study conciseness in my returns to the endearing and excellent letters which you send me, but I am so conscious of my own defects, and how uncapable I am of saying any thing worth postage, that I should spare you sometimes, did you not command me so absolutely to keep touch with you, which I can in number, though not in weight; for few in the world perhaps can immitate your pen, or entertain their Friends so agreably. the pleasure I took in reading my own, and also that which you address'd to Mr Duke made my Waters go down, and digest admirably well, and with better success this day then ever. here are many fountains in, and about this place, but three are most frequented. that in the middle of the Town with which I began, and which seems to have most of the Mineral; and two others about two Miles distant, amongst the rocks. on is called the Savoniere and
― 20 ―

is used by all those that drink Waters for the Stone and Gravel, or any diseases of the liver, and seems to be a lighter water then the fountain in the Town, otherwise the same in all respects; and I should chuse it but that the way to it is extreamly bad, and we have no conveniency but a cart to carry us, so that it is next to impossible to get at it; and when we are at it there is no conveniency either for men or women, both must creep amongst the bushes and Briers on all occasions, so that 'tis impossible to escape being wet in the feet, and having a dirty Tayle, be the peticoats shorter then the Ancles which is the mode of this Country. the same hardships attend those that drink of the Geronster, which has made us all hitherto keep to the fountain in the Town, Judging that neither of the other when carried, could be so good as these from the fountain head, but the last is so much magnified above the rest for all diseases of the Stomach and bowels, that I am at last perswaded to make tryal of it; this is the second day, and I think I do already find an advantage by it. it seems to warm and fortify the Stomach, I have eaten at another rate these two days then ever before since I came hither.†1 this Water of the Geronster taste<s>†a of the Steel as the rest, but has withal a strong smell and tast like Gun powder, which is supposed to be from Sulphur which is mingled in that fountain with the other minerals. they all operate alike with me, who am very well, and have perfectly recover the indisposition I was under when I left you at Utretch.†2 but I hope to give you a better account of my self in a little time, for the perpetual rains have made my drinking Waters hitherto very uncertain, and very irregular. our Glasses hold about 8 ounces and I have taken 5.6.7.8. or 9. as the Weather would permit. but you shall not fail to receive a Critical account of the Waters of all sorts, as soon as we can get Gauls.†3 this place does not afford any, or any thing else, but what is constantly brought from Liege, from whence I have taken care to have gaules as soon as it may be. our expectations are not in any thing more disappointed then in the company we have here, which is very little, and generally speaking very mean. here have been about half a score German Counts and Barons in the whole season, but no strangers of any other Countryes; yet that does not hinder but that we have 4. or
― 21 ―

5. Balles a Week, and the people of quality that are here are civill, and obliging, but we have had very little conversation with them the constant rains having made us prisoners in our own houses, for the greatest part of our time. but the terrible Thunder and Showers which have fall'n yesterday and to day, will I hope clear the Air, and bring us better Weather; or send us quickly to Amsterdam, or rather to Utretch; where we hope to meet you, whom we remember every day with much affection; and impatiently desire a nearer conversation with you; in which we hope to be happy again, within a very few days, my next perhaps may Set the time; but till then I beseech you Oblige us with your letters which are most Valluable, most acceptable, and the best expression of your generous Friendship, by which you have made me entyrely, and unalterably
Yours to serve you
ISABELLA DUKE
pardon this scrible, and pitty us that have no better Tools.
[Yonge:]
Dear Sir, I have beg'd leave to add a postscript to this to repair an omission I was guilty of in my last, in not paying you my humble thanks for the pains you have taken about Sueurs Histoire de l'Eglise,†1 I am extreamly ashamed it should give you so much trouble, and to put an end to it, must once more desire you to speak to Van Someren to let him know that I absolutely order'd the book to be bound in leather, so that I look upon my selfe to be no way obliged to take that which he has bound in Velom; And therefore I beg you to buy me the book in Quarto (if that be the best Edition) and bound in calves leather with gilded backs, where you can find it best bound and cheapest either at his or any other shop: I am with great affection
Yours W. Y.
[Elizabeth Yonge:]
Sir
I confess my Obligations to you are such, as Justly deserve a more particular acknoledgment, then by the hand of another, but had you not exspressly commanded it, I could never have had confidence to doe it with my own, for tho I have all the gratitude and
― 22 ―

affection that I ought to have for soe deserving a person, yet the sence I have of my own defects, and my desire to conceal them, made me unwilling to expose them to your view, whose good opinion I extreamly covet, but I have that defferance for all your commands, that I will endevour to obey them in the best manner I am able, and since this is only an instance of my Obedience, I beleive you have soe much goodness as not to improve it to my prejudice, but will rather pitty me, and endevour to cure what you find amiss. perhaps you will expect I should give you some account of the trust you comitted to my care when I left you, viz, my Brother Duke, were it not for fear of commending my own Goverment I could tell you he has generally liv'd very regularly, but as all men have failings, soe I could give you some instances of his, but I will spare him, since he has given you soe good an account of himself. for the spaa you have had a much better account of all particulars from other hands, and had you not, I should be at a great loss what to say of it, for should I give it a very good caracter, it would be more than it deserves, and should I say any thing that's ill my Brother Du: would not forgive me; soe I must defer the rest till I see you; which I hope will not be long, but the post tarry's for this, and I must beg your Pardon if I abruptly subscribe my self
Sir your most affectionate and obedient daughter EY
Address (written by R. Duke?): Aen Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Jan Lock ten huys van Mijn Heer Jacob van de Velde op de Hoeck van de Korte Niesel 't'Amsterdam

858. Dr. Caspar Sibelius to Locke, 4/14 August 1686 (852, 961)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, f. 107.
(English) 
Daventriæ 14.Aug.86.
Vir Nobilissime,
Ultimas Tuas Curam Lacteam in Phthisi ejusdemque Methodum continentes ante <aliquod>†a tempus ritè accepi et cum voluptate
― 23 ―

non sine aliquo fructu perlegi, Effectum tamen nullum Cura hæc præscripta Ægro jam conclamato adferre potuit. Hisce Tibi, Vir Doctissime, contenta Literarum D.Ten Rhyne†1 nuper ex Indiis allatarum transcribo:
(English) 1.†a Quid sit ficus Indica? vid. Clus. in Exotic†2 In suppressis lochiis et partu difficili plantis pedum, parum assata et transversim dissecta, applicatur.
(English) 2. Ne ex Acupuncturâ sequantur Convulsiones, loca notanda sunt, in quorum selectionis discrimine omne hujus Artis punctum consistit; adjectæ monstrant illa Tabulæ.
(English) 3. Inustio cum Moxâ sæpiùs una vice absque scrupulo administrari potest, in quâ tamen modum excedunt Japones. Ego (loquitur Ten Rhyne) communiter ter instituo, nisi malum pertinax altumque reclusa sit illius Causa: Meas de Inustionis Curâ Observatiunculas suo tempore et loco exhibebo, aliis jam nimiopere distractus. Haud adeò certa foret promissi sequela, ac si una Inustio omnem Podagræ Recidivam demeret: Levamen post Adustionem sentiunt plerique, tùm majus, cum plaga ichor sudat.†3
― 24 ―

(English) 4. Si mihi plus temporis suppeteret, tuæ expectationi in describendis variarum Asiaticarum gentium moribus ac ritibus etc. lubens pro meâ tenuitate satisfacerem, quod fortean aliquando fiet, si Deus vitam, valetudinem, et oportunitatem largiatur.
(English) 5. In Arithmetico <computo>†a nullum hactenus in Indiis populum offendi, qui denarium numerum transiliat; econtra illi hac in Arte ideò faciliores, quod mutatis solummodo rerum vel monetarum nominibus solo denario numero per Additionem vel Subtractionem omnia calculent, si ita fari liceat.
(English) 6. In Temporis computatione non septem dierum circuitum sed Lunæ cursum, juxta quem menses dimetiuntur, pleræque observant hæ Nationes.
(English) 7. Singularia, quæ hac de re, uti et animalibus, venenatis organis (sed diversæ indolis et efficaciæ sunt venena) necatis etc. quæris, longius, quàm mihi jam datur, requirunt otium.
(English) Hæc sunt quæ ex literis Amici Tibi communicare volui, ut Curiositati Tuæ aliquomodo satisfaciam. Si quæ ulteriùs Curiosa Tibi suppetant, et D.Ten Rhyne proponenda judices, modò mihi ea remitte ut literis eadem inseram. Literas Tuas ad me quæso tradentur à Mademoiselle Hoppesack logeant sur le Cingel op het hoeck van het koninghs pleÿn,†1 laquelle est la suœur de ma femme,
― 25 ―

qui vostre lettre me renvoÿera. Vale, Vir Nobilissime, salutatus à meâ Conjuge et omnibus Amicis meis. Dabam ocyssimè.
Nobiliss. Nominis Tui
observantissimus
C. SIBELIUS
(Latin) 
Deventer 14.Aug.86.
Illustrious Sir,
I duly received some time ago your last letter with the description of the milk-cure in phthisis and the way it should be employed, and I read it with [p. 23] pleasure and not without some profit, though the prescribed cure could do nothing for the patient, as by then it was all over with him. In this letter, learned Sir, I am copying out for you the contents of a letter of Mr. Ten Rhyne†1which recently reached me from the Indies:
(Latin) 1. What is the Indian fig? see Clusius on Exotics.†2 In cases of suppressed afterbirth and difficult parturition it is slightly roasted, cut up transversely, and applied to the soles of the feet.
(Latin) 2. To avoid acupuncture being followed by convulsions one should note the proper places for it, as the whole art of the process consists in the judicious selection of these; they are shown in the accompanying diagrams.
(Latin) 3. Cauterization with moxa can without hesitation be applied more often than once, though the Japanese are immoderate in this respect. I myself (Ten Rhyne is speaking) commonly employ it three times, unless the trouble is persistent and the cause of it deep-seated and obscure; I shall produce my Notes on Treatment by Cautery at the proper time and place; I am too distracted by other things just now. The promised result would not be so certain as it might if a single cauterization were to remove any recurrence of gout; most people feel some relief after it, and that greater when the cauterized spot exudes a watery discharge.†3
(Latin) [p. 24] 4. If I had had more time I would gladly have done what little I can to satisfy your expectations by describing the habits and customs of the various Asian races; this will perhaps be done sometime, if God grants me life, health, and opportunity.
(Latin) 5. In the matter of counting I have not so far met with any people in the Indies who go beyond the number ten; on the other hand they practise this art the more easily because by simply changing the names of articles or coins and using only the number ten they do all their calculations by addition or subtraction, if one may put it that way.
(Latin) 6. In reckoning time most of these nations observe, not a period of seven days, but the course of the moon, by which they measure months.
(Latin) 7. The particular questions you ask about this matter, as also about animals killed with poisoned implements (but their poisons are various in nature and efficacy), require more leisure that I am getting at present.
(Latin) These are the points I wanted to let you know of from my friend's letter, so as to satisfy your curiosity to some extent. If you have any further questions on matters of interest which you think might be put to Mr. Ten Rhyne, just send them to me to be put in a letter. Your letter to me should please be delivered to Mademoiselle Hoppesack, lodging on the Cingel, at the corner of the Konings pleijn;†1 she is my wife's sister and will forward your letter to me. [p. 25] Goodbye, illustrious Sir, my wife and all my friends send their greetings. I send this express.
Your most obedient servant
C. SIBELIUS
Endorsed by Locke: Sibelius 14 Aug. 86
859. Richard Duke to Locke, [10/20 August 1686] (855, 861)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 57. Fragment. The letter probably contained some offensive passages: no. 861. It was presumably Locke who mutilated it. Date from Locke's endorsement.
... greatest confidence imaginable. I have made trialls of the severall fountains here, as you desired, with galls as also with leaves of Oak and Thea, and the rind of Pomgranate, in all which the water of the Pohon (which is in the market place, and of which we drink mostly) had the deepest tincture, and was thickish and curdled, that of the Savvenier (which is about half a league to the Eastward of the Town) was of a bright violet color, and very clear, and that of the Gironster (which is about two English mile to the Southward of the Town) of a purple reddish color, and clear. It warms more then the other waters, and has a sulphureous tast which they have not, and smells like the washing out of a Gun.†1 The Pohon water is most generally transported, An Apothecary here told me that he was to send six hundred bottles of it which held two quarts a piece to the Governor of Rome which would cost him as many crowns.†2 He shewed me also some Pills which are made of an Extract of Spa water, and some purging ingredients, of which I intend to take a quantity to shew you when I shall have the happiness of returning to you in Holland. At my first coming I frequently drank 16 glasses, of nine ounces, being desirous to drink as much as my stomach would bear as I thought you advised, but since I have taken but twelve or
― 26 ―

thirteen, being not willing to be metamorphosed to a barrell. As for the Siesta, I make a shift to get rid of it, specially since you have givin it such a hard name, and perhaps can tell you that I have been more orderly then other people, and hope for a good effect of my course of waterdrinking, as I hope more fully to informe you herafter, and of some other experiments of the waters which we design to make. We are hither ...

860. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 14/24 August 1686 (857, 867)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 3.
Saturday Aug: 24th. 1686
Sir
This brings you my most hearty Thanks for the new expressions of your kindness; and assurances of your Freindship, which I received this Morning in your Obliging letter of the 20th of this Month, which was as welcome to me as you could wish it, and gave me a pleasure and satisfaction beyond what I can express, in promising us your Company this Winter, if we determin to pass it on this side the Water, to which nothing else could be so great so effectuall an inducement, the advantages being such as are no where else to be found; the daily conversation of so ingenious, so generous, so perfect a Friend, cannot fail to render us insencible of all other wants, and to make us compleatly happy even in a strang land. However we cannot yet come to any certain resolution, since we are not absolutely at our own disposal; the last letter Mr Duke received from his Father†1 did in a sort press his return to England this Autumn, in answer to which he begg'd that it might be left to his own discretion to return or tarry as he should then Judg it most advisable, yet promised to Obey any commands he should receive in his next, which we expect every moment, it being full six Weeks since his last came to our hands. Whenever it comes the contents of it will have a great influence on our settlement for this Winter, which if it be in this Country, will I guess be at Utretcht; a place which
― 27 ―

I hope will not be disagreable to you, and therfore I beseech you do not determin any thing concerning your self till we see you, which I hope will be in a few dayes. for we shall go hence monday next to Liege, and from thence in a day or two to Aix;†1 how long we may be tempted (by the Ladies and other pleasures of that place,) to tarry there I cannot tell, but if it answers our expectations no better then Spa did, I shall soon have enough of it; and since you do not prescribe the Baths I shall not adventure to use them, though all persons do that come to this place for the common Cause. but I am of opinion that I have no need of it, I think my self in every respect very well, and doubt not but you will be easily convinced of it when I come back to you. We have now done with the Waters, the constant rains having beaten us off from them some dayes sooner then we intended. they did not disagree with any one of us; nor any way incline me to purge after the first Week; neither have they exhausted me half so much as Tunbridge Waters use to do, and I hope may have better effects afterwards, though they have not made me so hungry, and so Vigorous in the time of drinking, as I have been at Tunbridge. Mr Duke has lately given you an account what tryals we have made of them with Tea, Gauls etc if you desire a fuller, excuse me till I see you, and then I will tell you at large what I have further observed, and answer as well as I am able all your curious questions; at least 'tis to be hoped that your Virtuoso Friend Mr Freke will be able to do it to your satisfaction; who is very well, and gives you his service; for the rest let him speak for himself. my Sister Betty has all the Gratitude she ought for your Elegant letter, for such are all yours though you quarrell so much at the Name; and we, know how to vallue them, and how to use them; and cannot be corrupted by your Apocryphal instructions. but I'le use the word no more since it does not please you, and since you can wrest it to a signification so empty, so different from what I intended it; but I desire one letter more, addressed to Mr Abraham Heldivier as Mr Duke directed in his last, though 'tis possible we may miss it, if this has the same ill fate with our other letters to be nine dayes on the Road, for which no reason can be given, but that we suppose they lay at Liege, where the post is very negligent; 'tis probable that this may have the same fate, but we have no other way of sending to you, and I owe you more thanks for your repeated favours, then 'tis possible for me to carry about me
― 28 ―

the long Tour that we are to make in our way back to Utrecht. for my Masters have resolved to pass by Nimmegue and Cleve, and some other Towns with hard Names; so that 'tis possible it may be yet three Weeks before we reach you, but I shall spurr on as fast as I can. you much obliged my Master with your News, he thirsts for more, and is your Obedient Servant. he has been regular beyond my hopes, and I believe will discreetly submit to all such prescriptions as you shall think necessary for him, I suppose he put it under his hand when he wrote to you last, and will not fail to make it good. but I must leave both him and you, to pack up, and prepare for my Journey towards you, heaven send us good Weather and a happy meeting. till then adieu, yet perhaps I may write once more, I am sure I will if I meet with anything worth imparting to you, at least 'twill give me the pleasure of writing my self once again, Dear Sir,
Your most Obliged faithfull Friend
ISABELLA DUKE
Address (written by Richard Duke): Aen Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Jan Lock ten huys van mijn Heer Jacob Van de Velde Boeckverkoper op de Hoeck van de Korte niesel tot Amsterdam.

861. Richard Duke to Locke, 24 August/3 September 1686 (859, 876)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 58-9.
Aix Sept. the 3d 1686
Sir
If my former letter charged you with calling names, or giving ill language you do me but Justice to believe they were not my naturall thoughts; and I must (with you) impute it to some evill spirit that made me write I know not what. I confess I endeavored to have carryed on that course of raillery that had been begun between us and if I performed it in too gross and dull a manner I hoped that the heavy constitution of a fat man might have exscused it, and that the friendship, and intimacy you had allowed me, together with the many, and great obligations I had to you would have secured me from such a misfortune, as your understanding what I writt to proceed from want of affection, and gratitude. But since I was so
― 29 ―

unhappy to expresse my self ill I must beg you to believe that it was wholely in my pen, and not the least in my intention. And therefore I hope you will not deny me the favor of your pardon, which I most heartily beg of you and shall continually solicite you for till I obtain it; for I cannot suffer a greater <affliction>,†a then by my error to lose a friendship for which I have the highest value and concern, and shall ever (if you please to permit me) cultivate with the best offices, and syncerest endeavors to serve you, since I covet nothing so earnestly as the title of
Sir
Your most obliged friend and faithfull servant
Ric. Duke

5 Sept.†a
Etiamsi subinde ab urbe errabundus absum, nunquam tamen domum redeo quin statim Wetstenium adeo, ut de te certior fiam, et ut sciam an vales et an harmonicè etiam vales. nuper apud ipsum vidi titulum Josephianæ Harmoniæ præfigendum, et dolui sanè nos adhuc hærere in vestibulo, et tam longe abesse ab illis Evangelii adytis in quibus possit animus acquiescere harmoniâ illâ delinitus. Quod illam harmoniam plurimi hic <expectant>†b avidissimè, certissimum
― 30 ―

est, nempe qui aliqua ejus specimina olim apud Elzivirium†1 et jam apud Wetst: viderunt, quorum etiam animos ego porro accendi justâ laudatione totius operis, quod integrum vidi.†a Sed cave tibi, et editionem accelara. amphora non meruit tam pretiosa mori,†2 undecunque efflagitant editionem; et, si non vult uxor, veniat ancilla, dicunt boni hi Lutherani.†3 Sed ut seriò tecum agam, matura impressionem, iterum iterumque rogo. præsentio enim si hâc hieme non fiat, nunquam futuram. Visionarium me, uti dicunt, vel Enthusiasten credas, si placet: modo tibi et nobis et reipub: Christianæ prosit Vaticinium; et tam egregium et proficium opus summo cum religionis damno ne intercidat. Sed hæc hactenus agitante nescio quo instinctu, quo et amore erga te sentio me incalescere. Scio horas tuas non inutiles nec <ἀμούσας>†b tibi transire. quod fortè etiam doleo quòd dum nova venaris, uti fit, quæ jam assecutus es et possides, cum neglectu habes. ― 31 ―

a Wet- missarum fasciculo intrusi cui non magnum addet pondus. Si Wetstenio etiam mittantur ad me literæ tuæ recte recipiam et commodius quam alibi. vive et vale ut omnia quæ sub manum vel in animo habes perficias et me ama tui amantissimum
J L†a
(Latin) 
5 Sept.
Though I am away from town now and then on my wanderings, yet I never return home without immediately going to see Wetstein for news of you, to know if you are well, and if you are also harmonically well. The other day I saw at his place the title-page to be prefixed to the Harmony of Josephus, and I was certainly sorry that we are still sticking in the entrance-court and are so far from that inner sanctum of the Gospel where the spirit may find rest, soothed by its harmony. It is very certain that that harmony is most eagerly expected by many people here, certainly by those who have seen some specimens [p. 30] of it before now at Elsevier's†1 and now at Wetstein's; I, too, have fired their enthusiasm still further by my well-merited praises of the whole work, which I have seen in its entirety ... But take heed and speed up publication; 'such precious wine did not deserve to die';†2 it is clamoured for on all sides, and 'if the wife is unwilling, let the maidservant come', as these good Lutherans say.†3 Seriously though, do hasten the printing, I beg of you again and again; for I have a presentiment that if it is not done this winter it will never be done. Think me a visionary, as they call it, or an enthusiast, if you like; only may my inspired utterance be of advantage to you and to us and to the Christian world, by preventing such an outstanding and profitable work from perishing to the great loss of religion. But enough of this; I am urged by some impulse which together with my affection for you I feel makes me grow heated. I know that your hours are not spent unprofitably or without the Muses, and I am possibly even sorry for that, since in the pursuit of new things, as so often happens, you have little regard for what you have already achieved and possess. I am delighted to hear that the Triumvirs are well; please give them my warmest greetings. I have slipped this letter into a sizeable parcel of [p. 31] papers sent by Wetstein; it will not add much to the weight. If your letters to me are also sent to Wetstein I shall get them safely and more conveniently than elsewhere. May you enjoy life and health to finish everything you have in hand or in mind, and love me your most affectionate
J L
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Toinard
Endorsed by Toinard: 17 Septre 86.
863. Edward Clarke to Locke, 30 August 1686 (849, 869)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 21. Printed in Rand, pp. 165-6. Answered by no. 872.
Chipley the 30th. of August 1686.
Deare Sir,
The Promise I made you in my last of the 10th. of July of visitting Mr. Stratton imediately after the then next Assises at Wells,†1 was fully intended to have been punctually performed at the time by mee, But tho I was gone as farr as wells towards it, and had spent two dayes of the Assises there, and was preparing to have gone to Sutton the day following, yett I was to my greate Losse as well as dissatisfaction utterly defeated of the opportunity either to performe my Promise to you, or to dispatch any other Businesse that I had appoynted in those Parts, by the suddaine Death of my cheife Servant in whose custody were many Writeings of greate value to mee, and severall others, And His Relations beleiveing Him to have dyed possessed of a considerable Personall Estate, press'd hard for a suddaine veiw of all in his Custody, for the discovery of such securityes as they supposed Hee might have money out upon, soe that my Wife was under a necessity of sending an Expresse for mee from the Assises, and my time hath been ever since wholly taken up, with such Councell as His Kindred made
― 32 ―

choyce of, to veiw all such writeings as were in his custody, and to seperate those belonging to mee, from such as they were interested in, and that being now done, and such Accompts as were between Him and mee being now stated and settled with the approbation of theire Councell, I have now gott time enough to acquaint you, That tho I was recall'd in such hast from the Assises by this suddaine accident, yett I had the good luck to find out Mr Stratton there and acquainted Him with the substance of your Letter of the 6th. of August to mee, and earnestly press'd Him to use his uttmost indeavours for the getting in of those Arreares of Rent due to you, and gave Him the best directions I could for that purpose, and promised to bee with Him at Sutton, as soon as the inconveniencyes and troubles occasioned to mee by the suddaine Death of my Servant were a little removed, and I hope to performe that before Michaelmas next, being resolved to bee with Him now with the verie first opportunity that my Affayres here will any wayes Permitt; I have little to add at present more then to tell you That your Kinswoman Joan Morris†1 is lately dead and soe your intended Charity towards Her is now at an End: I thanke God I am with my Wife, Children, and my whole Family at present in perfect health and doe rejoyce exceedingly in the Account I lately Received by Letter from your Freind Adrian of your Wellfare; The Cisterns†2 you sent mee are come safe to the little Baronetts house,†3 and I intend to send for them hither with the first opportunity, in the meane time I Return you Madam's and my hearty thankes for them, assureing you that wee are all here
Your humble servants etc:
Endorsed by Locke: E: Clarke 30 Aug: 86

After many days of almost continuous wanderings†2 I have at last returned here and am beginning to get some rest. I am now enjoying leisure and a place from which I can turn my attention to my friends and resume once more that [p. 35] converse with them which I have so much at heart. Accordingly it is you that I must greet first, my best of friends; I am most eager to know how you are, how your family are, and what you are doing. To be separated from you and not to make good that loss as far as possible by interchange of letters is exile, indeed almost death. I draw breath elsewhere but live with my friends, and with you most delightfully of all. Many things have drawn me to this city; whether they will keep me here I do not know. If I had my way I would soon return to Amsterdam to you and our friend Guenellon and Veen and the Collegie;†1 but this body needs a roof, bed, and lodging, nor are these things easy to find in that city, which I regret. I hope all the same to visit you all shortly, for I could not easily bear to be long without such desirable company. Meanwhile please give my best respects to your wife and to all my friends. Good-bye, and love me your most affectionate

JEAN LE CLERC
Jean Le Clerc was born in Geneva on 29 March 1657. His grandfather came to Geneva from Picardy as a refugee on account of his religion, and there, in 1588, married a sister of Étienne de Courcelles (Curcellæus: no. 1178). He left two sons who both became professors in the Académie of Geneva; the younger, Étienne, Jean's father, subsequently became one of the twenty-five magistrates who formed the governing body of the republic; he died in 1676. Étienne's elder son Daniel became a physician and medical author (no. 2121, etc.). In Étienne's time the traditional strict Calvinism of Geneva was being invaded by more liberal tendencies emanating chiefly from Saumur. He and his brothers welcomed them. The more orthodox, with other Swiss Calvinists, drew up the Consensus Helveticus (1674), an uncompromising statement of their creed. It was adopted by the magistracy of Geneva about the end of 1678.
Jean was educated at the Collège and later at the Académie of Geneva. The professor of philosophy at the latter was a Cartesian; there also Le Clerc read some Saumur theology. Leaving it in October 1678 he spent about a year as a private tutor at Grenoble, where he met Father Bernard Lamy (no. 1119); his later freedom from sectarian rancour was due perhaps to Lamy's influence. He returned to Geneva in 1680; there, after signing the Consensus Helveticus, he was ordained a minister on 2 April. Back in Grenoble he read and was converted by a book in which Curcellæus set out the Arminian as against the Calvinist views on the Trinity, original sin, and justification. He came to Saumur in the autumn and there in 1681 he published his first book, Epistolae Theologicae, in quibus Varii Scholasticorum Errores castigantur; the author is 'Liberius de Sancto-Amore'; the imprint, 'Irenopoli. Typis Philalethianis. 1679'. Young and impetuous, scorning
― 37 ―

theologians and all tradition, Le Clerc brings reason, his reason, to bear on the principal mysteries of the faith. During further wanderings Le Clerc read Richard Simon's Histoire critique du Vieux Testament (no. 469) and Spinoza's repudiation of the Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch in the Tractatus Theologico-politicus; he also entered into correspondence with Philippus van Limborch. He spent the later part of 1682 in London, failing to establish himself but learning to read if not to speak English. After a brief final visit to Geneva he settled permanently in Amsterdam in the autumn of 1683.
He preached in French in the Remonstrants' church there for about three months; he was then silenced by the civic authorities, apparently at the instance of the orthodox French ministers. In April the Remonstrants established a chair of philosophy for him in their seminary. The annual salary, 400 gulden, was increased from time to time, but was never sufficient for his needs; he supplemented it by profuse literary activity; he is credited with working fifteen hours a day. In 1691 he married Marie, a daughter of the notorious Gregorio Leti (no. 1374). Their four children died young. He continued to teach until 1731, when his health failed. Mme Le Clerc died in 1734; he died in his niece's house on 8 January 1736.
The identity of Liberius de Sancto-Amore became known while Le Clerc was in Geneva in 1683; henceforward he was reputed to be a Socinian or a promoter of Socinianism. It was a heavy charge. In the seventeenth century denial of the Trinity was blasphemy rather than heresy. On account of it two Englishmen were burnt alive in James I's reign; a Scottish youth was hanged in 1697 (nos. 2596, etc.; 2207). Socinianism as such scarcely took root in England; a succeeding movement, Unitarianism, although denied legal toleration, made some headway after the Revolution. In the United Provinces there were edicts against the Socinians. After their expulsion from Poland in 1658 the refugees who came to Amsterdam were not allowed at first to have a church of their own. The Remonstrants, in accordance with their spirit of toleration and despite the differences in doctrine, admitted them to their communion. That scarcely brought the Remonstrants into disrepute, but left Le Clerc exposed. His adversaries never spared him the opprobrious charge.
Le Clerc made enemies easily. He could be outspoken in his censure of other writers and scholars, apparently orally in mixed company as well as in his writings; as he regarded any censure of his own writings as an attack on his person his disputes degenerated into exchanges of abuse; he intensified if he did not originate them. His contentiousness was perhaps stimulated by his ceaseless toil and by fear of the loss of his livelihood. Exigencies of work may also have checked his development as a scholar: there was not enough time for reflection and reconsideration. He did not appreciate his limitations of ability or opportunity. He did too much too quickly, applying the facility that was requisite for some parts of his work to other parts where it was out of place. It was lack of consideration that allowed him to collect the fragments of Menander and thereby to expose himself to Bentley's savagery.
Le Clerc mentions some of his works in his letters to Locke. They include translations of, and commentaries on, the Bible, and a harmony of the Gospels; editions of classical and modern writers, including his great Erasmus; history;
― 38 ―

theology; criticism, including his Ars Critica; and three great periodicals, the Bibliotheque universelle et historique, and its successors, the Bibliotheque choisie and the Bibliotheque ancienne et moderne. The first, which ran from 1686 to 1693, is probably Le Clerc's greatest achievement. Before he began it he had contributed a notice of Leti's Il teatro brittanico to Bayle's Nouvelles de la Republique des Lettres. It differs in character from the Nouvelles and the Journal des Sçavans: miscellaneous notices of natural events are excluded; there are a few original articles of interest to the learned world, most notably the 'Extrait' of Locke's Essay; the notices of books are less incisive and more objective than Bayle's;†1 it is mainly through it that foreign readers became acquainted with English intellectual endeavour. Le Clerc had several contributors and associates, so that he was author of rather less than half this first Bibliotheque.
Le Clerc's letters to Locke are full of complaints. They leave an unpleasant impression of his character. It is probably fairest to regard them as the outpourings of a man in difficult circumstances to a sympathetic recipient. Le Clerc was unwise, querulous, and contentious; more important, he was sincere and conscientious in his duties, and more especially in the quest for truth and in its promulgation.
The principal account of Le Clerc is (Mrs.) Annie Barnes, Jean Le Clerc (1657-1736) et la République des Lettres, Paris, 1938; it includes judicious descriptions of his publications. The fullest bibliography appears to be that in Haag.
