BENJAMIN FURLY
Benjamin Furly was the fifth son of John Furly of Colchester. The father is described as a linen-draper (lintearius) in 1637 and a few months later as a gentleman. He was an alderman of Colchester in 1637 and mayor in 1638 and 1650. No linen industry is recorded at or near Colchester; it is likely therefore either that he was a leading retailer or that he was wrongly described. He was a Parliamentarian in the Civil War. He and at least two of his sons became Quakers in 1655. He was buried at Colchester in 1673.
Benjamin was baptized at Colchester on 13 April 1636. He was admitted to Colchester School on 21 August 1643 as a paying pupil. Two (or three) of his elder brothers had preceded him at the school. In their time the master was William Dugard (D.N.B.), a friend of Milton and probably an excellent master. Although he was dismissed some months before Benjamin was admitted the school is likely to have maintained its standard. Benjamin's later development suggests that he had a good grounding. In 1655, like his father, he became a Quaker. He was in Amsterdam in 1658. In 1659 he was a signatory of a Quaker petition to Parliament. Soon afterwards he settled permanently in Rotterdam.
Rotterdam was one of the leading European ports, with trading connections especially with the east coast of England and with the south coast westward as far as the Exe estuary and beyond it to Ireland. It lay also on a principal European thoroughfare, from London to Harwich and Brielle (the Brill) or Hellevoetsluís; at Rotterdam dividing, north to The Hague and Amsterdam, eastwards to the Rhine and the Empire. Furly was a merchant; there appears
― 40 ―

to be nothing to show whether he specialized in any branch. He married his first wife in or before 1665, He prospered and kept open house for Quakers and for English and foreign radicals. In early life he was conformist, publishing in 1663 The World's Honour Detected, a vindication of the Quakers' rejection of customary courtesies, and contributing to other Quaker publications; apparently also translating Quaker books. He received Penn and George Fox in 1677 and accompanied Penn on his visit to Princess Elizabeth at Herford. But he was not the man for conformity of any kind. In course of time he was repelled by the Quakers' insistence on externals. He could find no creed more to his liking, but his relations with the Rotterdam Quakers became uneasy and probably ended in complete separation. His quest for belief in combination with his love of novelty for its own sake is evidenced by the large number of suspect if not heterodox books in his large library and by his friendships with such men as F. M. van Helmont, Locke, and the third earl of Shaftesbury. His ardour for religious liberty emerged in his intervention on behalf of Foeke Floris and later on behalf of the French Prophets and Fatio de Duillier; for political liberty, in his friendship with Algernon Sidney and his sympathy with the popular movements in the Netherlands after William III's death.
Locke may have met Furly while he was in Rotterdam in 1683, but is more likely to have owed his acquaintance with him to John Freke (p. 58 n.). Freke could have been introduced to him through either his relationship to Penn (p. 114, n. 1) or his association with English radicals. Locke perhaps knew Freke from Shaftesbury's time; if not, they are likely to have become acquainted at Amsterdam in May of this year: this emerges from no. 851. Locke probably met Furly when he was in Rotterdam between 14 and 23 June, N.S., of this year; he mentions him first in his Journal on 8 October as providing information about the Quakers; letters from Mrs. Duke and Freke (nos. 867, 874) show that the friendship was advancing. When shortly before 12 December he was advised to leave Utrecht he probably went to Rotterdam: he enters information from Furly in his Journal on 9 December, and from Mrs. Furly on 20 December. After a visit to Amsterdam, where he failed to find accommodation, he returned to Rotterdam, where he spent most of his time until he returned to England in 1689. He perhaps lodged with Furly and in any case became attached to him and his family.
Furly's first wife died in 1691 leaving him three sons, Benjohan, John, and Arent. He married secondly in December 1693 Susanna Huys, widow of Jacob van der Tijt. He died in March 1714 and was buried in the Groote Kerk in Rotterdam.
The principal account of Furly is W. I. Hull, Benjamin Furly and Quakerism in Rotterdam, Swarthmore, Pennsylvania, 1941. It is very full but is uncritical and overrates Furly; the list of his writings seems thoroughly unreliable. Most of the letters in Original letters of Locke, etc., edited by T. I. M. Forster, 1830 (new ed., 1847), were addressed to him (the dates of some of those from Locke are wrong). Besides Hull I have used Register of the Scholars admitted to Colchester School, 1637-1740, ed. J. H. Round, Essex Archaeol. Soc., 1897; an account of the Furly family in Essex Review, viii (1899), 86-95; and C. L. Thijssen-Schoute, Uit de Republiek der Letteren, 1967.
― 41 ―

867. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 29 September 1686 (860, 873)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 4-5.
Otterton†1 Sept: 29th. 1686
Dear Sir
I hope you have made no unkind reflections on my long Silence, which has really been a great pain to me; at least I am sure you will pardon it when I have given you an account of our Travels, and the many hardships we have past through since I left you. The Winds were no more favourable to us at Sea, then at our first setting out; we contended with a very high Sea, and the Wind was full in our Teeth all the Voyage; so that we could make no way but by tacking, and that so slowly that we were four whole dayes and Nights on the Water; and reached not the shoar till Monday after sun set; the length of our passage, and the sickness we had laboured under had so disabled me, that 'twas impossible I could use a pen; the utmost that my brother or Mr Duke could pretend to, was to write two lines the one to his Father, the other to Mr Furly,†2 to let them know that we were in the land of the living, and the last was desired to communicate it to you and to Mr Fr:†3 which I hope he fail'd not to do. I slept more that Night at Harwich then I did all the whiles I were on shipboard, or almost ever since. for I have been extreamly ill all the way on the Road; the first meal I made was at Colchester where I eat a few oysters and a fresh Herring, which relish'd well to me, but before Midnight I was taken violently ill, and continued so all the night, but at last it wrought off in a looseness which has continued upon me almost ever since, and brought me very low; it being indeed hard service to travel seven dayes together in that condition, without resting in any place, which our pressing affaires necessitated us to do, we lay at an Inn in London, 'twas 8. at Night before we got thither, and as soon as it was day we were call'd up to set out for Devon, where att last we are safely arrived; and I have employed this first hour in which I have been able to hold up my head, in telling you so, being resolved not to loose another post, presuming that you will accept this testimony of my
― 42 ―

Friendship, this tender of my best services to you, in how hasty, and broken and confused words soever, it be expressed; since it comes from a sincere and gratfull heart, that is not more sensible of any thing then of it's great Obligations to you, whose Friendship I esteem invalluable, and I hope to be alwayes reaping the benefits of it. I every day regret my consenting to come away without you, which I should never have don had not my fears for your health, made me afraid to press you to accompany us, which I desired above all things, but I would not purchase my satisfaction at so deer a rate as the health of such a Freind, whose preservation and welfare shall ever be as much considered by me as my own; and my whole life shall be a perpetual return of the kindnesses you have heaped on me. the breaking out which I complain'd of when I parted from you is not yet over, but I think it Withers, therfore I shall forbear to do any thing to it as yet. but I apprehend it may have a hardness in the skin when the heat and itching is gone, pray advise me what I ought to do in such a case. I am afraid to venture on purging physick haveing lately suffered so much in the Gripes, a long Violent loosness, which is but newly checked; but pray let me know what you think of Daphee's Elixir†1 either for me or my Girle†2 as there may be occasion, and whither you do not think that Rhubarb alone is better for both of us; I find the Child well, but extreamly lean; and shedding her Teeth, which were pritty enough, but now they come yellow and ragged, and uneven; which troubles me a little, but I know not how to help her. yours Friends at Chipley thrive bravely, Mr Clark design'd us a Visit to morrow, but my Brother has for some reasons adjourned it to wensday next. after which you will quickly hear from me again; at present I shall only adde, That I have seen Escott,†3 which looks very well without, but there is very little done within, not one Chamber finish'd or fit to receive my Brother, I am afraid 'twill give him much pain, before he finds any pleasure there yet; but the affair that brought him Home is not so bad as 'twas represented, but much as I guessed it to be. I beleive 'twill be hard to get a good account from his ill steward; but that is the worst of it, I doubt not but he will be glad to be dismissed quietly, and will not give his Master any further trouble.
― 43 ―

I have not seen my Lanlady,†1 she went a dayes Journey into the Country, the very day before I came to Town; which you will easily believe was no small disappointment to poor me; but I was brought so low, and am so used to Crosses and afflictions, that almost all things come alike to me. I am unwilling However, to dismiss you so soon, but I trespass on many of my Neibours who are here to welcome me Home, and such to whom some cerimony is due, but I understand little, and practice less; yet now I must put an end to a conversation that pleases me much better than theirs can do, and hasten to subscribe my self what I am with the greatest respect and affection
Dear Sir
Your most Obliged faithfull Friend and Servant
ISABELLA DUKE
Your Daughter Betty gives you her duty.†2 and the Gentlemen kiss your hands.
Address (written by Richard Duke?): For Mr John Lock
Endorsed by Locke: I. Duke 29 Sept.86

868. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 1/11 October [1686] (865, 877)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 255j. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 305-7; postscript and address in Ollion, p. 168. Year from van Limborch's note.
(English) 
Utrecht 11 Oct.†a
Quanquam longo usu ad alia hujus vitæ incommoda occaluit aliquatenus mens mea, a consuetudine tamen tua (vir Doctissime et amicorum optime) me divelli sine magnâ animi ægritudine pati non possum. Tu enim me eruditione tua instruere: Judicio confirmare:
― 44 ―

consilio dirigere: amicitia et comitate solari solebas, quotidianum curarum mearum perfugium. Sed ita plerumque mecum agi solet, ut ubi et quibuscum esse maxime cupio, refragrante fortunâ raro permissum sit. Devorandum igitur ut potero hujus absentiæ tædium quod frequentibus tuis literis levare debes, jam præsertim dum tempus et otium tibi permittunt adversarii illi qui domi suæ prælia tibi meditantur.†1 Hoc te in quo jam sumus sæculo expectasse non dubito. Si candidè et ut veritatis amici argumentorum pondere tecum agant tibi scio non displicebunt qui veritatem amplecteris undicunque venientem. Sin Iracundè, veteratoriè malignè paucis placebunt nisi sui similibus. quicquid demum acciderit hoc certum est, quod tu illæsus victorque abibis quia veritatem quæris non victoriam. Sed ut verum fatear ego a rixosis hujusmodi disputatoribus non multum expecto qui in alienis convellendis, non suis astruendis quærunt gloriam. Artificis et laudem merentis est ædificare. Sed pugnaces hosce sibi et curis suis relinquamus. Si quid in Burneto†2 placidius et liberalius reperisti gaudeo, pacificorum vellem
― 45 ―

quotidie augeri numerum, præsertim inter reformatos.†1 inter quos nimium quotidie seruntur lites. Inimicus homo facit hoc.†2 Alterius sunt indolis amici quibus hic te favente familiariter utor. Uterque Grævius†3 salutem plurimam tibi dicit. Verynium†4 sæpius quæsitum nondum domi reperi, hujus septimanæ dies aliquot extra urbem transegit cum domum redeierit non diu insalutatum permittam. Vale cum tuâ tuisque et me ama tui Studiosissimum
J L
Ignoscas quæso quod inclusarum curam tibi committo
(Latin) 
Utrecht 11 Oct.
Although by long habituation my mind has become to a certain extent hardened to the other inconveniences of this life, yet to be forcibly separated from your company, learned Sir and best of friends, is a thing I cannot bear without much mental distress. For you have been accustomed to instructing [p. 44] me with your learning, to assuring me with your judgement, to directing me with your advice, and to consoling me with your friendship and kindliness; you have been the daily refuge of all my cares. But so it usually happens with me: adverse fortune rarely allows me to be where and with whom I chiefly desire. I must therefore put up as best I can with this wearisome absence, which you must relieve by frequent letters, especially now that you are allowed some time and leisure by those adversaries who are planning war upon you behind doors.†1 I do not doubt that you have expected this in the age we live in. If they were to deal frankly with you by weight of argument, like lovers of truth, I know that they would not be displeasing to you, who embrace truth from whatever source it comes; but by acting spitefully, in a spirit of malice and cunning, they will please few but themselves. Well whatever happens this is certain: you will emerge unscathed and victorious, since you seek truth and not victory. But to tell the truth I confess I do not expect much from such quarrelsome disputants, who seek glory in tearing the work of others to pieces, not in making good their own. The business of a craftsman who deserves any credit is to build. But let us leave these pugnacious folk to themselves and their concerns. If you have found signs of greater mildness and broad-mindedness in Burnet†2 I am glad of it; I would [p. 45] wish the number of peace-seekers to increase daily, especially among the Reformed,†1among whom too many quarrels are engendered every day; an enemy does this.†2 Very different are the friends whose familiar society I am enjoying here through your kindness. The two Græviuses†3 both send you their heartiest greetings. I have tried to see Verrijn†4 more than once but have not yet found him at home; he has been out of the city for several days this week; when he returns home I shall lose no time in calling on him. My respects to your wife and family, and love me your most devoted J.L.
Forgive me for asking you to see to the enclosures.
Address: Mÿn Heer Mÿn Heer Limborch
869. Edward Clarke to Locke, 2 October 1686 (863, 871)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 19. Answered by no. 872.
From this time until October 1688 Locke usually cut away Clarke's signature, or part of it, sometimes with loss of words on the other side of the sheet.
<Chipley>†a October the 2d. 1686
Deare Sir,
My last of August the 30th informed you by what Accident I was prevented from visitting Sutton and serveing you there imediately
― 46 ―

after our last Assises as I intended; And I write this to acquaint you, That I am now newly return'd thence, haveing spent the Greatest part of the last 12. dayes there, and that I found all your Rel<a>tions†a and Freinds in those Parts in good health, But your Businesse with Robert Haroll hath been permitted to runn into greate confusion, there haveing never been any Accompt stated or settled between Mr Stratton and Him for the Tenement Hee Rents since our La: day 1680. which as I understand was the time Mr Stratton began to receive your Rents, soe that to Bring Haroll to Adjust his Accompts with mee now home to the 29th. of September last, I was forc'd to Charge Him†b- with six-†b yeares and halfe's Rent, viz: From La: Day 1680. to Michaelmas 1686., which at 23l. per Annum being as Mr. Stratton tells mee the Rent agreed on amounts unto 149l: 10s:, Of which summe after much time spent in heare<in>g†a the Wran<g>les†abetween Mr Stratton and Him, it did appeare to mee partly b<y>†a Receipts produc'd by Haroll, and by Mr Strattons Booke, That there has been paid dureing this time by Haroll in money the summe of 88l: 04s: 00d: ½ And by a Byll of Disbursments allow'd Him by Mr. Stratton in the yeare 1682. the summe of 02l: 12s: 09d: ½ And by another Byll of Disbursements allowed Him by Mr. Stratton in the yeare 1683. the summe of 01l: 03s: 02d: which makes the summe Totall paid and disburs'd by Haroll to bee 92l. and noe more; soe that summe being deducted out of the 149l: 10s: above mentioned to be due for Rent home to Michaelmas last, there remaines still due from Haroll to Ballance that Accompt the summe of 57l: 10s:, And out of this 57l: 10s: Haroll claymes to bee allowed severall considerable summes pretended to be disbursed by Him in the yeares 1680: 1681: 1684: 1685: And in this yeare of 1686, But haveing never produced any Bylls thereof to Mr. Stratton, nor being now able to give mee any particular of <those>†c Disbursments, I refused to make Him any allowance, untill Hee shall <clear>ely†c and plainly manifest what the Particular summes are, and for what, and too whome paid, which Hee now pretends were soe laid out by Him, over and besides the two summes above mentioned to bee allowed and disbursed by Him in the yeares 1682: and 1683; The Accompt standing thus, and being by me reduced into Writeing under Harolls Hand and seale, I proceeded to the valueing of three Cowes, three Horses, six stacks of Hay, A small quantity of Barley, And His House-hold-Goods, which was all that Hee had on
― 47 ―

your Tenement, or elsewhere that I can heare of; All which, I was forc'd in the first place to seise upon and distrayne for the Rent Arreare before I could gett Him to come to any Accompt at all, And doe hope that these Cattle, horses and Goods, when disposed of, will rayse between 40. and 50. pounds of the debt, and the residue I doubt will prove a desperate debt, though Haroll promises fayre that what the Goods doe not rayse Hee will some other way make good to you; The three Cowes were by Harolls consent under his hand and seale sold for ten pounds before I came from Sutton, which Mr. Stratton is to Accompt for; And to prevent the charge and trouble of a judgment and Execution upon the Rest of the Goods distrayned, I have allsoe obtained His consent under hand and seale for the sale and disposeall of all of them, and have given Mr. Stratton my best directions therein, who appeares to bee now much pleased that there is soe much secured, being at first under apprehensions (by Haroll's stubborn Behaviour) that you would have lost the greatest part if not all the debt; I have allsoe given the best directions I can (Haroll not being in any Condition to rent it any longer) for the Letting of the Wynter Grasse, which I hope will bee disposed of to the best Advantage by Mr. Stratton, and before our Lady Day next Hee questions not but to gett a Good Tennant into it under the same Rent as Haroll had it, Provided the Tenement bee in the meane time well repayred, the defects whereof are cheifely these, viz: The thatch of the Barn is soe totally decayed that the Rayne beates through all parts of it, and if it bee not speedily New-thatch'd all over, the Tymber of the Roofe will be much injured, and the Barn rendred alltogather uselesse; The thatch of the Stable is allsoe much decayed, and I thinke must of necessity bee New Rigg'd, and the thatch on that syde the dwelling-house next the Highway is allsoe verie Ruinouse, The Well is allsoe decayed and uselesse, and must bee sunke deeper and repayred at the topp, towards which I saw in the furthest feild on the left hand of the Road that Leads towards Bristoll a Tree formerly Fell'd by Mr. Stratton's Order, And Hee tells mee Hee will take effectuall Care, that these things shall be done with as little Charge as may bee to you, And promises mee that Hee will never suffer any of your Tennants to runn soe farr in Arreare againe: As for the Treaty which Mr. Stratton hath formerly mentioned to you to bee had between Him and the widdow Shatter, upon a due examination of that matter, there appeares to mee a greate probability that the
― 48 ―

Life shee pretends to hold by is Dead, For at first shee affirmed the Person was resident in London, then shee said Hee was in Ireland, and now shee pretends Hee is out at sea shee knows not where, soe that untill it is more certaine whither there bee really a Life in Being or not, I thinke it in noe sort adviseable to proceed in that Treaty with Her, But I have given Mr Stratton such directions for the makeing of that discovery, that I doubt not, but if they are cauteousely pursued, will inforce the Widdow to produce the Life in case Hee bee liveing, and then wee shall bee the better satisfied what to doe further therein; And for the other Treaty soe often mentioned by Mr Stratton to bee had between Him and Veale, I beleive there is noe reall intent (at least at present) by Veale to proceed in it, For I sent twice to speake with Him whilst I was at Sutton, but could not gett him to mee to treate about it; And now I thinke I have Tyred you, and therefore will only add at present, that my Wife and all my Children are in perfect health, and give theire humble services to you as doth,
your most obleiged Faithfull Freind and servant
E:†a
The Sinkes are now come safe to Chipley, and will bee verie usefull when sett up, for which you have Madam's and my hearty thankes etc:
Endorsed by Locke: E. Clarke 2 Oct. 86
870. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 9 October [1686] (847, 882)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 138-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
From CCC.†1
In this Place where I received your last before, I have now received yours of the 6th of Sept: which I thought long of comeing, tho I perceive you are not in fault, since it has laine sometime at my owne House, to which I have beene a stranger about a Fortnight; You will think me I feare an Errant Gossip to be Gadding Abroad
― 49 ―

so soone Againe, And but an Ill Wife when I tell you that I have left my Good Man at Home alone by Himself, But the Little Being†1 I mention'd in my Last must be my Excuse for it, and I doubt not will seeme a Sufficient one since you have thought fitt to send me a Postscript of Consolation for being but at Thirtie Miles Distance, But I gave I Question not a Just Occasion for it, which tho it proceeded from a Cause I cannot Alter, your Letter has I Confess made me a little Assham'd of. But leaveing This subject Let me tell you that I am much Pleas'd with the Preference you have giv'n me over your Dutch Mistress; and that You can Think that Friendship may have the Ascendant over Love; I am Pleas'd Because it is Natural to All to Desire that Those whom they Esteeme should have the same Opinions with Themselves, were it onelie out of a Just Value for Truth; But I am more so (I was going to say) for a more Obliging Reason; But that I have Recall'd to my Remembrance You might Possibly not be in Earnest; and if so, that it would be in Vaine to Perswade you into it, (without which it must lose its Value) especially under the Disadvantages of my owne Absence, and your Misstreses Presence; And indeed should I attempt it now I think of That, it would more Argue my Little Opinion of the Latter, then my Great One of the Former. For what Signifies an Absent Friend? One sees them not; One Converses not with Them, but by the Tedious way of Letters; And one has never with any Freedome the most Proper and Pleaseing Sattisfactions of Friendship, To Laugh with Them when one is Merry; And to Complaine to them when one is Sad; So that to Confess the Truth to you, Tho I have now a Friend with me Less Agreable then you Are, (As perhaps your Dutch Mistress may in some Respect or other be then me) I injoy much more Pleasure from them then I should in You (were you Capable of haveing an Equall Regard for me) at This Distance. And yet after All, Haveing said this more to Justifie You then for any thing else, (Although it is not without much Truth) I am yet Pleas'd that you Remember me, That you Desire to Heare from me, And that you think I write not often enough to You.†a And to let you Know that if you had as Deserving
― 50 ―

a Friend, nothing could make them Altogether Useless and Insignificant,†a Philander†1 is a Name, that since I have seene you, has many times Reconcil'd me to the World when nothing else would; When I have beene in This Place Plagu'd with Theire Pedantry and scholastick Arrogance; when in Towne with the Noisie Fops There; And when with the Insipid Coxcombs of the Countrey; But Above All I have made use of it (though whether with so much Reason, or No, You and Heaven Can Onely Tell) when I Have beene Tempted to Beleeve that there was no such Thing Below (amongst your Sex at least) as an Undesigning and Honest Friendship; free from Unjust Ends; and Little Interests; which when either Disappointed; or Serv'd; turns to Hatred, Malice, and Revenge; Or to Coldness, and Indifference; Were I sattisfy'd that you ever had any Real Friendship for your Governess I should be Abundantly so that I was in the Right in Reflecting upon it to This End, and on These Occasions, But the Doubt Lies on That Side; and I Dare not Determine with Assureance whether I ever was more to you then an Agreable Acquaintance. But I know not whether I Have Rambled; from the Text I am Certaine, tho what you writt to me I cannot well tell, Haveing lost your Letter, A Misfortune which never before Befell me, as well as the Receiving it Open, which I wonder at. Twoo things notwithstanding I Remember in it The One that you chid me for not writeing sooner; The other that you was Angry with me for not Dyeing; For the first, my Apprehensions of the last was the Principle Reason of it; Since I envy'd any Body but my self the Pleasure of Reading a Letter of yours. And for the Last I Have no excuse to make for spoiling a good Epitaph; But can Assure you that I was so far a Prophetess as to be in very great likelihood of it; My Long Weakness after which, is Another excuse for my Former Fault, Who whether I write to You or No shall Always be Your Real Friend
and Humble Servant
PHILOCLEA
Oct: the 9th.
Address: For Mr Lock.
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 9 Oct.86 Answered 13 Nov:

871. Edward Clarke to Locke, 16 October 1686 (869, 872)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 20. Fragment: probably a quarter of the leaf is missing.
Chipley October the 16th. 1686.
Deare Sir,
My last of the 2d instant (which I hope by this time you have Received) gives a Particular accompt of your Affayres about Sutton etc: And after haveing ask'd your pardon for the Omission, I take this first opportunity to add what I then forgott to incert in that Letter, which is that whilst I was in those parts Mr Stratton paid mee for your use the summe of 31l: 10s. and told mee that was all the money hee then had of yours in his handes, but did not offer mee any Accompt, however (because you mentioned in your Letter of the 1st. of August last that Hee desiered to have his Accompts stated, and that you would have mee cast my Eye on them) I acquainted Him that if my seeing the state of His Accompt and communicateing of it to you would bee any satisfaction to Him, I was ready and willing soe to doe, But Hee declyn'd it, and therefore I said nothing further to Him on that subject: About 2. dayes since I Received from my Neighbour (who is Returned safe to her Brothers House neere mee) your Letter of the 27th. of August with your third Booke de Intellectu etc: sealed with your owne Seale,†1 and have taken it into my custody under the same conditions as you sent the former to mee, which you may bee assured shall bee most strictly performed, and I acknowlidg the particular Favour you have done mee (by permitting mee soe large an opportunity of peruseing those thoughts of yours on that subject) to bee beyond any thing I can Expresse, but must allsoe confesse that although the two former Bookes have been soe long in my Custody, and that my inclynations above all things have lead†a mee to a seriouse and deliberate veiw of them, yett such has been my unhappy circumstances ever since my Receipt of them†b that I can with the greatest truth assure you I have not passed one day which hath not brought its full Businesse with it, in soe much that I have not had any time to injoye my selfe in the Reading of that or any other Treatise

872. Locke to Edward Clarke, 21/31 October [1686] (871, 875)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 20. Printed in Rand, pp. 166-70. Year from Clarke's endorsement. Answers nos. 863 and 869; answered by no. 875.
31 Oct.
Sir
Though you have taken soe much pains in my businesse and recovered more of Haroll then I expected or I beleive I should have donne had I been there my self yet it is to be doubted whether you will permit me to give you thanks, But what ever pleasure you take in obleigeing your friends and what ever right you thinke you have
― 53 ―

particularly to doe me all the kindenesses imaginable I crave leave to be sensible of your favours and to be sorry it lies not in my power to make acknowledgments that may beare any proportion with them. I could not forbear saying thus much to you and send you half a dozen words of acknowledgment after you had spent the greatest part of twelve days in a most troublesome affair of mine. And therefor pray pardon me, and beleive that I have noe complements for you though I have all the true esteem and affection one freind can have for another. I feare Mr Stratton is but a slow man of London.†1 I put some thing into one of my letters to you to quicken him, whether you received it or thought fit to make use of it I know not, but in good earnest it were better that litle tenement were reduced into money then to yeild noe other income but trouble to me or my freinds, though I doubt whether chapmen are there to be had. I was sorry to heare by yours of 30 Aug: of the death of your man. I suppose without the help of instances in your view you know of what value a trusty servant is. Though I gave you an account by a memorandum that I thought Abel trees were to be got as good or better nearer home then from hence,†2 it was not to spare my self the trouble of sending them since I have not soe much pleasure in any thing as when I am doeing you some service. I have therefor taken order to have some got for you, therefor pray take order with Mr Elwill†3 about them for to him they will be consigned. With them you will also receive some Moscovie or Russia Cabbage seed and some bloud red cabbage seed, which they looke on here as the wholsomest of all and perhaps not without reason for let me tell you this as a thing worth your remembrance that it is one of the best remedys I know against the Scurvy, besides boyleing of it as we doe our cabbage ordinarily, they use it here also raw as their constant winter sallad, haveing always a store of them for the winter which I am told the gardners preserve by laying them in straw in deep holes dug into the ground on purpose. their way of useing them for salads is this, they take a cabbage and slice as much of itt off as will serve for the present meale just as you would slice a coucomber whereby the leaves being cut crosse fall into litle
― 54 ―

shreads which looke handsomely in the dish, and dressed with oyle and vinegar is noe ill sallad.
and if you keep your counsel will I beleive be scarce known what it is and the truth is being very wholsome if I were there I would bring it into use under some fine new name, for after I had been a litle accustomed to it I eat it with pleasure. I wonder you had not heard by the 2d of Oct:†1 of several sorts of seeds sent you by a neigbour of yours and the third book de Intellectu humano sent by the same hand, pray when you goe to market enquire after them if you have noe news of them sooner. But to return to the Abell trees, pray what doe you meane by soe great a number of them? tis true they are quickly up, but what are they good for when grown. If you cannot learne that the timber is good for something I advise you to plant noe more of them then you have need of for some present shade or shelter, for if they are not good timber they being not beautifull, there is noe thing recommends them but their quick grouth. and for me I litle value unlesse it be for some present need things that are soon ripe and soon rotten. Indeed I have heard that their bords are almost as good as deale for flooring of rooms and drie uses but I doubt it. In a rich soile like yours where all things grow soe well I should choose to have a walke up to the front of the house of limes only for beauty. two rows of a side and a space between them as broad as the front of your house or 10 or 15 foot broader as I formerly told you; but behinde the house I would have a walke of the same fashon of Elmes and on the sides of other usefull trees, (perhaps oaks should be one) which will serve for beauty and use too and pay for their standing. Abells I would only place either where others will not grow or where I have need of a present fence and then I would place oaks amongst them or behind them which is better which might doe the businesse when they are gon, but not knowing your designe I talke at random though with a good intention. Pray remember me to our Spa freinds,†2 pray observe nicely, without leting them perceive that you doe soe, how I stand in each of their books, we had some pleasant scenes here which would come into the history of my travells if I were with you to tell them. The promise of Limetree seeds has failed me, The seeds man tells me the skipper brings word that he came to late to Norway. I feare tis an excuse for I had bespoke them
― 55 ―

before you writ to me, but what remedy? I must be content with a promise for an other year. I feare by your silence you are not yet provided of a man such as we sought for my young master. let this (if it be soe) in the meane time satisfie you that none is much better then an unfit one and if I knew what state he at present was in as to learning I might perhaps thinke of some way, where in he might under your eye improve sufficently for his years without almost any trouble to you, and soe the principles of vertue sense and breeding which are the main businesse be preserved and nursed up in the way you have begun, and not all these, as is used, be sacrifised to a litle Latin under the management of an ill or imprudent tutor, unskild as it often happens in those Essentiall points. Though it hath hitherto scaped my pen yet it has been often in my head to enquire what course you tooke about your water and whether you are supplyd from the spring we examined when I was there. I have had many projects upon that affair in my head though I never troubled you with any of them, hopeing that your house is well supplyd with good water without them. Pray present my humble service to Madam. I had designed her a long letter by a Lady of her acquaintance I parted with not long since at the Brill,†1 but findeing other peoples letters were refused to be medled with I thought it good manners not to give the trouble of any of mine. soe that the two Ladys were excused one from carying and the other from reading a long letter from me. But pray tell her she has noe great losse in it. For it being past doubt that I am her humble servant with the utmost affection and respect any body can be I had noe thing to adde to it but complaints for my being at that distance which permits me not those oportunitys of performing those parts of duty and gratitude belong to me and enjoying sometimes at Chipley the company I most desire in the world I am
Sir
Your most obleiged and most humble servant
J L
Pray remember me to young master and my litle pretty mistris. I take it something amisse that you have said noething particularly of her to me this long time, but I am glad to heare from an other hand that all your litle ones thrive bravely for soe I am told in a letter I lately received. the news you may beleive was very
― 56 ―

welcome both because I have soe much reason to love father and mother and all the family. and also I am glad to finde that my plain rustick way of feeding and useing children has not such hardships in it as to hurt even the tender sex. For I flatter my self that Madam in breeding her daughters has inclined a litle to my method.
Address: For Mr Edward Clarck To be left at the Lady Kings in Salisbury Court near Fleetstreet London
Postmark: OC 28
Endorsed by Clarke: J:L: his Letter about Abeele Cuttings, Seedes, and other thinks etc: Received the 1rst of November 1686.
873. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 21 October 1686 (867, 883)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 6.
Otterton Octob: 21st 1686
Dear Sir
Though I have never been so happy as to receive a line from you since I left you, which is methinks an Age; yet I cannot doubt your Friendship, you have given me such assurances, such demonstrations of it, that my only solicitude is how to deserve it, and how to acknowledge it so, as to make you sencible how Gratfull, how Joyfull I am; I cannot forbear repeating my Thanks, and importuning you with my letters; how impertinent how insignificant soever they are, they will bring me to your Thoughts, where I beg that I may always have a place, since none can vallue, or Covet it more. I hope you have long since receiv'd my first, which had certainly been followed with another ere this, had not my Brother told me last week that 'twas his turn then, and that he would not faile to do me right to you, and to let you know that he took the employment out of my hands, but by a letter I received from him, this morning, I understand that the perplexity and multitude of his affairs would not permit it; he passes few minutes so agreably as he would do in addressing himself to you; really I pitty him, yet I believe the present Vexation, and the loss of some Moneys which his late unfaithfull Steward cannot account for, is the worst of his Case, all other apprehensions are over, and I beleive there was never any reason for them. he hopes to put his concerns in so good order that he may leave them and go to London before Chrismass,
― 57 ―

and my Master†1 resolves to follow him assoon as he can have any hopes of meetting you there. I lately met your Friend Sumshier†2 who this day begins his Journey for London with his Family, and talks of giving you a Visit at Utrecth if you do not incline to return into England, which I perceive he expected, and wonder'd to see both Dr Taffee†3 and your Otterton Friends return without you; yet he advises you nothing, but leaves you to be determin'd by your own reason, which he thinks can best direct you. but I am so selfish that I cannot forbear wishing you in England since I have no hopes of returning to you, nor indeed any reason to desire it; for the Air, and the drink of England agrees very well with me, and has already restored me to almost as good a condition of health as I enJoyed when I came first into Holland to you. but my particular disorder is as bad as ever, and I fear grows worse. also the roughness on my Thighs continues, but it seems to be withered and dying, and I hope will not trouble me long. I have taken Syrup of Fumitory every day, but have not applied any thing outwardly, but will follow any advice you will give me, which I shall impatiently expect, 'tis hard to live any longer without so much as a paper Conversation with you. pray let your next teach me how to Cure Agues with the Jesuits Bark; if it can be done by a recipe. and be pleas'd to be very particular as to Quartans, and Tertians, and Quotidiens, either in Children, or Elder people. abundance of my Friends and Neithbours now suffer in them, and if there be a certain remedy, I would be glad to be able to give them that relief. if you think this request ridiculous, let my Charitable intentions atone for my Ignorance and indiscretion, I presume upon your Freindship, and I know you have goodness enough to pardon all the errors, and mistakes that I have or may be guilty of towards you. and in confidence of it beg another Favour viz that you would wayt on Mrs Floyd†4 and Mrs Williams with my most humble service, and acquaint them with my health and safe arrival, and that I am passionatly desirous to serve them in all I am capable, if they please to Honour me with their commands, but that I forbear writing to them particularly, only because I am Tottally a stranger to all publick affairs, and this dull country place affords nothing that can entertain them, or be worth postage. remember me also if you please
― 58 ―

to Mr How†1 and his Wife, and to any other of our Friends. and Oblige me with a letter at your first leisure; which request I make with all imaginable earnestness, and with such respect and affection as becomes
Sir
Your Obliged faithfull Friend and most humble servant
ISABELLA DUKE
Your Daughter Betty is removed from me to Sir John Davies†2 for all this Winter. Mr Duke is at Escott with Sir Walter and my other sisters.†3 but all are well, and long to hear from you. adieu. pardon these hasty lines. and accept them.
Address: These For Dr Lock an English Gentleman att Utrecht
Postscript on cover: Pray send me your address, or make hast to us.
Endorsed by Locke: (i): Mrs Duke 21 Oct.86 Answered 18 Nov; (ii): Mr Duke

874. John Freke to Locke, 3/13 November [1686] (887)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 155-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
The writer, c. 1652-1714 or later, was a son of John Freke of Winterborne Stickland, Dorset. He matriculated from Wadham College, Oxford, in 1669 and remained there probably until 1672. He was admitted to the Middle Temple in 1669 and became a barrister in 1676. He was perhaps author of 'The History of Insipids', a satire against Charles II circulated in that year; proceedings against him on account of it were instituted but failed for lack of evidence. He associated with the extreme opponents of the court during the next few years, but kept clear of conspiracy. At the time of Monmouth's rebellion he was taken into custody; a few weeks later he was released on bail and was at Tunbridge Wells with Sir Walter Yonge and Richard Duke. He may have known Clarke since 1669, and perhaps became acquainted with Locke in Shaftesbury's time; from no. 887 it appears likely that he and Locke first became friends during his present visit to the Netherlands. He was a friend of Somers, perhaps from his first years at the Middle Temple or earlier. About the end of 1694 he and Clarke joined forces as 'the College' to promote Locke's and their own political views (no. 1821). Locke at Oates took the lead; Clarke spoke for them in the house of commons; Freke, who remained steadily in the background, had Somers's ear. The association appears to have dwindled in activity after about two years. Freke's radicalism appears
― 59 ―

also in his befriending John Toland (no. 1646) in 1694. In later years he probably limited his activities to advising his friends about their legal business: Philological Quarterly, xliv (1965), 472-83, a full account; Grey, Secret History of the Rye-House Plot, pp. 16, 18, 95, 104 (perhaps this man); p. 5 n.; Toland, Miscellaneous Works, 1747, ii. 292-4; E. Freke, Mrs. Elizabeth Freke, her diary, 1671 to 1714, ed. M. Carbery, 1913, pp. 48 n., 52, etc. (probably this man; there were several men of the name); letters below.
Rotterdam Nov: the 3/13
Dear Sir
Fryday night†1 I arrived at the Hague where I spent the next two days but had noe patience to continue longer though treated with all imaginable kindness by all I knew there yet still methought I wanted something and could not be easie and therefore on moonday I came hither where I still find the same want and now I perceive, twas the taste I had enjoyd for a week of your obliging and agreeable conversation that makes all other things loose their relish with me, which would make me change my Resolution of going for England and return to settle near you at utrecht were it not that I must goe to see whether I can find encouragement to take my American Journey (to which I am extremely inclined) and also that I think it a duty Friendship lays upon me to goe and endeavour my utmost to perswade our Friend†2 to spend some further time abroad. I received a Letter from him at my arrivall here dated from Chiply in which are these words [—try to put my affairs into better hands and a better methode then they have been of late but that I fear will be a work of soe much time that it will be near Christmas before I shall return to London and how long I may then adventure to be absent from my concerns I cannot guess—] by which you will Judge that he will not easily be perswaded to what I think his Interest unless one give him other reasons than can be sent in a Letter. He tells me Mr Clark intends to spend his winter in London which has made me stop your Letter to Mr Elwill and Address all to Sir W Y: to whom I have written both by the Ship and by post to take care of Mr Clarks†a as well as his own concerns which will be the best way since Sir Ws are not to be Addressed to Mr Elwill but to one at Apsham.†3
― 60 ―

I purpose to begin my Journey for Flanders Saterday next and resent†1 with all gratitude the good wishes you send with me they speak soe much of friendship that I want words to express the sense I have of them and the other obliging and endearing parts of your Letter but I shall always study to render you my acknowledgements by paying you on all occasions such Services as I can imagine will be acceptable to you and particularly by doing you all the good offices you desire towards our friends in england who however I'm sure know you too well to need any other recomendation to esteem you and value your friendship.
I deliverd your methode of common placing to Mr Furly who is very much pleased with it and says his own was much of the same nature. He this morning lent it to the Burgemaster†2 whom he found busie contriving a methode of putting his Notions in an order that he might know where to find them soe that it came in season. His business to the Burgemaster was to gett the Abeell Cuttings to put on board Hodder†3 who goes hence this evening and I believe by this time they are shipt. He had before put on board some black poplars which the Burgemaster said would grow but not White poplars or Abeel which the Burgemaster told him would not grow, They are cutt 5 foot long and that of purpose not onely for the easier carryage but because before they come into england if the ends are dry by dividing them in the midle they will have two plants each having one moist end to put into the ground.
I have met with little worth remark since I saw you onely that the Design I mentioned to you against —— is talkt of every where but none can tell what it is and my Author tells me that the Lord M: business at your Town has spoild it and either broken or alterd their measures as he is informed by a Letter last post.†4
I have searcht all my papers for that I promised you but cannot
― 61 ―

find it and therefore believe I left it in London where if I find it (as I doubt not) at my arrivall I will be sure to perform my word to you and if I see you before I leave that place it may be I may doe more than I promised and shew you my Instances†1
I†a- have given Mr Furly a Bill for 20 li and orderd him to pay it you as alsoe 47 Gilders ten Stivers which you laid out for the Trees deducting 4 gilders 10 stivers for the fraight of your 90 hither and alsoe your proportion of the other charges of Shipping them, Soe that when ever you write to him you may receive your money.-†a
As soon as I arrive in England you shall be sure to hear from me but I doubt whether I can find a way of sending to you from Flanders Soe that I hope you will not impute it to neglect if I am silent whilst I am in my Journey for I assure you nothing can afford me a greater pleasure than to write my self
Sir Your affectionate friend and humble servant
JOHN FREKE
I have sent you as much of the Green Salve as I could spare by Mr Scroops brother
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Jean Lock chez Monsieur Cross dans le Bode Straet a Utrecht
Endorsed by Locke: Mr Freke 3/13 Nov. 86
875. Edward Clarke to Locke, 5 November 1686 (872, 878)
B.L. MS. Locke c. 6, f. 22. Imperfect: part of leaf cut or torn away, containing presumably the signature and perhaps a postscript. Printed in Rand, pp. 170-1. Answers no. 872.
London the 5th of November 1686.
Deare Sir
your two Letters of the 28th. and 31th of the last moneth are both come to my handes since my Arrivall here, (which was the beginning of this weeke)†2 with my Wife and my two eldest children
― 62 ―

in my company, I thanke God they are all in perfect health, and soe are my other two children†1 allsoe, and my Wife joynes with mee in thankeing you for your Favours in supplying our Gardens and Plantations with such variety of the best things, and my sonn desires mee to assure you that Hee is perfectly your servant, and will Faithfully discharge the Trust you have reposed in Him touching the Lyme-Trees, concerning which I will write to Mr. Ellwell by the next Post, And my little Gyrle being unwilling to come short of her Brother in Civility towards you, sayes that shee is certaine shee Loves you much better then Hee can doe, and is Resolved never to forsake you; Thus you see how you are like to bee ingaged when ever you Return into England; You may bee assured the Lyme-Trees and other things shall bee taken all the Care of imaginable, And the Abeele Cuttings (for which I Return you my hearty thankes) I will dispose of as your guift to mee, and shall esteem them much if they grow though you are pleased to putt soe slight a value on them, But I must confesse I would not have sent for neere soe many of that sort of Cuttings, had I thought you would not have given mee Leave to pay for them: The Byll of Exchange that you say you have drawn on mee for twenty pounds sterling shall bee punctually paid in manner as you desire, And Madam is just now gott at my Elbow and commands mee to give you her particular thankes for your verie Kind Expressions in your Letter towards Her, and has strong inclynations of visitting you before Her Return againe to Chipley, as I hinted to you in my Letter of the 16th. of October (which I hope is in your handes), But when I know more of Her mind, and am a little better at leasure then at this time, it shall bee communicated to you, in the meane time I will only add that I spent one day with your Freind Adrian in my journey up, but received noe particular Orders from you by Him; Hee and His Lady and Lame Thomas†2 and his Spouse are all in Health, and give you theire services; your Spa-Freinds†3 I saw alltogather in Devon, and some of them were afterwards with mee att Chipley untill the day before I began my journey towards this Place, and all spoke of you with great Respect and Kindnesse; And because you aske mee how wee are supplyed with Water, I must tell you, It is from the spring neere the House that wee Examined when you were there, by one of Sir Sam: Moorlands
― 63 ―



Forceing Pumpes,†1 This is all that the time will permitt mee to write at present: I am
your obleiged Faithfull Freind†a
Endorsed by Locke: E:Clarke 5 Nov.86
876. Richard Duke and Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 10 November 1686 (861, 903; 857, 893)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 146-7.
[Duke:]
Escott Nov. the 10th 1686
Sir
Your most obliging letter from Utrecht of the 26th past to my Wife came safe to her hands, with which she would have paid you her thanks, had not I taken it out of them, alledging that it was my turn: And indeed I am sensible that I have been too tardy in making you my acknowlegements of the innumerable favors we received from you in Holland, as also of your kind remembrance of me in your last, and your concern for my health; which call for the quickest and deepest expressions of gratitude. But I hope you will have the goodness to pardon me, and accept of my syncerest respects, which I can never fail to pay you, whilst I have a memory, though I want language to express them as I ought. I can truly say I never knew any person that I was more disposed to love and honor then your self, and I have such a sense of my obligations to you as makes me entirely yours, and desire nothing more ardently then an opportunity of rendring you service. I must confess my incapacity in that point discourages me, but the experience I have had of your generous temper gives me confidence; so that I shall make no scruple of troubling you again with the affair of my health, Twas no small trouble to me to leave you on the other side of the water before I could have the benefit of your prescriptions, but I hope some good providence will bring us together again, I could wish it might be on this side with your convenience and inclination, I long for it with impatience, and should look on it as a particular blessing from heaven, I can onely now acquaint you that I find this
― 64 ―

air to agree much better with me then that of the low countries. I am not so subject to drowsinesse, and never sleep in the day but after some hard exercise, which has not happened to me since I have been settled at home. I believe I am much the better for the Spa waters specially in that which you may remember was my greatest complaint, but I know they have wrought but part of my cure, and therefore must apply my self to you to perfect it. I could make use of one Argument more to bring you over, which is that John Barber†1 has gotten an ugly Cough, and saies he finds himself decay as if he were threescore years of age, so that if you do not cure him, the new Gardens in the Row†2 will be spoild, and that I suppose you would not have ly at your door, I wish I knew how to retain Sill†3 as an Advocate for it having as good an opinion of his Rhetorick as you make us have of his Raillerie. I would beg the favor of you to put him in mind to buy me a good hone to sett my razors, as I desired him formerly. Sir W. has at length brought his perverse servant to an account in which he is very defective, but whither by negligence, or knavery does not yet appear, He submitts himself wholely to his Masters mercy, and was yesterday dismist his service, I think my Wife has also made her servant sensible of her ill behavior, she hopes you have received her second letter, and gives you her most humble service. I have left her at Otterton to take care of her Girle who is a full employment for her. Your Daughter Betty desires you to accept of her duty, who is now here Sir W.'s housekeeper, her elder sister having broken her arm by a fall from a horse in her way hither, we soon got a surgeon that sett it very well again, so that we hope she may come hither in a fortnights time, I have written a Catalogue of books on the other side which Sir W. desires you to buy at Auctions, or as you can get them for his friend the minister,†4 that has taken care of his business in his absence, but he referrs it wholely to your judgement, knowing no more of the books then he can learn out of the printed Catalogue,†5 so that you need not send any that you do not approve of, but Sir
― 65 ―

W. will write a postscript overleaf, and I make an end of troubling you here by assuring that I am unalterably
Your affectionate humble servant
R.D.

[Yonge:]
Dear Sir
I can not let a letter goe from Escott to you without a line or two under my hand, tho it be only to assure you of my best Respects,
― 67 ―

and that I am not the least passionate of all your friends in desiring your good company in the Row, but you are the best judge when to give us a visit; Only I can not forbear owning the satisfaction I should take in being restored to a conversation I value at the highest rate, and could not quitt without the greatest Regrett; The unhappy cause of my leaving the place where I last enjoyed that pleasure, continues still to take up all most all my time, I mean the dissordered state of my Affaires, which I fear will not be easily settled to my satisfaction, so that tis wholly uncertain when I shall adventure to quitt my Apartment here, though I must acknowledge your Gelinots†1 to be very inviting; All I can doe at present is to resolve to settle my business as well as I can before the holy daies which I purpose to spend in London, and there at leisure to take my measures for the future, which I should doe with greater satisfaction if you were with me, tho I should never perswade you to spend much time in that sink of sin and sea coale, when the Air of the Row is so much more pleasant and wholesome. As for the Catalogue of books on the other side I got the Parson to draw it up having a design to present him to the value of 20. or 30. crowns in books for the service he has done me in my business, and if you dissapprove of these or think any others better upon those subjects, pray buy only such as you like, only let there be some upon each subject, you may buy them at leisure and at the best hand, and send them hereafter with any books you buy for me, and I will return you the whole money with abundance of thanks as soon as I know what you lay out. I am called upon to conclude, so can only add our Services to all our friends at Utrecht, and that I am without Reserve
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate friend and humble Servant
WALTER YONGE
Address: For Mr John Lock at Utrecht.

877. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 14/24 November [1686] (868, 879)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 255k. Printed in Ollion, p. 169. Year from van Limborch's note and the contents. Locke puns on the word 'Te': see p. 70 n. and the poem.
(English) 
Ultrajecti 14/24 Nov:†a
Tu me jure accusare de Te potes (Amicorum Jucundissime) quod cum priores tuas literas a Te optimè conspersas conditasque acceperim nihil toto hoc tempore reposuerim. Credas, si velis, me sorbillando occupatum sermonibus non vacasse, Quicquid enim Te sapit pitissando,†1 qui diuturnior sit voluptas, degustandum Te enim frui vellem non absumere. Mihi sane maxime gratulor quod Te Virgilio et Horatio non ignotum ad nostra tempora servavit fatorum benignitas, quem igitur opto per longos annos incolumem ut Te habeam studiorum incitamentum, curarum solatium, et vitæ oblectamentum. Fac solum ut Te quantum possibile est possideam. Amicam tuam Te a Virgilio decantatam†2 cautè et Verecundè apud me habeo, unico meo populari viro ingenuo spectandam permisi,
― 69 ―

ejus copiam sibi fieri valde concupiscebat. respondi hoc non licere sine patris permissu: Quod si ea concederetur venia, ad ipsum forsan in Angliam (qua†a jam decessit) transfretaret aliquando.†1 Interim non est quod metuas tetricos illos qui Catonis nihil habent præter censuram, lusus tuos meas delicias mihimet servo, ut illis, epistolisque tuis suavissimis amicissimisque delinire aliquatenus possim tui desiderium. præsta igitur quæso quod videris minari, ut literæ Anglicanæ ad me semper veniant cum hujusmodi auctario, acceptiores inde erunt. imo vero ita invertes rerum ordinem, efficiesque ut pluris sit involucrum quam ipsa merx. Collegium in quo tam jucunda tam subtilia tam proficua et solida semper reperi mihi abreptum doleo. Sed audi vir humanissime quando ita in laudes et encomia prorumpere sit animus†b fac in posterum ut de te non de me instituatur sermo. Judæum sub prælo sudare gaudeo,†2 sed credo plus sudabit quando prælum in apertum aerem illum emiserit, nec facile reperiet in suâ metaphysicâ refrigerium. Alia me hactenus impedierunt quo minus votis tuis respondi sed non obliviscor vel
― 70 ―

monitorum vel beneficiorum tuorum, nam si Ciceronis verbis uti liceat Te plurimum amamus
J L
Tua<m>†a Tuos meosque quæso nomine meo salutes
(Latin) 
Utrecht 14/24 Nov:
You may justly accuse me on your own account, my most delightful of friends, seeing that since receiving your previous letter, so well ornamented and seasoned, I have been all this time without replying. Please believe that I have been so busy sipping it that I have had no time for conversation; for whatever smacks of you must be sampled in wine-taster's fashion,†1 to make the pleasure last longer; I want to enjoy you, not to gulp you down. I call myself lucky indeed that you, who are no stranger to Virgil and Horace, have been preserved to our times by the kindness of the Fates, and I therefore hope you may remain safe and sound for long years to come, for me to have you as the encouragement of my studies, the solace of my cares, and the delight of my life. Only see to it that I may possess you as much as possible. Your Mistress Tea, sung by Virgil,†2 I am keeping by me with due caution and attention to modesty; I have allowed her to be seen by only one [p. 69] gentleman, a countryman of mine; he was very desirous of being granted her favours; I told him that this could not be allowed without her father's permission, but that if this were given she might perhaps some day cross the sea to him in England, whither he has now departed.†1 Meanwhile you have no reason to fear those crabbed folk who have nothing of Cato in them but his gift for censure; I am keeping by me those delightful jeux d'esprit of yours, that with them and your most charming and friendly letters I may to some extent alleviate my longing to see you. I therefore beg you to do what you seem to threaten, to ensure, that is, that my English letters always reach me with this sort of supplement; they will then be all the more welcome; indeed you will so be inverting the order of things and making the wrapping more valuable than the actual wares. As for the Collegie, in which I have always found such delightful, such subtle, such profitable and solid converse, I grieve to be deprived of it. But listen, most obliging Sir: when you are moved to break out thus into laudations and encomia, see to it in future that the subject of discourse be yourself and not myself. I am glad that the Jew is sweating in the press,†2 but I fancy he will sweat even more freely when the press releases him into the open air, and that he will not easily find any cooling relief in his metaphysic. Other things have so far hindered me from meeting your wishes; [p. 70] but I am not forgetful of either your advice or your kind actions; for, if I may use Cicero's words, you are my most loved friend.
J.L.
Please remember me to your wife and family.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch by de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsars Gracht tot Amsterdam
Van Limborch's poem.
The numbers, etc., in angle brackets inserted in the margins are correct references where those in the manuscript are wrong, or are supplied where references are lacking. For Æneid i the writer follows an old text, which has four lines ('Ille ego qui quondam ...') preceding the opening 'Arma virumque cano'; the citations for this book are consequently higher by four than those found in modern texts.
The word cento means primarily a piece of patchwork, such as a quilt or garment; it is applied to poems composed of pieces taken from the works of other poets and relating to subjects other than theirs. Centos came into favour in late antiquity. Ausonius, who, at the emperor's command, had composed an epithalamium from the works of Virgil, and who was ashamed of having done so, sets out the requirements: a line should consist of two halves drawn from different lines in the source; a whole line and the succeeding half-line in the source is admissible, the second line being completed from a different line; to use two complete successive lines would be poor. The life of Christ was a favourite subject from Proba in the late fourth century onwards. Virgil, a heathen and sometimes obscene, was to be made a Christian. The leading English centonist is Alexander Ross (D.N.B.), who published Virgilius evangelisans in 1634 and a new version, Virgilii evangelisantis Christiados libri XII in 1638 (the Christus triumphans, Rotterdam, 1661 (L.L., no. 2502a) may be a third version). The cento could be used also for satires and occasional poems. For serious scholars it was a jeu d'esprit, the amusement arising from the contrast between recognized quotations and their application. The macaronic use of the word 'Te' in the present cento is exceptional: Philobiblon Soc., Miscellanies, vols. x-xi (1866-8), a full account by J. O. Delepierre, with catalogue and specimens.

Deare Freind
I had sooner answered your 2 letters if my seasure or Musidores stay in the country had permitted me to goe into Buckingham sheire whither I shall goe with him from this towne. I will looke after the coppy of Carolina Laws†1 if that I have be not what you meane and obey your directions therein. I have a kinsman who entends to goe to Carolina this summer with about 30 more. [Clarke:]
London November 25th. 1686.
Deare Sir
Soon after the writeing of my last of the 5th. instant to you, my Wife and your Little Mistris were seised upon with violent Colds, and before they were perfectly Recovered, my Eldest Son fell ill of a violent Feaver, which in 3. or 4. dayes time, (Notwithstanding all the Indeavours of Doctor Sydenham and Doctor Goodall to the contrary)†a gott soe into his head that Hee has layne ever since, (this being now the 13th. day since Hee was taken ill)†a in a Doz'd†2 and sleepy condition, and hath taken nothing but of theire Prescribeing, and is now reduc'd to a verie greate degree of weakenesse without the least appeareance of amendment, and what the Event will bee God only Knows; I have these two last dayes taken Doctor Thomas, being newly come to Town, allsoe into the Consultation with the other two, and heartily wish it were possible for mee to have your Assistance, but since that cannot bee, I shall acquiess in what they doe, and pray God to give a Blessing to theire indeavours, and restore the Child to his former health and understanding:†3 This is
― 75 ―

the only Reason that your Letter of the 25th. instant (which I received 5. dayes since) was not sooner answered, and this must bee my Wifes Excuse allsoe for not answering that obleigeing Letter of yours wherewith you Wellcom'd Her to the Town, shee being in truth at this time under a greate Concern: I will carefully imbrace all opportunityes of performeing every part of your Letter of the 25th., but am a little unwilling to remove those minutes of œconomy and husbandry†1 that you mention into the Square-Box without your further order, in regard I thinke they lye as safe and dry in the place where they now are, and for the second Booke of Velthusius in quarto.†2 I must bee forc'd to unpack and looke over all your Bookes (which are now putt up togather in a Narrow compasse) to find it out and dispose of it as you direct, however, if upon further thoughts you will have it look'd out and dispos'd of togather with the minutes of Œconomy Husbandry in such manner as is directed in that Letter, it shall bee done accordingly, These and all the rest of your Cosens things that were removed to and from St. Jones's†3 are plac'd under the Custody of Mrs. R: S:,†4 who gives her hearty service to you, in a House that Her sister and shee have taken neere theire former Lodgings, and are like to remaine there with Her as her owne Goods, untill you order mee otherwise to dispose of them, They are noe manner of inconvenience or trouble to the Lady or the House, and I beleive will continue as safe there as any where in the Towne, The Discourse de Intellectu I Brought to Town with mee that it might bee in a readinesse to bee disposed of as you should direct, which with mine and my Wifes Reall Love and service concludes this from†a

879. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 2/12 December [1686] (877, 905)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R. K., Ba 255l. Printed in Ollion, p. 170. Year from van Limborch's note. Probably written in Rotterdam: Locke enters information from residents there in his Journal, 9, 20, and 21 December.
(English) 
12 Dec.†a
De Tuâ (Vir Optime) et reliquorum apud vos amicorum benevolentiâ minimè dubito toties expertus. De expulsione†1 quod audivisti nec ita intelligo, nec aliquid dictum velim quamvis fortasse commodum erit ad vos iterum accedere. Hujusmodi sedis mutatio fateor aliquantulum incommoda est propter impedimenta. libros volo, quibus locum non adeo facile est reperire: Si alibi non reperio, rogo ut ignoscas si ad te mitto, ut in ædibus tuis in cænaculo vel alio quovis angulo requiescant, donec locum commodiorem invenero. Hoc unicum est quod me male habet, <quia>†b amicis molestiam creat: Quod reliquum est me non movet. Hi sunt
― 77 ―

fortunæ lusus, vel potiùs vitæ humanæ casus ordinarii nec magis quam ventus vel pluvia itinerantibus mirandi. Sed de his pluribus coram. propediem enim te invisam. Et quid tum factu opus est videbimus. Interim rogo ut de hospitio cogites et de hoc cum duobus amicis Doctoribus vicinis tuis†1 agas, Sed cavendum ne quid vel cogitetur vel dicatur de expulsione. Ita enim rem vulgari minime vellem; Optimos illos viros meo nomine salutes et Tuam et eorum lectissimas fæminas. Vale (Amicorum sincerissime) et me ut facis ama
Tui amantissimum
J L
Si quæ ad manus tuas pervenerint mihi destinatæ literæ retineas apud te donec venero
(Latin) 
12 Dec.
Of your own benevolence, O best of men, and of that of the rest of my friends in your circle I have not the smallest doubt, having so often experienced it. As to what you have heard about expulsion,†1 I neither understand the matter so nor should I wish a word to be said about it, although it will perhaps be convenient for me to join you all once more. Changing one's abode in this fashion is, I confess, somewhat inconvenient on account of the business with one's luggage. I want my books, for which it is not easy to find a place; if I fail to do so elsewhere please forgive me if I send them to you, so that they may repose in some attic or other corner of your house until I find a more convenient place. This is the one thing that distresses me, as it gives trouble to friends; the rest does not move me. These things are fortune's sport with us, [p. 77] or rather the ordinary accidents of human life, no more occasions for wonder than wind or rain for wayfarers. But more of these things when we meet; for I shall visit you shortly, and we will then see about what should be done. Meanwhile please consider the question of a lodging, and discuss the matter with our two friends the Doctors, your neighbours.†1 But take care that nothing is thought or said about expulsion; I should be most unwilling for such a description of the matter to get abroad. Please remember me to those good friends, as also to your excellent wife and to theirs. Good-bye, my most sincere friend, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J. L.
If any letters addressed to me have reached you please keep them by you till I come.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch by de Remonstranse Kirck op de Keÿsars Gracht tot Amsterdam
Postmark: Amsterdam (?).
