881. Locke to Edward Clarke, 7/17 December 1686 (880, 885)
Rand, pp. 175-7. 'This letter is in a very bad condition.' Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The transcription is unreliable. Answers no. 878.
17th Dec. 1686.
Dear Sir,
... [A desire to be] with you has been since the receipt of your last, which brought me the ill news of your son's dangerous sickness. Not that I think I could if I were present add anything to the prescriptions of those learned men you have consulted in his case, and are those very physicians to whom were I sick I should trust my life before any other that I know in the world. But yet I am troubled to be away from you in an occasion like this, wherein what I wanted in skill I might perhaps make up in diligence and some other offices of friendship, which in the state and concern I consider you and your Lady in might perhaps not be out of season. But instead of being at hand to [give] support or any way ease you, as I desire, I am in condition only to beg help from you. I am in great uneasiness ever since I received your letter two days since, and shall not be easy till
― 79 ―

I hear again from you. In the meantime I know not what to say, for I conclude before this comes to your hand the child's disease will be some way or other concluded. That it may be according to your and my desire in that of health and recovery [I shall] add the same earnestness of prayers and wishes that I would for my own, which I do with a concern as great as can be inspired from friendship, or anything else, but the great and unknown tenderness of natural affection. But whatever be the event, and how well soever the object deserves it, yet have a care it prevail not too powerfully upon you. Consider what reason was given you for, and that that, and religion, are of [value only if] they are to be consulted and hearkened to at such times as this when we have need of their counsels.
... If this find the child recovered, I then say nothing more to you concerning the things mentioned [to be put] into the square box, than that it would be a great satisfaction to me were it done. But if (which God forbid) this find you under sad thoughts for a loss which has no remedy, I then challenge the performance of your promised kindness to have it done, and that without delay, upon the receipt of this letter.... If you are angry with me on this occasion I shall not be much displeased. [If you] will have the truth of [the matter], I had rather you should have any occupation or any business to take up your thoughts, than those sad and melancholy ones I know you will be too forward to resign yourself wholly to, if this affliction should befall you....
The fourth and last book of De Intellectu Humano is now growing into some form, and then that will be sent or brought you; and then it will be in somewhat tolerable condition to be shown some friends and see wherein there be anything in it new or better than what [has appeared] in print in that respect, and so have their opinion upon it, or what is to be further done with it. In the meantime I could be glad you had as much leisure as to let me have yours.
The place where my cousin's things†1 are [such], that I leave it to you to consider, whether the trunk of deeds in Round Court were best to be removed thither, or that you should take them into the country, or be left where they are. Though I think very well of the care and honesty of the man with whom they are, and have no apprehension, but upon mortality, or fire, therefore pray dispose of them as you would of your own.
― 80 ―

If my noble friend†1 be in town, do me the favour to present to him my service....
I am most faithfully yours,
J. L.
Address: For Mr. Edward Clarke at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, London.
882. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, [7 December 1686?] (870, 896)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 136-7. The year from Locke's endorsement. The month as given by Lady Masham appears to be wrong: this letter and no. 870 can scarcely have been written within two days of one another. Further, this letter appears to have been written from the country; on 7 October Lady Masham had been absent from Oates for about a fortnight and probably had spent most of the time in Cambridge. In view of the dates of Locke's answers to no. 870, 3/13 November, and to this letter, 19/29 January, and of Lady Masham's statement in no. 930 that the latter might have been written a month sooner, the likeliest date is 7 December 1686.
Oct: the 7th.
Had I really had that Cause of Sorrow you Apprehended when you writ that Letter you afterwards thought needed so Large an Apologie I do Beleeve that notwithstanding the Postscript I should not have beene well Pleas'd with it, but have look'd on you as one who wanted Sensibilitie for the Afflictions of your Friends; Yet being now able to Judge without Any Prepossession I must acknowledge that I do not think I should have had much Reason for it; That you should therefore have beene so Uneasie upon that Score is extreamly Obliging and is no small Argument of the Realitie of that Friendship you Profess, Which if I did Doubt of, The Rareness of it in the World, And my want of Merrit to have Deserv'd it from you, may I think be Grounds Sufficient for my Excuse; Altho I do not Apprehend that this Cartesian Principle†2 ought at All to have offended you, the End sufficiently Justifying the use of it. Upbraid me not Therefore with what I owe you; Ingratitude is a Thing not in my Nature and I beleeve without Vanitie I may say it none better understands then my self the Value of a Sincere Friendship. For the Preference you Pretend to give me over
― 81 ―

your Dutch Mistress, You must Pardon me if not being willing to Question the Truth of what you say I beleeve notwithstanding what you tell me of her Merrit (which you Dare Compare, and I doubt not Justly enough May, with Anie in my Neighborhood) Tis yet more to some Defect in That, then to the Greatness of my Owne, Or Any thing else, that I am Indebted; It being Hard else to Conceive that Friendship should be Able to make its Party Good against Love under so Unequal a Disadvantage as Absence Think not that I would lessen the Obligation I have to You (If you Apprehend no Hazard of makeing me a Desperate Debtor I Know not why I should) But Friendship will have an Advantage not Inconsiderable if she should onelie Triumph over Beautie and Kindness; The first you have told me your Mistress has in a Verie Eminent Degree And the Last I have much Reason to Beleeve. It cannot Therefore be a Conquest too Little for me Altho she may not deserve to make you Hers; which Yet Perhaps you may be more then you your self are Aware, For I cannot Conceive how it is Possible (especially in a Countrey where Agreable Women are but Scarse) that she should Hang Long in that Strange Posture you speake of; If she dos, I am Confident the Fault must be Hers, and I have no disposition to blame you for it; A Mistress is the most Dangerous thing in the World to a Friend, and Therefore she must Pardon me if I cannot be verie much Hers, as I hope you will do too if I speake not of Her with All that Respect which from One Unprejudic'd against her may yet perhaps be her Due, For in spight of what you tell me of my worst Letters giveing you more Pleasure then she Can in Her Best Humour Tis verie Hard for me to beleeve so well either of my self, or your Preference of Friendship, when I Reflect on a Great Beautie on the One Side, And Yeares of Absence on the Other. However tis no small sattisfaction that I can stand my Ground, And the Obligation I have to you is not a little that whatever others have gain'd, I am no Loser; Since methinks Besides your telling me so, I find several Reasons to Perswade me I am still to you the same Person that I was when you could Indure to Pass so many Hours in my Companie; at least that I should be so, if your Health would permit you to see me in that Place you Pretend so much Curiositie for;†1 For I cannot find but that our Opinions of Absence after All are much the same, since you have no Reason from my last or any Thing else to Beleeve my Esteeme for my
― 82 ―

Friends can be Lessend by it; And in your Confessing it a Misfortune, you your self Acknowledge the Pleasure of Haveing Them Is,†aSince else it Could be no Misfortune. Could you find an Expedient to make it less so I should have a great Obligation to you for it But I can think of none, unless instead of Letters, you should write me Volumes. I Thought a good while since you had sent me One you writt Long Ago But I perceiv'd afterwards it was a Mistake. If Anie such thing were made Publick (tho I am now out of the Land of Philosophy) I suppose I should some way or other have known it But something that I had before heard at London gave me Occasion to Misunderstand you and Also to Put me in Paine on that Score for my Friends the Platonists and Cartesians On whose Accounts we have formerly had so manie Quarrels†1 But you will Perhaps, think now tis no longer Pardonable for me (If ever it were so) to Talk of Subjects of That Nature, and that Culpepper†2 and the Countess of Kents Receits†3 afford more Suitable Speculations for a Countrey Lady who has Children and a Familie to look after. Yet if you do, whilst you allow me so large a Share in Your Esteeme, and are so well sattisfy'd the World should Know that you Do So, I shall neither Quarrel with you for it, Or think I want Sufficient Reason to Value my Self; That, Haveing I assure you Always beene a Principle thing upon which I have ever done so; I am therefore so far Worthy of It; As well as with a Just Sense of my Many Obligations to You
Your most real Friend and Servant
PHILOCLEA
Address: To Mr Lock

883. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 10 December 1686 (873, 898)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 7.
Otterton Dec: 10th. 1686
My Dear Friend.
Though my Brother and Mr Duke both undertook to answer the Kind letter you sent me dated Octob: 26th. and I hope gave you a much better entertainment then I could have done, and paid you my Thanks as fully as 'tis possible for me to do; yet you cannot escape so, I must with my own hand acknowledg that Favour, and assure you that it afforded me the greatest satisfaction; for I was impatient to know what was become of you, and when I might hope to see you in England, but you took care not to say one word on that subject as if it had been a point quite out of Doors, no more to be thought off; however pray talk of it in all your letters for the future, there is nothing else which I can hear with so much pleasure; I can live on the hopes of it till the Spring, but I cannot live easily in this uncertainty wherin you keep me, as to the point which so nearly concerns me; take pitty on me, and send me good News on that Subject in your next, which pray hasten, methinks it has been long comming; but one letter in almost three Months, is very hard, upon a Friend that Vallues and loves you in Sincerity. 'tis True, Every one of your letters are enriched with more kindness, and more ingenuity then can be found in a hundred others, but that is not enough for me; I find that the more I have, the more I Covet; though you write incomparably, you must write frequently too, if you will keep me quiet. but I am satisfied that I have no reason to complain of you hitherto, but of my own ill fortune in having lost a letter you mention in your last to my brother concerning Agues, which never came to my hands; I defered this a full Week in hopes that it would come at last, but now I despair of it, and esteem it an irreparable loss; yet I hope you will bestow the same advice, or corrections on me, which that would have brought me; when you next give me an hours Conversation; for I vallue both as I ought, and I hope shall improve by both. and now all the ill effects of my Journey are over, and I am perfectly well; I hope you will pardon the irregularities of it, since I promise to be a most obedient Daughter for the future. Yet give me leave to ask you,
― 84 ―

why you Sing so constantly the Tune of Gelinots;†1 we that are here can see no reasons for it, but I will ever submit to yours, and pull that way which you shall lead and direct. in which I am sure I shall not erre, I durst follow you in every thing, even with an implicite Faith. which I would not any other Docter, or Father in the World. but I have an entyre Confidence in your Wisdom, and your perfect Friendship, which I beg may direct me in all my greatest concerns. 'tis an advantage I expect from your relation to me, you cannot honestly refuse it mee; and I will be sure to claim it in all exigencyes. nothing can be of more consequence to me then my Brothers Welfare, and I know you love him, and are concern'd for it; pray advice as you think necessary, with all imaginary freedom, which shall be answered with all possible Gratitude. I writ the first page of this att Otterton, but was interrupted, and brought it hither to Escott unfinished. where I found my Brother oppressed with cares and businesses to an incredible degree. so that I could not get one word from him the whole day, neither has it been possible for him to find one hour to write to you; but he is resolved to run away from all next Week, though he finds 'tis impossible to compass his matters, and bring his affairs into order, yet he well get to London and recruit a little, from thence you will quickly hear from him, at present he begs your pardon, not being master of one Hour. if this be the Case of men of quality and Estate, I shall alwayes pray I may be happy and poor; I wish our corner of the World afforded any thing that could be an entertainment or diversion to you; but since it does not, I will shew my civillity and kindness to you by hastening to conclude my self
Yours in all sincerity.
ISAB: <Duke>†a

884. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 12/22 December 1686 (862, 910)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 147.
<D>imanche†a ce 22. Decembre 86.
Vous reconnêtrez bien, monsieur, par la date de cete letre que le Triumvirat est rassemblé. Il vous salüe en cors. Le Capitaine de marine a desja des tables Greques et Latines que j'ay fait imprimer,†1 et il s'en sert utilement depuis long tems, aussi bien que plusieurs de mes amis. L'Ocasion de mon retour en Province soit doublement facheuse. L'une etoit pour la maladie de ma mere, et l'autre pour la mienne; et par l'evenement le tout a eté heureux. car ma mere se porte de mieux en mieux, et ma santé se retablit fortement. Je prens un bon augure de l'un et de l'autre pou. avoir la liberté de vous satisfaire harmoniquement à ce printems
Je m'informerai de la racine laquele etant pendüe au col, guerit les ulceres de la bouche,†2 mais vous me dispenserez de le demander à mr Godefroi mon ancien ami, qui nous a quité subitement par une malheureuse apoplexie depuis trois mois. Je le regrete extraordinerement. Il savoit bien des choses, et etoit inventif et communicatif.
A l'egard de la pierre au travers de laquele l'on passe les liqueurs, et les rend insipides, je me souviens que passant à Amboise avec monseigneur†b Le Card. d'Etrees†3 lorsque nous alions en Portugal, mr Borelli qui l'acompagnoit, trouva la une pierre qu'il jugea pouvoir avoir la même vertu; et un de mes amis qui a demeuré long tems à Cadis, m'a dit que lon en trouve de pareilles aux canaries.†4 Si j'etois à Paris, ou il est, je m'en informerois particulierement. Le Mr Borelli qui etoit avec monsieur†c le Card. d'Etrée n'est pas l'Illustre qui est en arrest à Rome, et qui faisoit de la Vierge une quatrième personne de la Trinité. c'est un autre qui est aujourdhui le distillateur de l'Academie.†5
― 86 ―

Ne dites point à mr Westein que je suis en Province s'il ne le scait pas. Scribebam Aurelianis.†1 Donnez moi une adresse à droiture pour vous. mais pour les letres que vous m'ecrirez, il†a- est bon les metre-†a dans le paquet de mr Westein quand il m'ecrira à Paris. Le port en coutera moins. Quand il y aura quelque chose de particulier, que vous craindrez d'etre ouvert en Holande, et qui concernera l'Harmonie.
Il y a etrangement de fautes dans les 16. pages d'essay,†2 mais on les peut corriger presque toutes à la plume. cela me convainc qu'il faut être prezent à l'Impression, et outre cela avoir un bon correcteur. Il y a quelque chose d'assez curieux dans mes notes.

886. Locke to Edward Clarke, 21/31 December 1686 (885, 890)
Rand, pp. 177-8. 'The paper is discoloured and the writing very much faded.' Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand.
31st December, 1686.
Sir,
You have here at length the [four]th and last book of my scattered thoughts concerning the Understanding, and I see now more than ever that I have reason to call them scattered, since never having looked them over all together till since this last part was done, I find the ill effects of writing in patches and at distant times as this whole essay has been. For there are so many repetitions in it, and so many things still misplaced, that though I venture it confused as it is to your friendship, yet I cannot think these papers in a condition to be showed anyone else, till by another review†4 I have reduced them into yet better order. Though bateing that, and the negligence of the style, you will find very little in the argument itself, that I think for the matter of it needs altering. Of what use it may be to any other I cannot tell, but, if I flatter not myself, it has been of great help to [our first enquiry], and the search of knowledge ever since has been in my thoughts, which is now five
― 89 ―

or six years.†1 For so long ago is it since some friends upon an accidental discourse [started me] upon this enquiry, which I am not sorry for. And if it has cost me some pains in thinking, it has rewarded me by the light I imagine I have received from it, as well as by the pleasure of discovering certain truths, which to me at least were new. For being resolved to examine Humane Understanding, and the ways of our knowledge, not by others' opinions, but by what I could from my own observations collect myself, I have purposely avoided the reading of all books that treated any way of the subject, that so I might have nothing to bias me any way, but might leave my thought free to entertain only what the matter itself suggested to my meditations. So that, if they at any time jump with others, 'twas not that I followed them; and if they differ 'twas not out of contradiction, or a mind to be singular. My aim has been only truth so far as my shortsightedness could reach it, and where I have misstated it in part or in the whole I shall be glad to be set right. Read it, therefore, as a friend's act, judge of it as a stranger's, and let me have your opinion with ... the greatest freedom, than which there can be nothing more obliging to
your most humble servant,
J. L.
31st Dec. 1686.

Dear Sir
I blush to think it is a full fortnight that I have been arrived here and have not in all this time paid my Duty to you in a Letter of thanks for the obligations you laid on me and the friendship you honourd me with when I had the happiness to be with you abroad. I could make some excuses for my silence but had rather rely on your goodness and from thence hope a pardon and promise my self you will not immagine that I could be guilty of ingratitude or neglect towards you whose good opinion and kindness make a great part of what I esteem my happiness. I have examined the matter I promised you and find the enquiry was made (as I supposed)
― 90 ―

and the matter answerd, and found as you and I could have desired and much to the honour and advantage of our friend†1 which I was very glad to hear. I expect Sir W. in Town next week and hear all his Relations and our friends in Devon are well which I'm sure will be wellcome news to you as it was when it was received this night by
Sir
Your obliged friend and humble servant

889. James Tyrrell to Locke, 26 December [1686] (842, 911)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 54-5. Year from Locke's endorsement. Answered by no. 911.
London Decem. 26.
Dear C.
I have long agoe returned you an answere to your last short letter, and presently after I orderd to be conveyed to you by the hands of Mr: A. C.†3 the bookes I mention'd; which I hope you have received before this time; and haveing bin now in this Towne all most this month I cannot well leave it without giveing you some account of the performance of your last orders as to uncle A.†4 who has bin with me, and†a- taken what bookes he desired, and amongst the rest your Philosophicall transactions, and history of the royall society-†a;†5 as I should have ventured without your expresse order to have let him have had what bookes he had pleased: since I know both his honesty, and your kindnesse to your Friends: as for that money I owe you; if you can doe me the kindnesse to forbear it till towards Midsummer, and then take it as I received it at 2, or three payments you will adde to those many obligations, I
― 92 ―

must still owne to you; for the truth of it is, that buying a new coach, and horses; with my wives goeing to the Bathe; for her health, and the unexpected sicknesse of my children, and Family have bin near 100l̷. out of my way this year. but yet if you please to command this 30l̷. I owe you all at once; and that at our Lady day; I doubt not but my credite and will are sufficient to take it up, rather then your occasions should suffer in the least there, since I know not how things goe with you where you are. therefore pray deal freely with me in your next: and allso let me know whether I shall send you any new bookes out of England, and what, in exchange for those you have sent me: I suppose you have seen Burnets new Theory of the Earth in latine; I should be glad to know whether you have seen it allso in English;†1 which is accounted much more Ingenious then the latine as haveing many new thoughts in it: if you think fit, I will send it you; and should be glad to receive your Judgment of it; this being a sort of correspondence which will not be dangerous: Dr: Sydenhams workes are all come out together with divers new additions,†2 and if you please I will send you that likewise: un: A. tells me you have transmitted your papers de Intellectu to your noble Friend:†3 I am glad they are in so good a hand: and I hope you will give him leave to make them publick; I could wish you would send for your papers in the red trunk which wee writ together; and out of them perfect your intended discourse concerneing Toleration, and Persecution,†4 which I'le assure you will be no ungrate subject to any party but one at this time; for I know none but the P.†5 of all partyes that can be offended at it: and of them most confesse the thing in Theory, tho' they deny it in practice. ― 93 ―

lately come out very good Phil: transactions if you command A. or I.†a †1 wee will make up your set. I have no more but wishing you <a>ll†b health this winter; and that the spring may inspire you with fr<esh>†b and more vigourous resolutions of returne to Old Eng: so hopeing to hear from you I am yours
M.

890. Locke to Edward Clarke, 31 December 1686/10 January 1687 (886, 891, 894)
Rand, pp. 179-80. Words in square brackets supplied by Rand. For Locke's preparatory notes see p. 88. Answered by no. 900.
Amsterdam, 10th Jan. 1687.
Dear Sir,
If the person answer the character you have received of him you will in the enclosed find news of a tutor for your son.†7 That which
― 94 ―

gives me great hopes he is such an one as you seek is the great opinion I have of the ingenuity and judgment of Monsieur le Clerc, who recommended him to me and has writ the enclosed to him. His study and design was divinity; but before he was called to the ministry the new conversion in France drove him from thence, and therewith made him leave the thoughts of being a divine, which in his present state must be forced to some other way of subsistence.†1 He tells me he is sober, discrete, and well natured, and well skilled in the politer parts of learning, without being infected with the pedantry of scholarship, and that he will be ready to follow any method of education shall be presented to him. If this be so we have the man we would, and by the influence of Monsieur le Clerc, his friend, and your namesake, we shall be able to manage him exactly to our design. But whatever character I upon report send you of him, it is but to encourage you to find him out, but not to hinder you from informing yourself of him with all the nicety imaginable; and there may possibly be this convenience, now you are in London, to have him some time with you in the house upon trial before you take him into the country. By such a trial you may see without the hazard of much experience, or a perfect engagement, [whether the] employment and conditions [are agreeable] and satisfy both sides. If he be not in London, Monsieur Cappel†2 can tell where he is, and will send to him, especially if you tell him your business and that the enclosed is from Monsieur le Clerc. When you go to speak with him, I think it convenient you should have with you a friend who can speak French, and is well instructed in the general plan of your design in the breeding of your son. Or at least by the interpreter you take with you Mr. Pepin may be informed, that your chief aim is to have the mind of your son formed to virtue and civility by all the sweet ways of allurements, persuasion and example; and that languages and letters are valued by you no otherwise than as they may be subservient to make your son the better, and the wiser, and fitter for civil conversation, and the employments of a gentleman; and that the age he now is in is the true time to teach him the mastery of his passions, wherein lies the great secret of wisdom and happiness in this life.
Pardon me that I prescribe to you so confidently in a matter which you understand more fully and can manage better than
― 95 ―

<one>†a that knows not what it is to have care and to deal with children. But for all that, my head and heart are both so set on this matter of the breeding of your son, that whenever that comes in my way, I cannot hold saying much more than I need, though it be always much less than what I think upon that subject, with you whose kindness interprets my actions as they are meant. My concern in the case will bear an excuse for my impertinence. The news of this tutor falling in so happily with [that] of his recovery flatters me with appearance of success, and makes me hope that the difficulty and dangerous passage of his health being now over, his stars are smoothing the way to all that may advantage his mind or body; my hearty prayers and wishes are that it may be so.
I answered yours of the 14th Dec. (which is the last I have from you) this week, and therein sent an inclosure to the young gentleman you writ about.†1 Pray present my humble service to Madame and the little ones. I wish them and you a very happy new year, with many more to come. I am,
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate humble servant,
J. L.
My service to our Tunbridge friends,†2 as many of them as are in town, and all the rest that think me worth the enquiring after. Pray tell Mr. Awnsham Churchill, the bookseller, as you pass by Amen Corner, that I have received Mr. Boyle's Book of Nature†3 and the other that he sent with it, for which I thank him.
Address: For Mr Edward Clarke, Esq., at Lady King's in Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, London.
― 96 ―

892. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 31 December 1686 (820, 1006)

Now deare Brother we are good friends againe lets make the best of that distance which cannot I veryly beleeve be prudently avoided and whilst its in our power not grudge each other such a commerce as becomes persons who have the same hopes, and feares,
― 97 ―

I am glad the Air you are in proves so kind to you. May it allwayes doe so whatever becomes of us hear, to sweeten all that lookes harsh abroad God has most tenderly fix'd me in the best and most friendly harbour this Isle afords, where could you but have a short view of the blessings I enjoy you would think as I doe that Providence has bin most signally tender of me and my Orphant, my Ghostly father†1 is such a man as you could not chuse but reverance did you know his progress and his christian resolution how much he is above all temptation to betray the peace of his conscience, how tender of his charge and obliging to all his inferiour brethren, and how much all for whome you have the highest value doe find themselves happy in the wise and good conduct of one they did some yeares past imperfictly know. Having given you this short image of a person whose Genious you will I doubt not be better acquainted with in a short time, I cannot denie you the plesure of letting you know that my son is as happyly provided for in Cambridg as his mother is in London we both seeme to be disposs'd of for others benifit as well as our own my youngster having all the advantages his age is capable of with less charge to me than I ever expected, and myself I have many opportunities alowed me to doe kind things without being involved in any worldly care or business and to make my being hear sound as well abroad as it is acceptable at home I have the friendship of a venerable Mother who uses me as mrs Foxcraft†2 and mrs Mary Colet†3 us'd to doe who is not a little pleas'd that she sees her only granddaughter the Bishopes only child in my care a fine child who by right must be a very considerable fortune but whose father dotes on no other greatness for her but that of having her truely good, this little damosel is given to me with so much respect and civility that I take the same method with her as if she were realy my own and my boy being grown allmost a man have I not don well to change him for a Girle. All my circumstances being realy beyond what you can fancy I can see nothing that looks alluring in other Palaces nor will I exchange my station for any preferment but that of a greater retirement for to be two much Esteem'd vissited or obliged to wander abroad is more dangerous than to be more a solitary where heaven and a mortified
― 98 ―

neighbour or to may wholy take up my thoughts, for to be forced from all the ease and plenty of this world into some melancholy straights will starle†1 human Nature tiriblie when from a scene of lower enjoyments we may encounter divers callamities with a nobler courage, this I speak as aprehensive of my own frailty, whilst I hear and behold what is greater than all the grandure of the world men wholy resign'd to the Will and Service of God.
Tis now time to assure you that all in Thames street†2 are as they ever were very good and kind, as for our distant relations†3I hear seldom from them, one reason may be my own Lazyness that will not suffer me to write to any that are near and may otherwayes hear of me then by my own writting, for though I haunt you and one more in Spaine†4 I am very much in debt to all the world besides and if you doe not reconcile me to the use of my pen I shall quite discard it. I desposs'd of your services as you would have me but none receaved it more respectfully than my good Lord who assures you of his service. the last day of the year 1686
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke
Endorsed by Locke: A G 31 Dec. 86 Answered 13 Jun.
893. Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 31 December 1686 (876, 902)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 148-9.
London December 31th. 1686.
Dear Sir
I have at length (thanks to my starrs) broke up, though my Task masters used me more rigidly then any of our country pedagogs doe their pupills, for the schooleboy's have some a fortnight some a week allowed them before the holy-daies, whereas I could recover but just two daies time to bring me to Ivy-ch:†5 to eat plum-broth and minced pye on Christmass-day; I then began to breath with more freedome, and amongst other thoughts that crowded upon me in that state of liberty, the sense of my Obligations
― 99 ―

to you was most urgent, and I applyed my selfe with great pleasure to doe you all the Right I could there by drinking your health frequently with your friends, and wishing you with us; And now I come to make you the best satisfaction I can for my long silence, a fault which is not a little aggravated by the confidence you were pleased to have that I would not thus neglect you; I confess business and building and planting and accounts and a thousand other torments I have undergone are no excuse for not writing to you (though perhaps whatever I had sent you would have savoured too much of the confusion I was in to merit your acceptance) and therefore if confession submission and the Apology my sister made for me†1 may not obtain my pardon, I shall wait to know what pennance you will impose upon me; only I beg you will not punish me in kind, by discontinuing your correspondence, which would be to deprive me of what I value at the highest rate, a severity no way agreable to your generous character, which makes me confident you will soon send me a pardon under your hand. In the next place give me leave to thank you for minding me of your Gelinots, and the many advantages of the Air you breath in. Learning, beauty, and pleasure are some of them great Temptations to a man of my complexion, and may well be thought to outweigh the entertainments of building and other country diversions; But there are some indispensible duty's a man owes his family, which must not be neglected, and my Affaires have been so disorder'd that 'twill require time to put them into good hands; besides I have some daughters†2 of yours upon my hands, which must be taken care of, and I wait to see the effect of a motion or two has lately been made me for them. So that in all probability I must content my selfe this year with Tunbridge instead of Spaw-waters; and I can not but flatter my selfe (from what I have learnt since I came to Town) that you will be so kind as to come and tiple with us on this side of the water; if you have any such good inclinations about you pray cherish them, and hasten to us as soon as your Affairs will give leave, you know some of your friends will want you to prepare their bodies for the cold waters, and the fatt gentlemans†3 constitution requires a long course, so that t'will be charity to allow him what time you can for preparation; besides about two months hence I must return to the builders to give them new
― 100 ―

orders for the†a summer's work, and particularly about the gardens and Library (your Province) wherein I would not willingly make a step without your advice; so that t'would be truly obliging in you to come over in the mean time and accompany me into the Country. And now I have mentioned my Library it minds me to explain my Request to you for the furnishing me with some books from thence, My intention is not to make a large collection of book to furnish my study (which is tolerably well supplyed already) the expense whereof will not so well suit with a builder; only I desire you would as it comes in your way pick up any books of great curiosity (such as Berniers travells,†1 Bossu du poeme Epique,†2 Xaviers new Gospell,†3 or the history of the Yncas of Peru,†4 which you recommended) and any other books which you judge may <be>†b of good advantage for my own reading (and amongst others Abbadée de la Verité de la Religion Chrêtienne)†5 in which you may be pleased to lay out to the value of 10. 15. or twenty pounds if you see cause; And as for the Parson's books since those he mention'd are not such as he took them for, I would only desire you to consider whether you can not find out some very good authors upon the subjects he is inquisitive after, particularly he would have a good Treatise of Ecclesiasticall History in Latin (being not frenchman enough to read my Sueur)†6 and some curious author that has made new discoveries in Anatomy, or any famous new Treatise in Divinity all latin; If you meet with any books of this kind that are curious pray lay out five or six pounds in them, for I am desirous to make him a present in books of about that value for the service he rendered me in my absence in having an eye upon my Affaires in the country. and I know no body whose Judgement I can relye upon to find out books fit to present him, but yourselfe. Be pleased
― 101 ―

to pardon this great freedome I use with you, and call upon Mr Furly for what money you shall lay out on my Account (I will write to him by this post to supply you with as much as you shall need) and beleive me to be unalterably
Your most faithfull friend and affectionate Servant
WALTER YONGE
Mr Freke gives you his humble service.
What books you buy for me you may send in a box with Maurier's memoirs†1 and such other books as I left with Mr Furly which pass the custome-house. Direct the box to be left with Mr Thomas Moor at Topsham, and let B.F. send it by one of our Topsham Skippers which he knows.
Address: For Mr John Lock at Utrecht.
Endorsed by Locke: Sir W: Yonge 31 Dec. 86 Answered 17 Jan. 87 enquiry about lime trees.

895. William Stratton to Locke, 13 January 1687 (848, 922)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 25. Forwarded by Clarke with no. 900.
Sutton the 13th. Jan 1686/7
Deare Cosin
I Received yours. Dated the 27th July and cannot return you An Answer by the same hand that brought yours, and by Reson of the decease of my Father Locke†1 whoe departed this life the 14th day of Desem I have not written soe sone as I shold, for I have beane under troble and have lost A worthy father and a most Emynent servant of god, I did aprehend a great los when ever god shold take him away but now I find it very great and likewise the Church of god on erth have a very great los in a faithfull member
As for Robert Horoll he is a very Idle fellow but Esquire Clarke have drawn a Wrighting that he hath made over all that he hath for securyty and I had 3 Cows at 10l̷ and he made over his horses for 10l̷ more whearof I have received 6l̷ and doe suppose I shall have the other 4l̷ shortly the reekes of hay being seven are attached and I have sould one and the winter lease which will amount to about 7l̷: when I have Rec the 4l̷ thear will be dew to you 37l̷ onely sum payments to be taken out, all that we have for securyty will be 7 hayreekes and all his goods besids and allsoe his 3 horses will be liable again to helpe pay the debt I will never trust him more unles I knew he was becum a new man and if hay shold be a cummodyty in any short time I hope the los will not be soe great as I did dout it would I shall quicken him till I hope to get good part of the mony but theare must be time
I have let the Estate to David Horoll and he keeps Cows and he lets Robert have part David is a very Just fellow If I mistake not and suffisient withall, for he bought his brothers Cows and payed redy mony and he hath bought Ould Down for his life and his wifes
― 103 ―

and a girells life besids I suppose he and his wife makes upward of a 100 years he is to give 28l̷ and 2s and 6d lords Rent I have heare inclosed sent the lease desireing you to seale it he is to pay halfe in hand and Make over the same for securyty till he pay the other part which i thinke is six munthes I have not the agrement at home at this writeing. he intends to pay more then the agrement in hand I accepted of this becawes Esquire Clarke would have accepted of it of Thomas Veale but he came not when he was Appoynted and is since dead
The widdow Shatter is very shatter witted now shee would have floryes life chainged and two added for 15l̷-10s- which was not my agrement with her and soe I shall say littell to her, flory was liveing lately for I was at london lately and spake with his wife and I found by her that he was at see and the land was two hot by reson of his debts and that he was in one of the Kings ships soe that I now doe not question but he was liveing Althou theare wa talke of his deth before I went for London I let your estate to david Horoll for but one year hopeing to see you heare next year
according to your order I paid 20s to my Father Locke whoe disposed of it to my Aunt Bonvills Children†1 Joane Morris was Decest a littell before I Received your letter my Wife presents her humble servis to you
I take leave your Faithfull Kinsman and humble ser
WILLIAM STRATTON

896. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 17 January [1687] (882, 930)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 140-1. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Whether or no it be longer then Ordinarie since I heard from you I cannot tell But it seemes to me a great while; I am in a Humour at Present that would not give me so much sattisfaction in Any
― 104 ―

thing as in the Assurance of the Remembrance of some for whom I have no Common Esteeme And the next Pleasure that I can find to That is to let Them see that they have mine. You must Pardon therefore to that Cause the Interruption that this may give you from some better imployment then the Reading my Impertinences
My Letters are Always such at the Best but I have Reason to think that this will be more then ordinarilie so since the Spirrit which Dictates it is a very Unreasonable One. I am at a loss Alreadie to Know what to Say and yet I cannot Perswade my self to give over the designe of Writeing you a Letter To what Purpose should you know that I am in an Ill Humor (since in short that is the thing which I would tell you) when perhaps before This comes to you I may be Return'd to a good One Or if I be not tis not in your Power to help it? Yet Could I certainlie tell <at>†a what Moment you received This it would at that verie time I fancie, bring your Idea so livelie into my Mind when you were wont to Chide me out of Vaine troubles that I verylie think it would have almost the same effect as if you your self were Present But this Cannot be and therefore I must be Content to waite till a Better Temper dos of its self or assisted by some other Happy Accident take Place and Dispell those Clouds of Melancholy that Represent everie thing either as Sad and Displeaseing, or at best Emptie and Insipid; and Onelie serve to Obscure the Light of Reason, and All good Understanding
Were I ever Capable of Philosophizing I beleeve I might find some Solid Argument now against Materialists since I clearlie perceive in my self that a Disturb'd Mind and Disorder'd Body such as will not permit the free Exercise of Reason in Any thing else besides, dos the more Indispose to those Spirritual Speculations which sometimes so well serve to beare up the Mind in such a due degree of Tranquilitie as is necessarie Both to the Injoyment of Life and performing the Duties of it as one ought. But I suspect you might not Allow of This whatever I thought; for that Reason therefore I shall not Attempt it, tho I assure you I am in so Dull and Earthy a Dispensation at This time that I am not Capable of Any Discourse of Reason upon anie subject whatsoever Neither do I now Know whether I express what I would say so as to be Intelligible But you have had this Complaint so often from me that I ought to feare wearying you with it, and I should do so did I not think you
― 105 ―

would beleeve I would not make it so often were not the very Complaining its self some releife to the Humor that Causes it, and then I cannot doubt but you will have the Charitie to allow of it. Besides it springing more from Internal then External Causes I should be Assham'd to Discover so much Folly to One that were less my Friend; Not that I esteeme not your Opinion of me more then most Peoples But you better Kno then They how to Value what is Well, and to make Allowances for what is not so. I must therefore tell you How Unreasonable I am; I Fancie sometimes our World Here is Alterd from what it was But I think againe that That is but a Foolish Thought and that I being more Concern'd in it the longer I live may think so onelie for that Reason. Otherwise there surely Always was Abundance of Malicious Ungratefull Censorious People and indeed very few besides; Could you teach me how to regard them no more then so many little Angry Wasps I should have a great obligation to you and methinks it is but a Reasonable Peice of Pride that I should do so; I Beleeve†a I want it not in other things since Besides All This a Thing that is really the most Uneasie to me Almost of Anie thing else, Is, that there are so very Few People that I can Possibly have Any High Esteeme for; Not but that since I have seene you I have had the good fortune to be Knowne to Diverse Whom All the World that can Judge, speake of with Honour, and I have been Oblig'd to them for some Particular marks of Respect and Good Will; But at Present I am onelie Capable of takeing my measures from a Countrey Conversation since the rest is like to signifie very little to me; I am Certainlie Plac'd in the Wretchedest Neighborhood in the whole World and never had so Violent a Desire in my life as now to good Companie. Tis in Vaine that I think (and therefore Pray say nothing of it) of Suiting my Mind to my Condition, for Business and the Impertinent Concernes of a Mistress of a Familie will never have Anie Place in my Heart, and I can at most do no more then submit to Them. I wish I could do otherwise with All my Heart but tis in Vaine to strive against the streame. You will perhaps Advise me to Converse with the Dead since Here are so few Liveing that are Worth it; I am indeed forc'd to do so more then I have of a long time done before But besides that I do not Naturally Love Reading My Eyes will not permit me to do it very much. The most Comfortable thing that you can say to me that I can Think of, is, still
― 106 ―

to Assure me you have some Esteeme for me. That Alone would make me think Life not Altogether Insignificant were there yet fewer things Pleasing in it to me then there Is; and Besides it will Continue in me some Value for my self which as Proud as I sometimes seeme I think I do at Others a little Want.
Did I not send you this Letter immediatelie I Beleeve I should not at All, since I am sensible it is a Horrid Impertinent one, and that at Another time I should be Assham'd of it; You will not (I suppose) think it want of Respect to You that you yet have it after that Thought, But an Argument of the Real Friendship of
PHILOCLEA.
Jan: the 17th.
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 17 Jan. 87 Answered 12 Feb:
897. Locke to Edward Clarke, [11/21?] and 18/28 January 1687 (894, 900)
Rand, pp. 184-8. 'The manuscript is dropping to pieces and so often illegible.' Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Rand's first date for the letter, 26 January, is questionable: Clarke mentions the letter twice in no. 901 and again in nos. 907 and 954, always giving the date as 21 January. Answered by no. 901.
Amsterdam, <21th>†a 28th Jan. 1687.
Dear Sir,
The backwardness I find in Mr. Stratton to show you his accounts or to communicate the bill of affairs has made me look back as far as I can into the matter, and by all the account I have received I do not [find more] than £130 10s. od.... But finding it necessary you should know, that when you come to examine that account, that that receipt may not mislead you. For I begin to doubt by his slowness what account I may expect. I intended [to speak] very plainly about it. But that I may not mistake in the matters I shall have occasion to mention to him, I would be very glad to know what money he has in the whole paid you.
My Uncle†1 left issue only by two daughters: Wm. Stratton's wife,†2 one of them, is thereby one of the coheirs of that little estate
― 107 ―

at Bel[u]ton, etc. My intention is, if he acquit himself well in looking after my affairs, in acknowledgment of his pains and kindness, to settle the whole estate on his son by my cousin, during the son's life and his sister's,†1 reserving a reasonable rent to my heirs. For the other daughter of my uncle has left a son†2 too, [to whom] I have very little obligation. This is my intention, if my cousin Stratton so look after my affairs in his hands [and] his negligence occasion me not either loss or trouble. But if I find he manages it so ill that I make little or nothing of it, I shall think of disposing of it some other way.... The best way [is] for both to propose to him the paying me constantly so much a year.... And then I to settle on his two children by my cousin during their two lives all that I have in fee simple [for] possession. I mean not out upon lease. This I take the liberty to propose to you to have your advice upon it, [as to whether you approve] of it, or can think of anything more advisable.
And now I am entered upon the affair of accounts I remember to ask whether Mr. Perce†3 has accounted to you for £100 received by a bill of 21st <March>†a , 1683-4 on Madame Daval. Item more <£200>†b by a bill ... [16]84 on Madame Daval. Item more £100 by a bill of R. Hill returned protested 16th May, 1685. Item more £399 10s. to Antoine Rodriguez Marquis in consideration of his bill drawn on Dr. Guenellon. In all £800.... If Mr. Oakley desires that the money in his hands may be forborne till Midsummer, [this may be done as] a kindness to him, on condition it be secured to you, in case he should die, for living I should take his word for a great deal more; and that it may be had on demand whenever occasions call for it....
Of Mr. Papin's proposition and design for your son, I would have him at present teach him [to speak] in French, and that only by talking till he can read English very perfectly. When he can read English well, then begin to read French. For it is not fit that children should be puzzled and <clogged>†c with too much business about reading [several] languages at once; and all the languages necessary, if a right method be taken, will be got time enough. And all the languages [wrongly taught] do not recompense half the injury is usually done to their health and humours by the exertion given
― 108 ―

them in learning them. Two languages, besides his mother's, are I confess absolutely necessary to your son, viz. Latin and French. But the use of them, if it be considered right, is far different. For the French is chiefly for French conversation, and the Latin for the understanding of books. If therefore a French tutor fall in [with your method] I should have him trouble your son with nothing else about languages, but barely to talk French into him, that [while young] he may form his organs to the right pronunciation of that language....
The language, I make [use as] a thing [to encourage] by example all the gentle ways of instruction to frame his mind toward [knowledge]. The best modes are by making him prefer reputation and praise to the satisfaction of any present excellency and passion. The method is by observing to what sort of knowledge his own natural inclination carries him, and to make [him] engage in it. For children should in things of learning and knowledge never be forced to that which [is a burden to them].... Encourage them by the credit and commendation they find attends it, you shall then see that they are as forward to learn as you are. They will with as much pleasure learn what is good and useful, as what is bad and hurtful; if [you lead them] to it by following their inclinations, and make it not at any time a task or a burden to them. This I think [may be done if you] begin with sensible, and especially visible objects, taking those that were most familiar and obvious first. They might practise drawing, a great deal of anatomy, botany, geography and astronomy whilst they are very young. For [earlier then we imagine if] children be delighted to know the situation and use of the parts of their own bodies, or the situation of town and countries, or the situation of the constellations of the heavens, which I think only as so many sensible objects [are to be impressed] on their memories, it would not only save them time and pain, and be of great use hereafter, but also [at the very] least engage them in the love and desire of knowledge. Being [certain also] not to weary.
As therefore I have advised heretofore, I am absolutely of the opinion that he should never be beaten, or so much as chid for his book, and I would have you give absolutely in charge to his tutor, whoever he be, never to strike him or chide him for his book nor drive him to the learning of anything by fear, unless it be the fear of shame or of displeasing you. But let nobody have the charge to strike him without your express order and direction. It is often the
― 109 ―

passion and insolence, but always the laziness of tutors that makes them beat and chide their pupils, they finding it much easier to impose hard and unsuitable things upon them, and correct them for not doing of it, than by studying their inclinations and suiting their instructions to their abilities, explain to them those things step by step, which they are willing to learn, and would with pleasure be led into, if their tutors would condescend and take pains to do it. I make sure it is so with your son, since I hear you not complain of [our] method, which you ought to have done if you had found those gentle ways I proposed of treating him any way insufficient. If the success hath hitherto [been good], I desire the continuation of the same method as of more consequence than all the French or Latin any tutor has to teach ... [For what gain is there to learn] all languages in comparison of a mind pursuing the ways of virtue and knowledge as you direct [and] that has never yet learned any aversion to the thing he is to do from the constraint and ill-usage that controlled him. I conclude this is so, for I expect to hear from you when our method fails. This I thought convenient to say concerning the instructions I think you should give his tutor, and the method you should put him in with your son, now that I have some hopes that [this one] will be fit to teach him French. If this man should not prove to your turn, and you should hereafter find a man with Latin, I think we must then change our method in respect of these two languages; but in all the rest keep to it, at least I yet see nothing to the contrary.†1

28th Jan.
Though I had got thus far of this letter, yet expecting every day the letter you had promised by the next post,†2 I [received them] all yesterday at the time three posts came together....
The [letter of advice]†3 should lie in London where you think safest, under your name as long as you are in town, and when you go out of town to be so in the power of somebody that stays in London, that it may be disposed of at any time by order from us, [as often] as there shall be occasion. Pray, therefore, send me word whom you think best to substitute in your place, when you go out
― 110 ―

of town, [and also] that may have the power to dispose of it as he shall receive advice....
I thank you for the [opinion of Stratton as]†1 I had rather have four words of yours grounded upon your unprejudiced observation than abundance of talk of people who speak of others as their passions have prepossessed them. I shall be very glad to do any service, but to do it well one must know the matter one has to work on....
I hope in your next to hear something about the tutor I sent you news of, and I shall be extremely glad if he so answer the character I have received of him that he prove suitable to your design. If a bill for £4 or £5 come to you writ in my hand, but signed by Sylvester <Brounower>†a having this mark   †2 under the name, pray pay it and put it to my account.
The last part of the philosophical essay I hope you will ere long receive,†3 and when the whole is together you will then be able to judge whether it be new or useful. For if it be nothing but what [is well known] and be not like to profit much the commonwealth of learning, the author will content himself with his own speculations....
My humble service to Madam and the little ones. I thank you and her for [the enquiries] for my health: I thank God I have not had it better these many years, and in the worst of winter fear not my cough.
I am, dear Sir,
your most affectionate and humble servant,
J. LOCKE.
Pray present my service to our Tunbridge friends,†4 as many of them as are in town, and let them know I writ to three of them above a week since.
I am more and more dissatisfied about my cousin Stratton, since I find by your silence he hath not yet answered the letter you have done me the favour to write to him to know what he has done in
― 111 ―

Haroll's business. And I believe he lets Shatter go on in the possession of that house without following your directions to discover, whether the life she pretends to hold by be in being or no. Pray tell me whether it rest not upon the tenant to prove the person alive by whose life he holds, and in case of doubt, whether it be not the Lord's way to enter. I only expect your answer and advice concerning what I writ in the beginning of this letter. And then I will write to him at large. For I fear matters will not go well in his hands, or at best that he is a very slow man of London.
Address: These for Mr. Edward Clarke at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, in London.
898. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 19 January 1687 (883, 903)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 8. Forwarded by Sir Walter Yonge: p. 121.
Otterton Jan 19th 1686.
Dear Sir
I cannot forbear Scribling on, though I can receive none from you; Your first of the 26th. of Octob: is the last, the only one that is come to my hands from you, since I left you, and that is almost worn out with often reading, in pitty to it, as well as to me, you ought to send me another. I heartily Thank you for any which you have design'd me, I hope you have many, for I am not willing to think that you have forgotten me; but I know not what hard fate it is that robs me of them; 'tis strange, that I can neither have letters from you, or safely Convey any to You, I am sure had all the letters I have addressed to you, found you out, they would have obtain'd some answer; You are too generous and too good natured, to suffer a Person that Loves and Vallues you as she ought, to Languish three whole Months without any account of you, and 'tis not much less since the 26th. of Oct: 'tis true Mr Duke has had a letter from you since, and I am greatly obliged to you for the part I had in it, and for the Pacquet you there tell me, you had dispatch'd to me, which is not yet come. what can I do to remedy this misfortune; I have already Tryed by way of Mr Furly, and by Mr Howes Bookseller at Utretch,†1 I will send this without any Superscription to London,
― 112 ―

and let my Brother or Mr Clark give it a more fortunate one; perhaps they may know where you are Transplanted, I hope 'tis into England, nothing else can make me amends. if you are upon the way towards us, 'twill be a very pleasing surprize, I begin to hope it strongly, and I know not how I shall bear the disappointment, if it proves otherwise; especially since I want you extreamly, for though in general I have had my health tollerably well ever since my return from Holland, yet my particular complaint grows I fear from bad to worse every day, and I have no hopes of retrieving that misfortune but by your care, and Skill; therfore I will not seek it else where, being desirous to be obliged to you only for the repairing of all my defects, and I hope you will be so Charitable as to take me into your serious consideration, and assoon as you can, without prejudice to your self; come and give me that aide, that assistance which I want, which you have promised me, and which you owe me as you are my Father, and my Friend. and at the same time perform those generous offers of your Services, which you have made to my Master; who Thankfully owns that he has the highest Obligations imaginable to you. he is at present at Escott supplying my Brothers place, who left us three Weeks since; but how he diverts himself, and whither wives or Gelenots run most in his Head, I know nothing; I doubt not but he has given you an account of himself, if you are where a letter can reach you; but if you are a member of the invisible World, I beseech you to find some way or other to let me know it, and put me out of the pain your Silence makes me to suffer; but if you are still one of us, Treat me with your wonted goodness, by which you have made me for Ever Dear Sir
Your most affectionate Friend and faithfull humble servant
ISABELLA DUKE
Address (not in Mrs. Duke's hand): For Mr John Lock These
Endorsed by Locke: Mrs Duke 19 Jan 86/7 Answered 22 Feb:
899. John Freke to Locke, 20 January 1687 (887, 909)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 159-60.
Temple January the 20/30th 1686/7
Dear Sir
Yours of the 7/17 Sir W Y deliverd me yesterday and by it I find that tis almost a month since I tendred you my service, for therein
― 113 ―

you speak of mine of December the 24th. I protest I could not have immagined it soe long since I wrote to you. I'm sure I think of you with honour and of your friendship with the greatest satisfaction much oftener than every day and believe the reason of my soe long silence was the oppertunity I had by our Salisbury court friend†1 to convey my respects to you which made me think it needless to give you the trouble of my useless Letters which otherwise out of self Interest I should certainly have persecuted you with that thereby I might be sure not to lose a place in his memory whose esteem I soe much value.
I am very glad I was able in my last to tell you that our Friend had Justice done him soe that his mistress is convinced that she has noe reason in any sort to condemn him or his deportment. I am now soe well assure<d>†a of it from further evidence that I believe I may adventure to say he stands right in her esteem and could not fail of her good graces if he were here and thought fit to make his applications soe much in vain have been the attempts and callumnys of his enemys†2
Your Friends in the West are all well and have a Just value for you and long to see you more than for the Spring. This the little Gentleman†3 who is here (and I believe will not for any good be perswaded to spend a year without seeing this Town) bids me, with his service, tell you and if I may speak my own opinion I think their nearest Relations are not more in every one of their esteem than your self soe little need have you of any ones assistance to obtain their good opinion or the continuance of it. And for Mr S:†4 I have given him soe Just a charracter of you that when you chance to see him you will find him not onely acquainted with you
― 114 ―

but disposed to be your Friend and begging to be admitted by you into that happy Relation
To your Quære concerning the Turkeys Heath poults and Gelinots I know not what to answer but must confess I have a great hankering after those wild Turkeys of America and am not sure I shall be at rest till I have found a way to taste some of them. I attend the return of a great American kinsman of mine†1 to this Town to see whether by his means I may not be enabled to eat of them and till then I adjourn my answer to your Question which of the three is best
I must not forget my promise to send you some of the marks of incredibility in a Witness and therefore you must pardon me if having filld one side of my paper I trouble you further and endorse†2 them
1 If he be a person unknown or of an ill reputation
2 If he speaks by hearsay and not of his own knowledge or what he has learn't from Authentick Records
3 If it be his Interest to have what he relates believed especially if in that case he pretend to inferr important consequences from what he relates which nevertheless doe not necessarily follow from the fact
4 If another of equall credit relate the matter otherwise though onely in Circumstances if he pretend to be particular as to the Circumstances
5 If he be partiall and it appears that he tells not the whole truth but omitts materiall passages whereby at least his negligence must appear
6 If he pretend to confirm his Relation by misapplyd evidence or proofs not Authentick
7 If he Asserts Impossibilitys for Truths
8 If what he says be inconsistent with it self or any other known truth
9 If he were Ignorant and yet relates Facts that it requires a prævious knowledge to comprehend
10 If he speak of things of publick note and Consequence and yet the Curious who were at the same time and place know nothing of them
― 115 ―

Some of these entirely take away others lessen the Credit of the Narrator as I conceive it and if you are of another opinion be pleased to convince me in your next and when I am soe fortunate as to see you as I hope I shall ere long in this Town I will shew you my Instances†1 upon all these with relation to the case we discoursed of which it may be will make the objections to the credit of the witness much more strong and evident. I am
Sir
your most obliged and affectionate Friend
JOHN FREKE
Address: For Mr John Lock
Endorsed by Locke: J Freke 20/30 Jan 86/7
900. Edward Clarke to Locke, 21 and 25 January 1687 (897, 901)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 26. Printed in Rand, pp. 181-3. Answers nos. 890 and 894; answered by no. 906.
London January 21th. 1686/7
Sir,
Verie lately I Received the inclosed Lease and Letter from your Cosen Stratton†2 with greate importunity to convey it forthwith to you to bee Executed, Which, at first I much wondered at, haveing frequently communicated to Him the ample authority I had from you for the Granting of Leases as well as for receiveing your Rents and other money's, But it seemes the Purchasour would not bee satisfied without your Executeing the Lease, and That being part of His contract with your Cosen Stratton (however Chargeable and troublesome it bee to you)†a I am obleiged to send it you, and am desiered by Him to acquaint you, That, 'tis the Purchasours request it may be seal'd (if possible)†a in the presence of English-men, And Return'd to your Cosen Stratton (who might have mannag'd this matter with lesse trouble)†a with the first opportunity: Mr Perce†3 hath three hundred ninety nine pounds and ten shillings of your fower hundred pounds in his handes (the other ten shillings being as Hee sayes allowed for Brokerage)†a And
― 116 ―

I have taken his Note for it in my own Name payable on Demand according to your Order; And now I begg leave to acknowlidge the Favour of yours of the 10th. and 17th. instant recommending a Tutor for my son, and to lett you Know that I have delivered the Letter that came inclos'd from Monsieur le Clerke to the Person Recommended,†1 And have mett him two or three times and discours'd him at large on that subject, But Hee being as yett altogather undetermined what course of Life to betake Himselfe to, or in what manner to dispose of himselfe here, I have not as yett any certain Answer from Him to my Proposealls, but hope in a short time to have his resolution therein; My Wife, son, and your little Mistris joyne with mee in theire true Love and Services to you, and with my hearty Prayers for the continuance of your health I rest,
your most Faithfull Freind and humble servant
E.†a
January 25th. 1686
Sir,
Just as I had finish'd and was sending away what is above written to the Post-house, with the Lease and Letter mentioned to bee inclosed, our Freind Mr. Fr.†2 inform'd mee of Mr. Furley's man's being in Town, and His intentions to make a speedy Return to Rotterdam, whereupon I declynd sending it by the Post by reason of the Charge, and will convey the Lease to you by Him, But the Letter I received from Mr. Stratton, I have here inclos'd, and since the Receipt of it have written to Him to quicken Him in the disposeall of Robert Haroll's Hay and other Goods and getting in the money etc: Which, (had Hee followed my former directions when I made the Goods lyable to your satisfaction)†b might have been done before this time, but I presume the death of His Father in Law has retarded His indeavours for you in that particular: Yesterday I againe mett Monsieur Papin, and with Sir W: Y: (who in all our meeteings hath been our interpreter when it was necessary) had a full discourse with Him upon our designe for the Education of my son, and the Proposealls I had made Him for that End, Which were to this Effect viz: That Hee should Live with mee by noe meanes in the Degree of a servant, But as my Freind,
― 117 ―

for whome I would have my son and all belonging to mee to have the greatest value and esteem imaginable, And that Hee should have the Liberty of my House and Servants in all Respects equally with my selfe, And twenty pounds a yeare Sallary, The Termes Hee made noe objection to, and of the Faithfull performance of them was in noe manner of doubt, But in this, as well as all his former discourses, Hee seem'd to thinke the Nature of the imployment, the instructing of a Childe, to bee altogather unpleasant, (Hee call'd it a Slavery)†aand beneath his undertakeing, and at last told us plainly that His Resolutions were now fix'd to persue his former designe in the study of Divinity, and to rely wholly upon That for his future Livelyhood, And therefore could not bee content to sett apart soe much of his time as would bee necessary for the instruction of the Child, But in case I would not expect Hee should spend above 3. or 4. howers in a day with the child, and permitt Him the residue of His time intirely to Himselfe, And allsoe Ingage, That, after 6 or 7. yeares time, or soe much as should bee thought necessary, spent in that manner with my Son, I would allsoe Advance Him into such a Benefice as might furnish Him with a comfortable subsistance for the Remainder of his Life, Hee would then undertake the imployment; But you will easily conclude 'twas not fitt for mee to contract with Him on these Termes, espetially when Hee had declar'd the Nature of the imployment to bee soe disagreable and uneasy, and that Hee could sett apart but soe small a portion of his time for my purpose, soe that after the ordinary Civillitys wee parted, And there remaines nothing but my hearty thankes to you and Monsieur le Clerk for recommending soe ingeniouse a Gentleman to mee, though it bee not my good Fortune to have the Pleasure and advantage of his Society in my Family: Sir W: Y: Mr. Fr. my Wife and the rest of your Freinds here give theire services, to you, as doth
your most Faithfull†b
Address: A Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Pieter de la Nove†1 ten Huÿse van Mÿn Heer Limburgh op de Keÿsers Graght bÿ de Remonstrancse Kerch tot, Amsterdam:
