901. Edward Clarke to Locke, 28 January 1687 (900, 906)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 27. Printed in Rand, pp. 188-91. Answers no. 897; answered by no. 906.
London January the 28th. 1686/7
Deare Sir,
In†a- Answer to that part of your Letter of the 21th. which concerns Mr. Stratton I must in the first place acquaint you, That I have Received of Him to your use (by Bylls of Exchange from Mrs Strachey)†b these severall summes following viz: On the 4th. of November 1683. 31l: 11s: 02d: On the 8th. of November 1684: 48l. On the 31th. of May 1686. 50l. And on the 20th. of September last 31l. 10s. In all the summe of one hundred sixty one pounds one shilling and two pence, (of which if I mistake not I have in some of my former Letters given you an Accompt) soe that by this, you find that Hee is not soe much in Arreare as you imagined,-†aHowever I thinke it would bee for your Advantage (when you write next) to desire Him to perfect his Accompt of what Hee hath Received and paid for your use, and to Pass it over to mee, by Which (if Hee makes it intelligible) it will appeare to you what is in Arreare, And how Hee hath mannag'd the Trust you repos'd in Him, and by a due consideration of the whole matter, You will bee the best Judge Whither Hee deserves the Kindnesse you intend Him or not; But most certainely you cannot in all probability take a Better course for your future ease and quiet in the mannagement of that Estate dureing your owne Life then That propos'd in your Letter of the 21th., And I thinke in case you settle on Mr Stratton's two Children by your Cosin for theire Lives your Estate in Fee that is now lett at a Rack-Rent, it ought to bee taken verie Kindly by Him, it being allsoe an ample incouragement for Him to bee obleiged to pay you constantly (by quarterly or halfe yearely Payments) the Rent that those Landes are now lett for dureing your Life without any Deductions, This Proposeall of yours carryes soe much Kindnesse in it towards His Children, and soe greate a probability of easing you dureing your Life in the mannagement of that Estate, that I cannot thinke of any thing more Adviseable in this Particular; In my Letter by the last Post I sent you one inclosed (which I had lately before Received from Mr
― 119 ―

Stratton) wherein you have His Accompt what postu<re your af>fayres†a in that Countrey are at present in, and particularly what Hee hath done towards the discovery Whither the Life that the widow Shatter holds by bee Liveing or not, and if what Hee hath written bee not satisfactory in that particular, it will bee on the Tenants part to prove the Life in Being that Hee holds by, and because of the uncertainty in this Case of yours, I formerly Advised Mr. Stratton to Enter and bring an Ejectment in your name, But by his Letter to you I found that Hee is now satisfied that the Life the Widdow holds by is Liveing; And†b- now I shall informe you That in April and May 1684. I Received of Mr. Perce†1 the first 300l. mentioned in your last Letter, And in August 1685. One hundred pounds in leiw of the Byll Return'd Protested, And I have his Note (as I inform'd you in my Letter by the last Post) payable on Demand for 399l: 10s. (the other 10s. being paid by Him for Brokeridge) which Hee lately Received of Antonio Rodriguez Marquis in consideration of His Byll on Doctor Guen.†2 In all eight hundred pounds (Wanting only the 10s. allow'd by Him for Brokeridg)-†b As for your money due from Mr. Oakley I have a Note under his Hand for the payment of it, which was long since payable, and I presume gave the occasion of that part of His Letter to you for farther forbearance: My last gave you a particular Accompt of my Treaty with Mr. Papin, and the Result of it, And therefore I will not now Repeate but heartily thanke you for what You with soe much Kindnesse writt in your last touching the Method to bee used in the begining of my son's Tuition, Which, I soe well approve of, That I shall use my uttmost indeavours that it may bee strictly observ'd by the Tutor I shall fix on, I have at this time severall Offers from amongst the French-Protestants, But find it verie difficult to have a true Character of theire Qualifications or Tempers, and therefore should have been much satisfied in Monsieur Papin, had the Nature of the imployment been agreeable to His inclynations, but that being Off, I must before I leave the Town (if possible) gett another that may Answere our Designe, or otherwise I doubt the Child will not only loose his time, but bee much injur'd by the Company of servants and others
― 120 ―

that Hee will unavoydably (in my absence) spend his time withall, of which I have allready this Experience, That as Hee increases in Age, Hee grows more and more fond of such People as divert Him most from the thoughts of Learning, in soe much, That since His last sicknesse, I have not by Reasoning and the other mild wayes that were formerly made use of bin able to prevaile with him to doe that which before his sicknesse was Easy and familiar, But have been forc'd into a seeming Breach of the ordinary Freindshipp betwixt us, and the acting over a feign'd displeasure towards him for whole dayes togather before I could prevaile with Him to doe that which I desiered, And I have (by late observations)†a greate Reason to feare That without a Tutor speedily Gott to keepe Him constantly from the conversation of such ill company, I shall never bee able to Govern Him intirely by our Method, but of this you shall heare more as I see Cause, and I will only at present acquaint you That Hee has perfectly recovered His former health of Body, but fayles in his memory much more then before his sicknesse, which probably may bee some part of the occasion why Hee applyes not to his Book now with the same ease and freedome as formerly, But I bless God Hee is Restored to the use of His Reason, and I have hopes that His memory with use may grow better, but without it I feare his Progresse in Learning will bee verie slow and difficult; The time will not permitt mee at present to say any thing more to you on this subject, And therefore shall only add that I will seeke an opportunity to take notice to Mr. Perce of the oversights committed by Him in his Late Byll and Letter of Advise, to prevent the like for the future; And doe further informe you, That amongst my acquaintance here (which are like to continue in Town)†a I know of noe Person soe propper to putt your money into the Power of as your Good Freind Mrs. R:S: who, I am certaine, will bee ready at all times to dispose thereof in my Absence as you shall order or direct, And therefore (if I heare nothing from you in the meane time to the Contrary) I shall before I goe out of Town soe place it in Her power, as (with Mr. Perce's Assistance) shee may bee able to Answer those Ends, and if there bee any thing further wherein I may bee capable to serve you, it shall with greate willingnesse and sincerity bee performed by
your most truly affectionate Freind and Faithfull Servant
E.†b
― 121 ―

I can noe longer pretend to any Excuse for my Wifes not Writeing to you, however hope you will not reject the hearty services that Shee, Her Son, and your little Mistriss sends you etc:
Endorsed by Locke: E. Clarke†a 28 Jan 86/7
902. Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 28 January 1687 (893, 915)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 150-1.
London Jan. 28th. 1686/7
Dear Sir
I think I am obliged to justify my selfe from the imputation you seeme to lay on me in yours of the 17th. instant, as if I prefer'd building and business to the conversation of my best friends, if you will take my word for it nothing but necessity could have made me ply it as I have done, and I have an eternall quarrell to it for hindering me so often of the enjoyment of my friends, but if you will not beleive me upon my bare word come over and be convinced by experience and ease me of part of that which is now my burthen, but would be rendred one of my greatest pleasures with your good company and assistance; and I assure you I was not in jeast when I told you in my last I depended on your coming over in the spring to set my Library in order, I dare hardly resolve to set up the wainscott and much less the books without your advice, therefore pray doe not dissappoint me, but since I am like to be condemned to summer in this country let me not want the pleasure of the best roome in My House, as I shall think that when you have helpt to furnish it, and are so kind to fill up one of the chairs designed for it; In the mean time I shall give you a farther demonstration of my readiness to answer my friends kindness in the way of letters by the empty scrible I am now sending you, which I can not delay (notwithstanding the hopes you give me of hearing more largely from you speedily) though it be only to thank you for your kind letter, and to be a cover to the enclosed from my sister;†1 who is much troubled to think that she has lost severall of your letters, what reason she has to be of that opinion I know not, but I hope she had your last which came inclosed in mine, for I sent it forward
― 122 ―

soon after I receiv'd it tho I have not yet an account of its safe arrivall at her hands. I beg your pardon for not acquainting you sooner that the Lime trees came safe, are all planted, and we hope will doe well. Mr Cl. is daily in search for a Tutor for his son but can not yet fix upon any, Monsieur Papin whom your friend recommended aimes rather at getting an establishment as a preacher, though with what hopes I know not, so that our friend is forced to look farther, and has hopes to find one for his purpose before the spring, when he returns to his House, and I to my building, in which durty work (however ill you think of it) I am too farr engaged not to goe on a little farther, especially since Mr Taylor is leaving our country after this summer, and I would willingly, get beyond the need of an Architect before he gets out of my reach. This will be enclosed to Mr Furly to whome I shall write by this post to buy me a back for my Kitchen-chimney†1which is a roome as necessary as any to furnished. Mr Cl. and Mr Fr. who are now with me oblige me to add their services, before I write my selfe
Dear Sir Your most faithfull friend and humble servant
WALTER YONGE.
Address: For Mr John Lock These.
Endorsed by Locke: Sir W. Yonge 28 Jan. 86/7 Answered 22 Feb:

903. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 29 January 1687, with postscript by Richard Duke (898, 918; 876)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 9-10.
[Mrs. Duke:]
Otterton Jan: 29th. 1686
Deare Sir
I am once more so fortunate as to receive a letter from you; Yours of 16th. instant is at last come safe to my hands; I need not adde that 'twas most welcome to me, Yours make themselves so whithersoever they are addressed, and cannot faile to be a most agreable entertainment to the most ingenious, though they have no share in the kindness that dictates them; how much I vallue
― 123 ―

them, will somewhat appear in the pressing Complaints you will find in my last, (of Jan: 12th. as I remember,) for want of them, and my impatient desires and expectations of hearing more frequently from you. You cannot bestow those Favours on any person living, to whom they are more necessary, or more acceptable; do me the Justice to beleeve it, and that I have all the Gratitude immaginable, for those and all other expressions of your Friendship, by which you have obliged me to the utmost degree. How can I thank you enough for the innumerable Obligations you have laid on me, how can I enough lament the loss of your second Packet, especially since I find that my loss is irreparable, and that 'tis out of your way to descend to repeat any thing. Your Neesing†1 Pouder would be of great use here, in our dull corner of the Country, where 'tis very difficult to keep ones self awake, I hope your store is not exhausted, but that I may have a frequent supply sufficient for my necessityes; which I assure you are greater then ever. for your Pills to purge Choler, I have no present occasion; Your Specifick to Cure Agues shall be used both Judiciously and Charitably; but I hope to see you, and to be more fully instructed by you, before I begin to Practice; and I will try no more experiments upon my self, till I have your Antidotes, to secure me from the ill consequences of them. I have learnt the Hebrew words Salemlec and Hephzibah, but I find they are no Charm, and I fear will do me no good, if you do not in your next explain the History of the Rabbi, and give me a larger account of his inventions; which pray do not faile to do, for I have a Terrible fitt of the Spleen at present, and it must be something very extraordinary, which can give me any disposition either to be gaye within, or pleasant without; I know not what a new way of making Love may do, and am sorry that your Essay†2 fell into any other hands then mine; the Treaty of Commerce must be renued, unless you will come in person and set all things right, which is infinitely more desirable. what Arguments shall I use to perswade you to it, would I had any Chain in my hand that could draw you to me. I would hold you no faster, no longer then you were willing; I would not be so selfish to serve my self, at your Cost; Trust me, and come and try; I fancy we shall agree that matter very well; perhaps when you return, you may draw the whole Rowe after You. and by that time the Weather may be better setled in the Country where you now are, which at present appears
― 124 ―

to me very Cloudy and uncertain. but you know best; if I were sure Travelling would not be prejudicial to you, I would importunately beg you to come and make us a Visit, you shall tarry as little while as you please, according as you find our Air agrees with you, I am of Opinion a few Hours discourse will settle this grand point to all our satisfactions. but I dare not urge it. whatever you do take care of your self, Your Health is the greatest concern of every one of us, and we would not hazard it, to purchase the greatest advantage to our selves, which we shall certainly find in your Excellent Conversation, whenever you make us happy in the enjoyment of it. think of this seriously, and be as kind to us as you can be without injuring your self. Heavens preserve and Bless you, wherever you are, and may you be always Easie, alwayes Happy, and may your enjoyments be Equall to your Merits; and may your Charity, and your Friendship to me, be rewarded an hundred fold. Your other Daughter is at Sir John Davies, whither I carried her about a Month since; she will be glad to hear some News of you, and perhaps may give you the employment you desire this spring, if you are within her reach. my Brother keeps us in ignorance of what he learns, sayes, or does, in London. but I suppose he will quicklie return to us, with your Friend Sumshire and his Family, who are retyring into the Rowe, which cannot be compleat without you. you see I cannot forbear that Toppick, but I will punnish you no further at present; but with the greatest respect <and>†a affection conclude my self
Sir
Your Friend and faithfull servant
IS: DUKE
[Duke:]
Having gotten leave to write in this I must also beg you in a postscript to accept of my most hearty thanks for the favor of yours, and to believe that I shall allways make it my businesse to deserve the kindness you express to me in it. I found nothing wanting in it but some better encouragement to hope to see you here in the Row this spring, which we now expect with no little impatience. Pardon me Sir if you find me often importunate with you on that point, 'tis not onely the effect of my necessities, but also of my inclinations, since you were once so kind to give us hopes of
― 125 ―

it, I cannot be content to forego that happiness. I am sensible that I have no other arguments to induce you to it, but such as must be drawn from your own charity and good nature, but if they do not prevail with you I shall be forced to stir up your daughters to persecute you so with their letters, that you will find their pens more troublesom at a distance then their tongues in your presence, which would so appease them, that we should have nothing but harmony in the Row. Pray let us receive a confirmation of your promise which would be the greatest comfort to us who can have relief no other way, and infinitely oblige
Your most affectionate friend to serve you R.D.
Address: For Mr John Lock
Endorsed by Locke: Mrs Duke 29 Jan 86/7

904. Thomas Papillon to Locke, 2/12 February 1687, with letter from — Broadnax
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 186-7. Thomas Papillon, 1623-1702, of London, merchant and a leading adherent of Shaftesbury; at this time a fugitive at Utrecht: D.N.B. Broadnax was a nephew of Mrs. Papillon.
[Written by Broadnax:]
Sir
The diseases under which I labour, and in which your advice is desired, are the consumption, and Feavor.
The fundamental Cause of the former I judg to be my Cough, which has been my troublesome Companion from the very first stage of my life. This having so long taken possession of me, I can rationaly no otherwaies conclude, then that it should considerably spend and wast me, it frequently opening my vessels so much as that with my flegm I frequently find fresh blood mingled. The more immediate Cause of my bodily decay, which is now very considerable, I attribute to my continual nightsweats, with which I have been beset more or lesse for about five weakes, I observe the violence of my Cough extraordinarily to open my pores, and give an opportunity to such a consequence. My Cough is never so exceedingly painfull as when I first raise up my self in the morning, in order to leave my bed, which is usualy about ten of the Clock, as soon as I am set at liberty by the departure of my enslaving sweat. The flegm I bring up is of a very viscous and Consistent matter. In order
― 126 ―

to the Cure of all which my discomposure, and bad state of body, by the Doctors direction, I have taken pills, powders, purges, and decoctions of many sorts, I cannot give you the ingredients, but in short they have all had but an ineffectual operation. My appetite, which is not altogether so good as formerly, is best at the evening. I am very weak and feeble, as you would ere this your self have Collected; My breath is short, and very painfully drawn after motion. To all which I beg leave to mention the gididiness of my head, which is most in the morning, I frequently by Coughing strain some blood from my head, as I fear; which generaly I do sensibly perceive, before it discovers itself. As to my digestion I cannot quarrel therewith, I find it sometimes tired, but desire to praise God that it is not worse.
My Feavor I can give no account of, I find my self in such a posture as is most commonly characteristical thereof, viz hot and dry.
[Papillon:]
Utrecht the 2/12 february 1687
Sir
Yours I Received in its tyme, as <also>†a advice from Mr DAranda†1 that you had paid him fl42: 10 for my account and according to your desire I paid Mr Crosse†2 the fl2 which was more then my mony Came to.

Guenellonem nostrum (uti reliquos collegas) quæso meo nomine salutes et dicas me gratias agere ob epistolam mihi transmissam
(Latin) 
14 Feb:
I hope now that frequent letters from England may reach me augmented by the company of your own, most scholarly Sir, so that if any unpleasant news is transmitted from those shores it may be mitigated by the amenity and elegance of your pen and tempered by its sweetness. There is nothing more savoury, nothing more delightful, than what is to be read in your letters, in which even German theology†1 itself does not show in an utterly unlovely light. I thank you for telling me about Magri's Hierolexicon.†2 I bought this book recently at Wetstein's, but those who are interested in it complain that it is sold too dear. I should therefore be grateful if you would kindly let me know in your next letter how much your own copy cost, for fl. 14-10 really seems more than enough, although it is bound in the French style.†3 The enclosed letter contains this and other exceptions, as I may call them, which I take to Wetstein's account; please pass it on to him, so that when his answer is received the money may be sent him. I am very sad at [p. 128] being torn away from you and the rest of the Amsterdam friends of whom I am so fond.†1 I hear little about politics where I am living now and so far still less about learning; so I beseech you to warm me to life again with your letters, lest I grow utterly torpid. Good-bye, and love me
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
Please remember me to our friend Guenellon, as well as to the rest of our Collegians, and give him my thanks for the letter that was sent on to me.

906. Locke to Edward Clarke, 8/18 February 1687 (901, 907)
Rand, pp. 193-7. 'The letter is in a very bad state, the paper being rotten and faded.' Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Some of the transcription appears to be faulty. Answers nos. 900 and 901.
18th February 1687.
Dear Sir,
By yours of 21st of Jan. I find that my cousin Stratton, who writes to me but once in two or three years, when he does it is in great haste. I thank you for not sending the lease by the post according to his silly desire; but some folks, so they may but please the people they talk with, and are in their neighbourhood, care not what trouble or charge they bring on those who are at a distance, although
― 129 ―

they ought to take more care of them. I have taken notice of this to him in the enclosed, and beg the favour also of you to do it when you see him. You will see that I have writ to him to pass his accounts to you as soon as may be. When he undertook the care of my rent there I left in his hands a rent roll by which you will be able to charge him, as also, I believe, by the little paper book of accounts, which, as I remember, you have of mine. A receipt you will find in his hand of mine for £31 odd money must discharge him of nothing, but being given for money which I have left in his hand, and is the same which was paid you, if I mistake not, 4th Nov., 1683. When he has passed his account and satisfied you therein, I then entreat you to open the proposition I mentioned to you in my last,†1 which upon further consideration I find to have two difficulties that will hinder me from settling it absolutely in his children by my cousin without a power of revocation. The one is, that he may die before me, and so my affairs there be set in the ends, and I fain to look out another into whose hands to put them. The other is, that I would not put the power of the little estate I have there out of my hands, so as not to be able to dispose of it as I please, whatever occasion I may have; and therefore I would make no such settlement, but with power of revocation. On the other side he will then have reason to object, that after he has [paid] such a rent without defalcation of taxes for some years I may resume my estate, and leave him not only unrewarded, but out of purse. To obviate this the remedy <I propose>†a is this. That the rent we shall agree for, or any part of it, being behind at any time six months, I will have an absolute power of revocation. 2nd. That, if I do revoke without any forfeiture of his, that then upon the tender of so much as you shall think reasonable for his pains, taxes and value of the estate (if there be any difference between then and now, for I would have him pay according as it was let by the rent roll I left with him, and that without any defalcation) by the year, according to the number of years that shall be charged from the time of the date of the deed to the time of the said tender. This is the best way which my ignorance in the law and these kind of affairs can make me think of. Perhaps you will think on something better. The truth is were mankind so as they ought to be, I know a better way than all this,
― 130 ―

and that is, that he should pay me constantly so much a year for all that estate there during my life, and that without any account, and then I would settle the estate as I design upon his children by will, which if at any time I altered I would some other way make him amends for his pains, and loss, if he had sustained any, but by his own fault. But in an age I cannot take other men's words, at least one of a 1000, I can scarce tell how to propose that another should take [them]. But I leave the whole matter to [your judgement] and kindness. I would be master of my estate whilst I live. I would make [disposal thereafter] with the least trouble. My thoughts are of no consideration: reasons intervene to the contrary to leave it to my heirs, with the advantage to my cousin Stratton's children as an acknowledgment of their father's care of it for me in my lifetime....
The man is come, but the lease [is not], being in his trunk, which he brought not with him in the Marguet boat, but sent on in a ship from London. But he tells me the ship [has sailed], so that I expect it every moment....
And now†1 I return to that which troubles me most, and that is, that our endeavours hitherto prove so unsuccessful in procuring a tutor. But, however, pray be not troubled about his loss of time, or the weakness of his memory; since his disease [is cured] you have nothing to apprehend from either of them. If you can maintain and increase his ambition and desire of praise, and keep him from ill habits and humours, trouble not yourself about his learning, it will come time enough. And I think that in the state he is now, wherein though he has no visible remains of his late disease in his body, yet his mind is not come to its former strength and alacrity, he should not be diseased†2 with his book, but left to the diversion of innocent delights to which his own inclination leads him, which, as you observe to have this or that tendency most successful in something amongst them that may be of use and [value] to him. [Do] not burden nor force him, especially in the matter of his book, which I am still in my old mind that [study should] never be made a burden or a business to him, but a sensible pleasure.
One thing, indeed, you have touched on which is of dangerous consequence, which is the [keeping] company with servants, and being pleased with their flattery and insinuations, which serve for
― 131 ―

nothing but to corrupt and mislead children. This is a mischief which, as I remember, I formerly took notice of as the most dangerous and the hardest to be prevented, and to which perhaps I think the great [depth] into which mankind is degenerated is more than to any one thing owing....†a They should never flatter him or play with him, unless some one sober servant to whose prudence you could trust [be in his company]. It is a great deal better that your children should be alone together to play in a place where [they may be watched], than to have them in the company of admiring servants who will be teaching of them one way or other ill tricks or habits.†1
But since his memory be not [diseased] I will answer for it that it will return again, but have [him constantly] under the notion of exercising of it now, [taking care] that you do not overburden it. Keep up his spirits that be not damped and broken, and so he fall into sober tameness, which is a dangerous quality in a child; and on the other side keep him from vicious inclinations and habits, and then trouble not yourself about his learning. I will undertake he shall have as good a share of it as any of his neighbours and make a better use of it. By the way, is there no such book as Æsop's Fables in English with pictures to entertain children, and to give him to read. If there be not it is a great pity, and were I in England, I would get it translated, and it would be of more use than a great many of those volumes which relate to serious matters.
I desire that when you see my cousin Stratton you would mind him to view all the parcels of land belonging to the tenement at Bel[u]ton often, for that some of them being mixed in amongst other may else be in danger to be lost, and that he take Robert ... ssell†2 with him to shew him them, who knows them all perfectly. I beg also that the half ... de Morbo Gallico,†3 which I left with R. Smith†4 sealed up in a little [box] about the length of a hand and about [half a] hand in breadth, may be sent into ... and the trunk be sent to my cousin John Bonville. And the box of books that I have [left], and a folio of the four Evangelists in Greek arranged in
― 132 ―

columns and interleaved (which book I delivered to my cousin Bonville myself and set an high value upon it, being not to be bought anywhere),†1 be put into the trunk, which being locked I would have left with him, and the key carried back and left with R. Smith,†2 and tied together with what other keys were left there before. You may easily [perceive] why I would have that tract De Morbo Gallico....
Pray present my humble service to her†3 and the little ones. Pardon the liberty with which I trouble you, and oblige me [if you] send your letters hereafter under such a convoy as your brother builder†4 does ....
your ... humble servant,
J. L.
Address: For Mr. Edward Clarke at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, in London.
907. Edward Clarke to Locke, 8 February 1687 (906, 924)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 28. Printed in Rand, pp. 191-2.

Deare Sir
Presumeing that my two last Letters of the 21th. and 28th. of January are in your handes, I shall at present only acquaint you, That since the last of them I have upon Monsieur Justell's Recommendation contracted with one Monsieur Foukett to goe into the Countrey with mee to bee my son's Tutor, well hopeing Hee will Answer the Character that Monsieur Justell, Sir Tho: Clarges,†5 and severall other Gentlemen have given of Him, And if soe, Wee have then such a one as was desiered, Hee approves well of the Method proposed in your Letter of the 21th. of January for our Begining towards†a- the Childs-†a instruction, and Promises carefully
― 133 ―

to pursue That, and such further directions as you shall thinke most Proper, which time and experience only can give mee a certainty of, and therefore I will not trouble you with any thing more of Him at present; But goe on to acquaint you that I much wonder I have not all this time had any Answer from the young Gentleman (that I lately gave you a Character of)†1 to the Letter which I delivered from you to Him, and cannot forbeare to acquaint you that Hee has something Lessen'd Himselfe (at least for the present) in my opinion, by the non performance of the Repeated Promises Hee made mee of Returning you a speedy Answer to that Letter, and untill Hee hath given mee some Reason for that neglect, I shall suspend my further Judgment of Him; Pardon mee that I speake thus Freely to you in this particular, my intent being only that you may not bee deceived by any thing I have Written, For 'tis my unalterable opinion, That unless the Gentleman imbraces your verie Freindly Offers of Assisting him in his studies with a Freedome and Kindnesse Equall to That wherewith you Propos'd it, Hee will not deserve your further Proceeding on that Subject, nor any wayes Answer the Character I gave of Him; And now I must tell you that Mrs Clarke finding mee a little Quarrelsome on the Poynt of not Answering our Freinds Letters, it imediately produced the inclosed from Her, with a Promise that for the future Shee will rather choose to be troublesome, then neglect the Acknowlidgments due to you for that Reall Freindship you have exprest towards Her and Hers etc: I am call'd out by Businesse, but shall ever Remaine,
your most affectionate Freind and Faithfull servant
E†a

908. Mrs. Mary Clarke to Locke, 8 February 1687 (809, 1013)

Deare Sir,
I have bin soe Long silent that I now know not what to say for my selfe and you haveing bin soe extreme kind on all occations to
― 134 ―

me and mine, that I dispare of ever haveing an opertunity to make any suteable Acknowledgment but doe sattisfye my selfe with the thoughts that you are most pleased when you are doeing works of Charrity to others which I doe assure you is very much showen by your Good Advice to us Concerning the Education of our Children which I thinke is the duty of all parances to discharge as well as they can In order to which Mr. Clarke did yesterday Fully a Gree with a tuter for our eldest sonn he being one that has a very Good Carrectter, and we haveing noe hopes of the persen you wase recomended tow for that purpose†1 made mr Clarke Conclude with him and I hope it will doe well; methinkes we have taken a Greate deale of paines and bin much Concerned it should doe soe, I phancy next Chuseing a wife for him thiss is as Great an afaire as any, nay it may be he may doe that wholely himselfe before we know any thing of the matter, but with thiss we must trust Providence I hope God Almighty that has soe Latley raysed him from the Grave beyond all Expecttation will Give him Live and oppertunity to doe some Good in his Genaration and make him thankefull to you and all that are Concerned for him and his Good; Mr. Freke at his comeing over did Give me some hopes of seeing you in a short time heare which I should very much rejoyce in; the room at Chipley being now redy Furneished and Ayred for you and you would be the wellcomest stranger that had ever bin in that House both to Mr. Clarke and
Your reall Frend and Most Ablidged humble servant
MCLARKE
all my Little ones are soe much in hast to be knowne to you and to present you with theyr humble services that I cannott tell which I must heare First

909. John Freke to Locke, 8 February 1686/7 (899, 915)

Dear Sir
Sir W Y who is very much your humble servant did me the pleasure to charge me with his commands to convey the enclosed to you and excuse his not writing. I gladly embraced the first part of his Commission because thereby I gaind an oppertunity of renewing the professions of my friendship and tender of my service to you together with my gratefull acknowlegements of my obligations, but for the second part I told him that his excuses would come better from his own hand when he shall have leisure to take pen in hand though they are thereby deferrd a Post or two, and I believe you will concurr with me in this opinion. I dayly see your friend and mine of Salisbury Court†1 and by his conversation am the more reconciled to the Town in which I did not think to have continued soe long as I have though now I suppose I shall remain here at least 6 weeks longer and then remove but whether into Italy or America I cannot guess (for my Cousin P†2 remains still in the country). Nay for my part I am not sure it will not be into Denmark for if Pr. G:†3 obtain leave to carry his princess thither (as tis said he endeavours) I believe I shall be inclined to wait on him. Your female Friends of Devon I suppose will be in London before I leave it for I am told one of the sisters†4 must come up within this fortnight to meet an honest Gentleman half way and tis probable the experienced marryd lady will not let her come alone. If soe I shall be happyer than I thought in an oppertunity of doing you right by representing to her the value of your friendship,†5which I shall not fail to doe with that affection which becomes
Sir
Your obliged friend and humble servant
J F

911. Locke to James Tyrrell, [14/24 February 1687?] (889, 932)
Boyle, Works, ed. Birch, 1744, v. 621. Excerpt from a letter of Locke's sent by Tyrrell to Boyle on 25 May 1687; it is not stated whether Tyrrell sent part of Locke's letter or a copy of the passage. The excerpt presumably comes from one of the two letters from Locke mentioned by Tyrrell in his letter of 6 May (p. 189). One of the two was probably that written on 14/24 February in answer to Tyrrell's letter of 26 December 1686 (no. 889); as in his letter Tyrrell asked Locke for his opinions of Burnet's New Theory, this excerpt may well come from the answer. Tyrrell was evidently dilatory in his correspondence at this time, so that the long period before he sent the excerpt to Boyle presents no difficulty. Answered by no. 932.
The New Theory of the Earth I have read in English, and cannot but like the style and way of writing upon thoughts wholly a man's own; but since you desire my opinion, as to the treatise itself, though it be a good while since I read it, and that but cursorily; yet there sticks with me still some of those objections, which rose in my way as I perused it, and which offered themselves against the truth or probability of his hypothesis, which made me not able then to reconcile it either to philosophy,†1 scripture, or itself. In the first part (as I remember) he makes the globe of the earth round, both by its schemes and hypothesis of its formation; and in the second part oval, without giving (as I remember) any reason for it. He makes the circulation of the water to be drawn up by the sun as now, but all the clouds to go and empty themselves at the poles only. How he makes out the physical reason of this motion, I do not well remember, but this I am sure of, by this means there could be no rivers; for all the water that should fall in those parts he designs for it, must needs in that state he puts the world in (the sun being constantly in the equator,) must needs have fallen frozen, and so remained in mountains of snow. But granting water, though without a sea, where lived the whales mentioned in the creation? But that, which seems to be the principle of his design, to make out (viz.) the history of the Flood, is that methinks, which he hath least succeeded in: for when this crust of earth broke, what hindered the broken pieces from sinking down into the abyss, and so being quite lost under water? And if the middle of the world, which lay under the sun, was that, which first failed, how comes it, that we find so much of the torrid zone above water? But if we may judge
― 140 ―

by the Andes (one of the highest and longest tracts of hills in the world) the crack (if there were any) seems to run the other way: but that which seems most incomprehensible of all is, how the water, that is now in the world, and was in his account no more then, could cover the tops of the highest hills, and remain above them so long a time as Moses mentions; for the flashing†1 of it, upon the falling in of the earth, (which is the cause he assigns) will be found (if considered) impossible to raise them†2 so high, much less to continue them there so long. I imagine, if I should trouble you with my fancies, I could give you an hypothesis would explain the deluge without half the difficulties, which seem to me to cumber this; but though I tell you, that I am not convinced of his doctrine, and have here sent you some of those doubts, which I had in reading of him, which is now almost two years ago; yet I must also assure you, that there are some chapters in him, that I cannot enough value, and the book is to be esteemed were it for those only.
912. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 16/26 February 1687 (905, 913)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 5-6. Answered by no. 913.
(English) Ecce iterum commodam te interpellandi, Vir præstantissime, oblatam occasionem. Epistola ex Anglia hodie ad me deferetur; alteram Wetstenius heri ad me misit; verum ego sera vespera domum rediens, eam non vidi nisi post tabellarii abitum. Duas itaque simul mitto. Mirantur omnes collegæ nostri, tam altum ubique de te silentium. Quid agas, quibuscum vivas, an tibi bene sit, plane ignorant. Harpocrati†3 te nimium familiarem credunt; orant, ne te
― 141 ―

totum illi consacres: Deus enim ille amicitiæ præses non est; et cum Dea Suada ac Gratiæ te sibi elegerint hospitem amicissimum, nullum cum Deo ipsis adverso commercium habeas. Hoc unum tibi persuasum habeto, nihil nobis gratius esse, quam ut tibi bene sit; non minima autem fœlicitatis nostræ pars est versari inter homines moribus ac studiis nobis similes, quibuscum aperte nos agere posse persuasi sumus. Si talium tibi copia adsit, gaudemus: si a talibus seclusus vivas, non miramur te illic Harpocratem agere: sed silentium illud tuum apud nos prolixiore confabulatione compensa. Postquam duobus conventibus de amœnioribus quibusdam ex itinerario alicujus manuscripto, quod prælectum fuit, aliqui sermones fuere habiti, nudius tertius tractatum D. Boyle de natura†1 legere incipimus: ita sensim exercitia intermissa repetimus. Tractatum meum contra Judæum ob summam typographi tarditatem gradu adeo lento procedere doleo: vereor ne partus sit futurus elephantinus,†2 aut si quis elephantino tardior est. Malim eum jam typis descriptum exstare: Vix enim mihi tempero, quin aliquoties in manus resumam, et inter relegendum quædam
― 142 ―

immutem, deleam, addam; utinam corrigam! Vale præstantissime vir, et plurimum salve a me et mea. Salutant omnes collegæ.
Tui amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 26 Februarii
 
(Latin) Once again a convenient opportunity of addressing you has presented itself, eminent Sir. A letter from England has reached me today; Wetstein sent me another yesterday; but coming home late in the evening I did not see it until after the post was gone. Accordingly I am sending you the two together. All our Collegians wonder at the profound silence which everywhere prevails concerning you. What you are doing, with whom you are passing your time, whether all goes well with you—of all these things they know absolutely nothing. They believe that you are too intimate with Harpocrates;†3 they beg [p. 141] you not to devote yourself entirely to him; for that god is not one that presides over friendship; and since the goddess Persuasion and the Graces have chosen you for their most congenial host, you should have no dealings with a god who is their adversary. You may be certain of one thing, that nothing is nearer our hearts than that all should be well with you; now, not the least part of our happiness consists in associating with people of like ways and interests with our own, with whom we feel able to deal freely. If you have enough of such with you, we are glad; if you are cut off from them, then we are not surprised that you play Harpocrates; but you must make up for that silence of yours by longer discourse with us. After we had held two meetings, at which there was some discussion on the more interesting points in a certain traveller's manuscript which was read to us, we started the day before yesterday on the reading of Mr. Boyle's treatise on nature;†1 thus we are gradually resuming our interrupted exercises. I am sorry that owing to the dilatoriness of the printer my treatise against the Jew is proceeding so slowly; I fear that the delivery is likely to resemble the elephant's,†2 or one even longer delayed, if such there be. I wish it were now in print; I can hardly resist the temptation of picking it up from time to time and whilst rereading it of [p. 142] making some change, erasure, or addition—I wish I could say correction. Good-bye, eminent Sir, my wife and I send you our warmest greetings, as do all our Collegians.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 26 February
Address: Præstantissimo doctissimo viro D. Joanni Locke
Endorsed by Locke: P.Limborch 26 Feb 87

(English) 
Mar. 8†a
Vir Reverendissime, Amicissime, Colendissime
Sine fati et ineluctabili prædistanationis vi experior in meipso quomodo peccandi initia <quandam>†b sensim afferunt secum peccandi necessitatem. Literis tuis amicissimis 9o et 15o Februarii datas respondendendi quam primum eas acceperam ansam mihi eripuit rei alicujus agendæ importuna tum festinatio. Sed cum peracto cum eo quocum mihi res erat negotio jam decessus illius in
― 143 ―

Angliam†1 mihi fecerit otium, satis ad literas scribendas vacare mihi videor, nondum tamen nactus sum eam quâ aliàs usus sum scribendi libertate. In hoc silentii crimen rebus aliis impeditus quasi inscius incidi miser, quod jam tempore auctum pene confirmat pudor. Sic delicta delictis cumulamus semel irretiti. et modesti pariter ac pervicaces in vitiis suis indurescunt. Vides quo in statu jam sum, et nisi credere me vis omnia certâ et immutabili necessitate evenire negligentiæ huic meæ ignoscere debes, ut redeat mihi antiqua mea apud Te parrhesia. De Germanâ Patrum Theologiâ†2 idem tecum plane sentio. maxima semper fuit semperque erit Germanorum natio, et pauci sunt in tanta scriptorum multitudine, qui non videntur eo sub aere nati.†3 Sed me hac de re a tua opinione non esse alienum non multum miraberis. aliquid amplius fateor est quod ego numeros tuos secretos notaverim, et quod tu hoc observaveris.†4 Cave tibi, et ignosce quam primum silentio meo, ne loquacitate mea tibi magis sim molestus, vides me in secretiora tua penetrare. Scire volunt secreta domus—et nosti quid sequitur—
― 144 ―

et inde timeri.†1 magicæ hæ metuendæ sunt artes nimis perspicaces, quibus ego non parum mihi placeo, quandoquidem ex tam jucundo tam laudabili enascuntur fonte et id mihi testatum faciunt quod ante omnia cupio. Scio jam mentem meam a tuâ, harmonicâ quadam sympathiâ regi plane et gubernari. Sic me orthodoxum semper fore certum est, O utinam et eodem modo et sciens fieri possim. Ut enim verum fatear inscius tuis numeris usus sum, sed gaudeo me prodiisse tenus. Vellem et in aliis rebus hoc mihi accideret. agnosco genium tuum, cui me ducendum totum libenter traderem. Gratias ago quam maximas pro omni tuâ curâ et operâ, in literis, in libris, et aliis meis rebus locatâ. utinam daretur et vices rependere. Vale et me ama tui Amantissimum
J. LOCKE
 
(English) Veenium Guenellonem reliquosque meos amicos meo nomine quæso salutes
Festinato opus non est ut hæc inclusa tradatur. Satis mature erit quando domum tuam venerit. Salutem ipsi meo nomine plurimam dicas
(Latin) 
Mar.8
Most revered, friendly and honoured Sir,
Without the compulsion of fate and ineluctable predestination I am learning by personal experience how first steps in sin gradually bring with them a certain necessity of sinning. The opportunity I had to reply to your most friendly letters of 9 and 15 February as soon as I got them was snatched from me by the troublesome hurry I was then in to deal with some matter of business. But as I have now settled the matter with the person concerned and [p. 143] his departure for England†1 has given me some leisure I seem to have time enough for writing letters, although I have not yet recovered the liberty in that respect which I have enjoyed at other times. It is through being hampered by other affairs that I have fallen, poor wretch, as it were unconsciously into this criminal habit of silence, which is now almost confirmed by shame, aggravated as it is by lapse of time. So it is that we heap transgressions on transgressions when we are once in the toils, and moderate and persistent offenders alike become hardened in their faults. You see what state I am now in, and unless you wish me to believe that everything happens by certain and immutable necessity you must forgive this negligence of mine, so that I may recover my old freedom of speech with you. About German patristic theology†2 I thoroughly agree with you. The German nation was always a very large one and always will be, and few there are in all that multitude of writers who do not seem to have been born in that climate.†3 But you will not be much surprised at my not differing from you on that subject. There is something more I confess: the fact that I dated my letters with your secret numbers, and that you observed it.†4 Beware then, and pardon my silence as soon as you can, lest I prove a greater nuisance to you with my loquacity; you observe that I am penetrating into your secrets. 'They want to know the secrets of the house'—and you remember what follows [p. 144] —'and to be feared for that knowledge'.†1 These too transparent magical arts are certainly to be feared; I plume myself not a little on them, seeing that they spring from a source as delightful as it is praiseworthy, whilst they afford me evidence of what before all things I desire. I know now that my mind is assuredly ruled and guided by yours through a certain harmonic sympathy. It is thus certain that I shall always be orthodox; would that by the same means I might be made knowledgeable as well. For, to tell the truth, I used your numbers in ignorance, but I am delighted to have made such progress. I could wish that this might happen to me in other things too. I recognize your genius, and I would gladly commit myself entire to its guidance. I give you my best thanks for all your care and help given me in letters, in books, and in my other affairs; I only wish I might be enabled to make a suitable return for it. Good-bye, and love me your most affectionate
J. LOCKE.
(Latin) Please remember me to Veen, Guenellon, and the rest of my friends.
There is no need for hurry in passing on the enclosed letter. It will be time enough when he calls on you at your house. Please remember me to him.
Address: Aen Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch by de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keysars Gracht tot Amsterdam
Postmark: Amsterdam 3S

Vir Ornatissime Doctissimeque
Nactus tandem commodam occasionem, mitto quod ante aliquod tempus promiseram Tralliani Græcum exemplar a Roberto Stephano editum, cui adjunctus est Rhazæ περὶ λοιμικῆς libellus.†1 Si textûs puritas æquet characteris nitorem spero hunc librum tibi non displiciturum. Utut sit boni consulas rogo tenue hoc munusculum, Quod etsi tam beneficiorum tuorum magnitudini, quam voluntati meæ parum respondeat ausus sum tamen ad te mittere apud quem exulantium jam pene ubique Græcarum literarum monumenta inveniunt perfugium. Suetonium a Te editum†2 frustra quæro. Vides quantam antiquis scriptoribus gratiam conciliat tua docta manus. Si quod apud bibliopolas vestros reliquum sit exemplar rogo ut mihi emas. (Latin)
10 Mar. 87
Accomplished and learned Sir,
Having at last got a convenient opportunity, I am sending you what I had promised some time ago, a copy of Trallianus in Greek, edited by Robert Estienne, together with which is Rhazes's small book περὶ λοιμικῆς.†1 If the text is as sound as the type is clear I hope that this book will meet with your approval. However that may be, please take this small gift in good part; though it corresponds as little to the greatness of your kindnesses as it does to my own wishes, yet I have presumed to send it to you as to one with whom the monuments of Greek learning, now in exile almost everywhere, find a refuge. I have been looking in vain for your edition of Suetonius.†2 You see the power of your scholarly hand in procuring favour for ancient writers. If there should be any copy left with your booksellers I beg you to buy it for me and to hand it to Mr Ward, the English knight,†3 by whom I am sending you this letter. He will repay you the cost of the Suetonius. He is lodging at [p. 146] a painter's, Van Gulick†1 by name, next to St. Peter's Church. If you also have anything you wish to tell me by letter about the matters we discussed together in our friend Sladus's garden,†2 please hand it to the same Mr Ward, who will see that it reaches me without fail. Nowhere do I so much enjoy and look forward to staying as at a place where I can have you and our excellent friend de Greve†3 as neighbours. Please give him my best respects. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and love me
Your most obedient servant
J. LOCKE
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Grævius professeur en histoire et Rhetorique à Utrecht

915. John Freke to Locke, 1 March 1687, with postscript by Sir Walter Yonge (909, 920; 902, 925)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 163-4.
March the 1/10 1686/7
Dear Sir
You are very unjust to your self and to me when you call your Letters idle and say their frequency needs excuse. Nothing can come from your pen that is not extremely entertaining: and I should think I had a very vicious pallat could I relish any pleasure (this Town can afford) like that of reading your ingenious and desireable Letters. Let me not then want what I soe much value! Bestow a few leisure minutes on me! as often as your goodness and friendship prompts you to it! and doe not fancy that any thing or any News
― 147 ―
can be more acceptable to me than that of your wellfare and the continuance of your kindness to me. you can at noe time nor in any place want what will render your Letters most valueable to me soe that you need not make such long pauses between your writing to find an occasion and a subject that shall be agreeable. I must confess I ought to blush when I thus sollicit the frequent repetition of your favours to me when I have soe long deferrd to thank you for your last of Febr the 2d but I hope you will pardon me when I tell you that I commissiond mr Cl†1 to doe it for me and to tell you that I deferrd writing till I could give you the history of the Fairy Gold which our friend this morning read in the very Notes taken by P B: (at the time it happen) and repeated to me to this effect. Anno 1658 The Gentleman was a Student of the Law and lodged in a chamber in E Court†2 in the Temple to which there was an Antichamber common to him and another but none had a key to his apartment but himself. One night coming into his chamber in the dark and laying down his Gloves on a table where he had a Tinderbox and going to strike fire he felt a piece of money which he thought a broad shilling†3 but having lighted his candle found to be a piece of Jacobus Gold worth 20s. about a fortnight after coming home late again in the same manner and in the same place he found such another piece of Gold which gave him many thoughts how the one and the other should come there and not being able to imagine how it could be put in that place by any humane creature he concluded it came there by an extraordinary and unaccountable means and flatterd himself with hopes that his good fortune would continue which made him every night for about 6 weeks look dilligently as soon as he had lighted his candell to find more gold but till his hopes were Worn out and he had noe more expectations of it he found none but then coming carelessly home again and laying down his Gloves as usually he felt two pieces which proved like the two former. In this manner at uncertain distances of time when he had noe thoughts of any such thing he found some times one some times two such pieces in all to the number of 2 or three and twenty (some of which his wife has yet in her custody) but at 3 Quarters End a Lady related to him visiting him saw in his Study one of the pieces of Gold and thinking he had got it by his
― 148 ―
profession congratulated his gain whereupon he told her the Story and she immediately prophesied he would find noe more which proved true though he continued to lodge in the same chamber severall years after. The Gentleman desires his name may be conceald in the story and made some scruple of shewing his notes but was at last prevaild on by our Friend on condition his name should not be made publick on this occasion which therefore I must desire of you. Our Friend that procured me the truth of this Story goes tomorrow into the country with his Family and our Devon friends†1 have taken coach for Fryday, but I suppose both the men will return hither again in Easter Term†2 without the Lady's though one of them hopes she shall and promises her self She shall meet you here by that time. I assure you both She and Mr D and all your fellow Travailers depend much on your coming and have their hearts soe set on it that I know not how they would be able to bear a dissappointment. There is not one of them but Esteems you as you desire and long for the advantages of your conversation and some of them think their life and health depend on it. The Fat Gentleman†3 would pine if he had not hopes of seeing you, and esteem him self in a desperate condition. And I must confess I am one of those also that wish you here since I am like to continue soe for my Cousin P†a †4 and I have met but are not like to accord, for he makes me noe overture but of Land for mony and I shall not turn planter†b nor will I ask any thing else of him. if he offer nothing I shall let the matter Dy Nor can I think of any other part of America†c through the discouragement occasiond by the News from Carolina†d where the Spaniards have made a Discent and Destroy'd and pillaged many plantations, though I doe not hear they have killd above Six persons.†e †5
― 149 ―
I acquainted Mr S:†1 with that part of your Letter which concernd him Just as he was going the Circuit and he bid me return you his thanks and says he shall enjoy it all his Journey and hopes noe better enjoyment till he is made more happy by your personall conversation which he likewise expects at his return to Town.
Your friend Mr Charleton who now likewise owns the name of Courteen†2 is alive and well but soe busie that he is seldom to be found at home. I was feign after many vain attempts to deliver him your Letter to leave it with his Laundress but I have once been soe lucky to see him and his Curiositys alsoe.
I shewd Sir W what you writt concerning him and got your Factum from Father Richardson†3 and deliverd it him this day. the old Gentleman seldom goes out of his chamber says he is ill perpetually troubled with the Stone but looks well and healthy and speaks hearty as he did when he commanded me to give you his service.
The Instances on the Charracters of Testimonys are obvious†4 but if they were not I should not write them but deferr the communicating them till by a personall conversation you make happy
Sir
Your affectionate friend and obliged humble servant
J FREKE
There is a proclamation of Indulgence in Scotland which we dayly expect to see here in print and then besure twill goe over sea.†5 Send therefore to our friend at Rotterdam†6 to get it for you for tis worth your reading

I desire the favor you doe me may be with as little trouble to yourselfe as may be, and that you would come and perfect my Library and reap some of

916. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 3/13 March [1687] (910, 919)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 150. Year from Locke's endorsement.

Jeudi ce 13. mars
Il n'est rien de si vray, Monsieur, que ceque je vous ay mandé, que les Pierres à filtrer se trouvoient aux Canaries, et même qu'eles y sont assez communes. Vous pourez en tirer de la par votre compagnie qui y fait grand commerce de vins.†1
Quelque perquisition que nous aions faite dans les ecrits et entre les pierres de mr Godefroi, nous n'y avons rien trouvé qu'une pierre qui est une maniere de fungus petrifié tres poreux, aiant des trous come une morille, mais je vous diray come le sachant d'ailleurs tres bien.
1. Que ce mien ami qui est à Paris, come je viens de laprendre de son frere qui est depuis peu de retour de la campagne, a deux pierres de cete nature qu'il a eües à Cadis. Eles sont à peu pres plates comme un bassin, aiant huit a neuf pouces de profondeur, et pres de quatre d'epais. Eles sont grisatres, et d'une matiere come de grez.†2 tienenent plus de trente livres d'eau, qui est assez long tems à passer. Il les a emportées toutes deux à Paris ou il s'est alé etablir,
― 151 ―
afin d'y passer l'eau de Paris, dont neanmoins il ne se sert gueres. Si j'etois à Paris, je tacherois d'en obtenir une de lui qui est cassée, et je vous l'enverrois pour que vous en fissiez vos epreuves.
2. Qu'une autre voiageur de mes amis qui est ici, en homme de creance m'a dit en avoir vu plusieurs en divers ports de mer, toutes venües des Canaries, et qu'il a eté dans un lieu ou lon en metoit trois l'une sur l'autre.
3. Enfin qu'il y a à Paris un marchand apelé de Laitre, demeurant dans la rüe St Denis proche les filles Penitentes, qui en a une belle, dont on vient de me donner avis, et je vous en donneray bien tost une ample instruction suivant les ordres que j'espere que l'on executera. On m'a ecrit qu'il la vouloit vendre, mais non pas donner: car il demande trente pistoles, et il dit aussi qu'ele est venüe des Canaries. Songez à en tirer de la. car la chose est assurée, aussi que tous les Triu<mvir>s†a vous salüent, et moi particulierement qui suis plus que <je ne le>†a saurois dire.
Votre—

918. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 14 March 1687 (903, 933)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 11-12. Forwarded by Freke on 21 March: no. 920.
Otterton March: 14th. 1686.
Dear Sir
Your silence is most unsufferable, I know not how to unriddle it, or how to bear it. that you should write to me but twice in six months absence; or three times, (for one letter I am told was lost in carriage;) is not congruous to the pleasure you once seem'd to take in my conversation, to the Freindship you profess to have for me. 'tis not I hope, of that sort that distance of place, or length of time, at least so short a time as six Months, can efface or blot out; 'tis impossible that the Excellent Mr Lock should be Changable, who understands Friendship so perfectly, and is a Pattern of it to all Mankind; and of Complaisance and good Nature too, how then comes it to pass that he uses me so ill, and gives me so much reason to complain that I cannot by any importunity obtain a more frequent Correspondence, or so much as a direct answer whither I may hope to see you in England this Spring or not; is methinks very hard. You cannot be ignorant how uneasie it makes me, for I sent you a letter full of Complaints the beginning of Feb: as I remember, and another about ten dayes after; and I cannot doubt their comming safe to your hands, since I enclosed them to my Brother, who sent them with the same directions, which have carried all his and all mr Frekes to you; but it seems mine are lost, for they have no influence on you, I now begin to despair of ever hearing from you more; for since my last, I have made a Journey to London, where I tarried a full fortnight, I am return'd and have been at Home again a Week, and yet my Doctor, my Father, does not remember me. Surely a post letter might more easily be conveyed, then my self, who have travell'd 300 Miles this last Month; why then are yours so long a comming; it puts me beyond all Patience; have you no consideration left either for the Health of my body, or the Ease of my mind, that you thus abandon me; You that were so tender, so kind before our last Separation; what have I done since, how have I forfeited your esteem, your kindness, in which I thought my self so rich, so happy. did you bestow it on me, only to make me know the worth of it, that I might feel the loss of it, sure it cannot be, you are not capable of doing so ill a thing, what
― 154 ―
then can it be; put me out of pain my dear Freind, and let me know what I must trust to. would to Heaven that I knew how to press you so as to prevail with You; if this does not procure me an answer, 'twill be in vain for me to write any more; and I will not, if I can so far command my self; I had almost resolved it when I wrote last, but I could not forbear making this one Essay more; which perhaps may be the last, for if it does not obtain a letter from you, I must conclude that you are willing to Ease your self of so impertinent, so troublesome a Conversation. but I will hope better things, and that you design only to try me, but not to shake me off. Yet 'twill be Charity to tell me so by the first; my Brother return'd from London with me, and is now with Mr Duke at the Assizes at Exeter,†1 so that I have no particular services from them to You; but I can assure you that they are, with much affection and Gratitude Yours, and I have made such an interest for you with my Lanlady, during my short stay in London, that there is nothing but your presence wanting to secure you a considerable share in her esteem, and Friendship too; which she is as capable of as any Woman I know; and nothing but your using me ill, can discourage her from desiring Yours. for your own sake then, as well as for mine be not inexorable, but write to me speedily, and write to me kindly, and tell me when I shall see you, when I shall meet you at London; I shall otherwise be in danger of ruining my self, by putting my self into the hands of some Quack Doctress; (to which I was earnestly prest, when I was last in Town.) for I will never apply my self to any of your sex, if you do not help me; and what will become of my Master, Heaven only knows; I am sure neither of us grow better. but a touch on this subject is enough, let my need of you, and my impatient desires of your Company, prevail with you to hasten to, Dear Sir,
Your most Obliged Friend and most faithfull servant,
I. D.

919. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, [17/27 March 1687?] (916, 923)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 151-3. The date at the head of the letter appears to be that of the account of the filter sent to Toinard from Paris. At this time Toinard usually wrote to Locke on Thursdays; hence the proposed date for the letter.
+
De Paris le 23. mars 87.
1. La pierre à filtrer que j'ay veüe chez monsieur de Lêtre,†1 marchand demeurant rüe st Denis proche les filles Penitentes, n'a rien de diferent des pierres ordinaires à bâtir.
2. Ele n'est point polie. ele a quinze bons pouces de diametre par le haut, de dedans en dedans, et presque autant de profondeur, et ressemble ainsi à un grand mortier.
3. Ele est carrée par le haut, eu egard aux extremitèz de dehors, qui font quatre angles, etant ronde en dedans.
4. Ele a trois bons doits d'epaisseur par tout, et plus encore par le bas, à cequi me paroist par ou les liqueurs passent.
5. Ele est d'une pezanteur extraordinaire, et dans un cercle de fer, soutenuë par quatre barres de fer, qui lui servent de pied.
6. Ele a un defaut, qui consiste en une fente d'un côté, mais qui ne penetre pas, de sorte qu'il ne passe jamais rien par la, à ceque l'on m'a assuré, mais par les extremitèz du bas du vaisseau.
7. Ele tient un seau de porteur d'eau de Paris.†2
8. Il y a prez d'un an qu'ele n'a servi, de sorte que si on vouloit prezentement la remplir d'eau, le tout passeroit en moins d'un demi cart d'heure.
9. Si ele etoit abreuvée, il faudroit un jour ou deux pour faire passer l'eau; cequi n'empecheroit pas que cequi passeroit ne fust fort clair et fort epuré.
10. Ele se netoie avec des balais ou brosses ou autres choses quand on a passé des eaux bourbeuses ou autres liqueurs.
11. L'année derniere 86. on la fit travailler jour et nuit pendant trois ou quatre mois parceque l'on ne pouvoit fournir aux pauvres et autres qui venoient demander de l'eau qui y avoit passé, et qui n'en avoient pas bu trois fois leur sou, qu'ils etoient gueris de fievres et autres incommoditéz.
12. On a observé que l'eau qui en sort, est quasi une fois plus legere que cele de la Riviere de Seine, dans sa plus grande pureté;
― 156 ―
et qu'ele n'incommode jamais, quelque quantité qu'on en puisse boire.
13. ceque je vous avois mandé dans ma precedente n'est pas vray, savoir que si l'on metoit une pinte d'eau dans le vaisseau, il n'en passeroit pas une goute qu'auparavant il ne fust tout abreuvé. Le tout seroit passé en un moment, si la pierre n'avoit point travaillé de long tems.
14. Je scai que le Pere du Moulinet†1 s'en veut acommoder par le moien d'un Religieux de la maison, parent du proprietaire.
Huc usque.†2
Voila, monsieur, ce qu'un tres honête homme de mes meilleurs amis, me mande touchant la pierre à filtrer, dont je lui avois recommandé de s'informer, pour satisfaire à lhonneur de vos ordres.
Je vous ay desja mandé que l'on la fait trente pistoles, mais aparemment ce ne sera pas le dernier mot.
mandez moi si vous avez envie de l'avoir, au quel cas je la feray negocier au meilleur conte qu'il se poura, et la païeray.
Que si l'excez du prix ou la dificulté de vous la faire tenir surement, vous en degoûtent, mandez moi si sa seule qualité colatoire, (pour me servir de ce terme,) est d'une si grande consequence dans la medecine qu'il ne faille pas manquer l'ocasion de l'avoir; car alors je la pourois bien prendre pour moi même.
Il est constant qu'il s'en trouve à Cadix, qui vienent de la grande Canarie, ou il y en a sur le bord de la mer, à cequ'un voiageur curieux m'a assuré: mais il ne s'en trouverra pas peutêtre de si grandes ny de si profondes à Cadix, et celleci est toute portée à Paris.
Le contenu en l'article 11. m'est suspect, et cequi est dans le 12. est absolument faux ad stateram; car j'ay autrefois ouï dire à monsieur Roberval,†3 grand mathematicien et fort exact, que l'eau de mer ne pezoit pas plus d'une quarante deuxiême au dessus de celle de la Seine. ainsi cete pretenduë legereté n'est tout au plus qu'ad sensum.†4
J'ay apris cete bele distinction d'ad stateram et ad sensum dans un petit livre De staticâ medicinâ, composé dans le siecle dernier par Santorio Santorini medecin de Padoüe.†5 Je l'ay preté il y a plus de trente ans à quelcun qui ne me la pas rendu, et onques depuis ne
― 157 ―
l'ay vu. Je crois que vous pouvez bien savoir la veritable raison pourquoi on perd souvent les livres que l'on prete, comme il ne m'est que trop arivé: c'est qu'il est plus aisé de retenir un livre que cequi est dedans.
Le P. du moulinet,†1 dont il est parlé, art. 14. est un de mes meilleurs amis; Il est religieux de ste Genevieve de Paris, ou il a un beau cabinet, dont il est fort communicatif. Il a les coins du Padoüan,†2 qui estoit un fameux faiseur de fausse monnoie du siecle passé, en matiere de medailles antiques. Il a aussi le congius Romain dont se servirent messieurs Peiresck et Gassendi pour trouver la proportion des mesures et poids des anciens avec les nôtres.†3 ce congius est tiré sur celui de Vespasien, qui est dans le Palais Farneze, dont Villalpandus sur Ezechiel donne les proportions et la figure.†4
Il y a 16. ou 17. ans que monsieur l'Abé Picard et monsieur de ste Colombe, aupres desquels je me suis fait honneur de votre connoissance, que je leur ay communiquée, firent la même experience. J'ay etois prezent, et je servois tout au moins et aussi tout au plus de soufleur d'orgues. monsieur l'Abé Picard avoit la plume et emportoit tous les calculs, dont il s'etoit chargé de faire les reductions. Je ne me suis jamais avisé de les lui demander de son vivant et l'on ne sait ceque cela est devenu. c'est une grande perte. Il y en a seulement quelque chose sans preuve dans le livret intitulé: Connoissance des tems, pag. 92. de l'Edition de 81. que j'ay sous la main.†5
L'Extrait que vous m'avez envoié des Acta Eruditorum anni 82. p. 389. n'est pas bien clair car Et cum in Galliis essem, vidi genus lapidis qui primâ statim vice liquores insipidos transmittebat, credoque adhuc vivere qui locum indicare possit.†6 semble à la verité dire que le lieu d'ou on tiroit ces pierres etoit en France, mais le peu d'exactitude qu'il y a dans
― 158 ―
ce raport, ou le lieu de France ou a eté veu ce genus lapidis, n'est point articulé, ny comment s'apeloit celui chez lequel il a eté veu, fait que ce voiageur auroit bien pu voir en France une de ces sortes de pierres, et qu'il auroit cru s'y trouver.
Je m'etois mepris touchant la pierre à filtrer à legard de feu mr Godefroi. Je reverray son fils touchant la racine, et m'en informeray aussi à d'autres.
Le deux Triumvirs vous salüent, et moi principalement qui suis
On me prie d'envoier en Holande ceque j'ay sur Lactance de Mortibus Persecutorum, parcequ'un Mr Galé de ce païs la en doit donner une Edition Variorum, dont il y en a desja trois, compris celle d'Aboæ à ces prochaines maisons en Finlande. mais je ne suis pas dans une conjoncture à pouvoir metre cela au net. De plus cela ne se peut bien imprimer qu'in quarto à cause des tables chronologiques, et les Hollandois ont l'octavomanie en tête.†1
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke Gentilhomme Anglois A Amstredam
Endorsed by Locke: Toinard 23 Mar 87
920. John Freke to Locke, 21 March 1687 (915, 934)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 165-6. No. 918 was enclosed.
March the 21/31 1686/7
Dear Sir
This comes onely as a wrapper to cover the inclosed but I must not let it goe without my thanks for yours of the 11/21 which was full
― 159 ―
of obligations I shall always very freely acknowledge to you. I have shewn your Cento etc: on Te†1 to severall of our Poets and many of them are not a little pleased with the conceit. I must confess I love to amuse my self with such things much more than I delight in any of our modern controversies or productions to all which I carefully keep my self a stranger as much a stranger as I believe I shall ever be to America though I was once soe much set on visiting it but my kinsman†2 has offerd me nothing but Land for mony and I tell him I had rather buy in Ireland than Pensylvania†a and should promise my self sooner to be enricht by it had I a mind to be Rich as I thank God I have not. I wish you had told me whither you intend to ramble this spring or stay where you are because I am undetermin'd what to doe with my self and would feign dispose of my self by your Judgement, for having quitted my profession I can be any where and should choose to be where I might be made happy by your conversation either at home or abroad for though I think I shall not be satisfyd without travailing once more yet I could be contented to deferr my Journey till towards Autumn if I could have your company here this Summer. As to the Story of the Fairy Gold I am apt to think the Gentleman came by it a way he do's not care to declare and therefore invented that Romance and writt it down that he might be sure always to remember to tell it the same way But I would be glad to know from whom the pieces were taken when given to him for they were coynd in England and not Fairy Land. The Lady you inquire after was the person that writt the enclosed who came to Town and stayd about a fortnight here in hopes to have marryd a sister but those hopes being vanisht she and her sister went with their brother into the country whence she hopes to return hither again to meet you as my last told you which is all I have time to tell you at presant saving that you shall always find me approve my self
Sir
Your most affectionate friend and humble servant
J F
Address: For Dr John Lock

il y a plus d'un mois que de jour a jour je differe a vous escrire. c'est bien le moindre de mes devoirs, mais tantost je vous crois a londres, tantost j'espere vostre retour et bien souvent l'embarras d'un bastiment tres difficile me met comme hors d'œuvre. vous aurez appris par Monsieur limburgh que la commission de Monsieur Cowls est executee: que je luy ay payé vingt ducatons et†a- 9 livres-†a cest a dire f66-12†1 pour le prix de l'option qui dure jusqu'au premier jour du mois de Mey prochain. je garde l'obligation datée du 1 mars jusqu'a vostre ordre, c'est assez plaissant que Monsieur Cowls a justement rencontré et marché avec le meschant voisin de mon beau pere†2 Le candele. combien chetif quil soit a nostre esgard il est pourtant assez bon pour vostre garant.
Monsieur charleton ma fait l'honneur de me respondre il me demande Gorlæi numismata†3 et bibliotheca orientalis et occidentalis.†4 le premier ne se rencontre que tres rarement a vendre, j'espieray l'occasion de quelque auction. pour l'autre, pas un des libraires ou je me suis informe ne le connoist. Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P GUENELLON

Dear Cosin
I Received your Dated the 17th Feb 1686/7 and have this evening according to your order Made up my account of your Conserns and find that I have in my hands If I mistake not 7l: 11s: 8d: which mony I shall redyly pay on demand†1 as for what you propose by Mr Clarke I Cannot but Gratefully receive and thankfully accept what ever kindnes you designe for my Children and shall redyly serve you as I have don or any other way you shall propose as I have made up my account you have theare in perticular how it stands with all your tenants wheare in you meet with any disapoyntment it is really my conserns and Indeade I cannot Justly Blame my selfe for any neglect unles in Robert Horralls Afaires for Indeade wheare we let small Parsells it must bee to poore men wheare mony is not to bee had at all times I shall Indever to let with all the securyty I can

your kinsman and humble ser:

923. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 24 March/3 April 1687 (919, 945)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 154-5. Toinard answers a lost letter of Locke's: see no. 916 endorsement.

Jeudi ce 3. Avril 87
J'ay dans ma famille, monsieur, des gens qui ont vecu bien au dela de ma mere, que j'ay perdüe le 25. mars. Dans l'afliction ou je suis, rien ne me consoleroit tant que de pouvoir la recommander à vos prieres, come j'ay fait à celes de tous mes amis.
Les dix exemplaires Adversariorum, dont vous voulez me regaler, sufisent. mandez moi en quel livre ils sont impriméz ensemble.
Je vous ay mandé que les pierres à filtrer se trouvoient proche de la mer dans la grande Canarie, come me la dit ici un curieux de notre ville qui la apris à Cadiz, d'ou vous pouriez en tirer. Il s'y en trouve pluzieurs, et il y a des gens qui en metent deux l'une sur l'autre pour une double filtration.
On ne scait pas si leau salée laisseroit sa salûre par cete filtration. si j'etois à Paris ou je ne puis pas aler si tost à cause de mes afaires domestiques, je tâcherois d'avoir l'une des deux qu'a un de mes amis.
Je vous ay envoié une ample relation de cele de mr de Laitre qu'il fait trente pistoles: qui est bien bien†a de l'argent.
Mon opinion que vous demandez, quo V.T. textu usi sint Judæi tempore J.Ch.†1 est qu'ils avoient une vulgate Chaldaique, ou si vous voulez Syriaque, faites sur l'Hebreu, (come nous avons une Vulgate Latine,) qui diferoit de son original en plusieurs endroits. Je nescai comment on peu douter que les Caracteres Samaritains n'aient pas eté en usage devant la Captivité: dans lequel tems les Juifs oubliant leur langue et leurs usages, prirent la langue et les caracteres du païs, et même la maniere de conter les mois à φάσει†2 inconnue depuis moyse jusques la.
De sene 83. annorum aliàs, et de aliis plura. Vale et c.†3
― 163 ―
Je vous ay mandé que j'ay de beles letres chronologiques de feu mr De st Asaph, du Pere Pagi et du P Noris, deux excelens Peres pour les publier.†1 Il y a un Canon Chronologicus Trajani de mr de st Asaph,†2 qui est un echantillon admirable, quoique l'Auteur s'y soit trompé plus d'une fois
Maux d'avanture sont de petis mots qui vienent aux doits, come ampoules, et des engelûres, et piqûres et c.
Come je †a letre, j'ay receu visite du Capitaine Grand vicaire avec une letre de Mylord Bishop de notre ville†3 sur la perte que j'ay faite. Il ne se peut rien de plus obligeant pour moi.
Le Cap. vous salüe. Je verray demain l'autre Triumvir.
Address: A monsieur Monsieur John Locke Gentilhome Anglois A Amstredam
