924. Edward Clarke to Locke, 26 March 1687 (907, 927)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 29-30. Printed in Rand, pp. 197-200.
Chipley the 26th. of March 1687.
Deare Sir
When I writt to you on the 23th. I had only time enough to lett you Know that I was then newly Return'd from Sutton-Court without being able to give you any Accompt of what success I had in those things your desires lead mee particularly to inquire into there, And therefore I take this first opportunity to acquaint you that imediately upon my Arrivall there (tho it was late) I sent to Mr. Stratton to desire that I might speake with Him early the next morning, and accordingly Hee came, and acknowlidg'd the Receipt of your Letter (which I convey'd to Him) and the Contents of it, But excus'd His not being ready with the Particulars of
― 164 ―
His Accompt, by the want of time to perfect the same, And seem'd to be much concern'd that Hee had it not ready for mee as you desiered in your Letter, and promised I should have it in two dayes time, I told Him I would tarry purposely for it, and resolv'd to spend that time in visitting my Freinds and acquaintance in those Parts, When that time was verie neere expired, He came againe to mee with the Beginings of a particular Accompt, Which (as farr as it went) appeared to mee to bee fayre and reasonable, and told mee that Hee intended to pursue the same Method for the Remaining parts of it, but said that Hee could not possibly perfect the same to lett mee have it unlesse my time would permitt mee to stay 3. or 4. dayes longer there, Which, I could not possibly doe being under an absolute necessity of Returning hither againe within that time, soe that I could not thinke of any other expedient, but for Him to perfect the Accompt by the Assises, and send it to mee from thence by some safe hand, Which, Hee promis'd Faithfully to performe, and I am in dayly expectations of it, the Assises being ended yesterday;†1 I am troubl'd that my occasions would not permitt my stay at Sutton untill this had been done, that I might have Examin'd the Particulars of the Accompt with Him, But if there bee any judgment to bee made by that small part which I saw, it will appeare to bee just, And I beleive Him to bee honest, but slow and uncertaine in all His actions, And therefore I was for some time in doubt with my selfe (the Accompt not being finish'd) Whither I should make your Proposeall to Him or not, untill I was determin'd in that by his asking of mee What you mean't by that expression in your Letter to Him, viz: That I had something to propose that would not bee to His prejudice, upon which (not being hansomly able to avoyd giveing Him an Answer to it) I told Him, That you had thoughts (when His Accompt should bee perfected to satisfaction) as an acknowlidgment of His paynes and Kindnesse in the lookeing after your concerns to settle on His two Children (by Mr. Lock's daughter) for theire Lives all the Estate you have in Fee at Belt<on>†a now in possession (not what is out upon Lease) Reserving a small <rent to>†b your Right heyres, And allsoe Reserveing, the same Annuall Rent, that the Estate was lett for when you
― 165 ―
delivered Him the Rent-Roll, to your selfe dureing your own Life to bee paid quarterly without any deduction for Rates Taxes Reparations or other charges whatsoever, with an absolute power of Revocation in you at any time upon default of payments of any part of the before mention'd Rent for the space of six moneths, And at all other times dureing your Life upon your Offer to pay Him Soe much as Hee shall make appeare to have been out of Pockett for the rates Taxes and reparations aforesaid, dureing the time that Hee shall have paid you the cleere yearely Rent aforesaid; Which Proposeall (when throughly understood) was well accepted, and Mr Stratton verie sencible of the Kindnesse you intended His Children therein, and sayes that when ever you please Hee will thankefully accept of such a settlement, and will take that Estate into his own propper mannagement and pay you the cleere yearely Rent aforesaid, soe that 'tis now in your owne Power to Please your selfe in this Particular, And I thinke a Settlement made by you in manner aforesaid is the only way whereby you can bee master of your Estate, and make the most of it dureing your owne Life, and with the least trouble, I am sure 'tis the best way I can thinke of, and therefore cannot but incourage you to proceed in it under this method, And when I have Received Mr. Strattons Accompt and perus'd it you shall have my thoughts thereupon, in the meane time give mee Leave to renew my thankes for your verie Kind Letter of the 11th. instant, and most particularly for your continu'd Care touching my Son's Education, in which, your method shall bee as punctually pursu'd as possible may bee, And I hope the Person that I have contracted with for that purpose†1 will answere our desires, but as yett I have had no experience of Him, by reason of a Feaver that seised Him about a Weeke or ten dayes before I came out of Town, Which confin'd Him to his chamber, and disabled Him from comeing into the Countrey with mee, But I heare of His Recovery and expect Him dayly here, and as soon as Hee hath been with mee for some time you may bee certaine I shall informe you particularly, and take the Liberty to aske your farther directions thereupon; And I beleive I shall allsoe imbrace your verie Kind offer touching the Freezland Ewes, but of that you may expect to heare further from mee in a short time, And allsoe of the Lyme-trees you sent mee, which are the finest I ever saw, and they being carefully Planted by John Barber†2 I Question not but they will grow and
― 166 ―
Prosper, but as yett I can have noe certainty of that, However give mee leave to send you my Wifes, my owne, and my sons hearty thankes for them, they are planted in a peice of Ground that lyes on the South-East-syde of my house, and will (if they thrive) afford greate Pleasure in a few-yeares; I will bee sure to have a good sound Ash-Tree fell'd on the 25th. day of May next as you direct, and shall waite untill you tell mee what use I shall make of it: The Poplar Cuttings that you sent mee I have Planted plentifully of both sorts of them, and have reason to beleive, the Populus Alba or Abeele Cuttings will grow as well as the other sort, your Spa Freinds have Planted severall of both sorts of them allsoe, and I beleive wee shall now in a little time bee certaine whither the Abeele Cuttings will grow or not, pray send mee word in your next which of the two makes the finest tree in Holland, and that will bee a further obligation upon,
Your most Faithfull Freind and servant
E.†a
Madam and all the younger Fry are Well, and give their best services to you etc:
Address: For Mr. John Locke These.

925. Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 29 March 1687 (915, 933)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 152-3.
Escott March 29th. 1687.
Dear Sir
If ever a letter from so perfect a friend could be unwellcome to me, your's of the 18th. would have been so, for giving me so fair a prospect of the advantages and pleasure of a former long letter you designed me (which never came to hand), and then telling me my loss is irreparable; but however mellancholy the subject of yours is I find it full of that friendship and Kindness (which I can never value enough) which will not suffer me to dispair of retriving what most concerned me in the lost letter, and since your fancy of being in my Library put you then into so gay a humour (of which I think I have reason to be very proud) pray put your selfe once more in the chair, and oblige me with some of those pleasant thoughts at your next leisure, especially what relates to the books and library, which I can not mention without telling you (once more) that I am at a great loss about the disposall of the roome designed for that use, and shall delay the fitting it up as long as may be in hopes of your assistance; And though the loss of these and other of your letters be a great grievance I could easily forgive the author of those dissappointments, if instead of making you uneasy in the place where you are, they could but dispose you to make us happy in your good company, to which methinks the season of the year joyned with the Charity it will be to severall of your friends should now invite you. My Brother and Sister Duke (who dined here to day) give you their best services, and she desired me to acquaint you that she wrote you a letter since her return from London, wherein she acquainted you that we had the company of our Sommersettshire friends†1 and Dr Tho: at Ivy-church, where you were much wished for by the whole company; and that she sent you that as her last unless she hears from you, being reduced to that low ebb by waiting so long in vain for a few lines from you that she has hardly faith enough left to beleive you have of a long time written to her at all; But I hope in a post or two she will receive a letter which will put an end to this quarrell, especially if you continue to write merrily as well as kindly; and never fear we
― 168 ―
shall complain of the length of your letters, which we esteeme one of our best entertainments in your absence. I am only troubled I have nothing to return from hence worth your perusall; what London affords you have from a better hand, and from hence I can send you nothing but the Love and services of your daughters with my humble thanks for your last favor and any other occasion you shall be so kind to give me of writing my selfe
Dear Sir
Your most obliged friend and faithfull servant
W. Y.
Address: For Mr John Lock These.
Endorsed by Locke: Sir W. Yonge 29 Mar.87 Answered 20 May
926. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 31 March/10 April [1687] (913, 931)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 255p. Printed in Ollion, p. 172. Year from van Limborch's note.
(English)
Apr. 10.†a
Dolendum mihi maxime est Te (Vir præstantissime) quod in me vitium agnosco esse frequens et inurbanum, velle imitari in scribendo sc: tarditatem. Hoc non dico quasi crederem tuam virtutem meo exemplo aliquo modo labifactatam, sed queror quod cum me miserè castiges, nihil enim gravius silentio tuo, id existimationi tuæ quâ me Tibi immitandum proponis, imputari velis. Sed nolo ego de me tam magnificè sentire, ut credam aliquid in me esse tam eximium quod vir Talis et Tantus debet imitari aut saltem si tibi
― 169 ―
persuasum sit hoc esse benevolentiæ et humanitatis tuæ, qui amicos tuos omni honoris genere cumulare satagis, quæso in posterum taciturnitas mea nunquam trahatur in exemplum. Vides quam in mea causa sum iniquus tibi non permitto quam mihi arrogo libertatem. Sed tu libertatis patronus ignosce in re mihi valde necessaria, Tuis enim literis carere nec possum nec debeo sic est in Fatis Tu videas. Opportune sane jam prodibit illud Episcopii scriptum†1 nec ille tam <instrenuus>†a miles cujus negligi debent subsidia cum jam undique vel infertur vel imminet bellum. Sed interim quo passu pergit contra Judæos scriptum? id potius quæro quia et tuum et Latinum. Dominum Le Clerc meo nomine quæso salutes, dicasque me nuper recepisse ex Anglia novum aliquod Sydenhami scriptum,†2 quod nondum legi, si librum ipsum vel ejus epitomen desideret, alterutrum, quod mallet, libenter ad illum mittam. Vale et me ama (Vir Spectatissime)
Tui amantissimum
J LOCKE

(Latin)
Apr. 10
It is a matter of deep sorrow to me, eminent Sir, that you choose to imitate what I acknowledge to be a frequent and unmannerly fault in myself, namely backwardness in writing. I do not say this as if I believed that your virtue was in any way undermined by my example; I only complain that when you punish me so cruelly—for there is nothing more distressing than your silence—you should be willing for this to be attributed to an opinion on your part that I am a model to be imitated by you. But I have no desire to think so highly of myself as to imagine that there is anything in me so superlative as to deserve imitation by one of your character and importance; or at any rate, [p. 169] if you are persuaded that this is consonant with your usual benevolence and considerateness—for you busy yourself with heaping every kind of honour upon your friends—I beg that for the future my own taciturnity may never be taken as an example. You see how unfair I am in pleading my cause: I do not allow you the liberty I claim for myself. But you, the champion of liberty, must exercise forgiveness in a matter that is one of sheer necessity for me: I neither can nor must be without letters from you; so it is ordained by the Fates. See to it, then. That work of Episcopius†1 will certainly be coming out at an opportune moment, nor is he so inactive a warrior that his support should be neglected at this time, when war is either launched or threatening on all hands. Meanwhile, however, how goes it with your writing against the Jews? I am more eager to know about that both because it is yours and because it is in Latin. Please remember me to Mr. Le Clerc, and tell him that I have recently received from England a new work of Sydenham's,†2 which I have not yet read; if he would like to have the book itself or an epitome of it I would be glad to send him one or other, whichever he might prefer. Good-bye, and love me, esteemed Sir,
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
[p. 170] I send my greetings to our common friends, and especially to your excellent wife.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch.

927. Edward Clarke to Locke, 4 April 1687 (924, 929)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 31. Printed in Rand, pp. 200-1.
Chipley Apr. 4th. 1687.
Deare Sir,
This serves to confirme what I writt to you on the 23th. of March last as to the time of my being in Town the next Terme,†1 And to lett you Know that I have now received Mr Strattons Accompt of your Rents under His Care and mannagement, with His Desires to convey the inclosed to you, by which you will see that on the Ballance thereof Hee makes himselfe Debtor to you in the summe of 07l: 11s: 08d½ The Accompt I have perus'd, and as far as I can judge of it (without haveing your own Rent-Roll to compare it withall, and the severall Bylls of Disbursements to Examine and consider of which are therein mentioned to bee allow'd and paid by Him)†a I beleive it to bee an honest and Just Accompt of those Rents soe far as Hee goes with it; But in regard the 31l. and odd money, which you left in his handes and gave Him a Receipt for in August 1683. when you Received the 5l. of Him, is not brought into this Accompt as it ought to have been, And to the intent you may bee the better and more fully satisfied in all other the Particulars of it, I will imbrace the first opportunity after my Arrivall in Town to send you the Accompt its' selfe to consider of, and thereby I beleive it will appeare to you (as it does now to mee) That Hee still owes you the 31l. and odd money over and besides the 07l: 11s: 08d½ that Hee makes Himselfe Debtor to you on the Ballance of the said Accompt; But I rather beleive this omission of His to bee through forgettfullnesse then by Designe, because that when
― 171 ―
I was last at Sutton and mention'd that Particular to Him, Hee readily own'd the truth of it, and said Hee would charge Himselfe with it; I shall not trouble you with any further observations of my own upon it, but submitt it to your better consideration and hopeing that my last of the 26th. of March is by this time in your handes, I conclude with all our hearty services to you, and Remaine in all sincerity,
Your most obleiged humble servant
E.†a

B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 68-9.
London the 12th of Aprill 1687
Dear Sir
Though I answered neither of your obliging letters till now yet sometime since I desired a verry good freind of yours and mine†1 to present you my service, and to send you a small booke which you formerly enquired after of which Dr. Barbyrac is said to be the Author†2 I hope it came to your hands. Dr. Goodall I presume ha's acquainted you that I gave him a draught of the Kinkina leafe you were pleased to present me, he told me that if he printed any thing Concerning it (if you saw fit) he would make mention of you,†3 and did at the same time tell me he would send me a letter for you, not knowing how to write to you, which letter I have expected ever since but I supose multiplicity of bussinesse prevented him, he is a verry worthy and ingenious Gentleman and I am verry much obliged to you for procuring me his acquaintance. A branch of the
― 172 ―
Cinamon tree you favoured me with amongst severall other raryties but I have none of the nutmeg tree either with, or without the fruit. I humbly thanke you for your designed kindnesse as to the draughts of the severall East Indian habitts,†1 but must request you to put me in a way of rendring you some service else I cannot with any Confidence Continue to be troublesome to you. I shall shortly send you a catalogue of such Curiosities as I want. In the mean time I desire that of your freinds†2 who am and ever shall continue to be
Sir
Your most devoted servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
It has pleased God to vissit my Lord Bridgewater's famyly with verry sad afflictions, the losse of my Lord Brackley and his brother, both were burnt in their bedds the last night about 12 a clock by the Carelessenesse of the servant that waited on them who was also burnt.†3

929. Locke to Edward Clarke, 19/29 April [1687] (927, 935)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 23. Written by an amanuensis (probably Syl) apart from the opening and closing words; some corrections by Locke and additions interpolated by him. Printed in Rand, pp. 201-12. Year from Clarke's endorsement. Answered by no. 935.
The letter belongs to the Education series: see note, ii. 624. Some passages are repeated in Some Thoughts concerning Education with little or no change; some are expanded; there are also connecting passages which correspond only roughly to passages in the book; and references to the Directions (K) sent to Clarke in 1684 and 1685. I have not tried to find all possible parallels for the last, and have not indicated textual divergences between the first (A) and third (C) editions of Some Thoughts.
Sir
Now that you have got a Tutor†a for your Son, and I set my self seriously to be thinke me what you should doe with him, I can
― 173 ―
hardly tell what to say; Not that I could not easily finde worke for him, but it is worke soe much out of the road, and thoughts, of those sort of people, that I am in doubt, whether he be not as much to learne that, as your Son is any thing he shall pretend to teach him.
That you may know, how well grounded this suspition is, give me leave to set before you again a short Epitome, of what I thinke, the true method of Education; and then be pleased to examine, how well these principles, and the pains must be taken to keepe to them, and instill them, agrees with the notions, and designes, of the Tutor you have got. 1°. He†1- that has not a mastery over his inclination, he that knows not†a how to resist the importunity of present pleasure, or pain, for the sake of what, reason tells him, is fit to be donne, wants the true principle of Vertue, and industry; and is in danger never to be good for anything. This temper therfor, soe contrary to unguided nature, is to be got betimes; and this habit, as the true foundation of future ability, and happynesse, is to be wrought into the minde, as early as may be, even from the first dawnings of any knowledg or apprehensions in children; and to be Confirmed in them by all the care and ways imaginable, by those, that have the oversight of their Education. 2°. On the other side if the minde be curbd, and humbled too much in children; if their spirits be abased, and broken†b- by too strict an hand over them,-†b they loose all their vigour, and industry, and are in a worse state then the former, for extravagant yonge fellows, that have livelynesse, and spirit, come sometimes to be set right, and soe make able and great <men>†c ; but dejected mindes; timerous, and tame, and low spirits are hardly ever to be raised; and very seldome atteine any thing. To avoid the danger that is on either hand, is the great art. and he that has found a way, how to keepe up a childs spirit, easy, active, and free; and yet at the same time to†a restrain him from many things he has a minde to; and to drive him to things, that are uneasy to him, he, I say, that knows how to reconcile these seeming contradictions, has, in my opinion, got the true secret of Education. The usuall lasy, and short way by correction, and the rod, which is the only instrument of government, that tutors generally know, or ever thinke of, is the most unfit of
― 174 ―
any, to be used in Education, because it tends to both those mischeifs, which as we have shewd are the Silla and charybdis which on the one hand or other ruine all that miscary, For. 1°. This kinde of punishment tends not at all, to the mastery of our natural†a inclination, of indulgeing corporeall, and present pleasure, and the avoiding pain; but rather incourages it; and soe strengthens in us, that, which is the root of all vitious, and wrong actions.
for what motives, I pray, does a childe act by, but of pleasure, and pain, that takes pains at his booke against his inclination, or abstains from eating†b unwholesome fruit, that he takes pleasure in, only out of the fear of whipeing? He, in this, only prefers the greater corporeall pleasure, or avoids the greater corporeall pain; and what is it to governe his actions, and direct his conduct, by such motives as these, what is it, I say, but to cherish that principle in him, which it is our businesse to root out, and destroy? and therefor I cannot thinke any chastisement usefull to a childe, where the shame of suffering, for haveing donne amisse, does not more worke upon him, then the pain. 2°. This sort of correction naturally breeds an aversion to that, which tis the tutors businesse to create a likeing, to. How obvious is it to observe, that children come to hate things, which they liked at first, as soon as they come to be whipd, or harased and teased about them, and tis not to be wonderd at in them, when grown men would not be able, to be reconciled to any thing, by such ways; who is there, that would not be disgusted with any innocent recreation, which was indifferent to him, if he should with blows or ill language be haled to it, when he had noe minde; or be constantly soe treated, for some circumstance in his application to it? This is naturall to be soe: offensive circumstances ordinarily infect innocent things they are joynd with; and the very sight of a cup, wherein any one uses to take nauseous physique, turnes his stomach, soe that noething will relish well out of it, though the cup be never soe cleane, well shaped, and of the richest materials. 3°. Such a sort of slavish discipline, makes a slavish temper. the childe submits and dissembles, whilst the feare of the rod hangs over him; but when that is removed, and by being out of sight, he can promise to himselfe impunity, he gives the greater scope to his natural inclination, which by this way is not at all alterd, but on the contrary heightend, and increased in him; and after such restraint breakes
― 175 ―
out usually with the more violence. or 4°.
If severity caryed to the highest pitch does prevaile, and workes a cure upon the present unruely distemper, it is only by bringing in the place a worse, and more dangerous disease, by breakeing the minde: and thus†a in the place of a disorderly yonge fellow you have a low spirited moapd creature, who,†b however with his unnaturall sobriety, he please silly people, who commend tame unactive children, because they make noe noise, nor give them any trouble, yet at last he will prove as uncomfortable a thing to his freinds, as he will be all his life an uselesse thing to himself and others. Beating then and chideing are not the punishments, fit to be used, in the Education of those, we would have wise, good, and ingeneous men, and therefor very rarely to be applyd and that only in great occasions, and cases of Extremity. On the other side to flatter children†c by rewards of things, that are pleasant to them, is as carefully to be avoided. He that will give his son apples, or sugar plumbs, or what he loves, to make him learne his booke, does but authorise his love of pleasure, and cocker up that dangerous inclination, which he ought by all meanes to subdue, and suppresse in him: but you can never teach him to master this inclination, whilst you compound for the checque you give it in one place, by the satisfaction you propose to it in another.†-1 I†2- say not this, that I would have children always kept from pleasant things, that are not injurious to their health; but they should have them only as the Consequences of the state of esteem, and acceptation, they are in with their parents, and governors; but never to be offerd them as the rewards of this or that particular action, that they shew an aversion to, or which they would not have donne without them.-†2 These rewards, and punishments being laid aside, what spur, or bridle shall we have left to governe unruly youth? will the tutor be ready to say. To which I answer, reputation, and shame. of which haveing spoke at large formerly,†3 I†4- shall only remarke here this one thing more of them, that though they are not the true principles of vertue, for that is the knowledg of a mans duty, and the satisfaction it is to obey his maker in following the dictates of that light he has given him, with†d- the hopes of acceptation and reward,-†d yet it is that
― 176 ―
which comes nearest to it, and being the testimony and applause that other peoples reason give to virtuous and right actions, is the proper guide and incouragement of children, till they grow able to judg for themselves, and make use of their owne reason.
But if a right course be taken with children, there will not be soe much need of the application of rewards, and punishments as we imagin, and is commonly†a made use of. For 1°. All their innocent folly, playing, and childish actions. are to be left perfectly free and unrestraind. If these faults of their age, rather then of the children themselves, were, as they should be, left only to time, and imitation, and riper years to cure, children would scape a great deale of misapplyd, and uselesse correction, which either failes to over-power the natural disposition of their childhood, and soe by an ineffectuall familiarity makes correction in other necessary cases of lesse use: or else, if it be of force to restrain the natural gaity of that age, it serves only to spoile the temper both of body and minde. If the noise and bustle of their play prove at any time inconvenient, or unsuitable to the place or company they are in, which can only be where theire parents are,†b a†b looke or a word, from the father or mother, if they have establishd the authority they should, will be enough, either to remove, or quiet them for that time; but this gamesome humor, which is wisely adapted by nature to their age, and temper, should rather be incouraged, to keep up their spirits, then curbd or restraind: and the cheif art, is to make all that they have to doe sport and play too.†-4 2°. As†1- to things they are to be taught in that age, as to read, dance, or some forraine language etc. which requires some application, and industry, this will be donne of it self, if you can but ingage their inclinations to it; which I thinke noe hard matter to doe, by ways formerly mentiond,†2 wherof I shall here only touch the generall heads-†1 1°. None†3- of these things should ever be made a burthen to them, nor imposed on them as a taske, or duty. when that is once donne, it presently becomes irkesome, the minde takes an aversion to it, though before it were a thing of delight, or indifferency. Let a child be but orderd to whip his top at a certain time every day, whether he has or has not a minde to it; let this but be
― 177 ―
required of him, as a taske, wherein he must spend soe many howers morning and afternoon, and see whether he will not soon be weary of any play at this rate.
Is it not soe with grown men? what they doe cheerfully of themselves, doe they not presently grow sick of, and can noe more endure, as soone as they finde it is expected of them as a duty? children have as much a minde to shew that they are free; that their owne good actions come from themselves; that they are absolute, and independent, as any of the†a proudest of you†b grown men, thinke of them as you please. 2°. As a Consequence of this they should never be put upon doeing, even those things you have got an inclination in them to, but when they have a minde, and disposition to it. He that loves reading, writing, musique etc. findes yet in himself certain seasons, wherein those things have noe relish to him,†c and if at that time he forces himself to it, he only pidders,†1 and wearys himself to noe purpose. Soe it is with children, this change of temper should be carefully observed in them, and the favourable seasons of aptitude, and inclination, be heedfully laid hold of, to set them upon any thing. by this meanes a great deale of time, and tireing would be saved. for a child will learne three times as much, when he is in tune, and inclined to it, in half the time, as he will with double the time, and pains, when he goes awkardly and unwilling to it. If this were minded, as it should, children might be permitted to weary themselves with play, and yet have time enough to learne, what is suited to the capacity of each age. And if things were orderd right, learning any thing, they should be taught, might be made as much a recreation to their play, as their play is to their learning: the pains is equall on both sides (nor is it that which troubles them, for they†d love to be busy) and the change and variety is that, which naturaly delights them; the only oddes is, that in what we†e call play, they act at liberty, and imploy their pains (whereof you may observe them never spareing) freely, but what they are to learne, they are driven to cald on, Compelled; this is that, that at first entrance balques, and cooles them. they want their liberty. get them but to aske their tutor to teach them (as they often doe their
― 178 ―
play fellows) instead of his calling upon them to learne, and they being satisfied that they act as freely in this, as they doe in other things, they will goe on with as much pleasure in it, and it will not differ from their other sports and play.
How a child is to be brought to desire to be taught any thing, you have a minde he should learne, I thinke I have already shewd. or if that part be any way dificient, we must perfect it.†1 The hardest part I confesse is with the first or eldest: but when once he is set right, it is easy by him to lead the rest whether one will.†-3 children†2- being more active, and busy in that age, then any part of their life, and being indifferent to any thing they can doe, soe they may be but doeing, Danceing and scotshoppers†a would be the same thing to them, were the incouragements and discouragments Equall. But to things we would have them learne the great, and only discouragement I can observe is, that they are calld to it, tis made their businesse; they are teased, and chid about it; all which is a prejudice to that natural freedome they extreamly affect, and tis that liberty alone which gives the true relish and delight to their ordinary playgames. turne the tables, and you will see they will soone change their application, Espetially if they see but the Examples of others that they esteeme, and thinke above themselves; and if the things they see others doe, be orderd soe, that they be perswaded it is the priviledg of an age, or Condition above theirs, then ambition, and the†b desire still to get forward and higher, and to be like those above them, will give them an inclination, which will set them on worke, in a way wherein they will goe on, with vigor, and pleasure, injoying in it their dearly beloved freedom; which if it brings with it alsoe the satisfaction of credit, and reputation I am apt to thinke, there will need noe other spur, to excite their application, and assiduity as much as is necessary. I confesse there needs patience, and skill; gentlenesse and attention, and a prudent conduct to atteine this at first: But why have you a tutor, if there needed noe pains? but when this is once establishd, all the rest will follow more easily, then in any other severe, and imperious discipline. and I thinke it noe hard matter to gaine this point: I am sure there will not be, where
― 179 ―
children have no ill examples set before them.
The great danger therefor, that I apprehend, is, from servants, and such other vitious, or foolish people, who spoile children both by the ill patterns they set before them in their owne ill manners and by giveing†a them†a togeather, the two things, they should never have at once, I meane, vitious pleasure and Commendation.†-2 Besides†1- the directing the busy temper of children, by the ways above mentioned, and insinuateing into them inclinations to the things, we would have them doe, another thing is to be taken care of is to checq, and subdue the vitious inclinations, they are apt to have, and bring them to an habitude of mastering of them; and here indeed there is need of reward and punishment. but still they should be those, I before mentioned, of reputation and shame: the pleased, or displeased countenance of father, mother, and those under whose government they are. for though to tempers that are active, and busy, as children are, it be†b easy to give them inclinations to any actions, they have an indifferency to, as I thinke it cleare they have to almost all sorts; yet if you will divert them from their natural inclinations, you must doe it by proposoll of some other good or evill; the only proper ones are those above mentioned.-†1 I†3- told you but now that children love liberty, and therefor they should be brought to doe the things are fit for them, without feeling any restraint laid upon them; I now tell you, they love some thing more, and that is dominion: and this is the first originall of all vitious habits that are ordinary and natural. This love of power, and dominion shews it self very early, and that in these two things. 1o. we see children as soon almost as they are borne, I am sure long before they can speake, cry, grow peevish, sullen, and out of humor, for noething but to have their wills; they will have theyr desires submitted to by others; they contend for a ready compliance from all about them, espetially those, who stand neare, or beneath them, in age, or degree, as soon as they come to consider others with those destinctions. 2o. Another thing wherein they affect dominion, is to have things to be theirs: they would have propriety, and possession; pleaseing themselves with the power, that seemes to give them, and the right they thereby have to dispose of them, as they
― 180 ―
please.
He that hath not observed these two humors, workeing very betimes in children, has taken litle notice of their actions; and he that thinkes, that these two roots of almost all the injustice, and contention,†a that soe disturb humane life, are not early to be weeded out, and contrary habits introduced, neglects the proper season to lay the foundation of a good and worthy man. to doe this I imagin these following things may some what conduce. 1°. That a child should never be sufferd to have what he craves, or soe much as speakes for; much lesse if he cryes for it. what then would you not have them declare their wants? yes that is very fit, and tis as fit that with all tendernesse they should be hearkend to, and supplyd; at least whilst they are very litle: but tis one thing to say I am hungry, another to say I would have roast meat. haveing declared their wants, their natural wants, the pain they feele from hunger, thirst, cold, or any other necessity of nature, tis the duty of their parents, and those about them, to releive them: but they must leave it to the choise, and ordering of their parents, what they thinke properest for it, and how much: and must not be permitted to choose for themselves, and say I would have wine, or white bread: the very nameing of it should make them loose it. This is for natural wants, which must be releived. but for all wants of phansy, and affectation, they should never, if once declared, be hearkend to, or Complyd with, by this meanes they will be brought, to get a mastery over their inclinations, and learne the art of stifeling their desires as soon as they rise up in them and before they take vent, when they are easiest to be subdued; which will be of great use to them, in the future course of their lives. By this I doe not meane, that they should not have the things, that one perceives would delight them, twould be inhumanity, and not prudence, to treat them soe: but they should not have the liberty to carve, or crave any thing to themselves; they should exercise themselves to keepe their desires under, and be content in the want of what they wishd for, and the more they practised modesty, and temperance in this, the more should those about them study to reward them, with things suited, and acceptable to them; but without telling them soe, but as if it were a natural Consequence of their good behaviour, rather†b then a bargain about†c- it. but-†c you will loose your labour, and what is more their love, and reverence too, if they can receive
― 181 ―
from others, what you deny them. this is to be kept very stanch, and carefully to be watchd: and here the servants come again in my way.
If this be begun betimes, and they accustome themselves early to silence their desires, this usefull habit will setle in them, and as they come to grow up in age and discretion, they may be allowd greater liberty; when reason comes to speake in them, and not passion, for when ever reason†a would speake, it should be hearkend to. But as they should never be heard when they speake for any thing they would have, unlesse it be first proposd to them; soe they should always be heard, and fairly, and Kindly answerd. when they aske after any thing, they would know, and desire to be informd about. Curiosity should be as carefully cherised in children, as appetite suppressed. 2°. As to haveing their wills, which is a contest often happens between children, that live togeather, who ever begins it, should be sure to be crossed in it; but not only that, but they should be taught to have all the deference, Complaisance, and civility one for another imaginable. when they see that this procures them respect, and that they loose noe superiority by it; but on the contrary they grow into love, and esteeme with everybody, they will take more pleasure in it, then in insolent domineering; for soe plainly is the other. The complaints of children one against another, which is usually but the desireing the assistance of another to revenge them, should not be favourably received, nor hearkend to: it weakens, and effeminates their mindes, to accustome them to Complaints; and if they suffer sometimes crosseing, or pain from others, without being permitted to thinke it strange, or intollerable, it will doe them noe harme, to learne sufferance; and harden them early. But though you give noe Countenance to the Complaints of the querulous, yet take care to suppresse all insolence, and ill nature; when you observe it yourself, reproove it before the injurd party, but if the Complaint be of something really worthy your notice, and prevention another time, then reproove the offender by himsel<f>†b alone, out of sight of him that complaind, and make him goe and aske pardon, and make reperation, for the injury he did. which comeing thus as it were fro<m>†b himself, will be the more cheerfully performed, and more kindly received, the love strengthend between them, and a custome of civility grow familiar amon<gst y>our†b children. 3°. As to haveing, and possessing
― 182 ―
of things, teach them to part with what they have easily, and freely to their freinds; and let them finde by ex<perien>ce†a that the most liberall has always most plenty, with esteeme and commendation to boot, and they will quickly learne to practise it.
This I ima<gin w>ill†a make brothers, and sisters kinder, and civiller to one another, and consequently to others, then twenty rules about good manners, with which child<ren ar>e†a ordinarily perplexd, and cumberd.†-3 There†1- is another ill disposition commonly to†b be†b observed in children, which I, who perhaps have noe more reve<rend op>inion†a of my two legged Companions, then others, cannot yet beleive to come from nature; and that is-†1 the delight†2- they take in doeing mischeif; whereby I meane spoiling of any thing to noe purpose; but more espetially the pleasure they take, to put any thing in pain that is capable of it. This I cannot perswade my self to be any other then a forrain, and introduced disposition; a habit borrowd from custome. people teach children to strike, and laugh when they hurt, or see harme come to others, and they have the examples of most people about them, to confirme them in it. soe by fashon and opinion it comes to be a pleasure, which in it self neither is, nor can be any. This ought carefully to be watchd, and early remedied, soe as to plant the contrary, or more natural tempers of good nature, and Compassion in the roome of it: but still by the same gentle methods, which are to be applied to the other two faults, before mentioned. But pray remember that the mischeifs, or harmes, which come by play, inadvertency, or ignorance; and were not known to be harm, or designd for mischeifs sake, though they may perhaps sometimes be of considerable dammage, yet are not at all to be taken notice of.-†2 If†4- the Tutor can be made to understand, and relish these things; and will at the begining apply himself, to put them in practise, he will afterwards finde his worke very easy, and you will I guesse finde your Son, in a litle time a greater preficient in both learning and breeding then perhaps you imagin. but let him by noe meanes beat him, at least without your consent, and direction. He must be sure also to shew him the examples of†c- the things he would have the child practise, and carefully keepe him from all
― 183 ―
bad examples,†-c espetially the most dangerous of all that of the servants, from whose company he is to be kept not by prohibitions, for that will but give him an itch after it, but by other ways, which I thinke I have formerly mentiond.†-4
As†1- to his learning, which as you know, I always count the least matter, his tutor if he be constantly with him, cannot choose but talke French into him, for with him he should speake noething else, and that will be enough of languages to learne at once. but whilst he learnes to speake, and read French, he must not forget to keep his reading of English, which his mother or any body may heare him doe sometimes;-†1 but†2- have a care still of cloging him with too much at once, or makeing any thing his businesse, but downright vertue, or rather abstinence from vice.-†2 If his Tutor†3- can when he understands him, teach him Anatomie, or Botaniques, Geographie, or the stars, or the knowledg of any other sensible parts of nature, that may be orderd soe, as to be noe burden to the child; but be made a Kinde of recreation, espetially if you give him the pleasure and pride to teach you, or his mother, or his sister, what he knows.-†3 I†5- know not whether it be time for him yet to learne to write, for I know not how old he is. But when that is seasonable, the first thing should be taught him†a is†a to hold his pen right; and this he should be perfect in, before he should be sufferd to put it to paper, for not only children, but any body else that would doe any thing well, should never be put to learne two things at once, or be set to perfect themselves in two parts of an action at the same time, if they can possibly be seperated. when he has learnt to hold his pen right. [to hold it betwixt the thumb and forefinger alone I thinke best. but in this you should consull some good writeing master, or any other person who writes well and quick]†b Then next he should learne how to lay his paper, and place his arme, and body to it. These preparatives being got over, the way to teach him to write without much trouble, is to get a plate graved, with the
― 184 ―
characters of such an hand as you like best, but you must remember, to have them a pretty deale biger, then he should ordinarily write, for every one naturaly comes by degrees to write a lesse hand, then he at first was taught, but never a biger. such a plate being graved, let severall sheets of good writeing paper be printed off with red inke, which he hath noe thing to doe, but to goe over with a good pen fild with black inke, which will quickly bring his hand to the formation of those characters.†a †-5 Yours of the 4th Instant with those of older dates I answerd the last post. I have reason to beg your excuse for this long addition concerning your son and his tutor, but you must give me leave to enlarge in this, haveing soe litle else to expresse that acknowledgment and zeale where with I am
Sir
your most affectionate humble servant
J L

930. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 27 April [1687] (896, 942)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 142-3. Year from Locke's endorsement.
You will perhaps ere This comes to you begin to Condemne me of some Neglect for not haveing Answear'd before now your twoo letters; I confess haveing Just now read them over I could be Almost Angry with my self for Defering so long to Put you in my Debt againe, But I should be Unjust if I should, since it has really beene next to impossible for me to have done otherwise then I have. I intend not This by way of excuse, since your haveing beene longer in Mine before makes it Needless. The Truth is I was very Impatient at it when I consider'd I had Writt two Letters However
― 185 ―
I was not so Sullenly Angry but that I resolv'd to send you a Third and Accordingly writt you a very long One, which that you had Not (if you regrett the Loss) You must lay the Blame upon a Certaine Thing which I am very seldome Guiltie of, Call'd Discretion, that Perswaded me it was not Always Best to Pursue ones Inclination; I therefore Condemn'd it to the Flames assoone almost as it was writt, when a Day or twoo after I Received Yours of the 12th of Feb: by which I understood you had writt me Another before That which I had not received then, but did a Week or Ten Days after in That Place which you ask me in it whether or no I had Renounc'd;†1 and from whence I am but just Return'd, Haveing had the Misfortune to Miss of our S:C: Friends†2 there, who were gone into the Countrey the Day before I came up; who should have beene very glad to have seene them There, since They would not be so Kind as to let me do so Here; My Good Lady†3 I Visited however as often as my occasions would permit me where you have so often beene, and where I assure you I could not be without rememb'ring it, tho it be so long since I have seene you There; and that I had a Thousand things to take up my Thoughts everie Day in that Busie Place, where besides the Ordinarie Affairs of Countrey Ladys who come to Towne but Once a Yeare I had a very great Varietie of Other Concerns, which the many Relations I now stand in, some Accidents, and a large increase of Acquaintance drew upon me; Acquaintance, suited I assure you as Agreably as the furniture of my Closet, of which I beleeve it would have beene One Pleasant instance to You, if you could have seene with me at the same time Mr Penn the Quaker, and Maids of Honour.†4 But in the Midst of All this Hurry I tell you of, though I writt not to you I assure you I found several occasions of Thinking of You; for which I beleeve you have at least as much Obligation to me, as I to you for being Inspir'd by either my Genius or your owne to write me a letter the 29th of Jan; which should have beene writt a Month sooner——
Thus far has been writt to you Almost a Week since, when I was Interrupted by the News of my Brother's Death, He to whom you use to send your letters,†5 which tho it Could be no Great
― 186 ―
Surprize to me will not yet let me be in a Humour to finish this as I ought in Answeare to Yours; It has Cast my Thoughts into Another Mould, and Decencie will Priviledge me from so much as Attempting to Change them whilst he yet Lyes Unbury'd. Not being Willing However to be Condemn'd too long (tho Unjustly) of forgetfulness, I send you this Letter as it is, and Beg your Pardon for the rest till Another time.
In the meane while Adieu.
If you think fit to write to me before you heare from me againe I think you must Direct for me to be left with Mr Guicheritte next doore to the Rose and Crowne in Shoemaker row in Dukes Place within Algate.†1 I Can think of no other Direction at Present, But it has hitherto prov'd unluckie to me.
April the 27th.
Address: For Mr Lock.
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 27 Apr. 87 Answered 27 Jun

931. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 6/16 May [1687] (926, 938)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 255q. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 309-11; postscript and address in Ollion, pp. 172-3.
(English)
16 May.†a
Quid illo facies homine Qui nec cantare par est nec respondere paratus?†2 Quid juvat libertate a te ipso concessâ uti sine viribus ad ea quæ decent præstanda necessariis. Jucundissima tua et floribus undique referta epistola ad ea quæ scribis iterum iterumque legenda maxime invitat, ut vero calamum sumam et aliquid meo more rescribam valde dehortatur et deterret Etsi enim grati sit animi,
― 187 ―
argutis et facetis amici sermonibus aliquid respondere, imprudentis tamen est et parum pudici, ornatis incondita, urbanis agrestia, pretiosis vilia vel in ipso literarum commercio reponere. Frustra igitur a Te Libertate donatus sum, munus sane in specie magnificum sed nisi aliquid de tuo etiam impertire possis ingenio plane inutile, frustra enim accusabis me tanquam in libertate tardum, cui tam parata et justa sit defensio hebetem non debere esse loquacem, nec dicere χάλκεα χρυσείων,†1 ut ut enim eo modo liber†a sim, parum certe videbor liberalis. Novi animum tuum, novi ingenium et quam paratus sis omnia ab amicâ voluntate profecta in bonam partem interpretari. hoc boni omnia consulentis non parva laus est, sed malè interim scribentis pessima excusatio. Eâ tamen fiduciâ fretus en te iterum compellare ausim melioribus studiis vacantem, si quid in eo pecco nolo incusare vim a fatis illatam causam sane si qua sit omnium maxime improbam, sed te ipsum qui ab omni vi et coactione longissime abes, Tua humanitas, tua benevolentia, tui lepores cogunt ut agnoscam, et ut fatear me tibi gratias habere etiamsi referre non
― 188 ―
possim. Si his conditionibus mecum agere velis en tibi ad legendas tuas epistolas paratissimum et cupidissimum: ad meas rescribendas etiamsi cupiam tardum, et sane tam necessitate quam officio tardum. Tu cum ista excusatione uti non potes et maturè scribas rogo et abunde. Id ni facias audies me graviter querentem Te non præstare et amico et egenti id quod potes et id quod debes quia <potes>.†a Si jam inciperem iniquo jure communem inter nos colere amicitiam hæc jam proponere vix animum inducerem, sed cum hac lege a primordiis amicitiæ semper viximus ut tu propere et cumulatè omnia officia benevolentiæ præstares ego vel in agnoscendo parcus et lentus essem pati jam debes mores meos quantumvis malos <vetustate>†b jam confirmatos in quibus nihil novum nihil insolens reperies. Vides quocum tibi res est, in hac tamen culpâ non prorsus ingratus videri vellem si id in se aliquid gratitudinis habet ut qui eam qua se destitutum fatetur, in te miratur et amplectitur vertutem; in eâ quæro mihi patrocinium quod mihimet præstare non possum. Sed de me satis ad majora nunc venio tua scilicet. Typographo haud parum irascor quod tuum tam utile tam doctum opus adeo procrastinet, spero jam accedente sole
― 189 ―
operarum diligentia magis incalescet. De Episcopii etiam tractatu gaudeo, de alio quod postulas tecum coram agam, ut enim quod res est fatear scripseram prius ad te nisi speraveram ante hac me Amstelodamum accessurum ut jucundissimâ amicorum illic consuetudine fruerer, imprimis tuâ, sine quâ hi ipsi veris non amæne transeunt dies. Vale Vir Præstantissime et ut facis me ama
Tui Studiosissimum

(Latin)
16 May.
What can you do with a man who is neither your equal in song nor ready to sing in response?†2 What pleasure is there in using the freedom of speech conceded by yourself without the necessary power to express oneself in becoming terms? Your delightful letter, replete as it is with every kind of ornament, strongly invites me to peruse your words again and again; at the same time it greatly discourages and deters me from taking up my pen and [p. 187] making some reply in my own fashion. For although gratitude demands that one should give some answer to the acute and witty remarks of a friend, yet it shows inconsiderateness and lack of shame if in the very business of correspondence one replies to the ornate with the disordered, to the polished with the rude, and to the valuable with the worthless. In vain, therefore, have you endowed me with liberty, in appearance, to be sure, a magnificent gift, but, unless you can also impart to me something of your own genius, a plainly useless one; for in vain will you accuse me of being slow to avail myself of that liberty, seeing that I have so ready and just a defence, namely that the dull should not be loquacious or offer brazen arms in exchange for golden;†1 for whatever liberties I may take in that way, I shall certainly appear deficient in liberal culture. I know your mind; I know your nature; I know how ready you are to put the best construction on anything that proceeds from the goodwill of a friend. This practice of making the best of everything is greatly to your credit, but is meanwhile the worst of excuses for a bad writer. However, in confident reliance on that nature I may venture, as you see, to address you once more, though your time should be given to better studies; if I transgress at all in so doing I have no wish to lay the blame on the compulsion of fate, which is surely, if any, the poorest of all pleas; no, I lay it on yourself, you who are very far removed from exerting any force or compulsion. It is your courtesy, your benevolence, your graces that compel me to acknowledge and confess the gratitude I feel towards you, even if I cannot [p. 188] repay your kindness. If you are willing to deal with me on these conditions, then behold in me one who is most ready and most desirous to read your letters, but slow at writing replies to them, much as I should wish to do so, and that, indeed, as much from necessity as from slowness to do my duty. As you cannot yourself use that excuse, I beg you to write soon and plentifully. Unless you do so you will hear me bitterly complaining that you are not doing for a friend and a needy one what you are able to do and ought to do because you are able. If I were now only commencing to cultivate a mutual friendship between us without having any right to it, I could hardly bring myself to make such a proposal; but seeing that the rule by which we have always lived from the beginnings of our friendship is that you should fulfil all the offices of benevolence promptly and in overflowing measure, whilst I should be chary and slow in so much as acknowledging them, it now behoves you to put up with my habits, bad as they may be and now confirmed by long usage, in which you will find nothing new or unaccustomed. You see with whom you have to do; yet with all my faults I should not wish to seem utterly ungrateful, if some measure of gratitude be implied in the fact that one admires and esteems in you a virtue of which he confesses himself destitute; it is in that virtue of yours that I hope to find the defence which I cannot furnish for myself. But enough of myself; I now come to more important concerns, to wit, your own. I am not a little annoyed with the printer for all these delays of his with your valuable and scholarly work; I hope that as we are now having more sun there will be more warming up of industry in his [p. 189] operations. I am glad too about the treatise of Episcopius; as to your other request, I will discuss it with you when I see you; for to tell the truth I would have written to you sooner if I had not hoped to come to Amsterdam before now, to enjoy the delightful society of my friends there, especially your own, in the absence of which these very days of spring are passing without pleasure. Good-bye, eminent Sir, and continue to love me
Your most devoted
J. L.
(Latin) Please remember me to your excellent wife and to our Collegians, especially Veen and Guenellon; kindly tell the last named that the box of pomatum and the accompanying letter have duly reached me, for all of which I am deeply grateful.

932. James Tyrrell to Locke, 6 May [1687] (911, 957)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 56-8. Part printed in King, pp. 169-70. Year from Locke's endorsement. The day may be wrong, or Tyrrell may have begun the letter on 6 May and continued it on the 7th: p. 192, n. 2. Answers no. 911.
London May 6th:
Dear Sir
I must in the first place confesse my self in your debt two letters; (besides all other matters of greater concernement) and I
― 190 ―
must beg your pardon that I have not discharged it sooner, since the ill estate of my wives health; in which I dayly expecting to see some alteration either for the better, or the worse, did for above two monthes keep me in a continuall suspence what would become of her. She has taken a bitter decoction in sack allmost all this winter: and yet her stomach has bin so bad as to be scarce able to digest any meat in two dayes time: she has likewise by your hint, and Dr: Dickensons†1 and Dr: Thomas's advice taken crude Antimony finely powderd about 10 gr: each morneing tho without any considerable advantage: but when about a month since she was brought downe so weake as to be scarce able to walk about the house a new preparation of steel she met with by chance hath strangely revived her: and before I came from home she was finely recruited, in strength, and found her stomach much better: and I suppose she now intends to forbear flesh all this month; and to live upon milk, and herbs boyled: pudding and other like things for a great part of this summer all flesh being very disagreeable to her stomach; besides this affliction of my wives long indisposition our Family hath met with another much greater: viz: the losse of my sist: Marg: who died at Shot: the begining of March last of the small Poxe of a very bad sort, so that they could by no meanes be brought out. which killed her about the thirteenth day:†2 my sister Bl:†3 is likewise ill near this Towne of an ulcer in the kidney and a dropsy: so that wee much fear her recovery. but she is now (God be thanked) somewhat amended. I am sorry I have entertained you with so much melancholy discourse: but the concerne I know you have for me; and mine I hope will excuse it.
I thank you for your kind; and generous offer of my keeping your money still in my hands till my conveniencyes will better allow me to pay it: I hope it shall not be much to your detriment whether I live or die. for I will if you please allow you interest for it at 5l. per cent: which is as much as money now ordinarily goes at. here and whenever your occasions call for it you shall have it at a month or 6 weekes notice with thankes. I am glad you have received the book†4 which I was afraid was lost it was so long a comeing to you: and if you please to give it your friend as you say: Ile
― 191 ―
assure you shall have another ready for you whenever you please to command it either when you returne or before, and am glad there is any thing it that can please so exact a Judg: I am extremely pleased with your true censure of the new Theorhy of the Earth; which as it shews me some difficultyes which I thought not of so it confirmes me in some other exceptions I made†a to it: before I received yours; and in which your conceptions, agreed exactly with mine, and for what you say of some chapters in the book (I suppose you mean those concerneing the providence of God, and non eternity of the world) I can never sufficiently value them. I should be glad to hear you would resolve to print your papers: or at least to communicate them to those you can trust to see how much of them is new; and fit for it: and now you have finisht that discourse†1 I should be glad to hear whether you have done what you intended concerneing the Law of nature:†2 which you have so often promised to reveiw:
<Your>†b discourse about Liberty of Conscience would not doe amisse now to dispose peoples minds to passe it into a Law whenever the Parliament sits. the thing gives so generall a satisfaction that more are displeased at the manner of doeing it then at the thing it self.†3 so that I find few but the high Chur: E: men highly displeased: but let the intent of those that doe it be as it will; I beleive whatever the chur: of England may loose the R.C.R.†4 will not gaine so much as they imagine more being likely to goe off to the Phanaticks then to them, among the ordinary people, who can neither expect offices nor pensions by the change: and if so I think the R.C.R. (as Osborne sayes) will onely change hearb John, for Coloquintida.†5 as for news I have not much to send you, onely to the great satisfaction of many, Judg Withins is put out, and one Sir Rich: Allebone. a R.C. of great integrity and ingenuity (as those say that know him) put in his roome and more such changes
― 192 ―
are dayly expected.†1 the vicechancellour, of Cambridge was suspended; and deprived this day by the commissioners Ecclesiasticall ab Officio, et beneficio. for refuseing to propose; and admit Father Francis a dominican Fryer to the degree of Master of Arts in that university; the rest of the Doctors who likewise mannaged that affair <or>†a signed the university plea, are to expect their doom but what that will be wee cannot yet tell.†2 and now I am in talking of Universityes I will give you a short account of the state of Oxon because you have not bin a stranger to it. in Christ church tho there hath bin a R.C. Head allmost this half year:†3 yet I cannot hear of one conversion among the students. the old Hall in Canter: Quaderangle formerly the Bishops Woodhouse is now fiting up for a chappel, for the Deane.†4 yet are there not, (notwithstanding Mr: W:s great endeavours to turne people)†5 above 6 or 7 schollers besides himself who have declared themselves R.C. Mr. W. prints books at his new presse for his Religion, but they have had no very good successe for one of them was answered as†b soon†b it came out:†6 and the other which is a kind of history of the Reformation has a very slight reception among the learned; being no more then a translation of Sanders and Gretsers storyes which have bin
― 193 ―
so long since confuted.†1 I doubt not but you have read Dr: B.s letters. which ar a patterne how a man should travell and what observations he should make. the book was forbid to be brought in, but it hath bin since printed here: and sells infinitely.†2 I forgot to tell you that Dr: Cl: the head of Maudlin Coll: in Oxon being dead the King sent downe a mandamus for one Mr: Farmour a new convert: a commoner Master of that house: but the Fellows refused to elect him but have bin so stout as notwithstanding to chuse one Mr: Hough chaplain to the Duke of O. for their President: my Lord Sund: has writ to them from the K. about it. but their answere was that they could not chuse Mr: F. with a safe conscience being under an oath and haveing received the sacrament upon it to chuse none but a fit man, whereas this man was not so being a person of ill fame; and debauched life; and allso not of any of those foundations they are by their statutes to elect their President out of.†3 I wish your cosens†4 affaires would suffer him to come over and see the face of things here for a month or two this summer; tho he returned againe at winter: he would find a strange alteration in mens humours: and need not doubt a favourable reception. I pray get me Grotius de Rebus Gothicis of the Elzivir Edition†5 if possible. but Paulus Diaconus is not in that collection:†6 and therefore if you can get him by him self pray buy it for me: I would be glad to send you over bookes in exchange for those I owe you if you will send me
― 194 ―
the names of what you would have. I sent up the bow†1 and directed it as you bad me; the person that was to have it I hear†a is a man of great learneing and worth: and I hope hath received it: but pray take care I doe not see you come over with a short wigh and plain linning and theeing all your acquaintance.†2 Unc: A. was lately in Towne but I saw him but seldome. Lisis is well and I hope to meet him as I goe downe. I have sent A. all the bookes you bad me as allso that you would have had burnt: he allso desires your Phil: transactions which I shall send him since you order me to deliver him whatever he desires. I have this morneing seald a note of my hand to†b you:†c for 30l: which I have deliverd to Mr: C.†3 for your use. so I hope I have setled that affair according to your desire at present. I have no more time nor paper but to write my self your reall Friend, and servant.
JT.
Mr: C. undertakes to direct this a shorter way. but if you think fit I should direct mine so, let me know it or els it is all one to me to write as I use to doe: since my letters seldome require hast. and whether they are received in May or June it is much at one.
Mr: B.†4 was well yesterday; and desired me to remem: his service to you
Address: For Mr John Lock

933. Mrs. Isabella Duke and Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 7 May 1687 (918, 940; 925, 939)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 13-14.
[Mrs. Duke:]
Escott May 7th.: 87.
Dear Sir
The last post brought me tw<o lett>ers†d from you, the want of wh<ich h>as†d really made me very uneasie. But now I am happy again, and though that of Feb: 22d. be more then two Months old,
― 195 ―
yet 'tis a most Valluable Nosegay, there are non such to be gathered on this side the Water, it had a Vertue to Calm all my disquiets, to silence all my Murmurings, to make me Live in your absence, and to make me hope again that Your Friendship, your Charity, would at last prevail with you to come and give us a Visit, and to Tarry with us, or take us with you, as you should Judge most Reasonable; And I beg that you would not frustrate my Hopes, you know how greivous that is, hope deferr'd makes the heart sick,†1 but the defeating ones hopes is extreamly dangerous, if not Mortall, therfore pray have some compassion of your Friend the Health of whose Body and Mind too, depends wholly upon you. you will be most welcome to me which way soever you come, whither in at the Window or Chimney Top, so you do but come I shall receive you with all imaginable Joy, and the Highest Satisfaction, a nearer conversation with you being what I want, and what I Covet above all things. And were I as much Master of my self as you are, I would not thus languish for want of it, no Considerations should keep me from you; surely the Wind does not alwayes blow the wrong way, I have been told that nothing is so Changable, I hope it has not changed its nature, only to make me Unfortunate, and that you by talking of flying, do not design to tell me that there is no hopes of my seeing you on any other Terms, but rather that you will be here very suddenly, and most agreably surprize me, and yet 'tis so long since that letter was written, that I am full of fears, and know not how I ought, how you would have me to understand it; and I am at the greater loss, because Yours of the 7th of Aprill tels me that you are a Wanderer, and must not be depended on as a Phisitian, is it impossible to prevail with you for once to wander this Way; speak Comfortably to me in your next, it most nearly concerns me, for in good earnest I am going with Mr Duke to london only upon the score of our Healths, he has a sharp Humour in his blood, which makes him almost alwayes complain that his Throat is sore, and keeps him alwayes under a perpetual loseness, but without any Pain. I am, (by his Favour) indifferent well, but you know I need to be set right in one particular, as much as he does physick, which I think he must have recourse to without delay, we purpose to be in London before the end of this Month, and my Brother has promised to accompany us, perhaps his stay there may not be very long, but we must do what shall be thought
― 196 ―
necessary for us, and he must trust some phisitian or other, and I must try what the Woman I mention'd can do for me, if you do not take pitty upon us. I am not without all the suspitions, distrust, and fears imaginable what will be the consequents of it; but if he is willing to go through a Method of Phisick to set him right, I must on my part do what is necessary for me; and I shall be forced to apply to that Woman for her assistance, if I can have no better, which I despair of unless you will give it me. for Heavens sake my Friend, do not keep me longer in suspence, but if you have any thoughts of comming over, tell me so plainly in your next, and hasten it to me that I may meet it at my first comming to Town, and take our Measures, and Resolutions accordingly. my Lanlady has had the Small Pox lately, which was no small suffering to me, who probably infected her when I were in Town, where I made some Charitable Visits daylie to a kinsman who was sick in that disease to a terrible degree; but they are both well again, only the weakness of her Eyes robs me of her letters, which is a great loss to me. but she sends me word by Mr Freke that her inside is not changed; though perhaps her outside may, but I know you will like both, when you are acquainted with them, and 'tis then you shall give me your Thanks; I shall never be compleatly happy till we are all three together, and I have done you that service with her which I promised you. I have a thousand things more to say, but have not time, nor yet to read this, which I have scribled in the greatest hast imaginable the post being going, and I could not delay it till the next, my kindness my Gratitude would not be any longer imprison'd; pardon what is amis in this, and accept the sincere affection that dictates it; and assure your self that I had not one hours time to dispose of, those few dayes that I were in london last, and I took what care I could to have you told so, and to get my self excused to you, but I did not find the secretary's so willing, Mr Clark absolutely refused it, both there, and at Ivye Church, of which I threatned him to complain to you for he said he would not, Mr Freke said he would, but it seems he did not; forgive all my faults, all my omissions, and let us begin upon a new score if you please; for I own my self a Bankrupt, and submit wholly to your Mercy. if you can forgive this and all that's past, you shall never more have reason to complain of me, who am by all imaginable Tyes become unalterably
Yours. ISABELLA DUKE
― 197 ―
I depend upon you to send, or rather to bring me the Antidote against drugs that skilfull Ladies destroy their healths withall. and your other secrets, my Recipe Book will be of no Vallue without them.
[Yonge:]
Dear Sir Yours of the 2d. of May came to my hands at the same time with that (I thought lost) of feb. 22th. which it seems was unhappily mislaid by trusty Mr Austin, who never failed me before, and has promised never to be so forgetfull again, so that you may continue to direct to him with the greatest confidence of your letters safe conveyance; and I should now beg your pardon for giving you the trouble of what you call repetition, but that both your letters though partly of the same subject were so full of variety and so pleasant together that I can not repent drawing the second from you, for which I have scarce time now to pay you my thanks; yet I must add that as in my former letters I gave you full power to buy me any curious books you meet with though they be not gilded or finely bound, so I am content you should buy me some latin books two in hopes that I may some time or other recover that tongue; But then give me leave in the generall to give you this caution, that I would not lay out much money nor buy a multitude of books, but only some that are very curious and such as you would recommend to me for my own reading, for my father left me a very good collection of books, which he was making till the year 70. (when he dyed) in which I shall <find plentifull>†a employment, and I have made some small addition to it, and amongst the rest, have severall books of buildin<g in>†a french and Italian and particularly Vetruvius (which you mention if you mean his Architecture) though not in latin; but I presume there will be no danger of your buying any that I am already furnished with; so that you <may>†b look upon your commission to be as ample as you can desire in every thing, but the expence of much money; in which I find I must confine my selfe, for there is no end of charge in building, so that I am abundantly convinced of the kindness of your wish that I could build with musick in that respect as well as for the sake of the damsells that would carry the hodds; yet I love the†c building so well that I should be glad to find a meet help to finish it, though it kept me from your
― 198 ―
Gelinotts, which I am sure I shall not (however) be at leisure to think of till towards winter. If this finds at Rotterdam pray give my service to our friend Benjamin,†1 and tell him I am at a great loss for want of an answer to severall letters I have sent him to know whether I am any way obliged to take the paving bricks I bespoke long since; if they were bought I would desire him to put them off (though at some loss) rather then be necessitated to pave my stables at so great a charge, since our ordinary pebbles will doe well enough, and I beg to hear from him by the first post, for I can not finish my stables till I have his answer, in which I beg I may also know whether he has sent me any iron backs,†2 and how many and <by>†a whome, for I hear nothing of them yet. Excuse my hast, for I fear least this post may be lost, and beleive me to be <unalter>ably†a
Dear Sir
Your most faithfull friend and obliged humble servant
W. Y.
You have the services of all the Row.
Address (written by Mrs. Duke): For Mr John Lock To be left with Mr Benjamin Furley merchant in Rotterdam
