934. John Freke to Locke, 10 May 1687 (920, 937)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 167-8.
May the 10th 1687.
Dear Sir
He that is famed for never speaking a silly thing nor doing a wise one†3 was wont to say (when he heard a strange story) Which is most proble that this story is true or that the teller of it lyes? I must confess I have ever thought this a pertinent Question and ever since I heard it have made it to my self on any such occasion and this made me soe backward in my belief of Fairys. But yours of Aprill the 15th has convinced me I yield my self vanquisht! There must be Fairys! even now in our days, or at least since King Arthurs to which time Chaucer puts them back.†4 How else could
― 199 ―
the Tradition of them and their manner of Acting with us have been continued down to us as it is? How could we know that as soon as one discovers the kindness they shew us their bounty ceases as our friends old kinswoman did and declared it to him, which proved true in the event? We know how slippery a thing Tradition is and how little able it has been to bring down the knowledge of things of greater moment and concern to us with any kind of certainty. Tis a great many Ages since King Arthur and we have noe other traditions of his time that may not Justly be reckond fabulous and can we think this which concerns us soe litle should or could be deliverd down soe particularly as it is from that Age and yet handed to us onely by old women. Your conceit that Dr H Ms vehicles†1 are of the race of Fairys pleases me much but I doubt they are displeased with him for searching soe much into their affairs and prying too curiously into their world for his head has sufferd by it he has for severall months been deprived of the exercise of his great reason and had a Just title to a fellowship in the college calld Bedlam but at presant is pretty well recoverd.†2 I am apt to believe this Disorder proceeded from the malice of these Fairys: for they are very malicious as appears by the tradition of changlings and they cant endure to be discoverd or known even by those they love and are kind to, for they make all their visits when they are absent nor doe they shew them kindness when they expect it and if their favours are once ownd and acknowledged though one tell it but to one single friend adieu! their friendship is at an end, Soe secret are they in their Amours! You seem to desire an acquaintance with these little modells of mankind but for my part I should be able to take noe pleasure in the love of those that I could not, I must not love again and whose favours I must not own. Tis the reciprocall affection and the gratitude I resent†3 in my self that compleats the enjoyment I find in Friendship and for their presents since they must rob another of what they bestow on me I should desire none of them. I never approved the practice of the cobler of Canterbury who stole Leather to make Shoo's for the poor.†4 We have a good English proverb that the Receiver is as
― 200 ―
bad as the Thief and these Fairys make a man a Receiver and yet think himself innocent which by degrees may lead one into an opinion that he may lawfully possess what of right belongs to another soe as he come by it cleverly and can't be detected a principle I like worse than taking an Ax or mattock in my hand and hewing out my fortune in †a a wild country though I am not inclined to that neither but absolutely resolved against that and all other ways of growing rich or great though ...†b †1
The Lady that you know is changing her family and furniture and on the brink of matrimony†2 and would feign engage me not onely to be at the wedding but to concern my self in my profession again and assist in drawing the Settlement which I am noe ways averse to provided I may doe it my own way but I doubt they will not like my methode since the presant Tenant will hardly be willing to be soe bound up as is necessary to support the contingent Remainders, prevent Waste etc: not onely in the Jointure but in the whole estate. Your Friends in Devon†3 will be Trustees in this Settlement if I make it. They are coming up to Town and I suppose all my fellow Travailers will be here within three weeks though I hope your daughter Betty will by that time have changed her name or at least resolved to doe soe and pitcht on that which she will use instead of it.†4 I could wish you would be here to rejoice with your friends on this occasion and assure you doe believe that your presence would very much increase if not double the Joy of the Company. I know they languish for want of you and twould be great charity in you to afford them that happiness. Tunbridge will be the rendevous but tis my misfortune that I doubt my occasions will call me into the west at that time with which fate I must be contented as I endeavour to make myself what ever befalls me. I suppose your publick Letters give you an account of all the News and then you know how the university of Cambridge has fared before the Ecclesiasticall comissioners which is all the important news now stirring and makes all the heads and fellows of Houses
― 201 ―
there (and at oxford too) tremble but I suppose had you continued a member of Christ church you would not have been affraid and therefore desire to know what you would give to be restored and whether I shall use my Interest to get you your place again.†1 Mr Clarke†a is with me while I write you this and is angry that I ask you this Question and doe not leave it to him who it seems intends you a Letter alsoe by this post and therefore lest you should be tired with reading Letters I shall enlarge this noe further but subscribe my self most sincerly and affectionately
Your friend and humble servant
J F
Address: For Mr Lock
Endorsed by Locke: J. F 10 May. 87 Answered 30 May

935. Edward Clarke to Locke, 13 May 1687 (929, 936)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 32. Fragment: upper half only of a large leaf, written on both sides. Printed in Rand, pp. 213-14. Answers no. 929 and a lost letter of 15/25 April, for which Locke made notes at the end of no. 924. Answered by no. 936.
London 13o Maij 1687°
Dear Sir
That Letter of yours (which in my last of the 3d instant I told you was sent to Chipley whilst I was comeing to this Place) being now Return'd to mee, I take this first opportunity to thanke you for it, but most espetially for the continu'd Care you take of my Son's Education, however cannot but wonder That you should rayse soe Kind a quarrell with mee for not finding fault with what you have with soe much Reason and Judgment written on that occasion, Which, I must tell you truly I cannot doe without Acting contrary to my owne understanding, and the strictest observation I have been able to make upon the Practise hitherto of those Rules you have therein given mee, Which, are all built upon the strongest Reasons imaginable, and therefore I beleive will never
― 202 ―
faile in case there bee a constant and steady Practise of them in the Education of Children; I hope the Tutor I have gott will strictly observe them, Hee being (as farr as I can Discern) throughly convinc'd that the Methods proposed are in all parts the most Rationall Hee ever mett withall, And that Prayse and shame are certainely the best Rewards and Punishments for all that's Good or Evill in a Childs Temper or Behaviour, And that they are the only propper wayes and meanes firmly to Roote Vertuouse and Good Principles in them, And that Children are to bee Ledd on by all the sweet allurements and perswations that can bee thought of, but never to bee forc'd or Govern'd by the Feare or Terror of those that are Plac'd over them, And this being declar'd to bee his Judgment I have reason to hope his Practise with my Children will bee pursuant to these Greate Truth's etc: And now give mee leave to Answere some of the Queries in your Letter of the 25th. of April with the plainesse and sincerity of a Freind, wherein I must tell you That from the first time you bidd mee observe how you stood in the Opinion of my Neighbours (your Companions the last Summer)†1 I have ever since in all ... hath pass'd with ...†a observations for your owne Private satisfaction: As for Thomas and Susan, Mrs. Perce and the Lady in whose House shee is,†2 I beleive they have all the same Kindnesse and Freindshipp for you as ever, and I am confident 'tis Lazinesse or forgettfullnesse rather then any disrespect that has occasion'd theire long sylence towards you, For they all constantly make the most kind inquieryes imaginable of mee after your Wellfare, And I never see any of them but they talke of Writeing to you, And the younge Gentleman (to whome I formerly delivered a Letter from you)†3 came to mee the begining of this Weeke and made greate Excuses for his not Keepeing his Word with you, and said that Hee had hitherto delayed Writeing to you, upon noe other reason but that of his Being from time to time ledd on with the hopes of Travelling abroade, and thereby haveing an opportunity to make His Personall acknowlidgments to you for the Kind service you intend Him, and sayes Hee have now obtain'd his End, is goeing into the Countrey
― 203 ―
to take Leave of his Father and Mother, and then is to sett out hence under the Care of a Scotchman (whose Name I have forgott, but is to Travaile with Him in the nature of a Governor)†1 for the Hague, and intends to waite on you in his journey thither; I hope what Hee sayes is Reall and not a feign'd Excuse, but that a little time will shew the certainty of, and the Conversation you will have with Him will direct you to make a Better Judgment of Him then any thing I can Write concerning Him: And now I come to that part of your Letter which relates to Mr. Stratton, whose Accompts I have this day sent hence,†2 with a Peruke of the Colour you did formerly weare (Mr Mol being gone out of Town) by the Person that by your directions I have paid for the Hatt Hee lately sent you, And when you have considered those Accompts I thinke it will not bee amisse if you Return them to mee, with your own observations on them by the same Bearer, and when I am ... Rent-Roll ...†a

936. Locke to Edward Clarke, 23 May/2 June 1687 (935, 943)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 36-8. Letter with enclosure. It appears to have been returned by Clarke; there is nothing to show at what date. For preparatory notes for the enclosure see p. 161, n. 1. Answers no. 935; answered by no. 954.
2o Jun 87
Sir
I here inclosed returned†b you my cosin Strattons accounts by the same hand you did me the favour to send them me. I have made some Quæres upon them which are severall of them of noe great importance but to shew how the account should have been made. The first indeed is material†c for if there be a mistake in it I may loose half a years rent. But if I mistake not it may be set right by
― 204 ―

the litle pocket book of account I formerly mentioned. As also by the same book you will see how far Eliz: Hopkins has paid her rent. and it will also shew you what part of the taxes William Gullock is to pay in Belton.
I finde by my Cosins accounts that he looks upon a lease that Robert Harol has of a litle peice of ground of mine in Beluton as of some value to make me some part of satisfaction in the arears are due from him. If the lease be lookd on twill be found he is to pay me the yearly value of the ground and soe that that lease is not to be recond much worth. however I would desire that care may be taken it be surrender'd, for I confesse I did foolishly to grant it him it lyeing soe neare the house.†1 when you see all that is to be got from him that can be in mony or other goods, allowance may be made him for that surrender as you thinke good
The ruels I have sent are necessary to be inculcated whether he accepts or not of the proposition I formerly made him. For if he should be as negligent and let the tenants run in arear as easily when he is to bear the losse of it himself as when he only received the rents for me. It would raise a great clamour against me if it should afterwards happen that I found it necessary to revoke that grant, Or else to prevent that clamour I must be at the losse. For†a- though we contract that I shall only repay him what he has laid out for taxes and reparations,-†a yet not only he and other people but you and I too shall thinke it unreasonable that he should be at the trouble to looke after my estate and at the end have noe thing but losse by it. This consideration of his naturall slownesse made me upon the reading of his accounts, wherein I founde notwithstanding all my repeated cautions to him of not leting the tenants run in arear, that there were two of the cheife of them in arear a whole years rent within three days when he made up his account. This†a- consideration I say made me write to you in my last soe doubtfully about the setlement I had proposed. But the offer haveing been made to him, you will see by my inclosed to him that I continue still in the same inclination though I have writ to him as you will see coldly enough about it,-†a or without takeing much notice of the Kindenesse or advantage it will be to him that
― 205 ―
what ever happens he may not say I was importunate with him or drew him in with hopes which he is deceived in. If†a- therefor when you see him next you finde him satisfied of the kindenesse I meane him by it and desirous I should put that proposall in execution I am willing as I said to have it don on these termes-†a
1 That he pay the cleare rent for all the whole estate in publoe pensford and Belton as it stands in the rent roll given him when he tooke upon him the management of that estate.
2° In consideration of which and the affection I beare his two children by my Cosin I will setle on them for their two lives after my decease all the estate Robert Harol rented of me reserving 23s: per annum rent.
With a liberty of Revocation at any time upon tender of what money†b has been disbursed for taxes and reparations, or without any such tender if at any time dureing my life the said rent agreed or any part or parcell thereof shall be unpaid six months after it is due. Perhaps†a- my Cosin knows me well enough to be content this should be don by my will which will be the shorter way,-†a but if upon that proposall you finde him scruple at it let it be don the other way. But†a- if that please him not or he seem not desirous of it pray enquire me out a Chapman for it which will put an end to all that trouble there to me and my freinds.-†a My service to your Lady and litle ones I am
Deare Sir
Your most humble and most obleiged servant
J LOCKE

[Written by Locke:]
Rules to be observed for the future
1° Never to let any tenant run six months in areare but always to get in one half years rent before the next half yeare be due. I finde reason to repeat this here again Because Sledg and others were within three days of being a whole year in arear when this account was given. Had this been observed as I always desired, I had not run the danger of looseing soe much by Rob: Harol and Barnes, or at least neither my Cosin Stratton nor you soe much trouble to recover it. I know noe surer way to bring losse on the Landlord, and ruin on the tenant then to let tenants run on in arear
2 The first mony you receive of William Sledg or at least as much of it as amounts to the rent of Buckfurlong, receive it as the rent of Buckfurlong. Because there being security given for the rent of Buckhill and not of Buckfurlong that I know, the arears when any should be left still upon the security.
3 If the Coleworkes goe on get a trusty man to Keepe the account and receive my due.
4 That the arears due from Haroll Barnes and Nath: Summers be got in or secured with all speed for if it be not paid or well secured to day twill be much harder to get it tomorrow

937. John Freke to Locke, 3 June 1687 (934, 941)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 169-70.
June the 3d 1687
You are (Dear Sir) altogether in the Right. Fairy affection will not serve my turn Whilst my body makes a part of me. I must have affections and desire a conversation suitable to Flesh and blood. Twill be time enough when I am divested of them to enter into and become a part of the spirituall world to learn to be pleased with such a Friendship in the mean time give me leave to preferr the real advantages and excellent fruits that I reap from yours
― 209 ―
before all the imaginary benefits of their fantasticall kindness. The onely good I ever heard they did their friends was bestowing a little Gold upon them but your conversation will make a man wiser and better. It may be they are endowed with an Intuitive knowledge†1 that is more than humane but they never doe (nor am I sure they can) communicate it to us nay I am apt to think they cannot since we must want both Ideas and words to express or understand them by. But a man is sure to be improved by your solid reasoning and admirable discourse soe that I should promise my self more satisfaction in the enjoyment of your Company but one hour than in a whole night of theirs a whole night I say for I think they never appear by day.
Tis noe small encouragement you give me to continue obstinate in this opinion that you tell me I thereby secure the fair Sex on my side for I am of your opinion that they pinch harder and are more dangerous Enimys than fairys and therefore I shall always desire to keep on good terms with them and am very glad I can have them of my party without the trouble of Courting them to it or dissembling my own opinion to get an Interest in theirs few men are soe lucky for this Creature calld woman is generally as coy as skittish as delicate as nice as humorous and fantastick in their kindness as any Fairy can be immagind to be Not that I think all women such there are some who have Souls that receive noe impressions from their Sex and are as plain open candid sincere and generous as the proudest He can boast of and such I reckon your daughters though one of them is soe dainty that she could not be brought to relish a good Husband of a fortune and family not to be dispised but greedily embraced because he has but one eye and smoakt Tabacco soe that on that and some other accounts that wedding is past hopes†2 And for the other wedding in which I was offerd to draw the Settlement I must confess I despair of its being ever celebrated†3 tho my kinsman†4 is still very confident it will take effect and if it do's, fear not, I will make the Settlement such as it shall be impossible ever to bring a question upon it into Westminster Hall be the partys concernd in it never soe litigious which is a presumptuous saying but I think soe well of my self that
― 210 ―
I speak it with great confidence and believe my self able to make it good in which I have the concurrence of our Salisbury court friend†1 to whom I have shewn the Breviate of the Conveyance
Tell my friend who is soe fond of a retirement amongst a few books and friends that I am sorry I exprest my self soe ill that he did not understand me when I offerd him my Interest to restore him to his ancient Seat. I thought when I had told how much that place was alterd and expected dayly to be more and more alterd for the worse he would never have desired to see it again and I believe when he reads it again he will see that I intended onely to Droll on that subject but most men tho otherwise very quicksighted are blinded with their affection to their Mistresses. This was his mistress and I doubt he has a blind side with respect to her.†2 We have noe News but what the Ecclesiasticall Comissioners make us moonday next Magdalen College is to appear before them and tis said their visitor the Bishop of Winchester†3 too. Then alsoe the university of Cambridge is to bring their Statutes to them to receive such Corrections and Alterations as their Lordships shall think fit and they say alsoe that Caius college statutes are likewise to run the same fate†4 and I believe few colleges in either university have such correct statutes as to need noe amendment if well lookt into and strictly examined
Give my service to Mr F†5 and family and tell him that my Cousins Agent that is going for America has soe long deceived my expectation of giving me a coppy of my cousins patent†6 that I begin to fear he will not perform his promise at all which would trouble me because I shall goe soe soon out of Town as I shall not have time to get it any other way however I will still doe my endeavour and doe not quite despair. Sir W Y and his Bro and Sister D did I suppose begin their Journey hither this day. Mr Somers†7 values your friendship as it deserves to be esteemd and passionately longs for a personall conversation with you in which
― 211 ―
I know you would be both extremly satisfyd. I am Sir above all the world
Your affectionate friend and humble servant J F
Address: For Mr Lock to be left with Mr Benjamin Furly merchant in Rotterdam

938. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 12/22 June 1687 (931, 958)
Staatsbibliothek Preussischer Kulturbesitz, Berlin. Transcribed from photograph.
(English)
22 Jun
Si tuum Vir præstantissime miratus sum silentium, id tuæ debetur amicitiæ, quæ non solita erat diu tacere: ut incusarem certè non permisit meæ tarditatis et negligentiæ conscientia; idque maxime doleo te corpore potius quam animo impeditum aliquanto plus solito tacuisse. Mallem enim ut offensus quam ægrotus a scribendo abstineres. Iræ enim tuæ (si amicis delinquentibus irasci quidem potes) parata semper in humanitate tua medela, morborum non felices semper nec faciles exitus. Sed video quocum mihi res est, cum ejusmodi scilicet viro, qui nulla ab amicis, etiamsi debita, exigit officia, nulla erga amicos unquam ipse prætermittit. Cura, rogo, valetudinem tuam, vides quantum meâ interest. Optime
― 212 ―
facis quod commercium omne cum Musis intermittendum aliquamdiu censes, Earum consuetudo etiamsi semper honesta, non tamen semper tuta; et quantum roboris menti addit, tantum corpori detrahit. Sed non probo frequentes hosce febrium recursus, relaxa subinde animum, ut corpori parcas. vereor enim ne studiorum amœnitate et amore deceptus, iis nimium aliquando indulgeas, nec quantum satis est valetudini vaces. sed credo hujus delicti te potius reum apud uxorem tuam quam apud te agere oportet. Hoc enim sub specie virtutis plerumque tectum ita latet, ut vix invenias qui velit fateri. Credes <forsan>,†a hoc modo incusare non est <consolari>†b (uti decet) valetudarium. Sed nihil est in hoc quod à me ægre feras, quum eam quam reprehendo culpam fateor in te esse, quod sciam, unicam: nec hac monendi libertate usus sum, nisi quod eum quam diutissimè salvum esse vellem, in quo omnia reliqua sentio esse laudanda. Cura igitur ut valeas, iterum repeto; et cura diligenter. Hoc si facis me amabis
Tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
inline image

Stylum nostræ linguæ non rectè intellexit is à quo ultimæ tuæ epistolæ inscriptionem mutuatus es.
(Latin)
22 June
If I expressed surprise at your silence, eminent Sir, it was owing to your friendly nature, which had not usually been wordless for long; as for finding fault with you, I was certainly too well aware of my own slowness and remissness to permit of such a thing; and what I am most sorry for is that the hindrance which kept you silent rather longer than your wont was of the body rather than the spirit; in fact I could have wished it had been resentment rather than ill health that kept you from writing. For your anger—if indeed you are capable of being angry with your friends for their delinquencies —there is always a ready remedy in your kindness of heart; illnesses are not always done with so happily and easily. But I see whom I have to deal with; it is with a man who demands no services from his friends even when they are due to him, whilst he himself never omits to do them to his friends. Take care of your health, I beg you; you see how much it concerns [p. 212] me. You are quite right in thinking that you ought to forgo all your commerce with the Muses for a while; though their society is always honourable it is not always safe, and is apt to weaken the body as much as it strengthens the mind. But I do not like these frequent recurrences of fever; give your mind a rest now and then, just to spare your body; for I am afraid that you are beguiled by the charm of your studies and your love of them and so sometimes indulge them overmuch without giving enough time to your health. But I fancy you ought to be charged with this offence before your wife rather than before yourself; for this sort of thing is apt to be so hidden under the appearance of virtue that you can hardly find any one who is ready to confess to it. You will think perhaps that this sort of lecturing is not the proper way to comfort an invalid. But there is nothing in what I say that should displease you, seeing that the fault I am rebuking is, I declare, your only one, so far as I know; nor would I have warned you so frankly if I did not wish that one in whom I feel everything else to be praiseworthy might live as long as possible safe and sound. Therefore see to your health, I say again, and see to it carefully. By doing so you will love me
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
[p. 213] The person from whom you borrowed the address of your last letter did not know how to write English correctly.
Address: Mÿn Heer Mÿn Heer Limborch à Amsterdam
939. Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 17 June 1687 (933, 944)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 154-5.
London June 17th. 1687.
Dear Sir
If I have any right notion of friendship, I know nothing that is a more infallible mark of the truth and sincerity of it, nothing that contributes more to the pleasure and happiness it brings with it, then a constant gayety and freedome in communicating ones thoughts without reserve, and saying every thing whereby ones friend may be profited; and therefore there was no need of an Apology for the discourse you made me from the fancy'd chair in my Library, nothing could be more kind and endearing then that first letter, except the repetition of it which shewed it proceeded not from a fitt of Kindness but a settled friendship, for which I hope I shall ever retain a Just sense, and study to deserve it by the best returns I am capable of; But Friend give me leave to tell you t'was not fair to give me such an Idea of happiness (as my having so perfect a friend with me at Escott and his being pleased to be a part of my family and to give me the advantage of his conversation in that roome and those hours wherein the enjoyment will be most undisturbed) unless at the same time you resolved to make me that happy man, as soon as ever your circumstances will permit your return, or rather your inclinations lead you to it; for I must needs own had you come over in the spring as I once hoped you would, I doe not yet see any reason you could have had to repent it; but when I have said this I would not pretend to judge of your Affaires, but can not forbear wishing your concerns would invite you to come amongst us; In the mean time I must own I shall never think my selfe well settled in the row till you are with me and think your selfe at home there; and I shall never fitt up my Library to my
― 214 ―
satisfaction without your assistance, though something must be done towards it at my return into the country; by which time I doubt not but the books you have taken the trouble of collecting for me will be arrived, the memoirs of Maurier†1 were left for me with our friend Benjamin together with the large book he presented me (giving an account of their principles)†2 they may both if you judge it fit be put up in the same box and sent with the rest. I purpose to enclose this to Mr Furly and to desire him to draw a bill upon me for all that he has disbursed for me for the trees, iron backs, etc. To which I beg you to add what you have laid out for the books, since I can think of no way so easy and proper to discharge those debts. You have been indeed an extraordinary husband for me in the purchase of this box of books, but though I confess I find my selfe more obliged to mind the saving of charges then ever I was inclined to doe or thought I should (thanks to building and the iniquity of the times) yet it is not so hard with me as to restrain you from laying out the other 10 ll. in books for me, if you meet with those that tempt you, only I would desire you to buy none but what are really curiosities in their kind, having already more good books then I can ever hope to look into. Our friend Chiply†3 goes home next week, but we hope to have friend John's†4 company as long as we stay in Town (which will be long enough to receive any commands from you) and then we shall remove but to Tunbridge, so that if I can serve you in any thing in the absence of your friend Somshire, you will much oblige by employing
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate friend and faithfull servant.
W. Y.
My Br. and Sister are your servants as she will tell you in a postscript, if she be not quite spent with hurrying up and down to the shops to rig out her country friends. Your daughter Betty's Affaire is quite off.†5
Our friend J. Fr. salutes you most kindly.
Address: For Mr John Lock These
Endorsed by Locke: Sir W. Y 17 Jun. 87. Answered 1° July with a catalogue of the books inclosed and a desire to know their prices in London

940. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 23 June 1687 (933, 953)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 15-16. Perhaps forwarded by Freke with no. 941.
London June 23d. 1687.
Dear Sir
Since 'tis impossible to prevaile with you to Visit us in person, 'twas Charitably done of you to do it by a letter, which was a favour I have not deserved, but shall ever own with all imaginable gratitude. 'twas with the greatest satisfaction that I received yours of 30th. of May, at my first comming to Town, yett it would have been more welcome had it brought me any hopes of seeing you here; However I am obliged to you for wishing me happy, though you will contribute nothing towards the making me so, now when 'twas wholly in your power; when all things smile upon you, and you have fairer invitations, and greater incouragements to set to sea then ever. but since you are determin'd, since it must not be, since 'tis a proposall so ungratfull to you, a subject you alwayes wave, I will do so to for the future, and not disease†1 a Friend, whose quiet, whose happiness I wish so Zealously, and would promote by all wayes possible, were I capable in any sort. how pleas'd should I be could I give you any instances of it, for once take a Womans word, beleeve me your Friend, and then you must beleive that I can have no greater ambition then to be serviceable, and usefull to you, and that I am in pain when I want occasions and opportunities of expressing how much I am yours. I do not hope to find any thing in this Town, that can compensate the want of your conversation, 'tis true my Lanlady is very ingenious, and alwayes kind; and I have my share of her time and Company; but had I many such friends Mr Lock would alwayes keep the place he Justly posseses in my esteem and affections; and should I neglect him I should think it an unpardonable sin. and though you are carefull to remember me of my being in Town lately a fortnight, without writing to you, 'twas because I were ignorant that a letter from this Town would be more welcome then from any other place, and I thought the perpetual hurry I was in, would be allowed for an excuse, since I writt immediatly before my comming up, and immediatly after my return. but however I submit to any pennance you shall lay
― 216 ―
upon me, and will not Justifye my self as innocent if you think me otherwise. I am sure I am always sincere, and alwayes sencible of my infinite obligations to you. I came to Town in very good health, but 'tis already a little impair'd by the physick my Doctress has given me, but she promises me fair, and I think I must go on, and try a little longer; whiles my Master is under the care of Doctor Syddenham; assoon as they will dismiss us, we shall away to Tunbridge Waters; which will I hope set me right again in all respects. I shall every day drink your health, and wish you with us. my Brother has promised us his company there, one fortnight, but now he is at Hampton Court;†1 Mr Duke begs you to accept his best services. pray tender both mine and his to Mr Furley, in doing which you will lay a new obligation on Sir
Your most Obedient faithfull servant
ISABELLA DUKE
Address: For Mr John Lock at the House of Mr Benjamin Furley Merchant in Rotterdam
Endorsed by Locke: Mrs Duke 23 Jun. 87 Answered 22 Jul.
941. John Freke to Locke, 28 June 1687 (937, 960)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 171-2.
You need not (Dear Sir) consult your Fairys to know where my treasure ly's recollect your self and you will remember I have told you who Comands my affections, whose conversation and friendship I have in the highest Esteem. Can you forget with what earnestness I have prest one that you know to spend a Sommer in a country I am forced to continue in till Autumn? And promised after that to accompany my friend to what part of the world that friend should choose? And if you remember this Can you doubt on whom my heart is fixed? you are therefore noe longer to seek for my Mistress but I have chosen soe well that I defy you to railly me on that subject. I was much pleased with the good wishes you bestowd on her and heartily thank you for the kindness you exprest to me in them but must tell you that had they been put in the right mood and tense they would have been but a just description of her. I need make you noe excuse for not returning you her answer to what you
― 217 ―
writt now that you know who and where she is. I am sorry I cannot send you the fresh Sea fish you desire but your fresh two leg'd Ling (which is what I suppose you mean) comes to soe good a market here that I find noe merchant willing to adventure any abroad in hopes of a better there Soe that if you have a mind to eat a Dish you had best come hither and here you may have plenty and a hearty wellcome but then you must make haste for we expect in a litle time to see our markets more stored with Turbats etc: than yours have been, for when the Fishermen have driven them from your shoar they will probably come to ours, for they seem to take delight in these seas since they found the way into them, and then I doubt twill be difficult for you to come at the Ling I talk of. I am sorry to hear the Fish women sing to soe ill a Tune and that soe many Join in Chorus with them. I am affraid if they have not ere this changed their notes it bodes a Storm.†1 I hope the enclosed assures you how zealous I am to cultivate a good opinion of you in those you desire to be esteemd by and I can with great truth tell you that there is not one of them but has a Just value for you and place your friendship amongst those things that are most dear to them.†2 But you cannot blame them to be a litle angry that you have disappointed or delayd soe long their hopes of being made happy in the enjoyment of your company, That's but a love Quarell which may easily be pardond (if it need any and may not be reckond merit). I cannot yet tell you whither I shall draw the Settlement you wot of my cousin sollicits the business very hard†3 and keeps me in Town to wayt the Success which when I know I shall communicate to you. In the mean time I busie my self here in the service of my other friends amongst whom your Landlord is not forgot. I have got a coppy of the pattent he desired (for him) out of the office†4 having tryd all other ways in vain. Tell him he shall receive it ere long by a Gentleman of my acquaintance that is making a step over the water to see what kind of bird a Stork is.†5 Tell him alsoe that the <name>†a of the man he desired to know is Mr Hackshaw and tell him alsoe (for news) that we are told the King is resolved
― 218 ―
to take the Government of all the plantations into his own hands even of Pensilvania and New Jersey†1 which tis supposed will be a means to people our plantations apace. All your friends in Town salute you and him and soe do's
Sir
Your most affectionate
JO: FR
June the 28th S:V:†2 1687
Address: For Mr Lock at Mr Benjamin Furleys a merchant in Rotterdam

942. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 29 June [1687] (930, 950)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 144-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
I can hardly Perswade my self that you stand upon Terms with me because you really ought not, But I am affraid either that you have not beene well, or the Direction that I gave you has fail'd. Pray when you do write, now, Direct to Mr Henderson a Stationer at the Signe of the Frying Pan over against the Mews at Charing Cross, He takes Care of All my letters, and little Affairs in the Towne. I Pretend not now that This should be look'd upon as a letter, But not Knowing when I may be able to do better I let you see at least that I do not forget You. I would not have you suppose me when you have read This, Under any Violent Greife, I am growne such a Stoick now that I Know not whether Any thing Could give it me But I am really under such a sort of a Melancholy that it not onely Hinders me from haveing Any Thought that can be Diverting But I am also affraid it should Grow a Disease upon me. It is not long you Know since I Bury'd my Brother, Since that I have also lost my Sister,†3 My Child has beene in the Greatest Danger Possible of the same Fate, and I am not yet freed from the
― 219 ―
Feares of it. Besides this I have Frequent Assaults of the most Painefull of Distempers, of which I had no Apprehension till very latly.†1 All these things together may I Hope a little excuse me; Since the last alone, is enough to give One a very Melancholy Prospect, it very seldome I suppose leaveing Any that have it but with theire lives. However I am indeavouring what I can against it, by the Direction of my Lady Ranelaugh†2 and Mr Boyle, who do me the Honour to be my Physicians in this Case.
If ever I do returne to Another Humour againe I assure you You shall Quickly Know it, in the meane time I shall have the Tryal of your Charitie, and You an Opportunitie of leting me see that you can write to me though there be nothing of a Dutch Mistress in the Case; Since I am not able now to say anie thing upon That Subject And the Gay Ideas of the World do not I assure you (as upon a Certaine occasion you told me they Did) now Dance in my Fancy, Afflictions being much more efficacious to that end then All the Weiwertisme†3 and Stoicisme we us'd to talk of. I have onely to Add that in whatever Humour I am in, I am always very much
Your Friend.
June the 29th
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 29 Jun. 87 Answered 5 Aug.

943. Locke to [Edward Clarke], 5/15 July 1687 (936, 954)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 24. Written by an amanuensis (probably Syl) apart from the opening 'Sir' and the subscription; there are also some corrections by Locke and additions interpolated by him. Printed in Rand, pp. 214-20.
Despite the address the letter was intended in the first place for Clarke. It belongs to the Education series: see note, ii. 624; and is a sequel to no. 929. It was perhaps accompanied by Locke's answer to no. 908.
Sir
You must not wonder that you finde me often addeing to my former discourse concerning Education tis what I warnd you of heretofore being sensible when I first undertooke it that I should in a subjet I was soe litle versed in omit many things necessary to
― 220 ―
be considered. Haveing been lately in an House where there were children†1 and takeing stricter notice of their actions then formerly I was wont to doe I finde that crying†2- is a fault that should not be tolerated in them not only for the unpleasant and unbecomeing noise it fills the house with, but for more considerable reasons in reference to the children themselves.
Their crying is of two sorts either stubborne and†a domineering or Querulous and whineing. 1°. Their crying is very often a Contention for mastery and an open declaration of their insolence and obstinancy†3 when they have not the power to obtein their desire they will by their clamour and crying maintain their title and right to it, This is an open justifyeing themselves and a kinde†b- of remonstrance-†b against the unjustnesse of the oppression which denys them what they have a minde to. 2°. Sometimes their crying is the effect of pain or true sorrow and bemoaning themselves under it. These two if carefully observed may by the meen, looks, and actions and particularly the tone of their crying be easily destinguished but neither of them must be sufferd much lesse incouraged. 1°. The obstinate or stomach full crying should by noe meanes be permitted because it is but another way of flattering their desires and incouraging those passions which tis our main. businesse to subdue and if it be (as often as it is) upon the receiveing any correction it quite eludes all the good effects of it and a punishment which leaves them in this declared opposition only serves to make them worse. The restraint and punishments laid on children are all misapplyd and lost as far as they doe not prevail over their wills, teach them to submit their passions, and make their mindes supple and <pliant>†c to what their parents reasons advise them now or their owne reason shall hereafter But if in any thing they are crossed in they may be sufferd to goe away crying they confirme themselves in their desires and part with a declaration of their right and a resolution to satisfie them the first opportunity. This therefor is another reason why you should seldom correct your children for whenever you come to that
― 221 ―
extremity tis not enough to whip or beat them you must doe it till you finde you have subdued their mindes till with submission and patience they yeild to the correction which you shall finde best by their crying and their ceasing of it upon your bidding without this the beating of children is but a passionate tiranny†a over them and it is mere cruelty and not correction to put their bodys in pain without doeing their mindes any good.
But as this gives us a reason why children should seldome be corrected soe it also prevents their being soe, for if when ever they are chastised it were donne thus without passion but soberly and effectually too laying on the blows and smart not all at once but slowly with reasoning between and observation how it wrought and stoping when it had made them pliant penitent and yeilding they would seldome need the like punishment again being made carefull to avoid the fault that deserved it besides that by this meanes as the punishment would not be lost for being too litle and not effectuall, soe it would be kept from being too much if we gave of as soon as we perceived that it reachd the minde and that was betterd. For since the chideing or beating of children should be always the†b least†b that possible may be That which is laid on in the heat of anger seldome observes that measure and is commonly more then it should be, though it proove lesse then enough. 2° Many children are apt to crye upon any litle harme they suffer and the least pain that befalls them puts them into Complaints and bawling. This few children avoid for it being the first and natural way to declare their sufferings or wants before they can speak, the†c- compassion that is thought due to that tender age foolishly incourages and continus in them long after they can speak.-†c Tis the duty I confesse of those about children to compassionate them whenever they suffer any hurt. but not to shew it in pyttying them help and ease them the best you can but by noe meanes bemoane them. This softens their mindes and makes the litle harmes that befall them sinke deep into that part which alone feels and make larger wounds there then otherwise they would. They should be hardend against all sufferings espetialy of the body and have a tendernesse only of shame and for reputation, The many inconveniencys this life is exposed to require we should not be too sensible of every litle hurt.†d what our mindes yeild not to, makes but a slight impression. and does us but very litle harme;
― 222 ―
tis the suffering of our spirits that makes and continues the pain This brawnynesse and insensibility of minde is the best armor we can have against the Common evils and accidents of life and being a temper that is to be got by exercise and custome more then any other way the practise of it should be begun betimes and happy is he that is taught it early That effeminacy of spirit which is to be prevented or cured as noething that I know soe much increases in children as crying, soe noething on the otherside soe much checks and restrains as their being hinderd from that sort of complaining In the litle harmes they suffer from knocks and falls they should not be pittyed for falling but commended and bid doe soe again, which is a better way†a- to cure-†a their falling then either chideing or bemoaning them.
but let the hurt†b- they receive-†b be what it will stop their crying which will give them more quiet and ease at present and harden them for the future The former sort of crying requires severity to silence it and where a look or a positive command will not doe it blows must. For it proceeding from pride obstinancy or wilfullnesse the will where the fault lyes must be bent and made to comply by a rigor sufficient to subdue it. But this later being ordinary from a quite contrary cause†c ought to be treated with a litle gentler method. persuasion or diverting the thoughts another way or laughing at them etc: may perhaps be at first the proper way but for this the circumstances of the thing and the particular temper of the child must be considerd. noe certain invariable rules can be given about it but it must be left to the prudence of the parents or Tutor But this I thinke I may say in generall that there should be a constant discountenancing of this sort of crying also and that the father by his lookes words and authority should always stop it mixing a greater degree of roughnesse in his looks or words proportionably as the childe is of a greater age or a sturdier temper but always let it be enough to master the disorder.†-2 I†1- must minde you also that Geographie and chronologie should have been put amongst these things which in the first place your son is very perfectly to learne I meane the general parts of them soe as to have a cleare and setled Idea of the
― 223 ―
figure of the earth and the positions of the parts of it, under its first and more general divisions and denominations;†-1 and†2- to have in his minde a view of the whole current of time and the several considerable Epochs that are made use of in history without these two history which is the great mistrys of prudence and civil knowledg and ought to be the proper study of a Gentleman or man of businesse in†a the world.
without Geographie and chronologie I say history will be very ill reteind and very litle usefull, but be only a jumble of matters of fact confusedly heaped togeather without order or instruction. Tis by these two the actions of mankinde are ranked into their proper places of times and countrys under which circumstances they are not only easier kept in the memory but in that natural order are only capable to afford those observations which make a man the better and abler for reading of them.-†2 The†3- globes therefor must be studied and that pretty diligently and I thinke may be began betimes if the Tutor have but discretion to destinguish what the child is capable of knowing and what not. For which this may be rule that perhaps may goe a pretty way viz that children may be taught any thing that falls under their senses espetially their sight as far as their memorys only are exercised and thus a child very young may learne which is the æquator which the Eclyptick etc. which Europe or England upon the globes as soon almost as he knows the roomes of the house he lives in if care be taken not to teach him too much at once nor to set him upon a new part till that which he is upon be perfectly and more then perfectly learnt and fixed in his memory.-†3 The†4- things that he will thus learne by sight and have by roat in his memory is not all I confesse that he is to learne upon the globes but yet is a good step and preparation to it and will make the remainder much the easier when his judgment is grown ripe enough for it.-†4 When†5- I speake of chronologie as a science he should be perfect in I do not meane the litle controversys that are in it. These are endlesse and most of them of soe litle importance as not to deserve to be enquird into though they could be known and therefor all that learned noise and dust of the chronologist is wholy
― 224 ―
to be avoided. The most usefull book I have seen in that part of learning is a small treatise of Strauchius†a which is printed in duodecimo under the title of Breviarum Chronologicum,†b †1 out of which may be selected all that is necessary to be taught a young gentleman concerning chronologie for all that is in that†c treatise†c a learner need not be cumbred with.
he has in him all the most remarqueable or usuall Epochs reduced all to that of the Julian period which is the easieast and plainest and surest method that can be made use of in chronologie.†-5 One thing more and I have donne for this time we†2- formerly observed that variety and freedome was that that delighted children and recommended their play to them and that therefor their book or any thing we would have them learne should not be enjoynd them as businesse This their Tutors and teachers are apt to forget and their impatience to have them busied in what is fitt for them to do suffers them not to deceive them into it but by the repeated injunctions they meet with childeren quickly destinguish between what is requird of them and what not when this mistake is made soe that his book is made once uneasy to him the cure is to be applyd at the other end and since it will be then too late to endevour to make it a play to him you must take the contrary course and observing what play he is most delighted with enjoyne that to him. make him play that play soe many howers every day not as a punishment for playing but as if it were the businesse requird of him. This if I mistake not will in a few days make him soe weary of his most beloved sport that he will prefer his book or any thing to it espetially if it may redeeme him from any part of the taske of play that is set him and he may be sufferd to imploy some part destined to scourge a top. or the like in his booke or such other Exercise as is really usefull to him This I at least thinke a better cure then forbidding (which usually increases the desire) or any other punishment should be made use of to remedy it for when you have once glutted his appetite (which may be safely donne in all things but eating and drinkeing) and made him surfet of what you would have him avoid you have put into him a principle of aversion†d and you need not soe much feare
― 225 ―
afterwards his longing for the same thing again.†-2 Play things†1- I would also have children have and of all sorts, but still be in the keeping of their tutors, or somebody else, whereof the child should have in his power but one at once and should not be sufferd to have <another but>†a when he restord that. This teaches them betimes to be carefull of not looseing or spoileing the things they have whereas plenty and variety of such things in their owne keepeing makes them wanton and carelesse and teaches them from the beginning to be squanderers and wasters. these I confesse are litle things and such as will seeme beneath the care of a Governor but noething that may forme childrens mindes is to be overlooked and neglected and whatsoever introduces habits and setles customes in them deserves the care and attention of their governors and is not a small thing in its consequences.-†1
I am
Sir Your most humble servant
J LOCKE
15 Jul. 87
Address: For Mrs: Mary Clarke at the Lady Kings in Salisbury Court near Fleet street London
Postmark: IY—
Endorsed by Clarke: J:L's Letter of Education Received the 22th July 1687.
944. Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 11 July 1687 (939, 960)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 156-7.
Tunbridge July 11th. 87.
Dear Sir
I had the favor of your's of the 2th instant about a week before we left London, but was then so busy in dispatching severall little concerns that I could not find a time to return you my humble thanks for it, and for your care and trouble in helping to furnish my Library, but by this delay I am now enabled to informe you that the books and other things sent by Hodder†3 are safely arrived at Topsham, of which I had yesterday an account from Escott. I had not the leisure to enquire the prizes of any of those books in
― 226 ―
London, but shall make a short stay there again in my way to Devon, and then I will endeavour to satisfy you in that particular. if you please in the mean time to let me know, which of the books you suspect your bookseller has over-rated, that I may not make a needless enquiry about the rest, be pleased also to write me at what places I may be most likely to receive satisfaction in that enquiry, and let me have the happiness of hearing from you speedily, because I purpose to be in London again within 3. weeks, and thence to hasten to Escott to quicken the builders and take their accounts that we may shutt up before winter. As soon as I come home I purpose to divide the books according to their marks, and shall send you word whether the parson desires any other books; you may be confident I will never part with those you so much recommend to me. I have too great a value for Mr L.s Judgement to doe that, or to recall the commission (I think) I gave you in my last to lay out such another summe of money (as the last) in any curious books you light on, which you judge fit for my use, not that I want furniture for my Library, for I beleive I have more books already than can be well placed in it, but I am willing not to loose so good an opportunity of being furnished with such choice pieces as I fancy can hardly be had any where but in Holland, and such as no body is so likely to find out as you, and I am sure I know no body whose recommendation in that kind I can relye on but your selfe, therefore pray use an entire freedome with me in this (as in all other things) and let Barclay and Maurier be sent with the next Cargo. We are much troubled at the report we have here of the misfortune befallen Monsieur Bele,†1 as well for the loss the publick receives by it, as for that acquaintance we had with him at Rotterdam, pray write me in your next how it is with him, and if the report be true who now writes the Nouvelles de la République des lettres. and whether they are as well done as they were by him.†2 Our friend Fr. went into the country a week since to see
― 227 ―
his Relations, but I suppose will be here within a fortnight to drink the waters; I know not whether he acquainted you that he was incommoded a week or ten daies together with a Rheumatism or Siatica, which made him very lame and was with difficulty enough removed; I wish you had the State of his case that you might advise him how to govern himselfe so as to prevent the like accidents, to which seems so very subject, I think this bout he was his own physitian. My Br. and S. Duke give you their most particular Respects, she is in daily hopes of a letter from you, they have just begun their course of water-drinking. I can not conclude till I have told you how much I was pleased with an expression in the conclusion of your letter, that does but suppose we shall once be so happy as to see you at Escott, every thing that assures me of the continuance of your friendship, and that you wish your selfe sometimes with us is most acceptable to
Your most obliged friend and Servant
W. Y.
Address: For Mr John Lock These.

Nous sommes delivréz ici <d'une>†a grande peine par la reception de votre derniere, et je vous ecris de chez l'un des triumvirs qui vous salüent tous. Il y a ici un fils du conte de Rochester,†2 fils du chancelier Hide aupres duquel est un mr Hill†3 que le Capitene de marine et moy voions de fois a autre, Il a beaucoup de merite et a commerce avec le Docteur Burnet qui n'est pas eloigné du lieu qui
― 228 ―
vous possede.†1 La grace que vous me voulez faire de m'aprendre à faire des pierres colatoires n'est pas de refus. mais j'aimerois bien mieux savoir en quoi il importe si fort de passer les liqueurs. Je scay bien que cela leur emporte cequ'eles ont de terrestre, mais aussi ces parties la sont quelquefois les plus alimentaires. l'interest que vous prenez à ma santé me porte à vous dire que depuis environ deux mois je prens le matin à jeun et le soir en me couchant une chopine de lait bouïlli sans sel ny sucre et que j'en ote la plure†2 qui se fait en se refroidissant, et que cela me fait extremement de bien. Je voudrois m'en avisé plutost.
Voila†a- enfin des feuïlles et de la graine de la plante que nos païsans apelent Baje, qui est le cynoglossum.†3 ceque vous en a dit mr Godefroi est constant, qui est que l'on sert ici contre les ulceres de la bouche en portant les racines au col enfileés dans un colier par rouëles. cela ma eté bien confirmé. cela ne pouroit-il point etre utile contre le scorbut. Il y auroit bien moien den faire l'experience au camp de Maintenon.-†a†4 Je travaille à sortir d'afaire d'avec mes coheritiers, et me metre en etat de pouvoir enfin vous embrasser. Dieu le veuïlle et au plutost.
Mandez moi prontement à droiture si celui vous aura eté rendüe
Mr L'Abé me dit prezentement que dans la Beausse il y a une herbe que les païsans apelent Chanquerole qu'ils pendent aupres de la cheminée et guerit à mezure quele seche les chancres qui vienent à la bouche des petis enfans, et mr L'Abé qui sen moquoit d'abord, m'assure l'avoir vu.†5 Nous saurons quele est cete herbe, et m'en feray aporter.

946. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 17 July 1687 (888, 982)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 58-9.

Deare Freind
Wayteing some days since on your noble Freind E P†1 and he not hopeing to see you in a short time and reteineing his former freindship desired me to write to you for the second part de Intellectu†2 and I beleeve you will much oblidge him by it
I have thoughts of makeing a Chymicall preparation of Reg [antimonii], [gold] and [silver] in the first volume of Petrus Johannes Faber Francofurti 1656 p 225:†3 taking the last number of pages in that volume. I suppose you may borrow the booke and therefore send not the processe. I desire if you canne satisfy me in the only doubt I have concerning that processe which is whether the [gold] and [silver] ought to be pulverized by an amalgama before they be imported into the melting Regulus [antimonii] or whether you thinke they will mix with it without the [amalgama] I know Chymists use to omitt some considerable circumstance besides I find in Poterii operum lib qui Pharmacopœa inscribitur p 636 de auro Diaph and p 637 de Theriac metall. both in the appendix to that booke†4 somewhat different preparations. I beleeve if the medicine be made right it will prove of great efficacy and I beleeve Faber both knowing and as a chymist honest. As to your Cousin Adrians concernes I find him incumbred in law but hopes an end by reference†5 before the next terme, but not soone enough to looke after his affayres in Holland though he much desired to make a short trippe over. If his voyage had held I would by him have writt more Chymicall doubts. However if you have any Chymicall freinds pray enquire. I have read 2 bookes of Gabr. Clauderus 1 de
― 230 ―
Cinnabari 2 de balsamandis corp. humanis.†1 I thinke him an industrious and ingenious Chymist. If any more bookes of his are printed I desire you to enforme me. My familly are all well and wee are learneing french of a french protestant minister. all present their services to you Especially Parthenice Will and godson. I am
your very affectionate A T.
I have never seene Lysis since I saw you but heare by Musidore that he is very much recovered

947. Locke to Benjamin Furly, 20/30 July 1687 (986)
Forster, pp. 18-20. Locke was in Amsterdam probably from 23 July to 15 August: Syl's accounts in B.L., MS. Locke f. 34, ff. 11v, 12.
30 July, 1687.
Dear Friend,
One cannot take amisse the kinde mistake of one's friends. But I should be very sory to have given any just occasion to your wive's†3 misapprehension. Had she been better acquainted with my way of liveing with those I am free with, she would have known that silence, when I have no businesse to write, is a liberty I take with none so much as with the friends I am most assured of, and with whom I think myself past all ceremony. But, to confesse the truth in your present case, I think I should have writ sooner, had I not every day expected that a letter from England would also bring me with it one from you, and that then I should have an occasion to answer. For I every day went or sent to Wetstein's, with hopes to finde one there from you. This be sure, I was any thing rather than sullen; and I was so far from taking any offence, that I am not displeased at the oportunity of acknowledging, once for all, that I was never any where with more freedom and satisfaction. This to your wife, to whom pray give my kindest remembrance. As for
― 231 ―
yourself, if I mistake not very much, you and I are past these discourses; and therefore let me tell you, that how acute, how subtil, how learned soever you are, 'tis not you alone have the privileeg to pass for a Jesuite; other people of lower rank may, I finde, sometimes arive at that honour, and, had it not been for an envious Englishman that sat at the other end of the boat, who discovered the truth, I had in my passage hither gon clear away with that reputation. This story is too long for a letter, and must be reservd to make you laugh when I come. Only I desire you to article with the Baron†1 that he shall not pervert me when I return again to his conversation. For being now got to be of the most orthodox society in the world, I would not be tainted with the least infection of heresie for all the gold our English chemist†2 there is like to make. And I make account to die in this unspotted reputation would doe one as much good as dyeing in St. Francis's owne frock. It is very convenient that you take care in this affair, for I finde the great desire I have to returne again to the enjoyment of his and your good company will not let me be long away. Pray salute him with my most hearty and best respects, and be assured that I am, with perfect sincerity,
Your unfeigned friend and servant,
J. LOCKE.
Remember me kindly to the litle ones, especially to my litle friend.†3 Bethinke yourself if I can doe you any service here, or for Mr. Van Helmont. I shall be glad of the occasion.
948. Dr. Charles Goodall to Locke [c. 25] July 1687 (1002)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 19-20. Forwarded by Charleton with his letter of 26 July (no. 949); presumably written a day or two earlier. Printed by Dr. K. Dewhurst in Journal of the History of Medicine, xvii (1962), 492-4. For the writer see no. 683, etc.
London July 1687
Sir
I thanke you for the figure of the leaf of the Kinkina tree you sent me by our worthy and good Freind mr Charlton.†4 I have compared
― 232 ―
it with some leaves taken out of boxes or bales of bark sent into England, which I have kept long by me. It doth very much resemble them and seem to be of the same kind. I thanke you for putting me in remembrance of perusing that treatise I intended upon that subject, which I have for some yeares laid aside,†1 having been engaged upon writing that History you mention,†2 as likewise hindered by sickness, loss of my Father etc. I now design in good earnest to fit it for the press, and am in hopes (whilst I am thus engaged) I may get better information about it from a learned and ingenious Physician (an intimate Freind of mine) who is speedily going to Jamaiaca†a with the Duke of Albemarle:†3 I have drawn up the following set of inquiries with which I intend to furnish him and some other Freinds, amongst whom I do particularly request your assistance.
Queries to be proposed concerning the Kinkina tree†4
To any of the Natives of Peru brought into Europe: To any Spaniards, who were born and lived some time in that Countrey: To any Merchants, who have long traded at Lima, Quito or other parts of Peru: To any Preists who have Spent some yeares there: Or in case None of these can be found in Europe, to Antonio Gimenez an eminent Physician of Lima, or any other inquisitive Physician or Naturalist, who may be found in that Countrey.
Where the Kinkina trees cheifly grow, whether they be wild or propagated by Art, or both; what their size, figure, number, colour (of the leaves, bark and wood) taste, and use amongst the Indians, and Europæans inhabiting that Countrey are; when and
― 233 ―
how the first discovery of these trees and bark was made: As likewise whether they beare flowers, seed or fruit; How and when the Natives bark these trees, whether the trees are not thereupon destroyed, if not, what use are made of them; how they manage the bark in order to its transportation, what quantity they have transported in late years?
Questions to be proposed concerning the Kinkina bark
To any Spanish or English Merchants living at Cadiz
When the Kinkina bark came first into Rome or Spain, when into other parts of Europe, what different prices it hath been sold at, how adulterated, what quantity hath been imported into Europe by the Spanish Galeons in one voyage, and how many they may have made of late yeares, especially since 1677 when this bark beganne to be generally used,†1 and how they have been fraighted therewith?
If you have any Freind at Rome, I begge the favour of you to write to him to enquire of the learned Nazarius†2 whether he hath published those observations he had by him de corticis Peruviani usu vique differenti in viris atque mulieribus quibus frustra datur.†3 which he mention'd in a letter wrotte to my learned and good Freind Dr Grew†4 An. 1680: If he would be pleased to transmit them to me either in print or Manuscript, I will do him all the right I can, when I publish my treatise on this subject.
If you have seen any books worth the reading which have been published about the Cortex since 80, be pleased to give me an account of them, as likewise how the Miscellanea Curiosa†5 are sold in Holland; I have the first set of them, but want 5 volumes of the second, viz 82.83.84.85.86.
My eldest Son†6 is now at home with me, He is 4 yeares standing at Cambridg next Christmasse; My youngest†7 is at Eaton, whom I
― 234 ―
intend to take home at the same time: I design them both for physic, be pleased to give me your advice about their education, and let me know what University you most esteem in Holland, whether Leyden or Utrecht, and what their yearely expence may be there?†a Charles (I feare) is inclined to a phthisis.
Dr Sydenhams Son†1 lives at home with him, hath severall Children and applies himself wholly to physic; He hath got the degree of Doctor in Scotland, and is to be admitted Licentiate of the Colleg.
My wife†2 and self give our humble service to you, being very glad to heare how well you enjoy your health in Holland. Sir I am
Your highly obliged faithfull Freind and humble Servant
CHARLES GOODALL

949. William Charleton to Locke, 26 July 1687 (928, 951)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 70-1. Copy or draft in B.M., Sloane MS. 3962, ff. 227-8. Part printed from B.M. version in Biographia Britannica, ed. A. Kippis, 1778-93, iv. 342-3. Answered by no. 951.
July the 26th 1687
Deare Sir
Inclosed I send you the long expected letter from our worthy freind Dr. Goodall, for who's extraordinary kindnesse and Civility
― 235 ―
to me upon your account I entreate the return of your thanks. It is now neare 3 moneths that I have been sorely aflicted with violent and Constant pains in my head accompanyed with great giddynesse insomuch that I was not able to read the letters on the back of a booke placed upon a shelf of an ordinary height without being ready to fall, In this Condition the able, and Compassionate Doctor, found me, and after he had taken a verry exact account of the circumstances of it he prescribed me severall things in order to my Cure, amongst others a sort of Lozenge by which I found benefit though he would receive none, it not being in my power to fix one single fee on him, he telling me that preceaving I was so Intimate a freind of yours I should have his advice gratis. I thanke God I am somewhat better then I have been but I feare that I shall scarsely ever be perfectly free'd from this unhappy distemper. Pray in your next let me know when I shall send the Moreri's Dictionary and the other Bookes you formerly mention'd, as to the Catalogue of the things I want it would be to large a one to be Inserted In this letter, I shall therefore take notice only of some few that I have formerly written to you about viz. the Phalangium Americanum a sort of spider, the Stella arborescens, and the larger sort of Echinus from the East Indies cum spinis, for other things there are severall which are set down in the Index Musaei Indici†1 that I want but which I supose will not be met with else where but if to be had I would willingly purchase them with money or in Truck, viz. the Salamandra ex Java Gecco. Avis Zeylanica, eleganti Crocato Colore Kahakurulla, Avicula Zeylanica mortem prænuncians, Manucodiata seu avis Paradisea Zeylanica ex albo et nigro variegata duabus in Cauda longissimis pennis donata Wathuhora, Conchæ Malabaricæ Chiancos dictæ uterus. In fine anything that is curious in nature either of shells, Insects, reptiles, birds, plants seeds etc will be verry welcome and though I may have them already they will serve to change for other things that I want. Sir you were pleased to give me this liberty and I have taken it. I am verry desirous of receiving a Catalogue from your freind†2 of what he would have from hence which I shall readyly furnish
― 236 ―
him with if I can upon the Consideration of his being your freind. I take my leave and am
Sir
Your Most Affectionate and most devoted Servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON

950. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 29 July [1687] (942, 967)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 146-7. Year from Locke's note. The reasons for the identifications of Urgunda and the Lady Abbess are stated in no. 815 n.
I am sorry you should once in your Life Owe More to the Impertinence of Others, then to my Friendship; who should not have Writt to you now but upon the score of the first. But I must have great Vanitie if I should really think this Letter could Oblige you Since tis onely to let you know I have depriv'd you for the Present of one that I am sure upon many Accounts must be much Welcomer to You then that would have beene (or Any from the same Hand) which you Quarrel with me for Burning;†3 However I have had so much regard for you as to take Care that it may not be a Total loss, Haveing refer'd the Person who wanted a Direction to you, to Mr C:†4 assureing them I knew not where you was, which was the Question Ask'd; though I suppose the Cheife Reason was not theire Ignorance; However it be I had no Mind to gratifie them any farther then I must needs, without being Unjust to You; Since the Picture they once Drew of Themselves at Urgundas House;†5 Theire Civilities to me There that time, And some Characters I have heard, make me Not Ambitious to be in the Number of Those whom they esteeme, and Consequently very
― 237 ―
Indifferent Whether I Oblige them, or Not, Who would not I suppose stand in need of my Direction to you if theire Business was of such Importance as that a Small delay would prove Prejudicial to it.
However do not beleeve that I think it can be so Inconsiderable Neither, as that this letter should make Any Amends for what I have done; which it would be impossible for me to do at Any time, But especially now, that I have begun it with telling you that Friendship Has no share in it, tho Perhaps if I should examine the Matter a little further I might find that I have done my self wrong in it, Since I am so tyr'd at this time with Writeing that I think Civilitie onely would scarse make me Continue it. Notwithstanding I find a great Disposition to tell you that that Black Cloud which overshaddow'd me when I writt to you last begins now to Disipate, and that if I am not yet Perfectly Gay, I am yet what is Better, Pleas'd; which I think a little Disposition to Melancholy, is no Hindrance to; However You must not expect from me Relations of London at this Distance of Time When All my Neighbours who have beene There this Summer as well as I, and who by theire Witts should have Transcendant Memories, have forgot them. Tis enough methinks that Amidst all the Divertions of That Place you were not forgot; Though I assure You my Principle One was Company, Haveing very little time to bestow on any others, which yet my Conversation with Some Persons had not made me renounce; Neither had I any Sute at Court to employe my Self, or Them in; whose Interest (whatever it be) I have very little Pretence to make Use of; altho I differ from the World (as it is not the first time) in my Opinion, and Esteeme for theire Persons, which you I hope will not make One to Censure me for; should Others ever do so; But I find you are not so far off of our World Here, but that you have All the news of it, Onely I suppose by your last Inquirie, it may be like our Countrey News letters, with large Additions; and sometimes False Storys; Of the first Number tis I imagine that to be which makes you ask after D: M:†1 who is indeed very ill in Body and Also Melancholy, as He Always was; though it now Dispose Him to be more unsociable, He not Careing for the Conversation of Any but his best Friends, which gives Occasion I suppose to some reports you may have heard, of which I Know no other Ground but an Impatience (which I think indeed below so much Philosophy) to be in that Happyer State he has so Well
― 238 ―
Describ'd;†1 the Thoughts of which, and those other Great Truths it is Built upon, being the onely support He says that the Mind of Man can have under so much Bodyly indisposition.
But tis Hard that a Man cannot be sick, but it must reach to Your Knowledge; I shall be affraid in time You will know what I do in This Closet. For those that make a Figure at Court, and Appeare There, I can be Content they should be Deliver'd up to You, to say what you Please of, Right, or Wrong, But if you once begin to Meddle with those in the Countrey, One knows not where you may stop; and I shall be affraid you will even Arrive to Urgundas Pretence at last of knowing Hearts;†2 to whom I may perhaps send to know, whether it is to Contribute towards the Nunnerie, or No, that your Lady Abbess†3 is in such Distress to Write to You; who I Fancie receives no Small Humiliation by the turne of Affairs†4 that she can Condiscend to Correspond with such a Reprobate as You are; who are so far I feare from that necessarie Duty of All good Christians, Fasting twice in a Weeke, as scarse to do it on Good Frydays, And I begin now to beleeve that a Deane who Eates Flesh in Lent and Can Preach on a Tuesday,†5 may be in Her Account something a better Churchman of the Twoo then Mr Ferguson;†6 Since the People of Her Stamp do not seeme to have Any Better Approv'd themselves, and are now but upon equall Terms; which I am sure is no small Greife to Abundance of theire Wise Admirers; though I beleeve very much better of Many of Themselves then to think tis so to Them. But should I once begin to Consult Urgunda, without doubt I should not stop Here, but have many more things to Ask Her But the little Specimen she has given of her skill may be her securitie from that Importunitie; Who notwithstanding that, and Her unjust Accusation of me for some Jesuitical Principles, I must say has Vertues enow to Attone for the Follys of her whole Sex, as well those of the Towne, as my Countrey Neighbours; whose Humour and Conversation you Draw more to the Life, then ever Kneller,†7 or Ryly,†8 can theire Faces. But I dare not venture to Give
― 239 ―
one stroke at Them my self; or say Any thing else for feare I should Ingage too far to leave roome to Add what I shall always desire You to beleeve of your old Governess, that she is your Constant Freind
and Servant
PHILOCLEA
July the 29th†a
