969. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 10/20 October 1687 (965, 979)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 255u. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 315-17; postscript and address in Ollion, p. 175.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Inter cardica et, uti nostri vocant, restaurantia, nihil tam efficax reperio quam amicorum benevolentiam. Tuis ultimis literis me maximè recreatum sentio. Jam diu prioribus tuis humanitatis plenis respondissem si quid certum de valetudine me pronunciare ausus fuissem, subinde enim cum me jam sanum salvumque credideram recidivam passus inter spem morbumque diu versatus distuli ad te literas dare donec certo aliquot dierum experimento
― 281 ―
me <prorsus>†a convaluisse confiderem. hæc cunctatio ultimas tuas amicitiæ plenas tibi expressit literas et mihi attulit remedium utilius eo et jucundius quod mihi a Domino Veenio per Helmontium misisti summâ cum curâ et festinatione: quanquam frustra, Famula enim per negligentiam eversâ phiolâ inclusum effudit liquorem. Sed jam spero non amplius opus erit remediis quamvis subinde levia quædam sentio symptomata quæ spero non recrudescentis mali esse minas sed abeuntis reliquias. Hæc ad te sigillatim scribere non vereor quia de valetudine mea ita solicitus es ut alio modo tuæ humanitati magis gratè respondere non possim. Gaudeo vehementer te pauco sanguine redimisse quod tibi impendebat malum. Spero te ea cautione et maturè semper usurum, quamprimum aliquam sentis gravitatem corporis præsertim capitis vel ventriculi ad venæsectionem tibi statim confugiendum. Hoc ni facias de te sano magis metuendum erit quam de me ægroto. Nos valetudinarii quoddam genus sumus hypocritarum qui eo non proficiscimur quo sæpius videmur tendere. Multum Tibi, collegis cæterisque amicis Amstelodamensibus debeo quibus mea sanitas ita cordi est, nec sperare possum vitam mihi satis diuturnam fore ut tantam benevolentiam tuam vero imprimis prout res meretur possim agnoscere, hoc velim tibi persuasum habeas me quantulus
― 282 ―
quantulus sim totum tuum esse. Salutes quæso quam humillime meo nomine Veeniosque Genellosque et Collegas omnes, illisque dicas mihi eos tam eximios esse medicos ut magis mihi prosint illorum vota, quam aliorum remedia. Lectissimam tuam fæminam quam officiosissime etiam salutes. Vale, et ego ut valeam, uti facis, me amando perge facere
Tui cum amore observantissimus
J LOCKE
(English) Hospes meus et Cl: Helmontius te plurimum valere jubent
Quando Tibi occurrit dominus Le Clerc ipsi dicas quæso me nuper et librum et chartas quas mihi miserat recte accepisse, et quamprimum aliquanto aptior ad eas res sit valetudo curaturum quod cupit, interim agnosco beneficium. Hanc schedulam inclusam mihi ante aliquot dies in manus traditam ut ad illum transmitterem detinuit non prona ad scribendum ægritudo, nunc quæso illi tradas, ut si bibliothecæ suæ inserandam judicet emendatam habeat:†1 si cupiat adhuc Porphyrii librum de vita Phythagoræ†2 ego curabo ut ad illum quamprimum mittatur

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Of all cordials and, as people like ourselves call them, restoratives I find none so efficacious as the kindness of friends. Your last letter has made me feel greatly refreshed. I would have replied some time ago to your previous letter, so full of generous feeling, if I had dared to say anything for certain about my health; for from time to time when I had believed myself thoroughly restored I suffered a relapse, and so in this prolonged hovering between hope and sickness I put off writing to you until I should be confidently assured by [p. 281] some days' trial that I had completely recovered. It was this dallying of mine that forced you to write your last letter, so full of friendliness, and brought me a more profitable and pleasant remedy than the one you sent me from Mr. Veen through van Helmont with such care and speed; though it was in vain, for a maidservant carelessly upset the bottle and spilt the liquid it contained. But I hope now there will be no further need for remedies, although I occasionally feel certain slight symptoms, which I hope are not threats of a recrudescence of the trouble but traces left behind in its departure. I do not hesitate to give you these particulars, since you are so solicitous for my health that I could not better show my gratitude for your sympathy by replying to it in any other way. I am exceedingly glad that you have found relief from the trouble that threatened you at the cost of a little blood. I hope you will always take that precaution, and in good time; the moment you feel any heaviness of the body, especially in the head or belly, you should resort at once to bleeding. Unless you do so we shall have to be more alarmed for you the healthy man than for me the sick. We valetudinarians are a species of hypocrites: we do not set out on the course to which we seem very often to be inclined. I owe much to you and to our Collegians and the rest of our friends at Amsterdam who have my health so much at heart, nor can I hope to live long enough to be able to acknowledge so much kindness, especially your own, as in fact it deserves; I would have you believe just this, that [p. 282] insignificant as I may be, I am wholly yours. Please give my most respectful greetings to the Veens and the Guenellons and to all our Collegians, and tell them they are such excellent physicians in my case that their good wishes do me more good than the medicines of others. Please also give my kindest regards to your excellent wife. Farewell, and, so that I too may fare well, continue to love me,
Your most affectionate and devoted
J. LOCKE.
(Latin) My host and the illustrious van Helmont send you their best wishes. When you meet Mr. Le Clerc please tell him that I recently received the book and the papers that he sent me, and that as soon as my health is rather more equal to such things I will see to his wishes; meanwhile I thank him for his kindness. The enclosed paper was handed to me some days ago to send on to him, but has been delayed as I was not well enough to write; so now please let him have it, so that if he thinks it suitable for insertion in his Bibliotheque he may have it in corrected form;†1 if he still wishes to have Porphyrius's book on the life of Pythagoras†2 I will have it sent to him as soon as possible.
20 Oct. 1687

Dear Sir
I hope you received mine of the 28th August which gave you notice of my having sent the manuscript into the Countrey as you directed, Since I have sent one halfe of the seeds and husks of the Fæniculum Sinense to Mr Jacob Bobert, and have now in my collection your noble present of curious draughts of East Indians and others, marked from 2 to 30, which I esteem amongst the cheifest raryties of it, not only upon the account of the Donor, but in Consideration of the greatnesse of their curiosity, and return you my most humble thanks. Sir Henry Hobart is still in Norfolke upon his return hither I shall be sure to put him in mind of his promise Concerning the herbe mention'd. Manucodiata Rex Clusii

972. Locke to William Charleton [1/11 November 1687?] (970, 992)
Messrs. Maggs Brothers, Catalogue no. 616, 1935, item no. 982 (for the contents of this item see no. 353 n.). Fragment. No date. If I have been long in returning an answer concerning that catalogue of curiositys which you did me the favour to send me, it has been because though I writ to the person they were designed for†3 yet I could not get noe answer from him till the last week I spoke with him which was the first opportunity I had to see him since the receit of yours. I finde by the discourse I had with him that all those things you have mentioned will be acceptable. He has in returne sent you the inclosed catalogue and shall be glad if you shall thinke all or any of them fit to have a place in your cabinet. I can answer for it he is in earnest in these offers or any
― 286 ―
other service he can doe you: and I found by talking with him that though he gave me other excuses for not answering my letter yet that the true reason was that finding your catalogue to consist of things which were great curiositys and which he had not, yet he was ashamed to say he was willing to have them all it being to great a present. When you finde an opportunity of sending them be pleased to addresse them to Mr Benjamin Furly an English merchant on the Scheepmakers haven in Rotterdam for me ...

973. James Tyrrell to Locke, 2 November [1687] (957, 985)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 62-3. Part printed in King, pp. 170-2. Year from contents.
Nov: 2d:
Dear C.
About two monthes since I returned you an answere to your kind letter, which I had newly then received, but not hearing any thing from you in so long a time; and considering the chief subject of that letter I can rather suppose that it miscarryed by the way to you, then that C. can be insensible of the afflictions of his friends: for in that I gave you perhaps too tedious an account of my poor wives distemper which grew so very bad both in her head; and stomach, that she desired to goe againe to the Bathe as the onely thing that might in all probability doe her some good; where she had not bin above a weeke ere I was sent for to come to her she being fallen very ill of the paine in her side which was very vehement: I came, but found her somewhat releived of her paine: but extreme weake, the waters nev<e>r†a haveing passed kindly with her; yet she growing indifferent well and her bowells and stomach being as wee supposed sufficiently emptyed by Glysters of any thing that might obstruct them; it was advised to trye once more whether the waters would passe with her by stool: so she tooke them 2, or three dayes, but found no benefite by them; they not passeing by stool; at all, nor was it any wonder she being able to eat nothing but a little thin water gruel: so that the waters finding nothing in her stomach to worke on; passed onely by urine. therefore
― 287 ―
finding her self dayly declineing in strength she desired to goe (and as she sayed) dye at home; so I went for her Coach; and she went thence the day, the K. and Queen came thither:†1 I found her still grow worse and worse: so that I feared I should not be able to get her as far as Oxford; but yet she forced her self so far, as to reach it in three dayes. I hoped to have carryed her home after a day or twos rest there; but it pleased God to disappoint me of those hopes: by takeing her to his mercy out of this vail of misery: the 16th: of August.†2 at the Angel†3 in oxford the third day after she came thither: I shall say no more of so sad a subject but that as I have lost an excellent wife so you have allso a good Friend; who to the time of her death did never omit acknowledging her great obligations to you; and would say that if any body could doe her any good she thought it was your self: and would often talk with some satisfaction of makeing a voyage to you, to see what change of air, diet, and above all your advice would have wrought upon her, but it pleased God to disappoint her in those designes and she onely particularly recommended my son James to your care: and therefore I have thoughts as I told†a- you in my last-†a of bringing him over to you, with an intention to put him to school at Utrecht, where Sir J. T.†4 tells me there is a French divine who teaches the latine Greeke and French with great accuracy. I would not bring him to be any trouble to you more then your care, and inspection over his education; therefore pray deal freely in your next to me; what encouragement you give me to bring him thither for without that I shall not stir farther. I have nothing els worth writeing but a short account how things have gone lately at Maudlin College before the Commissioners, whom the Ki: sent downe to visite that College: viz: the Bishop of Chester, the Lord Ch: Justice wright, and Baron Jenner:†5 when they came they summond the Fellows and President before them, and admonisht the
― 288 ―
latter to recede from the Goverment of the house; which he refuseing they expelld him; then they asked all the Fellows severally whether they would admit the Bishop of Oxford to be their head, which all of them refuseing except one Papist;†1 they admitted him themselves: by installing one of his chaplains, and giveing him the Oathes by proxy; then they sent to Dr: Hough for the Keys of the Lodgings which he refuseing to deliver they sent for a smith and broke them open. and put the Bishops Proxy in possession; then they sent for all the Fellows againe and asked them whether they would submit to and obey the President which the King had set over them: which Dr: F. (who was the first man asked:) utterly refused saying he neither would, nor could doe it with a safe Conscience; the rest of them signed a paper wherein they promised to submit to the Bishop <in>†a omnibus licitis, et honestis according to the Stat:†2 of the house; which submission was taken; and they much commended for it: but Dr: F. upon the third admonition still refuseing had his name struck out of the booke <and>†b was ordered to depart the College within 14 dayes: against which proceedings as null, and unjust he read and gave in a Protestation, as allso Dr: Hough had done before both appealing to the King in his Courts. etc: so there were no more expelld at present for denying their authority then the President, Dr: F. and the under porter:†3 but on Friday morneing upon receiving fresh instructions; the former submission not being looked upon as full enough they were farther requir'd to signe an addresse to the King wherein they were to confesse and beg pardon for their passed contumacy and promise absolute obedience for the time to come: but instead of that when they came together they made a quite other sort of Addresse to the Commissioners where in they first assert that they are not conscious to themselves of haveing acted any thing contrary to their oathes; and the stat: of the house; and therefore hope his Majesty will pardon them if they cannot render any more then a passive obedience to his Majestyes commands. since they cannot looke
― 289 ―
upon the Bishop as their lawfull head or words to that effect: and desire the Commissioners to represent their case fairly to his Majesty, at which paper (being signed by all the Fellows theire, except 2. viz. Dr: Smyth, and Charnock) they were very much displeased, and adjourned the Court 'till the 20th Instant:†1 when it is to be feared they will come downe againe and proceed very severely against all that signed that paper: this is the summe of what hath bin done hitherto. Dr: F. is very chearfull under it; and many commend his carriage as much more plaine and above board then the rest; who meant the same thing tho they darst not speake it out.†2 what will be the issue God knows but most wee fear a turneing out of most of the Fellows. I saw Lisis†3 at Oxford yesterday in his passage to Glo: he is perfectly recoverd and remembers his service to you; and so does Dr: F. my son; and daughter; do the same; and allso my man John; and his Wi: unc: A: was well lateley; and I have sent him†a your Phil: trans: which he desired. So doubting I have tired you, as much as I have done my self I remaine yours sincerely.
M.
Endorsed by Locke: Answered 25 Nov:
974. J. G. GrÆvius to Locke, 4/14 November 1687 (914, 978)
B.L. MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 30-1. Answers no. 914; answered by no. 978.
(English) Viro Nobilissimo Joanni Locke S.P.D.†4 J. G. Grævius.
Si pudorem, fidem et humanitatem omnem tibi decoxisse videbor, qui promissorum immemor, praesertim dono mihi acceptissimo, et litteris amantissimis postea lacessitus, tam diu nihil ad te litterarum
― 290 ―
dederim, dolebo quidem, sed de injuria mihi facta queri non possum. Tam diuturna enim procrastinatione officii, tuis in me meritis, et singulari benevolentiae debiti, quin meritus sim, ut hae notae mihi <inurantur>,†a caussam nullam invenio. Fateor me culpae inexpiabilis reum esse, quam sola tua bonitas et indulgentia potest eluere. Eluetur autem, si, ut clementi illi patri apud Comicum, tibi paullum supplicii pro magno crimine satis esse patiaris.†1 Nam hoc velim tibi persuassimum sit, me, licet tarditate nimia graviter peccarim, tui tamen memoriam religiosissime retinuisse: nec quenquam esse, cui in te amando et colendo priores partes concesserim. Cum vere superiore rediissem Amsterodamo, de negotio tibi noto egi cum amicis.†2 Illi testabantur litteras et a Bentingio,†3 qui Principi est a consiliis interioribus, ad Praetorem huius urbis perlatas esse, et dein alias a Dyckveldio†4 ad Consulem, nisi fallor, quibus significarint, illum, qui tum legati Regii personam gerebat,†5
― 291 ―
Regis nomine de te non nullisque aliis questum esse in aula, petiisseque, ut sibi potestas daretur, quorum edidisset nomina comprehendendi, et in Angliam mittendi. Cum ista huc perlata essent, veritos esse amicos, si res haec urgeretur, ne hic aliquando hominis tuae saluti insidiantis manus effugere nequires. Nam adjecerat urbes, in quibus degerent et latitarent, quos Regem sibi tradi velle contendebat. Existimabant autem amici nostri, qui haec mihi referebant, expectandum esse Dyckveldii adventum, ut illius sententiam coram audiremus. Differebatur is in mensem unum atque alterum. Cum vero ad nos tandem revisisset Dyckveldius, egi apud eum tuam caussam, testatus omnem criminis suspicionem apud Regem dudum per amicos tuos fuisse dimotam et expurgatam, id quod tibi certissimis argumentis et litteris fide dignissimis sit exploratissimum. Reponebat, nullum se dubitare, quin sic se res haberet. Tutissimum tamen se ducere, si Abbavillei reditum praestolaremur,†1 qui redux si querelas illas non iteraret, nihilque novi moveret, nihil superesse discriminis teque posse, ubi velles, sedem figere. Haec simul ac intellexeram volui ad te perscribere:
― 292 ―
sed nescio quo malo fato de die in diem scribendi munus protraxerim. Cujus culpam si detestanti et deprecanti remissam esse cognoro, magno curarum aestu liberabor. In posterum vero, si quid volueris a me sive in hoc, sive in alio negotio effici, senties me tanto majore studio, celeritateque tibi probaturum esse meum tuae voluntati et desiderio serviendi promtissimum et paratissimum animum, quanto longius <ante cessavi>.†a Nihil enim mihi poterit accidere optatius, quam si hoc crimen expiare potero; nihilque desideratius, quam si tuo gratissimo complexu mihi hic frui dabitur. Quicquid igitur curatum velis, mihi manda. Quicquid mandaveris et mihi commiseris, homini certo, et fidei pleno, et tutis auribus te commisisse†b intelliges. Trallianum et Rhezam editionis pulcherrimae inter κειμήλια mea reposui. Semper ii refricabunt mihi memoriam tui, quamvis illa sit tam alte meo infixa animo, ut nulla dies eam unquam sit oblitteratura. Lactantii editionis Antwerpiensis,†1 quae longe discrepat a vulgatis aliis, mentionem olim faciebas. Annus quo prodiit, et officina, unde prodiit effluxit ex memoria mea. Quae si mihi, ubi scribendi fuerit otium, indicare
― 293 ―
dignaberis, hoc etiam in accepti tabulas referam, sed addita hac ingenua confessione, me, cum solvendo non sim, semper totum tuum futurum nexu mancupioque. Vale vir eximie et me, si potes, amare perge. Trajecti D. XIV Novemb. CIϽ IϽCLXXXVII. Has praeterita die Saturni constitueram exarare, sed interveniebant, quae me abesse domo cogebant.
(Latin) To the illustrious John Locke greeting from J. G. Grævius.
I may well appear bankrupt of shame, good faith, and common courtesy, seeing that forgetful of my promises, especially when spurred by a very welcome present and after that by a most friendly letter, I have been so [p. 290] long in sending you a word in writing. If so, I shall be sorry indeed, but cannot complain of unjust treatment; for after such long delay in doing the duty I owe you for all you have done for me and for your remarkable kindness of heart, I can find no reason to plead that I do not deserve to be stigmatized in such terms. I confess myself guilty of an unpardonable fault, which only your kindness and indulgence can wash away; washed away, however, it will be if, like that lenient father in the Comedian, you can bring yourself to be satisfied with a small punishment for a great offence.†1 For please be assured of this, that however grievously I have erred by my too dilatory behaviour, I have yet kept you religiously in mind, nor is there anyone to whom I would yield in love and regard for yourself. Well, when I got back from Amsterdam last spring I had a talk with some friends about the business you know of.†2 They gave me to understand that a letter from Bentinck,†3 who is in the Prince's inner counsels, had been brought to the governor of this city, and later another from Dijkveld†4 to the burgomaster, unless I am mistaken, in which they intimated that the person who was then acting as the king's envoy†5 [p. 291] had complained at the palace in the king's name about you and certain others and had asked to be given power to arrest those whose names he had given and to send them to England. When this information was received here, they said, your friends began to fear that if the matter were pressed you might not eventually be able to escape the clutches of the man who had such designs on your safety in this place. For he had further mentioned the cities in which those whom, as he contended, the king wished to be handed over to him were living in concealment. Our friends, however, who told me of all this considered that we ought to wait for Dijkveld's arrival, so that we might hear his opinion from his own mouth. This was deferred for a month or two; but when at last Dijkveld came to see us again I spoke to him on your behalf, assuring him that any suspicion of offence that the king might have had had long been removed and cleared away through your friends, and that you were fully assured of this on reliable grounds and through trustworthy letters. He answered that he had no doubt that this was how matters stood, but that he thought it would be safest if we waited till Albeville came back;†1 if he on his return did not renew those complaints or make any new move there could be no further risk and you might take up your abode where you wished. I wanted to write and tell you about all this as soon as I learnt it; [p. 292] but somehow unfortunately I kept putting off that duty from day to day. If I may know that my fault in this respect has been pardoned at my earnest entreaty and prayer it will be a great load off my mind. For the future, however, if you want anything done by me in this or any other matter, you will find me making up for the length of my delay in the past by greater diligence and speed in proving to you that I have a prompt and ready mind to serve your will and desire. Nothing could meet my wishes better than to be able to expiate this offence, nor is there anything I could desire more than an opportunity of welcoming and embracing you here. If therefore there should be anything that you wish attended to, you may command me. Whatever the charge or commission may be, you will have reason to know that you have committed it to one who is reliable and trustworthy and a safe repository of your secrets. Trallianus and Rheza, in their fine edition, I have placed among my treasures. They will continually refresh my memory of you, though that is so deeply fixed in my heart that no lapse of time can ever obliterate it. You once mentioned Lactantius in the Antwerp edition,†1 which differs a good deal from other texts in common use. The year in which it appeared and the printing-house it came from have escaped my memory. If, when you have time to write, you will be kind enough to give me these [p. 293] details I shall book it in my accounts as a further debt, but shall add the frank admission that, as I am not in a position to pay, I shall always be entirely yours by bond and ownership. Good-bye, extraordinary Sir, and, if you can, continue to love me. Utrecht 14 November 1687. I had intended to write this letter last Saturday, but circumstances intervened which compelled me to be away from home.
Endorsed by Locke: Grævius 14 Nov. 87
975. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 7 November [1687] (967, 1003)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 150-1. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Since You were Writeing a Letter of Railerie when you received my last, it will be Hard for me to think you Date your recoverie from thence. However I am glad it has giv'n you an Instance of that skill which I can never teach you Unless I could give you more Friendship It being Certainly onely That Difference betweene Us, that Can make This; However the little that on any other Account I can Merrit, will keepe me from Complaining of you. But I can scarse forbeare doing so at my evill fortune for depriving me of that Letter you Mention, since it has fall'n out that I never in my life had more Mind to be Merry then at the receiving of This; which tho I very much Value, and would Part with for Nobodys else, I would willingly have exchang'd for that other of Your Owne.
I need say no more I suppose to tell you both that I am very well; and also what is much more Considerable to me, that my Mother is very much Better, Upon the Subject of whose Danger, all that You say I must owne is very Reasonable; and would not have beene I hope without some efficacie But should that loss ever befall me, I must beleeve for several Reasons that few Can be Capable to judge of the Greatness of it. But to Quit a Subject the very remembrance of which has almost Chang'd my Humour, I returne
― 294 ―
you my thanks for your Concerne for my Owne Indisposition, and shall be very glad (if you will give your self the trouble) to be entertain'd with some thing further upon that Subject, tho I Know Not how to Owne (unless A Fitt were upon me) that That, (how much soever so) will be more usefull then your Letters Ordinarily are; Since why I should prefer the Cureing of my Body, before my Mind I cannot tell, Which is an effect your Letters never fail of when there is occasion for it And Its evills are Capable of being remov'd by any Humane Meanes. I have just now beene Writeing a letter to my Lady R: to returne Her, and Mr B:†1 my thanks for theire advise about the Nephritick stone,†2 which I have beene Perswaded to; and Directed to a Man who sells them, But I Perceive Mr B: thinks it very Dangerous to make tryal of it unless I were sure of a Right one, in which I ought not to trust to a Shopkeepers Word, And that they would not have me use it unless I could get one at second Hand that had beene Experienc'd; which is scarse a thing to be thought Possible. Pray let me Know your Opinion about it, That which makes me Desireous to Venture is, the great benefit that the Bishop of Peterborough†3 has found by one from this Man I mention.
I am sorry you know not certainly my Author,†4 but I am sattisfy'd it cannot be the Person I nam'd to You, Nor had any Reason for it then but a Mistake; Whoever he is, I am very much his Friend, and Servant, and should be extreamly Pleas'd to Know Him But I Hope he will meet with a More Acceptable recompence then that could be if he Knew it.—It looks oddly to make such Kind of excuses for letters that go so far, But it so falls out that I must either not send you This now, or Conclude it. I Prefer my owne Sattisfaction in Heareing the sooner from you, and therefore shall onely add that I really am Your Friend and Servant
P:†5
Nov: the 7th.
Address: For Mr Lock.

976. Edward Clarke to Locke, 12 November 1687 (966, 981)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 39. Printed in Rand, p. 229. Answered by no. 981.
Chipley the 12th. November 1687
Deare Sir,
Your obleiging Letter of the 12th. of September I Received, and on the 29th. of that moneth in Answer I gave you the best Accompt I could of my Sonn's Tutor etc: with my hearty thankes (which will bee ever due) for the reall Freindshipp and Kindnesse you have done mee in the Particular of my Childrens Education, And I then promised to send your Letter that came inclos'd in yours of the 12th. of September to Mr. Stratton with the first opportunity, Which I have since done by a safe hand, with an earnest Repetition of such former Directions as were given Him for secureing the debt due from Robert Harol, and the better mannagement of the whole Affayre for the future, which I hope will bee carefully perform'd by Him, and my intentions were to have taken Sutton in my way this Terme†1 towards London, hopeing that by my Presence there I might have been capable of doeing you some small service, But by the unexpected Death of one that was concern'd in the Businesse that would have carryed mee thither at this time, I am disappoynted of my Journey and the satisfaction I propos'd to my selfe in the doeing you some little service in my way thither, However you may be certaine I shall willingly imbrace the next opportunity that offers of seeing mr Stratton, and doeing all that Lyes in my Power for your Advantage in your Concerns there, In the meane time pray accept Madam's and myne, with all the younge Fry's, hearty services, and bee assured that I am,
Your most affectionate and obleiged servant
E:†a
I heare nothing as yett of the Freez-land-sheep; but have Lodg'd a peice of the Wound-Wood with Mr. Elwill in Exeter with Directions to bee Conveyed to Mr. Ben: Furley with the first opportunity etc:
Endorsed by Locke: E Somerton†b 12 Nov. 87 Answered 2. Dec:

977. Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 15 November 1687 (960, 990)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 160-1.
Escott November 15th. 1687.
Dear Friend
I beleive you must long since have concluded me taken indeed since I have not till now found a time to thank you for the favor of yours of the 16th. of the last month, I wish I had so good an excuse for my silence, but having none I must even confess my fault and promise amendment in confidence of your pardon; But then how to answer your Question I know not, for perhaps I may be taken too (tho' not as you imagin) and that in such a manner as may confine me to this place for at least a year; To tell you the truth I am upon the list for Sheriffes with Sir William Morice†1 and Sir John Southcott,†2 and tho' tis most generally beleived the last will be pitch'd upon, yet some think there will be no Roman Catholick Sheriffes this year;†3 But if after all it should be your friends lott I know not how you will be excused from allowing me the favor of a visitt, which you so frankly promise me on another occasion, that to me does not appear more inviting, In this case there will be the fiddles of course, and no fear of any want of the Ladies, therefore be sure you shake off your Lazy distemper (which afflicts all your friends as well as your selfe) and prepare for a dance; I hope this will find you well recruited and that the coming on of the Spring will confirm you in your health as well in your kind intentions of visiting the Rowe, which can never be compleat without you. I have examined the books, you were pleased to take the trouble of procuring, by the Catalogue you sent me, and have sent Mr Cl.†4 Cowley's poems, and given the parson his books, and have just look'd into the designe of my own which I like extreamly well, but can not quite guess when I shall find a time to be better acquainted with them, for since I came home I have hardly had an hours leisure (having so much necessary business) and I fear I shall have little more till the summer comes. The Acta Eruditorum and Bibliotheque Universelle have been lookt into by a very ingenious
― 297 ―
neigbour of mine with great satisfaction, and I promise my selfe great advantage from Hofman's Lexicon, all the other books too I beleive are very good in their kind as I am sure the Italian book is, but however when I consider how poor a reader I am like to prove, and that I have already well nigh books enough to fill my Library, I would not have you give your selfe the trouble of buying any more books, but only such as are rarities indeed (such as Xavier's Gospell,†1 and the History of the Inchas of Peru)†2 and what you judge will be very advantagious and fitt for my own reading; which I mention only to let you see that I have no need to recruit and fill up my library, not to restrain you from buying any book either in Latin Italian or french which you have a good opinion of, and†a- judge ... for me,-†a which I shall alwaies esteeme an act of great friendship, and shall be carefull to reimburse you whatever you lay out for me with all thankfullness. As for the parson he has not given me a very particular account of his Opinion of his books, but I find some of those he sent for by name doe not much answer his expectations, so that he saies he will no more send for books upon any character he shall find of them in Catalogues; and I will find some other way to gratify him for his services. Upon the arrivall of the books the parson went to the Bishop†3 with the Catalogue, who made some difficulties at first (it being at a time when the Ec. Commission began to take place)†4 but after a little importunity I think the parson got them discharged without any other examination. I am with the greatest sincerity and unalterable affection
Your's W. Y.
My Br. and S. Duke went hence this morning, I presume she gave you a full account of the effects of the waters in her last about a month since, they both give you hearty services, as does your daughter Betty, who has of late been much disordered by a feavourish indisposition, which has weakened her very much; she was a week in Exeter under Dr Bidgoods care,†5 and is still under a course
― 298 ―
of physick of his prescribing, by which she is already much re cruited, and we hope will in a short time be set right again; the Doctor called her distemper an inward feaver; Our Somersetshire friends were lately well, I presume you hear often from them. If you see our friend Benjamin (to whome I shall direct this) pray tell him I have sent two hogshead of Syder by George Hodder of Topsham, one for him and another for Mr Venn.†1 I wish they may think them worth the freight, they are as good as any of those I keep for my own use, being chosen out of severall hogsheads, and I hope will prove tollerably well. I purpose to write to Benjamin by Hodder who I think may saile about a week or ten daies hence.
Address: For Mr John Lock at the House of Mr Benjamin Furly Merchant in Rotterdam
post paid to London 3d.
Postmark: No 18
Endorsed by Locke: W.†a Y 15 Nov. 87 Answered 20 Jan:
978. Locke to J. G. Grævius, 17/27 November [1687] (974, 1105)
Royal Library, Copenhagen, MS. Thott 1263-4°. Printed by C. Bastide in Revue internationale de l'enseignement, lv (1908), 387-8. Year from contents. Answers no. 974.
(English)
27 Nov:
Quanquam ignorare non potes, Vir Amplissime, literas tuas urbanitatis, elegantiarum, benevolentiæ plenas mihi semper esse exoptatissimas, absit tamen ut suspiceris me de illius amici silentio queri cujus verbis tantum debeo, et deberi me semper agnoscam. Tua fateor taciturnitas me aliquo modo solicitum habuit: Metuebam enim ne liber quem ad Te <miseram>†a rectè in manus tuas non
― 299 ―
pervenisset; Non quod crederem scripta illa antiqua jam ubique pene neglecta quidquam vel ornamenti vel usus locupletissimæ Tuæ allatura bibliothecæ; Sed quod minime decuit post tot accepta beneficia quibus pares referre non possum gratias me in tantillâ re vel promissi immemorem vel officii negligentem videri. Cætera securus eram, nec tua per aliquod tempus impedita vel dilata responsio tuæ vel benevolentiæ vel amicitiæ apud me minuerat opinionem: Quanquam Tu jam ita scribas ut abundè compensares omnem, siqua fuisset, moræ istius impatientiam. Ad Lactantii editionem Antwerpianam quod attinet, memini eam fuisse antiquam valde, et minore formâ, eâ ni fallor quam in 12° vocant; Annus vero et nomen Tipographi mihi plane exciderunt. Dic quæso si in animo habeas doctas tuas et medicatrices manus admovere Lactantio et Tuo hoc est optimo modo emendatum et illustratum edere.†1 Hoc vel hujusmodi aliquid si sit, dabo operam ut ad nos transmittatur liber iste. Quo animo in absentes sis satis <testari potest>†a amicus ille tuus cujus causam apud D†2 tanto cum studio egisti, an vero R†3 ipsum quoquo modo nominaverit aveo scire. Hoc si noveris vel data occasione ab eo expiscari poteris ut mihi quamprimum indices
― 300 ―
obnixe rogo, nec de nihilo est quod ego hoc a Te vehementius contendo. Si te jam diu non bene noverim in omnia benevolentiæ et humanitatis officia proclivem, parcius et meticulosius rogarem. Sed de Tuo benevolo de illius grato animo spondere possum Vale et me, ut facis, ama
Tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
Grevium nostrum meo nomine officiosissime rogo salutes
(English) Si literæ sub involucro (Aen Mÿn Heer Benjamin Furly tot Rotterdam) inscripto mittantur rectè accipiam.
(Latin)
27 Nov:
Though you cannot be unaware, excellent Sir, of my constant desire for your letters, with all their courtesy and grace of expression and kindly spirit, yet I would not have you suspect that I complain of the silence of a friend to whose words I owe so much, a debt that I shall always acknowledge. That silence of yours, I confess, made me somewhat anxious; I was afraid that the book I had sent you might not have duly reached you; not that I supposed [p. 299] that those ancient writings, now almost everywhere neglected, could in any way serve as an ornamental or useful addition to your well-stored library, but because after all the kindnesses I had received from you, for which I can never give you adequate thanks, it little became me to appear either forgetful of my promise or neglectful of my duty in such a small matter. Apart from this my mind was at rest, and if your reply was prevented or deferred for a time this did not diminish my belief in your goodwill or friendship. However, you now write in a way that fully makes up for any impatience I may have felt at that delay. As to the Antwerp edition of Lactantius, I remember that it was a very old one, of rather small size, what they call duodecimo, unless I am mistaken; but I have quite forgotten the year and the printer's name. Please tell me if you have any thought of turning your scholarly and healing hand to Lactantius and editing him corrected and illustrated in your own, that is in the best way.†1 If this or anything of the sort should be the case I will do my best to have a copy of that edition sent to us. Sufficient evidence of your heed for the absent can be given by that friend of yours whose cause you pleaded so zealously with D(ijkveld); but I want very much to know whether he mentioned the name of the K(ing) himself in any way. If you know this or can fish it out of him when occasion offers, I earnestly beg you to let me know it as soon as possible; I have good reason for pressing you [p. 300] rather urgently on this point. If I had not already long known so well your readiness in all things to render services of benevolence and humanity I would make this request with more moderation and diffidence; but I am in a position to vouch for your kind-heartedness and for that friend's gratitude. Good-bye, and continue, as you do, to love me,
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) Please give most dutiful greetings to de Greve on my behalf.

979. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 20/30 November 1687 (969, 1023)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 255v. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 318-20; postscript and address in Ollion, p. 175.
(English)
30 Nov. 87
Vir Amplissime
Cum nihil adeo corporis sanitatem foveat ac restauret ac animi tranquillitas, non dubitare potes quin jucundissimæ tuæ literæ amoris et benevolentiæ tuæ testes in hâc in quâ diu versatus sum infirmâ mutabilique valetudine mihi maximo fuerint Solatio.
― 301 ―
Aliorum medicamentorum me sæpe pertæsum reficiebant illa tua semper grata semper suavissima: et cum alia nauseabundus respuerem Salutifera illa sale tuo Attico condita appetentius semper desideravi. Cave igitur ut credas te mihi epistolis tuis creasse molestiam, nisi simul credere velis mihi ingratam fore convalescentiam, cujus tu amore, curâ, studio tuo maximus fuisti fautor. nec destiterunt tantæ amicitiæ indicia decumbentem me aliquo modo erigere. Si aliquanto tardius hæc cum gratiarum actione agnosco Nosti hominem, nec expectare debes morbum me expeditiorem reddidisse. Quanquam si hæc tibi justa satis videri possit causa aliquantulum procrastinavi, ut confirmatæ sanitatis nuncium tibi possem mittere et mihi tecum gratulari convalescentiam, quæ tibi adeo curæ et cordi fuit. Doleo Orobium nobis tam cito ereptum,†1 non quod in eo amiseris triumphi ornamentum, scio enim te, modo veritas vincat, de vincendi gloria parum esse solicitum, quamvis in illo vivente aliqua veritatis confessio non displicuisset: sed destinaveram in proximis ad Te literis petere exactam eorum quæ in inquisitione passus est historiam.†2 Ad hoc
― 302 ―
me impulit narratio cujusdam Galli quæ nuper prodiit de iis quæ ipse etsi Catholicus passus est ab inquisitoribus Lusitanis in Goa Indiæ.†1 Quæ a Judæo nostro confirmari omnia vel superari posse facile crediderim. Quandoquidem vero ille jam ad silentes migraverit, rogo ut tu quicquid istius rei tenes memoria velis chartis consignare ne intercidat quantum nobis restat methodi istius Evangelicæ testimonium. Doleo me non interfuisse Collegarum convivio non quod ostreis caruerim: in hujusmodi enim conventibus nihil mihi minus placet quam pars taciturna, et ejusmodi convivarum sermo aliquid magis sapidum et jucundius salsum habet quam ipsa ostrea Gaurana.†2 Salutes eos quæso meo nomine uti et optimam tuam fæminam totamque Veenii et Guenellonis familiam. Ante duas vel tres septimanas ad Dominum Le Clerc scripsi unàque chartas aliquas misi.†3 an rectè acceperit aveo scire jam enim istis rebus vacare incipio. ipsum meo etiam nomine salutes. Vale, et ut ipse valeam amando et scribendo effice
Tui studiosissimus
J L
― 303 ―
(English) Quo genere gallarum et vitrioli utaris quæso iterum indica nam ego uti scriptorum ita <atramenti>†a tui nitorem nullo modo assequi possum†1
(Latin)
30 Nov. 87
Excellent Sir,
Since nothing so promotes and restores the health of the body as does tranquillity of the mind, you cannot doubt that your most enjoyable letters, evidence of your affection and goodwill, have been the greatest comfort to me in my protracted condition of poor and variable health. Often when utterly [p. 301] weary of other people's remedies I was refreshed by those ever welcome and ever delightful specifics of yours; and when I was rejecting other sustenance with loathing my appetite was always the sharper for those health-bringing dishes seasoned with your own Attic salt. Beware therefore of imagining that I have found your letters troublesome, unless you are prepared at the same time to believe that I shall not be pleased with my restoration to health, of which you have been the greatest promoter by your affection, care, and solicitude, nor have the signs of such warm friendship ever ceased to raise me in some way from my bed of sickness. If I am somewhat slow in acknowledging all this by thanking you for it, you know your man, nor ought you to expect that sickness has made me more expeditious. However, if this may seem to you a fair enough reason, I have delayed a little longer in order to be able to announce to you that I am in settled good health and to congratulate myself together with you on my recovery, which has been a matter of such care and concern to you. I am sorry that Orobio was snatched from us so soon,†1 not that you have lost in him an ornament of your triumph, for I know that you are little concerned for the glory of victory so long as truth prevails; still, it would not have been unsatisfactory to have some confession of the truth in him while still alive. I had intended to ask you in my next letter for an exact account of his sufferings in the Inquisition.†2 I was impelled [p. 302] to do so by the narrative of a certain Frenchman which recently appeared, describing what he himself, though a Catholic, suffered at the hands of the Portuguese inquisitors at Goa in India.†1 I would easily have believed that it could be fully corroborated or even surpassed by our Jew. However, since he has now passed to the silent world, I beg you to be good enough to set down on paper whatever you remember of that affair, lest what evidence is left to us of that Evangelical method should be lost. I am sorry not to have taken part in the Collegians' banquet, though not for missing the oysters: nothing pleases me less at such gatherings than the tongue-tied part, and the talk of such table companions has a tastier and sharper relish than the very oysters of Gaurus.†2 Please remember me to them as well as to your excellent wife and to Veen and Guenellon with their whole family. I wrote to Mr. Le Clerc two or three weeks ago and sent him some papers at the same time;†3 I should greatly like to know whether he has received them, as I am now beginning to have leisure for such matters. Remember me to him too. Farewell and ensure that I may fare well by loving and writing to
Your most devoted
J L
(Latin) [p. 303] Kindly let me know again what sort of galls and vitriol you use; for I am as unable to achieve the brilliance of your ink as I am that of your writings.†1

980. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 21 November/1 December [1687] (984)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 81-2. Printed in Rand, Shaftesbury, pp. 273-4. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Ashley's movements are unknown. He was in England in May: pp. 202-3. On 5 November, N.S., he and Denoun left books with Locke in Rotterdam: B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, f. 80.
Paris De: the 1st
Dear Sir
Tho I expect now a letter from you very soon; yet the Concern I have least the Trouble you gave your self about me has done you ill, makes me not neglect this Post: nor am I willing to hazzard the Prolonging of it to one Letter onely. I am Removed since that, and come into a Pension, where now you may direct your Letters to me. t'is au Château Vieux dans la Rüe de St Andre des Arts
I have yet Pitcht on no masters of Exercise:†2 till I have done that, I can Prefix my self no hours to studdy: nor have I yet bought any, but French Books
There Plays here are very Ordinary either to read or see. Their Opera I have not seen yet, but shall tomorrow: I am affraid I shall
― 304 ―
like that but too well: for I am a perfect slave to Fine Musick. I find I can conform better to their diet here then their Manners. I have heithertoo had no disturbance from our own Country men. here are not as I am told by half soe many as were last winter.
Sir John†1 is this Moment Beginning his French, and his Master at his Ventilabria,†2 which Divert me from what I am doing, tho truly I have no more to say now but how much and with how great sincerity I am Your Obleidged Freind and Humble servant
A: ASHLEYH
Sir John desires me to give his Humble service and Mr Denoun Presents his to you.

981. Locke to Edward Clarke, [22 November/2 December 1687?] (976, 989)
Rand, pp. 233-4. 'In very bad condition, whole passages being entirely illegible or in part perished.' Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. He suggests January 1688 as the date, but the letter appears to answer nos. 966 and 976; Locke answered both on 2 December: endorsements. By its contents it appears to precede no. 989.
... And the sheep that I so long ago expected to be coming till lately, and not being yet sent, I was ashamed to write till I could tell you that they were on board, and therefore should have stayed a little longer could I with any countenance forbear now that I have a second from you which obliges me with all the speed I can to desire you not to give yourself the trouble you talk of about my Belton affairs, the concernment not being worth your journey thither, and therefore I beg you not to think of going so far upon so slight an occasion. It is enough that you concern yourself in it and look so much after my affairs there when any other business makes you go thither, and the journey which you have taken already on this occasion is more than I can sufficiently thank you for.
― 305 ―
I have now got ready three ewes and a ram, which I hope will now find a passage very speedily. He that brought them assures me that they use more commonly to bring 3, 4 and 5 lambs at a time than one or two. He means those of this kind, for these being young and this their first [being] with young, you are not to expect from them this time above one or two, but when they are at their full growth he says they will have four or five at a time. But they must be kept in good rich land that will feed them full and large. He talks about their going with the cows. The man in charge of them has by no means followed my direction. For I would have had ewes in their [separate folds which] might have shewed you what was the number of lambs they brought forth ...†a
Though I have told you somewhat a[larming] story of my health, let it not fright you no more than it has done me; it was uneasy, troublesome and long, more than it was dangerous, for my lungs having suffered very little in a great variety of indispositions I have been wearied with all they gave me not any apprehensions but of the trouble and continuation of them. It began with a looseness which it was a good while before I could master, and when with much ado it was stopped my stomach was so gone that I could scarce eat anything, and when I got some small matter down it was such a load to me that I wished it out again. When by very slow degrees I was got pretty well of those symptoms, a violent catarrh took me and held me not a little while in great disorder, which with ill weather that hindered my going abroad brought back some part of my former maladies; but now I thank God I am so well that were there nothing else to hinder it but the remaining untuneableness of my humour I should be able so [to order] that as to be in a condition to laugh with you. But it is time now to close, lest my robbing Madam so long of your conversation should make her long that I, too, should make my letters shorter. I wish her and you and all the little ones all happiness imaginable, and am
Dear Sir,
J. L.
Address: For Edward Clarke at the Lady King's, Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, London.

982. Thomas Herbert, Eighth Earl of Pembroke, to Locke, 25 November [1687], and Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 29 November [1687] (828, 1170; 946, 1042)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 195-6. Pembroke's letter and excerpt from Thomas's printed in King, pp. 158-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
[Pembroke:]
London Nov: 25
Sir
I receivd the second Part, and with it the hopes of all the rest in print, such thauts need no Epistle to recommend them, I do not say so to excuse my Name to it, for I shall alwayes be as desiorous (by my name) to testifye the satisfaction I have in any thing you are pleased to write, as I am and ever will be (by my Person) ready to vindicate any thing you do:†1 but pray do not let the hopes of seeing this in print, defer the satisfaction of seeing the whole att large, which I hope you will send me as soon as possibly you can; A chaine is not to be commended for its strength by taking it asunder; I shall not therfore pretend to commend this, since I can't do it without repeating the whole; but I will spare no pains where I may approve my selfe
Your friend and servant
PEMBROKE

983. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 3/13 December 1687 (921, 1029)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 3-4.
Monsieur
Ce nous est une joye extreme que vous este entierement retabli, et nous esperons que vous aurez tréve pour long temps, car pour une paix parfaitte on ne sen scauroit flatter dans cette vie caduque et malheureuse. nous aurions moins souffert avec vous dans vostre maladie, si vous aviez esté plus proche, et que nous eussions pu vous apporter quelque secours. car quoy que sans doubte il ne vous aye pas manqué d'amis ou vous este, il nous a pourtant manqué l'occasion de vous tesmoigner combien de part nous prenons a tous ce qui vous concerne. Vous nous pouriez†a pas mander une nouvelle plus agreable que la disposition de retourner icy.†1 je ne me suis pas enquis d'une demeure privée pour vous, parce que jay a vous demander du grace de prendre vostre logis chez moy et comme on n'estime jamais mieux une chose que quand on l'a perdue je puis vous assurer avec sincerité que ma femme a regretté plus d'une fois de ce que nous avons pas fait plus d'effort pour vous retenir chez nous quand vous y estiez. c'est pourquoy je vous conjure d'y revenir, et si vous <n'avez>†b dilayé vostre voyage plus que vous n'aurie<z>†b fait autrement, vous nous faitte assurement de l'injustice, puisque nous bruslons tous d'envie de vous embrasser et moy particulierement, qui suis comme je le doibs,
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant s<erviteur>†b
P GUENELLON
d'Amsterdam ce 13 dec: 1687
Toute la famille vous presente ses tres humbles respects.

984. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 12/22 December 1687 (980, 1169)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 83-4. Printed in Rand, Shaftesbury, pp. 274-5.
Paris. Decem: the 22d. 87
Dear Sir,
But that I am not Ashamed to Reveal my Greatest Frailtyes to you; I would not make you the Confession I am going, of having Deferd till now, the Answering of yours (tho Received but the day before Yesterday), But I hope the Ingenuity of this declaration will meritt your Beleife, when I tell you that it was the Effects of my Desire onely to doe it in better Order and when I had time Enough to myself to be some hours alone with you tho in absence whereby I hoped to Give myself as well as you more satisfaction.
But since I could not, nor have not yet obtained that wish; I must Content my self (as not the first time) with what I can gett: and make the Best use of it. the Reason of this has been, that I am Just now surprized by a Message from the Envoy†1 with a Journey to Versaills tomorrow at 6 a Clock, with whome we were Engadged to goe the next time he went theither. It is unnessessary here to speak of my Concern at your Not Receiving mine, mixt with the Joy for the danger I Escaped by writing my second: but I must needs tell you I am not satisfied that you speak nothing Perticularly of your Health as I desired you and this is no manner of Custumary or Ceremonious Question in me: but what I desire earnestly to be Resolved me: and I find by my self, that That Freindly Expression so often used by Tully, Cura ut Valeas,†2 is not ill Grounded: for I find your Health of such Concern to me, that I cannot but use that Expression to you here: and truly I have a Reason more incumbent on me; For that I fear I have been the Cause of some Badd to you, as I need not wonder, when you would run so many Hazzards so much against my will, on my account. To thank you for the Advice I have Received in your Letters as well as from your mouth; would be a subject too bigg for this Paper, or indeed for my Toung, and is what I shall never attempt, or att least never Pretend to speak of as it deserves. so that I
― 310 ―
Resolve to lay all that aside: and begg to be dealt by, as I doe. and I Flatter myself that if it were onely to satisfie me, Mr Lock would quitt every thing that might be a hindrance to speaking his Mind to me Freely and that might be so many Clouds to that light I Receive. It is now pretty late and I can onely lett you Know that for My Exercises I have yet begun none, nor shall I till the Hollowdays are over for itt will be but Loosing so much money. Lord Salisbury,†1 new Convert, is here, come since me, but Has, nor will Hardly Receive any Visit from me: which I find he resents. he Has with him 2 more English Converts, one Hales†2 is one, besides some Preists which he Caryes with him: Sir John Cropley Desires me to Give you his Humble service. and Mr Denoun gives you his. If you can Read this, I shall have my Intent, which is onely to doe better then loose tomorrows and stay till Next Post. Beleive me that I am with all sincerity your
Most Obleidged Freind and servant†a
Address: For Mr Lock att Mr Benjamin Furlys Op de Scippmakers Haven Tot Rotterdam Holland

985. James Tyrrell to Locke, 14 December [1687] (973, 1015)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 64-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
London. Decem: 14th.
Dear C.
I have received, and must now thanke you for your kind, and consolatory letter; and I wish I may be able to take all the good advice it brings: I hope time, and philosophicall as well as Christian considerations will enable me patiently to sustaine that losse which can never be repaired of so good a woeman, wife, and Mother as met in her. I shall never forget the concerne you allwayes expressed for her; were there no other obligations between us: and especially for what you so generously and kindly promise of leting it descend
― 311 ―
upon her children in the care you please to undertake of my sons education.
who hath the greatest mind in the world to be in so happy a condition: as to be under your direction; and therefore know not yet but that I may bring him with me at spring: were it not for one consideration, that I hope you will come over this summer and reside with us and perhaps not returne thither againe in hast according to your wonted humour of not careing to stir when your once fixed: besides I would be sure of a place where you could advise me to put him before I brought him over: which you doe not at all mention to me any more then in the generall you say it would doe well if I brought my son over with me: therefore if you have any thoughts of comeing over this summer; or have no certain place yet in your Eye where I may put him to school till he be fit for a university, pray let me have your opinion; whether it might not doe as well to put him to Mr: Sinclear†1 for a year or so; for I have seen some of his teaching; (and a son of Sir John Kings†2 in particular) who are very good scholars for their time; besides the other manly improvements he teaches with the learned tongues, he keeps a French protestant in the house out of charity who teaches those boyes French who have a mind to learne it: this I onely hint to you desireing you to deal freely with me for if you have thoughts of comeing over; or if you know of no good school you would advise me to; I will rather chuse to keep him here: but I will not keep him any longer time at home, for besides that I shall put off my Family at spring; I find he advances but slowly in makeing latine; or learneing Greek tho he can conster an Authour pretty well himself; and is a good way gone in Virgil: and Lucius Florus. But tho I shall put off my housekeeping yet I shall not my house for J.C. and his wife, are to live in it and take the land I hold in my hands: so that I shall be there some times. and your things will be as safe as if I were there my self. and I hope you will come over next summer to make use of them, for as things stand here you need not doubt of a good reception, and to be restored to your place againe if you thinke it worth while to confine your self any more to a collegiat life. wee may expect a Parliament in the spring; and in the meane time they are new regulateing the Corporations;†a and those who were
― 312 ―
turned out for Whigs, are now to†a be†a put in againe.
your uncle Ad:†1 has bin offred to <be>†b Alderman; or Major of his citty but hath refused it. if you will see upon what termes a man may be Justice of Peace or Deputy LeiuTenant pray consult the London Gazette of the 12th: Instant.†2 I saw your noble Friend lately who speaks very kindly of you, and I wish you were here whilst his interest lasts, for I fear it will not be long, for he has refused to propose the chuseing of such Members as will take off the penall laws and test: to the Gentlemen of his Countrey.†3 I am glad to hear from him; that you intend speedily to print your discourse. de intell: I should be glad to know whether you will doe it there, or here: I hope either to come over with uncle A. or by my self for I will not stay long for him, and I would be at home againe before Midsummer. I have bin in Towne this month and goe away to day. Mr: B. is well and remembers his service to you: he has lately published a very ingenious treatise of fineall causes. how far to be admitted in Philosophy.†c- †4 if you have a minde to it I will-†c send it you by Mr: C.†5 or you may send to him for it. there is a new booke come out with you. written by a Dutch man whose name I have forgot. it is as I think called Synagogus. Christianus. sive de Episcopis; et Presbyteris Christianorum:†6 I heer it much commended. pray inquire for it. Adrian Advises me to direct my letters to Mr: B.F. for there he says you are this winter if you like it I will continue so to doe. if not pray order otherwise. the best news I have to send you is that all our Friends are well. I hear that the Commissioners <Ecclesiasticall>†d have passed a new severe sentence disenableing all the late turned out Fellows of Maudlins from keeping or takeing any liveing or other Ecclesiasticall promotion:†7 and if so it will goe hard with poor
― 313 ―
Sir F.†1 who has a sine cure of about 40l. per annum: but they must even shift as well as they can: I have writ all that is worth writeing. and I doubt have tired you as well as my self. and therefore shall conclude with assureing you must ever be
your affectionate Friend, and obliged servant
J T.
Address: For Mr: John Locke at Mr: Benjamin Furleys house in Rotterdam Holland.

986. Locke to Benjamin Furly, 16/26 December [1687] (947, 988)
B.L., MS. Eng. letters c. 200, ff. 9-10. Printed in Forster, pp. 3-10, where the year is supplied as 1686. Forster further supplies the years for no. 988 (19/29 December) as 1686 and for no. 1004 (10/20 February) as 1687. The correct year for nos. 986 and 988 is 1687; this is shown by the mention of the Recueuil de diverses pieces concernant le Quietisme; that no. 1004 belongs to 1688 is shown by the mention of the Epitome (i.e. Locke's Abregé). Further the letters form part of a coherent sequence, exchanged by Locke and Furly while Locke was in Amsterdam; the latest being no. 1017, of 23 February/4 March.
The group of letters between Locke and Furly nos. 986-1012 passim contains some frequently repeated allusive designations. Apart from 'our friend' (probably F. M. van Helmont: nos. 779, 835), who is identified on all occasions, their identifications are not repeated after the first notices. They are the Commissioner, also called the Doctor Colonel or the Colonel; Colhans or Colans; and the book about the Quietists. Two further allusive designations are listed in p. 327, n. 1.
26 Dec
After my hearty commendations of the sheep†2 to your memory these are to acknowledg that I am indebted to you for two long, two kinde and two pleasant letters. Count not this as if you had been lately at the Hague for six when I meane but two in all. I finde by that of 23 that our thoughts chime as well at a distance as when we are togeather, and that you and I were thinkeing and writeing of our Commissioner†3 about the same time. If when the fellows head
― 314 ―
run against the post good wits jumpd, what wits I pray are we both whose heads run at the same time against the same post. Thinke not that I use the terme post here with any the least designe of derogateing from the worth of our author, for me thinks all authors may for some quality or other be termed posts, some for their uprightnesse, some for their stifnesse and others for some other qualitys that shall be namelesse. An other thing I observe from that letter is, that the quicker a man writes the slower others read what he has written,†1 this being a remarque that may concerne the writers of books as well as letters you may doe well to put it into our next letter of advice to our learned author. And now I come to the parts of that letter it self, and therein I shall begin with the later end first by a figure of elegancie cald hysteron proteron, a certain sort of leapfrog of use amongst the learned whereby they can when the matter in hand soe requires make a bishop as grave as he is who appeard not on the stage till Charles the fifths days leap over the heads of all that lived before him quite as far as to Charlemagne. He that can doe this I thinke may well deserve the reputation of a good jumper. Could you be soe silly as to imagin that you should subdue our Dr. Colonel†a with a paper potgun though charged to the muzle? to which side pray did you apply your battery? did you expect, to penetrate the warrier†b side on which the sword hangs or the learned side armed with an inkhorne? had you made the reflections you ought you must needs have concluded him
In warlike Scuffle most audacious
And with his pen most pervicacious†2
Is it possible it should enter into your mazard, unlesse it have a crack in it, that you should take in an ancient moniment of prowes that has soe many times stood the brunt of pen and pistoll and can still without flinching bid defiance to all your rhime and reason, and that he should surrender himself to your bare summons? could you expect that a man that will not give himself for the washing should sit still and let you pull his skin over his ears that you might make a new man of him. Authors I mean Coll authors
― 315 ―
at the head of their partys as easily part with their skins as with their stiles, their ways of reasoning, or the least of their assertions. The madnesse wherewith you expected to worke such a miracle deserves a diping and noe doubt but the Coll who is expert at it would doe you this kindenesse But whether when he had you under water he would not clap his hand upon your head and according to the method of his brother Doctor of Scotland,†1 keep you there till he were perfectly assured of your being tamed I leave you to consider.
In the midle of your Career with your man of war or man of god choose you whether you bring me into the broile and require me to answer concerning the Directory†2 whether guilty or not guilty. Truly Friend haveing always thought that travailing to heaven by a Directory was even as reasonable as to saile to the Canarys by a land map, I have not much made use of those way-wisers†3 and soe may be excused if I say noe thing to your soe peremptory demand. But this I thinke I may say safely upon the matter between you and your Author, that whether or noe according to the Directorian scheme the water of Baptisme washes away sin our diver will be neverthelesse in the suds, the argument you use sticking still as fast as birdlime.
That 16 or 17 false quotations may passe amongst soe many 100 good ones is spoke methinks like an old Soldier but if he were now a Commander in England or France I am afraid it would goe hard with him for false musters and the greatest part of his regiment would be found to be but men of clouts†4 that amounting to a great number in shew at a distance, would amout†a to a very few when it came to a close engagement.
But to leave him and come to the Irish†5 which me thinkes is much the better understanding I am very sory when you were advanced soe far that you were hinderd from comeing to a conclusion, for you went on very steadily and that tract you were in must needs have brought you to the very center of the matter. when you see him next I hope you will remember where you left of
― 316 ―
and begining from thence again take the two or three remaining steps which are as many as need to lead your man to Pisgay†1 or a precipice
You wish me with you and desire I should make hast and soe doe I too, but I doubt whether you would be of the same minde if you knew one of my reasons. a Caske of mum an Hoghead of Syder and without doubt ever now and then a bottle of wine or a zopie†2 among for a more effectuall remedy against phlegmatique humors and rainy weather, this I suspect in my absence will make brave worke and heresie will rise up a pace in the lanterne†3 when soe waterd, and the mischeif is I cannot finde any one to make my deputy-over-seer. Our old master†4 and you will I know be at it with tother glassie†5 and our Mistris though she will not partake yet will stand by clap her hands and incourage you to it for my part I thinke I were best make Arent my vice Governor who may often repeat to you his Wil ghy wel†a Laeten.†6
I see†b not that you need be soe much trouble about the Ducks how to keep them, tis but leting the tide come into your packhouse and there will be a pond of course and water enough tis but now and then throwing in a litle meat to them. Pray when you send them let the folk know the pains I have taken to procure them, and how often I have preachd to, ralied <and>†c dund the pore litle scotch man for them, soe that I know not whether by <my per>secution†c of him I have not driven him at last to steale them, but that <is noe m>atter†c as long as they have them the Ducks will neither breed nor looke the worse for <it. I>†c am troubled about pore Colhans.†7 The book cald Receuil des diverses pieces concernant le Quietisme ett†d †8 I have got for you and thought to have sent it to day, but it being misfolded it must be a litle reformd by the bookbinder and soe stay till next time. Pray remember me kindely to
― 317 ―
Mrs Furly, to Our good freind†1 and all the assembly in the Lanterne, the inclosed is for my litle freind†2 both as a token of remembrance from me, and as an item for him to show you what you deserve when you medle with your Zopies. I am Dear freind yours
JL
I have just now received the three crevats and a third letter for which I thank you: the water both in the Tye†3 and on the land side of the town is exceeding high, If it should get into the town I know not but you must come with a boat and fetch me from Dr Guenellons as soon as you hear it, without jesting if this northwest winde continue there will be danger

987. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 17 December 1687 (968, 997)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 21-2.
Escott Dec: 17th. 1687.
Dear Sir
I was extreamly glad of Yours of the 29th. of nov: but the ill Newes it brought me of your want of Health was a terrible allay of my Satisfaction; but 'tis better then worse, you are alive still, which is more then I could promise my self before, you had been so long speechless, that I was afraid what the Issue of it would be, but now that you are recover'd of it, all is well. I hope you will assoon shake off all those other troublesome Symptoms which have incommoded you; and with so much obstinacy afflicted, and diseased you. I can contribute nothing but my prayers and good wishes, which ever follow you; as a person that is a publick blessing, in whose safety all mankind are concern'd, as well as your Friends; and therfore I promise myself that you will be restored to us, since the world cannot well subsist without some such excellent Examples
― 318 ―
of Wisdom and Vertue; and there are so few left amongst Men, that they are hardly enough to keep the Age from corrupting, and degenerating even into Brutality. and Friendship is but a name, unless it be in your breast; and amongst a very few Heroick Souls more, Heaven increase the number, and may we go on to perfection. I read Seneca every day, and have run through Monsr l'Abbadées Treatise of the Verity of the Christian Religion†1 much to my satisfaction; and I heartily Thank you for sending them to my Brother. I have been a little conversant in some part of physick too; and do long to discourse some points with you, but I cannot do it by letter; if you can keep to your good resolution of comming over in the Spring I may have that satisfaction once more, and you better health; for the list of diseases which you sent me, are certainly entayled on all that dwell in Holland, and do not drink Brandy. therfore there is no mean, you must learn to do that, or leave the Country; I hope I shall some time or other hit upon an Argument that may be powerfull enough to bring you over to us, or at least to convince you that Your Company is much Vallued, and passionatly desired, by dear Sir
Your most Obliged and most affectionate Friend and most
faithfull humble servant
ISABELLA DUKE
My Masters best services attend you, and my Brothers, who is going to London.
Address: For Mr John Lock at the House of Mr Benjamin Furley Merchant in Rotterdam

Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 18/28 December 1687
Martin Nijhoff, Catalogue, etc., 1862, item no. 1391 (see no. 962 above). Probably the letter dated 28 December with no year, and here dated 1688: printed below, no. 1093.
