1004. Locke to Benjamin Furly, 10/20 February [1688] (998, 1005)
B.L., MS. Eng. letters c. 200, f. 12. Printed in Forster, pp. 15-18. The true year from the contents and Furly's answer, no. 1005.
20 Feb: 87
Dear Freind
Bank mony is here at 47/8 if you can have soe much for it there draw on Dr Peter Guenellon for 15000 guilders in bank and make your bill or bills payable at as short view as you please, Nay if you cannot get 47/8 take 4 and 6/8 rather then fail, for it will be lesse trouble then to get the bank mony sold here and then draw it in currant mony thither but pray let me heare from you about it as soon as you can that I may know what to resolve in it, for there is noe thing that now stays me here but the weather and the graveing of the plate which, doe what I could, I could not get the graver to begin upon till today, I presse it with all my might that I may get it don with all speed soe that I may have some copys of it printed whilst I am here pray therefor send me word what number you will have printed and upon what sort of paper, for then I will get ink and paper in a readynesse to have it don as soon as ever it is graved and bring both copys and plate along with me. your story of Master Peter†1 confirmes my former opinion of the man and when you soe much commend his books I cannot but think of Sir Ph: Sidnyes two verses
And if the man such praise must have
what must he that keeps the knave?†2
In good earnest we that lay out our mony in books have an ill bargain of it, if we are not to be thought as learned as our librarys and if soe Master Peter is I think one of the learnedest men within some miles of him. I pittyed him in that part of the story wherein he could not read your M.S.†3 and that for a reason which I must tell you because you would not else think of it, and that is that I found my self very much troubled upon the receit of your last of 18 when I found what ever longing I had to it, that I could not read
― 359 ―
it, however at last I groped out the meaning of the greatest part of it, though there are some words in it still as much beyond my reach as the story of the Beguine†1 was beyond your Rabbys. But pray remember (when you write next) the maxime I once minded you of before, viz that letters that are writ quick are long in reading.†2
Since the Colonel is gon I am glad with you that our MS staid tis something to comfort us in the losse of those notable discoverys we might have expected. I wish your heretical pravity and perversnesse have had noe hand in this tragedy. And may I not justly suspect what you cal Colick, was heart breaking? I warnd you long since what effects such kinde of dealeing might have on an old Soldier and Author. Pray aske our friend†3 what he thinks he will make in his next revolution for in the last he made noe small figure in several capacitys. To be serious this accident makes me reflect on the folly methinks it is to pudder our selves and vex others about questions which I imagin the change of the scene will shew us were not worth thinkeing on. But I will not make a funerall sermon I doe not use to preach in my letters and doe least of all intend it to you. Give my love and respect to the company in the Lanterne. I am
your very affectionate friend and servant
JL
Pray if you can finde any one goeing for England that will cary a litle book of philosophie but of 4 sheets and that has noething in it of any affairs doe me the kindenesse to send me word, for I am in distress to send one of my Epitomes.†4 It will take up noe more place then a letter.
1005. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 11/21 February 1688 (1004, 1007)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 22. Answers no. 1004.
Rotterdam 21/2 1688
Dear Friend
It was wel thou beganst thy last with business least thou mightst have forgot it, I will follow thy example, and tell thee, that tho I
― 360 ―
could not meet with occasion to draw f15000 in bank this day upon our poor exchange, yet I agreed for f1500 with Francesco Gallacini —not at 46/8 or 47/8 but at 5 per cent. But tho it be now neare 8 the brokers servant is not come for the bill. I have made it at 1 or 2 days sight, he promising the mony on second day that so I may have time to advise whether he has paid me before it can be demanded, which I shall not faile to advise munday night,†1 If the bill be called for to night, It will not be presented till Munday, And if the Doctor†2 be abroad when they come to present it, it may be as well, as otherwise, and if they should find him, I writing not to him till munday night, he may excuse the accepting it till next morning, having as yet received no advise from me of the drawing the mony. We live in a time that we know not who to trust, and so I would willingly have the mony before it be payd, or accepted, there. I do not so well like the putting me off till munday for the money which should have been paid today, according to the course of marchants. But I confess 'tis a kind of an idle day, when people go ordinarily in such fine weather a pleasuring, and that may be the reason. He is an Italian, and lives in Pomp enough. But I love to do things with the utmost security.
As to my letter of the 18 that was illegible, there was nothing, I presume, lost, but my idle pains of writing.
As to the Coppys I would have them printed upon the best thick writing paper, and 500 of them, in the palest yellow Inke that can be made and some of them 40 or 50 in black Inke. I have a letter from our knight. he takes no notice of any letter from me in which I told him that V.H.†3 had spoke with a bookeseller†4 about printing his M:S. but that he must give for the copy†5 100 crowns, and that without it, and restitution of the original I should not, without his leave, part with it. But he tels me he has been sick unto death, and is now recovering, and enquires if the M:S: be transcribed: I forbear to answer him because the printer has not yet been with me, which is none of the best signs of any great inclination to it. He askt me once coolely what manusc. that was that H. spake to him, I said a very curious thing. He askt wherein the curiosity consisted, I told him in the singularity; there being no other of the
― 361 ―
same time and places. He askt what it containd that was curious, I told him the opinions of the times: which would prove the truth of the histories. And no man would want it that would spare mony to buy an authentick piece of history as that was. He askt how the person came by it. I told him he got it in france—so he said he would come and see it, but has not been so good as his word. What will come of it I know not; but I would gladly see it abroad: But if I cannot find any here nor in Amsterdam that will undertake it, I beleeve he'le†1 soon remand it out of my hands unless he thinks it as safe with me, as with any man he can intrust it with.
If thou sendst me one of thy Epitomes over, I shall send it to Colchester, and from thence to London, safe enough, and perhaps directly to London from hence.
Our Colonel†2 was to wel armd and fitted de Cap a pé to receive any wound by such wooden darts, Peace rest his rags he was a very indefatigable methodicall man, and no doubt would now have produced something that should have out done all former things, for being resolved now to trust his own eyes onely, and being an exquisit Judge— we should have had some thing becoming him. This with deare Salutation from us all is all at present from
Thy affectionate Friend
B F
I hear nothing yet of any broker for that bill, and to morrow in the evening I shall go abroad, so that the bill shall not come hence till I have the mony if I can avoyd it.
Endorsed by Locke: B F 21 Feb. 88
1006. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 11 February 1688 (892, 1048)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 153-4.
London Feb: the 11 87
Deare Brother
You can have very littel reverance for me if you think me capable to endure your silence without murmuring, No I am not insensible how much it is my intrest to convers with you, and that few must pretend to entertain me as you doe whither you please to treat me
― 362 ―
with the freedom of a brother or the pleasantness of a seemingly Angry friend, your last found me at Ely, and chid me into good humour, but your not rebuking me for not answering you sooner is such a disapointment to me, that I look and Act sowerly and shall punish all that come near me with spleenitick prattle till you voutsafe to conjure me into better temper, but may you say to yourself, must I be punish'd with a silly little woman, and to free I know not who from her sullenness, stoope to a quick corrispondance with her, and because I have a way of expressing myself agreablie on all subjects must my pen be employ'd in writing obliging things to one that has not judgment or manners to answer me. Patience good Brother, tis expedient that you should humble yourself, tis dangerous in some ages to be frequently beset with the wise, and great men of this world, even whilst they reape the most considerable advantages by their conversation with you. And why should I not raise my spirits and tell you that it may be your intrest as well as mine to divert your thoughts from those perplexing scenes which may alarme your stoute heart too violently as well as strick terrour into one of a more feble and timerous frame. Be advis'd dont provok me to quarel with you least I became a shrew'd woman, and for fashon sake act unsuitable to all my obligations to you. I find it high time to leave wrangling and soberly assure you that I converse most with those who have a very particular Esteem for you, persons who know how to value you as much as those doe who make larger proffessions to you, As for the few particular friends with whome you us'd to abuse me they love, you, but raile at you as fircely as I myself can doe. My Son whome you I am sure wish well to is I blesse God very well, and a great favourite of his Tutors who makes me beleeve that the young Sophister is very good. To conclude let me tell you that I have bin forced to doe some violence to my timerous self to be able to write after this manner, pray let me hear from you whilst it is posible for us to be found, and consider me as happy as the present hurry of things will permit, I am where you directed your last and where I meet with the most kind and civil usage my proud heart can wish. farwell deare Brother May you never fall into any trouble here but what will make you the happyer hereafter
Address: For Mr Locke
Endorsed by Locke: A Grig 11 Feb 87/8 Answered 18 Apr:

1008. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 13/23 [February 1688] (1007, 1009)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 24. Month and year from Locke's endorsement.
Rotterdam 23—
Dear Friend
Thine of the 22 I have, and seing I am got into the favour by following thy footsteps, I think it best to continue the course I have begun. And so as to our business, tho I may not write to the Gentleman I drew a certain bill upon that the Value is not yet paid me—yet I may sub rosa tell thee, that when I sent my servant this morning, I met him timely abroad, and told him my servant was gone to his house, he replyed He must come in the afternoone, I told him I must have the mony today. He told me I should not need doubt of that—On the Exchange John†2 spake to him—and he said he would tell him before he went off—as if he intended to be punctuall to an houre—I ordred him to watch his Italianising and be punctuall to his appointment, and so went from the exchange to Leers his, for one of Scots catalogues†3 —And at my doore I found wayting the brokers servant, to tell me that the Gentleman was to go abroad apleasuring this afternoone, and to know if I must needs have the mony this afternoone, or if the morning would not serve
― 365 ―
turne—I was then forct to speak as the Dutch calls it, het hooge woord,†1 that it being not for a marchant but a Gentleman, he was resolved not to accept the bill till he heard it was paid here—and that he had wrote me so, I having advised him that I was not to receive the mony till this day—so he appointed my servant to come between 5 and 6 this evening—But about 4 he came to excuse the business, and feele my pulse, bespeaking my patience, for feare I should have thundred him a peale, he told me then, that he had been abroad, that he came in to the towne on purpose but there being a famous plea to be pleaded, betwixt a man and his wife, the man that should have paid him was there and the stadhouse being so throngd there was no getting to him, much less geting him out to pay mony—And would know what answer my friend would give today. I told him I knew not, he said he thought to have had a curtesy in having taken this parcell, and now it would be an injury —But intreated me not to write to him to night that I drew upon, which I promisd I would not do, and I think I have kept my word for I have not writ to him at all—But pray let not that be the answer, but rather decline if it can be, or if not, let the answer be, not that he has advice that the Value is not paid—But that he does not yet understand that the Value is received—as he had expected this morning and that he will not accept till he has such advice. He promises faithfully to pay it to morrow at 10 aClock so that if the acceptance could conveniently be waved it might be as well—yet secundæ cogitationes meliores†2 —If so, he might returne the bill with protest as non inventus†3 —and so pretend dammage; therefore if a Notary should come to protest Let the answer be—omdat men geen advys noch heeft dat de wardye, aan de Trecker is betaalt†4 —I am in hast and must break off abruptly—
Leers declines: do thy best there, but remember the poor Lady†5 that must have a feeling†6 out of it.
Address: aan Dr: Pieter Guenellon op de keysers graft bij het oude glashuys Tot Amsterdam Voor Dr: Jno Lock
Postmark: Amsterdam 3s

1009. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 14/24 February [1688] (1008, 1010)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 26. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Rotterdam 24 2/m
Deare Friend
I was last night intreated not to write to Dr. Guenellon, that I had not the mony, upon a Solemn promise that it should be paid at 10 this morning, but when my servant came there, he was told that he should at 2 aclock receive it elsewhere—And upon the Excha: my Gentleman told me that he had told my servant where he should have the mony at 2 aclock. So meeting a man of that name, I askt him if it were of him that my servant was to receive f 1575 for account of G.†1 he said no. I askt then if it were of his son, he said no—he seing me a little amazed told me, he had spoke to him about it, and if he would do something first he would pay it. But he knew not, in so much that I was afrayd I should have writ to night that it was not paid. But at length—he told me—he would pay it, and that my servant must come immediatly and receive it. So I came home in all hast to fetch John to receive it— which put me in mind of a device I once saw about 40 year a goe a kind of Riddle to children, in which were these words, in capitall Letters I/MONEY/Friend—and pieces of verses taking in those words to make up the verses—one of which was—At length with money came my Friend. which pleasd me wondrous well—So I got my mony but my friend away quite from me fell—If I had money and a friend, as I have had before, Ide keep my money and my friend and play the fool no more.
I would not however for the Loss of my Italian friend, have been without this experiment—could he have got acceptance there, I should have had many a fair dance for thy money ere I had got it. I met with one upon the excha: a good friend of his and mine, and told him the story, asking him the meaning. he said there was no reason of feare: I was in no danger—I said that was true but for a reason that he knew not, Viz because my friend would not accept till he had advice that it was paid; at which he smiled and shaked his head but said there was without that no danger: I askt him then, seing the man was in a strait to regain his reputation in Amsterdam,
― 367 ―
If I should go and tell him he might give me an assignation upon him, and that he would pay me, if he did—He said yes, if he sent him mony—but not else—But said he would go and speake to him as a friend. I told him I being out of danger it was needless, and that I beleeved, being so pincht, he would do his utmost—And I beleeve he was forced to pawn some bill or other, to get the mony— which pleasd me wondrous wel—and so theres an end of that story —So be pleased to give Dr. Guenellon, the Inclosed†1 —I have by a ship that is to go to London with the first wind to send to L.H. Sydney†2 a fother fat†3 of Rhenish wine—may I have to send him one of the Epitomes.
Leers, as I told thee, declines the printing this manuscript. try what may be done there—And, if it can be, bring with thee the mystery of planing†4 paper—that I may use the glewy water made by thee to fit my price Currants—our friend,†5 and my wife Salute thee as also does
Thy reall friend
B.F.

1012. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 16/26 February 1688 (1010, 1017)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 29-30.
Rotterdam 26 2/m 1688
Deare Friend
Thine of the 25th confirms thy former that Doctors are not wel skild in matters of Exchange, or else, after I had advised that I had the mony and desired the payment of the bill, you would not have writ of drawing it again, for once having the mony in my hands, I am not so easy as to return it him and put my self to the trouble, and hazard of seeking another bill—nor had he the confidence to demand it, but onely to recommend the payment per first, which I told him I had done, he askt if I had any answer. I told him yes— He would know what: I told him an order to draw it by somebody that would immediately pay, that it might be there paid without this trouble—he said he had sent the bill back, and I, that you being no marchants could not expect, or conceive that a bill once protested would be returned—He begd once more that I would recommend the payment, I told him he need not doubt but 'twas paid—of the coppys I intended half a Ream to be printed, but that wilbe nigh 2000 coppys—but 1000 wilbe enough, and some of them black†1 —
For the Lady I designe 100 Ducatons, and so I wrote the knight —But if it be 100 Rix Dollars rather then faile it may doe†2 —but I feare none will adventure till they see the book, And I am unwilling to send it to any man—Whats given must be given down upon
― 371 ―
receit of it, with an obligation for f500 to restore the coppy after Transcribed—
I am told the States have answerd the memorial concerning Dr. Burnet, and resolvd to protect him†1 —As also ordred 48 ships to be set out and 30 to be built—
Pray Let Syl. call at Jacob Clauses†2 with this Letter for a Dutch treatise the count†a †3 tels me is to be had at his Shop, being a translation of a Disciple of Pauls, stiled Hermas Pastor,†4 and let him pay for it—our old friend†5 comes in with news of a thorough thaw; and that we shall now soone expect thee, in the meane while we all salute thee and so I rest
Thy affectionate friend
BENJAMIN FURLYH
I heare John Spicer is coming from Exeter. I hope we shall have the boers sacks†6 by him—
Address: Aan Dr. Pieter Guenellon op de keysers graft bÿ het oude <glashuys>†b Tot Amsterdam for Dr: Jno Lock
Postmark: Amsterdam 3s

1013. Mrs. Mary Clarke to Locke, 16 February 1688 (908, 1020)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 181-2. Printed in Rand, pp. 246-9. Answers no. 999; answered by no. 1020.
London Feb: the 16th. 1687:
Deare Sir
I have nothing to shelter my selfe under for my Great neglectt in not returning you oft'ner My thankes for your many Favors to me and mine; but your Great Goodness and Charyty to forgive all offenders, and now Like one of our sex I take thiss opertunity to
― 372 ―
insinuate my selfe a Little into your Favor and Good opinion a Gen If it be possible by wrighting to you to Lett you know, that Mr. Clarke is now in the Countrey wheare some Exterordinary Buisness which wase of moment to him required his presence and Could not be dispatched without him†1 by which meanes he wase deprived the sattisfacktion of receveing or answareing your Last Kind Letter; but with his Leave I wase to open all Letters in his absence that came hither directed to him and in yours I find soe much thought and Frendly Care that you take about the Education of our Sone, that I know not how to Express my thankfullness as I ought to doe; though I have a true sence of it and will Continually keepe it in my mind in hopes of some opertunity att Least to shew my Gratfullness; I thanke God the Child is now very well and Growse very tall for his Age but thin, he is very much Improved in reading of his Inglissh since mounsr†2 came to him that being what he has most apployed himselfe to which indeede wase by my particuler desire he being after his Fevor†3 not able to read one word and very Little better when his Tuter came but now can read any chapter in the Bible very prittily and distinkly, he can alsoe Give an aCount of what he reads, he has alsoe made a prety Good progress in the discription of the Countreys Espeshally his one; and something in French which he has Larnt by heart and is now begining to read it, and he is very much pleased with his Larning to wright I hope he will in a short time be able to wright you a Letter of thanks himselfe, that way of Blacking of Coppyes is a very pretty and easey way of Larning, but that sort which we have Gott of them me thinkes is to sett but mr Clarke Likes the hand very well they tell me it is the modish round hand, I confess they know best but me-thinks it is a better hand for his sisters to Larne it Lookes to sett and formall for a man and Espeshally a man of Buisness as I would have him be, and I find by your Letter you are soe much for Buisness that you would have him of a trade and of all your trads you Could never have thought of one that would have pleased him better then that of a Joyner for ever since he Could take delight in any thing he wase never better pleased then with a hammer and a naile, the trade of a Jeweller and such like I feare will requier more Judgment then he may ever have without he delighted in it as much as his hammer.
I feare you thinke him forwarder then he is;
― 373 ―
he is a sort of a downe right honest Blockheaded boy, and what he has in him is pretty hard to find out mr. Clarke tells me he is Like me and my relations reserved, but I hope not for I should be Glad I knew any thinge worth communicateing, he has but a bad memory and it is pretty hard to him to Larne, but he is of a very Good nature, and Loves his Father extreemly and I beleve would doe any thing in the world that he sed he should doe or that he thought would please him, and seemes to be under Great Concerne when he is displeased with him soe much that he Changess Coler as pale as can be and seemes to tremble though his Father resons with him with as Great love and tenderness as can be soe that at Last he seemes to be quite dosed, and yett soone forgetts it, soe that I observe as yett a few words and a Little wipping dose doe more Good then all resoning alone till they are older and better able to Judge of it, not that I would have thiss Exercised†a used often or by any body but a Father or mother and then to be sure it will not be Immoderate, I have 2 daughters one you are pleased to honer with the tittle of your mistress, and not to recommend her to you but she is more afectted with one word then the other with five hundred without a Little of the rod some times though she is of a very Good nature and very Apprehencive for her Age and seemes to Looke mightily concerned when you tell her of a falt, and Like a Little Saint but next time tiss forgott <a>†b Gen without we have had a Little of the Lady Burches helpe, she is extreemely Like her Brother when he wase of her Age and exacttly of his humor, but more merry, he Loves his Tuter very well and is very willing to Goe to his Booke, I beleve becase he knowes he pleases his Father, tho it is hard to him to Larne and ofner calls on him to know If he is redy to Goe up to his Booke and tells him what it is a Clock then the Tuter doss on the Scoler though I must needs say they are both diligent enough and mounsr. is of a very Good nature I thinke and not at all Given to any Vice as swareing or drinking or such Like as I can perceve in the Least but rather an abhorer of it, the Greatest falt I can find with him he is prety formall and very tender and nice and carfull of himselfe and for doeing all things about himselfe just in such a time and methard more Like one of the Curiouse sort of Ladys then a distressed protistant that must shift in the world, but thiss is better to be borne withall then the above mentioned falts, and I confess I would have the Child to be brought up very neate and
― 374 ―
Clenly but not to formall which I the more speake a Gainst he being a Little that naturally, but thiss I hope as he Growse Bigger†a- and comes-†a to travell abrode they will soune Laugh him out of; I have taken the Libberty to inclose a Little of mounsrs. wrighting and a Little of his pupills which I happen to have in my pokett att thiss time which If you Like I shall have the better opinion of though I must needs say I Like such a hand for a man as sir walter young wrights or mr Bridgesses†1 which I thinke is rather the better but I know not whether you ever saw that or noe and thearefore Cannott Give me your Judgment; I am Glad you are Like to see your 2 Good Frends†2 you mention thiss spring, I am now at thiss place prepareing for another Little one my reconing being out about our Lady Day and If please God I doe well, and find my selfe Lighter you would have bin in some danger of seeing me alsoe If you had not told me I ought to stay tell you come in person to invite me soe that it may be now I may take state on me and stay till that time I brought only your mistress to towne with me for a nurss when I Lye in but insteede of that I have bin hetherto forst to nurss her she haveing had the measells, since her Father went into the Countrey but now I thanke God is very well a Gaine they Left a Great rume and weekness in her Eys but they are much better now to and I hope will be quite well before her Father coms home though I expectt him thiss weeke, she will needs have her service presented to you though I tell her I have hardly roome to subcribe my selfe what really I am as you may Emagin by the Libberty I now take,
Deare Sir
your Most affectionate and oblidged humble servant
M CLARKE,
I wright soe seldome that makes me now soe Impertinate and tediouse soe that one falt Creates another as is to usuall;

1014. Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 17 February 1688 (990, 1052)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 162-3.
London Feb. 17th. 1688.
Dear Sir
I fear it will be my fate alwaies to begin my letters with begging your pardon that I have been so long your debtor for the favors of that kind which you are pleased to confer upon me. It's now severall weeks since I have had your two last in my hands, and I have only my old excuse for my silence that I never think I have any thing worth the postage to send you, and that my sister wrote to you a little before she left the Town,†1 and this I hope may goe a great way to obtain your pardon; But it's now high time to pay you my hearty thanks for both yours, since my Sister is gone, and I can not pretend to be courting a Mistress, or to be otherwise so plunged in business as it seems you were about the 20th. of Jan. I confess after all the hints you have given me I can not guess what it is has so charmed you, I am most willing to hope (what would be my greatest advantage) that you were only busy in settling your matters, and packing up your books in order to your quitting that boggy country and making us happy with your good company this summer in the row; I am sure you can be no where so much desired, and if I can give any guess at matters we shall probably have a pacate†2 time to enjoy our friends; I am the more of this opinion because I am told by one of your friends that my Lord of P.†3 saies he hopes to see you here this summer. But whatever the Affaire is that has so taken you up, I should not easily forgive its keeping any thing from me that would have made me laugh (which is a matter of no small moment to a builder) but that you tell me I shall shortly see the effects of it, a pleasure I shall expect with the greatest impatience. About a month hence I reckon I shall turn my face towards Escott, where if I may be so happy as to see you this summer I dare promise you the Ladies and the fiddles, and if there be no Bride in the case I think I may promise you at least the parson of the parish and his brisk wife to countenance your dancing; I have seen Mr Charleton but once yet, but resolve to improve an acquaintance you have with so much friendship given me, in your next (which I beg may not be long in coming) pray write me
― 376 ―
whether you would have me keep the dictionary†1 he has left with me here in Town, or send it down for my Library in lieu of those you have bought for me; It is in two large folio's handsomely bound, and if there be a difference in the price, that may be adjusted betwixt us. Mr Stringer is yet in Town, but we have wanted Mr Clarks company this fortnight; He was called into the country to bury his Lady's old Uncle†2 who has left her sole Executrix, but what this Windfall will be worth to him I know not. I live in hopes of some happy opportunity to demonstrate the great value I have for your friendship, and my sincere desire to merit the title of
Dear Sir
Your most faithfull and most affectionate friend and servant
WALTER YONGE.
Address: For Mr John Locke at Mr Benjamin Furly's Merchant In Rotterdam
Endorsed by Locke: Sir W. Yonge 17 Feb. 88 Answered 19 Apr.
1015. James Tyrrell to Locke, 20 February 1688 (985, 1225; see also no. 1019)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 66-8. Part printed in King, p. 172.
Feb: 20th: -87/-88
Dear C.
Whilst I was under some concerne because I had bin so long without hearing from you, I had the good Fortune as to receive yours of the 3d: Instant S.N: which was a great satisfaction to me since it brings at once the assureance of your good health; (since you say nothing to the contrary) and allso of your continued Freindship, and Kindnesse to me, and mine; confirmed in so particular a manner, as both to administer comfort for the dead and good advice how to mannage those dear pledges of her affection which she hath left behind her to our care: I am very well satisfyed you concurre with me in the reflection I made of my sons incapacity of being improved as yet by his comeing over to you; and therefore I am resolved to put him out to school some where about London; but whether to Mrs: Tanner (who hath now got a new schoolmaster)†3 or els to Camberwell free school†4 (where he will be allso
― 377 ―
under the particular care of Dr: P.†1 my dear Freind, and Tutor) I am as yet unresolved; haveing at present some objections, and scruples as to both of them that I hope at least as to one of them to be satisfyed in before I carry him up. which I intend (God willing) shall be before Easter: for as to Mr: St. C.s†2 I am absolutely resolved not to send him thither for the ill character I hear of his wife and allso his owne want of prudence in mannageing boys as they ought, which I have from unc: A. who hath reason to know by a dear bought experience, and who gave me this advice in a letter about a fortnight since: when he was well. in the meane time I doe so far concurre with your opinion concerneing the method of teaching and breeding my son that one great reason of my takeing a Tutor into the house, hath bin (besides the more particular care I could have of his health) that I could have him taught my owne way: and tho' He may not perhaps be as ready as those who are taught in great schools; at makeing, and speakeing latine, yet as for that which is most truely usefull viz: constering an Authour; he is able to doe that pretty well with the help of a dictionary: his Master haveing not constered to him either in Virgil; or Florus above this half year: and he is pretty ready in the new Testament Greek; tho' to deal freely with you I doe not find that inclination in him to letters that I could wish and which I had my self at his Age: but nature is not to be forced; and his constitution will not endure; a too sedentary life; and so Gods will be done: if I can give him so much love for it as to make him bear staying at home; and to know how to spend a rainy 'tis well: and as much as I pretend to my self. and I hope whereever I put him I shall make his master†a persue your instructions: for I doe not know one boy in 10. that learns the better for much beating: and I abhorr that mechanic method in free schools where they administer the rod (as mountebanks doe their pills) to all tempers, and constitutions alike without distinction: but I hope to discourse more particularly with you of my sons education e're I am much older and hope to see your notes you have written upon that subject: I still continue my thoughts of
― 378 ―
visiteing you this spring tho I bring not Jemmy with me: therefore pray deal freely whether you had rather Unc: Ad: and I come together or that stay till his returne since it is indifferent to me; and perhaps so many of us at once may put you to some inconvenience; and therefore I desire to have your true sentiments of this before I goe; as likewise whether you desire I should bring over any of your Manuscript†a notes in Physick and other things which I have of yours: I have allso 3 volumes of the new Testament in French Latine and Greek: interlined with notes†1 which I am sure can never be filled up by a more judicious hand: if you have any desire I should bring them or any thing els of yours pray let me know it. as soon as you can conveniently; for I designe to breake up housekeeping at Lady Day, and to come up to Towne before Easter;†2 which is the reason that I have bin the quicker in answering your last that I may have time enough to performe your commands before I leave these parts: however I shall not fail to bring Mr: Boyles new peices†3 along with me: or at least to send them you. if I come not. I shall be glad to receive your commands in any thing that lyes in my power either in citty or Countrey. I know not what you meane by my Lord Primates Chronologicum muthicum; for I doe not remember neither can find any such booke you mention in my Lords life (which passed thro' my hands) onely there is mention made of his Chronologia Sacra amongst his other workes; which he left imperfect but as far as was finisht was publisht by Dr: Barlow: viz: from the Deluge. to the middle times of the Judges, and†b then after a chasme A shorte chronology of†c- the reignes-†c of the Kings of Judah and Israel: which is one of the most perplext things in the old Testament.†4 I am not wont to write much news: since you are so well furnisht in your Gazets in all things relateing to England; but know not whether you have heard that your right honourable Freind is dismist of his command of Wiltshire; as hath bin done with all Lords LewTenants that would not complye with his Majestyes commands: in the matter I suppose you know of: tho he hath bin continued in
― 379 ―
longer then any other: and was one of the last turned out.†1 and to let you see what encouragement those that were called Wigs now†a- meet with here:-†a all the Aldermen; and baylives of oxford that were lately put in by the late new charter are all turned out; and Mr: P.†2 your old acquaintance; and Ald: wright†3 with severall others put in their places, tho I hear the former refuses to act as such: your Unc A. is likewise named Alderman; and Justice of P. for S.†4 but refuses to act by reason of a misnomer: which is a good excuse: now if you would know the reason of all this they say there will be a Parliament in May: and in order to his Majestyes designes it is fit the Corporations should undergoe a new Alteration: the former Members growing weary, and not willing to drive out the whole stage; it was time the resty Jades should be unharnessed, and turned out to grasse: and those that before were so ready in giveing up their Charters now find the good effects of it in being the first that are turned out. nec lex est Justior ulla†5 —enough of the politicks: but wishing you all health; and us a happy meeting am.
Yours heartily
M.
Jemmy is much your servant; and highly sensible of your kindnesse.
Address: For Mr: John Locke. this.
Endorsed by Locke: Tyrrell†b 20 Feb 87/8 Answered 19 Mar
1016. Edward Clarke to Locke, 21 February 1688 (1000, 1020)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 43-4. Printed in Rand, pp. 249-50. Answers no. 999; answered by no. 1020.
London 21o. Februarii 1687/8.
Deare Sir
Soon after the Writeing my last of the 27th. of January, I was suddainly and unexpectedly call'd againe into the Countrey by
― 380 ―
the Death of my Wifes Old-Uncle Watts of Sydcott,†1 and am but now newly Return'd from thence, however cannot omitt this first opportunity of thankeing you for your verie Kind and obleigeing Letter of the 6th instant, which I have not as yet suffitiently considered, nor have I time at present to Answer as I ought, and therefore will now only speake to such particulars thereof as seeme to require a speedy Answere; My intentions are to continue here untill my Wife be Delivered and the Danger over, which I expect and hope will bee about our Lady Day next, and soon after that my Businesse will unavoydably carry mee hence into the Countrey, where I beleive I shall bee forc'd to continue for the space of a moneth or thereabouts, and then I shall Return hither againe, hopeing in a short time thereafter That Madam will bee in a Condition to begin her journey towards Chipley, And what ever Commands you thinke fitt in the meane time to obleige mee withall you may depend upon it they shall bee Faithfully performed, and you may bee allsoe assur'd that within a day or two (as I can gett time) Mrs R:S: shall have the ten pounds you have ordered mee to pay her etc Your other Letters (with the inclosed to your Noble Freind†2 of the 17th.) I have allsoe this afternoon Received, and shall bee verie punctuall in observeing every particular of your Directions therein as the Bookes come to hand, in the meane time (because you desire it) I must acquaint you that my Brother Builder†3 is in Town, and received your letter, but J:F: is amongst his Relations in the County of Dorsett; And I find that your Noble-Freind is not soe greate in his Interest at Court as Hee was being verie lately Discharg'd from those Honorable Commands which Hee had over his own County, to make room for some other more complying with That which is call'd his Majesties present Interest, many others are likewise turn'd out and putt in, and the World is full of change, But I am still the same unalterably,
your most affectionate Freind and Faithfull servant

1017. Locke to Benjamin Furly, 23 February/4 March 1688 (1012, 1114)
Forster, pp. 41-2.
Amsterdam, 4 March, 1688.
Dear Friend,
If lying be a sin that is put to account, most ordinary tradesmen will I fear have a hard reconing to even in the next world; for there is scarce one of them one can finde who thinkes it not a priviledg of his calling to breake his word whenever it may serve his turne.†1 But, however, they are all good Christians, orthodox believers, and such as one cannot but know to be marked for salvation by the distinguishing L that stands on their dore posts,†2 or the funeral sermon that they may have for a passport if they will goe to the charge of it. This preface will not be altogeather besides the matter, if you expect me (as 'tis like you doe) the same day you receive this. But, whatever businesse, desire, or resolution one has to see one's friends, those above mentiond Gent. I assure you, are first to be attended, and their leisure to be waited. And 'tis noe small joy that I am got soe far out of their hands that I can now say with some confidence that I hope to be with you on Saturday next. As an evidence thereof, I sent you by the day's Veer Scuyt†3 two boxes and a bundle of books; they are marked B.F. 1°. 2°. 3°. the least of the boxes is that which you sent my linnen and the apples hither in. The other box is twice as big, and has great iron hinges, and is fastened with a padlock; and the bundle of books is as long as the largest size of printing paper folded the long way. These you
― 382 ―
may receive as pledges that it will not now be long befor I intend to assure you in the lanterne that I am,
Your most affectionate friend and servant,
J. L.
1018. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 23 February 1688 (997, 1052)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 25-6.
Otterton Feb: 23d. 1687.
Sir
Being lately return'd from London, and having one Hour that I can call my own, I can no way imploy it so much to my satisfaction as in tendring my most affectionate services to you, to whose Friendship a large share of my Time, and Thoughts, and Soul are due. I blush every time that I reflect on the letters which I return you, for those Elegant ones with which you entertain me, especially on some of the last, which were so slight, so briefe, that they need a longer Apologie then I have now time to make; (for 'tis my fate to be alwayes limmitted, We are to Marry a Sister tomorrow,†1 and the good Company think the time stollen from them, which I employ in writing this, and several other letters, that must be dispatch'd by this post.) they were so defective in expressing the great Esteem, and kindness I have for you; and that Gratitude with which I resent all the Favours you so generously have heaped on me; so that I abundantly deserve your raillery, in taxing me with excesses in that point, and with writing your Epitaph; your advice against my reading and tampering with physick seems to be of the same Stamp, since you know I read very little of any thing, and that only for my own entertainment, being the most useless thing that ever read, or knew any thing; thus you call my faults to remembrance; as you do my infirmities of Body, by enquiring after my health; that part of your letter I take to be serious, and therfore shall answer it as fully as is convenient in this paper. Tunbridge Waters have still the same good effects on me as formerly; and the use of them secures both to my Master and my self, a very competent measure of Health, by sweetning and invigorating the blood, and delivering us from those complaints commonly called Vapours of the Spleen; but for our particular disorders we
― 383 ―
can find no remedy; my Woman†1 has left me as she found me, and Dr Sydenham has nothing more to offer, either to him, or me; all that I have learnt since I saw you either from Books, or discourse, is a right state of my Case; which I am certain is no more then a partial descent of the part, which lyes most commonly in an Oblique position. and is therby rendred uncapable of answering the end for which nature design'd it. perhaps there is no possibillity of setting it right, yet several Women would undertake it, but I dare not trust them, I am afraid of their phisick, and their Methods, and will never submit to any, but what you shall have examin'd and approved. and whither ever we shall be within reach of each other, so as to have a personal conversation, you know best, there can no more be said in a letter, but that I advance a great pace towards forty. I left my Brother in London, pursuing a fair Lady, I know not yet what will come of it; my next shall not faile to tell you, but now you must give me leave bid you adieu; being with all imaginable sincerity and Constancy Yours
Address: For Mr John Lock at the House of Mr Benjamin Furly Merchant in Rotterdam
Endorsed by Locke: Mr Duke 23 Feb 87/8 Answered 23 Mar
1019. James Tyrrell to Dr. David Thomas, 26 February [1688] (1027)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, f. 69. Year from Locke's endorsement. Tyrrell's preceding letter to Locke is no. 1015.
Feb: 26th:
Dear Friend
I thank you for your speedy answere, and more for your plaine dealing; for indeed I suspected you did not desire my company at this time or els you would have sayed somewhat of it at first; I suppose your businesse, or your brothers†2 at least is somewhat urgent since you cannot stay to take your son along with you, and that you goe way at a time of the year when the sea, and travelling in those parts is not very pleasant; I wish you a good voyage; and a safe returne; and pray let me know in your next (if it be worth
― 384 ―
while to write againe) whether you cannnot tell whether my company may not be convenient there; in respect of your self; or JL: for I would not goe thither to be troublesome to any body; neither will I goe at all till your returne; who perhaps may bring him over with you; and then one great part of my goeing will be taken off: I pray if you write to him againe before you goe (for I have writ too lately to write againe) let him know that I found out Will: Pen; and spake to him about that businesse; but <he>†a told me; the pardon was not for JL. but one Mat: Lock excepted in the proclamation:†1 so I desired him to meddle in no such thing as to JL. unlesse particularly desired; which he promised: and so much I could have told him; if he had writ to me about it: but that I am not worthy to be concerned in any businesse for him; which is all one to me; I have enough of my owne to doe: pray present my service to him and tell him I have answered his last; and hope he will have received it before you come to him: I humbly thanke your Lady for her kind remembrance; to whom I pray present my humble service who am
your reall friend; and affectionate servant.
J TYRRELL.
Your son is well, and promised to come to me at Shrovetide†2 but it seems something has fallen out that hinders him.
Address: For my honoured Friend Dr: Thomas at his house at Salisbury Carriage†b p'd†b

1020. Locke to Mrs. Mary Clarke and to Edward Clarke, 28 February/9 March 1688 (1013, 1220; 1016, 1021)
Rand, pp. 252-6. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Answers nos. 1013 and 1016; answered by no. 1030.
9th March, 1688.
Madam,
If you pay all your real debts after the rate you do an imaginary one to me, it would [be well if it were] convenient Mr. Clarke should have ever now and then such a business that he had lately at Sidcott. The letter you did me the honour to write me the 16th February brings such an overplus of interest for a little forbearance, that I fear you take me for a grievous extortioner that could not be satisfied for a few ordinary words I sent you some time since without receiving from you in return four times their number of such as infinitely exceed them in value. To confess the truth I do not find you are under any obligation to keep touch with me in writing, for being so much before hand with me in real and substantial kindness, you need not think that some thankful words I sometimes send you can give me any just claim to an answer from you in writing, though amongst all your favours there be none more welcome to me than those. And whatever were the cause I cannot but be extremely pleased that one of the kindest and one of the longest letters you ever writ in your life was to me, for so I think I may well say your last was. There is but one favour left beyond it to complete my happiness, and that I demand with some kind confidence, since your promise gives me a right to it, and your own purpose was to perform; which no pretence of state can excuse you from when you have laid down the great belly and are well up again. And I shall have reason to conclude you are willing I should languish away my life here under the dominion of a Dutch mistress that holds me fast on this side the water, if you will not come and by the unresistable power of your presence redeem me from it. In the meantime I with great concern wish you easily and safely delivered of another lusty boy. My young master gives such hopes of himself that I cannot but wish he may have more brothers and like him. I guess by what you say of him that he is a little more tender and soft in his nature than I imagined he would have been, which is
― 386 ―
a new reason for me to insist on my former rules against rough usage. Let not the rod I beseech you be employed either on him or my little mistress, but in case of obstinacy and direct refusal to obey your commands. I take the liberty to repeat it here, because your letter seems to intimate that the rod is of most prevalency on him, for his book which I am still in the mind should be made his recreation. And you have all the hold one can desire upon him, since you confessed he is solicitous so much about nothing as pleasing his father. Keep him in that temper of being afraid to displease you and his father, and you have him safe and need not use any blows to bring him what you have a mind to, provided you go not too fast and put him not beyond his pace. Now that he can read English let him every day read a chapter or two to you, or some other English body. But to his tutor let him read and speak nothing but French. Let him now get that tongue as fast as he can, for do what you can he will have English.
I am glad you [hit] upon so good a tutor for him. The finicalness and formality you take notice of in him is the least fault one could have met with; [but let him give] none of his niceness and formal ways to your son. It is much better to be borne with in a French schoolmaster than in a little gentleman. His tutor's hand (bateing a letter or two) I like exceedingly, and if your son leave out the long tails of his g's, p's and y's, and the impertinent stroke of his f's, and instead thereof will write them thus g, p, y, f, I could not wish almost to write a better hand. But if you like the enclosed better I will send you some of these yellow copies for him to go over with black, if you like that way to form his hand. The graver has misspelt Mr. Clarke's name, but that will do no harm to the writing.†1
Pray remember me very kindly to my pretty little mistress. I am exceedingly glad that the measles is so well over, which is a disease not without danger in the old way of tampering. I know if you had either Dr. Sydenham or Goodall they used neither hot remedies nor hot keeping, which is a rule I advise you to observe, if any of your children should have the same disease in the country. Madam, you will pardon me for talking thus to you of things you understand yourself much better than I do. 'Tis an odd way I am got into of entertaining you. Your own permission has encouraged me in it, and since I understand not the courtly way of compliments, give
― 387 ―
me leave in this to speak the true and sincere respect and concern wherewith I am,
Dear Madam,
your most humble and most obedient servant,
J. L.
Pray do me the favour to give Mr. Clarke so much of this paper as belongs to him.
Sir,
Never was letter more obliging in the seasonableness as well as other circumstances of it, than your lady's last, for it came very opportunely to ease me of a great pain your unusual silence had put me to. For having no doubt of your kindness nor forwardness to write I the more feared your health, or some of your family. That which it has proved does the least of any afflict me, since he died in a good old age and good right mind, which you know is a comfort since there is no remedy for mortality. Your lady having done me the favour to give me an account of your son I have taken the liberty to trouble her on that subject. And if I guess right at his temper by what I find in her letter he must be dealt gently with. And since the respect he has for you has a great awe upon him, keep it as much as you can in all your conversation with him from confounding him. The just measures of severity and mildness which is to be mixed in your words, looks, and carriage to him, it is impossible for any one absent to guess at, but only in general that if they be so tempered as to keep up your authority and his spirit, all will go well whatever little slips he may be guilty of, for you must neither endeavour nor desire to have him grave or staid beyond his age, nor proficient in anything beyond his natural disposition.
Sir, you need not make any extraordinary haste to answer that extravagant part of my letter of the 6th passato which concerns your son.†1 His age and that business will bear delay. Only I am of the mind, that it will not misbecome a gentleman to recreate himself from his other affair in some manual art. And the more skill and dexterity he has in it the more pleasure and diversion will he find in practice of it.
― 388 ―
I hope ere this you have received of the epitomes two bound, two stitched, and one in quires, that by several hands as I could light on them I have sent. That in quires I would have bound and gilded as the other are. Those three are to be thus disposed of: the first to my Lord Pembroke; and the other two, one to Mrs. Clarke, and the other to Mrs. Duke, which I desire you to send her by Sir Walter, who will be pleased to content himself with the reading of that, if it be worth it, till I can find an opportunity to send him that I <design>†a for himself. The other stitched up <in>†b marble paper are one for Mr. Boyle†1 and the other for Mr. Freke.
I would beg the favour of you to get me a good beaver hat made the diameter of the inside of the crown at the band, which I have here below marked by the two black lines, as also on the margin of the copy here enclosed. I desire the hat may be made as high as the fashion will bear: the rest I leave to your direction. I desire also a peruke very deep, the caul of a middle colour betwixt black and flaxen, and a little longer than a parsons. These Adrian or Mr. Oakley will bring with them.
Pray present my humble service to Sir Walter, and beg his excuse for my not writing to him this post as I designed, but have not now time scarce to finish this. And let him know he may, if he please, take Morery's dictionary that [he] had from Mr. Charleton into the country with him. So I designed it if he like it, and we shall well enough adjust the matter. I have more to say to you but have no more time, but to assure you that I am,
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate and most obliged servant,
J. L.
I hear that Thomas and Susan†2 are in town. I wonder I hear not a word from them. When I print my book, as I think now I shall, I would have my picture before it; therefore, pray get the picture they have of mine up to town whilst you are there, that I may take order to have a plate graved from it.†3
I am glad to hear the sheep are got safe to Chipley. The country man here I am told is very importunate to have his bags again wherein the provision of oats and beans were laid in for them
― 389 ―
during their being at sea, and which the master of the vessel carried away with him to Exeter. If it may be pray let Mr. Elwill send them back to Mr. Furly by the next ship.
Address: For Mrs. Mary Clarke, at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, London.

Deare Sir
Yesterday in the morning (and not before)†a I received from your Freind Mr. Charl: of the Temple Two Packetts, wherein were inclosed two of your Abridgments de Intellectu stich'd in Marble-Paper, one in loose Sheetes, and one verie hansomely Bound, That which was soe Bound, togather with the Letter which came inclosed in yours of the 24th. of January last to mee, I delivered in the Afternoon with my own hand to your Noble Freind, who received them both with all expressions of Kindnesse and respect to you, and seem'd to bee well pleas'd that the Abridgment was writt in French, And told mee that Hee had read over the greatest part of your Treatise at Large upon that subject, and that Hee was much pleased therewith, and to use His owne Expression, Hee said there were verie Fyne illustrations of your Notions all along in it, and promised mee that when Hee has gone through it, you shall have his thoughts therein more particularly, in the meane time by mee Hee Returns you His thankes for your Free communication of your Notions upon that subject to Him, and professes the continuance of a Reall Freindshipp towards you: One of the stich'd Abridgments in Marble-paper, I have since allsoe presented to Mr. Boyle in your Name and in such manner as you directed mee, which Hee received verie Kindly, and was glad to heare of your Wellfare, I found Him weake, and much indisposed, But Hee told mee hee had been much worse, and was now Recovering, and assured mee Hee would (as soon as possible) read over your Abridgment and give you his Reall thoughts without complement thereupon, and desiered mee to give you his thankes for it; The
― 390 ―
other two I Keepe by mee to bee disposed of as you shall further direct; And just now, whilst I was Writeing this, I received by the Penny-Post, one other of your Abridgments Bound, which according to your Directions was imediately delivered to Mrs. Clarke who, tho at present Shee understands it nott, yett values it exceedingly, and Promises to learn French on purpose that shee may thereby bee inabled to understand it, and will give you her owne thankes for it as soon as the Greate Belly is Layd, in the meane time Pray take my hearty thankes for that and all other your Favours, and bee assured of my being
Your most affectionate Freind and Faithfull servant†a
I forgott to tell you in my last of the 21th. of February that when I was at Sydcott to bury my Uncle Watts, tho my Businesse was such, and my time soe short, That I could not possibly goe to Sutton to speake with Mr. Stratton about your Affayres in those parts, yett I sent a servant on purpose to desire Him to come to mee in Case Hee wanted any Advise or Assistance in any of your Concerns there, but heareing nothing in return from Him, I had reason to conclude that all was well there etc:

Severall of your letters are before me and the curiosity's I mention'd had been with you sometime since could I have procured the Philosophicall Transactions you wanted which I hope will be to your satisfaction being from the yeare 1683 to 1685 and to page 834 of that yeare. if any thing be wanting upon notice I shall endeavour to procure it these I obtained with some difficulty and was beholding to Mr. Churchill the bookseller†1 without who's assistance

The other day I met with Sir John Hobart†1 being newly Come to towne and enquired of him about the herb that his grandfather Serjeant Maynard Commended so much which he told me Sir Theodore Meyerne†2 mention'd to him by the name of Hughwort which not being knowen to me by that name I asked him whether he knew not the Latine name. he replyed that it was either the Veronica mas or fæmina he knew not which but by his description it must be the former, for he say's it ha's a downynesse under the leafe and creep's upon the ground,†3 how it was to be made use of he could not tell me when I see him next I will endeavour to get a better account of it.
I delivered the 2 pacquets In Salisbury Court as you directed he†4 presents you his service. Inclosed you have the Catalogue of the things I send to Roterdam which are now pack't up in a small box mark't inline image and will be sent by the first oportunity, if I Could have a branch of the nutmeg tree it would be verry welcome.
As to the Costs of the books I sent you, wee will discourse it when I have the hapynesse of seing you, I hope you received a letter I sent you from Dr. Goodall†5 I kisse your hands and am
Dear Sir

1023. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 4/14 March 1688 (979, 1033)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256a. Printed in Ollion, pp. 175-6. Answered by no. 1033.
Locke returned to Rotterdam probably on 5 and 6 March, N.S.: B.L., MS. Locke f. 34, f. 15v.
(English)
Rotterdam 14 Mar. 88
Me authore et impulsore misit ad Te per Helmontium Furleius noster codicem manuscriptum,†1 ut inter manus tuas depositus maneat dum transigitur de impressione. Cum videris quæ contineat tu nobiscum credo senties mereri lucem. Continet enim authentica monumenta, rerum sæculo isto rudi gestarum, quas vel oscitanter satis vel perperam nobis tradiderunt†a historici. Mallem ego, et
― 394 ―
(ni fallor) omnes qui amant veritatem mecum mallent hujusmodi incomptas narrationes, ex ipsis fontibus haustas, quam flosculos historicos, qui ornant quidem scriptorem, sed lectorem failunt, et in errores inducunt. De edendo hoc libro cum Domino le Clerc ante decessum meum communicavi, Vos inter vos consulite quo pacto hoc fieri possit, nollem enim tam egregium istius sæculi monumentum intercidere, quod metuendum plane est, si restituatur illi cujus est,†1 antequam typis mandetur. In hoc est quod nos laboramus, et ad hoc vestram etiam petimus opem. Plura quæ ad hanc rem pertinent a Furleio accipies. Si quam hac in re tibi creo molestiam mihi credo ignosces dum tuum secutus exemplum publico, quantum possum, inservire studio. Ut vales et tu et tui nostrique omnes, et quid agitur in collegiis fac me subinde certiorem, ut commercio jucundissimarum tuarum literarum, quantum fieri possit, fallam absentiæ tædium. Vale et me perge amare
Tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
Inclusas oro datâ occasione tradas
(Latin)
Rotterdam 14 Mar. 88
On my suggestion and incitement our friend Furly has sent you through van Helmont a book in manuscript,†1 with a view to its remaining in your keeping whilst arrangements are made for printing it. When you see the contents I think you will agree with us that it deserves to see the light; for it contains authentic records of events in that rude age, of which historians have given us either negligent or faulty accounts. I would prefer, and, unless I [p. 394] am mistaken, all lovers of truth would be with me in preferring, such artless narratives, drawn from the very fountain-head, to the flowers of rhetoric offered by historians, which are ornaments in the writer, indeed, but deceive the reader and lead him into errors. I had a word with Mr. Le Clerc before my departure about publishing this book; you and he must please consult each other about how this can be brought about, for I should not wish such a remarkable record of that age to be lost, as is clearly to be feared if it shoulp be restored to the person it belongs to†1 before it is committed to print. This is the difficulty we are in, and we are seeking for further help from you both in dealing with it. You will hear more relative to this matter from Furly. If I am giving you any trouble in this business you will, I think, forgive me, seeing that I am following your example in exerting myself to serve the public interest to the best of my ability. Let me know from time to time how you and yours and all our friends are, and what is going on at the Collegie meetings, so that I may cheat the tedium of absence, so far as may be, by means of your delightful communications. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
Please deliver the enclosed when you find an opportunity.

1024. Fredericus Van Leenhof to [Dr. Pieter Guenellon?] 4/14 March 1688.
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 152-3. Identifiable as the letter forwarded to Locke by Guenellon on 15/25 March: no. 1029. The writer, 1647-1713, was pastor in Zwolle c. 1681-1711. Influenced by Cocceius and Descartes, he was accused of Spinozism on account of his Den Hemel op Aarden (1703): J. P. De Bie and J. Loosjes, Biog. woordenboek van protestantsche godgeleerden in Nederland, 1919— ; no. 3331, etc.

(English) Mijnheer
'k heb het boekie van d'Heer uw. vriend my onbekent met het versoek daar omtrent wel ontfangen; als ik't in't rouw overlas; en nog meer, als ik't wat begon te overwegen, heb ik't met goed genoegen moeten aanschouwen, en erkennen 't vernuft, de gesette, en door veele overdenkingen en ervarentheydt beproefde gedagten, die daar in doorgaans te speuren sijn: dog ik moet mij beklagen, dat ik door veele beletselen werd afgetrokken; om soo een vernuftig en doorwrogt werk met een vervolg van gevestigde overpeinsingen te konnen doorsoeken, en de maniere van voortgaan, en spreekwijsen, en onderscheidingen van saaken en woorden mij soo eigen te maken, dat ik omtrent verseekert kan zijn, van niets verkeert en buiten de meininge van uw. vriend optevatten: waarom ik mede versoeke, dat ik niet mag geoordeelt worden de palen van onze vriendschap te overtreden; indien ik uwe verwagtinge niet voldoen om een volkomenden oordeel te vellen, 'k zou mij sulx ook niet wel derven betrouwen aangaande 't werk van soo een verstandig schrijver.
― 396 ―
(English) 'k zal nogtans iets seggen, opdat ik toonen mag, wat agtinge ik omtrent u versoek heb moeten opnemen, en ik bid vriendelijk, dat hier mede alles mag wezen afgesneden; alzoo uw. wel kond denken, dat mijn gedurige bezigheden, die van een andren aard zijn, mij verbieden; om mij veel met diergelijke oordeelvellingen; of conferencien, en correspondentien, en wat meer van die nature is, te bekommeren.
(English) 'T is dan zeeker, dat u vriend erkend moet zijn voor een man van veel leesens, en veel erkauwens, van sterke en gesette gedagten en van een diep oordeel, die de gevoelens van de hedensdaagse geletterde weereld wel doorsien heeft, en schijn en waarheid, en waan en regte wijsheid van elkanderen heeft leeren schiften. Sijn Ed. toont genoegsaam van soo een edelmoedige geest te wesen, dat hij wil door eigene oogen zien, en alle gezag verwerpende, zig wil verlaaten op dat gene, dat door vaste betoogingen, zoo veel ons mogelijk is, gevestigt staat; en wat kon men grooter Edelmoedigheid betoonen; als dat men 't Edelste naspeurt, dat is ons verstand; in de beschouwinge van welkens aard, en kennisse van welkens werkingen, kragten, en volmaakinge 't grooste genoegen van een wijsbegeerige gelegen is? als bekent moet staan. (English) Om evenwel ook iets aanteteekenen van 't gene, dat mij als nog wat hard, of duister voorkomte, heb ik niet ondienstig geoordeelt sulx in een staaltie twee à drij voor oogen te stellen; als bij voorbeeld, dat u vriend de ziele begrijpt als een tabula rasa sonder ingeschapene denkbeelden; ook van God, die niets met de zinnen gemeens heeft; en van gemeene verkundigheden en werkinge van 't verstand en de zuivre reden. Swolle den 4/14 Maart 1688.
(Latin) Sir
I have received the little book by your friend, who is unknown to me, and the request relating to it. As I read it cursorily, and still more as I began to think about it, I had to regard it with approval, and to acknowledge the genius, the considered thoughts, tested by many reflections and experience, which are to be perceived throughout it. But I must regret that on account of many hindrances I was unable to investigate so ingenious and well-wrought a work with a sequence of well-based considerations, and to make myself so familiar with the manner of proceeding, terminology, and distinctions of things and words, as to be able to be sure that I do not interpret anything incorrectly or beside your friend's intention. I must therefore ask not to be judged to have broken the bounds of our friendship if I do not satisfy your expectation of a complete judgement; I should indeed not dare to give one with regard to the work of so understanding a writer.
(Latin) [p. 396] I shall nevertheless say something in order to show how highly I esteem your request, and I beg that this may end the whole matter since you will understand that my regular duties, which are of a different nature, do not allow me to concern myself very much with such judgements, or discussions and correspondences and the like.
(Latin) It is certain then that your friend must be considered a man of wide reading, of much reflection, of strong and considered thoughts, and of profound judgement, who has penetrated well the opinions of the contemporary learned world, and has learnt to separate appearance from truth, vain from real wisdom. He shows sufficiently that he is of so noble a spirit that he wants to see through his own eyes and, rejecting all authority, will trust that everything, so far as possible, is established by sure demonstrations. And how can one show greater nobility of mind than by investigating the noblest, that is, our understanding, in the contemplation of whose nature and in the knowledge of whose processes, powers, and perfections, lies—as must be acknowledged—the greatest enjoyment of a philosopher? Are not his thoughts always pleasing? Has he not a penetrating judgement concerning the notions of sensations and reflections; of simple and complex, which concern the modes, substances (to use his word), and relations? of the imperfections and misuse [p. 397] of languages, from which so much mischief has sprung, even among learned men, and the means of improvements? of the certainty of knowledge and its degrees, etc.? Beyond any doubt there are many high and excellent thoughts in it, worthy of seeing the light in this understanding age to the great profit of the learned world. I foster the hope of drawing great advantage from this great work when once it is printed and when, as I desire, some intervals of leisure may be given me.
(Latin) In order however to mention also something of what seems to me difficult or obscure I have thought it not unserviceable to present two or three examples of that: as for instance that your friend conceives the soul as a tabula rasa, without innate ideas; even of God, who has nothing in common with the senses; and of ordinary pronouncements and operations of the understanding and pure reason. There is therefore nothing but a sensitive knowledge; thence should come reflections, etc. I can conceive no soul without idea; or one must understand something else by the soul; although what I cannot excogitate with any thoughts; or whatever opinions I imagine of the Ancients, or Hobbes, or Descartes, or whomsoever else.
(Latin) Also I know no processes of the soul other than addition, subtraction, and [p. 398] comparison, with its consequences; whether it occurs in ideas or propositions; and it is acknowledged that everything in arithmetic and geometry must be reduced to these processes.
(Latin) How an extension of duration (which is not to be confused with time) truly constitutes the notion of eternity, without speaking of ordinary people, I also cannot understand; for how we can conceive of infinity through an infinite addition of finite numbers, since, taken in its full sense, it comprises nothing but perfect existence through itself; and we know that no single number, no matter how often multiplied, can express the square root of a rectangle; as for instance of 15 or 3 times 5, which can be given only in lines.
(Latin) I cannot but think that the error is a lack of knowledge. This appears from the fact that where there is sufficient knowledge one cannot be subject to error. The greater the knowledge one obtains of the matter, the less one errs in it, as experience teaches.
(Latin) The four things of your friend are, it seems to me, nothing but reasons for lack of knowledge.†1 Let that suffice.
(Latin) A word is enough to the wise,†2 and it is not necessary that I enlarge further upon these and similar matters.
(Latin) [p. 399] I hope that your friend will take this small liberty in good part, and will serve the learned world for a long time with a healthy soul in a healthy body, and make himself free through the truth.
(Latin) To conclude, there is no writing in which there is nothing to censure, whether rightly or wrongly; there is nothing without some blemish. The best painters have minor flaws, those who, observing what is most important, either overlook them, or will not thereby obstruct the grandeur and magnificence of their inventions. Farewell. I remain, after the presentation of my service to that worthy gentleman
Worthy Sir and friend
Your affectionate servant
Fredericus van Leenhof
Swolle the 4/14 March 1688.

(English)
Observationes
In Tractatum Dn. J. Locke de Intellectu: secundum doctrinam Hebræorum et Philosophorum antiquorum.
― 400 ―
(English)
In Lib. i. pag. 1.
Quod Intellectus sit tabula rasa†1 non docuerunt antiqui Hebræi, et qui illorum fundamentis institerunt Philosophi, Pythagoras nempe et Plato:†2 quia Scientiæ ortum statuerunt esse Reminiscentiam: quæ opinio nata est ex Hypothesi de Præexistentia Animarum, à qua nec Aristoteles fuit alienus.†3 Sano sensu tamen admitti etiam posset hoc simile: si nimirum (1.) intelligatur de prima Animæ origine: ubi Deus infinitè luminosus (Hebræis Æn-soph, Aristoteli Infinitum dictus;) constituto intra se loco in quo creaturæ subsistere possent, (quem Hebræi Makom panui; et Aristoteles Vacuum appellant;)†4 cum productione Animæ Messiæ, quæ totum illum locum occupabat, omnes simul animas producebat, quæ in uno corpore Messiæ†a unum constituebant Syntagma luminosum, cuius unus erat intellectus et una voluntas, quarum facultatum beneficio
― 401 ―
in contemplatione et Amore Dei à Messia†a informabantur, ad unionem cum Deo summumque adeo Bonum suum obtinendum.†1 Ibi Intellectus dici poterat tabula rasa, quia nihil in se continebat, quam quod à Luminibus divinis ipsi imprimeretur.
(English) (2.) Idem status quoque rursus erit Animarum, quando Christus regnum tradet Patri, Deusque erit omnia in omnibus: ubi abrasis omnibus ideis prioribus, Intellectus iterum erit tabula rasa, nihilque contemplabitur, quam Summum illud Visionis suæ beatificæ Objectum.
(English) (3.) Cui statui quo proximior evadit Anima etiam in hac vitâ Asceticâ, eò magis Intellectus eius tabula rasa dici meretur. Quò respexit Pythagoras in hoc Axiomate: Ἅπλωσον σεαυτόν. Fac te ipsum simplicem.
(English) (4.) Si tamen rectè consideretur modernus Animarum in hoc corpore status, postquam scilicet dispersi fuerunt isti filii Dei, dilapsæque à primæva cum Deo unione, Animæ; variisque propterea tenebrarum, falsorumque luminum Corticibus†2 obductæ:
― 402 ―
Similis mihi videtur Anima parieti, cui Anus illa Chinensis applicuisse dicitur folia Scriptorum Confutii Philosophi; superinductâ postmodum argillâ et calce, politoque extrinsecus pariete, ut nobilia hæc Scripta Tyranni illius effugerent incendium, qui omnes sui temporis libros quaquaversum comburebat.†1 Atque hoc respectù extrinsecus quidem Tabula rasa sive Paries rasus et dealbatus est Intellectus: interius tamen latent Scripta quædam, Confutianis longè digniora.
(English) (5.) Si enim post hanc vitam in statù Separationis in Anima manent ideæ in hac vitâ conceptæ: quomodo dici poterit, eandem dum hîc vivit carere ideis, in vita anteactâ conceptis, qualis ab iis præsupponitur, qui Præexistentiam statuunt?†2
(English)
Ab Lib. ii. cap. 1. p. 2.
Origo idearum hîc dicitur duplex: Sensatio et Reflexio.] Rectè quidem si (1) admittatur Sensus sextus vel (connumeratis internis) octavus vel nonus: id est: Visio interna: quæ vel est passiva, nimirum perceptio rerum divinitus (per somnium, Visionem, Ecstasin etc.) vel ab aliis Spiritibus intrinsecus <communicatur>†a : quales
― 403 ―
Spiritus sunt Messias,†a ejusque Spiritus: Angeli boni et mali: nec non Anima alia sive per Embryonatum (Hebræis Ibbur)†1 in nobis delitescens; sive tanquam Maggid i.e. Annunciator aliquid nobis aperiens: quo etiam pertinent Habitus infusi. Vel activa, cum Anima beneficio proprii luminis quædam percipit: ut cum Teresia clausis oculis per frontem vidit; aliique oculis obvelatis objecta cognoscunt; vel in morbo res extra domum vident etc. quo pertinet totus Labor Sophiæ.†2 (2.) Si admittatur divisio Sensationis in eam, quæ est hominis, et in eam, quæ est Archæi,†3 <seu>†b spiritus vitalis.
