Plurá aliàs
(Latin) Observations on the treatise of Mr. J. Locke on the Understanding: after the doctrine of the Hebrews and the ancient philosophers.
[p. 400]
(Latin)
On bk. i, page 1
That the understanding is a tabula rasa†1 was not the teaching of the ancient Hebrews or of those philosophers who built on their foundations, namely Pythagoras and Plato.†2 For they determined that the source of knowledge was reminiscence; this view derived from the theory of the Pre-existence of souls, a theory to which Aristotle too was no stranger.†3 But it could also reasonably be argued like this: (1) (if there were no doubt in our minds concerning the prime origin of the soul) God, being infinitely luminous (known to the Hebrews as Aen-soph, to Aristotle as the Infinite), having established within himself a place where creatures could subsist (which the Hebrews called Makom panui, and Aristotle a Vacuum),†4 with the production of the Soul of the Messiah which occupied the whole of that place, at the same moment produced all souls, which in the single body of the Messiah constituted a single luminous mass with one understanding and one will, by [p. 401] means of which faculties they were fashioned by the Messiah in the contemplation and love of God in order to obtain union with God and the greatest good for themselves.†1 By this argument the understanding could be called a tabula rasa, since it contained nothing that was not printed on it by divine light.
(Latin) (2) The same state of souls will obtain again when Christ delivers his kingdom to the Father and God will be all in all: all previous ideas will be erased and the understanding will once more be a tabula rasa and nothing will be contemplated but that supreme object of his beatific vision.
(Latin) (3) The closer the soul approaches to this state even in this ascetic life, the more its understanding deserves to be called a tabula rasa. To which notion Pythagoras was referring with his axiom, 'Be simple'.
(Latin) (4) But if the present state of souls in this body is correctly considered, by which I mean that, after those sons of God were scattered, and the souls sundered from their primeval union with God, and wrapped accordingly in changeable husks†2 of darkness and false lights, then the soul seems to me like [p. 402] 2the partition wall to which that old Chinese woman is said to have attached the writings of the philosopher Confucius; they were covered afterwards with plaster and lime, and the outside of the wall was smoothed, so that those famous writings should escape the fire of the tyrant who was indiscriminately burning all the books of his time.†1 And in this respect on the outside the understanding is as a tabula rasa or a smooth whitewashed wall; but on the inside lie hidden certain writings, worth much more than those of Confucius.
(Latin) (5) For if after this life in the state of separation there remain in the soul ideas conceived during this life, how can it be said that, while it lives here, the soul lacks ideas conceived in a former life such as is presupposed by those who assert Pre-existence?†2
(Latin)
On bk. ii, ch. 1, p. 2
The source of ideas is here said to be twofold: sensation and reflection.] Rightly indeed if (1) the sixth sense is acknowledged or (counting the internal ones) the eighth or ninth, that is, internal vision. It may, on the one hand, be passive, i.e. perception of things communicated internally either divinely (through a dream, vision, trance, etc.) or by other spirits—such [p. 403] spirits are the Messiah and His spirit(s), angels good and bad—or by another soul, whether through an embryo (Ibbur in Hebrew)†1 concealed within us, or a Maggid, i.e. a voice expounding something to us, to which also infused feelings are relevant. It may, on the other hand, be active, when the soul perceives something by means of its own light—as when Teiresias sees through his forehead though his eyes are closed; and others recognize objects when blindfolded; or in sickness see things outside the house, etc., to which is relevant the whole Labor Sophiæ.†2 (2) If the division of sensation into that which is of the man or of the Archeus†3 or vital spirit is acknowledged.
(Latin)
Ibid.
Supposition: that ideas of sensation are the first acts of thinking, etc.] If the above are admitted, the following examples also have their place: that John the Baptist while still in his mother's womb was filled with the Holy Spirit; also that certain infants laugh immediately after birth whether awake or asleep; also that they cry immediately; also that the Archeus of children [p. 404] contracts in fear of the plague and so infects their body with this disease;†1 and so on.
(Latin)
Ibid., p. 3
It is denied that ideas are innate or natural.]
In support of ideas being connate the following arguments present themselves. (1) If beasts, plants, etc., bring their own knowledge into the world, so much more does man. (2) Whatever is common to every man is also natural to man: such are those principles which are called 'common knowledge'. (3) That which may be known of God is known inwardly to man, Rom. 1: 18.†2 (4) Christ is the light which lighteth every man that cometh into the world. John 1: 9. (5) The Gentiles do by nature the things contained in the law. Rom. 2: 14. (6) The work of the law is written in their hearts. Rom. 2: 15. (7) Rubble of the image of God remains even after the fall. Gen. 9: 6. (8) If sick ideas are connate, why not also healthy ones?
(Latin)
Ch. 2, p. 4
It is denied that any spirit can produce a new idea by itself.]
Here I should like to consider more deeply what van Helmont says generally [p. 405] about ideas; especially where he says that in man there is some definite faculty of creating, etc. De injectis materialibus § 16.†1 Again De morbis Archealibus § 7,†2 etc.
More another time.
Endorsed by Locke: Knor Jun 88†a
NOTE: Knorr sometimes places a tick over the letter u: e.g. Tractatúm. I have regarded this as part of the letter and consequently ignored it except when it falls on a final u; it may there represent an accent and I have therefore reproduced it.

1026. Locke to Edward Clarke, [9/19 March 1688?] (1021, 1030)
Rand, pp. 256-8. Words in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Rand suggests 11 March as the date, but the letter is Locke's answer to no. 1021 which, according to his endorsement, he answered on 19 March. Answered by no. 1030.
... [I am glad] at last some of the abregée has got to your hands. That in loose sheets may be bound as Mrs. Clarke's was, and then sent to Mrs. Duke by Sir Walter [Yonge], as he will be the best [able] to correct it. And pray desire him to content himself with the reading of [that copy], if he think it worth while, till I get an opportunity to send him one for himself. It is so difficult to meet with people to send them by that my friends must not take it amiss that they have them not all together, nor so soon as I could wish them. The remaining one in marble paper [give when] you can to [Mr. Freke] ...
I was surprised [to hear] that W.P. had procured your cousin a pardon.†1 I know not how to understand it, since if there be any truth in your cousin's professions he knows nothing of it: you will therefore do well to inform yourself as dexterously as you can from Mr. P. by a third and skilful hand what there is in it. For your cousin thinks himself concerned to know; though in a business of the nature it will not become him to appear inquisitive. Adrian tells me he communicated the same piece of news to you. When you
― 407 ―
inform me of the truth and particularities of the story you shall have my opinion concerning the case, for as this may be I know not how far this may alter his measures. I think, therefore, it will be of concernment to him, that you without any stir inform yourself particularly of all that has passed in the affair, if there be any such thing.
Adrian will be some time this month in town. He will receive £20 in St. John's Court†1 to buy books here for the young gentleman,†2 which I desire him to pay you. I write the same thing to him, but if that letter should miss him your minding of him will be enough, for in his last letter is my order to dispose of it. I desire him also to wear over a chamlet†3 cloak for me, which I have desired Mrs. R. S. to buy for me. I would have it of the best boiled†4 chamlet that is to be got, that will endure wetting and of a dark colour, not apt to stain; for I am past fashion and finery, and am now only for things of use. The lining I would have of a very good shalon,†5 unless there be anything else lighter and as strong. I have writ to her to the same purpose, but it will not be amiss (if you hear not of her before) to send to her for the cloak when Adrian comes to town. She sends me word she has the £10, for which I thank you.
The 9th instant I writ to your lady in answer to hers of 16th February. I hope ere this it is come to hand, for there was in it something for you too. If you looked in the little bound abregée, that came single, there was a short letter in it, wherein I desired to know your opinion of the hand printed on the paper it was wrapped up in, whereof I have sent another copy since, printed in red with Madame's letter. If you like that hand and that way I will send you more of them for young master.
Madame, I remember, solemnly promised me heretofore to let me see her on this side the water. I think she cannot do a better thing at any time than to keep her word, especially now after she has got up again; when at the same time she may join health, pleasure and charity together. Resolve on it you and she together. It is not so much as a journey to Tunbridge, and has ten times the advantages in it. And I long mightily to speak with you about my
― 408 ―
Bel[u]ton estate. You will do me a kindness whilst you are in town to draw a grant of all the land I have there and in St. Thomas†1 to J. N.†2 whilst you are in town and send me it by Adrian, or Mr. Oakley, or rather bring it yourself, for I cannot do as I would without talking with you. I am extremely beholden to you for the care you had of it when you were at Sidcott, but unless Wm. Stratton be pressed upon that point I fear the rent will run again into arrears, for he is a slow man of London. But if you will come we shall both settle that matter and discourse many points concerning your son, which whole sheets of writing will not do half so well. At Abel Ropers, a bookseller, at the sign of the Sun, in Fleet Street, you will find Æsop's Fables, English, with cuts.†3 Pray buy it for him, and get a Latin one too of that edition out of which the English one was translated. I will tell you hereafter what use to make of it. Get it also in French if you can.
I am, Sir,
your most affectionate and most humble servant,
J. L.
My little treatise has drawn on me some compliments, and I doubt not but that I shall receive others upon the same occasion, but amongst them all I dare say there will be none that will come near Madam's in the case. For nobody but she will go so high as to tell me they will learn French on purpose to understand it. Tell her I expect she should keep her word, for whatever the book be good for the French may be worth the having, and since she has as much to say to the purpose as other people, I would have her have as many fashionable languages to express it in. This is spoke methinks with the air and authority of an author, but I am so little and so new an one that I can easily lay by that to express myself in my ancienter and more natural temper, which is that of being with a very great respect and affection her most humble servant. Pray remember me kindly also to my little mistress.
I have writ to Adrian to bring my cloak and to J.T.†4 to bring my hat and peruke.
Address: For Mr. Edward Clarke, at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, London.

1027. James Tyrrell to Dr. David Thomas, 9 March [1688] (1019)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, f. 70. Year from Locke's endorsement. Tyrrell's succeeding letter to Locke is no. 1225.
March 9th:
Dear Sir
I thank you for your last and I hope this will come time enough before you goe, to wish you all happynesse; and a good voyage, and to carry my service to our good; Friend; for as for waiting on him now my self I must beg both his, and your pardon; the warneing being soe short and the time of the year soe cold for sea voyages: nor doe I know whether I shall goe this summer or not; for I have businesse of my owne; and besides I have great hopes that JL. may returne with you; for his expression to me in one of his (when I had promised him to come over with you) was, that if wee did; perhaps He might be even with us; or to that effect which I understood in that sense; and pray therefore farther those thoughts what you can; for he will have now all the summer before him and he can never have a more favourable time for men in his circumstances then now; and when he has seen his Friends; and setled his affaires; he may returne againe at winter; if he thinks the air of England will not agree with his constitution; tho I cannot see any reason why Salisbury; oxford, or any Countrey Towne where the air is not too cold may not doe as well for his lungs as where he is; but of this he must be the best Judge. I speake as I would have it; pray tell him I writ lately to him; or els I would have done it now by you, I shall carry up my eldest son to school in Easter week; and shall then be either in Towne or neer it, and hope to receive his commands by that time. I wonder you goe to stay for so little a while as a fortnight or three weekes at farthest; and if you designe to be as good as your word and be backe at Easter; I suppose you goe to see how you like the education of utrecht, or some other university for your son. in order to the sending†a- him; if you doe,-†a Sir John Busby†1 a Gentlemen of our Countrey has lately brought over both his sons
― 410 ―
from Leyden; and gives a very ill character both of the discipline and improvements of that place:
All the news I can send you is of the good health of all my relations; allmost all the Justices of Peace of this county are turned out and my self among the rest: Sir Peter Tyrrell, and Sir Thomas are put in Commission, and a great many honest Gentlemen who will not act in that capacity to my knowledge:†1 I hope if I have time before I travell into Cheshire with my daughter to come over; and passe a few days with you at Salis: when I hear you are returned; which I wish may be with all imaginable speed and safety so w<ith>†a my service to your Lady I remaine
Your most assured Freind; and faithfull Servant.
J TYRRELL
pray tell JL. that if there be any thing in London or any where els I can serve him in I hope he will imploy his old Freinds before new ones. if you can †a in †a

1028. Thomas Stringer to Edward Clarke, 12 March 1688
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 110-11. Given by Clarke to Dr. Thomas to be delivered to Locke: p. 414. Stringer's last extant letter to Locke is no. 754. Locke answers this letter in no. 1038.
Ivychurch march 12th. 1687.
Dearest Sir
I just now Received yours of the 10th instant, with mr Locks Commands to send up his Picture†3 and because doctor Thomas is
― 411 ―
coming towards you, to morrow morning I have been the speedier to returne you this Answere. I have that esteem and Respect for mr Lock that I cannot but be glad of any occation to heare from him, tho it be to my losse, For it must needs be much to my dissatisfaction to parte with that Picture, first because if I keepe it, it may be a means for me to heare from him againe; next that because I can't see him here for whome I have soe harty a friendshipp, I doe think my selfe not a little prowde that my best Roome is adorned with his Resemblance, where he hangs amongst good Company and can be noe where better welcome, And lastly I am not willing to weaken my Title unto it, I have his word, and my wife hath his hand to shew how he hath once disposed of it, and wee are now too old for Childrens play to have a thing given and then to have it called for againe; You know Possession in this case is a good Confirmation of my Title, and unlesse he will give me good security on that poynt, I am resolved (tho I have noe leggs) to stand stoutly in defence of it; It is the veneration I have for my old friend makes me thus valew his Picture, and untill I am well assured of its Returne to Ivychurch, the high sheriffe with the Posse Commitatus shall not be able (under any pretence) to fetch it forth of my hands; What you write of engraving a Plate from it, I take to be but a Colourable Excuse, because doctor Thomas hath one that is generally thought better paynted and is of a much lesse size, and Consequently may be better secured from danger of hurt in Carriage, Whereas mine is soe large that it cannot well be packed in the Country (without hazard) for soe long a Journey;†1 Besides such plates are always engraven not from paynt but draughts in black and white,†2 and those draughts may be truer taken from the life, then any Picture, and more Exactly and advantagiously done in holland, (there being better Artists) then in England; When you write againe to mr Lock, If I may take the liberty to be soe troublesome unto you, Pray doe me the favour to lett him know, that because I can't gett the Substance to keepe here, I will make as much of his shadow as I can, he may see what difference is made between him and an other of our old acquaintance and housemates,†3 For his Picture I always look upon with pleasure and delight, but the others I should think would scandalize the meanest office. Tho I doe not obey his Comands in this, I am still his harty servant, and
― 412 ―
shall with my life or any thing I have always sincerely and Faithfully endeavour to doe him Reall service, And he will ever finde that my wife and selfe shall deserve the same opinion as when he gave us his Picture; I beleive it wilbe a lessening of your trouble if you send him this letter, and lett him read my minde under mine own hand; I am sorry we doe not heare how your good Lady and little misse doe, we hope well because we don't heare ill, We truly wish all happinesse unto them, and with harty thanks for all your Favours, I subscribe
Dearest sir
Your most affectionate Faithfull and obleiged servant
Tho: Stringer
Address: For Edward Clarke Esqr at my Lady Kings house in Salisbury Court in Fleet streete London
Postmark: MR 14

1029. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 15/25 March 1688 (983, 1037)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 5-6.
Monsieur,

Deare Sir
Since my last I have gotten the Abridgment which came to mee in Quires Bound and Guilded as the other was, and according to your order have plac'd it in Sir Walters handes to bee conveyed to Mrs. Duke, And the other which remaines in Marble-Paper I shall allsoe send by Him to Mr. Freke about a fortnight hence (when Hee designes to goe out of Town)†a if I have noe other opportunity

by a safe hand in the meane time to convey it to Him; I have allsoe gotten you a Good Beaver-Hatt made the diameter of the inside of the Crown at the Band exactly according to the Dimention mark'd by the two Black-Lynes in your Letter of the 9th. instant; A Peruke I have allsoe bought for you pursuant to your directions in the same Letter as neere as possible I could, And these togather with six Flannen-shirts (bought and made up by your verie good Freind mrs. R:S:) And a Cloake (which in the Buying and makeing up I gave Her my best Assistance)†a I have sent hence by your old Freind Adrian, who staid but one day in Town, and is this day sett out from hence towards you, and 'tis possible may bee with you as soon (or before) this can come to your handes,†1 Hee promised mee to take particular care of them All, and to see them safely Delivered to you, which I hope Hee will doe, they being all, in my Opinion extreamly good of the Kind, and I beleive will give Content in the Weareing; By Him you will allsoe Receive a Letter that I had from Mr. Stringer†2 in Answer to what by your order I writt to Him touching your Picture, By which you will find that Hee is resolved not to part with it; And I would by Him allsoe have sent you a Grant of your Estate at Belton and St. Thomas to J:N: as you desire, could I have gotten time dureing his stay here to have done it, but now I thinke I must take a time by your directions and in your Presence to doe it, Which, if God Blesses my Wife with an happy Lying-in, and noe Extraordinary Businesse prevent, my Inclynations doe verie strongly Prompt mee to, But since there are soe many Accidents which may contradict my Intentions in this particular, I Dare Promise nothing, But Trust on Providence to send us a happy meeting, Which, I earnestly desire and Long for; In the meane time give mee Leave to assure you that I will use all imaginable care and caution to find out the Truth of what was done in that Affayre touching W:P: and my Cosin, that in your last you mentioned to mee, And I will allsoe take Care to gett Æsops-Fables, in Latin, English, and French with Cutts, as you have ordered, and will waite your further Directions for makeing the best use of them: just now I received the Inclosed from my Sonn,

Ce 28. Mars.
Non seulement au même jour mais encore à la meme heure que je receus lhonneur des vôtres l'on maporta un grand mortier à filtrer l'eau acheté à Cadis, et venu par Roüen. Jugez combien de
― 416 ―
joye pour moy en un même tems, cependant ele fut bien temperée par la reception de ce mortier, car un de mes amis à qui il avoit eté remis depuis long tems ne recevant point d'ordre de ma part, s'etant imaginé qu'il m'a fait savoir qu'il etoit arivé, me la envoié aiant trouvé une ocasion commode. 1032. John Freke to Locke, 19 March 1688 (990, 1821)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 175-6.
Dear Sir
Yours of the 17th of Febr: I received the beginning of March with a due sense of my obligation to you for it. It found me reading Cardinall D'Ossat's Letters†4 and put me in mind that it was to you I was indebted for being at that time in soe good company that it was you recomended that book to my perusall and procured it for me for which give me leave to render you many thanks but many more for the better entertainment your own afforded me and the much better which it promised me (and which since you have
― 418 ―
promised I expect and long for) Your Tract de Intellectu, when it comes (which I fancy will be by the welch Doctor†1 who I hear is with you) I will be sure to treat it as you prescribe and faithfully give you my opinion both of the matter and the expression neither approving nor condemning any thing without giving you my reason why I doe soe In which employment I perswade my self I shall reap more pleasure and profit than ever I did in my profession or any other Comerce I have had whilst I was concernd in the business of the world. I must confess I once thought by my endeavours to have contributed something to the happiness of a family I extremly value in making the match and Settlement†2 (soe often mentiond to you) and then I should have thought my time and pains had been spent to the best purpose, but there is soe much falseness and knavery mixt in the affairs of the world that I find I am by noe means fit for such transactions which has made me quitt them though I still believe that all the tricks that are playd will not doe the business and that at long run they will be glad to come to the Terms I proposed if they will then (as I am not sure they then will) be accepted. My Cousin†3 blames me for desponding and has written hither to me and tells me that a nearer view of things would make me have a better opinion of them and with great confidence speaks comfortable things but he talks in generall and I see noe cause to repent of my recess†4 and have taken such delight in solitude and privacy (since I have tasted it) that I fancy I shall never be tempted from it or be able to relish Crowds and business again. Not but that women and dancing and Fidles may possibly retain as much power over me as you and therefore if I understand our friend S W†5 by them invites you to London I shall be apt to be of the party and meet you there but I fear he will not give us that occasion of meeting this Spring though he writes me (since I received yours) that his stay in Town is not without that prospect
I had once thoughts this summer might have afforded me another occasion of seeing you for I had found a companion that was willing to ramble a few years about the world with me on condition I would have first visited Holland and Flanders but the late proclamation that recalls home our forces†6 is pend in such Terms that my Gentleman is affrighted from his purpose
― 419 ―
We have noe news here but that since the French imposition on our Cloath†1 soe many clothiers leave off trade that tis hard to sell our wooll at any price and this makes it an uncomfortable inhabiting amongst the poor in a country whose chief riches is sheep as this is where I reside soe that I am sorry my Companion leaves me and hinders my travail, for I know too well what it is, to travail alone and therefore must be content to stay at home where I scarce put on a hat or pair of shoes above once a week to goe to church and where I resolve to abscond†2 my self till I have an oppertunity of losing my self in a voiage with some agreeable companion to find which is now the chief of my wishes except those by which I desire to approve my self sensible of my obligations to you and Sir
Your affectionate friend and humble Servant
J Fre:
March the 19th
When you see B:F: let him know I forget not my obligations to him and should gladly serve him
Address: For Mr John Lock at the House of Mr Benjamin Furly Merchant in Rotterdam.
Endorsed by Locke: J F 19 Mar 88 Answered 7 May
1033. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 20/30 March 1688 (1023, 1034)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 11-12. Answers no. 1023.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Veniam dabis, quod morbo impeditus tardius ad tuas respondeam. Sententia aliquot medicorum circiter octiduum immuratus fui; postea vero benigna eorundem sententia e muro dimissus, sed detractis prius septem vel octo unciis sanguinis: quam pœnitentiam
― 420 ―
ultro in me recepi; licet illi sibi suisque successoribus servaverint potestatem me ad murum revocandi, si res exigat, et ego alio remedio ad sanitatem reduci nequeam. Vides me librum illum manuscriptum non abjecisse, ita phrasibus illius jam sum imbutus, ut mihi familiares evaserint.†1 Doleo morbum meum etiam illius operis editioni fuisse intempestivum. D. Clericus me inscio convenerat Wolfgangum:†2 mallem ego convenisse Wetstenium, qui cum studiis imbutus sit, rectius de ejusmodi operibus judicare potest.†3 Gaudeo mihi illum librum exhibitum: omnino ere Christiana judico, illum edi: et quo plura lego, eo vehementius editionem illius cupio. Omnia valde curiosa sunt, et procul dubio placitura. Quæ de Guil. Ruffi narrantur quibusdam videri possunt incredibilia: mihi vero nequaquam: similia enim hoc et superiore sæculo in patria nostra vidimus. Solent hominibus probis quidem, sed quandoque ignaris et superstitiose devotis sese immiscere homines nequam,
― 421 ―
vel spiritu quodam vertiginis abrepti, qui vel errore quodam, vel malitia incautos ad se pelliciunt. Interim si ab autore nomen suum sequacibus imponatur, sicut ab Ario Ariani, a Pelagio Pelagiani, ita a Ruffi ruffianos denominatos credo.†1 Ego omni ope allaborandum censeo, ut opus hoc æternæ memoriæ consecretur, et quamprimum edatur, neque ullo modo committendum, ut in tenebris delitescat, et a blattis et tineis corrodatur. Scripsi ad D. Furlæum quid egerim cum Wolfgango et Wetstenio: si crastina die vel perendie ulterius quid efficere possim, ad vos scribam. Nunc, quia et Hagam literæ sunt scribendæ abrumpere cogor. Vale Amplissime Vir. De collegio alias scribam. Uxor mea, omnesque collegæ plurimam Tibi scribi jusserunt salutem.
Tuus
P. A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 30 Martii

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
You will pardon my slowness in answering your letter, as I have been hampered by illness. I was immured for about a week by the sentence of certain physicians; after this I was indeed released from confinement by a favourable judgement of the same authorities, but only when seven or eight [p. 420] ounces of blood had first been drawn, a penance to which I readily submitted, though they reserved to themselves and their successors the power of recalling me to confinement if the case should warrant it and if I could not be restored to health by any other treatment. You observe that I have not thrown away that manuscript book; I am now so imbued with its expressions that they have become second nature to me.†1 I am sorry too that my illness has been so untimely for the publication of that work. Mr. Le Clerc went to see Wolfgang†2 without my knowledge; I myself should have preferred to see Wetstein about it; he is at home with studies and better able to judge of such productions.†3 I am glad to have seen that book; in my opinion it is entirely in the interests of Christianity that it should be published, and the more I read of it the more eagerly I desire its publication. The contents are of great interest throughout and will undoubtedly appeal to readers. The stories told of Guillaume Ruffi may seem incredible to some; by no means, however, to me; we have seen the like in our own country both in this century and in the last. There are persons of worthless character or carried away by a kind of spiritual vertigo who are accustomed to mix with [p. 421] people who are honest enough but sometimes ignorant and given to superstition; such persons allure the unwary, whether being themselves in a way misled or with malicious intent. Meanwhile if followers are given a name from their leader, as the Arians from Arius or the Pelagians from Pelagius, so, I suppose, ruffians may get theirs from Ruffi.†1 I consider, then, that no pains should be spared to keep this work in perpetual remembrance, and that it should be published as soon as possible; it must on no account be allowed to remain hidden in darkness, to be gnawed by moth and bookworm. I have written to Mr. Furly telling him about my dealings with Wolfgang and Wetstein; if I should be able to effect anything further tomorrow or the next day I will write and tell you. I must break off now as I have a letter to write to The Hague as well. Good-bye, excellent Sir. I will write about the Collegie another time. My wife and all the Collegians ask me to send you their warmest greetings.
Yours
P. VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 30 March 1688
Address: Reverendo Amplissimo Viro D. Joanni Locke.
Endorsed by Locke: Limborch 30 Mar. 88

1034. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 24 March/3 April 1688 (1033, 1051)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 13-14.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Non descivi negotium editionis manuscripti ad me missi quantum in me fuit urgere: Verum emptores detinentur pretio. Wetstenius satis se promptum ostendit, et jam convenerat D. du Cene,†1 inquisiturus quo pretio tædiosum describendi laborem suscipere vellet: Ille vero singulas paginas æstimat decem stuveris nostratibus: cum vero volumen contineat ultra quadringentas paginas, ducenti floreni nostrates soli descriptioni impendendi forent: Si vero descriptionis jus centum ducatis argenteis, qui valent trecentos et quindecim florenos nostrates, redimendum sit, non poterit sibi apographum comparare Wetstenius, nisi numeratis plus quam quingentis florenis: Quod pretium ipsi immane videtur, cum totum volumen excudi posset quinquaginta aut sexaginta foliis. Crediderim tamen ego alium me reperire posse, hominem Germanum, qui minoris conduci posset. Tandem post commutata aliquot verba, Wetstenius dixit, se apographum quidem emere velle, a possessore voluminis sibi tradendum; et obtulit centum imperiales,†2 seu ducentos et quinquaginta florenos Hollandicos. Nescio an possessor
― 423 ―
tantum minuere velit de pretio, præsertim cum et pretium descriptioni insumendum detrahi debeat. Credo Germano illi non solvendum dimidium illius, quod petit D. du Cene. Si D. Furlæo et Tibi consultum videbitur, volo quidem eum convenire, ac cum ipso agere, quasi mihi esset descripturus. Si Wetstenius non abiisset Francofurtum, fortassis persuaderi posset, ut trecentis florenis apographum redimat; verum ipso absente nihil ultra pretium ab ipso indicatum promittere possum. Si Germanus ille tot habeat solidos,†1 quot D. du Cene petit florenos, posset apographum haberi sexaginta circiter florenis. Velim ut cum D. Furlæo hoc expendas: Omnino enim e re Christiana judico hoc tempore librum hunc edi. Ego in gratiam Wetstenii aliqualem concepi titulum, quem ipse catalogo Francofurtensi, quo libri proximis nundinis evulgandi continentur, inseri curabit.†2 Credidi hac ratione ipsum magis magisque ad illius editionem induci posse; et ipsi volumini MS. aut illius possessori nullum fit præjudicium. Collegæ nostri omnes bene valent. Legimus in collegio Epitomen tractatus tui de intellectu, qui sæpe nobis disserendi materiam præbuit. Nonnunquam de
― 424 ―
mente tua strenue disputatur, non consentientibus inter se collegis, quid pag. 7. per ideam, et per qualitatem intelligas;†1 quod mihi tamen minime obscurum videtur; et quo sensu, ideam voces objectum immediatum. Atque ita disputando tarde progredimur. Volupe nobis est prolixe tecum confabulari, quod nos facere credimus tua legendo. Tu præsentia tua omnibus ejusmodi disputationibus finem imponere posses, et inter contendentes Palæmonem agere.†2 Vale Vir Amplissime: Uxor mea omnesque Collegæ plurimam Tibi salutem scribi jusserunt
Tuus
P. A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 3 Aprilis
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I have not failed to push forward to the best of my ability the business of getting the manuscript sent to me published; but purchasers are deterred by the price. Wetstein shows himself ready enough, and has already seen Mr. du Cene†1 with a view to ascertaining at what price he would be willing to undertake the tiresome work of transcription; du Cene estimates it at ten of our stivers a page; since, then, the volume contains more than four hundred pages this would mean an expenditure of two hundred of our gulden on the transcription alone; but if the right of transcription must be purchased for a hundred silver ducatoons, which are worth three hundred and fifteen of our gulden, Wetstein will not be able to obtain a copy for himself without paying more than five hundred gulden, a price which seems to him enormous, seeing that the whole volume could be printed on fifty or sixty sheets. I fancy, however, that I can find another man, a certain German, whose services could be secured for less. Eventually after some discussion Wetstein said that he was willing at any rate to purchase a copy, to be made over to him by the owner of the volume, for which he offered a hundred rix-dollars†2 or two hundred and fifty Dutch gulden. I do not know whether the owner [p. 423] would be willing to abate so much of the price, especially as the cost of transcription would also have to be deducted. I believe that one would not have to pay that German the half of what Mr. du Cene is asking. If you and Mr. Furly think it advisable I am prepared at any rate to see him and put the matter to him personally, as if the transcription were to be done for myself. If Wetstein had not gone away to Frankfurt he could perhaps have been persuaded to pay three hundred gulden for the copy; but in his absence I cannot promise any more than the price he has indicated. If that German were to get as many schillings†1 as Mr. du Cene is demanding gulden, the copy could be had for about sixty gulden. I hope you will consider this matter with Mr. Furly; in my judgement it is all in the interest of Christianity at this time that this book should be published. To oblige Wetstein I have composed some sort of title; he will see to its insertion in the Frankfurt catalogue which contains the books to be offered to the public at the next fair;†2 I thought that in this way he could be induced more and more to undertake the publication of it, and no harm is done to the book itself or to its owner. Our Collegians are all well. We have been reading in the Collegie the epitome of your treatise on the understanding, which has often provided us with material for discussion. From time to time there is vigorous [p. 424] argument about your meaning, our Collegians not agreeing with one another as to what you understand on page 7 by 'idea' and 'quality',†1 which to me, however, seems in no way obscure; and in what sense you call the 'idea' the immediate object. And so we proceed slowly by the method of argument. It is a great pleasure to us to hold long conversations with you, as we feel ourselves to be doing in reading your work. You could by your presence put an end to all such arguments, and act Palaemon between the contending parties.†2 Good-bye, excellent Sir. My wife and all our Collegians bid me send you their warmest greetings.
Yours,
P. VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 3 April 1688
Address: Amplissimo ac Reverendo Viro D. Joanni Locke
Endorsed by Locke: Limborch 3 Apr. 88
1035. Dr. John Hutton to Locke, 27 March/6 April 1688 (1025, 1889)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 251-2.
Honored Sir
Yowr leter off march 28 which†a came to my hand but last night makes me blush, when by it I under-stand that my Landslord†b has
― 425 ―
not sent yow the books our worthie as well as Learned freind Mr Stanly bought for yow; I have desired him to send yow this from the Hague under his cover, by which†a yow'l know how yow may have these ware bought, and why the others†b yow mentioned in yowr cattaloqüe could not be porchased for yow, the summe laid out is but small I ow it him, which†a I shall pay, and yow shall pay me att meeting: the air here is somewhat colder then att the Hague, yet I am warmer, and more in Love with yowr abregé att this Instent then when I writ to yow Last, since that tyme, I have the approbation and commendation off some more off our frinds, off it, as well as off the author for his designe; whose Largness off soul, and clearness off judgement all doe and most allow to be beyond ordinarie writers, yea, beyond any who have writ upon the Subject; Only one learned persone told me that He wisht, that, that part off the booke had bean the strongest which he thought was the weakest; which was concerning the proving a Deietie; I told him it was easie to object but not to say much that was stronger upon the subject; I turned up to him for answer the pages 71: 72: 81: 82: etc:†1 for my part I never object where I am not able to, make the solutione in some degree att lest; nor am I Criticque eneuch†c to condemn where I can find nothing can be easily emended; please Accept off my synceritie in what I writ upon the matter I cannot flater a man I valüe soe much; my Respect or duety may by accident seeme wanting, but my affection and candor for yow shall be uninterupted, because I am in great fathfullness
Honored Sir
Yowr most humble and most obledged servant
JO HUTTON
Loo April 6th 88

1036. John Stanley to Locke, 29 March/8 April 1688
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 186-7. The writer is perhaps John Stanley of Grange Gorman, co. Dublin, c. 1663-1744; cup-bearer to Queen Mary II; at various times assistant or secretary to the Lord Chamberlain of the Household; a commissioner for Stamp Duties 1694-1700; created a baronet 1699; Warden of the Mint 1699-1708; a commissioner of Customs 1708-44: G.E.C., Baronetage, iv. 179; etc. The future baronet is mentioned below, nos. 1577, 1760, 2253 n.; as baronet, no. 2668, etc.
Hague Ap. 8. 88.
Sir†a
Upon Doctor Huttons letting me know how it might lye in my power to oblidge a man of your worth I undertook readily the care of getting you the books you had desird him to buy for you at Auction, tho I was so unhappy that I could only procure for you these four books at the rates you had markd down. Thevenot†1 I bought for 7 gild: the Spanish book†2 2 gild: 10 stiv: and the other at 12 stiv:†3 Philosophicall transactions, Calvini Lexicon Juridicum†4 and some other of the best books you desird, went off at almost double the rate you allowd me to bid for them: some of the others I mist of by not being always present; for they changd so often from one part of the catalogue to another according as any old customer desird them, that it must have taken up the whole day to have watch'd them. Sir if you have any other service for me here pray employ me, for I should be very glad to oblidge a man of your reputation
Your very humble servant
JOHN STANLEY

Monsieur,
je ne peu tousjours que vous faire mes protestations sur les complimens que vous me faitte. c'est renouveller incessamment la confusion que je doibs avoir de respondre si peu a l'amitié dont vous m'honorez mais Monsieur comme vous m'en faitte souvenir je tacheray de m'en mieux acquitter dans l'advenir. les livres que Sylvestre a emporté par megarde sont de si peu de valeur que je ne scay bonnement sil sont a moy. mais pourtant il n'a rien commis en ne vous portant pas le livre de Monsieur Dellon,†1 car mon neveu†2 ne l'a pas achetté. sil vous plaist de regarder vostre notice. vous aviez donné commission a 15 sols et mon neveu ma fait voir dans son cataloge quil a esté vendu a 19 sols de maniere quil n'a osé encherir sur ce pris pour ne pas passer vos ordres. 1038. Locke to Thomas Stringer, 6/16 April 1688 (754, 1028, 1045)
London, Victoria and Albert Museum, Forster Collection, MS. 364. Draft, with slight variants, written on cover of a letter from Edward Clarke(?) to Furly, in B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 261. Printed in Rand, pp. 260-2, with date 11 April, from a source not stated. Answers no. 1028; answered by no. 1045.
Rotterdam 16 Apr. 88
Sir
By a letter you writ to Mr Clarke, which, according to your desire, is come to my hands I perceive my old friend Mr Stringer is contrary to my expectation grown a great Courtier, and I cannot but wonder that a man I thought of a quite other make, amongst soe many professions of affection and respect in words should in the same letter mix things soe litle consistent with either of them. Childrens play and colourable pretences are accusations that savour but litle of esteem and kindenesse: At least whatever I might have deserved from others, I might justly expect our old acquaintance and friendship might have preserved me with Mr Stringer from any such suspition till some manifest injury had forced him to alter his thoughts of me. It is I confesse noe small humiliation to me that I have not deserved soe much confidence as that from a man that I have for many years called and beleived my friend: And if the rest of the acquaintance I have left in England entertein the like thoughts of me I thinke it will be best for me to stay with my Dutch friends who treat me with an other kinde of respect and affection. There is an other insinuation in that letter as if you had reason to complain that you never hear from me. Were I given to complain I think I might with some reason say that it was a very silent respect and affection that would not in fower or five years bestow fower or five
― 429 ―
words upon an ancient acquaintance. If I have forborne to write to any of my friends it has been purely out of regard to them, to whom I thought I could not doe either more civily, or more friendly then to leave it to them to judg, whether they thought it fit to hold any correspondence with me: and I never was silent to any one, who gave me a reason to thinke such a commerce would be acceptable to him. Mrs: Stringer must be my witnesse in this point, to whom I never failed to write soe long as she thought my letters worth the answering, And, if I mistake not, till she plainly said she would write noe more to me.†1 For I made use of the intercession of some friends in England to obtein a leter from her, which though for these two or three last years was a favour I was not thought worthy of, yet I made noe unkinde reflections on it nor had ever mentiond it but in my own defence, Now that this undeserved reproach for not writeing, forces me to take notice, what tendernesse my absence has procured for me in some of my freinds, who soe readily impute to me those neglects which they themselves are guilty of. But to returne to the main subject of your letter. If you beleive your self when you say I gave you my picture, I beseech you to consider, what you think of your self, when you deny it me upon this occasion; Sure I am you will never perswade any body else, that you think bonâ fide I gave it you whilst you dare not trust it again in my hands. For you will not finde any one who knows me, that will imagin, I deserve to be suspected of a designe to cheat any one of what is his, much lesse a friend of what I my self had given him. To all your skilfull discourse about pictures and draughts I shall say noe more but that I hope I may be allowd to be of age enough to know, if I would have a print of my self, what kinde will best please me. But Sir I that am very slow to entertein hard thoughts of my friends will not determin which part of your letter, either the friendly, and complemental; or the unkinde, and disobleigeing is the most in earnest. I leave you the free liberty of interpreting: And your compliance or not with the desire I sent you by Mr Clarke will fully resolve me what is the friendship and esteem I am to expect from you. in the mean time I am
Sir
Your most humble servant
J: LOCKE
― 430 ―
Pray present my humble service to Mrs: Stringer
This being in answer to what you writ to Mr Clarke I have sent it to him open, to be seald and conveyd to you, that he being our common freind may see how well I deservd those very civill things you writ to him of me, if they were said in earnest
Address: For Mr Thomas Stringer at Ivy church these
1039. Lady Guise to Locke, 7/17 April 1688 (1044)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 128-9. The writer was Elizabeth, daughter of John Grubham How of Langar, Notts., and sister of Scrope How, first Baron Howe (D.N.B.), and of Jack Howe (ibid.); wife of Sir John Guise, c. 1654-95, of Elmore, Gloucestershire, second baronet 1670; M.P. 1679-81, 1689-95: G.E.C., Baronetage, iii. 218-19. He was now resident in Utrecht; he participated as a colonel in William's expedition to England: Calamy, Life, i. 143; Papillon, Memoirs, pp. 338, 343.
Sir
I can noe longer lie under the seeming Ingratitude of not returning you my real acknowledgments for your most acceptable present and oblidging leter, by the last I find you have met with some friend of mine that has given you soe favourable a character of me, that I blush when I consider I merit it not, nor Could any thing render that partiallyty pardonable; but its haveing perswaded you to some Esteeme for me; Curiosity is you know Insident to my sex; neither am I exempt from it in some perticulers. that was it which first perswaded me to looke into your booke, and when I had don soe, noe wonder if the charmes in it prevail'd with me to persue that atempt, which I did with soe great a delight that it had ben to doe a violence to my Inclinations to have quited it, and ware any thing Capable to taint me with vanity, I had Certainly ben debaucht into it by the Easy perseption I had of your way of reasoning, but Insteed of ascribing any praise to my selfe I give it wher tis due; and owne Sir that tis to you it belongs, for haveing with such admirable fasility offer'd to our sences what has ben but obscurly treated of by others, and tho I am perswaded your flight is not lesse Exalted than that of other Philosophers, yet does it not remain in the clouds; but descends with a quicke tho Easy touch upon the aprehention and if it leaves not an Impresion, the fault must be wholly asigned to the reader, since I can't but believe you
― 431 ―
have Extreamly well perform'd your part, but I am senceable my aprobation will add very litle Luster to the worke and therfore leave it to more Competent Judges, who may be Capable to give it its true value. all I will say more is, that you have soe admirably handle'd the subjects you have hitherto treated of, that tis pitty your pen should be Idle, and I am sure the advantages it would Convey to the world will not be more Esteem'd by any, then by my selfe whome you have oblig'd to be
Sir
your reall friend and Humble Servante
E. GUISE
Ap: the 17th utrecht.

1040. Lady Masham, formerly Damaris Cudworth, to Locke, 7 April [1688] (1003, 1322)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 17, ff. 154-5. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Though a Varietie of Accidents such as are Incident to one who has so many Relations and Interests in This World dos at this time more then Ordinarilie Disorder my Thoughts, that I have not that Command of them I could Wish Yet I cannot resolve to let you think as you say if I Writt not soone you should, That the Book you did me the favor to send me, for which I returne you many Thanks, is Condemn'd to the Prophan Side (as you Call it) of my Closet.
You are indeed in the Right to Beleeve That I do not Practice all the Rules of the Neighborhood; And that my Kitchen and Dairie, do not ingross All my Time. But how much you were so, if you Thought me Any Judge of the Essay you sent me when I shall tell you I have made very little Improvment of that Kind, it will be needless to Say; I do not I confess think my self altogether Uncapable of Things of that Nature; And I am sure I have a Universal Love for All usefull Knowledge†1 Beyond that Capacitie; But as I was Diverted from It when I was Young, first by the Commands of Others And Afterwards by that Weakness which Hapned in my Sight, The World through long Acquaintance begun almost
― 432 ―
to Claime All my Thoughts; And from my many Concerns now in It, Thinks to Justifie that Title; But as it is a True Bondage in my esteeme; and a very Ignoble One too; I assure you it is my Principle Care and Business to Free my self from It; But for one so much Ingag'd, and whose Time is so far spent, the Shorter Methods are Certainly the Best: Besides that being my self Cur'd of some sort of Scepticisme by arguments that However Solid in them selves have beene to me effectual, I think that I may much more Advantageously employ my Houres in Pursuing the End of these speculations then in indeavouring to Extricate those Difficulties that the Witts of Men have Intangled them with, Which being Needless to my self, can be no Part of my Obligations; who should not be likely to be in any Capacitie of Dispensing to Others: The Duty Certainly of those that Are.
Religion is the Concernment of All Mankind; Philosophy as distinguish'd from It, onely of Those that have a freedome from the Affaires of the World; Which as They would Hinder the latter; May well Manag'd be Great Inforcements of the Former: And indeed the Pleasures of This life are so Triffling and Transitorie, And Its Cares so many and Bitter, That I think one must be very Miserable and Stupid, not to seeke Ones sattisfaction in some thing else; If one beleeves that it is to be found; especially as the Conjuncture of some Certaine Times may Be;†1 Which may stir up a more then ordinarie Desire of being of so Confirm'd and Settled a Judgment as should secure one from the Danger of foregoing Solid and Real Goods for Imaginarie; Or on the Other Side indureing Real Inconvenience for meere Humour, and Opinion: Which I Beleeve will afford as little Sattisfaction Hereafter, as Here. I Know not what Thoughts this will make you Have of me; But I suppose none of Them will be That I intend to set up a Lecture of Divinitie, Or Enter into All the Disputes and Differences of Religion; Since I beleeve to Know whatever Truth I am Concern'd in is†a an Easier and Better Way to Overlook†2 them; But I tell you This, to let you see that in All this time the Spirrit of Goverment dos not yet so Possess me but that I am as readie to give an Account of my self as receive one of my Charge; Though Principally indeed it be to Answr That Part of
― 433 ―
your Letter in which you say It will become me to show you your Mistakes: I confess I have a Desire to Know them my self (Because Yours) if there be Any; And Accordingly as opportunitie Serves, shall employ better Judgment then my owne to find them out; which if to me unanswerable, You will give me leave I Know to Propose them from a second Hand.
For my owne Part though I think of several things Confus'dly that I would say to you if you were in this Closet, I find them not well enough Deliberated to send so far: Though I should be glad more Clearely and fully to understand the Difference betweene you and some friends of Mine, about that Principle thing, of†1- the Souls Haveing no Actual Knowledge; Being not sure the Difference betweene You, is Really so great as it Seemes; Since by actual Knowledge They say that they meane not That there is a Number of Ideas flaring and shineing to the Animadversive Facultie like so many Torches; Or That there are Any Figures that are legibly writt there like the Astronomical Characters in an Almanack; But onely an Active Sagacitie in the Soul Whereby something being Hinted to Her she runs out into a More Cleare and large Conception; Her Condition being like that of a Sleeping Musician who dos not so much as Dreame of, Or has any representation of Any thing Musical in Him, till being Wak'd and Desir'd to Sing, Somebody repeating twoo or three Words of a Song to Him; He Sings it all Presently:-†1 And such†2- are the Objects of sense to the Soul; which seemes to me Plainly to have a Facultie in Her above that of Sense Which is that that Judges of, and often Detects Impostures of it; As when the Atomick Philosophers say that Heate and Cold Bitter and Sweet Red and Blew, are not real Qualities in the Objects, onely our owne Fancies, These being not Intelligible Things: But Magnitude figure site Motion and Rest, into which They resolve them, We have not onely sensible Ideas of Passively impres'd from without, But also Intelligible Notions exerted from the Mind It self.-†2 Tho you seeme
― 434 ―
indeed to make them but the same thing to us; And under the Name of second Qualities to exclude All Account of the first more then that They are so.†1 But I beg your Pardon for this, which I did not intend; not Knowing distinctly enough my owne thoughts to undertake to tell them to Another; Which in a fitter Humour for It then Any I have beene in since I received your Book, are not much Inclin'd now to dwell long on these Matters; Haveing onely regard to them so far as they may Weaken, or establish in the Minds of Any the foundations of Natural or Reveal'd Religion; I am not therefore Dissatisfy'd that Men (even those I most Esteeme) differ in these things as well as others Whilst They Agree in Those: And tho (so far as I can Judge) I do Think the Demonstration of a God from His Idea Conclusive,†2 Yet were there no Other but yours,†3 I should think it sufficient. Tho I can scarse think the Idea of Eternitie should be Form'd from That of Time repeated;†4 Since no Succession but must once have beene all of it to Come but one moment; And there is no Imagining (I think) an Eternal Succession. But it is surely from what you say in that last Place, That nothing could ever have Come from Nothing; Or Any thing ever have beene if there once was nothing;†5 From whence, One Cannot but Imagine the Necessarie Existence of Something; which is the same thing with Eternal Duration; which is not Properly, but onely Applicatively Successive; Containing in it Virtually all Successive Duration as the Channel of a River is always Present to the Water that Passes through it; or a Permanent Rock to the River that runs by it. For the 3 last Things about Revelation†6 I fancie I need not say that I am so far of your Mind; And think it Had beene Happy for the Christian World if everie body else had always beene so. But I think I ought to beg a great deal of Pardon for this long and Impertinent Letter which I doubt will make you affraid to send me more Books.
I suppose you have before this time received a letter from me by the Young Man I told you of;†7 Who I Hope is now well againe, But I Heare upon his going over was very ill with a Flux which He fear'd would bring Him into a Consumption; The Account came
― 435 ―
from Himself else we should have beene more Concern'd; However tho He I think would make the Worst of it, It would be a Sattisfaction to me to be assur'd He is in no such Danger, Since he is one I should be very loath to lose tho I have so many. Pray if he ever continue neare you to be so Kind as to give Him Any Councel you may see Him to Stand in need of; He has so much good Nature and Sence That I am sure He will take It as he ought And you will therein very much Oblige me; who tho I know no Ill or Extravagance†1 by Him, Cannot but Apprehend so Young a Man left wholly to his Owne Goverment may easilie be drawne into Any.
I have a great deal of Concerne for Him on many Accounts But all are not fit to be put in a letter. If he has not yet beene with you I am Confident it is that he has not beene well enough to leave the Hague; which I should be sorry to Think. Pray when you write to me do me the favor to let me know if He has recover'd all ill effects of His distemper tho I expect to Heare from him before that time. Pardon this Addition to the rest I beseech you and beleeve me always your faithfull Friend and Servant
Philoclea
Apr: the 7th.
I had almost forgot to Date my letter which you did Altogether.
If you see not Harry enough to be so free with Him as I desire; You will However Oblige me if you can let me Know what Advise he will Most stand in need of. I know nothing How well He has Hitherto behav'd Himself; But I perceive He has a great many friends which makes me Hope the Best And I suppose He will have one Now that will have more then Ordinarie Concerne for Him; whom you would find a very Honest Gentleman if you were Acquainted with Him And much Better Company then most Young Gentlemen of His Profession. You will wonder at first I suppose to find a Son of Mine So little an English Man as I do at your little Gentlemens speakeing French.†2
Endorsed by Locke: Philoclea 7 Apr. 88 Answered Jun. 1

1041. Sylvester Brounower to Locke, 18/28 April 1688 (2141)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, f. 176. Locke states the circumstances of Syl's journey in no. 1050. Syl left Rotterdam on 17 April, N.S.: Journal.
Francfurt Apr 28: 1688:
Sir
I cannot leave to present my humble duty to you, and to thanke you for all your kindnesses, but espetially those at my parting of which I am Extreamly sensible, and wish noething more but that I might have occasion to shew that I am soe, I arrivd last night here in Francfurt and shall goe again to day with the Land-Coach to Heydelberg. I have hitherto had a tedious and chargeable Vojage and the best Comfort my Countrymen give me here, is that it will be worse the rest of my journeys. I have deliverd Mr. Furlys letters at Ceulen†1 and Francfurt and am just now a goeing to receive my money at Mr. van de Walle. Noe more at present but I hope this Letter will meet you in good health as I hope I shall again e're long and in the meane present my humble duty again and shall rest for ever
Sir
your most humble and dutifull servant
SYLVESTER BROUNOWER.
Address: For Mr. John Locke at Mr. Benjamin Furlys Marchant op t' schipmakers haven tot Rotterdam.

1042. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 25 April 1688 (982, 1049)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 60-1. Thomas left Rotterdam on Wednesday 11/21 April: Locke, Journal.
Sarum Ap 25 88
Deare Freind
Mr E C†2 gave you an account of my returne to London two days later then I expected our master mistakeing the hills by Callis for the North foreland could not carry us beyond Dover by fryday night though the wind was right From whence I came to London Sunday night†3 and to Salisbury the Saturday night followeing not
― 437 ―
without fireing our Ax†1 twice and at Stockebridge breakeing our ax. I delivered all your letters. your N.F†2 sayth he longs to discourse you about your booke haveing more to ask and to receave answeres to then canne be well done in one letter and that he longs to see you. Aunsham Churchill was not in London nor have I seene him since his brother†3 told me that for good bookes of which they may venture to print 1000 or 1120 they give sometime 20s sometime 30s the sheete for the coppy if writt fitt for the presse. I desire your farther direction. I have ordered some bookes to Mr Furly to whom and his wife and Mr Van Hellmont pray give my humble service my Lord Ashley hath writ to his grandmother who shewed me his letter, in which were neither excuses or respects wanting. he says hee entends to travaille farther I suppose over the Alpes. The honorable†4 says he will writt to you concerneing your booke I entend to send my young man (his name is Thomas Davys)†5 to the Surgeon at Amsterdam but desire to be farther enformed by you when and if I canne where to place him for dyet and lodgeing in that towne and I beleeve if nothing extraordinary fall out to send my sonne Will to your Doctor of Physicke†6 by midsummer at the farthest but in both shalbe governed by your advice
As to the Chocolatte nothing is to be altered save that the cinnamon is to be poudred fine and sifted and then the Venella to be put to it and to be beat with the cinnamon till it come to a finer pouder and then sifted againe
your godson is very proud of his godfather and token. my familly are all well and Present their services to you. I am
your affectionate ADRIAN

1043. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 29 April/9 May 1688 (1031, 1062)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 159.

Ce 9. may 88.
La perte qui me cause l'afliction dont je vous ay parlé par ma derniere, ne me regarde pas seul; mais vous encore, et tout le genre humain.†1 Il faut que vous n'aiez pas de coutume de lire les Gazetes d'Amstredam ny de Brusseles†2 puisque vous l'ignorez. Cequi me desole au lieu de me consoler, c'est que vous semblez me faire esperer que vous pourez venir joindre le triumvirat, en m'ecrivant bibemus aliquando invicem in salutem alii aliorum δύο και δύο:†3 car cete agreable harmonie de διὰ τεσσάρων†4 n'est plus.
J'ay une extreme joie de ceque vous n'avez jamais eté ny ne serez in eadem cymbâ cum illo διδασκάλῳ πολυθρυλλήτῳ.†5 Je vous avouë que j'en avois un facheux soupson. Si donc vous avez la liberté de venir ou j'ay eu le bonheur de vous connêtre autrefois, donnez jusques au lieu ou vous etes desiré, je vous y donneray un apartement agreable dans un lieu qui m'apartient et par consequent à vous; et qui est telement à la campagne qu'il ne peut pas etre moins hors de la ville. cependant vous y serez incognito comme dans un desert. Vous y orez de bonne eau et de bon lait, et du vin qui ne vous deplaira pas; il n'y a que la biere que je ne vous promets pas. Vous y ferez l'experience de Lapidis Colatorii,†6 que vous emporterez avec vous. Que si l'etat de vos afaires ne vous permet pas de me regaler et consoler par votre presence dans la conjoncture ou je suis, je ne laisserez pas d'envoier cete pierre à votre adresse, apres que je lauray fait monter suivant que je l'ay dessiné, car il faut pour sen servir aisement qu'ele soit suspendue, et lon travaille à cela.
Je n'ay pas encore les livres, que j'ay impatience de voir. On m'a fait esperer une maniere de faire des trochisques thanatotiques†7
― 439 ―
plus efficaces et plus pronts que ceux dont vous avez la composition; Vous l'orez des que lon me l'ora donnée. Je suis

1044. Lady Guise to Locke, 30 April/10 May [1688] (1039, 1056)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 130. Year from contents. Answered by no. 1056.
I know not Sir whether my silence, or the trouble I now give you requiers the greater apologie, yet I had not omited the returne of my thankes for the oblidging yours but that I have ben from home and in a perpetuall hury Ever since the receiving it, this may paliate for the first, but what will sofen the defects of the last I know not, unles it be the goodness you are soe absolutly the master of, and from which springs the favorable opinion you are pleas'd to Conceive for me. you have hitt right when you request me to peruse your booke; since I doe it with all the pleasure Imaginable and shall ascrib it wholy to my owne dulnes if it be not as well to my advantage; but you must choose some other person to discrie the Errors you would have found ther, since in my opinion there are non, I know not how fare Emulation or a mistaken Zeal may prevaile over the minds of some, to Cavill with your philosophey: or question your religeon, but I leave them to answare for their Ignorance, and only say for my selfe that if any thing can perswad me I am otherways then soe, tis that I value what is perfect, and Estimable, as in my opinion is the litle treatis you favor'd me with, and which with many other prevailing sircumstances in your character meritts the Esteeme of
Sir
your most oblidged Humble Servante
E GUISE
May the 10th utrecht
1045. Thomas Stringer to Locke, 30 April 1688 (1038, 1046)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 155-8. A copy or draft, in Stringer's hand, without address or endorsement, in P.R.O., S.P. 30/24 (Shaftesbury Papers), bdle.
― 440 ―
47, no. 23; there are very slight verbal differences. Printed from the latter version in Rand, pp. 262-7. Answers no. 1038; answered by no. 1046.
Ivychurch Aprill 30th. 1688.
Sir
I was soe sincere in Every thing I wrote to mr Clarke Concerning you that I was Strangely surprized at the Reading of your Answere unto it.
You know we live in a Country which somtimes at this time of the yeare doth not want heat, And a Reinforcement of soe much Sharpnesse out of Holland, was enough to putt a Colder Constitution then mine into such a fermentation, As to take time for deliberation, drinck large draughts of whey to coole, and Read some of your former letters for an allay, before I did dare trust my temper to adventure upon a Reply; I think I have heard of a treatise you have eyther printed or are about to print, that sayth words are of noe other use then to Convey mens sence and meaning from one to the other,†1 And if a man out of dulnesse or want of skill, should blunder upon words that are of a doubtfull or double interpretation, I suppose it hath always been a Rule in Friendshipp to take them in the best and most Favourable sence, harty Friends will streyn hard of that side, to make them mean well, Rather then use learning and skill by melancholy Fancyfull Arguments to interprett them otherwise; I have still soe much Respect for old Friendshipp as not to enter into Particulars, besides being of all men very unfitt for animadvertions. But in the generall I cannot but be very much of the opinion, that if the best new Dutch Friend you have should give himselfe the trouble of soe much impertinence as to Read over what I then wrote to mr Clarke, And at the same time be acquainted that it was from an old Friend, whoe had a most sincere esteeme and true affection for you, and hath soe still, but that he is become a Cripple, and soe not serviceable, That this old Friend doth say (and truly beleiveth himself when he doth soe) that when we were in our most intimate Friendshipps and obleiging indearments, you at two severall times and places gave him your Picture (the one at Exceter House the other in the Longwalke at Bexwells)†2 And afterwards upon some occation wrote to his wife to borow it, to take a Copie of it, with a Promise that you would not
― 441 ―
deprive her of it, but Returne it safe to her againe, etc.
That all this being forgott you somtime sinc sent to this old uselesse Friend for this Picture and told him you eyther had or would dispose of it otherways, whereupon he claymed a title to it, and Refused to deliver it, That now a Gent in London†1 informed him you had Comanded him to write to this old friend to send up your Picture thether from his house in the Country to ingrave a print by it, But he Remembring upon what occation you had before sent for it, wrote that letter to the Gent, and would not send it unlesse you would promise to Returne it to him againe; Lett this new Dutch Friend have never soe much Respect Esteeme or kindnesse for you, and be as perfect a Stranger to me, I dare hold a bett of any odds, he will make quite an other Construction of it then you have done, And then you may Judge how very slow you have been to enterteyne hard thoughts of me (whoe still must and doe pretend to be your Friend) when you have soe hastily determined the matter, with soe much severitie against me as to Act such a very Angry parte before (you say) you know whether I am in earnest or in Jest. But sinc you are pleased to appeale to mr Clarke as the Common Friend between us, tho he is a Person I am sufficiently troublesome unto in other more necessary Concerns, yett if you will send back my letter againe I will Request the favour that he will Compare yours with it, and Consider whether from a Person that hath a true Friendshipp that could possibly deserve such a very Angry and severe Returen; To be accused of Falsnesse, indirectnesse, Rudenesse and incivilities etc. are hard Charges (which I should be sorry to deserve from any but Especially mr Lock) And all about a shaddow or somthing lesse, For one Parte of your letter seems to carry the heat unto an old Peque to my wife, And (tho for some yeares you have travelled with it, and for want of a better occation hath Catched at this to bring it forth, yett) if you will impartially Examine the matter, I am apt to beleive you will finde but little Reason for such a Conjecture, She professeth her selfe a perfect Stranger to every parte of your Charge, not in the least Remembring that she was ever solicited to write or denyed to doe it, For she did lately write and intended to send it by the Doctor,†2 but for an other cause then I perceive you apprehend she omitted it, And I am sure when ever your name hath been mentioned or she hath had an occation to talke of you, She hath always shewed a
― 442 ―
Concerne for mr Lock by all the marks and appearances of the truest and Faithfullest Friendshipp and kindnesse that is possibly to be Expressed by the hartyest and best Friends, And of this she can appeale to many witnesses, and with as great assurance Challenge the whole world to testifye the least thing tending or inclineing to the Contrary, which was the Reason she was more surprized then I when she saw that parte of your letter. However She Jocularly bid me tell you that matrimony hath not yett wasted soe much of her good humour that she could make such a Construction or for soe little Reason harbour a Peque of soe long standing against her greatest Enimie, But for mr Lock she doth hold her selfe in many Respects soe much obleiged to him, that if nothing else could hinder prejudiced or lessening thoughts, yett Gratitude will not suffer any other opinion of him but what doth deserve the highest Esteeme and she did not a little delight her selfe to provide brown bred and milke against his coming with the Doctor. From hence you may see there could be noe such strange mediums to Represent things amisse between England and Holland, if some were not very much disposed to be wrong interpreters there, And this I take to be an other Evidence of your slownesse to enterteyne hard thoughts etc. My wife doth Really doe what you say, makes noe Reflections but beleives if it please God she lives Ever to see you, she shalbe able throughly to satisfye you, that you are much mistaken, and she is not in the least guilty.
But as for the Picture, which you make another cause of this quarrell, You may be well assurd I should not have deteyned that any more then I did any other of your things which you left in my Custody,†1 nor devided it from them to carry it to Bexwells, If I had not been throughly satisfyed that you did Really and bona fide give it to me, and that in Justice and Right it was mine. And therefore your Clayming to have it againe is a manifest injury which (as it is demanded) I have noe Reason to Comply with, And tho I have had an Exceeding valew for it, not for the Paynt and intrinsick worth, For that (as the case is) I should dispise, but for the sake of the Person it Represents, which I can strongly averr, I truly loved, yett I doe now begin to beleive by the Course you are taking that it may be in your power to bring the MAKE BATE†2 to suffer a punishment answereable to the offence.
― 443 ―
How sharply soever you accuse me for not beleiving my selfe when I say you gave me the Picture, I may with more Confidence Returne the same upon you, when you say I denyed you the use of it upon any occation whatsoever, soe as I might have it Returned againe; If I should have done soe mean a thing, you might too justly have bestowed some of those before mentioned Epethites upon me, and bring me under the Reproach of those that enterteyne Suspicions of theire friends, apprehends them to be Cheats, and mix inconsistencys between theire words and Actions. But I am sure you know other things of me, And if you will Lay aside an unprejudiced minde, and turn the Tables, I doubt not but you can much easier Reconcile all those hard things to satisfye a true Friend, then finde in it such appearances or Relishes of distast.
The skilfull discourse you mention about Pictures and draughts is what I learned from mr White when my late Lord sate to him to draw his Face in black and white in order to ingrave a plate for a print of him,†1 and he being a man of that Enimency and Reputation in that art, I thought he might have soe much skill to know which way was best in his own Trade. However I did not presume to write that by way of instruction, or beleive that you wanted eyther age or discretion to Choose, but only tell mr Clark a story of what I both saw and heard from him, which I could not apprehend would be any Lessening to you. I know all men are not born with like partes, nor doe they acquire Equall Learning, and tho I cannot pretend to much skill in any thing, yett you may beleive noe man loves to be upbraided with his ignorance.
I have the same Excuse you make for not writing, and more, notwithstanding you call it a silent Respect. But you being then in your Retirements, etc. (it may be for good Reason) not desireing any more Correspondence then was necessary for your buisnesse, I must Leave you to Judge whether silence in that Respect did not looke more like Friendshipp in me, then impertinently to interrupt it, Especially I knowing mine own Circumstances and indiscretion, which at that time might occation ill to a Person I wished well, and whether in such a Case I might not reasonably Conclude, that in any of your Removes not to give me direction to write, was not a modest way of forbidding it. However I soe little Regarded the Ceremonyall or Formall (which is the troublesome) parte of
― 444 ―
Friendshipp, that I always desired you should Act with what Freedome you pleased towards me, it being as great Satisfaction to me, and I was as well pleased to heare the news of your health by mr Clark or any other hand, as tho I had the Favour of Receiving it from your owne.
I understand not your deviding my Letter into partes or that there is any thing Complementall or disobleiging in it; Complements are more sutable to Travellers to make addresse to new acquaintanc, and to disobleige old Friends is fitter for those that are Fond of new. I don't know that I am guilty of eyther of them, Plainesse and true hartednesse is what I pretend to, And that I should be sorry any Dutchman should out doe me in.
I think without Force or injury I may mention one instance more of what kinde thoughts you enterteyne of me, that after the Experience of soe many yeares acquaintance and friendly Conversation, you should Contrive a Test to trye how Farr you may trust or putt Confidence in me. If I should Act soe little a parte to gratifie your humour in that Particular, such Phantasies usually increase, and are seldome satisfyed. But this seemes the harder because you have not left me liberty to choose, you having already prejudged the Cause, and the question you have putt to trye me at the end of your letter, you have fully decided by all the other partes of it. For whoe (that knows mr Lock) can be perswaded that he is growen soe Touchy, Fancyfull, or nice humoured, as to be provoaked or putt into such a fitt of Anger and Choller against an old Friend, for a letter which he beleives may be only mirth or Jesting, or that he doth looke for soe much Respect and observance, as to quarrell at Freedome and Familiaritie; You may think of me as little and narrow as you please and putt what tryalls and tests you will upon me, But you will still finde I shall endeavour to preserve an Eternall Esteeme and Respect for old Friendshipps, and Particularly for you, whatever opinion you may Conceive of
Sir
Your most humble servant
THO: STRINGER
Address: For my much Respected friend mr John Lock at mr Benjamen Furley s house a merchant in Roterdam
Endorsed by Locke: T. Stringer 30. Apr. 88
