1046. Locke to Thomas Stringer, [c. 6/16 May 1688] (1045, 1542)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24 ff. 262-3. Draft, with many alterations not recorded here. Date: This draft is preparatory to an answer to no. 1045; Locke enclosed a letter to Stringer in his letter to Clarke of 6/16 May (no. 1047); the letter was probably an answer to no. 1045; the date of the draft therefore is probably 6/16 May or a day or two earlier. Locke wrote to Clarke about the dispute in no. 1047 and more fully in no. 1050. He corresponded with Mrs. Stringer in 1689: no. 1165, etc.
I received your civil and obleigeing letter and you have taken a great deal a pains by an other of the same strain to convince me in what sense I was to take your former to Mr Clarke and which part of it was in earnest. I am not soe versed in this kinde of conversation as to returne you my thanks for it in the same stile that you have thankd me for the picture you say I gave you. you have justified the kinde expressions of your letter to mr Clarke and have made me know that childs play and colourable pretences were meant in earnest. But in good earnest doe you thinke that those were kind and freindly expressions. But†a- I should have straind hard say you to have given them a kinde interpretation. I know not what I could doe more then to leave to your self their interpretation for when the interpretation of words lies only in actions tis not in any mans power to give them what sense he pleases if you have that faculty I desire thus much of your freindship to beleive the same of me that you did before any mention was made of this beloved picture, or thinke that any body will beleive the same of you you would have them when they hear your story of it.-†a how they were meant noe thing but your actions could interpret, for when by Mr Clarke I sent to desire my picture was it the great freindship you boast of that made you deny me that request. you say I gave it you because it was yours then you denyd it me excellent freindship. I will write you downe amongst the ancient examples of it the Pythias†b of our age denyd pore Damon his picture to have a draught made of it only because it was his. Had it been another mans tis like free liberall friendly Pythias could have found in his heart to part with it. But what if the picture should not be yours. I gave it you say you. a good title I allow could it be made out. you say it and I deny it both very honest fellows the case is thus far equall here lies the oddes I sat for it and paid 15 pounds for it methinks therefor till
― 446 ―
you can shew some better title to it. you will say again I gave it you at Exeter house, in what year I beseech you. and in what room since you remember it soe well. But did you ever heare amongst those ancient freinds or amongst people of more moderne date that any one beleive that his freind gave him something which he afterwards denyd to have don that ever this reall freind would prevaile soe far of the possession he had as to keep what the other said he never gave him and of which gift he had noe witnesse nor proof. Perhaps you will say the gent is mistaken, let it be soe but I aske you whether ever any one that thought him self a civil man ever kept from an other upon colour of a gift what the other denyd to have given him. but thus to give and take is childs play let it be soe let him be the child and you the man the freindly man you boast of. tis not talkeing of themselves that makes mens characters, their actions paint them truer then any pen or pencil can. If I am melancholy capsious false to my freinds your keepeing my picture will not give me another credit or opinion in the world pity these faults in an old freind who was just the same when you cald him soe as he is now. though he has the misfortune to fall into your displeasure and that for noe other reason but because he would have his pin box again. if you thinke he deserves to be whipd <because>†a he asks for it again consider whether you will not be <thought>†b a very harsh schoolmaster and a litle out of season. Noe but tis not a pin box tis the picture of a friend I love. I keep it for his sake and cannot part with a thing soe dear to me. Hey day whip the boy and Keep the pin box for his sake cast of the friend and treat him with all the roughnesse imaginable to say noe thing else and yet to keep the picture for his sake. noe but now you begin to dislike it as a Makebate soe then your freind is soe dear to you that you dislike that which has been the occasion of any difference between you and him. If this were said in truth the remedy were easy send me the make bate and all were well again. Noe but you will punish him for occasioning the difference between you and your dearly beloved friend. Here one might aske you again whether you beleive your self whilst you say this that you will burne or destroy the picture because it makes bate betwix you and a man you are a freind to and to whom the world thinks you have noe reason to be otherwise. Methinks now you have said it you should not choose but doe it to give the world this indisputable proofe of the greatnesse
― 447 ―
of your thoughts and freindship. But you cannot suffer as you say to have a test put on your freindship what is the meaning of that that your freindship after soe much glittering in professions cannot bear the test. Freindship Sir is like gold <known>†a by the test trial shews us it and if yours will not bear the triall of 15 or 30 ls for soe perhaps the picture may be valued doe not bost any more of it I beseech you. But you will not haveing†b- soe asked for it.-†b
I have indeed heard crosse children and humersom women and men like them say I would have don it if you had not asked me but I never heard yet it given for a reason from the mouth of a man a man of businesse. But here you seeme to insinuate that if it had been sought as it should, one knows not what might have been don. but in the way I knew not a civiller nor more acceptable way to aske it in then by Mr Clarke pray tell me what was the fault of it. Sometimes it is for love of me some times because it is yours some times because you will not have a test put upon your freindship and some times because it has not been demanded as it ought that you deny your freind his picture to have a draught made by it, for how doe you know that if you had let him have it for that occasion he would not have sent it you back again. Noe but he desired it formerly to have it to take a copy by it and what then I refused it him for the same reasons or what were the reasons that you refused him then I beseech you. were <they>†c these or any other pray tell me
What I said about pictures and draught I did not thinke could have been brought to be a reproach to your parts or learning, noe man you say loves to be uppraided with his ignorance give me leave in this point to be lesse touchy then you. if any one will tell me I am ignorant in Arabique and Syriaque that I understand not navigation that I am a Novice in Algebra parts of knowledge of much more importance and use then skill in painting I should not be offended at hearing soe undeniable a truth from others for not affecting to be thought skilfull in all things I can without exceptions allow any one to tell me that I am ignorant of a great many nay almost all soe far am I from being infallible. But give me leave to tell you that your information wherever you had it was a litle out concerning draughts for graveing. There is not one of an hundred of the gravers that can draw from the life though copy well enough
― 448 ―
  
from a picture what they would grave, and by Mr Whites takeing the other course one may see what a print he made of it. But if an old Batchelor had a minde to appear in a peruke and 20 years yonger in print, by haveing a plate copyd from a picture drawn soe long agon. me thinks an old freind should have found some other way to expresse his complaisance then to have sent him to another picture or his own old countenance†1 neither of which he liked soe well and therefor however opportune your advice may be on some other occasion you might (how skilfull soever you are in painting for I doe not upbraid your ignorance) have spared it in this, as not like to be hearkend to not haveing on it the clear marke of freindship whose directions use to be for the sake of the receiver and not the giver
Pray remember me to Mrs Stringer and tell her I can expect noe thing from her but civility when she hearkens to noe thing but her good nature and tell her she cannot refuse to beleive me when I tell her I caryed noe grudg
unlesse she has some body by her that has soe good eyes that at this distance he can looke into my heart and see something in it which I that cary it about with me never observed in it. for men that are soe quicksighted and know soe well how to use both ends of the perspective ought to be credited
Not being versed in that sort of rhethorique wherein you have been soe liberal to me I shall not returne you my thanks for your letter in the same stile where in you send me your first thanks for the picture you acknowledg I gave you. But there being in it some seemeing contradiction concerning which I shall propose you some few questions that when you have resolved these doubts I may know which parts you would have passe for true and which you acknowledg not to be soe I may not trouble my self to answer that which you allow not to need any
why if you valued the pictur only for the true love you had for him whom it represented you keep it now that you love him noe longer, or if you have that true love for him still how you can refuse him a picture he desires of you.
How you can designe any thing against the picture as a punishment to the Makebate when you know the picture is innocent or whether you can that way expresse your dislike of the difference when you know it will not end it
― 449 ―

whether a man can take it amisse that his words were not taken in a contrary sense then what they were meant when he himself has not the confidence nor will soe to interpret them
1047. Locke to Edward Clarke, 6/16 May 1688 (1030, 1050)
Rand, pp. 267-9. Word in square brackets supplied by Rand.
16th May, 1688.
Dear Sir,
I could not read your kind letter of the 27th passato without great shame to see how great and unkind some troubles I had given you, in sending you on so many small errands with my inconsiderable treatise. I know not what to say to you to excuse it. Find some arguments in your own friendship and goodness to do it, or else I am undone. For it is without a compliment that I assure you that there is nothing so dear to me as my interest in you, nor anything that I should so unwillingly lose any part of. But your tried friendship secures me of that fear, and the share you allow me in it is what I possess in this world with greatest satisfaction. When your lady is well laid, which I hope every day to hear, and well up again, which I mightily long for, I hope I shall have an opportunity to tell you so to your face, and then you will be convinced that I have all the reason in the world to think myself so happy in nothing as the enjoyment of so good a friend.
You will here enclosed find a letter to Mr. Stringer in answer to his about my picture. The truth is, he deals with me after a way I could scarce have believed under any other assurance but that of his own hand. He tells me his wife has it under my hand that I gave it to him. I am afraid he strains the matter too far, for having never purposed but to have that picture in my chamber in Oxford when I came to settle there I am sure I could never give it away in a letter to anyone, or say anything like it unless I were drunk when I writ it. But if you can, pray get a sight of that letter that I may know what it is, for I have not the least remembrance of any the least thing towards it, nor can I believe it. For I think such a thing as that I should not possibly forget.
As to Mr. Somerton's cousin,†1 he has certainly the oddest state in
― 450 ―

the world. He desires nothing but to be quiet in the world, but cannot obtain that of his friends. Adrian he says will inform you what has been done in his affairs without his least knowledge or privity. But now it is done I find he is brought into straights by it. For to refuse what is granted is to bid defiance; to blame, or talk of P is to affront and make an enemy of him  †a And to that I now scarce see a remedy, which Mr. Oakley's imprudent meddling in the case upon his own head has yet made more difficult, so that if great care be not taken I think your cousin will receive all the inconvenience is possible in this affair and none of the benefit. That which he thinks best I find is to let the matter sleep as much as may be at present; but if the matter should go on and he by Mr. Oakley's meddling be left out of it, he asked me whether his reputation would not be altogether in as bad a case and [even] a much worse, to which I could not tell what to say, though I were willing a little to ease his mind, which I find mightily troubled with this odd business.†1
I have herewith sent some copies for your son. I like the hand he writes already very well, and particularly because it has no flourishes in it, which is carefully to be avoided in children when they learn to write. Pray let him have my answer with my thanks for his pretty letter, and make him as proud of it as you can, that he may take a pleasure betimes in writing of letters.
My most humble respects to your lady. I hope the pain and danger is already over, and she is rejoiced in another lusty boy. I am with the utmost reason,
Dear Sir,
your most humble servant,
JOHN LOCKE.
If he like the copies I have sent for your son, the use I would have him make of them is this: to go over one of the yellow copies with
― 451 ―

black ink, and then setting another before him endeavour to imitate it on fair paper. The one I think will teach him to fashion the letters, the other will give him a freedom of hand; if these two <ways>†a be used alternately.
Address: These for Mr. Edward Clarke at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, London.
1048. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 8 May 1688 (1006, 1065)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, f. 155.
May the 8th 88
Deare Brother
You deserve not a Meek and well tempor'd sister that can find in your heart to make so il use of her submissions. I thought when she humblie bow'd and conffess'd her weakness in not answering you Nimbler, that you would with a quick hand and many good words have rais'd her spirits and secur'd the peace, but instead of that civility which is due to her nothing will serve your turn but a sever beating the poor feble smale creature if she throu a modest fear of sining as most of her sex does, should chance to be more silent then you expect. Well had not this winter added to my Naturall dulness I would trie which of us should swager most to the life but as the case stands all I can doe is faintly to shew what a Virago I would be were it in my power. After this wilde begining what brave account may you hope for of the Book you sent me, I know you look to be diverted with my jargon, but to cros you all I could I made hast into wise and learned company to whome I said, what would you give to see a Book own'd and publish'd by Mr Locke all replied who can give enough for any thing so grave and good a head peice thinks fit to make publick, having soon put them in a longing condition and then set them a reading they all agreed to say finer things then I will pretend to repeat. the English having paid you true respect, I next concluded it for my honour to shew the present you sent me to Monsieur Capel,†1 who having gredily examined it, made this return. Madame You have trusted me with a rarity of very great value, no man that has not the clearest and
― 452 ―

best understanding can with such force and conviction lead men to the knowledge of what is most Essentiall to them, his expressions are so pertenent and happy that one must be as dul as an Ox not to be firmly perswaded of the truth of all he says; All this, and a world more did the transported man speak, and to Ease his mind he preach'd to me upon Every page and realy he did it so affectionately†1 that he made me very attentive. Now deare Brother what would you now give that I could truely tell you that I understand the weighty Volum, that you have refin'd my thoughts and made me sensible of the great importance of all you have don to make Mankind wiser, I am sure You could not have a plainer demonstration that you have outdon all that are gon before you, but for your humiliation I remaine the very same pittifull ignorent soul I was long agoe, Except you will call it an improvement to be more afraid of myself and all mankind then ever I was, methinks the world is now so impudently bussy in laying snares and so prosperous in all insincere practices that I allmost worship good and undisguis'd souls who never were easier to be discover'd in this island than at this time, but tis a pain to behold how many pricipitate themselves and importune their friends to be like commets, not considering that they will most probablie quickly die like fooles, And if ever an immorall friend was to be treated with cautiously tis now, This is the time wherin a thoughtfull and well resolved Christian begins to shew its true spirit and dignity, and by principles that command regard will convince the world that Truth is superiour to all the polacy of fallen Angels and the best Laid divices of Ambitious man.†2 All in England to whome I am most obliged give you their service and are glad to heare from you, pray consider that you cannot be slow in answering me without ofanding as faithfull a friend as any you have in the world, tho she dos not wish as yet to se you in this new modeled country, God Keepe you deare Brother
Address: For Mr Locke at mr Benjamin Furlys Merchant on the Scepe Makers Haven In Rotterdam
Postmarks: -8; -B
Endorsed by Locke: A G 8o May. 88 Answered 15 Jun

1049. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 10 May 1688 (1042, 1063)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 62-3.
May 10 88
Deare Freind
Aunsham Churchill says they doe not give a value for a coppy of a booke to be printed but it is first reade by some whom they trust, but that he will print a booke at his owne charges and the author shall have the halfe cleare proffitt. I ordered his brother†1 to send some bookes to Mr Furly but know not whether he hath done it. What your N F†2 objections are I know nor canne you know them unlesse in England but I suppose the Honourable†3 will write something to you of your book. he says the aphorismes are very methodicall but that the author either knew not or concealed the menstruum†4 for the greate worke. I know your letters were delivered especially that to your mistris†5 and your booke also though shee was affrayd that I would have cheated her of your booke and I suppose you may expect some animadversions on it from her hand more materiall then any of Dutch Divines canne write. I am glad any French Saynt hath so much favor for Holland as to send good Clarret and that state so much religion as permitt the retayleing of it for the benefitt of tender consciences. I have receaved an answere from Musidore who says WP told him that it was Josia†a Locke not JL†6 and that with this Musidore thought I was satisfyed and that he will goe to WP and make that apology I writt. I use his owne Words if I thinke it necessary and if it will doe you any service I have by this post May 21†7 writt to him againe that he told me he desired
― 454 ―

W P not to move for you and that to say as I writt was very reasonable for a freind. perhaps he hath forgotten it. I will if you thinke fitt send you both his letters if worth the postage however I would retard this no longer for feare you may agen have some grumbling in the gizard. My familly is well and I am
your affectionate AD
all mine send you their services pray give mine to all with you I thinke E C is not yet returned to London
Address: These for Mr John Locke.
Endorsed by Locke: D Thomas 10 May 88 Answered Jun. 11 and 15
1050. Locke to Edward Clarke, 11/21 May 1688 (1047, 1055)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 26. Printed in Rand, pp. 269-74. The letter (with an enclosure) was sent to Rabsy Smithsby for delivery to Clarke: p. 469. Answered by no. 1060.
21 May 88
Dear Sir
Yours of 7th and 27th Apr I received, and in them, as in all yours, new matter of thanks. I wish I could pay them such as I owe; but in my inability I have this satisfaction, to thinke you beleive, I heartily wish it. I fear, my Beluton affairs give you more trouble, then they are worth. I scarce know a remedy, whilst they are in the hands of an undexterous, and slow man.†1 and how to take them out, cannot be thought on till I see you. I have lately drawn a bill on Mr Perce†2 for £50, which I hope will be answerd according to advice. Pray be pleased to receive of my Lady S £20, which she gave me Commission, to lay out in books, for the yonge Gent. and to get commission for £20 more. I heare he has writ lately to her, pray enquire whether he takes notice of it to her. for I sent him word of it.†3 If you light upon an excellent servant, fit for me, pray secure him, till you can give me notice of his age, qualifications, and termes. He must be trusty, sober, diligent, well conditiond, read and write well, and some other good qualitys, in fine excellent, for none, is better, then as the ordinary sort are, and tis better to
― 455 ―

stay and take Syl again then one that is not better.
He had occasion to goe home, and asked me leave. I told him twas not fit, what ever might happen, that he should be obleiged to come back, or I be obleigd to wait without a servant, till he returnd: on these termes we parted, though I beleive, he hopes to returne to my service. However if in the meane time fortune should doe such a miracle, as to bring such an one in your way, as you could wish me and I would have. I would be glad; but would not have you, give your self much trouble in seeking. If you saw Adrian since you writ, he will have told you, what I have desired him to write to Mr Oakly in your absence. It is necessary, and that for fresh reasons, that he should unsay to W P†1 and own to him, that it was without the order or privity of the person concernd, and soe take off the suspition of slighting or affront, which it cannot but be prejudicial for his freind to lie under with a man of that interest. This must be the reason, and it must come only from you, or Adrian. But you must be sure, to let him know, noe part of the contents of the inclosed,†2 for†a- he loves to be talkeing,-†a and therefor you must charme him to say just soe much and noe more as is desired of him in the fit place, and noe thing noe where else, but let it die. If I tell you, what you thought was quite laid by, is now again on foot. you will thinke it necessary, that Mr Oakly should forth with redresse, as much as is possible, what his medleing, without order, in a businesse, he was wholy a stranger to has don. I know not what stars governe my friends at this time, Mr Oakly quarrells with me, and thinks himself injurd, because I doe not imploy him, and without any communication with me will be doeing though to my cost. But what is beyond all, is Mr Stringers answer to that letter, you delivered him from me, wherein I allowd his freindship the leisure of second thoughts to recollect it self, if ever he had any; and gave him leave to turn the harsh things, he had said of me in his letter to you, into jest, if he pleased. But in his answer, he has taken pains to second it with such an overflow of gall and spite, as required noe lesse then two whole large sheets of paper to wrap it up in, and that leaves noe roome to doubt, but that he would have, what he writ to you, understood in the most provoaking sense it could beare. And if any one should see this letter of his, that knew not
― 456 ―

what had passed between him and me, he must needs think me the most inveterate enemy he ever had in the world; and that in that letter I had treated him with the utmost outrage.
What, he said in his letter to you, his wife had to shew under my hand, that I had given him my picture (and noe doubt if he have any such he has shewn it you) is it seems by his letter to me, this. (viz) that I writ to his wife to borrow it to have it copyed. I always imagind the deed of gift, he bragd of was some such matter as this, that at best would amount to noething but an evidence against him. I must therefor now explain the whole matter to you. After my returne out of France speakeing, upon an occasion at Bexwells, of removeing my picture, I was told I should have it noe more, and findeing by the discourse, that it lookd more like earnest, then I could have expected, haveing never once in my life thought of parting with it, I was not a litle surprised. but not haveing then any place, where I was setled, to remove it to, I thought best not to presse it any farther, but to wait an oportunity to get it into my hands by fair means, not being willing to come to a heat upon this occasion, which soe feirce and positive a man as Mr Stringer, was but too apt to break out into. which way of proceeding how necessary it was, if I would not indanger breaking with him the event witnesses. Tis like then I might, pursuant to this intention of not haveing a quarrell with him to recover my picture, write to her some thing to that purpose. And if it should now be asked why he let me not have it upon that request, it will be hard to finde any answer, but what will cary with it a plain confession, that he was conscious to himself it was not his, which joynd to his desire of keeping it right or wrong, is that alone, which can explain all his cariage in the whole affair since. But that I gave it him, or ever intended to give it any body, whilst I thought of returning to Ch: Ch:, where I had all a long designd out a place for it in my chamber, has been always soe far from my thoughts, that I can assure you with the greatest truth, I never did it. However he affirmes and I deny: on whose side lies the proof? But take it, that our opposite words are equall, there will still be this oddes, that it cost me the pains of siting and fiveteen pounds drie mony†1 to boote, which he pretending noe consideration, but a bare word, by which it came to be his, I think gives me the better title. It appears more then enough, that he has an unreasonable desire it should be his; It may
― 457 ―

be too he has talked himself into an opin<ion>†a that it is, or an opiniatrity that it shall be soe: For some men, you know, haveing once said a thing are forever after infallible in it.
But grant I were mistaken, I aske whether any body, but Mr Stringer though he did beleive the word had been said, would yet strain it to such a degree, when he was told it was not remembred, or was not in earnest: For a friends picture is I thinke of all things the least to be kept as a gift where tis declard not to be so intended. Nay if it had been given with the formalitys that transfer a right, and been deliverd before witnesses. I think noe body but he would have refused to give it back again, to a man he cald his friend, and for whose sake alone he pretended to value it, if he knew it was desired; much lesse would have refused it, as Mr Stringer, has don me, when I mentiond borrowing of it (as he himself says) formerly, and now that I had occasion for it, and made use of you our common freind, who were upon the place, to get it of him. If you finde any thing in all this (whether I gave him the picture or noe) that deservd his reproaches, I beseech you tell me, for I will make him satisfaction. But pray tell me, has not siting still crippled his understanding too. For 'tis hard to thinke a man not under some decay should be willing to have it thought of him, that, haveing got his friends picture into his hands (which came there with other things only as a depositum) he is malitious enough to thinke of dest<roy>ing†b it, if he may not keep it without being asked for it. His words are these, put a better construction upon them if you can. I doe now begin to beleive by the course you are takeing, that it may be in your power to bring the MAKEBATE to suffer a punishment answerable to the offence. Can you hold laughing at the Pithy Expression of MAKEBATE writ in great letters, as if he valued me more then my picture, witnesse his cariage; Or that if he spoiled the pictur, that would compose the difference. The pore man had ill luck to betray his forwardnesse to destroy it: For the wisdom of Solomon could not (you know) think of a surer mark, in the want of other proofs, wherby†c to judg, which of the two pretenders had noe right. But he lays the blame on the course I am takeing. What course could be more gentle then nine years <patient>†d attendance, I would fain have any one tell me: For it should have been restored to me with my other things upon my returne out of France, it being with them left in his custody dureing that absence.
― 458 ―

But if Mr Stringer be soe elevated, that he thinks he has a right, not only to keep what was barely intrusted to his care, but to give ill language when you only asked it, that there might be a plate graved from it; and to quarrell with me since, because I did not interpret kindely what he writ of me to you with soe much unkindenesse, that he either could not, or would not put a friend†1 interpretation on it himself, though I left him at liberty to give it what sense he pleased: Or if findeing that I am not like to beare his ill language with the same patience I have hitherto borne the detention of my picture, he be very uneasy, to think that I should now insist on my right, and make the whole matter appear in its true colours, I cannot help that. I am sorry he has soe soar a place, that the least touch galls, and the very pointing at it puts it out of temper. Noe course I have used could disease any one, who did not suffer more from his own conscience than from me. And to shew what regard I have stil to the familiarity has been between us, and the friendship I am sure has been on my side I will not refuse any amicable course, you or any of our friends shall advise, for the obteining what by all manner of right is mine. But if noe thing else will serve his turne, and he will needs paint himself to the world in indelible characters, I shall not leave him till he has don it. That the profession of friendship without the reality is the masque of low mindes that change with every look of fortune is noe new thing; and what I might expect should I have any real need of him this compassion to my indisposition and absence cannot but satisfie me. Pardon me Sir that I tire you with soe long a story, you are a freind whose least good thought, I value above any picture can be drawn of me, and therefor I cannot suffer my self to lie under any imputation on that account: Besides you know all the offices of Civility and Friendship by the surest way that is by practiseing them. I thinke I have transgressed none of them in this whole affair; I am sure I will not be obstinate in what you shall finde blameable in my proceedings. I am extremly glad that Madam and her litle one are soe well. Three boys and three girles†2 looke me thinks very gracefully, Pray with my service let her know I wish her joys may increase with her stock. Now your Lady <is>†a up again, think I beseech you on what you
― 459 ―

made me hope for, I long for noe thing soe much since there noe thing soe much pleases me as the affection and sincerity where with I am
Dear Sir
your most humble servant
J L
The inclosed I think were best be sealed up in a Cover superscribed to yourself and left with her that brings it you†1 to be ready at hand when there shall be occasion. But let noebody read it but your self.
Address: For Mr Edward Clarke
Endorsed by Clarke: J:L's Letter to Receive 20l. of the Lady Shaftesbury layd out in Bookes for the Lord Ashley etc: And about Mr Stringer, and the Picture etc: Received 26th May 1688.
1051. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 12/22 May 1688 (1034, 1054)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256b. Printed in Ollion, pp. 176-7.
(English) 
Rotterdam 22o May 88
Vir Amplissime
Expectatus optatusque tuus ad Synodum†2 adventus silentem me hactenus tenuit, spe liberioris, quam per epistolas et scribendi tædium, tecum sermonis. Sed ista jam spes celebrato solutoque sine te conventu evanuit, et in ejus locum de valetudine tuâ sollicitudo successit. Non ex collega tuo Pontano†3 de te rebusque tuis certior ut cupiebam fieri potui, Quippe qui adesse eum non noveram
― 460 ―

priusquam decesserat. Exime mihi quamprimum oro hanc curam, et si vales, Furleium, quid de codice†1 statutum sit vel quo in loco ea sit res moneas, nam reversum jam tandem Wetstenium heri intellexit. Quando illum convenias hanc inclusam Epistolam per otium quæso tradas, in quâ de Manuscripto ne verbum quidem, id negotium tuæ curæ in integrum committitur ut solus transigas. Salutes quæso optimam tuam Uxorem, Veeneosque Gunellosque et integrum collegium meo nomine. Dicasque Domino Guenellon me antehac novos ipsi gratulatum fuisse lares si scirem quomodo rectè inscribenda esset ad illum epistola. Helmontius Furleiusque te salutant Vale et me ama tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
(English) Dominum Le Clerc et Du Cene plurimum salvere jubeo
A Wetstenio per inclusam quæro quid factum sit de quibusdam meis libellis quos Toinardo destinatos, Lutetiam transmittendos suscepit,†2 si roges et dicas te quæ responderit ad me perscripturum et illius operæ parces et ego citius cognoscam.
(Latin) 
Rotterdam 22 May 88
Excellent Sir,
My expectation and ardent wish that you would come for the Synod†2 has kept me silent till now, in the hope of a freer sort of converse with you than through letters and the tiresome method of writing. But that hope has now vanished, as the assembly has been held and dispersed without you, and its place has been taken by anxiety for your health. I was not able to learn anything about you and your affairs, as I wished to do, from your colleague Pontanus,†3 for I did not know he had been here until after he had gone. I beg [p. 460] you to relieve me of this anxiety as soon as possible, and tell me if you are well. Please let Furly know what has been decided about the manuscript,†1 or how the matter stands, for he learnt yesterday that Wetstein has now at last returned. When you meet him please hand him the enclosed letter at your leisure; there is not so much as a word about the manuscript in it; that business is entrusted entirely to you for you to manage it alone. Please remember me to your excellent wife and to the Veens and Guenellons and the whole Collegie. And tell Mr. Guenellon that I would have congratulated him before now on his new abode if I had known how to address the letter correctly. Van Helmont and Furly send you greetings. Good-bye, and love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) Please give my best wishes to Mr. Le Clerc and Du Cene.
I am asking Wetstein in the enclosed letter what has been done about some books of mine, intended for Toinard, which he undertook to dispatch to Paris;†2 if you will ask him and tell him that you will write and tell me his answer you will save him trouble and I shall know about it more quickly.
Address: Mihn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch bij de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsars Gracht tot Amsterdam

1052. Mrs. Isabella Duke and Sir Walter Yonge to Locke, 12 and 16 May (1018, 1061; 1014, 1401)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 27.
[Mrs. Duke:]
Otterton May 12th 88.
Dear Sir
Your most Welcome letter of March the 23d came to my hands above a Month since; but my Brother, who was then in London, kept the Book till now,†1 not being willing to let so great a treasure go out of his possession, till he had well acquainted himself with it, and made his best improvement of it. so that by this contrivance I am as ignorant, and defective as before, (having not yet read one page in it.) unless I have learn'd self deniall by wayting for it; for I can never desire any thing with more impatience, or receive it with more satisfaction, and Thankfulness. Your remembring me at so great a distance, and bestowing on me so valluable a present, is a vast addition to the favours you have formerly heap'd on me. the kindness of it makes deep impressions on me and I hope the Reason of it will do so too, and that in my next I shall be able to give you a better account both of it, and my self; so that you will not think it thrown away upon me. Thus much I might have told you many Weeks since, before I receiv'd the Book, and my inclinations led me sufficiently to it, but I perceived that you did not like the humour I was then in, and that 'twas as disagreable to all the rest of my absent Friends; who accused me of Gravity and of being deeply tinctured with the spleen etc which greatly surprized me because I was at Peace with my self; and my Friends that were with me, did not bring in any complaints against me; besides I had read Senecas Moralls three or four time over, this Winter, which could not fail to cure any ill Humours that otherwise might have hung about me; so that I concluded that the Plannet that then predominated was adverse to me, and that I ought to impose a total silence upon my self till some more favourable Starr gott the ascendant; and so I kept my resolution till the Merry Month of May. I am afraid it has had no good effects on me yet, for it has been Wett and Cloudy hitherto, we have not had one fair day. I am now newly return'd from Escott whither I went to welcome Home my Brother, who is much Yours, and so is Mr Duke and your Daughter
― 462 ―

Betty, who sends you her duty, and hopes that you have not Vowed a perpetual Bannishment from your Native Country, and best Friends; who want nothing but your presence to render them as happy as this World can make them. but 'tis my despair of it that puts me into a Mellancholly humour whenever I am writing to you, and not the thoughts of forty which is an Age I have long wish'd to arrive at, as the best time of ones life; and I find it to answer my expectation as I approach it; I live more in one year now, then I did in the first 20. and am growing on a great pace, and with great pleasure, unto life Eternall. I hope I am not the same that I were when I saw you last, but you may like me the better perhaps. could I get you near me I am sure you would make me so, for the present your book shall supply your place, when you think I have learnt that lesson, pray come and give me a new one. let me not alwayes pray in vain, but remember that I am most sincerely, and unalterably
Your Friend and faithfull servant
ISABELLA DUKE
[Yonge:]
Escott May 16th.
Dear Sir
My Sister has very sensibly obliged me by entrusting me with the conveyance of her letter, for I have thereby an opportunity both to pay you my due thanks for your kind letter and most valuable present, without giving you the trouble of another letter for what may as well be transmitted in a postscript, and likewise to rectify some little mistakes which I find she has drawn you into; for I can assure you there was really neither Mistress nor Courtship in the Case,†1 whatever my designe or my sisters might be, to occasion my stay in Town, but now my other business is over I am returned to Escott, as Errant a Batchellour as I have been these seaven years,†2 and I think should be as Idle a one could I as easily get rid of the builders as the matchmakers, but instead of that One shoulder of mutton (as we say) draws on another,†3 As fast as I can finish one thing I see others as necessary to be done, so that I see no greater Argument for matrimony then that I may have a helpmeet to draw me out of the mortar, and to ease me of some part of
― 463 ―

the burthen of a numerous family.†1 And though I am so overladen with business at present I doe not dispair but I may find a happy leisure in some short time to give my selfe the pleasure and advantage to read your little Tract, which I know can not but answer the satisfaction I felt in receiving so signall a Testimony of your friendship; which I prize at the highest rate at this distance, but shall never be satisfyed or think myselfe well settled at Escott till we have you here amongst us, till that One day comes when you will makes entirely happy in your conversation, a pleasure I find you will not have us dispair of, though at the same time you take great care we should flatter ourselves with the too near approach of that felicity; In the mean time we must content our selves as well as we can with seing your thoughts in your book, in the reading of which I confess I ought before this to have done you Right, as I find my sister presumes I have done. The two volumes of Moreri are in the House amongst my other books, but I think the library will hardly be finished till you come to direct how it should be; I desire you would take Benjamin Furly for your paymaster for them and any thing else you buy for me; and when you see him next pray give him my hearty service, and desire him by any of our Topsham Vessells to send me halfe a dozen more of the lesser sort of the Iron backs†2 he sent me last year, which I have now measured and find to be about 18. inches wide and 2. foot 2. inches high; I have six roomes more to be finished where I designe to use them, but he may take his own time during the summer to send them, which whenever he does I desire he would draw a bill upon me for the value of them and for what you have laid out for me. And I beg the favour of a line or two at your leisure either from yours or his hand to advise us how to cleanse and colour those Iron backs, so as they may look well now in the summer when we make no fires as they doe in Holland. Be pleased to excuse this and command the utmost services of
Dear Sir
Your most obliged friend and most faithfull servant
W.Y.
I desired Mr Clark to write you that I have bought the history of the Incas of Peru in English;†3 but I shall be glad to have Xavier's Gospell†4 too of which I formerly wrote to you.
― 464 ―

Excuse my not writing to our friend Benjamin. I shall be glad to hear that the Eggs I sent the burgemaster produced young ones. I hear nothing of the flowers he mentions.
Address (written by Mrs. Duke): For Mr John Lock at the House of Mr Benjamin Furly Merchant in Rotterdam
In another hand: post pd to Lond° 3d
Postmark: MA 18
Endorsed by Locke: Mrs Duke 12 May 88 and Sr W. Yonge
Answered 29 Jun Answered 17 Sept
1053. Joseph Bowles to Benjamin Furly, [May 1688]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 4, ff. 148-9. Date from Locke's endorsement. I cannot identify the writer.
Mr. Benjamine Furly.
Sir I must allwayes retaine a due sence of your late kindnesse, for which you are desir'd to accept my most intire and affectionate Acknowledgments, assureing you I shall with all cheerfullness Imbrace every occasion in which may doe any Act of Service or office of friendship for you, or those Gentlemen with you in whose Conversation I took so much delight, that makes me desire to Establish a Commerce of thoughts (and other buisness too as occasion offers) on those subjects you gave me a tast while in your company—I have not yet had time to consider the Doctors Abridgement, and therefore am yet stumbling at the threshold—I find the soule call'd tabula rasa. that is, without Ideas or knowledg—I take it that our first notion of vitality is power and capacity, of perception, of appetition, and of Action (for any one of these wanting the other two would remaine useless) And if it be true, that this being while wrapt up in the Notion of power might remaine to all Eternity, to no purpose, equall to a Nonentity, 'till exited†1 by the proposall of Objects, I say in this case, if it be possible to conceive a vitall being to subsist in such a state, it may then be called tabula rasa, without Ideas and knowledg, perception or thought, but how this Differs from nothing, is hard to conceive.
But. (first) may wee not conceive an immateriall vitall being to Exist Unorganiz'd? (secondly) that there hath, or may be, no such thing as body, (thirdly) that such a Vitall being must in such a
― 465 ―

Case, be without Ideas, that is Imagination of body, or it's affections. But (fourthly). wee need not say it should alsoe be without knowledg, and perception of its owne being, or thought, and consequently some Notions of those Various Objects which of necessity are allwayes present with it, as God, time, space, Eternall Truth, and whatsoever doth Exist of Uncaused, and Absolute Necessity, togeather with whatsoever may be created that is not Corporeall—Nor ought wee to suppose that the Uniteing such a Vitall immateriall being with Organiz'd matter, should destroy those primary and essentiall properties of it's being, as perception, thought. etc.—And therefore Under this consideration it seemes the soul is not Tabula rasa.—But by Tabula rasa, some understand white paper and soft wax, Equally receptive of all Impressions, Good or Evil, right or wrong, true or false, And in this Sence 'tis alsoe Questioned whether these Termes may properly be predicated of the Soul, because it can never be Indifferent to those things, nor can contradictions be reconsiled to it.
'Tis yet in doubt whether Sensation and Reflection doe fully and playnely express the Source of all our perceptions and conceptions of things, for if it be suppos'd that without Sensation, men could never have come to Experience and the Scientificall Knowledg of things, Yet the power or faculty of Reason and Understanding is (at least in Order of Nature) before Sensation, for the power of Sensation, doth not begett the power of <Ratiocination>,†a any more than Colour begetts the power of seeing. And may wee not rather think, that Sensation, (which is nothing Else but Organization)†b are but the Instruments which the soul makes use of to discover (Onely) body and the affections thereof, so that wee must ascribe to the soule a distinct mode of perception, superior to sensation, which may be call'd Intellection,†1 Reason, or what you think more fitt to express it:
And then the Question is, Whether it be not more probable that this superior faculty doth Exite sensation, than that sensation should Exite this superior faculty—first Because this Power or faculty of the soul hath its proper Objects, about which it may be more directly Conversant than it can be with bodily Objects, for it can Converse with Immateriall things immediately and without
― 466 ―

the help of sence—Secondly, there is No such thing in us as a Power of Sensation distinct from this supreme faculty, for Sensation Is but Instrumentall. And 'tis this faculty that corrects all the Misprisions it makes by Sence, as is Evident in the whole Doctrine of Refraction and other Instances.—Thirdly, It seemes wee are passive in all Sensation, but 'tis the Activity of this faculty, That often setts the Instruments of sence on worke, and can restraine them when it will—Fourthly This is the most permanent and Essentiall faculty of the soul, for should all Sensation be Suspended (as most of them often are) through defects in Organ or Medium) Yet wee cannot think that the soule at any time should be without thought, or Conception while it hath Variety of Objects to think upon, Compare, Diversifie etc. Nor can it ever want variety of such Objects, as are properly suited and adapted to its faculties as before mentioned.
Sir Your free Conversation makes me Expose my weake and impertinent thoughts to your Correction, which I know can Easily be done, and shall be gratefully accepted—I should much Esteem an English Copy of the Doctors Abridgment, for I feare to misinterpret the french to a friend of mine etc.—Our friend Mr. John Ward†1 is comeing for Holland in three or four dayes, by whome shall send you Burnetts Regalia†2 and Parliamentum Pacificum,†3 if can get it, for hear 'tis called In. One Mr. Philips a Gentleman of my Acquaintance hath translated into English Mr. Vanhelmonts Alphabetum Naturæ,†4 If he please to Give leave, and lend his Cutts it shall be printed: And if you send me Les Oracles†5 you will Increase the Obligations of
Your Assured Friend
JOSEPH BOWLES.
Address: For Mr. Benjamin Furly <Merchant>†a In Roterdam
Endorsed by Locke: J: Bowles May: 88 Answered 4 Jun.
― 467 ―

1054. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, [c. 31 May/10 June 1688] (1051, 1058)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256c. Printed in Ollion, pp. 177-8. Date from van Limborch's note.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Nos per triduum inter eadem fuisse mœnia sine Colloquio sine conventu adeo mihi impossibile videtur ut vix credam Tibi etiam fatenti. Ista negotia tam improbe importuna valde accuso. Te etiam parum insimulo, non quod ad me non accederes id enim in tanto rerum expediendarum cumulo non oportuit: sed quod me per puerum te in urbe esse et in vicinia non monueris. Ego tam vacuus quam tu plenus rerum addesse tibi quavis hora vacanti poteram, etiam expectare domi tuæ otii brevioris intervalla. Vides quam grata quam Chara mihi sit tua Consuetudo, cum eâ præter spem frustratus, de te apud te ipsum queri non abstineam. Cum Amstelodamum profectus fuero me probe ulciscar non te fugiendo sed sæpe et importune domum <tuam>†a ventitando interim pax. nam ita te amo ut patienter ferre non possim mihi eripi tuum vel unius horulæ consortium, ita etiam amo ut non diu possim irasci. Sed hæc raptim, oblatâ hâc scribendi occasione cum jam decedendi tempus
― 468 ―

instaret tabellario. Saluta meo nomine omnes tuos nostrosque. Vale et ut facis me ama
Tui studiosissimum
J LOCKE.
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
That we should have been for three days within the same city walls without conversing or meeting seems to me so impossible that I can hardly believe it even on your confession. I lay the chief blame on those business affairs of yours that are so unconscionably pressing. With you too I find fault a little, not for failing to visit me, which would not have been proper for you with such a load of business on your hands requiring dispatch, but because you did not let me know through a servant that you were in town and in my vicinity. I who am as idle as you are full of affairs could have been with you at any hour when you were free; I could even have waited at your house for your all too brief intervals of leisure. You see how welcome and how precious your society is to me, when being disappointed of it I do not scruple to complain of you to yourself. When I get to Amsterdam I shall take a proper revenge, not by avoiding you but by making myself a frequent and importunate visitor at your house; meantime a truce; for I am so fond of you that not only can I not patiently bear to be robbed of your company even for one little hour; but also I am so fond that I cannot be angry for long. But this in haste, as I got this opportunity for writing when the post was just about to leave. [p. 468]Remember me to all your family and to our friends. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most devoted
J. LOCKE
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch by de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsars Graft tot Amsterdam
Postmark: Amsterdam 3s

1055. Edward Clarke to Locke, 5 June 1688 (1050, 1057)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 48-9. Printed in Rand, pp. 274-5. Answered by no. 1057.
London 5th. of June 1688.
Deare Sir
Saturday night last I Return'd hither from the West, and found my Wife and Children well here; I was with your Cosen Stratton at Sutton-Court, and at his own House about a fortnight since, but could not bee soe serviceable to you there as I design'd by reason Hee had not, nor could not possibly (as Hee said) make out your Accompt for mee, But Promised to Return fifty pounds of your money hither to mee with the first opportunity, And make His Accompt perfect against my comeing againe into that Countrey; There are generally greate Complaints of the Difficultyes to rayse money amongst Tennants, but I meete with none greater then those I have hear'd from Mr. Stratton, the Tennants thereabouts being much worse then formerly, and (as Hee sayes) are grown soe Poore and scarce, That unlesse they are permitted to have theire Rents Left in theire Handes for a considerable time, and other Advantages besides, there is not a Tennant to bee had for any thing in those Parts, By all which I presume there are some Arreares greater then Hee was willing to lett mee Know the Particulars of at that time, espetially haveing a Prospect that the Greatest part of them will bee
― 469 ―

speedily gotten in; Mr Stratton hath followed the method I directed, and without any difficulty or trouble hath gott into His handes your Lease to Robert Harol of the Home-close at Beluton etc: which will bee a further security for what remaines due from Him to <you and>†aprevent Him in his designe of makeing such unreasonable Advantages upon you as Hee intended by it, my time at present will not permitt mee to give you a more Particular Accompt of your affayres in Somersett, but if I can bee soe happy as to see you this summer, as I intended, you will then bee more fully inform'd, but ever since I fix'd my thoughts on that Injoyment, every thing has seem'd to conspire against mee in it, First, many Crosse Accidents in my own Affayres have happen'd, besides the Death of my Lady King which brought mee into a Trust for Her Children, And imediately upon that the Sicknesse and Death of my Cosen Clarke's Lady here, Hee being at that time extreame ill and since Dead in the Countrey,†1 Leaveing the Care of His Estate, and Fower younge Children upon mee, hath soe much increased my Affayres and troubles, that at present I can hardly see a Way through them, but Notwithstanding these and many other unexpected Misfortunes that have happened, yett Madam and I are not totally without hopes of seeing you before wee Return into the West, if there bee a Possibility of my getting soe much time as to come to you, which I most earnestly and heartily wish for; Your Freind mrs. R:S: is just now come in with your Letter that came inclosed the last weeke to Her for mee, and gives you Her Reall Love and Service, but at present the time will not permitt mee to Answer any part of it, but you may bee certaine I will carefully performe what is therein desiered, and Answere it with the first opportunity, and for ever remaine
Your most affectionate Freind and Faithfull servant
E:†b
Madam gives her service to you etc:
Address: For Mr. John Lock These
Endorsed by Locke: E. Clarke†c 5 Jun. 88 Answered 22

1056. Locke to Lady Guise, 11/21 June 1688 (1044)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 51-2. Probably written for dispatch, and then treated as a draft. Answers no. 1044.
Rotterdam 21 Jun 88
Madam
If I continue to importune your Ladyship with my letters you must thank your self for it; and you must not think to ruin, as you have don, that litle modesty I once had without feeling some of the ill effects of it. I was wont not to be able to bear without pain and confusion, undeserved commendations and thanks, that were bestowed upon me. This I am sure, I was never farther from haveing a title to any than those which your Ladyship has been pleased to heap upon me of both kindes: But yet I know not how you put them into such words that tis impossible to avoid being pleasd in reading them. I can not be convinced that you give the merit you seem to acknowledg for I finde after all I have it not. But yet you doe something that approaches it and what I receive from you does almost as well. For provided one be happy it matters not whether it be, by ones own purchase or the bounty of another. Think me soe Madam I beseech you as often as I receive those marks of your Ladyships esteem and favour: And beleive that however I have thus long forborne to trouble you with my thanks out of considerations of respect, yet it is too much to live always silent under the sense of such obligations, and not return one word of acknowledgment. I see by your Ladyships letter there are men touchy enough to be put into a heat by my litle treatise, which I think has none in it. If they are soe concerned for truth and religion as becomes sober men, they will answer the end of its publication and shew me the mistakes in it. But if they are of those religious men, who when they can shew noe faults in his book can look into the heart of the author and there see flaws in the religion of him that writ it, though there be noe thing concerning religion in it, only because it is not suited to the systems they were taught I leave them to bethink themselves whether they are his disciples whose command it was Judg not. Such gossiping talkers who supply the want of knowledg with a shew of zeale, and who if censure and tatle were reason and argument would certainly be very infallible I leave to their own good humor and charity, It haveing seldom been observed that any are forward to suspect or question others religion but those who want
― 471 ―

such a masque to cover some defect in their own. I have soe sincerely proposd truth to my self in all†a- I have-†a writ and doe soe much prefer it to my owne opinion that I shall think my self obleiged to any one who will shew me where I have missed it.
Endorsed by Locke: JL to L: Guise 21 Jun. 88
1057. Locke to Edward Clarke, [12/22] June 1688 (1055, 1060)
Rand, pp. 276-8. Words, etc., in square brackets are supplied by Rand. Date: The day from Locke's endorsement of no. 1055; Clarke's date in the endorsement is the old-style date of receipt. Answers no. 1055; answered by no. 1060.
[22nd] June, 1688.
Dear Sir,
It was very good news by yours of the 5th that you were come up to town, and that all the family were well, but better that you intended not that the farthest of your journey. I wish for nothing more, but how much soever I wish it, I cannot consent it should be with the least straitening to you or your affairs.
I see you have been, as you are wont, careful of my affairs more than I have the confidence to desire. I expect no other news from Sutton than what you send me. My cousin is a slow man and let them get in arrears, when complaints and backwardness of tenants was not at that pitch it is now, and therefore it is not to be wondered if he in the common distemper yields to what is grown almost a fashion. I dare say he is not one of those who shall reform it. But who can help it? I must either suffer this or resolve to part with what I have there. But of that [later when] we talk with one another. In the meantime, though I love not to be cozened, yet I have no great reason to be afflicted, for I have meat and drink and clothes as much as I need, and what should I complain of?
I see your stock of orphans increases every day. Worth and honesty I perceive produces children, as well as love and matrimony. I am your eldest charge and must desire to keep the place; and I fear the great boy will not give you the least trouble. Should they all write so many and so long letters as I do to you, that were enough to wear you out. I confess my fault, but fear I shall not much
― 472 ―

mend it; for if I knew anybody I loved better, I might talk with you less.
Since my last I have read a letter from Mr. Oakley†1 whereby I find he has done what Adrian desired of him. But has not been able to forbear what I presume Adrian also desired him. He loves to be a man of business. At any rate it would choke him, if his tongue might not go, whether with rhyme or reason it matters not. The very mention of holding his peace is like a cork that makes perfect bottle beer of it, and yet it must sputter. He tells me himself he has been talking of it to my ... F.†2 If he, when he sees you, takes any notice of it to you, you must tell him that Mr. Oakley meddles in business wherein he has neither commission nor knowledge, and loves to be talking he knows not what. This I think is best to be said to him, for I think not seasonable to discourse to him at large that whole affair, nor to show him how my name has been brought in question without any desire or so much as knowledge of mine....†a But at present I think there be reasons why it should not be mentioned to him.
By a letter I received just now from Adrian I find Mr. Oakley is gone into the country. He has left two books of mine with Awnsham Churchill to be sent me. Though they be but little ones, yet I value them very much, and sent to him for them only upon presumption he would bring them himself. I desire you to take them into your custody till you can meet with a safe hand to send them by, and if you go out of town before that happens pray leave them with Mr. R. S.†3 You will do me a favour also to tell Mr. Churchill that Adrian gave him order to send me some books which I never yet heard of, and which therefore I desire him to send me by the first opportunity, and also an octavo, or one of the least quarto Bibles, that are printed with the chronology set down at the top of every page.
Pray present my most humble service to Madam. Tell her she must hold her resolution. I am,
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate humble servant,
J. L.
― 473 ―

Address: For Mr. Edward Clarke, at the Lady King's in Salisbury Court, near Fleet Street, London.
Endorsed by Clarke: John Locke's letter 18th June, 1688, about Mr. Oakley, and about 2 books to be sent to him.

Vir Spectatissime
Quantumvis obfirmato animo minas meas non expavescis, senties tamen aliquando datâ occasione quid sit irritasse crabronem in eo enim genere meritò numerari possit provocatus iratusque amicus. Nondum vidi Acta illa Lipsiensia ubi tu coram sisteris,†1 sed euge jam salva res est. Incæpi de istius operis merito pretioque aliquo modo dubitare, quod nemo ex systematicis illis reperiret in eo tractatu quod displiceret, nihil enim argumenti aut boni aut novi deberet continere nec quod supra vulgus saperet si vulgo placeret. sed jam vapulas, laudo, nec vibices metuo. benignior his paedagogis si non voluntas, saltem vis est quam ut eorum virgæ
― 474 ―

vulnera vel cicatrices relinquant. Conditiones subscriptionum†1 plus semel in Angliam misi sed hactenus responsi nihil accepi, ego data occasione iterum et ad alios mittam quo successu nescio, hæc enim et hujusmodi nisi præsto adsis, et hæsitantes impellas, immemores moneas plerumque negliguntur. Quod de Judæo narras†2 valde placet, brevi habebitis spero quæ sufficient ad justum volumen in quo Sanctitas officii ad plenum depicta omnium oculos animosque in sui admirationem arripiat. Dolendum plane esset tot et tanta sanctitatis exempla in tenebris latere, prodeant tandem in lucem ut quibus fundamentis stabilitur et propagatur fides tandem innotescat. Simonii historia critica Novi Testamenti jam diu sub prælo est et post mensem unam vel alteram prodibit†2
(Latin) 
22 June
Esteemed Sir, 
You may refuse as obstinately as you like to be frightened by my threats; yet some day if I get the chance you will feel what it is to have roused a hornet; for a provoked and angry friend may justly be reckoned as belonging to that species. I have not yet seen that number of the Leipzig Acta in which you appear in person;†1 but bravo! now all's well. I began to have some doubts about the merits and value of that work of yours, as none of those systematical gentry found anything to disagree with in that treatise; for it must have contained no argument either good or new or anything above the heads of the herd, if it was to please the herd. But you are now having your whipping; I commend you, and I have no fear of weals. These schoolmasters, you know, if their intention is not too kind, are at any rate too weak to [p. 474] make their rods leave wounds or scars. I have sent to England more than once giving them the terms for subscriptions,†1 but so far I have had no reply; I shall send again and to others when I get an opportunity, with what success I do not know; for unless one is standing at their elbow, urging them on when they stick and jogging their memory, things of this sort are apt to be neglected. I am very glad to hear what you tell me about the Jew;†2 you will, I hope, soon have enough material for a regular volume, giving such a complete picture of the holiness of that Office, as may draw all eyes and minds to admire it. It would be a crying shame for so many striking examples of holiness to remain hidden in darkness; may they see the light at last and make known on what foundations the faith is established and propagated. About the MS. volume I have nothing to say; our friend Furly wrote to you about that two days ago. I guess from this that you see Wetstein from time to time; when you do, please hand him the enclosed letter, which I take the liberty of sending to you. I wrote to him a fortnight ago; I also sent him some books and asked for others to be sent to me, and speedily; but I hear nothing; he does not answer. I am the more worried by his silence because I had sent [p. 475] at the same time two volumes of Garcilaso de la Vega†1 to be returned to Mr. Veen, from whom I had borrowed them some time ago; there was also a letter from me to him with them. Please remember me to him and the rest of our Collegians. Good-bye, my dear friend, and continue to love me
Your most devoted
J. L.
(Latin) I send my best wishes to your excellent wife.
Simon's critical history of the New Testament has now been in the press a long time and will come out in a month or two.†2
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch by de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsars Graft tot Amsterdam
Postmark: Amsterdam 3s
1059. Awnsham Churchill to Locke [c. 7-18 June 1688] (2566)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, f. 95. Date: On the assumption that the books are those ordered by Thomas (p. 453), Locke could not have received the letter before 12/22 June, when he wrote to Clarke asking him to instruct Churchill to dispatch them and to include a Bible (p. 472); Churchill could not have written the letter long after 18 June, O.S., when Clarke received Locke's letter, or he would have mentioned the Bible.
Awnsham Churchill, d. 1728, was a son of William Churchill of Dorchester, Dorset. The father was a bookseller, active from about 1655 to 1688. Awnsham began to publish on his own account in 1681; his brother John joined him in 1690. The brothers and Jacob Tonson were the leading Whig booksellers. The Churchills published, besides much else, the Collection of Voyages
― 476 ―

in which Locke was interested, Bishop Edmund Gibson's edition of Camden's Britannia, 1695, and Rymer's Foedera, 1704-15. Awnsham was M.P. for Dorchester from 1705 to 1710. Notice in D.N.B.; his character emerges in his surviving letters to Locke, mainly from 1700 onwards.

1061. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 30 June 1688 (1052, 1085)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 28-9.
Otterton June 30th. 88
Dear Sir
Though I have written to you very lately, and very largly, yet I must beg leave to trouble you again with two lines, to propose to you a Material Question which was then forgotten, and which nearly concerns me. to witt whither you think that the use of the Bathe may be a propper and effectual remedy, for the disorder I have so long lain under; I know 'tis Vulgarly esteem'd a great strengthener of all those parts, and many Women have found great Benifit by it; but my Case is particular, and I am no competent Judge whither it may be good for me, or not, or whither it may not be injurious to my Health in General. Good Sir give me your Opinion fully, and freely, and send it me assoon as possibly you can, for I shall go into that Country about fortnight hence, to wayt on my
― 480 ―

Sister that was lately Married,†1 from whose house I may go to Bath with Ease; and before the Year be too far past. If you send me thither, I beg instructions which Bath to use, and for how many dayes, and whither any other remedies must be used together with it, as assistants; and with your Opinion give me Your reasons for it, I beseech you. not but that I would follow it to a tittle, with an implicit Faith, but for my better instruction, which you have promised to contribute to, on all occasions. forgive Dear Sir my Freedom, my Brevity, and all other Omissions, which my haste makes me Guilty of, since I am in danger of losing this Post, which would be a great inconvenience to me, since the sooner I have your answer, the greater will the favour be; Your Friends are all well, as Mr Clark will tell <you>†a more at large, who I hear is on his way towards you. I do not envy him that Happiness, but I wish I could share it with him. adieu. I am Ever
Sir
Most affectionately and most faithfully Yours
ISABELLA DUKE
I remember you once told me a present remedy if a Lance should happen to prick an Artery in Bloodletting; I have quite forgotten it, pray repeat it in your next. adieu.

Deare freind
I have all ready answered your former letter as I now doe this of Jul 2d. and thanke for your advice therein to send my sonne Will to Dr Sidneham which I entend to doe the next month.

1064. William Molyneux to the authors of the Bibliotheque universelle, 7 July 1688.
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 92-3.
The writer became a correspondent and friend of Locke in 1692: no. 1515. He was a brother of Dr. (later Sir) Thomas Molyneux (no. 800). His problem appears to be loosely connected with Abregé, II.vii (pp. 6-10), which deals with Perception, and corresponds to the Essay, parts of II.viii and ix. Le Clerc and Locke ignored it at this time; Molyneux repeated it in a letter to Locke, 2 March 1693, and Locke then incorporated it in the second edition of the Essay: no. 1609; see also no. 1984.
The problem attracted much attention in England and abroad in the eighteenth century: K. T. Hoppen, The Common Scientist in the Seventeenth Century: a study of the Dublin Philosophical Society 1683-1708, 1970, pp. 172-4.
Dublin July. 7. 88.
A Problem Proposed to the Author of the Essai Philosophique concernant L'Entendement.
A Man, being born blind, and having a Globe and a Cube, nigh of the same bignes, Committed into his Hands, and being taught or Told, which is Called the Globe, and which the Cube, so as easily to distinguish them by his Touch or Feeling; Then both being
― 483 ―

taken from Him, and Laid on a Table, Let us suppose his Sight Restored to Him; Whether he Could, by his sight, and before he touch them, know which is the Globe and which the Cube? Or Whether he Could know by his sight, before he stretchd out his Hand, whether he Could not Reach them, tho they were Removed 20 or 1000 feet from him?
If the Learned and Ingenious Author of the Forementiond Treatise think this Problem Worth his Consideration and Answer, He may at any time Direct it to One that Much Esteems him, and is
His Humble servant
WILLIAM MOLYNEUX
High Ormonds Gate in Dublin. Ireland.
Address: Pour Les Auteurs de la Bibliotheque
A Monsieur Monsieur Waesberg Merchand Librair a Amsterdam Paid to Lond. 6d.
Postmark: IY 16
Endorsed by Locke: W. Molineux 7 Jul. 88
1065. Mrs. Anna Grigg to Locke, 22 June and 8 July [1688] (1048, 1121)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 156-7. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Dr. Francis Turner, bishop of Ely, of whose household Mrs. Grigg was a member, was one of the Seven Bishops sent to the Tower on 8 June for petitioning against James II's order that his Declaration for Liberty of Conscience should be read in all churches on two successive Sundays. The bishops were released on their recognizances on 15 June and were tried for seditious libel on the 29th; the verdict of acquittal was delivered on the 30th. Two of the four judges summed up in favour of the accused and were dismissed on 7 July.
Deare Brother
Tho my head and heart is very full of what now fils all Gazets,†1 I will as well as I can answer your kind caveling letter; The Book you sent me is againe entertaining a Gentleman who has a world of Wit, and who is so pleasd with what you write that I cannot obtaine
― 484 ―

of him to find the least fault, I have tried others but all are Obstenatly bent to commend it as much as Monsieur Capel,†1 who by the by told me that discoursing with Mr Boyle, the Noble Gentleman complaind only of your being too Abstracted.†2 The Deane of Canterbury†3says this to me, in truth Mr Locks Book is a mervelous ingenious piece, it has no fault but that its writ in french, and this fault is the reason I send you no larger account of it, divers of my new and very learned friends being deprived of the pleasure of reading it. This lame Answer you must pardon, for till you think fit to make use of your own Country Language, I cannot speak more particularly.
I was begining such a letter to you as would have bin sad and large enough to shew you how willing I am to convers with you and according to my former freedom was ready to tell you my whole heart, but honesty and truth are often so il used that I durst not venture to utter what I every moment deplore and cannot but muz on perpetually, nor am I alone in my raveries, Many hundred Thousands doe as I doe; Nor would you know England were you in it, all that you and I use to call worthy persons are full of affliction,†4 and more inclin'd to vissit you than wish you here, Now are the spirits of the children of men tried, and for my comfort not one of those I did or doe love depart from the paths of righteousness and peace (tho extremly provoked) but such as cald the Bishops papist are drudging slaves to father Peters.†5
I cannot say that any true friend of yours is well but divers remember you very respectfully, and particularly those to whome I am beyond expression obliged and for whome I have the tenderest concerne, such as shall make me a sincere sharer in all their distreses.
I cannot enough thank you for your affectionate enquiries after my son, I thank God I hear nothing but good of him, he is now an old Sophister, and will be batchelor next Christmas (if the Universities stand so long), poor Lad he sees Clouds and darkness about him, but I hope he will consider the more, and learn in adversity that wisdom which is so often neglected in the dayes of prosperity.†6
― 485 ―

If you continue in the mind of sending over a box of Books to be keept for you please to send them to Mr Smith at the Princes Armes in St Pauls Churchyard.†1
June the 22th 88
but in your letter of advice Name the books you send, this letter was designed by the post the day it was dated, but tis no matter what becomes of it tis so madly put togeather, but realy brother I have not a moments rest but whilst I sleepe so great and continued a Court attends the 7 Champions of whose conduct and diliverence the worthy barer of this†2 will give you a large account, and by him I may without doing you mischief assure you that the very good Bishope of Ely is your true friend speak often of you with great respect, what next is to be don with us I know not hitherto those arts which have bin us'd to root out the Church and with her the Laws of England have by the goodness of God don much good, having served to demonstrat who are the men that keep innocence and fence us from Popery and Slavery, you need not be told how much business the present contests cut out for ingenious men, nor how all our thoughts are employ'd, dayly new papers come abroade and those of greatest spirit and use are said to be yours,†3 you are in a glorious spot of the world Keep you in it a while longer, I have faith enough to cheer my heart and to fancy strongly that popery is spending itself and will soon expire by its extreme violence,†4 let me hear from you or I will be spitefull
I may be with you before you expect me, pray Brother don't continue a stranger to the Hague nor be afraide to apear where we are so like to be driven for sanctuary. My pen you se rambles already but my heart is very steady to my friends
July the 8th

1066. William Charleton to Locke, 12 July 1688 (1022)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 80-1.

Dear Sir
Though I did not give you my thanks for the several curious things you sent me before now by reason of my Lady Dowager of Exeter's decease and the obligation that lay upon me to go down with her body to Burleigh,†1 yet so favourable an occasion as offers it self at present of Conveying my thanks to you by a worthy friend of yours and mine†2 Could not be omitted, and as I am satisfied that the great civility he ha's shew'd me has been upon your account, so I return you my acknowledgements for the kindness you have done me in procuring me his acquaintance. I am verry sorry that Sir Henry Hobart is still at his seat at Blicklin In Norfolk but I shall not be unmindfull of your desires when he comes to town. I am much obliged to you for the favor of the book you sent me and being sensible how unfit I was to pass censure on any thing that came from your pen, I did without naming it's Author†3shew it to some persons of my friends who were more fit judges and they did much commend it. wishing our freind and you a happy meeting I take my leave that am Dear Sir
Your most humble and most obliged servant
WILLIAM CHARLETON
