1067. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 13/23 July 1688 (1011, 1069)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 23-4. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 28-9. Answered by no. 1069.
A Amsterdam le 23 de Juillet 1688.
Monsieur
Voici le neuviéme Tome de nôtre Bibliotheque,†1 dont j'ai cru <qu'il>†a valloit mieux vous faire coûter le port, que de trop tarder à vous l'envoier, en attendant une occasion. Il a paru un peu plus tard qu'il n'avoit accoûtume non par ma faute, mais par celle de M de la Crose.†2 Je vous prie d'examiner à la rigueur l'Essai touchant la Poësie des Hebreux†3 , et de m'en marquer vos sentimens, avec cette liberté Philosophique qui fait, selon moi, le plus grand assaisonnement de l'amitié. Car il m'est important de reconnoître au plûtôt mon erreur, si je me suis trompé, puis que, comme vous savez mieux que moi, il en est de l'erreur comme de la Renommée Crescit eundo.†4 M. Meibom†5 qui l'a vu en a parlé, selon sa coûtume, avec indignation, quoi qu'il avoüe qu'il y a quelque chose de bon. Il croit avoir trouvé le secret de la Poësie des Hebreux, qui est, dit-il, different, et qu'il ne donnera jamais au public qu'on ne lui comte cinquante mille francs. A dire la Verité entre Vous et moi, quoi que j'estime sa science, je ne le crois pas capable de découvrir une chose de cette nature, parce qu'il faut quelque raisonnement, et que le bon homme n'excelle pas de ce côté là. Je me persuade que pour être bon critique, il faut avoir consideré les Langues d'une maniere bien plus philosophique que lui ne sauroit faire. Pour moi j'ai tâché de le faire autant qu'une vie cousuës d'occupations aussi embarrassantes que la mienne me l'a pu permettre. Vôtre troisiéme Livre m'a
― 488 ―

beaucoup confirmé en diverses pensées que j'avois euës touchant la maniere d'expliquer les écrits des Anciens, et m'a ouvert l'esprit pour faire attention à des choses où je n'avois pas assez pensé. Vous verrez dans le X Tome de la Bibliotheque, que je dois composer moi seul, si j'ai profité de vos idées, car il se trouve qu'il y a des livres qui me donnent occasion de m'étendre sur cette matiere, ce que je fais volontiers, parce que je vois qu'elle est presque inconnue.†1 Je suis vôtre tres-humble et tres-obeissant serviteur
J LE CLERC
On m'a dit que la Critique du N.T. de M. Simon étoit imprimée. Leers n'en envoiera ici que le plus tard qu'il pourra. Si elle est en vente, je vous supplie de m'en acheter un exemplaire et de l'envoier en blanc par le bâteau, adressé à Wetstein. Je vous rendrai ce qu'il aura coûté
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke tot Mynheer Benjamin Furly Tot Rotterdam
Endorsed by Locke: Clerc 23 Jul 88

1069. Locke to Jean Le Clerc, 20/30 July [1688] (1067, 1082)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 258u. Printed in Fox Bourne, ii. 76-9. Person addressed and year from contents. Answers no. 1067.
Rotterdam. 30 Jul:
Sir
I know not why you should excuse the slow sending the ninth tome of your Bibliotheque, unlesse you have made to your self some law I know not of, and which I cannot suppose without a mighty increase of the obligation. Your discourse of the Hebrew Poetry I have red with mighty satisfaction, and am soe far from haveing any thing to say against your hypothesis that it seems to me as clear as any demonstration can be concerning such matters for soe I call such evident probabilitys as ariseing from the things them selves leave noe counterballance on the other side. I know not what cavils prejudice or party may raise against you, for some men who are devoted to a sect and not to Truth are never to be satisfied, and tis noe great matter whether they are or noe. If it were necessary to adde any thing to that full proof you have given of the Hebrew Verses being in rhime, I thinke one might say that the other by measure is unnaturall and had never been in the world had
― 490 ―

not the variety of dialects, of the Greeks useing the same language in several distinct communitys, by their various placeing and formeing their words given occasion to it.
The Romans who derived their language and learning from the Greeks were almost under a necessity to follow their way of Poetry too, but wanted soe much of the conveniencys of that language to doe it, that it was very late before poetry got any footing amongst them and then it was only Hexameters, which have the greatest latitude except their Dramatique Trimiters etc: which differ litle from prose, For Horace was the first as well as almost the last amongst the Romans that durst venture their tongue at Lyrick poetry. And he too with his great witt and command of expressions, was fain in many places to transgresse the rules of his language and with Gretian†a liberty use forain ways of speakeing to accomodate his words to the measures of the Greek verses he imitated. Besides these two languages I think there cannot be another produced wherein their way of versifying is not in rhime. For however you have Quoted the English for writeing verses without rhime, yet I know but one man that has don soe, and he too one much versed in, and addicted to the Greek and Roman politer learning, whose admiration of their poetry put him as I imagin on that way of writeing.†1Some translations I thinke there may be too in that way of blanck verse, as we call them, but they are litle regarded and scarce thought different from prose. And we see as you your self have observed, that as soon as the Greeke language began to be out of vogue and use amongst the Romans rhimeing poetry came in also in their language, which as I said I think is the most naturall way of verses. which the Greeks alone (who affected to be Originals in every thing) had the conveniency and boldnesse to transgresse. For the Romans I count only their schollers. If there be any thing in the whole essay wherein I differ at all from you, it is only in this, that I wish you had left out the supposition you make p. 239 that perhaps sometimes here and there they neglected the rhime, which is not very probable, if their poetry consisted in it, and we never see it don in rhimeing verses, any more then the feet are neglected in
― 491 ―

metrical. for this would be to write half verse half prose.
This though it be a reason to me against that supposition, yet is not that for which I except against it. For I sho<uld>†a not be much curious to enquire into the Ancient Poetry of the Jews, if it terminated in a bare speculation concerning this peice of Antiquity. That which affects me in it is, the prospect I have that it may be of mighty use to correct many errors and give us a great light into the present state of the Hebrew text as we have it. But if it be once granted that in their poetry they neglected the rhyme, it will be apt to stop mens farther enquiry where they can make out the sense of the text without it. But on the othersid I should rather conclude that where ever the rhime is wanting there our copys differ from the original. Nor are we to think there was noe rhime because we cannot now make it out with as good sense as it carys in our present reading without it. For if to the difficultys (you mention) one adde this, That the books written in Hebrew which are come to our hands can not be supposd to contein the whole compasse of that language, one†b- shall quickly loose the hopes of reforming all the faults of the Copistes.-†b They had noe doubt many words and expressions which are noe where in the scripture. And had we noe other remains of the Roman language than what is to be found in the writeings of Tully and Livy (which are a great deale more than our old Testament conteins) we should thereby be very ill able to re-establish a very imperfect copy of Horaces Odes writ like prose if such an one alone had been all could have been found of him. But I think we should not from thence conclude that the Romans used to neglect the just measure of their feet, because we could not at this distance reduce them into that exactnesse by any change of words we could finde to supply the defects of the ill written copy. I shall make noe apologie for taking this liberty, haveing donne it in obedience to your commands or rather to provoake you to the same with me on some other occasion. The discovery you have made I thinke of great use and I wish as your leisure will permit you would goe on in reduceing the Psalmes into their Original rhimes as far as out of the state they now are <in>,†c it is possible to be donn. I have some farther questions to propose to you on this subject but my letter is already grown beyond the measure I at first designed it: And yet I must not conclude it without telling you that I wonder you soe litle esteem the Gent, you mention, capable of
― 492 ―

penetrateing far into the Eastern Poetry.†1 Methinks he has the most poetical head of any man I ever met with. His visions are beyond the reach of those dull people who conduct their thoughts by paltry reason, And he must needs have a large Farme in Parnassus who can expect soe great an income from it. The truth is in all but his meat drinke clothes and some such other foolish accoutrements of life he is very rich, and if the world would but take off those commodities he has at his rate, he would be noe small man. The mischeif is the ignorant world Knows not how to value them, and soe the exchange of knowledg for money is not made, though wanted on both sides. and I see noe remedy for it, but we must be condemnd to ignorance and he to threadbare clothes. though who can but thinke it great pitty that a head which is the treasury of such a masse of pretious knowledg should be coverd with a peruke soe much weatherbeaten and out of repair? About two months since I was told at Leers's that P. Simons Hist: critique du N.T. was in the presse and that it would be don about this time, but being last week at his shop I saw fower and twenty sheets of it, all that was then printed of threescore which they say it will amount to, soe that according to this reconing we may expect it will be published about fower months hence.†2 I longue to see your next volume and shall not be a litle confirmed in my opinion concerning the whole businesse of words as I have treated it in my third book, if I finde your thoughts concur with it and that it may be applyd with any advantage to the understanding of ancient writers which I have been apt to thinke the ordinary way of Criticks leads not to. I cannot, nor I ought not to finde fault with this ninth tom of your Bibliotheque But yet I cannot forbeare to tell you that it wants the Asteriscks of distinction†3 which you have don me the favour to place at the begining of some of the other toms I am
Sir your most humble and most obedient servant
J LOCKE

1070. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 20/30 July [1688] (1058, 1090)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256e. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 322-3; omitted sentence and address in Ollion, p. 178. Year from van Limborch's note.
(English) 
Rotterodami 30 Jul.†a
Vir Spectatissime
Sive iratum me sive gratum existimari vellem sentio me jam nimis diu tacuisse. Amicum amico respondisse, crabronem irritanti vindictam retulisse citiùs oportuit. Sed ego nescio qua ingenii tarditate nec amici nec inimici partes rectè ago. An tibi hoc modo placere possim nescio, me Slado nostro (si cum eo ita <agerem>†b ) valde displiciturum sat scio, qui hujusmodi Lentulos æquo animo ferre non potest. Editionem M.S. de quo cum Wetstenio transigebas dolendum plane est non procedere, et metuo si jam non procedat <illius>†c impressio ne intereat tam luculentum historiæ monumentum, quod sane multis quæ jam omnium manibus versantur libris longe anteferendum existimo. Multâ cum voluptate legi Clerici nostri tentamen, ut ipse vocat, de antiquâ Hebræorum poesi. Non parum lucis inde affulsurum psalmis, reliquis quæ in S. Scriptura extant scriptis metricis minime dubito, Totum psalmorum librum sibi ita restitutum edi optarem, incites illum
― 494 ―

rogo ut quantum per alia negotia liceat hoc opus festinet. Cuidam meo amico in literis Hebræis versatissimo†1 cum hoc dixissem credere non potuit, exemplo persuasus jam credet. Plura habui dicenda, sed adventus amici ex Anglia†2 hic me interpellat, adeo ut in aliud tempus sint rejicienda. Optimam tuam Fæminam, Collegas et amicos saluto Vale et me ama
Tui studiosissimum
J LOCKE
(Latin) 
Rotterdam 30 Jul.
Esteemed Sir,
Whether I wanted to be thought angry or grateful, I feel that I have now held my peace too long. A friend should have replied to a friend and a hornet should have taken vengeance on the provoker more quickly than this. But through some sort of temperamental slowness I do not play the part of either friend or foe aright. I do not know whether you may be pleased with me for this behaviour; I know well enough that our friend Sladus would be highly displeased if I treated him in this fashion, for he cannot put up with such slowcoaches. It is certainly a pity that the publication of the manuscript for which you were negotiating with Wetstein is not going forward, and I fear that unless the printing of it is now proceeded with we may lose such an excellent historical monument, which I consider far superior to many books that are now in general circulation. I much enjoyed reading our friend Le Clerc's essay, as he himself calls it, on ancient Hebrew poetry. I have little doubt that much light will be shed by it on the Psalms and the rest of the metrical passages to be found in the Holy Scriptures. I should like to see an edition of the whole Book of Psalms thus restored to its proper self; I beg you [p. 494] will encourage him to hurry on with this task so far as his other affairs permit. I mentioned this to a certain friend of mine who is well versed in Hebrew learning,†1 and he could not believe it; the example will now persuade him to believe. I had more to say, but am interrupted by the arrival of a friend from England,†2 so I must put off the rest to another time. Remember me to your excellent wife, and to our Collegians and friends. Good-bye, and love me
Your most devoted
J. LOCKE
Address: Mÿn Heer Mÿn Heer Limborch by de Remonstransce Kerck op de Keÿsars Gracht tot Amsterdam

(Latin) 
Rotterdam 5 August 88
I hope you will have understood before now from my letter of 9 July†3 why I was so late in answering your previous one. If I have been guilty of the [p. 495] same fault once again my excuse must be the claims of certain friends who are travelling through these provinces; their reason for coming here from England was, I might almost say, the hope of seeing me, and they wanted my company for the rest of their journey; so it was only when I returned home two days ago that I got an opportunity to read your latest letter of 16 July and to write in return. That letter now makes your reason for sorrow sufficiently clear, and it affects me in the same way in no small degree; I shall miss the kindly companionship of a very dear friend and the judgement of a most experienced man. It is sad indeed that the fates take no account of skill and merit; if that were so, a man of such eminent character and learning would have lived longer. Reflect on this, I beg you, and then perhaps you will give more thought to your Harmony.
(Latin) I am glad to receive the Corrosive Troches; I embrace the friendship of his kinsman with gratitude and with equal warmth and I hope to have some correspondence with him. Wetstein has let me know that six of my booklets have at last been sent to the Paris bookseller Esclossan for you, together with Volume 1 of Kabbala Denudata.
(Latin) In case Wetstein's dallying should have kept you waiting too long I sent one copy of my epitome to Paris by the hand of a friend to the address of Mr. de Noyers;†1 I hope this and the other items have reached you some time ago. [p. 496] Please let Mr. Deshais Gendron have the copy which was intended for his uncle.
(Latin) Your last letter arrived safely and in good time. My best respects to the Captain; I eagerly await your opinion and his, as also of others, on what I have written. Good-bye. J L

1073. John Shower to Locke [17/27(?) August 1688]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 93-4. Shower is likely to have been in Rotterdam rather than elsewhere; the letter apparently refers to Clarke's final departure; hence probably Friday 27 August, N.S.
John Shower, 1657-1715, nonconformist divine; at this time evening lecturer at the English Presbyterian Church in Rotterdam. He was associated with Sir Samuel Barnardiston and John Howe, and his present wife was a niece of Thomas Papillon: D.N.B.
Kind Sir,
Being hindred this Evening beyond my expectation from paying my respects to you and Mr. Clarke before you goe from hence, must crave your Pardon; which could hardly hope for, (after so many obligations as I am under) from any but so Generous a Friend as you. I deny my self the honour of seeing you with the more regret, because have not yet been able to fasten any testimony of my Gratitude for your extraordinary Kindness to me and mine; but hope to see you at your Return, wishing a safe and prosperous voyage to your worthy friend Mr. Clarke, I beg you would believe that I am (as very sensibly obliged,)
Sir
Yours to honour and serve you
J. SHOWER.
Fryday Evening.

1075. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 6 September 1688 (1068, 1084)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, f. 67.

Deare Freind

your obliged ADRIAN

1077. Edward Clarke to Locke, 16 September 1688 (1060, 1080)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 52. Printed in Rand, pp. 278-80.
Deare Sir
I hope my Letters from Dover and London are before this time in your handes; By this you will see I am not yett gott home, being forc'd to leave Madam in London, Bartlemew-Fayre affording soe much Businesse, t'was impossible to procure such a Dispatch as to gett Her out of Town with mee, however shee Promised to overtake mee here this Evening, where I have been forc'd to spend the greatest part of the Weeke past in the Execution of the Trust for my Cosen Clarks Children, But heareing that your Noble-Freind†1 was prepareing to leave Wylton for the Wynter-season, I went with Adrian to waite on Him, where I presume wee were the more kindly Received by the Intelligence wee brought Him of your Wellfare, your Letter Hee Received from mee with greate Kindnesse, and upon a long discourse with Him touching your Treatise de Intellectu, Hee gave mee this in Commission to Write to you, That what ever Hee had to say upon that subject, was in noe sort any objection either to the Notions in your Booke, or the Reasons made use of to support them, but purely relateing to those repetitions and other small Errors therein, which you have allready Corrected, and therefore Hee desires you to proceed in your designe of publishing it, with the first opportunity, as a Performance that will not only exceedingly obleige Him, but all the Considering and Learned part of Mankind, This Hee bidd say to you to speed the Worke, but promised Hee would Write to you Himselfe upon His Return to London, but when that may bee is alltogather uncertaine, Hee being now gone with his Lady†2 to Sir Robert Sawyers,†3 where Hee intends to spend some dayes, and by that time Hee getts to London 'tis possible his Lordshipp may forgett his Promise in that particular, therefore pray goe on in fitting it for the Presse, and what ever Commandes you shall please to give mee concerning it, or any other of your Affayres, you may bee assur'd shall be most Willingly and Faithfully perform'd by mee: I thinke in my last I forgott to tell you that I could not speake with
― 501 ―
Captain Greenhill, Hee being at Tunbridge, but I have inform'd Adrian in every Particular touching Mr. Champnes,†1 and of your Care and concern for Him, Hee thinkes there is a Necessity of removeing Him from Utrecht, and will with the first opportunity consult his Brother Greenhill what methods will bee most convenient for the doeing of it; I allsoe acquainted Him what care you had taken in the settling Mr. Davy's at Amsterdam, for which Hee Returns you his Thankes; your Freinds at Ivy-Church†2 were verie inquisitive to Know what you said to mee touching the Picture etc; I told them that you shew'd mee Mr. Stringers long Letter, and that upon my peruseall of it, I had Censur'd it as a Paper Writt in Heat and not fitt to have Pass'd between Freinds of soe long and soe intimate an Acquaintance, Mr. Stringer in Excuse said, That Hee had the same Respect and Freindshipp for you as ever, But t'was your Letter that Provok'd Him to write in such a manner, I answered, That I thought there was noe occasion in that Letter of yours to induce such an Answere, and a further Dialogue wee had upon that subject, which I thinke would bee troublesome to repeate, But I cannot gett a sight of That Letter of yours, which, conveys the unquestioned right you once had in the Picture, and the Post being ready to goe off, I am forc'd to conclude, with an Assureance that I am,
Your most obleiged Faithfull Servant,
E†a
Salisbury: September the 16th.

1078. Thomas Davys to Locke, 19/29 September 1688 (1074, 1091)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 193-4.
Amsterdam September 29th: 88
Honoured Sir
I received yours and a letter from Dr Thomas with a bill of exchange for fifty Guilders wich I have received and a letter for Dr Gwenellon which I delivered to him and he was soe kinde as to Invite me to come to his house as often as I have any difficult Case. wich I will most willingly doe and doe returne you most humble thanks for all your favors you have conferr'd upon me. I did Sir assone as I came to Toune deliver your booke to Dr Gwenellon (who does present his service to you) and doe humbly beg your pardon for not giving you an account before I am now settled with my Master and hope that this place will answer the Doctors exspectation which for him and you I am bound ever to pray for and should accept it as a great mercy from God that If at any time I could but make an acknowledgment of all your favors II remaine
Sir your most obliged servant att command
THO DAVIJS
Address: For Mr John Locke To be Left at Mr Benjamin Furlys on the Scipmakers haven in Rotterdam

Monsieur
Monsieur Toinard m'ayant tesmoigné que Je vous fairois quelque sorte de plaisir de vous communiquer le dernier corrosif de Feu Monsieur L'Abbé Mon oncle, J'ay eté bien aise de me servir de cette occassion, pour vous tesmoigner en méme temps la passion que J'ay de connoistre une persone qui est d'une merite aussi distingué que vous, Enverité J'ay les dernieres obligations a Monsieur Toinard de me procurer L'avantage de pouvoir par ces lignes vous tesmoigner la passion que J'ay de lier avec vous un commerce
― 503 ―
de lettre, et de meriter L'honneur de vostre connoissance que Je regarde comme un bien considerable; Monsieur Toinard poura vous Marquer les soins que J'ay eu de m'enrichir de tout cequi m'a paru de plus curieux en La medecine. J'entens en recherchant tout ceque L'on a inventé de meilleur, Je vous communiqueray tout ceque vous souhaicterés, si de vostre costé vous avés quelque chose de curieux pour cequi regarde les maladies de L'oeil, vous me fairés un sensible plaisir de me le communiquer; mon addresse est a Deshais Gendron rüe st. andré des arts vis a vis le chapelet. Si Je vous puis etre de quelque utilité a paris, Je vous prie de me commander, et de me donner occassion de vous marquer par effect combien Je souhaicte vous rendre service en tout ceque vous me jugerés capable, Je suis
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
DESHAIS GENDRON
A Paris ce 9e octobre 1688
Corrosif†a- de Monsieur L'Abbé Gendron.
℞ mercure sublimé corrosif trois onces, Sel armoniac deux onces, L'un et L'autre mis, faut mettre le tout dans un matras avec une Livre de bonne eau forte que L'on fera evaporer sur un feu de cendre moderement chaud, jusqu'a ce que toutte La matiere se reduise en consistance de paste, sur la quelle faudra adjouster huict onces de Vinaigre radical, faut encore faire evaporer le dict Vinaigre sur le meme bain de cendre, Ensuitte la masse etant deseichée faudra le reduire en poudre pour s'en servir selon l'art.-†a

Vous avez l'usage de cete poudre au chapitre des Trochisques du petit livre de monsr l'Abé Gendron.†1 Son principal efet est pour la carie des os, et pour les chairs que l'on veut consumer

1080. Edward Clarke to Locke, 30 September 1688 (1077, 1083)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 53. Printed in Rand, pp. 280-1. Answered by no. 1083.
Deare Sir,
Your Kind Letter of the 17th has been now a full weeke in my handes, for which you had imediately Received my thankes had I been able to Write, but soon after my last of the 16th from Salisbury to you, I was taken ill of an Ague, with an ill Feaver that attended it, Which soe much weaken'd mee, that t'was not without Greate difficulty I gott hither, by the use of the Cortex Perue, I thanke God I am now able to tell you that I am at present free from both, and doe hope shall continue soe, but am not in a Condition to goe abroade to dispatch the Businesse I came into the Countrey for, which, you may imagine (my circumstances considered) is noe small disappoyntment and trouble to mee: You have exceedingly obleiged my Gardener by the Junkills and the large Nasturtium Indicum seed you have sent Him, which wee heare are safely arrived at Topsom†1 by Spicer,†2 and I hope some time the next weeke to gett them safe hither, The Lyme-tree-seeds, and the Turnipp-seeds you mention will bee noe lesse acceptable when they come, but I heare nothing as yett of theire Arrivall: I am intirely satisfied in every Article of yours and Mr. F.'s†3 Accompts, and doe not doubt but Mr. Percyvall will make punctuall payments of the Byll that is drawn on Him for £: 110: 13: 11: mention'd in your Letter, but I have neither strength nor time to thanke my Good Freind Benjamin as I ought, either for his greate Kindnesse to mee whilst I was in Holland, or the Extraordinary Care or trouble Hee hath taken for mee since, and therefore I begg you to make Him sensible of my hearty Acknowlidgments, and ea<rne>st†a hopes that I may some time or other bee happy in an opportuni<ty to>†a serve Him; And I heartily thanke you for opening the Complement<al>†a Letter you mention that was directed to mee, and I wish you had done the like by the other allsoe, for I cannot guesse at the Hand by that part of the superscription you sent mee, therefore Pray open that allsoe, and in your next lett mee know the contents of it, if materiall, and by whome it was Writt, and with mine and

your most affectionate Freind and obleiged servan
E†a

1081. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 1/11 October 1688 (1076, 1087)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 163. Answered by no. 1088.

ce 11. Oct. 88
Voila enfin, monsieur, ceque <j'aten>dois†c depuis long tems. J'ay pensé à ceque vous m'avez ecrit touchant la pierre que je voudrois bien etre entre vos mains. les ouvriers dont je n'ay pu venir à bout pour la montûre sont cause de cela. On m'en devoit envoier une otre de Cadis, mais j'ay donné ordre que l'on l'envoie à droiture à Amstredam à une adresse sûre d'une personne de ma connoissance qui y fait de grandes afaires. nous sommes ici dans latente de ce grand evenement, mais je n'ay pu encore me persuader que la foudre tombe du coté quele gronde; il y ora dans cete afaire plus de sudoüest que de nordoüest, ou je suis bien tronpé.†1
Le Capitene est devenu depuis dix ou douze jours homme de cour. Je nescai quand il reviendra de Fontainebleau.
Il n'est que trop vray que notre ami Mogol, a fait le grand voiage.†2 et cequi me fache cest que monsieur Du cange est aussi fort mal. Je lui ecrivis la semaine derniere. on atend de jour a autre la Chronique Alexandrine imprimée au Louvre avec ses notes. Il luy a donné
― 506 ―
le Titre de Chronicon Paschale,†1 que je luy indiqué en luy en pretant la Preface manuscrite il y a plus de quinze ans. Je luy ay marqué la joie que j'avois de cete aprobation. Je pense que vous savez bien que j'ay bien des choses sur cete Chronique que je n'ay point voulu mêler avec les productions de monsieur Du Cange. Les mienes sont presque toutes chronologiques. Son edition servira à les metre en marge.
Je suis actuelement à ma maison de campagne, ou je feray demain mes vendanges. Je passeray du vin blanc tout frais fait par la pierre, pour voir si cela leclaircira sans qu'il ait bouïlli.
Address: A Monsieur Holande Monsieur Benjamin Furley pour Monsieur JL A Roterdam
Endorsed by Locke: Toinard 11 Oct 88 Answered 10 Nov.
1082. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 4/14 October 1688 (1069, 1089)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 25-6. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 33-4.
A Amsterdam le 14 d'Octobre 1688.
Je ne sai, Monsieur, par quel malheur il arrive, que lors que je vous envoie un Volume nouveau de Nôtre Bibliotheque, je suis obligé de commencer ma lettre par une excuse. Il faut que je m'en serve encore cette fois, car il y auroit huit jours que vous auriez ce volume si un rhume incommode ne m'avoit tenu au Logis, et ne m'avoit empêché de retirer mes exemplaires assez promptement. J'avois interêt à <le>†a faire, pour apprendre le plûtôt que je pourrois vôtre sentiment, touchant tout ce volume et particulierement les Regles, qui commencent à la p. 309.†2 Comme je ne les ai données que par occasion, et que le terrein me manquoit j'ai été plus obligé de me rétressir que je ne le serai lors que je donnerai un petit Systeme sur cette matiére. J'aurai soin de rapporter plus d'exemples que je n'ai fait, et de suivre même une méthode plus exacte. J'ai déja plusieurs additions, et j'espere que peu à peu je pourrai si bien approfondir
― 507 ―
cette matiére, que je n'oublierai rien de considerable. Mais pour cela j'ai nécessairement besoin des avis de mes amis, et particuliérement des vôtres, Monsieur, qui me seront d'autant plus utiles, que vous avez examiné les principes les plus abstraits de la science que j'entreprends de traiter. Je suis obligé de supposer tout ce que vous avez dit dans vôtre troisiéme livre comme démontré; parce que mon dessein n'est pas tant de donner les principes Metaphysiques de la Critique, que de reduire ces Principes en pratique. C'est ce que j'ai tâché de faire dans le petit Discours que vous verrez dans ce volume. Voila mon dessein; vous pouvez voir là dessus ce qui manque à l'execution. Si vous faites un tour ici cet Hyver je pourrai vous lire ce que j'ai ajoûté dans un exemplaire où il y a du papier entre-deux. Cependant faites moi la grace de m'avertir des fautes que vous pourrez remarquer dans ce petit Ouvrage, de ce qu'il y faudroit ajoûter, de la méthode qu'il faudra suivre eta. Je suis encore un peu embarrassé à l'égard des bornes que je dois me prescrire, et dans une matiére si étenduë et si délicate, il ne peut pas manquer d'y avoir de la difficulté. Je ne veux écrire ni une Grammaire, ni une Rhetorique, et par consequent je ne dois point descendre <ju>squ'aux†a préceptes de ces sciences, mais me tenir dans des idé<e>s†a générales, qui servent à l'intelligence de toutes les Langues, sans donner aucuns préceptes particuliers, pour bien parler et pour bien écrire. J'ai cru vous devoir marquer plus distinctement mon dessein, que je n'ai fait dans l'Ouvrage même, qui a été fait trop promptement pour prendre mes mesures, comme je l'aurois souhaité, instituebatur amphora, sed currente rotâ urceus exiit.†1 J'attends donc, Monsieur, de la bonté que vous m'avez témoignée tant de fois, que vous voudrez bien lire mon petit Ouvrage avec application, et me marquer tout ce qui vous viendra dans l'Esprit. Je suis toujours de tout mon coeur Monsieur Vôtre tres-humble et tres-obeissant Serviteur
J LE CLERC
No address; at foot of f. 25, Le Clerc writes: Pour Monsieur Locke.
Endorsed by Locke: J Le Clerc 14 Oct.88

1083. Locke to Edward Clarke, 9/19 October 1688 (1080, 1086)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 27. Faded and torn. Printed in Rand, pp. 281-3. Apparently written from Amsterdam: Locke went from Rotterdam to Leyden on 12 October, N.S.; he was probably in Amsterdam on 15 October, continuing there until he returned to Rotterdam on 30 October, N.S.: Journal. Answers no. 1080; answered by no. 1086.
Dear Sir
I cannot be pleased that you should be sick at all but of all other I can best bare with an ague if you must have any desease, because as you have got rid of it (which rejoyces me) soe I think it is in your hands to hinder its return if you please. To that purpose I advise you to continue on your use of the Cortex Peruv at the rate of at least ℥j every week dureing all the month of october 3/4 of an ounce every weeke all Novemb. and ℥s all December drinking a glasse of good wine after every dose. I think if you can swallow pills that the best forme to take it in least the nauseous tast grow soe offensive to the palate and it make the stomach refuse it. Let it be very finely pouderd and made into pils with syrop of july flowers†a †1 There needs <scarcely>†b other rule in takeing it but that it be not just before or after eating though the morning fasting be thought generally best. You may safely enlarge the dose and time of takeing it for I never yet knew any body receive harm by takeing too much but often suffer by takeing too litle. Be sure to get that which is good for which I think you may trust Mr Shipton†2 and never be without it in your house. Thus much for your ague which I hope I shall hear noe more of nor of any other sicknesse in your family. In hopes therefor of your healths and good stomachs I have been just now takeing care about your garden belly timber.†3 Since Madame has been pleased to value them of this country soe much, I have therefor bought winter Turnep seeds ℥vi Sommer turnep seed ℥vi yellow Turnep seeds ℥vi Carot seeds ℥iij and Red Cabbage seeds ℥iiij and Limetree seeds as much as all the other togeather. I have now taken the first of the season to provide them to make some amends for my tardynesse last year and you may expect them
― 509 ―
time enough to trie some of them yet this <season if>†a the winde hinder not <for>†a the vessell they are designed by waits for noe thing else. I am very glad your gardener was soe well pleased with what was to be got for him whilst you were here. The truth is the Nasturtium Indicum with that brave large glorious flower is an excellent plant both for shew and use. I hope the seeds though of the last year†b will grow. When I consider what a returne I make to Madam for those flowers she throws on me in hers of 29 Sept. my cheeks (as cold as I am) glow with shame. She knows I am the pittifullest Gallant in the world and she will not thinke it much besides the matter if I make my addresses to her like old father Winter cround with Turneps and Carrots†1 let her but take in the stove under my feet (which I have whilst I am writeing this) in stead of a pan of Charcoals and the peice will be perfect. But yet I am not out of hopes to entertein her (whether you sweat again or noe) under the shade of the limetree grove but it must be in some of the butterflye months for in the winter I am as dead as they. Your complementall freind therefor mistook my constitution when <he soe kindely offerd>†a me his service if I would make any advance. I am soe <far from any>†a advances towards <love or>†a mistris or Courtship when the son is on tother side the line that I think on noe thing but the Chimny <corner>,†a which I think not to be left for a beauty or Fortune wherein a man otherwise disposed might hope <to finde a>†a paradise. Madam therefor may be sure of this that though she may easily finde more diligent usefull and agreable†c Gallants yet she can never have one more constant and more faithfull than I am who prefer my apartment at Chiply with her company, to all the noise and grandure that tons of gold promise; and to all those fine <castles>†a in the air which Love uses to build on the hopes of a rich match. The other letter according to your order I <have opend>†a a Copy of it you will finde on the other side†2 which though it be of businesse yet perhaps scarce worth the portage <and therefor>†a I have transcribed it. Pray present my humble service to Madam and tell her that though I writ to her the last <week>†a yet her letter which she lately honourd me with will draw
― 510 ―
on her the trouble of another from me speedily. The Doctor†1 and his Lady whom I saw to day were glad to heare of your safe arival at home and their yonge Gallant Peter desires to have <his service>†a to Mis Betty and yesterday her other Gallant Paul†2 who presented her with Amsterdam asked for her. How she will doe between these two yonge apostles I know not unlesse she will Rob Peter to pay Paul for they both pretend vigorously to her and I cannot blame them for I love her mightily my self. Remember me kindely to her and to all the litle ones. I wonder that in all your letters I finde not any mention of J:F: I hope he is only stolen out of the croud not out of the world. I wish you what you can wish your self and am
Dear Sir
perfectly yours J L
19 Oct 88
I have not yet presented your complements to Benjamin not being at present within reach of him
Endorsed by Clarke (part lost or concealed by mount): ... 20th of October 1688.
1 How to take the Jesuits bark
2 About Lyme-tree-seeds and other seeds etc:
1084. Dr. David Thomas to Locke, 20 October 1688 (1075, 1138)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 20, ff. 68-9.
Oct 20 88
Deare Freind
I receaved 2 letters from you some time since both opened and doubt whether this or any other of mine have or may come safe to your hands.†3 I have writt to Mr Furly to supply Mr Davijs with the mony he shall want not exceeding 10l per annum beside what is to be payd to his master Mr Peter Adrianz for dyet and teaching
As to what you write concerneing the sleeves the length of the
― 511 ―
wrist bands is 7 Inches and a quarter of an Inch and length of the sleeves beside the wrist bands 21 Inches
I receaved the chymicall processes and have read Philalethes†1 more then once and doubt whether water in the receavor in the purification of the [mercury] may prejudice it That being in other processes prescribed. I desire you to read Jodocus Greverus in Theatr Chym vol 3: p. 699†2 to the same purpose. I entend and am now prepareing materialls for the [aurum] potabile which mr Boyle assures though formerly of a contrary opinion is of very greate use and efficacy in physicke. I have made a preparation of his for at least cureing the faynty sweates of persons consumptive and am now trying it and the effect you shall know assoone as I can be assured of it. I have only Juvenall and Persius and Virgill of the Delphine Edition†3 and shall buy Horace here and if I buy any other I will give you speedy notice of it however I shall not refuse what you buy but shall part with the double to one of my sonns
Your N. Freind†4 promised to write to you to print your larger treatise de Intellectu humano long since. He mentioned something to me of the Extention of space which is not body†5 in which your opinions differed. I perceave Mr Davijs have receaved of you at twice 8l which I will pay on any bill drawne on me or to E.C. I suppose I have writt a letter long enough to answere 2 and my neglect in writeing my wife hath beene very ill of a violent payne in her shoulder and arme but is now much easier. all send their services. I am
your A T:

1085. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 20 October 1688 (1061, 1118)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 30-1.
Otterton Octob: 20th. 1688.
My Dear Friend
I humbly beg pardon for my long silence, which nothing could have occasion'd but the earnest confident expectation I had of your returning into England with Mr Clark. I knew that whiles he was
― 512 ―
on that side the Water, your kindness to him, and Complaisance to the Ladies, would carry you from Town to Town, rambling with them, so that 'twould be next to impossible for a letter to find you; and I depended upon your Comming Home with them, and with great pleasure Fancied my self already in possession of you, for this Winter at least; But how miserably was I disappointed; since instead of embracing the best of Friends, and being happy in the enjoyment of your most agreable, Excellent Conversation; I am entertain'd with nothing but Rumours of Warrs, and the daily Alarums of an expected invasion, both from the Dutch, and French, so that 'tis to be fear'd we may suffer all the extremity's of a Winter Warr. 'tis full three Weeks since that we, were told the Dutch were on our Coast and would be landed before the Newes letters could reach our remote contry,†1 as yet we hear nothing of their being come, but we are told that we owe our quiet only to the Winds that have been cross to their designes; but you know best who live amongst them. 'tis too late to wish that you had given me some hints of this storm, I could have avoided it, by comming over to you, and Wintering with you; which your daughter Betty and I would certainly have done; whereas now we must take our Fate; for we did not believe common reports, because we had so good a Friend on the place that gave us no intimations of any such thing; but since 'tis so; I hope you will pray for us; and do me the right to believe that no person can have more gratfull resentments of the Favours they have receiv'd from you, then my self, or be with so much respect and affection
Your Friend and Servant
ISABELLA D:
I came Yesterday from my Brother, who salutes you with much affection, as does Mr Freke who is now with him, but espetially my Master.
Address: For Mr John Lock att Mr Benjamin Furley's House Merchant in Rotterdam
In another hand: post paid to London-3d
Postmark: OC 24
Endorsed by Locke: Mr Duke 20 Oct.88 Answered 19 Nov: and 25 Jan

1086. Edward Clarke to Locke, 24 October 1688 (1083, 1098)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, ff. 54-5. Printed in Rand, pp. 284-5. Answers no. 1083.
Chipley the 24th October 1688.
Deare Sir
By reason of my Absence for about ten dayes past from this Place, Your verie kind Letter of the 19th came but late to my handes, soe that this is the first opportunity I have had to return you my thankes for it, and to assure you that I shall carefully performe your Directions in takeing the Cortex Peruv, by which I hope to prevent the Return of my Ague; from the ill Effects of Which I thanke God I am now pretty well recovered againe, and shall at all times readily imploy what strength I have in your service; I am allsoe to return you Madams and my thankes for the plentifull provision of Belly-Timber you have gott togather for us, The turnip-seeds, Carrott-seeds, and Red-cabbage-seeds, will bee verie welcome to the People in the Kitchin as well as the Gardener when ever they come, But the Lime-tree-seeds will bee as much more esteem'd by mee as I value a good Plantation of Tymber, and of Beautiful Trees, beyond any Belly-timber whatsoever, the one, if taken sufficient Care of when first planted, Being a go†a < >ion†b for Posterity, and the other only serves as a <helpe to>†b please the Pallatt and distroy hunger, but I heare nothing as yett of the Arrivall of either sort of them; My Gardener is not a little proud of the large Nasturtium-Indicum-seed and the other things you sent Him, and returns his humble thankes for them, and all other your Favours, and would bee verie glad to heare, that all the above mention'd seeds were safely come to hand, because if they come not in a verie short time Hee feares this season will bee lost: My Wife gives her service, and bidds mee tell you, that whilst I was the last weeke at Sutton, she Writt to you, and sent one inclosed from Mr. D'eully,†1 which shee hopes is gone safe to your handes; Your Cosen Stratton was with mee at Sutton a good part of the time I was there, which I spent with him cheifely in directing the most prudent methods I could thinke of, for getting in those Arreares of Rent that are now due to
― 514 ―
you, they are indeed much more considerable then I could wish they were, and I doubt will not bee gott in without greate difficulty, For there was never Known a time when, Sheepe, Cattle, Corn, Wooll, and every thing else that the Countrey-man should rayse money by, Sold at such Poore meane rates as now they doe, in soe much that in many places, the Proffitts of the Lands will hardly pay the Workemens Wages that are imployed to Manure it; Mr. Stratton†a- approv'd of the Directions I gave Him, and promised to follow them carefully;-†a I received one hundred pounds of Him to your use, and at the request of my Aunt Strachey left it with Her, upon her Byll payable by Mr. Lynn†1 in London before the end of this Term, which is a conveniency to Her, and will bee I hope noe disadvantage to you: J:F: was lately with mee here, and is now at Escott, Hee gives you his hearty service, and thanks for your Kind inquiery after Him, Hee acknowlidges the receipt of yours of the 7th. of May last, and assures mee that Hee hath written twice to you since that time; The little Barronett†2 hath received the Bookes you last sent Him, and Hee and the rest of that Family, togather with Madam, and the younge Fry here, give theire Services, and you have allsoe the hearty good Wishes of
Your most affectionate Freind and Faithfull Servant
E:†b

N.T vidi manibusque tractavi sed nondum legi, nondum enim prostat venalis, sed credo me hâc septimanâ empturum. quod araverit in vitulâ cujusdam amici mei facile crediderim nam utrumque ita factum suspicor ut alter non sit nimis cautus, alter non nimis candidus. (Latin)
10 Nov.
I have been away from home, so am late in answering.†1 Please excuse my slowness to Mr. Gendron†2 and keep me the friend you have given me; his very name cannot but be most welcome to me, but over and above that he has moved me by the services he has done me. I have been waiting impatiently to learn what happens to new wine when strained through the stone; and now I understand from your latest letter of the 4th that it did not pass through. If I had been there when it was too thick to pass I would have poured it on after clarifying it by filtration through three or four sheets of paper, so that when the thicker and stickier part of the juice had been removed I might possibly squeeze out a drop or two, so as to see whether the taste of liquors can be removed in this way. The vintager did quite right to add water immediately, to prevent the viscosity drying in the pores and obstructing the passages. I doubt whether the starch adhering to the bottom on the outside would have had any taste.
(Latin) 'Here is harmony disturbed once more'—the old sad song; so I must go on complaining, groaning, rebuking, but all in vain. I have seen and handled [p. 517] the Histoire critique of the New Testament, though I have not read it, as it is not on sale yet; but expect to buy it this week. I can easily believe that the writer has ploughed with the heifer of a certain friend of mine, for I suspect what has happened on either side: the one party has not been too careful and the other not too scrupulous. But what am I to say of a man who is prepared to minister to other people's reputations and to hand over his work to be rifled by plagiaries (for such that fellow is, if I am right), rather than to meet a universal demand by publishing it entire under his own name? As soon as I get hold of this new critique I shall read it through carefully to see what it is made of, though the columnar book†1 that I should compare it with is not here. That book is carefully put away; for it is the one out of all I possess that I am most anxious to preserve safe and sound; would that he who alone has the power and the duty to do so might some day relieve me of my anxiety. I hear nothing about the books that were sent to Esclassan; I wonder what has happened. You shall have a copy of the Histoire shortly, if there is any way of sending it. As to edulcorating sea-water, the thing is well known, but fire must be used; the edulcorated liquid is quite clear and good to drink; it can be kept a very long time without going bad. You should appropriate the Chronicon Paschale some time and publish it with illustrative notes; I say this in accordance with my usual practice, not that I have any hopes of it.
(Latin) [p. 518] My best respects to our Duumvir;†1 I know he is a courtier even in the country, that is to say kindly and polite; he will therefore be content with the good wishes of myself, his useless friend. Good-bye; keep me in mind and enjoy your affairs and learned studies.
J LOCKE

1089. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 7/17 November 1688 (1082, 1103)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 27-8. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 34-5.
A Amsterdam le 17 Novembre 1688
Je suis quelquefois, Monsieur, si embarrassé de rien, que mes petites affaires me font oublier ce que j'ai le plus envie de faire, ou de dire. J'avois résolu de me donner l'honneur de vous aller voir une seconde fois, avant que vous partissiez, mais je ne pus le faire, comme je l'aurois souhaité. C'étoit pour implorer vôtre secours, en une rencontre où j'en ai extrêmement besoin. Vous savez que je dois
― 519 ―
faire le XII Volume de la Bibliotheque seul;†1 mais vous ne savez pas que les Livres de Francfort, sont en si petit nombre et si chetifs†2 que je n'aurai jamais de quoi remplir ce volume, quoi que je les ramasses tous. On en imprime ici si peu de bons, qu'il n'y a presque rien à prendre; et la France et l'Angleterre nous sont fermées.†3 Je voulois donc vous prier de voir si vous ne pourriez point me fournir quelque petite piéce de Physique, par exemple, ou de quelque partie de la Philosophie qu'il vous plaira. Vous m'avez dit, si je ne me trompe que vous aviez prouvé dans un Chapitre de vôtre Essay of the understanding qu'on ne peut avoir aucun Systême de Physique parfait.†4 Si vous pouviez, Monsieur, m'accorder ce Chapitre, je le traduirois le plus exactement qu'il me seroit possible, et je vous en ferois voir la traduction, pourvu que je l'eusse de bonne heure. Voiez, je vous en supplie, si vous pouvez le démembrez du reste de l'ouvrage, et soiez persuadé que vous ne sauriez faire de plus grand plaisir au public et à moi en particulier, que de faire paroître de temps en temps quelque morceau d'un ouvrage si utile, jusqu'à ce que vous le donniez tout entier. Si cela vous paroit faisable, et que vous veuilliez qu'on vous en tire quelques exemplaires in 12o ou in 8o vous n'aurez qu'à me le marquer. Ce n'est pas que si vous trouvez cela embarrassant je voulusses vous gêner le moins du monde; et que si vous aviez quelque autre piéce détachée de la même nature, je ne l'inserasses volontiers; mais il faut que je vous avouë que ce sujet me paroit digne d'être éclairci, pour desabuser une infinité de gens. Faites moi la grace de me répondre un mot le premier jour de vôtre loisir, et de me croire toûjours, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et tres-obeissant serviteur
J LE CLERC
Marquez moi, s'il vous plait, si vous avez trouvé les deux exemplaires du X Tome que j'avois envoiez à Rotterdam.

Famulus meus†1 Amstelodamum res suas agens profecturus meam non prius rogavit veniam quam instaret decessus adeo ut ad Te scribendi tempus non dabatur. (Latin)
Rotterdam 24 Nov. 88
Excellent Sir,
My servant,†1 when about to go to Amsterdam on his own business, did not ask my permission until it was almost time for him to depart; so I was not given time to write to you. I am sorry indeed to hear of this loss of health in members of your family; I hope, however, that your son,†2 as also the rest, will soon be better. About his illness and its treatment I dare not give any opinion in absence, nor indeed is there any need for it, seeing that you have such skilled physicians ready to hand among your friends. Let me, however, offer one piece of advice: if, as you seem to expect, smallpox should eventually break out, I should wish you, both in dosing the patient and in covering him up, to beware of keeping him too warm, for this excites heat in the blood, not without great trouble and danger to the invalid. I was forced against my will to say this much by my affection for you and yours, and I speak from experience. The state of your son's health is, I hope, such as permits me to speak of other matters, especially of the kind you like to hear about. Our friend Furly waited on the Prince before his departure and addressed him personally, to implore his [p. 521] succour against a case of persecution which has now, if ever, most unseasonably begun in this province. He pressed the matter so urgently that the Prince was pleased to write a letter to the bailiff of Kenmerlant, who by the authority of the Synod had ordered Foecke Floris, a minister of the Mennonite Church, to leave the district within eight days and pass out of his jurisdiction, unless he preferred to be imprisoned. You will learn the story of this Foecke Floris from others better than from me. Our Furly did not know him even by sight before this case arose; but considering that his liberty was a matter of common concern to all Christians he took up his cause with enthusiasm and conducted it energetically, for unless he had spoken out he would have made no progress. I hear that the brake applied by this letter has checked the zeal of the persecutors for the present. If you should come to know anything more of this business amongst your Mennonite friends please tell us of it.†1 May you enjoy good health, my excellent friend, with your whole family; such is the heartfelt wish of
Yours most devoted
J. LOCKE
[p. 522] Furly sends you his best wishes.
Remember me to your dear wife and to the rest of our friends.
Address: Mÿn Heer Mÿn Heer limborch bÿ de Remonstrantse Kerck op de Keÿsers Gracht t'Amsterdam

1092. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 15/25 November [1688] (1090, 1093)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256g. Printed in Ollion, pp. 179-80. Year from van Limborch's note.
(English)
25 Nov.†a
Vir Amplissime
Magnâ me curâ et sollicitudine liberarunt gratissimæ tuæ mihi heri redditæ literæ. ex tuo silentio si non male ominabar, metuebam certè, et ut amantium mos est, quia quæ optaram, non audivi, quæ timebam finxi. Sed gaudeo jam omnia in tuto esse, et periculosum filii tui morbum ita præteriisse ut nihil restet†b jam ad perfectam sanitatem nisi quod diætæ regimine perfici posse existimatur. Quandoquidem prior illa mea de morbo illius monitio tibi adeo grata fuit, liceat mihi et alteram addere. Non quod credam meo tibi opus posse esse consilio ubi doctissimus et longo usu prudentissimus Veenius adsit, sed ut persuasum tibi sit me tibi fidem habere cum testeris tibi acceptum esse quod cum re non possim <voluntate>†c tamen et studio adjuvem. Post hujusmodi morbum solent nostri medici semel atque iterum purgare, et præcavenda mala, quæ ex reliquiis miasmatis variolosi in corpore hærentibus oriri possint, mihi etiam et alia causa hujusmodi iteratam purgationem requirere
― 524 ―
videtur. Nempe, quod solent convalescentes ex hoc morbo, magno appetitu laborare, unde, si non caute et moderate alantur, metus est ne eduliorum nimio onere nondum penitùs defæcatus oppressus sanguis succrescenti alicui morbo materiam præbeat. Sed qui tuto convalescere volunt cavere debent ne nimis propere <convalescant>†a , et in eo utplurimum peccant mulierculæ præsertim clinicæ, quod nihil credant ad vires restaurandas tantum conferre quantum nutrimenti copiam, cum assumendorum vis et quantitas sensim tantum augenda sit prout augentur vires. Quod enim bene subigit ventriculus, bene digerit sanguis id†b solum robur addit corpori, vigoremque spiritibus impertit, quicquid justam illam mensuram superat non solum <inutile>†c onus est, sed in humores noxios et morborum causas degenerat. Hæc ego fusius hic mihi dicenda existimavi, quia nostrates in hac re plerumque peccant. apud vos forsan hoc, uti cætera, prudentius et moderatius. Furl. noster maximas tibi gratias agit ob utramque quam misisti historiam sed insuper avet scire quo jure quibus formulis vel quam ob rem e carcere liberatus fuit Foeke Floris et in exilium missus.†1 Nihil habeo hoc in genere quod
― 525 ―
tibi jam rependam vel si habeam non credo jam tempestivum esse, aliis extraneisque rebus cum tuis civibus jam intentum, minusculis nuntiis interpellare. Satis jam vobis est ad plurium dierum sermones vel saltem quod ab amico nostro accipies satis erit. Ego interim deum O.M. precor ut ecclesiæ suæ hoc est bonis omnibus eam largiri velit pacem et libertatem quam plurimi passim promiserunt, pauci hactenus præstiterunt. Vale cum filio totâque familiâ et me ut facis ama
Tui amantissimum

(Latin)
25 Nov.
Excellent Sir,
Your most welcome letter, which I received yesterday, has relieved me of great concern and anxiety. If I drew no bad omens from your silence, yet it certainly caused me some fear, and, as is the way with those who love, because I did not hear what I had hoped for I imagined what I feared. But I am happy that all now is safe, and that your son's dangerous illness has passed off so well that nothing now remains for his complete restoration to health but what is considered can be effected by a regulated diet. As you were so glad to have that previous warning of mine about his ailment, may I be allowed to add yet another? Not that I suppose you can have any need of advice from me when you have with you such a skilful physician as Veen and one so wise by long experience, but in order that you may be sure that I believe you when you declare that you are grateful for what help I can give you by goodwill and devotion, though I cannot do so in practice. After a sickness of this kind our physicians usually purge the patient more than once, as a precaution against troubles which may possibly arise from remains of the variolous infection that may be lingering in the body; in my opinion there is also [p. 524] another reason calling for such a repeated purge. I mean that persons recovering from this disease are apt to be troubled with an inordinate appetite; hence, unless caution and moderation are observed in giving them nourishment, there is a risk that the blood when not yet thoroughly purified may be oppressed by the excessive burden of food, and may therefore afford material to some incipient ailment. The fact is that those who wish to recover their health safely should not be too hasty in recovering it; the commonest offenders in this respect are females, especially sick-nurses; they believe that nothing contributes so much to the restoration of strength as abundance of nourishment, whereas the strength and quantity of what is taken should be increased only gradually in proportion to the increase in the patient's bodily powers. It is only what is well digested by the stomach and well distributed by the blood that adds strength to the body and imparts vigour to the spirits; whatever exceeds that just measure is not only a useless burden but degenerates into noxious humours and causes of diseases. I thought it proper to speak about this at some length since our people are usually at fault in this matter; with you perhaps this, as other things, is managed with more prudence and moderation. Our friend Furly sends you his best thanks for both the accounts that you sent; but he is further desirous to know by what legal authority and under what regulations or for what reason Foecke Floris was released from prison, and sent into exile.†1 I have nothing of this [p. 525] sort to repay you with just now, or if I had, I do not think this is the time to interrupt you with small items of news, when you and your fellow citizens have your minds on other and external affairs. You now have enough to talk about for several days, or you will have with what you will hear from our friend. Meanwhile I pray that Almighty God may be pleased to bestow upon his Church, that is upon all good men, the peace and liberty which many on all sides have promised, but which few so far have provided. My best wishes to you, your son, and your whole family, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J L
(Latin) Please remember me very kindly to your belovèd wife, to our friends Veen and Guenellon with their whole family, and to all our Collegians.
I wish your son the best of health.

1093. Locke to [Philippus Van Limborch?], 18/28 December [1688?] (1092, 1100)
Uppsala University Library. Transcribed from Xerox print and plate ix in Messrs. Maggs Brothers' Catalogue no. 286 (item no. 1735. The plate is repeated in Catalogues no. 306 as pl. xvii and no. 322 as pl. xi. The letter, without a plate, is already in Catalogue no. 269, item no. 526). The letter probably came onto the market from a member of van Limborch's family: no. 962 n. The contents suggest that it was addressed to van Limborch himself. The place of writing and the son's illness establish the year.
― 526 ―
(English)
Rotterdam 28 Dec
Vir spectatissime
Si per juvinem Anglum†1 ut Tu tuique valerent rogaverim, non eo feci animo ut tuum accusarem silentium, sed ut de filii convalescentiâ certior fierem, cui, ut fateor verum, ex tuo silentio metuam, satis gnarus in isto morbo, si gravius laboraverit aliquis, cum in ipso portu videtur navigare sæpius suboriri tempestatem, et quasi in momento naufragium. Sed gaudeo maxime, jam diu omnia in tuto esse. Si languescat appetitus non cohibendus sed excitandus potius est frequenti apricatione et deambulatione in ære aperto, <quamprimum>†a frigori assuescere potest, et abstinendum ab omnibus quæ oculos vel animum exerceant: fruaturque pingui et hilari otio. Vides quam pronè me rebus tuis immisceo, nec immerito meæ enim sunt semperque erunt. De Slado nostro tanto impensius doleo quod ea quæ scribis facile credo, et metuo ne sit immedicabile vulnus. morbi qui originem trahunt ex animo non facile reperiunt medicinam, præsertim in eâ ætate ac indole, quæ adversa non leviter ferunt, nec adsunt domestica vel consilia vel
― 527 ―
solatia. Adhibe, quantum potes, fomenta: meretur illius integritas, doctrina, candor, omnia amicitiæ subsidia. Uti tu de nostris ego itidem de vestris rebus bene ominor, utrique jam in eadem sumus navi. De literis cambii rectè et in tempore mones. ego omnino solvendas jam censeo, ea conditione ut more apud mercatores recepto syngrapham in manus tuas recipias. de hoc uno si cautum sit, in reliquis fac ut lubet. Faustum fælicemque Tibi tuisque omnibus animitus exopto annum. Vale Vir Amplissime et me ut amas ama
Tui studiosissimum
J LOCKE
Uxorem filium filiamque saluto. Furleius noster te salutat.
(Latin)
Rotterdam 28 Dec
Esteemed Sir,
If I inquired through the young Englishman†1 how you and yours were, I did not do so with any intention of finding fault with your silence but to be informed about your son's recovery, for which, to tell the truth, I might have fears from that silence. I know well enough that in that malady, when someone has had a serious attack of it and his ship seems to be in the very harbour, there often arises a storm, and shipwreck, as it were, happens in a moment. But I am delighted to know that all has been safe for some time now. If his appetite tends to fail he should not be kept indoors but rather roused by frequently sunning himself and walking in the open air, as soon as he can get accustomed to the cold, and he should keep from anything likely to exercise his eyes or mind; he should enjoy complete and cheerful leisure. You see how ready I am to busy myself with your concerns, and with reason, for they are my own and always will be. About our Sladus I am the more deeply grieved because I can easily believe what you say in your letter, and I am afraid the wound may be incurable. Sicknesses that derive from the mind are not easily remedied, especially at an age and with a temperament which do not bear adversity lightly, and when there is no advice or consolation in the home. Do all you can [p. 527] to alleviate his trouble; his uprightness, learning, and sincerity deserve all the help a friend can give. I augur as well for the affairs of your people as you do for ours; we are now both aboard the same ship. You give me right and timely warning about the bill of exchange; I think it should be settled completely now, provided always that you have the written agreement given into your hands according to mercantile practice; if you are careful about this one thing do as you like in other respects. I heartily wish you and yours a prosperous and happy year. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and continue to love me
Your most obedient servant
J. LOCKE
My greetings to your wife, son, and daughter. Our friend Furly sends you his.
1094. Carey Mordaunt, Viscountess Mordaunt, later countess of Monmouth and, later, of Peterborough, to Locke, 22 December [1688]/1 January [1689] (1099)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 99-100. For Mordaunt see p. 573 n. His lady is Carey, c. 1658-1709, daughter of Sir Alexander Fraizer (D.N.B. and I.H.R., Bull. v (1928), 183-5); married Mordaunt c. 1678. Mordaunt was in the United Provinces in 1686: p. 60, n. 4. He returned to England, but about the end of 1687 was in charge of a Dutch squadron in the West Indies. He was in the United Provinces again by the autumn of this year and accompanied William on the expedition to England. When Lady Mordaunt came to the United Provinces is unknown. She and Mordaunt perhaps became acquainted with Locke through Furly.
Lady Mordaunt's writing and spelling are extremely bad; it is impossible to be certain of spellings, and sometimes of words.
― 528 ―
hage the 1 of january
Doe you think fitt to undoe mee with vanité or make me doubt your sinsernes: two things equally fatall: the first had Lyke to spoile a weeks humiliasion:†1 so prone is nature†a- to believe-†a what whee wishe yeet i had reather ere in that then think you kane in enny thing: with this condission that you will andswer att the great day for every proude thought i caried to church with mee at crismas: i am unraisonable enofe to Laude you with all my future falts uppone this subject iff I could flatter my selfe so fare as to emagine i could impose and give a rainon for a oumans vanitté beyond her one conceite: but i swear by all things that truë that i have receave<d>†b addission for this moment i have so ille anopinion of my selfe, so great a one of you that i dread this Letter as my vergine fears mayd mee aprehend my forst wryting to your ungratfull sex hoe seldom gained believe wich is the forst steep in Love, so unwilling i was to sette a value one those itransitory things. had they bribed mee pride with Mr Locke aprobasion though y was sensible i did not merite itt twould at Least a mayd a violent deseier twer possible: wich y never had for enny otther: you may reproche your selfe iff i have nott andswerd your Letters souner for when I heard you excuse crude notions y Left of wryting and believed none could disjest or wryt one word of sence, wich raised my fears to that degree that i had onc resolved not to expose my selfe to so unmerciful a juge: i plead noe merite but a vast inclinasion to your frinship wich is Lyke to Last for i have brock but feü and not one my side as ouers was att forst sight i hope the proportions†c whee found in ouer humore will increes as whee are more aquanted though i fancy y have knone you all my Life: this advantage whee have of Loveaers†d hou all ways Louck with parsiale eyes tell att Last thay find thay are so i will reade your bouck†2 sence you have forgiveven the profanasion if you will keepe the secret i shall be more obleged for I dare not pretend to understand things so much above mine that Littel judgment i have will only serve to convince mee how necessary tis that i should ever
― 529 ―
valeü you and how raisonable never to hope for a returne though none is more your friend and humble sarvant then
CARY MORDAUNT
thank the baron†1 for his present with my service to ouer friend.†2 i will wryt no wews for you know it as soune as whe doe
Endorsed by Locke: La: Mordaunt 1 Jan. 89 Answered 6.

[Dr. Guenellon:]
Ma femme pour reparer sa faute de vous avoir pas salué au bas de ma derniere vous charge presentement dune grande lettre et pour ne pas tomber dans la mesme faute je vous diray seulement que je vous remercie de vostre belle responce qui nous flatte que vous ne partirez si tost comme nous l'apprehendions.
Je vous souhaitte une heureuse entrée dans cette nouvelle année et que nous vous puissions voir bientost en bonne santé. Toute la famille vous remercie de vostre bon souvenir. je suis
Monsieur, Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur

1096. Dr. Charles Goodall to Locke, 27 December 1688 (1002, 1137)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 23-4. Printed by Dr. K. Dewhurst in Review of the History of Medicine, xvii (1962), 495-6.
London Dec. 27. 1688
My worthy and deare Freind
I know you can be no stranger to the wonderfull successe which God Almighty hath given to the Prince of Orange in his late undertaking to deliver our miserable and distressed kingdoms from popery and slavery, which mercy we in England esteem no lesse then the Isralites deliverance from Ægypt by the hand of Moses, God grant that we and our posterity may live our mercies.
I presume you have heard that the King went privately from Whitehall some few daies before the Prince came to St James's,
― 531 ―
with a design for France, but was stopped by some Fisher-men, and then return'd againe to whitehall on the Sunday in the Evening, but on the Tuesday (being the day the Prince came to London) he retired to Rochester, and is said to have left the kingdom last Sunday.†1 On Munday being the 24th. of this month, the Lords spiritual and temporal met at Westminster and pass'd the following Order.
We the Lords Spirituall and Temporal assembled in this conjuncture do desire your Highness to take upon you the administration of publique affaires both civil and military and the disposal of the publique revenue for the preservation of our religion, our rights, liberties and properties and of the peace of the nation.
And that your Highness will take into your particular care the present condition of Ireland and endeavour by the most speedie and effectuall means to prevent the dangers threatning that kingdom, all which we make our request to your Highness to undertake and exercise till the meeting of the intended convention the 22th. of January next, in which we doubt not such propper methods will be taken as may conduce to the establishment of these things upon such sure and legal foundations that they may not be in danger of being again subverted.
yesterday the Knights, Citizens and Burgesses which were in town and served in any of the Parliaments that were held during the reign of K.Ch.2. As likewise the Lord Mayor and Court of Aldermen of the City of London and 50 of the Common-Council of the same waited upon the Prince and concurred with the Lords in the foremention'd request.†2
Sir I hope that this news will encourage you to returne to London as soon as you can settle your affaires in Holland; if you please to come to my house you shall freely command what conveniencies that will afford, which I hope may not be unacceptable to you. My wife and self give you our heartie service and do wish you a prosperous and safe returne to England. I am
your faithfull Freind and humble Servant
CH: GOODALL
Sir Since my writing this letter Mr Church-hill†3 hath printed
― 532 ―
the foremention'd Order, and the Princes answer, which he desired me to present you, with his service.
Sir Walter Young and Mr Clerk I saw this day, who give you their service.
If your affaires will not permit you to returne speedily I hope you will not deferre your returne longer then the time when the Princesse comes for England, which I expect may be the latter end of Jan. or beginning of Febr.†1 give my service to Dr Stanley,†2 if you see him.
Address: This For his deare and Worthy Freind Mr Locke†a at mr Benj. Furleys. marchand. Rotterdam:
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Goodall 27 Dec: 88
