1097. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 9/19 January 1689 (1088, 1109)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, f. 165. The date is complete, January being understood as in no. 802. The letter evidently answers a letter later than no. 1088.
+
Mercredi 19. 89.
J'ay trop d'impatience de vous temoigner la joie que j'ay de votre derniere pour ne vous pas marquer que de toute l'annee je n'ay receu aucune nouvele plus agreable. A legard du reste je suis un de ceux qui presseroient ledition de l'ouvrage dont nous avons vu et admiré l'essay.†3
La c. du P.S.†4 n'a point eté encore renduë. Je la crois perduë, parceque l'on lora prise au porteur.
J'ay fait partir aujourdhui pour Paris les exemplaires de Pollux et Hesychius de mr Henri de Valois, ou il y a bien de ses notes.†5 Je
― 533 ―
les ay obtenus d'un de mes amis, qui a acheté ses livres. c'est monsieur Spanheim†1 à qui la cour a donné son congé qui les portera en Holande, pour servir à ledition que l'on y fait de ces deux Auteurs. Je les adresse à mr Grævius. Je nescai si vous savez que c'est aussi à moy à qui le public a obligation de l'Harpocration de mr de Valois, que je donnay à mr Daniel Elzevier.†2 Un monsieur Thompson savant anglois à qui j'ay preté ici cet exemplaire d'Hesychius de mr de Valois, m'a dit qu'il y a un de vos Eveques qui y a beaucoup travaillé.†3 ce mr Thompson etoit venu voir Madame <sa>†a sœur qui etoit entre les mains de mr L'Abé G.†4
Le P. Pagi m'a envoié depuis peu par present un volume contenant une critique des 4. premiers siecles contre Baronius. C'est un excelent ouvrage, et qui est encore plus surprenant, etant fait par un Cordelier, et quidem Provençal.†5 J'avois lié commerce entre led. Pere, et Monsieur de st Asaph, dont il cite souvent des fragments de letres que j'ai toutes entieres, et que je garde precieusement, aussi bien que les copies de celes que le meme mr de st Asaph m'a addressées pour le P. Noris de Verone, travaillant à Florence à un excelent livre des Epoches de villes Syromacedonienes.†6
Ce P. Pagi n'a entendu qu'a demi mon opinion que je luy avois communiqueé de la double maniere de conter la Puissance Tribu<ni>ciene†b des Empereurs tant dans les medailles que les Inscriptions.†7 Il la publiée sans mon aveu, et puis a voulu la refuter, et cequ'il raporte ne fait pas la moindre chose contre moy, car concedo totum, ergo gly.†8 Voila ceque cest que de n'entrer pas dans le principe.
― 534 ―
Je ne le luy avois dit que de vive voix à Paris, et il n'en a retenu que cequ'il a pu. cela m'obligera a etendre mon opinion au net, et à la faire imprimer. Je nescai s'il est venu jusques à vous que je me suis fait quelque nom pour l'explication des medailles, et principalement pour les Greques ou il y a des Epoques. c'est à quoi je ne pretendois nullement, mais quelques principes de Chronologie dont je me suis garni et dont les soy disans Antiquaires sont ordinairement fort depourvus, ont pu m'atirer cet avantage, par lequel on a voulu m'engager a entreprendre des ouvrages bien eloignéz de l'Harmonie, et je m'en suis jusques à prezent defendu.
J'ay un furieux Rhume qui m'a empeché depuis 4. jours de voir le Triumvir. J'espere pouvoir aler demain. Je n'ay pas voulu lui doner la peine de venir ici en lui en donnant avis. J'ay pris ce tems la pour lire le nouveau vol. du P. Pagi ou il y a de tres excelentes choses, mais je ne suis pas pour cela toujours de son avis. Il ecrit fort bien en Latin, et ce n'est pas un style Fratesque.†1 Il seroit trop long à vous conter comment il ma obligation du privilege. car cest a prezent une opera en France que pareille chose, cequi fait extremement tort aux letres, et à l'etat.
Je suis ——
Endorsed by Locke: Toinard 19 Jan. 89
1098. Locke to Edward Clarke, 18/28 January [1689] (1086, 1102)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 176. The earlier part, on the upper part of the first page of the letter and continued overleaf, is written by Syl, with corrections by Locke; the later part, on the lower half of the first page and continued overleaf, is written by Locke; the address also is written by him. The letter is badly damaged, strips about an inch wide being lost from the upper and lower parts of the right-hand margin. The missing parts of the letter are indicated here by angle brackets. Printed in Rand, pp. 285-8. The year from the allusion to Lady Mordaunt, etc. One of the Education letters: no. 782 n.
28 Jan. 8<9>
Sir
You may remember that I have formerly told you that children whilst very yonge should be treated as rational <creatures and> that therefore you should always cary this in your minde in all the
― 535 ―
managment and discipline of your son.†1 This I perceive <needs some> litle Explication it being liable to some mistake. Tis true your son and all children should be treated as Ration<al creatures and> therefor argued with as grown men. Longe†a discourses†2- and philosophical reasonings at best doe but amaze and confo<und but do> not instruct them. When I say therefor that they must be treated as rational creatures I meane that you should ma<ke them sensible> by the mildnesse of your carriage and your composure even in your correction of them that what you doe is reasonable in you <and useful and> necessary for them. And that it is not out of caprichio passion or phansy that you command or forbid them any thing. <This they are> capable of understanding and there is noe vertue they should be excited to nor fault they should be kept from which I doe <not think> they may be convinced of but it must be by such reasons as their age and understandings are capable of and those prop<osed always in very> few and plain words. The foundations on which several dutys are built and the fountains of right and wrong from which they s<pring are not per> haps easily to be let into the mindes of grown men not used to abstract their thoughts from common received opi<nions. Much less> are children capable of reasonings from remote principles. They cannot conceive the force of long deductions. <The reasons that> move them must be obvious and level to their thoughts and such as may (if I may soe say) be felt and touched. But <yet if their age> temper and inclinations be considerd there will never want such motives as may be sufficient to convince them. <If there be> noe other more particular yet these will always be intelligible and of force to deterr them from any fault <fit to be taken> notice of in them (viz) that it will be a discredit and disgrace to them and displease you. But of all the ways w<hereby children> are to be instructed and their manners formed the plainest easiest and most efficacious is to set before their E<yes the examples> of those things you would have them doe or avoid which when they are pointed out to them in the practise of persons <within their> knowledg with some reflection on their beauty or unbecomingnesse are of more force to draw or deterr their imita<tion than> any philosophical discourses can be made to
― 536 ―
them. Vertue and vices can by noe words be soe plainly set before their understandings as the actions of other men will shew them when you direct their observation and bid them view this or that good or bad quality in the practise. And the gracefullnesse or†a ungracefulnesse†a of many things in good or ill breeding will be better learnt and make deeper impressions on them in the Examples of others then from any rules or instructions can be given about them. This is a method to be used not only whilst they are yonge but to be continued even as long as they shall be under anothers tuition or conduct. Nay I know not whether it be not the best way to be used by a father as long as he shal <think fit, on> any occasion to reforme any thing he wishes mended in his son. Noething sinkeing soe gently and soe deepe into <men's minds> as example. And what ill†a they either overlooke or indulge in themselves, they cannot but dislike and be ashamd of <when they see> it in another†-2
Sir†b
The letter you did me the favour to write me the day you came to town I receivd last Tuesday†1 and the same day returnd you my thanks. I since that receivd yours of the 1st instant and could not have receivd a wellcomer new years guift. I thank you for the good wishes and inclosed print in it. One thing troubles me that I see you looke not after your election,†3 but I hope you will have it some where without lookeing after. I wonder at N F. what he means.†4 I think the treatment he receivd from others, lay noe obligations on him to be froward now. Your sons tutor†5 will I <doubt not> finde himself out in his account, however you doe well to seek an other. I wish one to our purpose. you <will see from> what is above that I still continue on in my wonted liberty, it was designed you a good while since <but I had no> mind to send it till I had hopes it might come to you. Your last makes me doubt whether this will f<ind you in> town or else I had writ some thing to you which I have now writ to the Gent†6 who put some thing into your last letter,†c who I
― 537 ―
told you in my last I d<esired to> draw up the setlement of a match I had in my thoughts but I have writ to him to communicate it to y<ou when you come to> town. Doe not laugh at me when I talke of a Match at this time of day for I can tell you that one <of the finest> ladys at this court,†1 came not long since to this town on purpose to see and be acquainted with me <although> I am not like to be a Courtier. where are any of your yonge spruse blades that have such complements <paid to them?> I have since returnd her her visit and we are very well pleasd one with an other, if ever you be soe happy as <to meet her> you shall acknowledg she is an extraordinary fine woman. This perhaps you will thinke as strange news <as any I> receive from you but tis fit I return you some in exchange for yours. But pray tell Madam for all that, <that nothing> can shake my service to her. My humble service to her and the litle ones. I thinke of returning some <bills of exchange> speedily to the same hand as before, and now if you think fit to looke abroad for placeing some mony for me out either in a lump <or in small> parcels I have noething against it. I am glad you have those papers from Ivy church, we shall talk m<ore fully> when I see you, which you may be sure I long for above all things there. I return all your good wishes with <whatever> mine can adde to them. Upon the comeing of the first news of successe I received the kindest letters both <from> the Doctor and his wife†2 and my friends at Amsterdam that you can imagin, they always remember you and your company <with great> kindnesse and respect. I intend to goe and see them as soon as the weather is fit to travell, but can scarce tell how to thinke†a
My service to all my freinds in City or Country as they come in your way I am perfectly
Dear Sir
your most humble and faithfull servant
J L
... folkes†b as well as John an Okes†3 salute you and yours.
Address: For Mr Edward Clarke To be left with Mrs: Rabsy Smithsby in Dorset Court†4 in Chanell row Westminster

1099. Carey Mordaunt, Viscountess Mordaunt, later countess of Monmouth and, later, of Peterborough, to Locke, 21/31 January [1689] (1094, 1397)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 101-2. Year from Locke's endorsement.
hage the 31 of january
Wher the impresions receaved from Mr Lock Liabel to tyme or decay: you might with some j'ustice acuse mee: but i fynd you nether kno your selfe: nor merite by suspecting: others should: or when thay doe: fancy them so slight: as to bee worne out in a months styme: no thay will grow and thrife haveing taken deepe route in a soile that is nott sandy though in a wman hart: i fear iff my Lord†1 seeses that expresion he will revock is promis you must give him Leave in his turne to bee jelous sence you wher because y did not wryt to you a Lese raison iff you heard his complants uppone that subject you will forgive mee and triomfe over a hussband: a common thing in your caise: i have beene very ille this fornight: the begining was: what is called the disease of one contrey: inpasience to bee ther: but ended yesterday with voilence as all great things doe but kings: ouers whent out: Lyke a farding candele: and has given us by this convension an occasion not of amending the goverment: but of melting itt downe and make all new: wich makes mee wish your ther to give them a wryt scame of gorverment: having been infected by that great Man Lord i'asbury:†2 by reading the barons boack†3 i am apt to flater my selfe in this opinion that Soals may slide in to frindes when sens doe not deserve them i supose when he died: he did nott know his grand
― 539 ―
son worthe: so well as my daughter†1 now: hou i cured of an†a agùë by the old mdcine frightig her with the wews of my Lord acheles†2 being taken by the king of franses onders: without just: this abligasion she has to him: so one fier drives out the otther: i am so weake that y shall nott undertake my jorny to Amsterdam till Monday or tuesday next: in case you may have your convennient way of traveling: i intend the jorny so: make mee no more excuses for rustick words: for you doe nott think your selfe gilty of them: as for mee i kno my falts are so crose in wryting that tell i am convinct i hold you fast you shall have as feü of my Letters as is possibel: wich i shall nott bee tell you Leafe making escuses ther is some thing in that Louckes Lyke possessing one selfe and shoes y doe nott in Lovers Lungage disorderd wordes have most eloquence: and as long as you ranche yours so well: and have such a care of what you say: i will not give you aname†a you atribute your selfe in one of your Letters: but this y may. that noe boddy have stile her selfe more your friend then shee hou is your sarvant
C MORDAUNT
Endorsed by Locke: L Mordaunt 31 Jan.89 Answered 2. Feb.

Vir Amplissime
Subitus hic et nondum inexpectatus Principissæ decessus†3 conturbat omnes rationes meas. et id impedit quod ante omnia mihi
― 540 ―
constitutum erat et imprimis homini beneficiis maximis cumulatissimo. et non ingrato necessarium, ut Te aliosque Amstelodami amicos inviserem et coram valedicerem. Hoc non magis exigebat officium quam animus meus in id maxime intentus, ut hominum optimorum et de me optime meritorum, congressu, vultu, sermone, per aliquot dies, mutuoque amplexu discedens fruerer. Non potes ignorare quam commoda hæc sit navigandi occasio in tam læta turba inter tot naves bellicas cum jam mare undique piratis infestatur.†1 sed ut verum fatear hæc me non omnino movent, nec me a vobis his commodis ita ingratus me abstrahi paterer nisi gravior me reluctantem urgeret causa. Quidam ex magnatibus Anglis qui hinc cum <principe>†a in Angliam profectus est ad me nuper scripsit ut vellem Uxorem ejus Hagæ commorantem†2 in reditu domum Comitari. Suscepi lubens hoc quod esset officii, petentis dignitati et amicitiæ, et multo minus ornatissimæ fæminæ meritis, non negandum. Sed nec illa nec ego de tam maturo decessu ne per somnium quidem cogitavimus. Illa et ego <cogitavimus>†b Ad Amstelodamum hâc septimamâ. sed nosti quid intervenit, festinatione incredibili in Angliam tenditur. hujus festinationis illa me certiorem fecit nudius
― 541 ―
tertius, et monuit illico convasandum†a esse mihi ad hoc minime parato. Quid dicam? deest (quod doleo) salutandi, compellandi, amplectendi occasio non voluntas. hoc tibi persuasum esse ita firmiter credo, ut Te adversus alios tanquam patrono et defensore uti non dubitem. Me abire insalutato Optimo Venio Nostro totâque illius familiâ plane ægre fero. quod in hoc casu dictu opus est pro me dicas rogo, nihil pro me spondere potes quod non præstabo. Scio enim qualia et quanta <sint>†b eorum erga me merita, et quo ego in illos sum animo. de mea erga Te Vir Clarissime amore et gratitudine nihil dicam. Velim ex tua hoc cognoscas amicitia. De literis cambii hoc unum rogo quod prius monui, nempe ut cautum tibi omnino sit, ut autographam in manus tuas sine dubio retrahas, reliqua tuæ permitto prudentiæ.

(Latin)
Rotterdam 5 Feb. 89
Excellent Sir,
This sudden departure of the Princess, which was not expected so soon, upsets all my calculations. It also interferes with what I had resolved upon [p. 540] above all things, and which was a prime necessity for one on whom the greatest kindnesses had been heaped and who was not ungrateful, namely to visit you and my other friends at Amsterdam and say good-bye to you all in person. I was in duty bound to do this much; but what moved me no less was my own keen desire to have the pleasure for a few days of meeting, seeing, and talking to the best of men and my greatest benefactors, and of a mutual embrace at parting. You cannot be unaware what a convenient opportunity this is for me to make the voyage in a light-hearted company among so many ships of war, now that the sea is everywhere infested by pirates.†1 To tell the truth I am not in the least influenced by these things, nor would I be so ungrateful as to let myself be torn away from you by these advantages if I were not pressed against my will by a weightier reason. One of the English notables who set out from here for England with the Prince wrote to me recently asking me to accompany his wife, who is staying at The Hague, on her return home.†2 I readily undertook to do so, as it was my duty and a request not to be refused to the position of him who made it and to the claims of friendship, far less to the deserts of a most illustrious lady. But neither she nor I so much as dreamt of such an early departure. She and I both had in mind to go to Amsterdam this week; but you know what has prevented this; the voyage to England is being unbelievably hurried on. The lady informed me of this [p. 541] haste two days ago, and warned me to pack my belongings instantly, little prepared as I was for it. What can I say? I am to my grief deprived of the opportunity, though not of the desire, to greet and talk to and embrace you all. I am so sure you are convinced of this that I have no hesitation in using you so to say, as my advocate and defender against the others. The thought of going away without saying farewell to our good friend Veen and his whole family distresses me deeply. I beg you to say for me what needs to be said in this emergency; you can promise nothing on my behalf that I will not fulfil. I am conscious of all they have done for me and of my own feelings for them. Of my affection and gratitude towards yourself, distinguished Sir, I will say nothing; I trust that you as my friend recognize it. As to the letter of exchange, I ask only what I warned you of before, namely that you should by all means be careful to get the original back without fail into your hands; I leave the rest to your own good sense.
(Latin) This in haste, as they say we must leave tomorrow; the west wind which has now died may possibly advise otherwise by then; but princes must be obeyed on land as winds must at sea. Please give my best greetings to your excellent wife and family; also to my good friend Veen together with his wife, both his daughters, and his sons-in-law, as well as to all my friends and Collegians. If there should be anything I can do for any one of you in England [p. 542] I shall not fail to give all my care and attention to it. Again and again good-bye, and continue to love me,
Honoured Sir,
Your most obedient and devoted
J. L.
1101. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 27 January/6 February 1689 (1100, 1106)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 15-16. The date should perhaps be two days earlier: n. 1.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Ita mox indicat mihi D. Guenellon Te cras cum Celsissima Principe Auriaca abiturum in Angliam.†1 Gratulor Tibi et nobis res Angliæ in eum statum restitutas, ut securus illuc redire, ac penates tuos revisere audeas. Equidem tantam et tam subitam tanti regni mutationem sine speciali Dei directione contigisse nemo sanus crediderit. Ego hic ineffabilem divini numinis benignitatem gratus agnosco, quod Angliam æque ac patriam nostram ab imminente Papatus jugo auspiciis Principis Auriaci benignus liberaverit.
― 543 ―
Utinam omnes Angli id grato animo agnoscant, et mutua inter dissentientes charitate generosum Principis Auriaci propositum promoveant: Si enim Presbyteriani cum Episcopalibus eadem qua hactenus acerbitate de primatu contendere velint, quid aliud quam cœptum hoc egregium pessumdaturi? Metuo Scotos seditiosum suum Convenant urgentes. Quod si pax Ecclesiastica inter tam pertinaciter dissidentes obtineri nequeat; saltem ea vigeat inter omnes moderatio, ut quam quisque sibi libertatem cupit, eam alteri lubens largiatur, neque cujusquam conscientiæ, qualiscunque tandem sit, vis inferatur: Libertas enim ex æquo omnium est. Ita tandem mansuefient animi, et fortasse ad arctiorem pacem præparabuntur. Opto ut hunc florentem patriæ tuæ statum brevi videas. Quoniam temporis angustia non permittit, ut præsens Tibi valedicam, paucis animum Tibi explicabo meum. Magnam fœlicitatis meæ partem statuo, inter amicos tuos numerari. Fortunam tuam meliorem ex lege amicitiæ aliquatenus etiam meam credo. Quare licet a Te non sine dolore avellar, non possum non acquiescere statui tuo, qui ex diuturnis erroribus tandem senex quietus et securus patriam revises. Nulla dies, quoad spiritus hos reget artus,†1 memoriam tui animo eximet meo; sed et mei te fore memorem
― 544 ―
persuasus sum. Quare vivet inter nos dulcis nostræ conversationis commemoratio, et dum corpore non possumus animo erimus conjunctissimi. Vale itaque Vir Amplissime, et Amice inter paucos mihi chare, fruere deliciis patriæ et consanguineorum, gratiâ divinâ contra incertos vitæ hujus casus tutus, ac semper pace ac gaudio bonæ conscientiæ exultans. Interim memor mei vive, et in Angliam reversus literarum commercium, unicum amicitiæ inter absentes conservandæ medium, noli intermittere. Uxor ac liberi omnia Tibi fausta apprecantur. De literis Cambii nihil hactenus actum ob frigus intensum. Sed eas quamprimum commode fieri poterit curabo. Vale animæ dimidium meæ.†1 Salveat D. Furlii.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
So soon as tomorrow, then, Mr. Guenellon tells me, you are to sail for England in company with Her Highness the Princess of Orange.†1 I congratulate you and ourselves that English affairs have been restored to a state which permits of your venturing to return thither without apprehension, and to see your own home once more. Truly no sane person can believe that so great and sudden a change in such a mighty kingdom can have come about without the especial direction of God. For my part, I acknowledge in this with gratitude the inexpressible loving-kindness of the Deity, in that he has in his mercy brought about the liberation of England as well as of our own country, under the auspices of the Prince of Orange, from the threat of bondage to the [p. 543] Papacy. May all Englishmen acknowledge this with grateful hearts, and by the exercise of mutual charity between those of differing opinions may they promote the noble enterprise of the Prince; for if Presbyterians and Episcopalians are minded to contend for predominance with the same bitterness as heretofore, what else will they effect but the ruin of this notable beginning? I fear the Scots with their zeal for their factious Covenant. If, however, peace in the Church cannot be achieved amongst such determined adversaries, at least may so much restraint prevail amongst them all that each may willingly grant to another the liberty which he desires for himself, and that force be done to no man's conscience, of whatever persuasion he may be; for liberty is the right of all alike. So at length tempers will grow milder and will perhaps be prepared for closer bonds of peace. I hope that you may soon see this prosperous state of your native land. Since shortness of time does not permit of my bidding you good-bye in person, I will unfold myself to you in a few words. I account it no small part of my happiness that I am numbered among your friends. This betterment of your fortune the law of friendship leads me to feel as in a measure my own also. Therefore although I am not separated from you without sorrow I cannot but acquiesce in your situation, now that after long wanderings you are at last in old age to see your native land once more in peace and security. No length of time, 'whilst breath of life shall rule this frame',†1 will erase your memory from my heart; but I am persuaded that [p. 544] you too will remember me. Thus there will endure between us the delightful recollection of our intercourse, and whilst it is not possible in the flesh we shall be most closely united in spirit. Good-bye then, excellent Sir and friend dear to me as few others; enjoy the delights of your native country and of your kindred, ensured by the divine grace against the uncertain chances of this life and ever exulting in the peace and joy of a good conscience. Meanwhile keep me in mind, and when you are at home again in England let there be no interruption in our exchange of letters, the one sure means of preserving friendship between the absent. My wife and children wish you all prosperity. Nothing has so far been done about the bill of exchange on account of the intense cold. But I will see to it as soon as it can conveniently be done. Good-bye, thou half of my soul.†1 My respects to Mr. Furly.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH

1102. Locke to Edward Clarke, 29 January/8 February 1689 (1098, 1128)
B.L., MS. Locke b. 8, no. 28. Apparently written in haste. Printed in Rand, pp. 288-90.
8 Feb. 1689
Dear Sir
Yours of 22 Jan is the third I received from you since your last comeing to London for which I cannot forbear to returne you my thanks by the post this†a same day that I receive it, though it be a doubt to me whether as it may happen this or I shall get to you first.†1 I have seen the Princes letter to the convention,†2 which carys weight and wisdom in it. But men very much wonder here to heare of Committees of Priviledges of Greivances etc as if this were a formall Parliament and were not something of an other nature and had not businesse to doe of greater moment and consequence, sufficiently pointed out to them by the Princes letter. People are astonishd here to see them medle with any small matters and When the setlement of the nation upon the sure grounds of peace and security is put into their hands, which can noe way soe well be don as by restoreing our ancient government, the best possibly that ever was if taken and put togeather all of a peice in its originall constitution.†3 If this has not been invaded men have don very ill to complain. and if it has, men must certainly be soe wise by feeling as to know where the frame has been put out of order or is amisse and for that now they have an oportunity offerd to finde remedys and set up a constitution that may be lasting. for the
― 546 ―
security of civill rights and the liberty and property of all the subjects of the nation. These are thoughts worthy such a convention as this, which if (as men suspect here) they thinke of them selves as a parlament and put them selves into the slow methods of proceeding usuall there in, and thinke of mending some faults peice meale or any thing lesse then the great frame of the government, they will let slip an oportunity which cannot even from things within last long. But if they consider forain affairs I wonder any of them can sleep, till they see the nation setled in a regular way of acting and puting it self in a posture of defence and support of the common interest of Europe. The spring comes on apace, and if we be, France will not be Idle. And if France should prevaile with the Emperor for an accomodation (which is more than feard) I beseech you consider how much time you have to loose in England. I†a- mention not Ireland because that is in every bodys eye.-†a I writ some time since to J F. suspecting you might be out of town, concerning one point, which if gaind will goe a great way to keep all right, I desired him to communicate it with you if you were not gon into the country. I could tell you severall other considerations I have, which I need not trouble you with who I am sure will thinke of the very same or better. I doe not perceive that you stood to be chosen any where, which when I see you I shall quarrell with you for not a litle, make not the like omission the next Election. I writ to you the same time I did to him, but supposeing it would finde you in the country it was only upon the old subject of your children.†1 I am glad to heare their mother and they are well. I am their and
Dear Sir
Your most affectionate humble servant
J L
The news comes just now from a good hand that the Emperor and the French King are agreed.†2 I have by the two last posts remitted mony to Mr Percivall. The bills of exchange are five that I have sent him, the sum how much you will see by the bills, pray whilst you are in town when you goe that way looke a litle after it, and minde him to be carefull of it. My <service>†b to Mrs Smithsby
― 547 ―
and the rest of my friends that are in town espetially your Westerne neighbours amongst whom I recon J F:†1

1103. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 2/12 February 1689 (1089, 1104)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 29-30. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 35-6.
A Amsterdam le 12 de Fevrier 1689.
Monsieur
J'avois appris de nôtre Ami Mr. Limborch, que vous étiez sur le point de partir, et je me serois d'abord donné l'honneur de vous écrire, si j'avois pu deviner que le vent vous retiendroit encore quelques jours ici. Sans les glaces je vous aurois aussi renvoié vos deux livres,†2 avec le Volume XI de la Bibliotheque, que je n'approuve guere à la verité, mais qui est une suite de ceux que vous avez. Je croi que je pourrai envoier ce paquet par le bâteau de Lundi,†3 si les glaces sont rompuës. Avertissez moi, s'il vous plait, en cas que cette Lettre vous trouve encore à Roterdam, si vous voulez que j'envoie à M. Furly le XII qui sera bientôt imprimé, ou donnez moi quelque adresse à Londres où je puisse vous le faire tenir. Je vous suis infiniment obligé des offres que vous me faites, et je vous puis assurer, sans compliment, que je me ferai toute ma vie un plaisir de vous témoigner en toute occasion l'estime que je fais de vôtre amitié. J'espere que vous m'accorderez la faveur de me marquer vôtre adresse, dès que vous aurez arrêté une demeure fixe en quelque part, et de me permettre de me consoler, en vous écrivant quelquefois, de la perte que vos amis font ici par vôtre départ. Pendant que vous avez été en Hollande, quoi que vous ne fussiez pas dans la même ville, il me sembloit que vous étiez présent, par la facilité de vous écrire et de recevoir de vos nouvelles. Mais il me semble que je vous vois aller en un autre monde, lors que je pense que vous allez au delà de la mer. Je ne m'en consolerois
― 548 ―
pas, si je n'esperois de recevoir encore quelquefois des Lettres, par où j'apprenne que vous vous portez bien. J'ai encore deux choses à vous demander: la premiére c'est que vous ne supprimiez pas davantage vôtre Essay concerning the†a Understanding, et que vous nous ôtiez de la crainte où nous sommes de le perdre: la seconde c'est que lors que quelques uns de vos amis auront quelque piéce, qu'ils veuillent faire connoître deça la mer, vous ayez la bonté de vous ressouvenir de nôtre Bibliotheque. Après cela il ne me reste rien que de faire des voeux pour vôtre heureux passage, et de prier Dieu qu'il vous fasse trouver un lieu tranquille, où vous puissiez passer le reste de vôtre vie aussi doucement que vous le méritez. Je vous supplie de croire que je fais cette priére de tout mon coeur, et que je me ferai toûjours beaucoup d'honneur d'être, Monsieur, Vôtre tres-humble et très obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC.
Comme je ne doute pas que vous ne voiyez Mrs. Boyle et Burnet,†1 j'ose vous prier de les assurer de mes respects.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke chez Monsieur Benjamin Furly Marchand A Roterdam.

1104. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 3/13 February (1103, 1126)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 31-2. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 36-7.
A Amsterdam le 13 de Fevrier 1689.
Voici, Monsieur, vos deux livres, dont je vous suis extrémement obligé. J'ai lu celui qui traite de la Béatitude avec bien du plaisir, et j'en ai fait même un extrait assez long.†2 Pour l'autre il n'y a rien de particulier, et je m'étonne qu'un geometre comme M. Wallis ait voulu publier si peu de chose.†3 J'ai joint à ce paquet deux exemplaires
― 549 ―
de la Bibliotheque, quoi que j'aie apris depuis peu que l'Auteur de ce Volume, qui l'a dédié à mon insu, avoit commis de grandes extravagances à la Haie, et que Madame la Princesse l'avoit fait menacer de le faire mettre aux petites maisons. J'en suis faché, mais aiant séparé mon travail du sien, j'espere qu'on ne me rendra pas responsable de sa fureur.†1 J'ai crû devoir vous en dire un mot, Monsieur, afin que si quelcun vous en parloit vous aiyez la bonté de lui dire que j'ai rompu depuis plusieurs mois avec cet homme-là, qui m'a fait éprouver que les maladies du cerveau sont incurables, car je puis dire que j'ai fait depuis 3 ans tout ce que j'ai pu pour le rendre sage, mais il est toûjours devenu plus fou entre mes mains, et présentement qu'il en est sorti μαίνεται οὐκ ἐτ' ἀνεκτῶς†2 Sa folie n'est plus tolerable. Je vous demande pardon de vous entretenir d'une chose, dont vous n'avez que faire; et je vous prie encore une fois de croire que je suis et que je serai toûjours, Monsieur, Vôtre tres-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC

(English)
Hage 14 Feb. 89
Vir Amplissime
Ante aliquot septimanas dedi ad Te literas, quas Janetto traditas fuisse certò scio, an tu vero eas rectè acceperis, ex silentio tuo valde
― 550 ―

dubito, præsertim cum de ea re scripsi quam me scire mea non parum interesset. Champneium†1 a parentibus revocatum ita decedere cupiebam ut omnia prius præstaret quæ tuis in eum meritis et meæ expectationi responderent. Sed ne turpissime in extremo actu deficeret, quid Tibi honorarii vel quocunque alio nomine deberetur per epistolam quæsivi ut cum aliqua saltem gratiarum actione Tua agnosceretur cura. Quid actum sit plane nescio, cum nec Tu aliquid respondisti, nec ille roganti aliquid dicere potuit, utpote qui Te insalutato inurbanus dicam imo insulsus et stupidus se subduxerat. De his omnibus rebus me coram certiorem fieri speravaram, cum Te soluta hieme uti destinaveram domi tuæ inviserem. Id meum consilium turbavit jam prorsus principis præmaturus decessus, quem etsi ventus Anglorum votis contrarius in hunc usque diem distulerit tamen ad Te Amstelodamensesque amicos excurrendi tempus in tam incertâ et instabili morâ non dabatur. Ego jam patriam revisurus id doleo, me non prius te complexum fuisse et tibi coram dixisse ultimum vale. Hoc habet aliquid obæratorum fugæ simile, qui cum non sint solvendo clam abeant. Pares tuis in me beneficiis
― 551 ―
gratias referre nunquam potero, habebo semper. sed ideo quia non sum solvendo te cupiebam videre et agnoscere quæ deberem. Me ita avelli ut te non <prius>†a salutem pudet sane pigetque. Hanc tu ægritudinem mihi aliqua ex parte levabis, si spem amicitiæ tuæ tuarumque aliquando literarum abeunti permittas. Tuæ enim amicitiæ gloria amplissimus erit peregrinationis meæ fructus. Fac modo ut ego in Angliam reversus Tibi aliqua in re possim esse utilis, et beabis. quæ meæ sunt partes vellem aliquo modo meritis tuis respondeant, de tua enim in me voluntate nullus dubito. Ea confisus alium Tibi sed alterius indolis et frugi Juvinem commendo. Ille jam ab aliquo tempore serio apud vos literis incubuit, et quærit studiorum subsidia, quæ nullibi, paratiora sunt quam apud te, currentem quæso dirige, dubitantem confirma, cæcutienti lumen, laboranti auxilium præbeas, permitte saltem ut Te domi aliquando invisat, et de rebus literariis consulat: ingenuum ipsum, amicos ejus gratos reperies. Frater ejus Dominus Paulus D'Aranda†1 inter primarios Anglorum apud Amstelodamenses mercator multis nominibus mihi charus est. Nec quicquam cupio magis quam ut
― 552 ―
sciat, meam commendationem Fratri illius Benjamino D'Arandæ†1 apud Te profuisse. Hoc mihi nihil gratius facere potes. Vale Vir Colendissime et me ama ut facis
Tui Studiosissimum

(Latin)
The Hague 14 Feb. 89
Excellent Sir,
I wrote to you some weeks ago, and I know for certain that the letter was delivered to Jannettus, but as I have heard nothing from you I seriously doubt [p. 550] whether you duly received it, especially as I wrote about a matter on which I was much concerned to be informed. When Champneys†1 was recalled by his parents I desired that he should not leave without first fulfilling his obligations in such a way as might answer to all you had done for him and to what I expected of him. Lest, however, he should fail disgracefully in this final performance I wrote to ask what was due to you as your professional fee or on any other account, so that the care you had taken of him might be acknowledged at least by some expression of gratitude. I am quite in the dark as to what was done, as you sent no answer, nor was he able to tell me anything when I asked him, seeing that he was so unmannerly, shall I say, or rather so boorish and stupid as to slip away without taking leave of you. I had hoped to hear about all these things in person when I called on you at home, as I intended to do when winter was over. That plan of mine has now been completely upset by the premature departure of the Princess; though this has been put off even till now by a wind adverse to the wishes of the English people, yet in such an uncertain and changeable period of delay I could not get the time needed for going to see you and my friends at Amsterdam. Now that I am to see my own country once more it distresses me that I have not first embraced you and bidden you a last farewell in person. This is something like the behaviour of runaway debtors, who abscond because they cannot pay. I shall never be able to thank you adequately for all your kindness, though I shall always be [p. 551] grateful for it; but it was just because I am insolvent that I longed to see you and acknowledge my debt. To be snatched away like this without first saying good-bye to you fills me with shame and disgust; but you will relieve my distress in some measure if you will allow me to depart with the hope of your continued friendship and of hearing from you now and then; for the honour of your friendship will be one of the richest rewards I have reaped of my sojourn abroad. Only give me the chance to be of use to you in some way when I return to England, and you will make me happy. I can only wish that anything I can do might correspond in any way to all you have done for me, for of your goodwill towards me I have no doubts. It is in reliance on this that I am recommending another young man to your notice, but one of a different character, an honest man. He has for some time been devoting himself seriously to learning in your country and is looking for help in his studies, which is nowhere to be found more readily than with you; I beg you to direct his steps, encourage him when he is in doubt, enlighten him when he cannot see, and assist him in his difficulties; permit him at least to visit you at home from time to time and to consult you on learned matters; you will find him well bred and sincere and you will earn the gratitude of his friends. His brother Mr. Paul D'Aranda†1 is one of the leading English merchants in Amsterdam and is dear to me on many accounts; it is my most earnest [p. 552] desire that he should know that my recommendation to you has been of use to his brother, Benjamin D'Aranda.†1 You can do me no more welcome favour. Good-bye, honoured Sir, and continue to love me
Your most devoted
J. LOCKE
(Latin) Whilst this west wind is blowing letters sent to Furly at Rotterdam will find me, as I am thinking of going there tomorrow, in readiness to sail with the rest of the company when the wind is favourable.
My best wishes to our de Greve, a friend whom I shall always have cause to remember.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Grævius professeur en Rhetorique ett à Utrecht

(English) Amplissime Vir
Non credideram patriam nostram hactenus te hospite fore beatam. Si suspicari potuissem, discessum tuum tot diës differendum, jam alteras ad te dedissem; neque enim amicitia nostra ex
― 553 ―
earum genere est, quas Erasmus ait melius ali silentio, quam colloquiis aut literarum vicissitudine.†1 Velocissimo calamo ad Te ultimas meas scripsi, quia sero monitus. Affectum meum tibi testatum esse volui, qui incondito et rudi, sed nativo et infucato sermone se plenius tibi exhibuit, quam operoso verborum ornatu tectus. Ita est, Vir Amplissime multisque mihi nominibus Venerande, quò propius discessum tuum instare video, eò me gravius affici deprehendo: præsertim quando hæc animum meum subit cogitatio, nullam fore diëm quæ nos iterum conjungat. Vere prædico me nec candidius pectus, nec amicitiam sinceriorem, nec judicium rectius in quoquam familiarium meorum reperisse. A tali itaque amico avelli non potest non esse grave. Verum gratulor Tibi felicem in patriam reditum, precorque ut diuturna ac solida illic quiete fruaris, quam nulla posthac Reip. tempestas turbet. Si Te corpore sequi negatum est, animo tamen sequar, et in ipsum domicilium, quin et Musæum tuum penetrabo; et si alloquentem me coram audire negetur, literis meis in ædes tuas irrumpam, Tibique tuas extorquebo, ut saltem inter absentes aliqua sermonis sit vicissitudo. Non gravaberis tum epistolas meas, licet verbosiores, legere; et si
― 554 ―
garrulitate mea tibi sim molestus, potes simili vel duplici epistolarum tuarum prolixitate mihi vicem reponere. Interim Vir Amplissime et Amice dilectissime, omnia Tibi precor prospera, et quoniam præsenti non licet, absens Te per epistolam hanc complector, Tibique ex animo valedico. In Angliam ubi appuleris monebis nos quò epistolæ nostræ dirigi debeant ut tuto ad Te perveniant. Hasce inclusas rogo D.Doct.Burneto tradas. Ecce quam familiariter, qui Te hinc discedentem mox literarum mearum onere gravem. Salutat Te amantissime uxor mea ac liberi, omnesque dolemus, præreptam nobis occasionem ultimum Te alloquendi, affectumque nostrum, quod sine lachrymis non fieret, coram testandi.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I had not supposed that our country was to be so fortunate as still to have you for its guest. If I had had reason to suspect that your departure was to be so long deferred I would have written again before now; for our friendship is not [p. 553] of the sort that Erasmus says thrives better on silence than on conversation or exchange of letters.†1 My last to you was written in great haste, as I had such late warning; I wished it to give proof of my affection for you, which was better shown to you in language that was rough and unstudied, but natural and sincere, than if it had been dressed up in laboured ornament of words. The truth is, excellent Sir and on many accounts to be honoured by me, that the nearer I see the approach of your departure the more deeply I find myself moved, especially when the thought occurs to me that the day may never come when we shall meet again. I can say truly that in none of my intimate friends have I found greater open-heartedness, sincerer friendship, or sounder judgement, so that separation from such a friend cannot but be grievous to me. However, I congratulate you on your happy return to your country, and I pray that you may there enjoy long and assured peace, never henceforth to be troubled by any tempest in the state. If it is denied to me to follow you in the flesh, I shall nevertheless do so in the spirit, and shall make my way into your very dwelling, and even into your study; and if it is impossible for you to hear me speaking face to face, I shall break into your house with my letters and extort yours from you, so that there may be at least some exchange of speech in absence between us. You must not then find it tiresome to read my letters, wordy though they may be; and if I should happen to [p. 554] annoy you with my garrulity you can retaliate with letters similarly long-winded, or even twice as long. Meanwhile, excellent Sir and my most beloved friend, I wish you all prosperity, and, since I cannot do so in person, I embrace you in absence by this letter, and bid you farewell with my whole heart. When you land in England you will let us know to what address our letters should be directed so as to reach you safely. I beg that you will deliver the letter enclosed herewith to Dr. Burnet. You see what familiarity I use with you by burdening you with my correspondence at the moment when you are leaving us. My wife and children send you their most affectionate greetings, and we are all distressed at being robbed of the opportunity of speaking a last word to you and giving you in person proof of our affection, which could not have been without tears.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 15 February 1689
Address: Reverendo Amplissimo Viro D. Joanni Locke

1107. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 6/16 February 1689 (1106, 1120)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256i. Printed in Some Familiar Letters, pp. 325-8; postscript and address in Ollion, p. 182.
(English)
Rotterdam 16o Feb. 89
Quod imprimis hinc decedens desideravi ut scilicet Te Vir Amplissime reliquosque Amicos Amstelodamenses amplecti daretur, in eo omnia quasi deditâ operâ mihi maxime adversari videntur. primo glacies et festinatio, deinde in ipso itinere pluvia intercæpit. Die enim Sabbati ultimo†1 hinc Hagam profecturum, ut ibi Nobilem Fæminam†2 ad Amstelodamum etiam cogitantem compellarem, imber satis violentus me Delphos transeuntem perfudit, quod incommodum Hagæ etiam passus sum. Ita totus madidus accessi ad illam quæ nocturnum illud iter quo ad vos ea nocte perrecturus eram, tanquam sanitati meæ nimis periculosum non dissuasit solum sed et prohibuit. Sic pluvia illa quæ jam a duobus mensibus pene unica quasi designatò, unius dieculæ vobiscum spem, qua hinc gestiens decessi prorsus abstulit. In aula omnia tam parata ad abitum, tam moræ impatientia inveni, ut primo favente vento principem classem conscensuram nemo dubitet. Istud destinatum
― 556 ―
iter ad vos incæpi non tam vento quam principis religioni confisus†1 quam vix credidi die dominica velle iter ingredi etiamsi ventus orientalis invitaret, sed jam nihil aliud expectatur, quam ventus navigationi idoneus, quo simul ad naves convolandum erit. Heri vesperi huc redii et quam diu hic languescendum sit nescio. hoc certò scio nihil molestius esse quam ad fastidium usque laborare otio, et tamen ad id quod maxime velles tempus non suppetere. Quam vellem mihi dari apud vos horam unam vel alteram. Vultus, sermo amplexus amicorum nescio quid habent quo se explere anima†a mea†a anxie desiderat, Quo vos in me sitis animo, quo ego in vos nullum credo est dubium, nec augeri posse mutua nostrum amicitia, valedicentium alloquio, opto tamen videre, dextras jungere, et me iterum vobis totum tradere cujus totus sum. Hoc si mihi jam non concessum fuerit alias spero futurum, non enim de me tam male ominor ut nullam credam fore diem quæ nos iterum conjungat. Multa sunt quæ hanc navigandi occasionem non mihi omittendam suadent. Amicorum expectatio; res meæ privatæ jam per aliquot annos neglectæ, piratarum frequentia, et parum tutus alias transitus,
― 557 ―
et nobilissimæ Fæminæ sive cura sive amicitia, quacum iturus sum. Velim hoc tibi persuadeas me hic aliam patriam reperisse et pene dixeram parentes, quod enim in illo nomine charissimum est, benevolentiam amorem charitatem, quæ ad conciliandos homines conjungendosque fortiora sanguine habent vincula, apud vos abunde expertus sum. Habeo hic amicos semper mihi colendos, imo et invisendos si res et dies patiatur. Hoc certo scio, quod decedo cum animo revertendi ut cum illis solidum aliquando et illibatum capiam gaudium, quorum humanitate effectum est ut a meis absens et in communi omnium mærore nullam sentirem animi ægritudinem. Te quod attinet (Vir omnium optime amicissime dilectissime) cum <tuam>†a cogito doctrinam animum mores candorem suavitatem amicitiam satis in te uno reperi (ut cæteros taceam) quo mihi semper gratulari potero optime locatam et fructuosissimam aliquot annorum apud vos moram: nec scio an aliquod mea vita tempus æque jucundum habitura sit, certè magis proficuum nondum habuit. Deus O.M. Te omni fælicitatum genere cumulatum, familiam, patriam incolumes conservet et custodiat, ut diu sis ecclesiæ et omnibus bonis utilis. De meo erga Te animo qualis jam sit qualis futurus sit nihil addam, cum meum spero amorem non magis mihi
― 558 ―
notum et certum esse quam tibi, cujus in me amicitiam tot beneficiis testatam habeo, ut quicquid de ea literis tuis jucundissimis dicas, jam jam penitus persuaso facile persuadebis. Optimæ tuæ uxori liberisque, Veeniis Gueneloniisque omnibus plurimam salutem dicas. Te mihi apud illos advocatum et patronum relinquo nequid gravius statuant in hominem tot beneficiis <devinctum>†a si non fugientem, minus urbane certe quam oportuit valedicentem. Sed ita sunt fere res humanæ ut nihil præter voluntatem in nostra sit potestate. eâ totus ad eos feror, eâ singulos amplector; quæ mihi nunquam ad beneficiorum memoriam, ad grati animi confessionem defutura est. Vale Vir Colendissime et me ut facis ama
Tui in perpetuum amantissimum
J LOCKE

(Latin) Rotterdam 16 Feb. 89
My chief desire on leaving this country was to be given the chance of bidding a warm farewell to you, excellent Sir, and to the rest of my Amsterdam friends; but in this everything seems to be opposing me as if of set purpose. First, there was the ice and the hurry, and then on the journey itself I was caught by rain. I left here last Saturday†1 for The Hague, in order to have a word there with the noble lady,†2 who was also thinking of going to Amsterdam; but when passing through Delft I was drenched by a pretty violent downpour, an inconvenience which I also suffered at The Hague. So I was wet through when I reached her; I had meant to press on that night to see you all, but she not only advised me against this but absolutely forbade such a night-journey as too dangerous for my health. So it is as if that rain, almost the only drop we have had for the last two months, was expressly ordained to rob me finally of the hope I was full of at starting, that of having one short day with you all. I found everything at the court so ready and so impatient of delay that nobody doubts that the Princess will embark with the first favourable wind. When I started on that intended journey to see you I trusted not [p. 556] so much to the wind as to the Princess's religious scruples,†1 for I hardly thought she would be willing to start on a journey on Sunday, even though an east wind might invite it; but now they are waiting for nothing but a suitable sailing wind, and as soon as that comes we must rush to the ships. I returned here yesterday evening and do not know how long I shall have to dawdle here. I am sure of this, that nothing is a greater annoyance than to be saddled with inactivity until one is sick of it, and yet not to have time for what one wishes to do most of all. How I wish I could be granted an hour or two with you all. There is something in the sight and talk and embraces of friends that my spirit yearns to take its fill of. Of your feelings for me and of mine for you I think there can be no doubt, nor could our mutual friendship be increased by a farewell talk; yet I long to see you, to clasp your hand, and once again to commend myself to you as entirely yours, which indeed I am. If this is not to be permitted to me now I hope it will be at some other time; for I do not augur so ill for myself as to believe that there will never be a day which may bring us together once more. There are many things which make it advisable that I should not lose this opportunity of sailing. My friends expect me; my private affairs have been neglected now for some years; there are many privateers about, and the passage would otherwise be rather unsafe; [p. 557] and there is my responsibility, or might I say friendship, for the noble lady with whom I am to travel. Of this you may feel assured, that I have found here another fatherland, and I had almost said other kinsmen; for all that is dearest in that name, benevolence, love, and charity, which have power to unite men and hold them together with bonds stronger than those of blood, I have experienced in abundance with you. I have friends here whom I must ever cherish, whom indeed I must visit if time and circumstances permit. This I know for certain, that I am leaving you with the intention of returning one day to enjoy the full and unimpaired delight of their company whose kindness brought it about that in my absence from my own people and at a time of general despondency I felt no mental distress. As for yourself, best of men and my dearest friend, when I think of your scholarly mind, your candid and upright character and your kindly friendship, I feel that I have found in you alone, to say nothing of the rest, enough to enable me ever to call myself happy that my sojourn of these years among you has been put to such good and profitable use. I know not whether there is ever to be an equally delightful period in my life; there has certainly never yet been one more advantageous. May God Almighty abundantly bestow every kind of happiness upon you, and may he preserve and protect you, your family, and your country, that you may long be of service to the church and to all good men. I will say no more of what my feelings towards you are now and will continue to be, as my affection is, I hope, not better or more certainly known to myself than it is to [p. 558] you; I have evidence of your friendship in so many acts of kindness that whatever you may say of it in your delightful letters you will have no difficulty in persuading one who is already fully persuaded. Please give my best wishes to your excellent wife and children, and to all the Veens and Guenellons. I leave you as my advocate and defender with them, lest they pass too severe a sentence on one who is under obligations to them for so many kindnesses, seeing that, if not actually running away from them, he is certainly saying good-bye less courteously than he should have done. But it is commonly the way in human affairs that we have nothing in our own power except our will; with that will I am borne to them heart and soul; with it I embrace them one and all; nor will it ever fail to move me to the remembrance of benefits received and to the acknowledgements of a grateful heart. Good-bye, honoured Sir, and continue to love me
Your ever most affectionate
J. LOCKE
(Latin) I wrote to our friend Guenellon last week, and two days ago from The Hague to Mr. Le Clerc; I received the books from him yesterday, both his own and ours; let him know that I am indebted to him on both accounts. I should like to know what our friend Sladus is doing; I am much concerned for his welfare, and rightly so. Tell him he must not vegetate, now that the affairs of his friend and his country (for he is a countryman of ours) are prospering, and whatever further may proceed from a sincere friend, for I value [p. 559] him highly and am very fond of him. I send my repeated good wishes to all our Collegians. I wish I might find something in England with which to acknowledge the honour that has been done me by so distinguished and scholarly a company.

(Latin) To the illustrious Mr. Locke, from Joh. Verrijn, greeting.
It is now some time since I heard that you had left this country rather hurriedly; now, however, late this evening I understand from Mijnheer van Limborch that you have not yet started; accordingly I send you this note, both in order to have someone by whom I may send my respects to Mr. Burnet, and also to avoid your leaving us without a word of farewell. I thank you for not having judged me entirely unworthy of some part in your friendship; and although that friendship has been very dear to us, yet I congratulate you and all your countrymen on the safety and security that have fallen to the lot of your kingdom and churches, not without signal proofs of divine providence. For the future God grant that your people may enjoy those [p. 560] blessings as long as possible, and that you too may always enjoy good health and sufficient leisure to remember us sometimes.
Good-bye.
Amsterdam 16 Febr. 1689.

1110. J. G. Grævius to Locke, 8/18 February 1689 (1105, 1200)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 32-3. Transmitted by Benjamin to Paul D'Aranda; by him apparently forwarded to Furly, and by him to Locke: pp. 567, 569. Answers no. 1105; answered by no. 1200.
(English) Vir Nobilissime.
Incredibilem ex tuis litteris cepi voluptatem. Primo vehementer gaudebam, cum ex iis intelligerem, te molestiis et periculis, quibus aliquamdiu conflictatus es indignissime, nunc liberatum esse, reditumque in patriam adornare. Quamvis ego caream aegerrime tua suavissima consuetudine, non possum tamen non tuis gaudere bonis, cum tibi vivere licebit cum tuis sine insidiis, sine incommodis. Volo haec tibi esse propria, nullisque rebus adversis interpellari, ut quicquid temporis et aetatis hic exigendum erit, molliter ac suaviter sine aegritudine molestiaque transigas. Dein quid gratius mihi accidere poterat, quam tantum virum, quem ut vidi, ut deperii,†2 singularis sui in me studii et amoris tam illustria argumenta edere? Quantas enim significationes prolixae hujus tuae
― 563 ―
voluntatis hae litterae habent? A te, Locki, amari pluris, mihi crede, duco, quam dynastarum ac Regum gratia florere. Velim enim persuasissimum tibi sit, me, a quo tempore virtutes tuas mihi cognoscere datum, tanti te fecisse, ut neminem tibi quos norim anteposuerim. Idque in omni sermone apud omnes, ubi fuit occasio de te loquendi, prae me tuli, me non modo mirificas ingenii tui suavitates, et varietatem doctrinae, sed in primis probitatem vitaeque integritatem, studiumque bene de bonis omnibus merendi propensissimum mirari et colere. Nunquam haec ex meo effluent animo: semper quam diu mei memor fuero, tui quoque memoria illi obversabitur. Et si quando ullo officii obsequiique genere id tibi testatum facere potero, cognosces quantam mihi in te observando constituerim pietatem, et quam in te amando nulli mortalium cedam, qui vel longo annorum usu, aut sanguinis necessitudine tibi sunt conjunctissimi. Cum vero litterarum quoque tuarum spem mihi facis, cumulas ingenti accessione gaudia et nihil mihi poterit afferri optatius et desideratius. Si me vis saepe frui hac voluptate, qua nunc me affecisti, quam fidem dedisti libera. si non crebro, fac saltem non nunquam tuas epistolas videam. Equidem non ante rerum quoque jucundissimarum quicquam me juvabit, quam te salvum et incolumem ad tuos rediisse intellexero. Ad laetitiae, qua
― 564 ―
me perfudisti, omnibus numeris absolutæ cumulum mihi potuisset†a accedere, si tui quoque complectendi copiam et facultatem ante discessum tuum non invidisset mihi fortuna. Sed haec, ut cetera quae haec vita fert acerba, sunt ferenda. feram aequiore animo, si, cum te non licuerit videre, tuas epistolas videro, et hic viam invenero tibi probandi meum animum et observantiam. Praestantissimus D'Aranda, quem ante jam amabam, quanti ponderis apud me sit tua commandatio cognoscet spero. Nam quamvis mihi eum dudum commendarint ejus dotes, et desiderium, quo flagrat, optimas artes imbibendi, a te tamen mihi traditus non modo semper erit in oculis, sed et in sinu meo.
(English) Quas litteras ad Jannettum misisti, nullus vidi. Champneium non miror insalutatis nobis abiisse. Qua lingua enim valere dixisset, cum patriam eius linguam ignorem? De honorario nunquam a me potuissem impetrare ut ullam facerem mentionem, praesertim cum fructum ex nostra disciplina aut nullum, aut perquam tenuem, ceperit Champneius, nisi toties id urgeres et tam acriter. Ne igitur et in hac re mea voluntas a tua discrepet, uti nolim unquam nostras rationes discrepare in ulla re, significo tibi quicquid est honorarii id nec Janettum, nec ejus alumnum, vestrum civem, mihi numerasse.
― 565 ―
Ceteri mihi solverunt triginta florenos pro annuis scholis. Sed pudet pigetque harum nugarum. Deum precor ut secundis ventis hoc anni tempore, satis adhuc alieno, quo olim clausa erant maria, feraris in patrios portus. Vale et me amare perge. Amabis sane hominem tui studiosissimum et observantissimum. Trajecti D. XVIII/VIII Febr. 1689. Tuae, quas Hage scripsisti 14/4 Febr. heri mihi demum redditae sunt.
(English) Praestantissimo Grevio, <quem>†a credo cras me visurum esse, salutem dicam tuo nomine. Jannettum quoque compellabo de tua epistola. Hodie prodire mihi districto non licuit. Iterum iterumque Vale.
(English) Furleium quaeso ut meo nomine salutes. Librum ejus†1 non sine fructu legi, quem mecum communicarat amicus, ut et si vobiscum est, et si†b videris, Helmondum.†2
(Latin) Illustrious Sir,
Your letter gave me unbelievable pleasure. In the first place, I was overjoyed at learning from it that you are now set free from the troubles and dangers you have contended with so long and so undeservedly, and that you are preparing to return to your native land. Though I shall be deeply distressed by the loss of your delightful company, yet I cannot help rejoicing at your good fortune, seeing that you will be able to live with your own people without discomforts and exposure to insidious attacks. My wish is that these blessings may remain yours as of right, uninterrupted by any kind of adversity, so that whatever time you may have to live here below may be passed in ease and comfort without distress or trouble. And then, what could have gratified me more than that such a great man, who had won my heart the moment I saw him, should give me such signal proofs of his remarkable interest and affection for me? For what manifest tokens your letter contains of [p. 563] your abundant goodwill towards me! To be loved by you, my dear Locke, I account, believe me, of greater value than to bask in the favour of potentates and kings. I would have you be fully assured that ever since it was granted me to know your excellent qualities I have valued you so highly that I would not place anyone I know before you. Whenever an occasion to speak of you has arisen in any conversation and in any company I have made it known that what I admire and respect in you is not only your wonderful charms of intellect and the variety of your learning, but chiefly the honesty and integrity of your life and your earnest desire to deserve well of all good men. These things will never be effaced from my mind; as long as I remember myself your memory too will always be present to me; and if I should ever be able to prove this to you by any service or the fulfilment of any wish you will realize how firmly attention to you is fixed in my mind as a sacred duty, and how in affection for you I would yield to no one on earth, even to those who are most closely united to you by long association or the ties of kindred blood. But when you go on to give me hopes of hearing from you, you heap the measure of my joy with a mighty addition; nothing could better meet my wishes and desires. If you wish me often to enjoy the pleasure that you have now given me you must keep your promise. If not very frequently, manage at least to let me see your letters from time to time. Indeed, nothing even of the most delightful kind will please me until I know that you have returned safe and sound to your own people. The joy you have filled me with to [p. 564] overflowing, complete as it is, might have been increased if fortune had not begrudged me the power and opportunity of embracing you before your departure. But these things must be borne, like the other bitternesses of life. I shall bear them more easily if, since I could not see you, I may see your letters, and if I can here discover some way of proving my affection and regard for you. The excellent D'Aranda, whom I was already fond of, will, I hope, come to know what weight your recommendation has with me. For although his natural gifts and his ardent desire to acquire the highest arts have long won my approval, yet now that he has been entrusted to me by you I shall not only always watch his progress but shall make him my special care.
(Latin) I have not seen the letter you sent to Jannettus. As for Champneys, I am not surprised that he went away without saying good-bye to us; for in what language could he have said it, seeing that I am not acquainted with his native tongue? About my honorarium I could never have brought myself to say a word, especially as Champneys got no value, or very little, from my instruction, if you had not pressed the matter so often and so sharply. Well, then, to avoid a clash between my wishes and yours in this matter, as I should never wish our accounts to disagree in anything, I inform you that whatever was due to me in that way was not paid to me either by Jannettus or by his protegé, your fellow country man. Others have paid me thirty florins [p. 565] for a year's instruction. But I feel shame and disgust at these trifles. I pray God you may have favourable winds to carry you to your home ports at this time of year, which has so far been unpropitious enough, and which once used to keep the seas closed to shipping. Good-bye, and continue to love me; you will surely be fond of one who is full of devotion and respect for you. Utrecht 18/8 February 1689. Your letter written at The Hague 14/4 February reached me yesterday at last.
(Latin) I believe I shall be seeing the eminent de Greve tomorrow and will remember you to him; I shall also have a word with Jannettus about your letter. I was too busy to go out today. Good-bye again and again.
(Latin) Please remember me to Furly. I read a book of his,†1 which was sent me by a friend, not without profit. Please also give my respects to Helmond†2 if he is where you are and if you happen to see him.

1111. Benjamin D'aranda to Locke, 8 February 1689
B.L., MS. Locke c. 3, ff. 26-7. D'Aranda's date must be old style because the only letters of Locke's and Grævius's with which his can be associated are those of 4/14 and 8/18 February (nos. 1105, 1110); it is clear from them that there can have been no exchange in the preceding fortnight. This letter, with no. 1110 enclosed, was apparently forwarded by Paul D'Aranda to Furly, and so reached Locke.

Ultrajecti, 8o Febr: -89
Præstantissime Vir
Quas a Fratre, heri, accepi litteras Tuas Grævio clarissimo tradidi; in quibus me beasti sane quod Ei commendare dignatus sis. Ego vero, quamvis nihil habeam, hoc potissimum tempore, quod tanto beneficio dignum reponam, gratias tamen saltem, (quas semper habebo maximas) cum coram agere non erat fas, (quod doleo) non potui mihi obtemperare quin per litteras referrem, quanquam ne tam molestæ sint verear quam indignas Te, indignas tanto in me honore, satis sciam: audacem tamen fecere candor et humanitas Tua, quæ jam abunde expertus sum, in impetrandâ illâ Tuâ ad Grævium commendatione (quâ nihil potuit mihi optatius accidisse, tum propter illius viri summam eruditionem, tum propter meam in id doctrinæ genus, in quo Ille tam gloriose versatur, propensionem et amorem, adeo ut, tanto præeunte duce, haud dubito quin exinde fructus accipiam maximos. hasce igitur meas litterulas (gratitudinis summæ pignora) non gravabere, spero, blande accipere et fovere; atque utinam id mihi fælicitatis aliquando contingat ut Tibi pro tantis Tuis in me beneficiis paria saltem si non (quod vellem, modo

(Latin)
Utrecht, 8 Febr. 89
Eminent Sir,
I have handed to the renowned Grævius your letter to him, which I received from my brother yesterday, in which you have been so very kind as to recommend me to him. For my part, though I have no means, especially at the present time, of making a worthy return for such a great kindness, yet since I am, to my regret, unable to thank you in person, I cannot help expressing at least by letter the very deep gratitude which I shall always feel, though I fear that my thanks may be as troublesome to you as I am fully aware that they are unworthy of you and of the signal honour you have done me; I was emboldened, however, by your open-hearted generosity, which I have now experienced in full measure in obtaining your recommendation to Grævius; there is nothing I could have wished for more, both on account of his great learning and because of my own inclination and love for the kind of studies in which he is engaged with such distinction, so much so that with such a scholar for guide I have no doubt that I shall reap the greatest profit from his instruction. I hope therefore that you will not be unwilling kindly and favourably to accept these few lines, the pledges of my heartfelt gratitude, and I hope that I may some day have the happiness to be able to make you at least an equivalent return, if not, as I could wish if it were possible, a greater, [p. 567] for your great kindness. As for yourself, most generous Sir, since you are resolved to depart, I pray that you may see your own country again in safety, and that you may enjoy a long and happy life there; meanwhile, if you know of anything in which I might do something pleasing and useful to you, be assured that I shall always be ready and forward to serve you and desirous of no greater glory than the ability to do so.
Your most obliged and obedient servant
BENJAMIN D'ARANDA
P.S. I enclose a letter to you from the renowned Grævius which has just been brought to me.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Lock

Sir
Doubting whither this Letter will reach you while in holland I dare not increase its bulk any more than to thrust in this bit of Paper which though small brings you very many thanks for your Letter to Mr: Grævius in my Brothers favour, you have so many ways, and those in so obliging a Manner, made me your Debter,
― 568 ―
that till you put me in some way of proving I am as sensible of your favours as I ought to be I shall not dare shew my self to you again. but to say truth I am desirous to know where I may pay respect to you in London, with, the Beggars fee, Thanks for the good advice you gave me at the Delft boat, I have not since tasted wine and, believe I shall continue to abstain from it, I will allways own that the benefit I may receive by not using it is from you who I hope will do me the favour to remember that you have in me left here one who by being your Convert is under strong bonds of continuing
Sir your m: faithfull servant

1114. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 12/22 February 1689 (1017, 1115)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 32-3.
Rotterdam 22 [[sic]]m february 1689
Dear Friend
I know not whether I should have wrote to thee, till I heard of thy safe arrivall had not the 2 Inclosed for thee come to hand the One from Amsterdam the other from Toinard.†4 a third came from the Briel, but that I judgd not worth the sending, being that from Rivall from on board the Isabella†5 —I doubt not, hearing that you put to sea about 3 aclock, but you arrived safely last night, at Harwich,†6 if so, I hope thou wilt stay and repose thyself a while at Colchester;†7 where I am sure thou wilt be most heartily welcome,
― 570 ―
I met Stoop going down the river—And the next morning, (having no time to go to the Inn or our lodging to pay and take my Gown) I sent John†1 down to do it, and the chocolate pot by him, who gave it yong Papillon†2 for thee—Stoop, and his ship, and David Rall, and Richard Martin were all before the Briel, flattering themselves that the Princess was not yet put to sea, and that they should overtake her, but I beleeve they found the contrary—All in the Lanterne salute thee, and do regrett thy absence, which I shall not be willing to beare longer then needs must, the change is already so sensible, as if the sun were departed from our hemisphere; my affaires, for ought I see, sound a retreat out of this Cuntry, my chiefest spring of Irish Commissions are perfectly stopt—And in this chargeable cuntry to stay without Imployment, is nor prudent, nor long practicable for me—But quo me vertam nescio,†3 therefore if any thing fall under thy consideration, having spoken with those upon whom I depend, I shalbe glad to be advertised thereof. I have remitted my Lord the mony my Lady gave me,†4 this post, in the bills of Van Twedde,†5 and one of my owne—If our Friends E: Clark and J. Fr. Sir Walter and his brother Duke†6 be there give my service to them, and account me always among the number of thy friends, who shall never forget the proffit I have reaped by thy converse, which makes me so desirous of a continuance thereof if it may be—
Our Virginy man†7 is yet here, and the wind strong in the old corner so by him, if this post come in, in any time, and bring any incouragement I may yet come—in the meane while I rest
Thy most affectionate friend
BENJAMIN FURLY

1115. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 19 February/ 1 March 1689 (1114, 1140)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 34.
Rotterdam 13 March 168<9>†a
Deare Friend
Tho, Since mine Last post, we heare of the Queenes safe arrival at Whitehall,†1 and have none from you that I presume arrived all of you at the same time, yet I find myself under the obligation of writing again, for the conveyance of the two Inclosed, not knowing what hast they may require. The one is from Toinard,†2 the other from England.
We heare that both houses are at last agreed, which is great satisfaction to us, generally, what the Instrument of Government is we long to heare, but if it be not some thing more then what we can pick out of all the letters and printed papers they have shewed themselves a most gratefull confiding people to a wise prince to whom they leave all— So we must expect from his generosity that he will go on to perfect that excellent worke he has begun; and from his experience, concerning the convenience of an universal liberty of conscience, in this Cuntry we must expect the same there. For when the Prince shews an inclination to it, no English Parliament at this time a day surely will hinder so good a thing. And in particular we may hope by an Act of Parliament to be relieved from the 2 snares the convention have brought us under for the present.†3 Was there no body among them could think upon those sufferings and sufferers, that upon that account have been so visible, and of so long a continuance? For if we cannot be relievd by a Law, theres no hopes of being relieved by dispensation or connivance. I hope I shall soone have a letter from thee certifying us of your good healths, and what I am particularly to expect. Three days since the Earl of S. was dismist.†4 I was this day to have seen him but he was gone
― 572 ―
abroad in a coach with Jurieu;†1 I sent him one of the Inclosed papers which his uncle sent me from France 1666 and which I found accidentally yesterday looking among old papers, which I showing to Denis Verburgh, he went and printed it in E. and Dutch.†2 It is remarkeable that it should have layne neglected as a loose paper 23 years, and be at this time found unsought for—as was my old Almanack. pray enquire after the Mirabilis Annus 1663. and after John Coughen, whose Almanack it was.†3 <He>†a uses much to frequent Peter Kids Amsterdam coffeehouse.†4
It is remarkeable that this Son of man, is one that uses not to carry in his Arms the unicorns†b that are used in the land of wool. And that the Lilly is to lose his crowne and he to be crowned therewith, as also that the Emperor should return triumphant out of the East parts to help this king of England. But there seems to be a bitter cup to be drank in the land of the Lion, and a large viall of blood to be shed there if all be true thats there told. I have this night writ to John Freak, about a business of consequence, which I hope to have the management off if I come over. Tis the recovering of £3000 taken from some friends of mine by the African company.†5 Against which tho they could not get Justice formerly, yet its hoped now they may, If J F. Judge it fit to ingage in it and write to me, concerning it, that If I will undertake, on my part, to do to my utmost, he will do his, it may make the owners
― 573 ―
dispatch the business of Hartsoecker†1 the sooner that I may come to serve them in that affaire, and reap some advantage by it. Therefore let him say little to the <seamen>,†a and tell them hele consider it and write to me—we al salute thee and so I remain
Thy most affectionate friend
B F—
I hope the bill and bond too are paid. my service to my Lord, and Ladys M. and C. and Earl of M——†2
Address: To Ansham Churchil Bookeseller in Pater Noster Row at Amen Corner In London
For Dr. Locke These
Postmark: —25
