1116. Locke to Charles Mordaunt, second Viscount Mordaunt, later earl of Monmouth, and later third earl of Peterborough, 21 February 1689 (1150)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, f. 198. Apparently the letter sent or ready to send. Printed in King, pp. 173-5.
The person addressed is Charles Mordaunt, c. 1658-1735; second Viscount Mordaunt of Avalon 1675; created earl of Monmouth 9 April of this year; succeeded as third earl of Peterborough 1697; the general: D.N.B.; for Lady Mordaunt see p. 527. Mordaunt was appointed a privy councillor between 14 and 18 February. According to Lady Masham Locke 'had his choice given him of goeing as Envoy to the Emperour, the now King of Prussia [Frederick III, elector of Brandenburg, from 1701 king in Prussia as Frederick I] or to a third place which I remember not': letter to Le Clerc, January 1705. The present letter suggests that what was offered was the mission to the Elector.
Whitehall 21 Feb. 1689
My Lord
I cannot but in the highest degree be sensible of the great honour his Majestye has don me in those gratious intentions towards me which I have understood from your Lordship: And it is the most touching displeasure I have ever received from that weak
― 574 ―
and broken constitution of my health which has soe long threatend my life, that it now affords me not a body suitable to my minde in soe desirable an occasion of serveing his Majestie.
I make account every English man is bound in conscience and gratitude not to content himself with a bare slothfull and inactive loialty, where his purse his head or his hand may be of any use to this our great deliverer. He has venturd and don too much for us to leave roome for indifferency or backwardnesse in any one who would avoid the reproach and contempt of all mankinde. And if with the great concernes of my Country and all Christendom I may be permitted to mix soe mean a consideration as my owne private thoughts I can truly say that the particular veneration I have for his person carys me beyond an ordinary zeale for his service. Besides this, my Lord, I am not soe ignorant as not to see the great advantages of what is proposd to me. There is honour in it enough to satisfie an ambition greater than mine, and a step to the makeing my fortune, which I could not have expected. These are temptations that would not suffer me easily to decline soe eminent a favour, as the other are obligations to a forward obedience in all things where there is hopes it may not be unusefull. But such is the misfortune of my circumstances, that I cannot accept the honour is designed me without rendring my self utterly unworthy of it. And however tempting it be I cannot answer to my self or the world my imbraceing a trust, which I may be in danger to betray even by my entring upon it. This I shall certainly be guilty of, if I doe not give your Lordship a true account of my self and what I foresee may be prejudiciall to his Majesties affairs. My Lord the post that is mentioned to me, is at this time if I mistake not one of the busyest and most important in all Europe, and therefor would require not only a man of common sense and good intentions, but one whom experience in the methods of such businesse has fitted with skill and dexterity to deale with not only the reasons of able but the more dangerous artifices of cunning men, that in such stations must be expected and masterd. But my Lord supposeing industry and good will would in time worke a man into some degree of capacity and fitnesse, what will they be able to doe with a body that hath not health and strength enough to comply with them? What shall a man doe in the necessity of application, and variety of attendance on businesse to be followed there, who sometimes after a litle motion has not breath to speake, and cannot borrow an hower or
― 575 ―
two of watching from the night, without repaying it with a great wast of time the next day? Were this a Conjuncture wherein the affairs of Europe went smooth, or a litle mistake in management would not be soon felt, but that the diligence or change of the minister might timely enough recover it: I should perhaps thinke I might without being unpardonably faulty venture to try my strength, and make an experiment soe much to my advantage. But I have a quite other view of the state of things at present. And the urgency of affairs comes on soe quick, that there was never such need of succesfull diligence and hands capable of dispatch as now. The dilatory methods and slow proceedings, to say noe worse of what I cannot without indignation reflect on in some of my Country men at a season when there is not a moment of time lost without indangering the Protestant and English interest through out Europe, and which have already put things too far back,†1 make me justly dread the thought that my weake constitution should in soe considerable a post any way clog his Majesties affairs. And I thinke it much better that I should be laid by to be forgotten forever than that they should at all suffer by my ambitiously forward undertakeing what my want of health or experience would not let me manage to the best advantage. For I must again tell your Lordship that however unable I might prove there will not in this Crisis be time to call me home and send an other. If I have reason to apprehend the cold air of the Country there is yet an other thing in it as inconsistent with my constitution and that is their warme drinking. I confesse obstinate refusall may breake pretty well through it. But that at best will be but to take more care of my own health than the Kings businesse. Tis noe small matter in such stations to be acceptable to the people one has to doe with in being able to accomodate ones self to their fashons and I imagin whatever I may doe there my self the knowing what others are doeing is at least one half of my businesse. and I know noe such rack in the world to draw out mens thoughts as a well managed Bottle. If therefor it were fit for me to advise in this case I should think it more for the Kings interest to send a man of equall parts that could drinke his share, than the soberest man in the Kingdom.
I beseech you my Lord to looke on this not as the discourse of a modest or lazy man but of one who has truly considerd himself and above all things wishes well to the designes which his Majestie
― 576 ―
has soe gloriously began for the redeeming England and with it all Europe. I wish for noe other happynesse in this world but to see it compleated and shall never be spareing of my mite where it may contribute any way to it, which I am confident your Lordship is sufficiently assured of, and therefor I beg leave to tell your Lordship that if there be any thing wherein I may flatter my self I have atteind any degree of capacity to serve his Majestie it is in some litle knowledg I perhaps may have in the constitutions of my country, the temper of my Country men and the divisions and interests amongst. whereby I perswade my self I may be more usefull to him at home, though I cannot but see that such an imployment would be of greater advantage to my self abroad would but my health consent to it. My Lord misseing your Lordship at your lodging this morning I have taken the liberty to leave you my thoughts in writeing being loath that in any thing that depends on me there should be a moments delay, a thing which at this time I looke on as soe criminall in others. I am
My Lord
your Lordships most humble and most obedient servant
J LOCKE
Address: These present To the Honourable the Lord Mordaunt
Endorsed by Locke: J L to Lord Mordaunt 21 Feb. 88/9

(Latin)
London 8 Mar. 89
Excellent Sir,
Great as is my happiness in the embraces of friends congratulating me on my return to my country, it is hardly greater than the sadness I feel at leaving [p. 577] all of you; though there is no link of blood or nationality between us, yet friendship and goodwill have assuredly bound us together with a stronger tie. You, especially, best of friends, I shall always hold in remembrance and honour. When I recall all that you have done for me I realize how great is the power of affection and human kindness that can presume to vie with love for one's native land. May I perish if in the universal rejoicing in which I am taking part I do not miss you and yours most grievously. To tell the truth, indeed, now that my lung-trouble is upon me once again, my one consolation is that, if the cough which attacked me immediately I arrived should get worse every day, as it threatens to do, and should compel me to be an exile once more, the same remedy will give me back both my health and you, who are as dear to me as my health. If I am not absolutely panting for such a fresh sojourn abroad, seeing that I am scarcely yet at home, I certainly think of it whilst I pant.
(Latin) I wrote to Dr. Guenellon as soon as I landed to tell him about our voyage and how well timed it was, for I felt that the first thing to be done on returning to my fatherland was to give evidence of a mindful heart to those who had provided me with a fatherland on foreign soil. Please give my kindest remembrances to your excellent wife and to your daughters and sons-in-law; [p. 578] and let me know of your doings and how you all are from time to time. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most respectful and obedient
J LOCKE
Address: Mijn Heer Mÿn Heer Veen
Noted by Veen: accepi has viiij aprilis
1118. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 9 March 1689 (1085, 1125)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 32-3.
Otterton March 9th. 88.
Dear Sir
Your old letter, which came lately to my hands;†1 is however a new Obligation on me, who am already indebted to you for a Million. I was almost afraid that you had blotted me out of the Catalogue of your Friends, and were resolv'd to have no more to do with me; but this letter convinces me that I were not wholly forgotten, and does me as much good now as if I had receiv'd it soon after it's date; but it would have spared all the affliction which your Silence made me suffer, which was much greater then any danger I could have run by receiving it; and how ever it were interpreted you could not have been hurt by it, who were safe on the other side of the Water. but since you are so Peaceable, I will be as Thankfull, and make no more words of it; Especially since we have a New Scene, and so Glorious a one, as Transports us, and makes us forget and forgive whatever is past. or else I should have a new quarrell to you for not giving me notice of your Comming over, which would infallibly have kept me in Town, and without doubt brought Mr Duke thither. and then I should have had my share of your good Company, and been as Happy as this World could make me; wheras now I can only please my self with fancying you are in England, London and Amsterdam being both at a fatal
― 579 ―
distance from poor me; for I came so lately thence, that I should be excommunicated should I propose going thither again. Yet I cannot forbear congratulating most heartily your safe arrival on this side of the Water; And if you do not make hast to Chipley, that I may wayt on you there, I know not what extravagant Course I may take; for I am impatient to ask your blessing, and to offer you the utmost services of, Sir
Your most Obedient daughter and Faithfull humble servant
ISABELLA DUKE
Mr Duke begs you to accept his best services.
Address: For Mr John Lock att London

Apres vous avoir dit, monsieur, que j'etois dans une extrême inquietude par votre silence, je vous prieray de trois choses à l'avenir touchant celes dont vous voudrez m'honorer.
1. De ne point marquer le lieu.
2. D'User Stylo novo.

A legard de lotre je ne vous saurois rien prometre, etant un livre rare et memes peu connu.†2
Je vous prie d'assurer madame Caverly de mes tres humbles respects. Nous avons bien parlé d'elle depuis son depart monsieur l'Abé et moy.

Le petit neveu du feu Triumvir†2 monte à g<rands>†a pas sur le grand theatre. Il fait tous les jo<urs>†a de merveilleuses decouvertes par sa sagaci<té>†a en medecine et chirurgie. N'oubliez pas de salüer de ma part celui à la maison duquel j'ay obligation de la plus douce et plus avantageuse connoissance que j'ay jamais faite.†5
Maux davanture sont ampoules aux doits, Gerzûres, ecorchûres, picûres, et cæt.
Je reçois tout prezentement votre letre du 28. Febr. quand ce seroit stylo veteri, ce seroit bien tard.

Vereor ne nomine negligentiæ tibi suspectus sim quòd tam

diuturno utor silentio, quod nec tuis meritis, nec meæ voluntati, nec nostræ denique amicitiæ omnino convenit. London, 12 Mar. 89
Excellent Sir,
I fear you must be suspicious of me on the score of negligence because of [p. 583] this long silence of mine, which was by no means suited either to your deserts or to my wishes, or in short to our friendship. I would have you know that my change of place has not brought with it a change of mind, which is the same towards you as of old and will be the same wherever in the world I may be, a heart full of affection and respect. The truth is that since my return to my native land I have been much occupied: there is the converse with friends who come to see me or whom I must see; or the labour of seeking out my private effects, which are scattered in various places, and collecting them, for present purposes; or, if not some kind of entry upon the service of the state (if I may mention that service without boasting), at any rate my efforts, and justification of those efforts, to make sure that I shall not surrender my private leisure in exchange for public business; and worst of all, there is the bad effect on my health of the malign smoke of this city. All this has kept me so busy that I have hardly been left a moment of free time ever since I landed here. As soon as ever I stepped ashore, amongst the greetings of a crowd of people, I wrote hastily in my own tongue to Mr. Guenellon, asking him to give my best wishes to you and the rest of my Amsterdam friends; for whatever joy and delight I found here told me that something had been left behind there which gave me no less pleasure in recollection than what I saw with my eyes here. Burnet is designated bishop of Salisbury.†1 The question of toleration has now been taken up in parliament under [p. 584] a twofold title, namely Comprehension and Indulgence.†1 The former signifies extension of the boundaries of the Church, with a view to including greater numbers by the removal of part of the ceremonies. The latter signifies toleration of those who are either unwilling or unable to unite themselves to the Church of England on the terms offered to them. How lax or how strict these provisions are likely to be I hardly yet know; this at least is my impression, that the episcopal clergy are not very favourably inclined to these and other proposals that are now being mooted here; whether this is conducive to their own advantage or to that of the state is for their consideration. As to the payment I wrote to you about before I left I am daily expecting a word from you. Goodbye and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J. Locke
(Latin) Remember me to your dear wife and your whole family. I send my best wishes to the Collegians and to all my friends. Please give my best regards to Mr. Le Clerc, and tell him there is hardly anything of any importance in the commonwealth of learning appearing here at present; the press is now hard at work in the interests of the commonwealth of politics. The second part of [p. 585] Burnet's Theory of the earth came out not so long ago, in Latin;†1 also a small book entitled A Brief History of the Unitarians;†2 as this is not on sale I will, if he wishes, send him a copy at the first opportunity. He must excuse me for not writing to him at present; I hope shortly to have leisure again for learning and books; then perhaps there will be an opportunity for sending more plentiful information about books; for since I returned here, being drawn away by other matters, I have hardly entered a bookshop.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch

Dear Sister
Now I am come to England where I had promised my self a full Satisfaction I finde I want still two things very deare to me, that is You and my health. (English) Amplissime Vir; Salvum te in Angliam appulisse ex literis tuis ad D. Guenellonem intelleximus; et, si literas meas recte ad te dirigere novissem, e vestigio hanc tibi fœlicitatem gratulatus fuissem. Quamquam enim quævis terra viro forti patria sit,†2 animusque tuus fortunæ lusus diu contemplatus et expertus cuicunque sorti acquiescere
― 587 ―
didicerit; tamen quietas post multos errores in patria et inter consanguineos tandem nancisci sedes, præsertim ingruente senectute, alias per se satis molesta, non inter minima vitæ hujus commoda numerandum censeo. Quare ex animo hanc tibi gratulor fœlicitatem, Deumque precor, ut nulli motus civiles eam perturbent; sed regnum Anglicanum optata fruatur pace; eaque sit in illo regiminis moderatio, ut omnes ex æquo protegat; nec leges patrias defendisse, et Deum juxta conscientiæ dictamen coluisse, ulli in crimen unquam imputetur. Ac certe non possum quin omnia mihi moderatiora spondeam, cum Te negotiis civilibus admotum considero: ita enim verba tua interpretor, aliqualem tui ad Remp. factam accessionem: quibus modeste munus aliquod politicum Tibi demandatum significare mihi videris. Equidem non tam Tibi, quam patriæ tuæ gratulor, cujus negotiis curandis adhibetur vir eâ animi integritate, eâ rerum mundanarum peritiâ, eâ eruditione, eâ longo usu et variis casibus probatâ prudentiâ, eâ denique moderatione ac morum probitate, qualem in Te novimus et admiramur. Nec in negotiis tantum politicis, sed et Ecclesiasticis, eandem voveo moderationem; ut Ecclesia Anglicana, in quam plures aliarum regionum Ecclesiæ, tanquam eximiam, oculos conjectos habent,
― 588 ―
exemplar omnibus præbeat Tolerantiæ vere Christianæ, quæ sub duobus titulis, Comprehensio et Indulgentia, optime repræsentatur. Utinam omnium, quos Euangelii regulâ cælo non exclusos constat, comprehensione Ecclesiam nobis exhibeat vere Catholicam et Christianam! Verum, ut quod res est dicam, quando attentius considero, quantum Ecclesiasticorum, præsertim Præsulum et potestate ac jurisdictione Ecclesiastica pollentium, animis præjudicium ingenerare soleant antiquorum Conciliorum decreta, et primorum Ecclesiæ Doctorum, quos magno veritatis præjudicio augusto Patrum titulo venerari solet Theologorum vulgus, temerariæ decisiones, vereor ne angustis nimis cancellis ea circumscribatur. Papatus omnibus hominibus est naturalis, olim aiebat Lutherus:†1 Cum itaque tantâ apud vulgus probabilitate se commendare potest, vix eam sperare possumus humanarum rerum felicitatem, ut qui suffragiis potiores sunt, omnes naturam exuant. Non inficior tamen, præteritorum recordationem saniora posset suggerere consilia. Quod si tamen Comprehensio angustior sit, per laxiorem Indulgentiam posset omnium prospici securitati, si, quos conscientia, sive erronea sive recte instructa, τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ μεγάλῃ se unire non permittit, sine metu pœnæ privatis in cœtibus de Deo permittantur docere, Deumque colere, prout sibi in Euangelio revelatum
― 589 ―
credunt. Verum hæc eorum prudentiæ commissa sunto, ad quos ea cura spectat. Quæ tua sint consilia, quam justa et Christiana, novi. De Rever. D. Burneto eadem mihi persuadeo; quia nunquam de illo viro credere possum, dignitatem Episcopalem ullo modo animum ipsius, quem mihi sæpius tam candide ac rotunde aperuit, ullatenus immutaturam. Quamprimum episcopatum, ad quem designatur, in ipsum collatum audivero, gratulatorias ad ipsum dabo literas. Solutio, de qua scribis, in quatuor partes est distributa; tres jam solutæ sunt; quartæ solutionem intra paucos dies exspecto. Sed velim ex Te scire, quid epistolis et chartis eò spectantibus fieri velis? an a me asservari? an Tibi remitti? an vero flammis aboleri? Quicquid jusseris, faciam. De reliquis brevi in proximis meis literis, quas solutione plene peracta mox Tibi scripturus sum. Vale Vir Amplissime, et, quod facis, in amore mei persevera. Valetudinem opto Tibi ex voto. Salutat Te plurimam uxor mea.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
We learnt from your letter to Dr. Guenellon of your safe landing in England, and if I had known how to address my letter to you correctly I would at once have congratulated you on this happy event. For though it may be true that any place on earth is a brave man's fatherland,†2 and though you yourself have learnt by long observation and experience of the caprices [p. 587] of fortune to bear with any lot, yet I think that to attain at last after long wanderings a haven of rest in one's own country and amongst one's own kindred, especially when old age, a thing vexatious in itself, is coming upon one, is not to be counted among the least blessings of this life. Therefore I congratulate you heartily on your happiness, and I pray God that no civil commotions may disturb it, but that the realm of England may enjoy the peace it has longed for; may there be such moderation in its government as may protect all men alike; nor may it ever be accounted an offence in any man that he has stood by the laws of his fathers and has worshipped God according to the dictates of conscience. And indeed, I cannot but assure myself that there is in fact greater moderation in all things when I consider that you are entrusted with public affairs; for such I take to be your meaning when you say that you have made some sort of approach to the business of the state; which, it seems to me, is a modest way of signifying that you have been appointed to some political post. For my part, it is not so much you as your country that I congratulate, now that its business is in the hands of a man of such integrity of soul, such experience of worldly affairs, such learning, such wisdom approved by long use and in various emergencies, in fine, such moderation and moral probity as we know and admire in you. And it is not only in political affairs but also in ecclesiastical that I hope for the same moderation; that the Anglican Church, to which the eyes of many churches in other places are directed as to one of distinction, may afford to all an example of truly [p. 588] Christian toleration, which is well represented under the two heads of Comprehension and Indulgence. God grant that, by embracing all who by the rule of the Gospel are manifestly not shut out from Heaven, it may give us the spectacle of a truly Catholic and Christian Church. But, to state the fact, when I consider more carefully the amount of prejudice that is commonly engendered in the minds of churchmen, particularly of prelates and those enjoying power and authority in the Church, by the decrees of the ancient Councils, and by the rash pronouncements of the earliest Doctors of the Church, whom the generality of theologians are wont to venerate, to the great prejudice of the truth, under the august title of Fathers, I fear lest that Church of yours may find itself hedged about too narrowly. Popedom is a natural thing to all men, as Luther used to say in his time.†1 Since therefore it is able to recommend itself so plausibly to the multitude we can hardly expect that happiness in human affairs, that those who have the greater power by their votes should all shed their nature; yet I would not deny that recollection of the past might suggest saner counsels. If, however, Comprehension should prove too narrow, then wider Indulgence might offer a way of providing for the security of all, if those whom their conscience, whether wrongly or rightly informed, does not permit to join themselves to the Great Church were allowed to meet together by themselves without fear of punishment, and so to teach concerning God and so to worship Him as they believe [p. 589] to have been revealed to them in the Gospel. But these things must be entrusted to the wisdom of those who are concerned with the care of them; as for your own plans, I know how just and how Christian they are. I feel the same assurance about the Reverend Mr. Burnet; for never can I believe that the high office of bishop will in any way or in any degree change that worthy man's mind, which he has often so frankly and roundly expressed to me. As soon as I hear that the bishopric to which he is designated has been conferred upon him I shall write him a letter of congratulation. The payment which you write about is divided into four parts; three are already paid; I expect the payment of the fourth within a few days. But kindly let me know what you wish done with the letters and papers relating to it. Am I to keep them? are they to be sent back to you? or are they to be destroyed by fire? I will do whatever you tell me. About any remaining matters I will tell you shortly in my next letter, which I shall write as soon as the payment has been completed. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and remain constant, as you are, in affection for me. I heartily wish you the best of health. My wife sends you her warmest greetings.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH

1123. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 2/12 April 1689 (1095, 1135)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 9. The absence of an address suggests that the letter was enclosed in no. 1124.
Amst. ce 12 avril. 1689
Monsieur,
Comme nous ne pouvions qu'a peine esperer que vostre traject put estre achevé avant la tempeste,†1 nous estions dans des apprehensions continuelles avec toute la nation, que vous ne souffriez pas moins de tourmente sur mer, que nostre coeur estoit agité de crainte et de douleur qu'une si grande Princesse et tant d'illustres personages qui l'adsistoient couroient risque de souffrir, jusqu'au neufrage, je vous jure Monsieur, que peu de gens croient que vous pussiez avoir atteint l'autre bord avant l'orage, et il faut de necessité que le vent aye esté plus favorable en mer quil ne parut icy; jugez Monsieur, combien agreable nous a esté vostre lettre qui nous a tiré de doubte et remis nostre esprit en repos; ce n'est pourtant pas un repos parfait, estants tousjours allarmé de vostre eloignement, et ce sont des pauvres esperances ou plustost des nouveaux chagrins pour nous, que nous ne pouvons vous revoir que par l'accablement de vostre poitrine, et la crainte de ne pouvoir supporter l'air de vostre patrie; c'est exciter en nous un estrange combat, puisque il faut se flatter par cela mesme qui nous afflige, et que nous esperons que vous surmonterez. ce nous est veritablement un plaisir que connoissant vostre merite et vostre solide, nous sachions combien vous pouvez estre utile a vostre patrie dans la conjoncture presente des affaires, ou elle est devenue comme l'ame de toute l'Europe affligée. et dans le plaisir mesme de vous posseder nous ne delaisserons pas de regretter la perte que feroit la cause commune en vous eloignant du timon des affaires. Plutost donc Monsieur que de vous revoir avec des conditions si desavantageuses, nous souhaittons de tout le fond de nostre cœur, que vostre santé se puisse r'affermir, et que quand apres cet orage des affaires communes le calme sera revenu, vous vouliez bien nous consacrer quelques jours de vostre loisir, pour vous revoir. Cepandant Monsieur vous nous†a marqué pas le caractere precis de
― 591 ―
vostre employ, que nous nous impatientons de scavoir pour vous en pouvoir feliciter duement et pour vous donner le titre qui vous appartient. c'est pourquoy nous vous conjurons de le faire par la premiere que vous aurez la bonté de nous escrire. Ma femme a recu le pacquet que vous avez eu la bonté de luy envoyer: elle vous remercie de toute la peine que cela vous a donné, et vous conjure den agir librement avec elle, et de nous faire scavoir a combien montent les frais que vous avez deboursez, autrement vous l'obligerez de s'en rapporter a ce qu'elle en poura scavoir par autruy. elle se ressent fort obligée a Mademoiselle Smitsby de son honnesteté et vous prie si vous en avez l'occasion de luy en faire son compliment. nous voudrions scavoir de quoy on peut regaler les dames en Engleterre de ce que nostre pays produit.
Monsieur Sladus vend une partie de sa bibliotheque. sil avoit publié le catalogue†1 plustost je vous en aurois envoyé un, pour scavoir de vous et de monsieur Charleton quels livres vous en souhaitteriez. la vente s'en tiendra la sepmaine prochaine et il ny a que quatre jours quil a fait distribuer le catalogue. Ma femme vous auroit escrit si sa santé l'eut permis. elle vous salue tres humblement, et nostre pierot†2 qui profite a veu d'œil, vous presente ses tres humble respects. si vous voyez Monsieur Sylvestre,†3 je vous prie de luy dire que je ne luy ay pas escrit manque de scavoir son adresse et dans l'incertitude sil reste de dela. Monsieur Cohe de Zutphen†4 nous est venu voir et je luy ay rendu son livre. je vous suis obligé de m'avoir procuré sa connoissance. pour nouvelle. liege qui avoit nouvellement fait un traitté de neutralité avec la france, s'est declarée absolument pour l'empire. on dit que la paix avec les turks s'eloigne de plus en plus. nous nous preparons pour des grandes joyes au jour du couronnement de sa majesté britannique par des ordres de l'estat. vous avez presque mesprise a Mon adresse, c'est au coin du nieuwe spiegel straet et vous avez marqué vÿsel straet. je suis avec un profond respect et toute la famille.
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
GUENELLON
Endorsed by Locke: Guenellon 12 Apr. 89

1124. Dr. Egbertus Veen to Locke, 2/12 April 1689 (1117, 1159)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, f. 3. Answers no. 1117.
(English)
Amstelodami. xij Aprilis 1689.
Spectatissime Vir
Quam volupe nobis fuerit audire felicem tuum in Angliam appulsum, id ipsum per Guenellonium nostrum jam scies, ex altera autem parte gravius nostras perculsit aures et Animum, quod pectus tuum offendat Aer Londinensis præ carbonibus gravis, sed tu, qui nosti quantum aer valeat ad sanitatem tuendam, etiam facile cognosces tibi eligere salubriorem, qui, si ibi inveniri non detur, ecce nostrum, quem sanum constitutioni vestræ expertus es, ultro offerimus, quo si iterum frui cogaris, ambabus ulnis veterem hospitem amplexuri sumus, et si gratum tibi, simul offerimus ædes nostras, ad quas et Uxor et ego te invitamus ex corde toto, magisque gratus advenies ad Venios tuos, quo magis has ex libera voluntate eligas. profecto quantopere me tædeat absentiæ tuæ vix possum dicere, adeoque ut mihi præteritos referri annos exoptem, si id sine tuo incommodo posset. sed quod hanc nobis felicitatem invidere minatur, est quod ex literis Domini Limburgii et Guenellonii obscure significas ad munus aliquod promotum te iri, aut omnino nunc esse, sed cum, ut soles, de te ipso tuisque
― 593 ―
modeste loquaris et caute, molesto nunc desiderio id ipsum aliquando apertius significes oramus, quo tibi debite gratulari possemus tecumque gaudere.
(English) Interim nobiscum quid agatur cum scire aveas: Valemus, Deo favente, adhuc dum omnes. Dr. Sladus, qui diu se collegio et praxi medicæ negarat,†a nunc iterum prodit, Lugduni nunc est, unde reversurus brevi, cum bibliothecam patris sui forte et ex parte suam etiam hoc mense venalem exhibeat.†1 Uxor generi mei De Wilde intra tres quatuorve menses quinto prole suam familiam augebit, quod bene vertat Deus. Guenellonii uxor adhucdum principissat, ego illis Utrisque ut Lucina favere dignetur opto ex animo, quod nec Angliæ nec nobis ingratum esse potest, faxitque Deus ut porro talia regiæ familiæ subveniant prospera, qualia cum omnib: bonis civibus ex-optamus vovemusque. Deus, qui huc usque nobis et vestris in hac expeditione tam benigne et bene voluit, animos civium vestrorum ita conjungat, ne quisquam postea hanc vestram tranquillitatem turbare ausit. Quo omine desino, ubi primo te, humanissime vir, ex uxoris ut et ex meo nostrorumque nomine

salutaverim. Vale itaque et Vive felix, nosque sæpius literis vestris bea—

(Latin)
Amsterdam, 12 April 1689
Esteemed Sir,
How pleased we were to hear of your happy landing in England you will already have learnt through our friend Guenellon; on the other hand our ears and hearts were much distressed to hear that the air of London, so heavy with the fumes of coal, is troubling your chest; but you, who are aware of the importance of air in preserving health, will also easily know how to choose a healthier atmosphere for yourself; and if that should not be obtainable over there, then here is ours, which you know by experience is good for your constitution and which we willingly offer you; should you be obliged to enjoy it once more we are ready to embrace our old guest with both arms, and at the same time, if you like, we offer you our house, to which my wife and I invite you with our whole heart; your arrival will be the more welcome to your friends the Veens the more you make the choice of your own free will. Certainly I can hardly say how irksome your absence is to me, so much so that I could wish for these past years to be recalled, if that could happen without trouble to you. But what threatens to begrudge us this happiness is that in your letters to Mr. van Limborch and Mr. Guenellon you allude darkly to some post to which you are about to be promoted, or which you may actually hold now; but since, as your way is, you speak modestly and cautiously of [p. 593] yourself and your affairs, we must trouble you to satisfy our desire, begging you to say at last more openly on what we may duly congratulate you and rejoice with you.
(Latin) Meanwhile, as you would be glad to know how things are with us, I can say that up to now by God's mercy we are all well. Dr. Sladus, who for a long time had absented himself from the Collegie and from medical practice, has turned up again; at the moment he is at Leyden, meaning to return from there shortly, as he may perhaps put up his father's library and even†a part of his own for sale this month.†1 My son-in-law De Wilde's wife will be increasing her family with a fifth child in three or four months' time; may all go well with her. Guenellon's wife has so far imitated the Princess; I sincerely wish that Lucina might see fit to bestow her favour on these consorts; such an event cannot fail to be welcomed both in England and in our country, and may God grant that the royal family may in time be provided with such happy supports as is our hope and prayer and that of all good citizens. May He, who has thus far shown such mercy and favour towards our and your peoples in the matter of this expedition, so unite the hearts of your citizens that none may hereafter dare to trouble the peace you now enjoy. On that word I close, having first sent you all good wishes, most kind Sir, in my wife's name as well [p. 594] as in my own and in that of all our family. Good-bye, then, and may you be happy, and give us the pleasure of often hearing from you.
Your most obedient servant
EGBERT VEEN
Address: Myn heer Mynheer Lock at Dr. Goodals at the Colledg. of Phÿsitians in Warwick lane. london.
In another hand (Locke's?): Mr J Locke
Endorsed by Locke: E. Veen 12 Apr.89
1125. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 5 April 1689 (1118, 1149)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 34-5.
Otterton Aprill 5th. 1689.
Dear Sir
All possible Thanks is due to you for your endearing letter of 14th. of March, and the only acknowledgment that I can pay you, at this distance; but how can I make my letter worth postage, or what can I say from Devon, that can atone for my interrupting your better entertainments. to profess my deep sense of my Obligations to you and the perfect Freindship I have for you, would be a tedious Tautologie, since you have been so often assured of it, that it needs no confirmation. To beg you to hasten into the Country is to no purpose, since you tell me your affaires will not permit it. and to Talk of my comming to you at this time, is worse then saying nothing, because it sets me a longing for what I cannot obtain; nor never shall, unless you can find out a better reason then comming to see the Coronation. I have seen Sights enough to exhaust my whole stock of Curiosity, so that I can relish our Happiness of having a Protestant King and Queen, by the hearing of the Ear, as well as if my Eyes saw it; and as effectually enjoy the Blessings of their Government; but I cannot find it so in the Blessings of Friendship, therfore I would get nearer to you if it were possible.
― 595 ―
but I know not how to contrive it; I do not envye my Dear Lanlady, or any of my Friends the pleasure and advantages of your Conversation, but I wish I could have my share, and be sometimes amongst you; but since it cannot be, I must read Seneca, which (how much soever you laugh at it) does me great service on such occasions. I am glad to learn by Mr Clark that your Lungs are freed from what Oppress'd them at your first comming over; I hope you find the same Ease as to what lay upon your Heart and head; and that all things will contribute to make England agreable to you. in which I wish well to my Self, for I shall not be always in this state of separation; which is very Grievous to Sir
Your most Obedient Daughter and Humble Servant
ISABELLA DUKE
Mr Duke commands me to assure you that he is your most faithfull servant.
Address: These Are for Mr Lock att London
Endorsed by Locke: I: Duke 5 Apr.89
1126. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 9/19 April 1689 (1104, 1154)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 33-4. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 37-8.
A Amsterdam le 19 d'Avril 1689
J'ai vu, Monsieur, dans vôtre Lettre à Mr: de Limborch, des marques obligeantes de vôtre souvenir. Je vous suis extrémement obligé des offres, que vous me faites de m'envoier the History of the Unitarians; le soupçon que j'ai que ce ne soit peu de chose fait que je n'ai pas grand empressement pour cet ouvrage. Cependant si vous trouvez une occasion de l'envoier, sans vous donner la peine de la chercher, je serai bien aise de le voir, et lors que vous aurez le loisir de me marquer seulement les noms des livres, qui viendront à vôtre connoissance, et que vous jugerez passables, j'aurai soin de les faire venir par la voie de nos libraires, qui ont des correspondans à Londres. Je voudrois voir bien tôt dans les Catalogues, An Essai of the Understanding, et vous devez vous attendre à être souvent importuné†a de moi pour cela, jusqu'a ce que vous ayiez tenu vôtre
― 596 ―
parole. Je vous ai envoié dans une balle du Sieur Wolfgang adressé à Daniel Bernard†1 Libraire François à Londres deux exemplaires du XII Volume†2 adressé à Mr. Ansham Churchill, que vous aurez la bonté de faire retirer, parce que je crain qu'il ne soit pas ponctuel à les rendre. Je suis occupé à traduire en Latin pour mon Auditoire,†3 mes Regles de Critique, ou plûtôt à faire un nouvel Ouvrage rangé plus méthodiquement, où elles entrent. L'Abregé de vôtre Essay m'a été de grand usage pour cela, mais si j'avois eu tout le Livre, j'en aurois bien mieux profité. Je suis toûjours sur le Roose graft,†a †4 où vous pourrez adresser vos lettres, lors que vous aurez quelque moment à perdre. Je suis assez en repos présentement, que je suis seul. Je vous souhaite aussi de la tranquillité, et de la santé, et je vous prie de croire que c'est très-sincerement que je suis
Monsieur
Vôtre tres humble et tres-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC

1127. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 12 April 1689 (1122, 1131)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256k. Printed, less the final paragraph, in A. des Amorie van der Hoeven, De Joanne Clerico et Philippo a Limborch Dissertationes Duae, 1843, pp. 144-5; in full in Ollion, pp. 183-6. Answers no. 1122; answered by no. 1131.
(English)
London 12/22 Apr. 89
Vir Amplissime
Heri Regis et Reginæ inauguratio sive ut dicunt <coronatio>†a summo cum splendore et maximo concursu plausuque populi
― 597 ―
celebrata est, eodem die utrumque in Scotia istius regni regem et reginam solenni modo promulgatum sive uti nos loqui amamus proclamatum credimus, nam Nostro Gulielmo et Mariæ solium istud ante aliquot dies ab ordinibus istius regni designatum et decretum fuisse expeditis nuntiis constat. Burnetus jam Episcopus Salisburiensis in hesternâ solennitate suas habuit partes, Concionatus est coram rege et regina et ita concionatus est ut omnes laudent, edi concionem non dubito, exemplar quam primum occasionem nactus fuero ad vos mittam.†1 Hæc heri, hodie gratissimæ tuæ redditæ sunt literæ, unde renovatum gaudium, nec enim in privatâ re aliquid jucundius credo esse quam quos maxime velis amicos bene valere et de te bene sentire certiorem fieri. Gratulationes vestras amoris et benevolentiæ plenas eo quo debeo animo accipio. tantòque hilarius præsentibus et domesticis utor amicis quod tam faventes habeo absentes et peregrinos multis nominibus mihi non minus charos. De tolerantiâ apud nos stabiliendâ non prorsus despero etiamsi lente admodum procedat et de præsulum ingenio recte judicas, spero tamen.†2 Hodie Burnetum vidi: dixi te parare literas
― 598 ―
gratulatorias quamprimum certum tibi foret illum pædo Episcopali donatum, gratus nuntium hoc accepit. Scoti Hierarchiam Episcopalem tam acriter aversantur quam nos amplexamur, et in gravaminum catalogo primas ei dederunt.†1 Temperatum aliquid ex adversantibus extremis optant omnes boni quibus sana et moderata placent. An Burnettus tuus eodem uti tibi persuades animo futurus sit Salisburi quo fuit Amstelodami nonnulli dubitare incipiunt, interim dicam tibi quid accidit, cum primum, post consecrationem†a suam Episcopalem ad regem accessit Burnetus†b observavit rex quod galerus illius solito amplior erat, rogavitque quid sibi vellit ista fimbriæ ampliatio, respondit Episcopus convenire istam formam ordini suo, cui Rex Galerus spero non immutabit caput tuum. Venii Guenelonisque epistolas una cum tuis accepi quibus cum jam respondere urgentibus negotiis impeditus non possum rogo ut gratias quam maximas iis meo nomine reddas, et tuis id est efficacissimis verbis excuses hanc tarditatem scribendi, quam si qua ex parte compensare potest animi propensitas hoc spondere possem neminem uspiam esse qui ad omnia amicitiæ officitia
― 599 ―
paratior sit. Video vos omnes cupide percunctari quodnam munus publicum mihi demandatum sit, breviter respondeo nullum, valetudinis excusatione usus, munus evitavi satis honorificum quod florentibus viribus et ætate sine dubio ambirem, ego jam solum et meæ et patriæ quieti studeo, nec fatiscenti et res suas componenti magnum æquor temere ingrediendum est. Utor jam fateor valetudine aliquanto meliore, respiratio liberior est, et tussis moderatior quam sub primo adventu, an hoc veris <aere calidiore>†a an consuetudine aeris maligna vis minus noxia sit plane nescio hoc scio stultum esset humeros meos oneri publico submittere quibuscunque phalaris ornato. quod mihi in oblato honore maxime placuit hoc fuit quod vos, saltem in transitu, iterum invisendi occasionem præbuisset. Etiamsi publica munera non attingo, publica tamen negotia et amicorum privata nescio quomodo ita me occupatum tenent ut a libris omnino aveller, maxima hic jam librorum etiam bonorum habetur auctio quam ne quidem invisendi datur tempus,†1 brevi spero mihi restituetur antiquum et optatum otium, ut ad rempublicam literariam reversus aliquid habeam quod ea ex parte ad Dominum Le Clerc scribere possim.
― 600 ―
Interim oro eum officiosissime meo nomine salutes, et roges ne meum silentium oblivioni aut negligentiæ imputet sed præsentibus curis a re literaria longissime remotis.
(English) Quando solutio facta fuerit literæ Vulcano tradantur nec enim opus est ut huc remittantur si quid est quod ad me mittere velis invenies Anglum <quendam>†a nomine Hunt†1 Hagæ comitis ille nobilem Anglum nomine my Lord Willam Paulet†2 nuper illuc comitatus est, qui eo profectus est ut Hagæ <duceret>†b in uxorem Dominam regis nostri ni fallor consanguineam vel affinem. Celebratis nuptiis meus Amicus Dominus Hunt mox reversurus est et quicquid pro me ei tradetur sedulo curabit. Sed meus famulus†3 adhuc credo Roterodami est, ille navem <quâ>†c libri mei vehuntur conscendit ante meum decessum.†d Nautæ negligentia qui otiose Roterodami hæsit amisit navigandi nobiscum occasionem, ante aliquot dies cum præsidio bellicarum navium solvit et ad Littus Angliæ accessit tam prope ut pene manu tangi potuisset, sed vi tempestatis ab ancoris avulsus, et fluctibus diu jactatus tandem
― 601 ―
summo cum periculo Masam repetiit, quando iterum navigaturus nescio. Quicquid pro me ad Furlei ædes mittetur uxor illius vel famulo meo vel cuipiam alteri ad me transportandum tradet. Furleius ipse apud nos est, et eadem in tempestate maximum adiit discrimen et miraculo pene evasit.

(English) In posterum si placet ita inscribantur literæ
For Mr John Locke at Mrs: Smithsbys
in Dorset Coort in Chanell row
Westminster
Dilectissimam tuam uxorem omnemque Optimi Venii familiam Collegas cæterosque amicos saluto
(Latin)
London 12/22 Apr. 89
Excellent Sir,
Yesterday the inauguration or, as they say, coronation of the king and queen was celebrated with very great splendour amid the acclamations of [p. 597] a vast concourse of people; we believe that on the same day in Scotland they were both solemnly promulgated, or, as we usually say, proclaimed, as respectively king and queen of that kingdom; for it is confirmed by express messages that that throne was some days ago designated and decreed to our William and Mary by the estates of that realm. Burnet is now bishop of Salisbury; he had his place in yesterday's solemnity; he preached before the king and queen, and did so in a manner that won general approval. I have no doubt that the sermon is being published; I will send you a copy at the first opportunity.†1 So much for yesterday's doings; today your most welcome letter has come to hand, bringing me a renewal of joy; for in one's private concerns there is nothing, I think, more pleasurable than to be assured that one's most valued friends are well and that they have kindly feelings towards one. I accept all your affectionate and kind congratulations with the feelings that they deserve, and I am all the gladder of the friends I have with me here at home because I have such good ones absent from me in another land, who are on many accounts no less dear to me. As to the establishment of toleration in our country I do not altogether despair, though it is proceeding very slowly, and you are quite right about the disposition of the prelates; still, I have hopes.†2 I saw Burnet today; I told him you were preparing to write him [p. 598] a letter of congratulation as soon as you knew for certain that the bishop's crosier had been bestowed on him, and he was grateful for the information. The Scots are as keen in their aversion to episcopal governance as we are in holding to it, and they have put this first in their list of grievances.†1 All right-minded persons who favour sane and moderate counsels hope for some relaxation in the attitude of extremists on either side. Whether your friend Burnet is likely, as you feel sure, to be of the same mind at Salisbury as he was at Amsterdam is a thing that some people are beginning to doubt; meanwhile let me tell you what happened when he had his first audience of the king after his consecration as bishop. The king noticed that Burnet's hat was wider than usual, and asked him what was the meaning of this enlargement of the brim; the bishop answered that it was the shape proper to his order; on which the king remarked 'I hope your hat will not work a change in your head'. I received Veen's and Guenellon's letters along with yours; as I am prevented by pressure of business from answering them at the moment, I beg that you will give them my very best thanks, and that you will make my excuses in your own, that is in the most effectual, terms for my dilatoriness in writing; if this can be in any way compensated for by my earnest intention, then I can promise that no one anywhere exists who is readier to [p. 599] fulfil all the duties of friendship. I see you are all very eager to know just what public post I have been appointed to; I can answer in a word, to none. I have used my health as an excuse for avoiding an office which is honourable enough, and which I should undoubtedly seek if I were in the prime of life and in the enjoyment of my full powers; as it is, my only concern now is for peace and quiet for myself and my country; one who is breaking up and putting his affairs in order should not rashly launch out into the open sea. I confess I am in somewhat better health now; my breathing is freer, and the cough I had on my first arrival is less severe; whether this is due to the warmer spring air, or whether I am growing accustomed to the pernicious atmosphere and so suffering less harm from it, I do not know; this I know, that it would have been folly to shoulder a public burden, with whatever trappings it might be decked out. What pleased me most about the honour offered to me was that it would have given me an opportunity of seeing you all once more, at least in passing. Although I am not undertaking any public duties, yet public affairs and the private concerns of friends somehow keep me so busy that I am entirely torn away from books; at the moment a big auction sale of quite good books is being held here but I have not time even to go and see it;†1 I hope that my old and longed-for leisure will soon be restored to me, so that I may return to the commonwealth of learning and have something to write about to
[p. 600] Mr. Le Clerc in that field. Meanwhile I beg you to give him my best respects and to ask him not to ascribe my silence to forgetfulness or neglect, but to charge it to my present affairs, which are far removed from learned pursuits.
(Latin) When the money is paid the papers may be consigned to Vulcan; there is no need for them to be sent back here. If there is anything you wish to send me you will find a certain Englishman, Hunt†1 by name, at The Hague; he arrived there recently in company with an English nobleman, Lord William Paulet†2 by name, who made the journey in order to marry Madam at The Hague; she is, unless I am mistaken, a connection of our king either by blood or marriage. My friend Mr. Hunt will return soon after the wedding, and he will carefully attend to anything that is handed to him for me. But I believe my servant†3 is still in Rotterdam; he embarked before my departure, on the ship that is carrying my books. Through the negligence of a mariner who hung about doing nothing in Rotterdam, he lost the opportunity of sailing with us. He put to sea some days ago with a convoy of warships and came so near the English coast that it could almost have been touched with the hand; but he was torn from his anchors by a storm, and after prolonged tossing on [p. 601] the waves he at last got back to the Maas at considerable risk; I do not know when he will sail again. Anything for me that is sent to Furly's house will be handed by his wife either to my servant or to someone else to be brought across to me. Furly himself is in this country; he ran into great danger in that same storm and escaped almost by a miracle.
Good-bye and continue to love
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
(Latin) Please address my letters in future as follows, [etc.].
My greetings to your dear wife, to the excellent Veen and his whole family, and to our Collegians and my other friends.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch bij de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keysars Gracht t'Amsterdam
1128. Locke to Edward Clarke, [13] April [1689] (1102, 1130), with fragment of later letter
Rand, pp. 290-2. 'In very bad condition'. Words, etc., in square brackets are supplied by Rand. The date of most of this item is 13 April; the paragraph near the end containing news is later and belongs probably to 20 April. In his answer Clarke says that while Locke dated the letter 13 April its postmark was dated 16 April: p. 605. His answer relates only to the earlier part of the letter. Rand apparently combined parts of two letters.
London, [13th] April [1689].
Dear Sir,
I am sorry to find by yours of the 11th that you had not then received mine, which I writ to you this day seven night, which had
― 602 ―
more business in it that required your speedy answer then and there I was then in treaty with a French tutor†1 for your son, of whom I shall say no more now, but that Mr. Furly who has known him a good while gives him a very good character. J F likes him very well, and I [likewise] approve of him upon two or three discourses I had [with him. But I] put him off for a final answer to the end of this week, in hope of receiving one from you by this, and accordingly he came to me this morning. The terms I told him as well as I knew them. The main one, which was the salary of £20 per annum, I perceived he would willingly have accepted. I told him, that both the tutor you formerly had and he whom you had agreed with, I thought, had neither of them the promise of any more; but this you undertook to him, that his terms with you should be sure not to be worse than either of those; nor, indeed, do I think they ought, for by what I see of him I like him better than either of them. He has lately had the tuition of two young English gentlemen, and Mr. Furly, who saw them with him in Holland, and at whose house he was with them a fortnight, gives an excellent character of his care and government of them; and says, moreover, that his wife, who has no great opinion of Frenchmen, was in love with him, and this was at a time when he thought not Mr. Furly would ever have occasion to give any account of him. He wishes you were in town, that you might see him and him you, to be both the better satisfied each of other. I like him not the worse, and in my discourse with him I find him not forward to [claim knowledge] he has not, nor to undertake anything in the breeding of your son for which he is not prepared; which signifies more to me than a forwardness [to attempt some]thing, and a presumption of his own abilities †a [Let me know in your] next the particular of the terms (for I have once more remitted him for another week) that I may conclude with him. And then let me also know how to convey him down to you, and the proper [directions] to me about the going abroad with your son whenever he went abroad without his mother; and whether he must lie in the same bed, or chamber. As to the bed, I answered positively no. As to the chamber, I left that to your determination. And I think it would be convenient [to permit] him in the same chamber, for that will
― 603 ―
gain so much time and talking. But then it would be convenient he should at least have a closet adjoining, but unless I know your house better than my memory now retains it I can say nothing to that. To these particulars pray give me an answer and add all others you think necessary.
The other business, I writ to you of at the same time, was a project I have in my head to get my Cousin Somerton†1 to be Auditor to the Queen's Majesty. My Lord Coote†2 is treasurer to her. The salary is but £100 per annum. The perquisites, I am told, about so much more; the business not much, and such as Mr. Bridges†3 says he will quickly perfect my Cousin Somerton in. It is not the present advantage that put me on this for my cousin, but the entrance it gives him into the court, and the countenance it gives him in the country. And I will tell you how far I am advanced in it. The Bishop of St. Asaph†4 has promised me to move it to the Queen. Mr. Dacome†5 has promised me to second him with both these; I have made an acquaintance for this very purpose. And my Lord Coote has promised (who is very hearty in it) to do all he can when once the matter is moved. Pray assure my cousin that though I have done this without his knowledge I hope [he will not be offended] that I endeavour to engage him in such small affairs; if I had power or interest to reach to greater I should employ it [with equal zeal] for him....†a
[Scotland has] proclaimed King William and Mary.†6 It is agreed there is a great fleet ready to [sail] at Brest, and that there are 14 or 15,000 land soldiers drawn down thither. If it is so, and that [be done it] must be for a descent somewhere on our King's dominions, it is hard to guess where. I wish [it may not be] in the West. But
― 604 ―
the House of Lords refusing to consent to the Commons that the Bishops should be obliged to take the oaths, and both Houses adhering to their opinions that being to-day puts a stop to the bill, and consequently to the settlement of the country....†1
I grow more and more sick of this world....
Let Madam [be assured] I am her most humble servant. Remember me kindly to your little ones, and believe me,
Dear Sir,
your most affectionate humble servant,
J. L.
Address: For Edward Clarke, Esq., at Chipley near Taunton.
Endorsed: ... Received the 20th April, 1689.

B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 40.
Sutton the 19th: Ap: 89
Dear Cosin
According to your Appoyntment I have this day waited on the Gentlemen Att Hounstreat†2 to know what they demand for two lives In Revertion of yours In your Estate Att Buck Hill, and I can have noe price unles I will let then know what Rent you make of it I conceive theyr demand to be unresonable and therfore did put it of, they desired me to meet them att Hounstreat the 29th: of this Instant and by that time they would Inform them selves of the vallew of it they have already had halfe a years time to Inform them selves If you have any Inclination to know their price I will wait on them but not accept I Receive an answeare from you I hope you will have this by munday and when you have Considered It I may know your mind by saterdayes posst at Bristoll If it be left att Mr Walter Chapmans†3 House in broade Meade I shall be shure to have it
Sir I hope you Received my letter that I writ to you the day after my Retorn from london whearin I gave you sum account of A Vacancy of a surveighers place in the Costom House In Bristoll I now understand Commitioners are setled for Altering and Filling up Vacancies In the Customs, If It ly In your way I hope you will

1130. Edward Clarke to Locke, 20 April 1689 (1128, 1167)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 56. Printed in Rand, pp. 292-4. Answers no. 1128.
Chipley April the 20th. 1689.
Deare Sir,
Your Letter dated the 13th was not sent out of London 'till the 16th (as appeares by the Office marke on the outside)†b and soe came but last night to my handes, which I was exceedingly troubled at in regard some parts thereof required a speedy Answer, And I could heartily wish that all my thoughts were as cleerely and fully laid before you upon every part of your Letter, as they at this present appeare to mee, and then you would in them plainly see the most gratefull and hearty acknowlidgments that can bee made by one that has a true sence of those many, reall, and Extraordinary Acts of Freindshipp, and particularly those mentioned in your last Letter, that you have done for mee; As to the French-Tutor now in Treaty with you, which Mr. Furly commends, I have upon his judgment a greate opinion of, and shall willingly give Him 20l per Annum as I gave Mr. Duely,†1 and shall contentedly
― 606 ―
beare the charge of his comeing into the Countrey, when ever wee agree the certaine, But at present I am under greate perplexity of thought in that particular, the true Reasons that occasion it I thinke not soe propper for a Letter, and therefore I shall deferre them 'till I see you, or have an opportunity by a private hand to convey them to you, and only tell you that my Wife and I have some thoughts at present of seeing you in London, and spending some part of this summer at Tunbridge, and of bringing the Children with us, and if That should happen to bee Resolved on, it would bee altogather improper to send for the Tutor hither at this time, And therefore my desire at present is, That you make noe absolute Agreement with Him in that poynt, untill you heare from mee againe, unlesse you have allready obleiged your selfe, And if soe, I shall punctually performe it, bee the Agreement what ever it will: As to the other part of your Letter, I know not how I shall deserve either the Honour or the Favour design'd mee by you, If the Place doe not obleige mee to a constant residence in Town, and I am capable of performeing it (of which you and Mr. Bridges that know my Fayleings are the best judges) and it can be obtain'd, I shall Faithfully performe the service, and the Trust that shall bee thereby reposed in mee, and shall ever acknowlidge your Favour and Kindnesse therein whilst you permitt mee the Tytle of,
Your Faithfull Freind and servant
EDW: CLARKE
I am much rejoyced to heare that our Good Freinds Mr. Furley and his Wife†1 are safe in England, Pray give Mrs. Clarks and my true Love and service to them, and accept the like your selfe from us, And when you have read the inclosed, if you thinke fitt, pray seale and send it to my Lord Coote, who was soe Kind to write to mee upon the same subject by the last Post etc:
Endorsed by Locke: E:Clarke 20 Apr 89

1131. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, [c. 12/22 April and] 26 April/6 May 1689 (1127, 1134)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 20-1. Copy by van Limborch in Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., IIID 16, ff. 195-6. Excerpt from the copy printed in Ollion, p. 187 n. The later part of the letter answers no. 1127.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Fœlicem rerum vestrarum successum speramus, non ignari, res Europæ magnam partem exinde dependere. Ex Scotia quæ nuntiantur, blanda nos spe fovent, regnum illud sub eodem rege se Angliæ regno uniturum.†1 Sed ex Hyberniâ nuntiantur minus grata. Spero tamen omnia obstacula regni Anglicani viribus superanda, ut ita tandem conjunctis copiis nimia illa Galli potentia, seu verius impotentia, in <ordinem>†a cogatur. Deliberationibus de rebus religionis fœlicem voveo successum; neque is deësse potest, si omnes qui eas tractant, non res suas, sed Christi et Ecclesiæ agant. Prodiit hic hisce diebus libellus elegantissimus de Tolerantia, per modum epistolæ scriptus, non expresso autoris nomine.†2 Nihil quicquam in hac materia legi, quod æque arrideat. Neque dubito, quin hoc rerum statu magno in Anglia cum fructu legi possit, adeo solide, et fundamentis
― 608 ―
hactenus non ita indicatis omnem religionis ergo persecutionem et religionis genio, et juri naturæ adversam ostendit, ut, qui illius lectione conscientiarum libertatem omnibus ex æquo concedere non persuadentur, non ratione duci, sed aut cæco preju dicio, aut proprio commodo præcipites agi credi debeant. Recusa etiam hic est Samuelis Strimesii, SS. Theologiæ Francofurti ad Viadrum Professoris de Pace Ecclesiastica Dissertatio:†1 hæc Comprehensio, alter libellus Indulgentia seu Tolerantia merito vocari possit; ita argumentum utriusque per omnia deliberationibus de negotio religionis sub utroque isto titulo conforme videtur. Instigabo quantum possum bibliopolas, ut quamprimum exemplaria aliquot in Angliam mittant. Quod si illi cunctentur, prima quæ hinc solvet navi spero me aliquot utriusque exemplaria Tibi missurum, si forte mitigandis rigidiorum animis aliquid momenti afferant. Jam solutio plene peracta est: Exspecto quid epistolis et chartis eò spectantibus fieri velis. Inter amicorum et consanguineorum turbam precor ut lætus annos, quos Tibi divina benignitas adjicere dignabitur, expleas; ita tamen, ut nostri memor vivas, et, quo facilius
― 609 ―
absentiam tuam feramus, crebris epistolis nobiscum confabuleris, Teque hac ratione quantum potes præsentem exhibeas.
(English) Hasce huc usque ante duas hebdomadas scripseram per proximum tabellarium Tibi mittendas: Verum alia intervenerunt, præsertim migratio in alias ædes, commodiores et prioribus vicinissimas, quæ ita omnem meam supellectilem librariam conturbavit, meque ita occupatum detinuit, ut epistolam jam scriptam reperire, aut de ea mittenda serio cogitare non potuerim. Interim certiores oblatam regi et reginæ coronam Scotiæ nuntii attulerunt;†1 quod et tuis, quæ nudius tertius mihi redditæ sunt, literis confirmatum voluisti. Audio rigorem circa res ecclesiasticas aliquatenus mitigari. Faxit Deus, ut omnes aliis faciant, quicquid sibi fieri vellent. Acutum regis de ampliato galero dictum narras. Memini a viro quodam gravi ac cordato, mihi amico, aliquem, cui splendida offerebatur conditio, sed non nisi ejuratâ quam veram credebat doctrinâ obtinenda, serio hisce verbis monitum: Jam probaris utrum vere sis Christianus. Res secundæ vix habent modum, nec is nisi invicto animi robore servari potest. Cui autem animus doctrina Christi probe est imbutus, is omnia mundi blandientis irritamenta facile
― 610 ―
contemnit. Valetudinem Tibi minus adversam gaudeo: Spero brevi plene fore confirmatam. Tu pro tua peritia ipse facile remedia accommodatissima investigabis, quorum optatum effectum Tibi intra paucos diës voveo. Quod valetudinem causatus munus Tibi oblatum declinaveris, equidem non improbo: Quamvis enim, si publica regni et totius Europæ negotia considero, Tibi Tuique similibus Reip. habenas committi optem; tamen quod vitam privatam honori Tibi oblato prætuleris, minime reprehendere possum. Ex alieno sæpe arbitrio dependent politici, et, quod ipsi improbant, nonnunquam urgere et exequi coguntur. Interim cui vita placet privata quandoque aliis salutaria suggerere potest consilia, et ipse extra omnem periculi aleam positus fœlicem suorum consiliorum successum exspectare securus. Quanquam maxime gratus fuisset tuus conspectus, nolim tamen eum tanti, hoc est, valetudinis tuæ detrimento, emtum. Eum Tibi precor statum, in quo ipse totus acquiescas. Brevi D. Aranda hinc in Angliam proficiscetur:†1 illi (non enim nimio fasciculo eum onerare audeo) duo vel tria quæ Tibi tradat exemplaria epistolæ de Tolerantia committam: per famulum tuum, quem tam misere tempestate jactatum doleo,
― 611 ―
cuique brevi feliciorem trajectum precor, etiam paucula mittam, si forte nondum a bibliopolis in Angliam missa sint, ut tam utilis tractatus illic legi possit. Episcopi Salisburiensis concionem in coronatione regis habitam ad se missam in linguam Gallicam transfert D. Clericus, brevi credo edendam.†1 Veeniis Guenelloniisque epistolam tuam ostendi, qui omnes Te quam officiosissime salutant, omniaque Tibi fausta precantur. Sladus publica auctione elegantissimam suam bibliothecam distraxit:†2 profectionem in Angliam meditatur, fortasse brevi Tibi adfuturus. Chartas, ut jussisti, hodie Vulcano, vel ipso Harpocrate fideliori custodi, tradidi. Credo me brevi Hagam profecturum; illic quæram D. Hunt: nihil enim mihi gratius est, quam amicis tuis innotescere, ut, dum præsentia et alloquio tuo frui negatur, tuorum amicorum sermonibus, qui absque crebra Tui mentione haberi nequeunt, me oblectem. D. Clericus, qui Te salutare jussit, D. Aranda suarum literarum latore utetur. Filius meus, cui, quamprimum Regi ac Reginæ sceptrum oblatum audivit, præ gaudio lachrymæ erumpebant, D. Locke precatur perpetuam cum D. van der Linden†3 conjunctionem, et ut nulla Reip. procella alterum ab altero divellat. Uxor autem mea et
― 612 ―
filia mecum omnia affectu propensissimo Tibi precantur, quæ ipse Tibi optare possis. Vale, Vir Amplissime, et in amicorum ac consanguineorum turba ne obliviscaris
Tui Amantissimi
PHILIPPI A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami prid. Non. Maji.

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
We are hoping for a happy issue in the affairs of your country, being not unaware that the affairs of Europe depend in great part upon this. The news from Scotland encourages us to hope that that kingdom will unite itself with England under the same king.†1 But what we hear from Ireland is less pleasing. I hope, however, that all obstacles are eventually to be overcome by the strength of the kingdom of England that so at last the excessive power of the Frenchman, or to say more truly his outrageousness, may be restrained by the united forces. I hope that the deliberations on matters of religion may have a fortunate issue; nor can this fail to be achieved if all who are conducting them consult not their own interests but those of Christ and the Church. There has recently appeared here a very well-written pamphlet concerning Toleration, composed in the form of a letter, but without giving the name of the author.†2 I have never read anything on this subject which appealed to me so strongly. Nor do I doubt that in the present state of affairs it could be read with great profit in England: it demonstrates so [p. 608] irrefutably, on grounds never hitherto so set forth, that all religious persecution is contrary both to the spirit of religion and to the law of nature; so that any who are not persuaded by reading it to allow equal freedom of conscience to all must be believed not to be led by reason but to be carried headlong either by blind prejudice or by concern for their own advantage. There has also been reprinted here a dissertation on Peace in the Church by Samuel Strimesius, professor of theology at Frankfurt-on-the-Oder;†1 this may justly be called Comprehension, the other treatise Indulgence or Toleration; the argument of each seems in all respects similar to deliberations on matters of religion under each of these heads. I shall do my best to induce the booksellers to send some copies to England as soon as possible; but if they are slow I hope to send you some copies of each by the first ship sailing from here, on the chance that they may have some mitigating influence on the minds of the more inflexible. The payment has now been completed, and I await your wishes as to what is to be done with the letters and papers relating to it. I pray that you may live happily amongst friends and relations for as many more years as it may please the goodness of God to grant you, provided, however, that you keep us in mind and that you make your absence from us easier to bear by conversing with us [p. 609] in frequent letters, and in this way make yourself present with us as far as you can.
(Latin) This much I had written a fortnight ago, meaning to send you the letter by the next packet boat; but other things intervened, notably our move into another house, more convenient than the old and quite close to it; this upset all my library equipment and kept me so busy that I could not find the letter I had already written, nor was I able to give any serious thought to the business of dispatching it. Meanwhile we have received more certain information that the crown of Scotland has been offered to the king and queen;†1 you too, in your letter which I received the day before yesterday, expressed a wish that this news might be confirmed. I hear that rigour in regard to Church matters is abating to some extent. God grant that all may do unto others as they would be done by. That was a shrewd remark which you tell me the king made about the widened hat. I remember that when someone was offered a splendid match,†2 but one that he could not obtain without abjuring the doctrine which he believed to be true, he was seriously warned by a certain grave and judicious friend of mine in these words: 'You are now on your trial as to whether you are truly a Christian'. Prosperity knows hardly any bounds, and to keep within them requires invincible strength of mind. He, however, whose mind is rightly imbued with the doctrine of Christ can easily spurn all the blandishments and incitements of the world. I am glad that [p. 610] your health is improved, and I hope that it will soon be fully established; with your practical skill you will easily discover for yourself the most suitable remedies, which I pray may have the desired effect in a few days. As to your action in declining on the ground of health the post that was offered you, I do not disapprove of it. It is true that, when I consider the public business of the kingdom and of all Europe, I should wish that the guidance of state affairs might be entrusted to you and to those like you; I can, however, find little fault with you for preferring a private life to the proffered honour. Politicians are often dependent on the will of others, and they are sometimes compelled to further and execute measures of which they themselves disapprove. Meanwhile he who prefers the private life can sometimes offer salutary advice to others, and in a position which does not expose him to any risk or danger he can await without anxiety a happy outcome of his counsels. Although the sight of you would have given me the greatest pleasure, yet I would not wish it purchased at such a price, I mean with anything bad for your health. I only pray that your circumstances may be such as to keep you entirely contented. Mr. D'Aranda will shortly sail from here for England;†1 I will entrust to him (not presuming to load him with too bulky a parcel) two or three copies of the letter concerning Toleration to hand to you; there is also your servant, who I am sorry had such a wretched buffeting in the storm, but [p. 611] who will, I hope, shortly have a better crossing; I will send a few more by him, in case none has yet been sent to England by the booksellers, in order that so profitable a treatise may be read there. Mr. Le Clerc is translating into French the bishop of Salisbury's sermon at the king's coronation, a copy of which was sent to him; I believe it is to be published shortly.†1 I showed your letter to the Veens and the Guenellons, who all send you their heartiest greetings and wish you all prosperity. Sladus has dispersed his very choice library by public auction;†2 he is considering departure for England and perhaps will soon be with you. I handed over the papers today, as you bade me, to Vulcan, a trustier keeper than even Harpocrates himself. I believe that I shall be going to The Hague shortly; whilst there I shall try to see Mr. Hunt; for nothing gives me greater pleasure than making the acquaintance of any friends of yours; thus, though I am denied the satisfaction of speaking to you in person, I can enjoy the conversation of your friends, which cannot be without frequent mention of yourself. Mr. Le Clerc, who sends you his greetings, will employ Mr. D'Aranda as the bearer of his letter. My son, who shed tears of joy as soon as he heard that the sceptre was offered to the king and queen, prays that Mr. Locke may ever be closely united to Mr. van der Linden,†3 and that no tempest in the state may sunder the one from the other. [p. 612] My wife and daughter join me in sending you our most affectionate greetings and in wishing you all that you yourself could desire. Good bye, excellent Sir, and in the company of your friends and kindred do not forget
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 6 May

1132. George Walls to Locke, 29 April 1689 (745, 1175)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 49-50.
Hamburgh Ap: 29th 1689
Honour'd Sir
Beinge surpris'd both with mr Mans cominge hither and the suddennes of his goinge away, I am trobled that I have not had opportunitie to shew him anie civilitie as I would certainly have done, beinge a gentleman soe intimately acquainted with you and one that I had the honour a little to know elsewhere: I have now onlie time to tell you that I tooke the libertie to write to you addressinge my letter to mr Shepherd merchant in London.†1 but I did not then know of your beinge in England, which I have since learn't by the favour of my Lady Joanna's letter.†2 If my former be come to your hands I hope you'le believe the sinceritie of everie part of it. and

nothinge would be more acceptable to me then that you would plese to trie me in the most suspicious part of it, if anie be such. yesterday night late was the first time that I knew who this gentleman was, and this morning earlie he unexpectedly departs, which is the reson that I have onlie time to assure you in this odde manner that I shal ever be sensible of the great obligations which are due to you from
Sir
your most oblig'd humble servant
G: WALLS
