1133. Locke to [Lady (Mary) Calverley], [early May 1689?] (1164)
B.M., Add. MS. 4290, ff. 52-5. Copy made by or for P. Desmaizeaux. Printed, presumably from this manuscript or a copy of it, in A Collection of Several Pieces, pp. 266-70, where it is said to be addressed to Lady Calverley. Date: Locke probably received a letter from Lady Calverley about April: p. 618 (where the date 5 May for Locke's letter is probably new style). In her letter of 23 July 1689 (no. 1164) she writes about two letters from him. This may be the earlier of the two. In 1689 Easter term lasted from 17 April to 13 May; Trinity, from 31 May to 19 June; Parliament sat from 22 January to 20 August. Perhaps answered by no. 1164. For Lady Calverley see no. 781.
To my Lady — in Yorkshire.
Madam
Whatever reason you have to look on me as one of the slow men of London you have this time given me an excuse for being so; For you cannot expect a quick answer to a letter which took me up a good deal of time to get to the beginning of it. I turnd and turnd it on every side, lookd†a again†a and again at the top of every page, but could not get into the sense and secret of it till I applyd my self to the middle. You Madam who are acquainted with all the skill
― 614 ―
and methods of the Antients have not I suppose taken up with this Hyroglyphical way of writing for nothing: And since you were going to put into your letters things that might be the reward of the highest merit, You would by this mistical intimation put me into the way of virtue to deserve them.
But whatever Your Ladyship intended this is certain, that in the best words in the world You gave me the greatest humiliation imaginable. Had I as much vanity as a pert Citizen that sets up for a wit in his Parish, You have said enough in your letter to content me, and If I could be swoln that way You have taken a great deal of pains to blow me up and make me the finest gaudy bubble in the world as I am painted by your colours. I know the Emperours of the East suffer not strangers to appear before them till they are dressd up out of their own wardrobes,†1 Is it so too in the Empire of wit, and must you cover me with your own embroidery that I may be a fit object for your thoughts and conversation? This Madam may suit your greatness but does†a not at all satisfy my ambition. <He, who has once flatter'd himself with the hopes of your friendship, knows not the true value of things, if he can content himself with these splendid ornaments.>†b As soon as I had read your letter I lookd in my glasse, felt my pulse and sighd for I found in neither of those the promises of 30 years to come. For at the rate I have hitherto advancd and at the distance I see by this complemental way of treatment I still am I shall not have time enough in this world to get to you, I do not mean to the place where You now see the pole elevated as You say 64 degrees.†2 A post horse or a Coach would quickly carry me thither. But when shall we be acquainted at this rate? Is that happyness reservd to be compleated by the Gossiping bowl at your Grand-daughters lying in? If I were sure that when You leave this durty planet†c I should meet you in the same star where You are to shine next, and that you would then admit me to your conversation I might perhaps have a little more patience. But methinks it is much better to be sure of something than to be put off
― 615 ―
to expectations of so much uncertainty. If there be different elevations of the pole here that keep you at so great a distance from those who languish in your absence who knows but in the other world there are different Elevations of Persons. And You perhaps will be out of sight among the seraphims while wee are left behind in some dull planet. This the high-flights of your Elevated <Genius>†a give as†b just augury of whilst you are here. But yet pray take not your place there before your time, nor keep not us poor mortals at a greater distance than you need. When you have granted me all the nearness that acquaintance and freindship can give, You have other advantages enough stil to make me see how much I am beneath you. This will be only an enlargement of your goodness without lessening the adoration due to your other excellencys. You seem to have some thoughts of the Town again. If the Parliament or the Term which draw some by the name and <appear>ance†c of business, Or if Company and Musick meetings and other such entertainments which have the attractions of pleasure and delight were of any consideration with you, You would not have much to say for Yorkshire at this time of the year. But these are no arguments to you who carry <your>†a own satisfaction and I know not how many worlds always about you. I would be glad you would think of putting all these up in a Coach and bringing em this way. For though You should be never the better, Yet there be a great many here that would and amongst them
The Humblest of Your Ladyships servants
J LOCKE.
1134. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 6/16 May 1689 (1131, 1146)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 22-3. Answered by no. 1147.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Vides hic tria exemplaria Comprehensionis et Tolerantiæ: conjunxi in unum volumen utramque, ut aliqualis voluminis moles
― 616 ―
esset, et quia argumentum aliquatenus est homogeneum: alias novi Tolerantiam multis modis tractatum de pace Ecclesiasticâ superare.†1 Ad ædes D. Furlei misi sex exemplaria incompacta, quæ per famulum tuum Tibi tradantur, ut pro arbitrio tuo ea compingi cures. Res meæ non permiserunt, ut Hagam excurrerim; et jam, quantum audio, D. Hunt iterum in Angliam abiit, quod doleo. Acta Inquisitionis adhuc describuntur: verum Fellingerus†2 aliquamdiu ægrotavit; sunt tamen jam duæ tertiæ partes totius voluminis descriptæ. Salutant Te omnes Collegæ. Sladus ubi hæreat, ignoramus: rus creditur petiisse: si in Angliam discedat, ante suum discessum nos procul dubio est salutaturus. Omnes Collegæ recte valent, Tibique firmam ac solidam et stabilem precantur valetudinem. Vale Vir Amplissime et nos ama.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Amstelodami 16 Maji
inline image
― 617 ―
(English) Prolixas per ordinarium tabellarium 6 hujus mensis dedi ad Te literas, quas Te jam accepisse nullus dubito.
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Here are three copies of Comprehension and Toleration for you; I have put one of each together in one volume, in order to make a book of appreciable size [p. 616] and because the subject-matter is to some extent of a piece; otherwise I am aware that Toleration is in many respects superior to the treatise on Peace in the Church.†1 I have sent six unbound copies to Mr. Furly's house, to be handed over to you by your servant, so that you can use your discretion as to having them bound. My affairs did not allow me to make an excursion to The Hague; and now, as I hear, Mr Hunt has left for England again, for which I am sorry. The Acts of the Inquisition are still in process of being transcribed; but Fellinger†2 has been unwell for some time; still, two thirds of the whole book have now been transcribed. All our Collegians send you their greetings. We do not know where Sladus is sticking; he is believed to have gone to the country; if he is leaving for England he will no doubt say good-bye to us before his departure. All our Collegians are in excellent health and wish you a sound and settled confirmation of your own. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and keep us in your affections.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 16 May
1689
(Latin) [p. 617] I sent you a long letter by the ordinary post on the 6th of this month; no doubt you have received it by now.
Address: For Mr. John Locke at Mrs. Smithsbÿs in Dorset Court in Chanell row Westminster
Endorsed by Locke: Limborch 16.May.89
1135. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 8/18 May 1689 (1123, 1139)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 10-11.
Monsieur
Je ne scaurois voir partir Monsieur Daranda sans le charger d'un mot de lettre pour vous. Monsieur limburgh nous a resjouï de la nouvelle du restablissement de vostre santé. nous esperons que pendant cette saison douce vous aurez le temps de vous munir et accoustumer contre le meschant air de l'arriere saison. je crois que vous verrez cet esté Monsieur Sladus, puisqu'il a envie de passer en Engleterre. Sil n'estoit pas dans un age si avancé, il pouroit y ceuillir plus de fruits de son erudition et de son scavoir, quil na fait icy. je remarque que la vente de sa bibliotheque, sa maladie derniere, son rebut pour la practique, vient principalement de chagrin de voir icy le merite si mal recompensé; mais il faut quil songe a se reposer, et il le peut faire avec moin de perte pour le public que vous, qui dans le chaos ou se trouve l'Europe seriez un instrument capable de denouer bien des choses. on ne scauroit pourtant que loüer vostre modestie et la force que vous avez de vous vaincre, en ne vous laissant pas entraisner dans ce torrent des affaires publiques, qui a ses peines et ses dangers: que vous preferez le repos et la vie privée pour dire avec ce philosophe, bene vixit qui bene latuit.†1 pardonné pourtant a la licence que je prends de Juger de vos actions qui passent ma portée et que je ne doibs que venerer.
toute la famille vous presente ses tres humbles respects. Ma femme fait des nouvelles instances pour scavoir ce que vous avez deboursé pour elle. Pierot demande souvent quand il reverra
― 618 ―
Monsieur Lock, je luy promets que quand il sera grand il vous ira faire la reverence. je souhaitte que vous vivrez jusque la, en santé et prosperité, et que je ly puisse mener, pour vous dire de pres avec combien de respect, je suis
Monsieur,
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P. GUENELLON.
Amsterd. ce 18 mey 1689
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur j lock a Londres
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Guenellon 18 May. 89
1136. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, 9/19 May 1689 (1119, 1180)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 171-2.
+
Jeudi ce 19. May.
On ne peut pas, monsieur, avoir plus de joie que j'en viens de recevoir par la votre du 5. du courant. J'avois bezoin d'une pareille consolation dans la disgrace qui m'est arivée par une chute qui m'a causé presque une dislocation du gros orteil du pié gauche, et me fait garder le lit, qui est pour moy un etat fort violent.
Je vous prie de marquer ma reconnoissance à tous les messieurs qui me font l'honneur de se souvenir de moy, et à Madame de Caverlye.
J'aprehende que la guerre future n'interrompe la douceur que je goutois par notre commerce. mandez moy à quoi en est le Josephe de mr Bernard.†1 Il a fait un traité de Ponderibus veterum,†2 dont je voudrois savoir votre sentiment. Je ne l'ay pas vu. J'ay ramassé à Paris un grand nombre de ces poids la, dont une partie avoit eté à mr Peiresc; et quoiqu'ils m'aient couté quelque argent, je ne suis pas faché du marché. J'y en ay ajouté d'otres trouvéz par cy par la.
Je m'etonne qu'un homme aussi eclairé qu'est monsieur de st Asaph puisse dire que nota L nullo modo est Lambda Græcorum, car c'est le L de lancien Alphabet Ionique, dont les monetaires se sont servis par menage pour marquer ἒτος, qu'il ne pouvoient metre en abregé par E, qui auroit fait de la confusion avec le
― 619 ―
nombre quinaire, et metant le A ordinaire, il en oroit fait un otre avec le tricenaire, sed hæc alias pluribus ex professo.†1
Si monsieur de st Asaph a receu le livre du P. Pagi qui lui etoit destiné par l'Auteur, il y poura voir comment il a mal entendu la belle decouverte que je lui avois communiquée de la <dou>ble†a maniere de conter la Puissance Tribuniciene des Empereurs. Le bon Pere m'en a ecrit depuis, et en est demeuré d'acord, et cela et otres choses qu'il a quelquefois mal prises, m'engageront à en detronper le public.
J'ay receu le livre ou le plagium harmonicum est publié.†2 c'est sur le denouëment de la question de la derniere pasque ou je faisois voir que parare Pascha n'est otre chose que perquirere fermentum et panis fermentati frustula in cænaculo in quo postridie manducandum erat Pascha.†3 Vous entendrez cela à demi mot. les characterismes en sont dans l'harmonie, que je ne vois pas se devoir avancer dans un tems de troubles comme celui cy, pendant lequel quand je voudrois à ce dessein passer en Holande par la Flandres ou l'Angleterre je ne le pourois plus.
mandez moi pourquoi on ne se sert pas à Londres du secret de mr Boyle pro edulcorandâ aquâ salsâ, dont j'ay ici le projet en un petit in 8†4
Si vous savez quelcun qui parte de Paris pour Londres adressez le à mon hôte, et m'en donnez avis auparavant. Il y trouverra la nouvele Concordia Evangelica,†5 et peutetre la Philosophia Vulgaris.†6
Je nescai pourquoi je reçois seulement ce jourdhui 19. la votre du 5. un de mes amis m'aiant remis des nouveles de Londres du 12. ou il est parlé d'une letre de l'Electeur de Treves sur l'avenement à la couronne du —†7
Excusez ma mauvaise ecriture, etant dun clinique†8 bien chagrin.
J'ay des choses plaisantes et surprenantes à dire sur l'edition de la chronique Alexandrine faite au Louvre par feu mr Du cange.
― 620 ―
mandez moi le nom de l'Archevesque d'York qui a eté Eveque d'Excester, et qu'elle est sa naissance et ses emplois devant qu'il fust Eveque d'Exceter.†1
s'il est vray que l'Eveque de chester†2 qui a passé par ici, ait eté empoisonné à Dublin par deux pretres Irlandois, parcequ'il portoit le Roy a pardonner aux Protestans Irlandois detenus dans les prisons, combien de fois ne dira-on point: Tantum Relligio —†3
Quoiqu'il y ait des fables dans le malela, on ne laissera d'y trouver de bonnes choses pour la chronologie.
Le triumvir est à la campagne qui est un surcroist d'afliction pour moy. Si mr Jonston est à Londres, faites lui mes complimens, et au Πολλυτρηλλ. Διδασκ. Βουρνῆν†a Επισκ.†4
Address: A Monsieur Angleterre Monsieur Awnsham Churchill near Amen Corner London
Postmark: MA 16
Endorsed by Locke: Toinard 19 May 89
1137. Dr. Charles Goodall to Locke, 17 May [1689] (1096, 1292)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 25-6. Printed by Dr. K. Dewhurst in Review of the History of Medicine, xvii (1962), 496-7. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Friday May 17th
Deare Sir
My son Thom was this week to wait upon you, but missed of you at your lodgings; He is this morning gone into Suffolke and after 5 or 6 weeks stay there designs for Northamptonshire, if you please to write to him at your leasure, it may answer the end which your good advice was design'd for; I will let him know how kind
― 621 ―
you have been to him in the books you have sent him, and do intend to send them into Northamptonshire; But as for the books sent to my deare Son Charles (the son of my hopes and staff of my Family) they can be of no use to him, He dying at Oxford on Saturday last to the greif of all that knew him or had heard of him.†1 I am sure you cannot but pity his poore Mother and sympathize with your afflicted Freind. who is and ever shall be Sir
Your Obliged faithfull Freind and Servant
CH: GOODALL
I received of your Man the 1l-6s-4d laid out for your use.
Address: This For his worthy Freind Mr Locke.
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Goodall 17 May.89

1139. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 20/30 May 1689 (1135, 1161)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 12-13.
Monsieur,
Souffrez que j'interrompe vos grandes occupations pour un moment. Monsieur de Mauclaire qui a l'honneur de vous connoistre de reputation, m'a fait des instances pour luy procurer l'occasion de vous faire la reverence. il est bien difficile, Monsieur, de se deffendre de cette importunité quand on a attiré les yeux de tous les scavans sur soy, et acquis leur estime, Monsieur Mauclaire est de ce nombre: et comme il espere de s'establir en Engleterre appuyé de la faveur du Lord Macelsfield,†1 il conteroit pour un bonheur et un avantage particulier, s'il pouvoit s'acquerir vostre bienvueillance, j'ay une experience en moy mesme combien elle vaut et combien vous este facile a la donner; c'est pourquoy je massure que Monsieur de Mauclaire qui a beaucoup de scavoir et de merite, ne manquera pas de vous y enguager. je le souhaitte dautant plus que jay conceu une veneration particuliere pour toute cette famille. vous avez veu une ou deux fois Monsieur de Norois†2 son beau frere chez nous. ce son de fort bonnes personnes et de naissance, et d'integrité. toute nostre famille vous presente ses tres humble respects, et je suis comme je le doibs,
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur,
P. GUENELLON
Amsterd. ce 30 May 1689.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur J: Lock chez Monsieur Dr Goodall an college de Medicine in Warwick lane A Londres.
Endorsed by Locke: P:Guenellon 30 May. 89
1140. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 22 May [1689] (1115, 1141)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, f. 37. Year from Locke's endorsement. Furly came to London on or before 12 April: p. 601. He was now perhaps staying with Lord and Lady Monmouth (formerly Mordaunt) at Parson's Green: p. 626;
― 623 ―
with John Osgood at Mortlake: p. 638; the Penny Post area extended about ten miles around London.
May 22†a
D.F.
I just now received yours of this date with the books†1 and have onely so far transgrest thy orders as to read the first pa: of both— and the first I prefer as the clearer, hitherto. My physick has wrought tollerably. I have had nine stooles. Mrs Popple†2 has
― 624 ―
sent me some sirope of Capulare†1 to take a spoonfull in a glass of cold spring water, but I intend not to use it, till I have thy approbation, she says its much used in France, and experienced by herself as very cooling and stopping the Cough for some while night or day. my Hospes and his wife I expect this evening—I shall not faile to write every at 7 or 2 aclock by the penny post, and shall be glad to understand what your senators do—In the meane while, with hearty thanks for all your kindness I rest
D.F.
Yours
B.F.
3 aclock by the French Precepter—going to London
Endorsed by Locke: B.Furly 29 May. 89
1141. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 24 May [1689] (1140, 1151)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 9, ff. 35-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
24 May
D.F.
I have this afternoon had my Brother Stephens wife†2 to visit me, having heard that I was here at a widdows house,†3 a stranger to me, dangerously weak. She came mighty concernd, and with order from the Countess of K.†4 to fetch me back. They would take care of me, and Dr. Lower,†5 who comes dayly to visit my <sisters>†a daughter that has had the smallpox, should come dayly to me. While she
― 625 ―
was here in came my Bristol friend and after him some time R Hains with Letters from home, one from my W.†1 one from John,†2 and one 3 days later in Spanish from our wild reasoner; telling me my w. is disconsolate about that company business, with that yong man, and that he could not but be of her opinion in it. desiring me to desist, and make hast home if I will not have my w: fall into a sickness. I have answerd that I would immediatly come, could I, tho, I ought to go to the Bath for my arm, but that I am neither in condition to go home, nor to the bath at present—Pray when the box is sent to the Earls†3 send a few lines with it to my w. or to him, mentioning my great illness, and necessity of going to the bath when I can, but not as from me.
I find little advance because I dare not venture into the aire, our folk are not come home yet, I have got 12 ounces of pearle barly at 12d per lb, but I fancy hen-barly of a farthing a lb would have done as well; if anybody else wants any in the Village they must come to me for it now. I have Just now finisht the book about the penall Laws.†4 I confess the provocations were great, and tis hard keeping that people in any order, where they have the favour of the prince, as they have had of all our kings since the Reformation—So that as my Lord Faulkland says they had the name and honour of a persecution without feeling the Inconveniences of it.†5
I have an answer of my letter writ into Scotland my friend is mightily shockd, troubled grieved, what deny my own Testimony of 30 years and upwards? so fickle? so uncertain? fears self Interest is concerned in it. 'tis to comply for some end, but prophesyes I shall find it otherwise. All rather praise constancy, and integrity etc.†6 —I have answerd him, this day. That I am sick of anything that looks like sectism, singularitys, and authority — That I detest the thoughts of doing any thing against my mind, for any base
― 626 ―
interest—That tis not what I thought of things one or 30 years agoe, or even yesterday that should govern a reasonable man to think so today. That no honest man can think as he will, much less as others would have him. That I had lately been prest by an ingenious man†1 who, discernd by my answers, that I rather defended other mens Judgments then my own, And that I could not avoid to confess it, and that I did severall things rather in complyance to others, then to my own sense. That I intended no sect, or division about trifles, that if men could leave me to my liberty I could forbeare things, which I should not perhaps, if they would compell me to them—
What hele answer time will shew. I durst not yet looke out into the garden, tho I am weary of this imprisonment, and spoon meat yet I keep both—
But last night Smelling egs and bacon so delicate to my Stomach I had much adoe to forbear yet did—I have not to ad save the salutations of our old friend†2 to thy self and the countess of M—†3 and my own, and so I rest.
Thine
B F
24th evening
goes away to morrow by 7 A'clock
[On a separate scrap of paper attached to f. 36:]
I forgot to tell you I have had to day much proneness to vomit and have in the violence of coughing vomited up my Grewel, and that I swallow with some difficulty the Lappet of my throat hanging downe—dos thy booke go on?†4
Address: To Dr. John Locke at mrs Smithsbyes in Dorset court in channel Rowe in Westminster
Postmarks: London Penny Post: W SAT; W Af 4(?)
Endorsed by Locke: Furly 24 May. 89

1142. Benjamin Hawkshaw to [—— Flood?] 27 May [1689]
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 152. The writer, c. 1672-1738, was a son of Locke's old friend Eleanor Parry, now Mrs. Hawkshaw (no. 48, etc.), who had recently come to Wales as a refugee from Ireland: p. 640. He entered Trinity College, Dublin, in 1688; he was now to go first to Oxford and then to Cambridge; later he returned to Ireland and was ordained. He published a volume of poems in 1693: D.N.B. The letter was addressed perhaps to Mrs. Hawkshaw's 'brother Flood' (p. 644) and passed on by him to Locke. Hawkshaw wrote to Locke on 12 November (no. 1202) and later.
(English) Charissime Avuncule
Ingruentibus hisce procellis, patriâ orbatus re, imò per omnem vitam te verè Mæcenatem reperi, tu carinæ vela laceratæ Indocilis pauperiem pati†1 renovasti; tuisque gaudet Auspiciis. Tu Patrem æque ac virtutis alumnum exuli consulendo agis, unde fit ut non sim solvendo: cujus salutari modò frui liceat consilio tanquam Anchoræ, immotus triumphet
Tuus omni Observantia et cultu Devotus Servus Neposque
BENJAMIN HAWKSHAW
Bewmaris 27 dies Maii.
(Latin) Dearest Uncle,
Assailed by these storms, deprived of my paternal estate, indeed throughout my whole life I have truly found a Maecenas in you; you have renewed the sails of my battered craft, 'untaught to endure poverty',†1 and it rejoices under your auspices. You act the part both of a father and of one schooled in virtue in your care for the exile, whence it comes that he is unable to pay the debt. If only he may be permitted to enjoy your salutary advice as it were his anchor, he may then triumph unshaken,
Your most respectful and devoted servant and nephew
BENJAMIN HAWKSHAW
Beaumaris 27 May.
Endorsed by Locke: Hawkshaw 27 May. 89

1146. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 5/15 June 1689 (1134, 1147)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 24-5. The letter was carried by Dr. Sladus, who did not reach England until about October: pp. 649-50, etc.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Rerum nostrarum statum amicissimus noster D. Sladus, harum lator, abunde tibi significabit. Aliquot horas, licet occupatissimus, impendes amico hinc ad te in Angliam usque provolanti. Licet enim scribendis epistolis otium tibi desit, præsens tamen amicus etiam occupatissimo aliquantum temporis suffurabitur. Spero te jam epistolam de Tolerantia e manu D. d'Aranda accepisse. Multi hic curiosi sunt noscendi autorem: verum ille latet, nec quisquam eum indagare potest. Rogatu D. Clerici, quæsivi e typographo autorem:†2 verum ille respondit, Epistolam ad se missam
― 631 ―
involutam brevi epistolio sine nomine et manu ignota scripto; se itaque ne divinando quidem assequi posse unde ad se venerit. E Remonstrantium officina prodiisse quidam colligunt ex argumento et tractationis modo: Verum quando consideramus ingenia et stylum singulorum inter nostros, neminem reperimus cui fœtum adeo eruditum et ornate scriptum attribuamus. Contraremonstrantem fœtus tam moderati parentem esse credibile neutiquam est, nisi forte sit vir quidam eruditus in magno illo cœtu latens, qui moderationem Remonstrantium animo fovet; quales illic multos esse certum est: paucos vero a quibus talis epistola prodire possit. Itaque certiorem te de autore reddere nequeo. Sed aliud est. Rumores hic sinistri de Doct. Burneto, nunc Episcopo Salisburiensi, sparguntur, quasi regiis consiliis plane sit adversus, ideoque summam regis offensionem experiatur: eumque confirmant plures ex Anglia reduces, interque eos tales, quos de eo certissimos esse oporteret; quorum relationibus effectum est, ut rumor hic totam civitatem nostram adeo pervaserit, ut qui illi contradicit nullo modo audiatur. Miraculi instar mihi est, hæc de illo viro dici et credi, qui semper maximo animi ardore causam regiam promovit, qui cum rege hinc in Angliam trajecit, et pluribus concionibus, etiam in
― 632 ―
ipsa solenni inauguratione, regem summa animi contentione toti regno commendavit, fortunamque suam, qua nunc gaudet, totam regi debet; adeo ut nihil rebus ipsius magis adversum videatur, quam regias deserere partes. Hæc mihi totidem argumenta sunt, quibus impedior, quo minus rumori isti fidem habeam. Interim gratissimum feceris, si vel paucis verbis quicquid hujus rei sit ad me perscribas; ut si falsus sit rumor, uti mihi persuasum habeo, eum diluere possim.†1 Reliqua D. Slado committo. Vale Vir Amplissime, et per epistolam ostendito, te nostri vivere non immemorem. Salutat te uxor mea et liberi.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 15 Junii

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Our good friend Mr. Sladus, the bearer of this letter, will inform you fully how things are with us. Busy as you may be, you will surely spare an hour or two for a friend who is rushing all the way from here to England to see you. Though you may not have leisure for letter-writing, still, the presence of a friend may fairly steal a little time from even the busiest of men. I hope that by now you have received the letter on Toleration by the hand of Mr. D'Aranda. Many people here are curious about the author of it; but he remains hidden, and no one is able to track him down. At Mr. Le Clerc's request I asked the printer who the author was;†2 but he replied that the letter [p. 631] had been sent to him wrapped in a short note with no name and written in an unknown hand, so that he could not so much as guess at the person it came from. The subject-matter and the manner of its treatment lead some people to infer that it is a product of the Remonstrant workshop; but when we consider the natural gifts and literary style of particular persons amongst ourselves we cannot discover anyone to whom we could attribute so learned and elegantly written a production. That any Contra-Remonstrant could be the parent of such temperate offspring is utterly incredible, unless it be that there lurks in that numerous company some scholarly man who fosters at heart the Remonstrant spirit of moderation; it is certain that there are many such among them: few, however, from whom such a letter could proceed. So I cannot tell you anything certain about the author. But there is something else. Sinister rumours are being disseminated here concerning Dr. Burnet, now bishop of Salisbury, making out that he is flatly opposed to the royal policy, and that he is therefore in the deepest disfavour with the king; and this is confirmed by a number of persons returning from England, some of them being such as should be best informed in the matter. From their reports it has come about that this rumour has gained such currency throughout our city that no one who contradicts it can get a hearing. It is a marvel to me that these things should be said and believed about that man, who has always displayed the utmost zeal in furthering the king's cause; who accompanied him on his crossing from here to England, and has in many public utterances, moreover at the inaugural [p. 632] ceremony itself, recommended the king to the whole realm with all the force at his command, and who owes the good fortune which he now enjoys entirely to the king; after all this nothing would seem more opposed to his own interests than that he should abandon the king's party. These, then, are so many arguments hindering me from putting any faith in the aforesaid rumour. Meanwhile you will do me a very great favour if you will write and tell me, even in a few words, anything that may have a bearing on this matter, so that if the rumour be false, as I feel sure that it is, I may be able to dispel it.†1 Any further matters I must entrust to Mr. Sladus. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and pray show us by a letter that you have not forgotten us. My wife and children send you their greetings.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 15 June

(English)
Londini 6 Jun 89
Vir Doctissime
Tolerantiam apud nos jam tandem lege stabilitam te ante hæc audiisse nullus dubito.†1 Non eâ forsan latitudine qua Tu et Tui similes veri et sine ambitione vel invidiâ Christiani optarent. Sed aliquid est prodire tenus. his initiis jacta spero sunt libertatis et pacis fundamenta quibus stabilienda olim erit Christi ecclesia. Nulli a cultu suo penitus excluduntur, nec pænis objiciuntur nisi Romani, si modo juramentum fidelitatis præstare velint et renunciare transubstantioni et quibusdam dogmatibus ecclesiæ Romanæ. De Juramento autem Quakeris dispensatum est. nec illis obtrusa fuisset malo exemplo illa quam in lege videbis confessio fidei, si aliqui eorum istam fidei confessionem non obtulissent, quod imprudens factum multi inter illos et cordatiores valde dolent.
(English) Gratias tibi ago pro exemplaribus tractatus de tolerantia et pace ecclesiasticâ quæ mihi misisti, compacta recte accepi, incompacta nondum ad manus meas pervenerunt. In vertendo de Tolerantia
― 634 ―
libello aliquem Anglum jam jam occupatum intelligo.†1 Opinionem illam pacis et probitatis fotricem ubique obtinere optarem. Acta inquisitionis jam pene descripta gaudio, uti spero brevi proditura, Opus utile et expectatum. Legem de tolerantia sancitam ad Dominum Le Clerc misi, quo interprete intelliges quousque extenditur hæc libertas.
Vale et me ama Tui Amantissimum
J LOCKE
Dilectissimam uxorem tuam liberosque reliquosque amicos meos meo nomine salutes
(Latin)
London 6 June 89
Learned Sir,
No doubt you will have heard before this that Toleration has now at last been established by law in our country.†1 Not perhaps so wide in scope as might be wished for by you and those like you who are true Christians and free from ambition or envy. Still, it is something to have progressed so far. I hope that with these beginnings the foundations have been laid of that liberty and peace in which the church of Christ is one day to be established. None is entirely debarred from his own form of worship or made liable to penalties except the Romans, provided only that he is willing to take the oath of allegiance and to renounce transubstantiation and certain dogmas of the Roman church. In the case of the Quakers the oath has been dispensed with; nor would the confession of faith which you will see mentioned in the law have been thrust upon them—a bad precedent—if certain of their number had not offered this confession, an unwise step that is much regretted by many of the more judicious among them.
(Latin) Thank you for the copies you sent me of the treatise on toleration and peace in the Church; I duly received the bound ones, but the unbound have not yet reached me. I understand that some Englishman is just now at work [p. 634] on translating the pamphlet on Toleration.†1 I could wish that that opinion, which is calculated to foster peace and righteousness, might everywhere prevail. I am glad that the Acts of the Inquisition are now almost transcribed and I hope they will shortly appear; a useful and much-desired work. I have sent Mr. Le Clerc the law enacted on Toleration; with him to translate you will understand how far this liberty is made to extend.
Good-bye, and love me
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
Give my greetings to your dear wife and children and to the rest of my friends.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Though I availed myself of the same opportunity to write to you yesterday, I now greet you again. The reason is that, your name having come up in conversation, the earl of Pembroke, our king's ambassador extraordinary,†2 [p. 635] desires to see you when he is in your country and to have some talk with you. Please therefore be good enough to call on him when you have an opportunity. He is a thoroughly cultured man and devoted to the liberal arts, and is a friend to scholars and honest men. If you approach him in my name his kindness for me will ensure you ready access to him, especially if you first make contact with his private secretary.†1 I have written this in a hurry when the earl was leaving, as the present piece of paper will inform you; it was all I could lay my hands on. 1149. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 8 June 1689 (1125, 1157)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 36-7.
Otterton June 8th. 89.
Dear Sir
I have been so unfortunate in all my Addresses to you, since your return to England, that I have hardly the Courage to offer at it any more; my letters of the 8th. and 17th. of Aprill, are not the only ones that I have had the pleasure of writing to you, though none of them have ever come to your Hands, as I am told by my Sisters, who ought to know, for they were all enclosed to Sir
― 636 ―
Walter Yonge. I never suffered so many disappointments of that kind in my whole life as I have this last six Months. and 'twas my hard fate to lose those letters which most nearly concern'd me, and were directed to my best Friends; whose conversation was necessary to my Happiness, and well being, and in Whose Memory, and good Opinion I were very Solicitous to preserve my Self. I cannot express the regret it has occasion'd me, but now that Honnest Mr Wildman has the Post Office,†1 I hope all these faults will be mended, and my fortune too. at least that all I write will not miscarry, and for Lucks sake I will direct no more to my Brother. if this finds you at your lodging, I shall soon follow it with another, in which I may speak my Thoughts more freely then I dare do, till the Charm is broke, and I hear that one letter is come safe to you. Though my Health is very imperfect, yet I am under no threatning Symptons at present, and I hope my Violent ilness in the Spring, was not from so fatall a Cause as I at first imagin'd, since it does not return and I know a very healthy Woman that has since been much in the same Condition; However I ought not to neglect it, but must beg leave to send you my Case once again, if my letters can find a way to you. this last Week I have been troubled with swelling of my Gumms, which run up over my Teeth, or rather between them, and are very tender, I wish you could direct me to a Remedy, I have been so several times this last Year, and I am much afraid 'twill spoyle my Teeth, which are yet indifferent good, and I would be glad to preserve them, if you can help me you will oblige me extreamly. You see my dear Friend what freedom I use with you. I hope you can pardon it, as your Goodness has done all my faults hitherto, and that you will also forgive my abrupt conclusion being in danger of losing the post, and I have but too long already neglected my duty in tendring you the best services of Sir
Your Obliged faithfull friend
ISABELLA DUKE

1151. Benjamin Furly to Locke, 10 June 1689 (1141, 1243)

Mortclack, from the Sugar house, at
John Osgoods.†3 10/20 June 1689
D.F.
Yesterday I omitted to write, But Saturday our Oxford friend†4 (whose name for my life I cannot call to my <mind>),†b will have informd thee, that I was pretty well and free from my Cough, he walking with me to Holland house,†5 where I met with my Ingenious friend at last, and stayd dinner with him; where I met with a scrupulous Cambridge schollar, that thought nothing, "could discharge him of the oath of Allegiance that he had take to Ja: 2.
― 639 ―
and his successors". I had pleasant sport with him upon Sir R: Filmers maggot,†1 which he soon quitted, because he saw he could not make it bear to his purpose. And tho he were at every turn reduced ad non loqui,†2 he had the wit to hold fast the conclusion. Last night after our meeting was ended, I met with the like scruple in one of our folk, who, when I thought I had fully convinc'd him, gravely told me I had more experience of these things than he, and had said much which he could not answer. But that I had not satisfyed his reason. I told him I could not help that at present there being no more time, but might perhaps another time. In the meanwhile I see not, that university learneing, nor inspiration, does make all that pretend to it wise, or give them Common Sense.
It remains now onely that I tell you how I find my self. saturday all day, I tooke no medicine of any sort. Nor yet at night, to try if I could sleep without it, and so I did yesterday and this night, saturday night I slept very well, and on my right side, last night (being a little heated in the meeting, and my change of bed and beer, I was a little at first kept awake and coughed—I return today to my barly water so soone as its cleare. And doubt not of getting rid of my cough in few dayes. I am told that upon some allarm, or Jealosy of some being up, or ready for K.J: my Lord Delamer had in actuall arms 3 days 4000†a men—Is it true? have you any such thing there reported?†3 I am here so far from the city that I shall soon grow weary because I cannot hear what the senators are doing. I shalbe glad to receive a line from thee, be pleased to salute all my friends and acquaintance as occasion presents—and account of me as
Thy most affectionate friend
B F

1154. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 25 June/5 July 1689 (1126, 1216)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 35-6. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 38-9.
A Amsterdam le 5 de Juillet. 1689.
J'ai reçu, Monsieur, le paquet que vous aviez remis au Sieur Aubert,†4 et je vous suis obligé de la peine que vous avez prise de me marquer les titres de quelques livres nouveaux dans vôtre Lettre précedente. J'ai bien de la joie d'apprendre que vôtre Traité est sous la Presse;†5 et je ne me dédis point de la promesse que je vous avois faite de le mettre en Latin, pourvu que vous n'exigiez pas de moi que je le fasses trop promptement. Je suis chargé seul du soin de la Bibliotheque; au moins ai-je cherché vainement quelcun pour m'aider. Mr. Le Cene,†6 qui a fait le Volume XIII, l'a fait si
― 642 ―
miserablement, que malgré les corrections infinies, que j'y ai faites, j'en ai honte moi même. Le Sieur Behagel†1 qui va à Londres, pour y lever une boutique de Libraire, vous en remettra deux exemplaires en blanc. Je souhaite que cet honête homme s'y établisse, afin que nous puissions avoir plus promptement ce qui se fait là; et je croi qu'il n'aura pas de peine à le faire, dans Westminster. J'ai lû avec plaisir l'Acte de la Tolerance;†2 c'est une démarche vers la paix; et je souhaite que celui de la Comprehension paroisse bien tôt. Lors que les Puissances favorisent des sentimens moderez, ils l'emportent bien-tôt sur les opinions factieuses, que l'on ne soûtient que pour plaire aux Princes qui les protegent. Si l'on ne va pas tout d'un coup aussi loin, qu'il seroit à souhaiter, c'est toûjours quelque chose que de témoigner quelque sorte de moderation.
Je n'ai point encore vu l'Histoire des Unitaires,†3 et je crain que Mr. Furly n'ait négligé de l'envoier, parce que le Sieur Aubert m'a dit qu'il étoit tombé malade en Angleterre. Je vous suis cependant obligé, Monsieur, de la bonté que vous avez eu de le lui donner de bonne heure, et je vous prie de croire que je ne perdrai aucune occasion de vous témoigner ma reconnoissance pour les soins que vous prenez à m'aider à soûtenir la Bibliotheque Universelle. Faites moi encore la grace de m'apprendre si le Dr. Pococke a commenté tous les petits Prophetes, et si cet Ouvrage est tout imprimé, où s'il n'y a encore que sur Michée, comme on me l'a dit. Comme je ne fais pas de difficulté de faire des extraits de Livres Anglois peu connus ici, lors qu'ils sont curieux, je tâcherai d'avoir Pocoke, sur tout s'il a commenté les 12 petits Prophetes.†4 Je croi que vous verrez à Londres L'Amant de vôtre Reine,†5 si vous lui pouvez procurer une place à Bedlam, vous ferez un oeuvre de charité, car assurément il n'en reviendra jamais, puis quil a eu l'effronterie de me soûtenir qu'il n'avoit rien fait qu'il ne dût faire, quoi que je lui montrasse les originaux de ses Lettres. Il m'a causé bien de la perte et du chagrin, Dieu le lui pardonne, et le fasse sage. Au lieu de vous entretenir de ces sottises je voudrois avoir quelque chose de bon à vous mander
― 643 ―
d'ici; mais il ne s'y fait qu'une grande abondance de sermons, et peu de bons livres. Vous connoissez le païs aussi bien que moi. Je prie Dieu qu'il vous conserve dans une parfaite santé. Je suis de tout mon coeur, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC
Au commencement des Feries, c'est à dire dans 15 jours d'ici j'irai à la Haie, pour avoir l'honneur de faire la reverance à Mylord de Pembroke.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke Docteur en Medecine at Mr. Ansham Churchill Bookseller near Amen Corner London
Endorsed by Locke: le Clerc 5 Jul. 89 Answered 23.

1157. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 3 July 1689 (1149, 1168)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 38-9.
July 3d. 1689.
My Dear Friend.
Your Obliging letter of 11th. June came safely to me, in due time; Which will make it the more strange that I should be so long in answering it; and craving that assistance which I so much need, and you with your wonted Goodness offer me; But it hapned to be a Critical time, and I was willing to observe my Self a little further before I gave you a state of my Case. which the more I consider, the more I am at a loss how to put it in writing; neither do I see what service I can do my self, by giving you the Trouble of reading it; unless my circumstances would give me leave to follow your advice, and to go to London, or Tunbridge, if you should think it necessary for me. My Master is very much concern'd for me, but we are under such Difficultyes at present, that we dare not absent our selves from Home; and I am afraid shall hardly be able to make an escape for the whole Summer. to what end then shall I punnish you with telling you an unpleasant story; since I understand my own disease well enough to know that I cannot be reliev'd by any remedies this Country affords, or at this distance from my Physitian, unless it be by mending the Habit of my Body in general, and sweetning my Blood, which doubtless is Scurbutical in a high degree, as appears by the swelling and Bleeding of my Gums, a frequent Lassitude of my whole Body; inward Convulsions, and a mighty faintness, and dispiritedness, with a trembling of my Heart, and all my Nerves; much the same complaints I have formerly laboured under, only the swelling and bleeding of my Gums is new. if you can substitute any thing in the room of Waters, for this
― 646 ―
Year; or any way help me, you will do a great piece of Charity, for I am at a non plus, and can have no further recourse to any thing but Castle Cary Waters;†1 which I have this day sent for; and I purpose to give them to my little Betty for two or three days, unless you think them impropper. I heard a Bird Sing that Mr Clark and his Lady were returning to Chipley, and that 'twas thought Mr Lock would accompany them; would to heaven you could confirm that good News to me, who suffer more then I can express by my distance from him; for whom I have all the Esteem, affection, and Gratitude that my soul is capable of, being with the greatest sincerity and respect Unalterably
Yours.
ISA: DUKE
Mr Duke is your Humble servant.
Address: For Mr John Lock at his Lodging in Dorset Court in Channell row in Westminster

1158. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 8/18 July 1689 (1148, 1163)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 26-7. Answers nos. 1147 and 1148; answered by no. 1172.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Tolerantiam apud vos stabilitatam gaudeo. Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ exemplum apud alias Reformatas magnæ est autoritatis, nunc præsertim, regnante Principe Arausionensi, quem Presbyterianis minime male velle persuasum sibi habent; ac proinde autoritate sua regia utriusque partis nimium zelum temperaturum augurantur.
― 647 ―
Et sane, negari nequit, si alterutra pars sibi permittatur, quin alteram alias quærere terras sit jussura. Si itaque una solummodo protectione regia ac parliamentaria gaudeat, facile vires nacta alteram potentiâ suâ opprimet: Optima est temperatura, quemadmodum omnes boni sunt cives, etiam omnibus civitatis jura concedere ex æquo, et nulli, <quamdiu>†a civitatis jura non violat, denegare quod jure naturæ ex æquo omnium est. Si fortasse arctioribus limitibus Tolerantia sit circumscripta, spero ubi suavitatem illius æquitatemque degustavit Anglia, plenam tandem inde emersuram tolerantiam, per quam nullius conscientiæ ulla, vel minima, vis inferatur. Quakerorum quorundam factum, ut recte notas, imprudens est: Verum illi fortasse metuerunt, nisi confessionem illam exhiberent, se a communi protectione excludendos: Nunc liquet, superabundantem cautelam nonnunquam nocere. Tractatum de Tolerantia in linguam Anglicam verti gaudeo. Hic in linguam Gallicam versus est a D. de Cene,†1 et credo brevi proditurum; etiam in linguam Belgicam versus est;†2 ita ut jam brevi quatuor linguis legi possit. Spero non sine fructu fore ejus lectionem; et
― 648 ―
maxime gaudeo in linguam Gallicam, nunc omnibus, etiam magnatibus ac principibus, communem esse translatum. Hic eum a Remonstrante quopiam conscriptum credunt, quia quæ defendit Remonstrantium placitis sunt consentanea. Nullum tamen inter Remonstrantes noverunt, cui eum attribuant. Quare alii credunt, licet in Remonstrantium cœtibus non vivat, esse tamen Remonstrantium doctrina imbutum. Ego mihi plaudo, librum adeo eruditum, et communi rei Christianæ adeo utilem, credi non aliunde quam ex Remonstrantium officina prodire posse. Apud typographum inquirere voluerunt, unde in manus ejus devenisset: verum ille se id ignorare respondet: ad se missum libellum epistolæ sine nomine sine dië et consule inclusum. Venio ad alteram tuam epistolam, in qua certissima amoris tui in me sinceri documenta ostendis: Vis me amicitiæ tuæ cum Comite Pembrokiensi facere participem. Occasionem mihi suppeditas innotescendi viro, quem eximiæ suæ dotes jam in patria nostra reddidere celebrem et venerandum, cujusque laudes jam passim prædicantur. Ego hactenus Hagam excurrere non potui; verum fortasse brevi dabitur illuc eundi occasio; tum tua fretus amicitia Generosum comitem compellabo, licet hactenus Magnates adire non assuetus. Verum adeo se omnibus affabilem exhibere audio, ut fiduciam eum compellandi
― 649 ―
concipere ausus fuissem, etiam commendatione tua non munitus; multo magis nunc per tuam amicitiam aditu mihi facili præparato. Verum audio multos adhuc ex Episcopis recusare juramentum fidelitatis:†1 Nescio an fictus sit rumor eorum, qui præ nimio presbyteratus studio Episcopis male volunt. Alii hic rumorem divulgarunt, Episcopum Salisburiensem sese regi ostendere adversarium, ideòque gratia regis penitus excidisse: qui rumor ita hic invaluit, et per plures ex Anglia adventantes ita fuit confirmatus, ut frustra illi contradiceretur: mihi tamen nunquam creditus fuit. Jam paulatim evanescere incipit. Credo eum multis hic remonstrantismi esse suspectum. Memini mihi a Matrona quadam Angla, cui ego eram ignotus, ante duos vel tres menses dictum, Doctorem Burnetum esse quidem virum egregium, verum arminianum.†2 Tales autem hic facile creduntur gratia regia excidisse, quia eos ea indignos judicant. Prolixius de eo scripsi in epistola, cujus amicum nostrum Sladum latorem fore credideram.†3 Verum ille ante tres hebdomadas et quod excurrit in Angliam abiturus nobis valedixit;
― 650 ―
nunc per civitates et pagos Hollandiæ oberrat, incertus quando profecturus, imo an profecturus. Si proficiscatur, meas Tibi exhibiturus est. Collegæ omnes bene valent, Teque quamplurimum salvere jubent. Liber Sancti Officii jam totus descriptus est. restat index ille præfixus. Cras contendo cum uxore et liberis Roterodamum: si D. Furlæus redierit, eum compellabo. Plurimam Tibi salutem precatur uxor liberique. Vale Vir Amplissime, meique memor vive.
Tui amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 18 Julii
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I am glad that toleration has gained a firm position in your country. The example of the Anglican Church is of great weight with the other Reformed churches, especially now that the Prince of Orange is on the throne, who they feel sure is by no means ill disposed towards the Presbyterians; they augur from this that he will use his royal authority to temper the excessive zeal of [p. 647] each of the parties. And, to be sure, it cannot be denied that if either of them were allowed to have its way it would probably tell the other to betake itself to some other part of the world. Accordingly if one alone is to enjoy the protection of king and parliament it will easily become strong enough to crush the other by its own power; the best rule is that all alike, in so far as they are all good citizens, should be allowed the rights of citizenship in equal measure, and that no one, so long as he does not offend against the laws of the state, should be denied what belongs to all alike by the law of nature. If toleration should happen to be confined within narrower bounds, I hope that when England has had some taste of the prince's agreeable and equitable nature we may at last see the emergence of complete toleration, by which no man's conscience may be forced even in the smallest degree. The action of certain Quakers, as you justly remark, is ill advised; but perhaps they feared that unless they made that confession they might be excluded from the general benefit of protection; it is now plain that superfluous precautions are sometimes harmful. I am glad that the treatise on Toleration is being translated into English. Here it has been done into French by Mr. de Cene,†1 and I believe will soon be published; it has also been translated into Dutch;†2 so that people will now soon be able to read it in four languages. I hope that the reading of it [p. 648] will not fail to bear fruit; and what pleases me especially is its translation into French, a tongue which is now generally familiar to all, even to great men and princes. People here believe that it was written by some Remonstrant, because the positions which it defends agree with Remonstrant tenets. They do not, however, know anyone amongst the Remonstrants to whom they can attribute it. Others therefore suppose that, although the writer may not be living in Remonstrant circles, he is nevertheless imbued with Remonstrant teaching. For my part I congratulate myself that so scholarly a book, and one of such service to the common cause of Christianity, should be thought incapable of proceeding from anywhere else than the Remonstrant workshop. They have tried to find out from the printer the source from which he received it; but he says that he knows nothing about it: the pamphlet was sent him enclosed with a letter bearing no name or date. I come now to your second letter, in which you give me the surest proof of your sincere regard for me: you desire, in fact, to make me a sharer in your friendship with the earl of Pembroke. You are giving me the opportunity of making the acquaintance of one whose remarkable gifts have already made him well known and respected in our country, and whose praises are sung on all hands. I have not so far been able to make a visit to The Hague, but perhaps an opportunity will offer itself shortly; in that case I will in reliance on your friendship pay a call on the noble earl, albeit I have not hitherto been accustomed to approaching the great. I hear, however, that he shows himself so affable to everyone that I [p. 649] would have summoned up courage to call on him even without the support of your introduction, much more so now that your friendship has provided me with easy access to him. I hear indeed that many of the bishops still refuse to take the oath of allegiance;†1 this may possibly be a false rumour put about by those who have no liking for bishops, out of excessive zeal for Presbyterian government. Others here recently put about a rumour that the bishop of Salisbury was showing opposition to the king, and that he was therefore completely out of favour with him; this rumour gained such strength here, confirmed as it was by many people arriving from England, that it was useless to contradict it; for my part, however, I never believed it. It is now beginning to die out by degrees. I believe that many people here suspect him of Remonstrantism. I remember being told two or three months ago by a certain English lady, to whom I was a stranger, that Dr. Burnet was certainly an excellent man, but an Arminian;†2 now, in this country such persons are easily believed to have lost the king's favour because they consider them to be undeserving of it. I expressed myself at greater length about him in a letter which I believed our friend Sladus was to carry.†3 It is three weeks and more, however, since he said good-bye to us as about to leave for [p. 650] England; now he is wandering through the towns and villages of Holland, undecided as to when he will go, or even whether he will go at all. If he goes he is to give you my letter. Our Collegians are all well and send you their best wishes. The book of the Holy Office is now completely transcribed; there remains the index prefixed to it. Tomorrow I journey to Rotterdam with my wife and children; if Mr. Furly has returned I will call on him. My wife and children wish you the best of health. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and keep me in mind.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 18 July
1689

(Latin)
Amsterdam 25 July 1689
Esteemed Sir,
There have been many reasons for this rather late reply, but the chief one is that I was ill for a week and more, after which, when the sickness abated, [p. 651] I betook myself out of the city in company with my wife, my daughter Cornelia, and my sweet little grandson Peter,†1 in order, that is, to recover my strength and spirits, both of which I felt to be much impaired. Now I am well again, thank God, and on returning, though rather tardily, to my usual occupations I felt it my duty to make haste and tell you how heartily we thank you for the large knives and the novel contrivance, which one of us at first sight said was the hilt of a Spanish sword and another a spit. We shall put our dishes on it and turn it, with you in mind, as we have found that it serves admirably for such a purpose. When my wife put these things amongst her household equipment it occurred to her that it was also her duty to think of something in return, which might show how welcome the gift is as coming from such a friend.
(Latin) If you wish, kind Sir, to know how things are with our Collegie, I must say that it is much depleted and we often hardly make a quorum, ever since Dr. Cyprianus†3 has been in your country and Dr. Sladus has threatened to make his way to you. But that gentleman hastens very slowly; in the words of our proverb 'he goes crab-fashion'.†4 He said good-bye to his friends some time ago as if on the point of departure. First of all he made for Utrecht to see [p. 652] his friend Hubert;†1 from there he went to Haarlem, where he stayed for some days with Arminius and his cousin Margaret; from there to The Hague; then into the country not far from here; now he is at Utrecht once more, and yet he wishes it to appear that he has not changed his mind; when you see him in person you will find him not so shy of explaining himself. Mijnheer van Limborch is away from town just now on account of the holidays. Quina and Bernagie, who were the only ones at the Collegie in our house today, send you their best wishes, as I do also with my whole heart, praying that all may go well for you and for peacefulness in your native land; some are spreading reports that that peace is not so certain and secure, which may God forfend; may He inspire all your countrymen to unite in harmony with such an amiable king and keep them loyal to their country and to a religion that is truly Christian. Good-bye, from your
EGB. VEEN.

1161. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 16/26 July 1689 (1139, 1179)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 14-15.
Monsieur
il y a longtemps que je doibs une responce a vos deux dernieres lettres, et des remerciements pour toutes vos honnestetez et les presens dont il vous a plu nous honorer. pendant qu'on vous demande conte de ce qu'on vous doibt, vous nous engagez dans des nouvelles obligations, qui nous mettent hors d'etat d'y pouvoir satisfaire. si vous vouliez en agir librement avec nous et nous mander ce quil y pouroit avoir icy de vostre service, nous aurions quelque esperance de nous pouvoir acquitter avec le temps. nous vous supplions d'estre persuadé que nous le souhaittons veritablement
― 654 ―
et que nous nous fairions un plaisir extreme d'estre honoré de vos commandements. je vous envoye une carte nouvelle du Palatinat sur le plan de celle d'Angleterre qui a parue avant vostre depart.†1 en peu de jours paroistra celle de France, et on travaille a celle d'Irlande, suivant la mesme methode pour trouver facilement les moindres endroits et peu connus. si ce plan vous agrée je vous envoiray toutes celles qui paroistront, je vous envoye cette carte du palatinat avec quleque autres petites bagatelles que la famille vous envoye dans la mesme petite caisse dans la quelle estoient les chemises de laine de ma femme. Monsieur Gunston, l'associé de Monsieur daranda nous a fait la grace de l'addresser a un de ces correspondans, Mr. Peter Delmé†2 merchant in lyme street in London. le maistre du bastiment qui s'en est chargé se nomme mr. Aldred, son vaisseau se dit, the lion. la caisse est marquée I.L. le contenu sont douze aulnes de toile d'hollande. une medaille d'argent, un pain d'espice, une carte, trois portraits de princes. et quelqu autres petites bagatelles a jouer pour un enfant. le vaisseau doibt partir cette sepmaine d'icy: je laisse a mon beau pere et a ma belle mere, et ma femme a se defendre de vous oser presenter si peu de chose. pour moy je vous envoye rien du tout qu'un eschantillon d'une carte et quelque portraits pour mandier vos commandements. Monsieur Limburgh n'est pas en ville, depuis quelque<s>†a jours, il est parti en bonne santé. Monsieur Sladus rhode la campagne sans trouver le chemin qui mene en Engleterre. le voyage de Monsieur cyprianus surprend icy bien des gens, veu quil est partis a l'insceu mesme de sa femme et de la plus part de ses amis, laissant travailler icy ses competiteurs, qui ont beau jeu presentement. nous sommes icy comme en langueur, voyant que vostre gouvernement a tant de peine a s'affermir. quil y a tousjours des mal intentionez pour une si bonne cause, et a la quelle toute l'europe est si interessée. Mais il faut esperer que Dieu qui a commencé cet œuvre avec des marques si specieuse de sa grace, la parachevera. vous me faitte bien de l'honneur de me dire que Mylord Pembroch vous a ouï parler de moy. vous scavez trop bien Monsieur que je nay pas des talens pour oser paroistre devant un si grand et si excellent personnage, a moins quil suffise d'avoir le bien d'estre de vos Amis. je crois fort que
― 655 ―
son Excellence qui connoist parfaittement vostre Merite, s'imagine, que vous n'avez fait icy dautres connoissance qu'avec d'habiles gens. et ainsy j'aime mieux quil me croye habile homme sans me voir, que de diminuer ce credit par Ma presence. je scay pourtant fort bien que vous ne me voudriez pas exposer, ca esté un effet de la bonne volonté que vous avez pour moy. et je vous en remercie.
encore une fois Monsieur consideré moy je vous prie comme un homme qui vous est tout acquis, et qui souhaite estre d'effet.
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P GUENELLON

1163. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 21/31 July 1689 (1158, 1172)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 28-9. Answered by no. 1172.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Nullam Te salutandi occasionem prætermittere possum. Lator harum est filius D. Christiani Hartsoekeri,†1 nuper ministri in Ecclesia
― 657 ―
nostra Roterodamensi, viri dum viveret mihi amicissimi. Filius hic mercaturæ sese dedit, et nuper ex Lusitania rediit: Nunc in Angliam proficiscitur, tum ut linguam Anglicanam addiscat, tum ut cum mercatoribus quibusdam, qui commercia cum Lusitanis habent, familiaritatem contrahat. Juvenis est, quantum quidem mihi innotuit, bonorum amicitia non indignus. Ob memoriam viri mihi amicissimi et intimi eum Tibi commendatum ut habeas obnixe rogo. Scimus in regione peregrina juvenibus nihil magis esse necessarium directione et consilio virorum prudentium ac benevolorum. Fretus nostra amicitia ego illum Tibi de meliore nota commendo. Quicquid illi præstiteris, mihi factum credam, ac gratus agnoscam. Non dubito quin se Tibi morum suavitate ac modestia sit probaturus. Scio vitæ genus quod amplexus est a tuo quammaxime esse alienum; nec enim Mercurio cum Musis quicquam est commune: Attamen honesta vita, morum candor, commercium cum bonis, omnibus, etiam diversissimum vitæ genus amplexis, communia sunt. Nolo eum pluribus Tibi commendare, ne amicitiæ nostræ diffidere videar. Scribo hanc inter amicorum sermones, ubi cum uxore mea haustu Theæ sanitatis tuæ memores sumus. Roterodami sum, brevi hinc Amstelodamum rediturus. D. Furlæum nondum rediisse intelligo. Spero omnia tandem fœlicem sortitura exitum, ut finito
― 658 ―
luctuosissimo bello tandem pax alma omnium miseriarum oblivionem inducat. Audio et hic eosdem de Episcopo Salisburiënsi sinistros rumores: Verum nulli eos abundantius spargunt, quam presbyteriani: Unde mihi suspicio est, credidisse eos, Episcopum in ipsorum partes transiturum; quæ spes cum eos fefellit, jam, præ odio quo omnes Episcopos prosequuntur, ipsum acutius traducere. Quam suspicionem et alii ipsorum sermones mihi confirmant. Ex Te certiora scire aveo. Vale Vir Amplissime: uxor reliquique amici plurimam Tibi precantur salutem.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH
Roterodami 31 Julii

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I cannot neglect any opportunity of writing to you. The bearer of this letter is a son of Mr. Christiaan Hartsoeker,†1 who was lately minister in [p. 657] our church at Rotterdam, a man who in his lifetime was a very close friend of mine. This son of his has taken up a mercantile career and has just returned from Portugal; he is now going to England, both to learn English and to become acquainted with certain merchants who have dealings with the Portuguese. He is, from what I have come to know of him, a young man not undeserving of the friendship of good people. In memory of the man who was my valued and intimate friend I earnestly beg that he may find a welcome with you. We know that for young men in a strange country nothing is more needful than direction and advice from wise and kindly persons. Relying, then, on our friendship I recommend him to you in the highest terms; whatever you may do for him I shall regard as done for myself and shall acknowledge it with gratitude. I have no doubt that with his amiable and modest nature he will win your approval. I am aware that the walk in life which he has chosen is far removed from your own, for Mercury and the Muses have nothing in common; still, uprightness and candour and habits formed by intercourse with virtuous folk appeal to all alike, even to those who have adopted an entirely different way of life. I will not recommend him to you at greater length lest I should seem to mistrust our friendship. I am writing this with friends talking round me, where in company with my wife we are drinking your health in tea. I am at Rotterdam, returning shortly to Amsterdam. I understand that Mr. Furly has not returned yet. I hope that everything may turn out well in the end, so that when this most lamentable war [p. 658] is over kindly peace may at last make us forget all our troubles. Here too I hear the same sinister rumours about the bishop of Salisbury; but those who spread them most freely are Presbyterians; hence I suspect that they believed the bishop was about to come over to their side, so that being disappointed of this hope they are now all the more eager to disparage him, out of the hatred they evince towards all bishops. Other things too that they say confirm me in this suspicion. I should like to have more certain information from you. Good-bye, excellent Sir; my wife and the rest of our friends send you their warmest greetings.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Rotterdam 31 July
1689

1164. Lady (Mary) Calverley to Locke, 23 July [1689] (1133, 1305)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 5, ff. 1-2. Year from Locke's endorsement and contents. Perhaps answers no. 1133.
Chopwell†1 July 23d
Dear Sir
In spight of Monsieur Pelisson†2 I shall begin my letter with telling you, that I received Yours, Mais quelle lettre! Quell tresor de belles choses! what heat from your Climat! but these things Apart, I have since I writt you last made an Effort upon the laziness of my Constitution, I retir'd to produce a letter—and hop'd to succeed to a Miracle such vanity had your first epistle fir'd me with, thus easy is it for you mighty people in oratory, (when you make it your bussiness) to impose upon us Mortalls, especially when you think it below you to prove any thing but impossibilitys, I found so, for after all the fine thing you had made me in my conceit, upon the essay I wanted all that was necessary to acquitt my promiss, I found neither the inventive faculty, nor the garnishment, and that when I promisd you quelque chose de vostre façon, I was unacquainted with my self, but I was come but from reading your letter, that was the reason I took le vol trop haut, meme que Je me donnois dans le Phebus, now all I have to say, is, you must blame your self for those altitudes you had put me in, I thought as you ought to be treated with nothing that is Common, and nothing but what is new unsaid or unthought of before can be worthy of you, so I hop'd to entertain you, thus was I puffed up after what I read from you, Mais Mons: vous m'avez bien donnee dans le panneau, pour vous dire franchement la verité, I see I may try my heart out, before I find out the accomplishments you have mark'd to me, or any advantagious way to sett of my Meritts to you, without lying: after this evident tryall, this taste of my disabilitys, had you not given me leave in your second letter to converse with you in my old dunstable†3 freindly way, I durst not have sett pen to paper, and with all my plainness if you consider what it costs me to write a letter to you, you wou'd grant your civility to be due to me, for I dare not write you News
― 660 ―
of our Dundees and Mackay's,†1 least I shou'd invade the priviledges of those who gett money for their labour, nor any thing relating to the beau monde or galantry, least I shou'd make a breach into your prerogatives etc, nor dare I enter into the polities for then I shoud draw upon me the forces of the D,†2 and all, send you news at rebound, etc, but as strictly as I am tied up, I will never quitt the service so long as you will suffer me in this way, to assure you with how reall a respect and to what epreuve I am
Your most faithfull servant
M C

1165. Locke to Mrs. Jane Stringer, 25 July 1689 (748, 1166)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 24, ff. 259-60. Draft. The letter was delivered to Mrs. Stringer by Clarke: p. 664. Answered by no. 1166.
London 25 Jul. 89
Madam
After the conversation you and I had in town since my returne I thought there had not been any quarrell or suspition of a quarrell remaining between us. But by a message I lately receivd from you by Mrs Clarke I finde you thinke there is need of some Apologie for your soe positive breakeing off all correspondence with me when I was in Holland. I confesse I was a litle surprised at it when it happend, and could not hear a freind that I esteemd soe much soe abruptly tell me I must expect to heare noe more from her without thinkeing it a losse, espetially at a time when freinds†a- were most of value and use to me.-†a However I can assure you I made noe unkinde reflections on it, but gave all the allowance to the caution wary people thought necessary in those times, that you could desire: And had never thoughts of mentioning it to you or any body
― 661 ―
else, till Mr Stringer by upbraiding to me with†a severall years silence†1 forced me to allege soe unavoidable a reason for my justification. But with all this I assure you I had not then nor since any quarrell to you. And I count it the greatest misfortune I have had since I came to England that by the continuance of some hard usage upon me I am kept away from a place and company wherein my health and inclination would other wise have perswaded me to have spent a good part of my vacant time, and I know not what wast I should have made on the milke and cheescakes you soe kindely offerd me if Mr Stringer were not as it seems weary of his old friends, and did not value me at a rate I am ashamd when I thinke on, for I know not a meaner character can be given a man than not to be thought worth his picture, and that one that calls himself his friend had rather have with him the†b shadow than person of him he pretends to love. I have examined all the parts of my past life and cannot finde in any one of them a reason why mr Stringer of all the men I know in England should have the least complacence for me. And I doe not finde that I am soe contemptible or ridiculous to any body else that whilst they call me friend allow soe little to the consideration of that name But Mr Stringer is pleased to have it soe and I say noe more: but thus much a late accident forces me to say. For seeing lately my Picture drawn by Greenhill at a painters where I was siting for an other†2 I thought (though it had been sent for without my knowledg) that it came very oportunely for the desire I had to have a print of it before a booke of mine to which I thought to prefix it being now in the presse†3 and therefor a litle before Mrs Clarke went out of town when I saw the painter where it was had noe more to doe with it I sent for it to my lodging to have a plate graved after it. This I thought in the familiarity was amongst all that were any way concernd I might have don without offense to any body. But I found Mrs Clarke at her goeing away was uneasy about leaveing the picture though for a purpose she thought soe reasonable. This made me see in what state matters were still and how litle it was permitted me to presume on <the
― 662 ―
good will or civility>†a of my old friends at Ivy church, without direct askeing leave and their positive allowance. I confesse I had it from the painters without askeing Mrs Clarkes consent and I did not doubt but I should have yours but since I perceive this scruple I thinke it convenient to aske now that I may have it by your consent till there be a plate gravd from it. I will not set the graver on worke about it till I have your answer. For I will not give†b- those who are concernd the uneasinesse that-†b the picture shall be in any hands, or a plate be graved from it without your permission. If you please to consent to let me have it soe long I shall receive it as a marke that your former kindenesse is not quite past recovery. I tell you truly I esteem you as I ever did and desire very much we may live and laugh as we use to doe Doe not suspect that if I have got any new freinds I doe the lesse value my old ones or am lesse concerned or rejoyced to be valued by them. at least do me Madam the Justice to beleive that I am
your most humble servant
J LOCKE
Pray remember me to Mr Stringer and the rest of the good company with you:
I designed to write by Mrs Clarke but as they know I had not then time

1166. Mrs. Jane Stringer to Locke, 29 July [1689] (1165, 1171)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 101-2. Year from Locke's endorsement and contents. Answers no. 1165.
July the 29th
Sir
Mrs Clarke can be my wittness that I had imediately returned you my humble thanks for the great favour of your Letter if she had not kept me out att Salisbury till it was too late to doe it by that post. I am hartily glad to heare your picture came so seasonably to give you the satisfaction of a coppy to put before your
― 663 ―
book and tho I am told tis above my capacity I rejoyce the understanding part of the world is like to receive so great a benifitt as I heare that will be. I hope you canot doubt but your picture is att your own dispose both for time and place. I beceech you beleeve if we had any thing that were a thousand times the vallue we should rejoyce to serve you with it. I hope you beleeve me truly sencible of the great debt I owe you for your abundant great favours to me and mine and tho some things unaccountable has pas'd amongst us I doubt not but you that are strong can forgive the infirmitys of weak brethren and I dare engage if you please to ease you self of a load of buisness and company and honnour us with your company att Ivey church but one month I will give you a good account of all that has passed but I dare not atempt it att this distance nor in less time. I promise you faithfully if you come you shall not repent making us happy. I confess you may suspect self Love prevails and that my hart is very deceitfull, and I beleeve all this however I allso veryly beleeve I am not so deceived but that I can truly say I am farr more delighted with an opertunity to serve my friend that has oblidged me then in receiving any other conciderable benifitt. I know very well more is due to you then I can posibly pay and when ever you give me an opertunity to say or doe any thing towards it my obligation still encreacess as I desire it should who am
Sir
your most oblidged faithfull humble servant
JANE STRINGER
