1168. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 31 July 1689 (1157, 1230)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, f. 40.
Escott July: 31st. 1689.
My Dear Friend
Some dayes since I were made Happy by the receiving your endearing letter; which surpass'd in kindness, if it be possible, all
― 665 ―
that ever I have receiv'd, even from your self, who know so well how to excell in Friendship, and all the most touching expressions of it. I know not what influence your prescription will have on my Body, but I am sure your kindness has charm'd my Soul, remov'd all uneasiness from it, and made me Tast such pleasures as nothing else can afford me. Those assurances of your continued affections to me, are more desirable, more acceptable, more necessary to my well being, then Health when I am sick, Ease when I am in pain, or any other enjoyment whatsoever; and make me more rich, and Happy. Methinks I am now Elevated to the height of my Wishes, and look down on every Body, and every thing else. and am insensible of my wants of Health, or any thing but Words to express my Gratitude to you, and my deep sense of what I owe you, for so great goodness. that when you are encompass'd by the most excellent persons in the World, who all Court your Freindship, you should allow me a share of it; because I beg it, and know how to Vallue it, but have nothing else to recommend me to you. and am also most unfortunatly at a most deplorable distance from you. which I esteem my greatest unhappiness, but cannot help my self at present. but must support it as patiently as I can. We are under such circumstances as make our presence at Home absolutely necessary, at least my Master thinks so, which is the same thing to me; so that I must pray, and wayt for your comming into the Country, and live upon the hopes you give me of it. I am now better in health then I have been, the Purging Waters which I drank six days, intermitting three between did me good I believe; my Gumms are very well again. However when I go back to Otterton, I will make the Gargle you advise, which may be of use to keep them so. my Girle has seldom been free from pimples and Blisters about her Nose and Mouth since she came Home, and 'twas for that I gave her Castle Cary Waters; otherways she is perfectly well, Plump and vigorous, much mended every way by the fresh Air of the Country; my sisters also are well, and pleas'd with their retirement; they beg that their best services to you may conclude this from Dear Sir
Your most Obliged affectionate Friend and Humble Servant
ISABELLA DUKE
The Country affords nothing worth your notice. Mr Duke is at
― 666 ―
Exon being one of the Grand Jury,†1 and very much your humble servant. he longs to get you into the row.
Endorsed by Locke: Mrs Duke 31 July 89
August
1169. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, [August 1689] (984, 1195)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 85-6. Partly printed in King, pp. 183-6. Dated from Locke's endorsement.
Sir
I was so concerned att not being able to explain myself on some Notions that I had onely started to a discourse, which, to excuse myself, I must say was begun by You; that whether it was onely the affection that every one has to his own, that made me fond of them; Yet rather then they should dye soe, I resolved to engage farther in their defence the next day with the same impudence that I have used you to: Butt as Good Luck would have it for you, You were gon abroad: soe I Missed the Gain of an hour or two by you, and You the Loss of as much upon mee:
Yet so far was I from learning the discretion that I mought by this; that I grew wors then before: those thoughts that were not so well satisfied with themselves, but feared their doom from you; Proud and Insolent with this repreive, thought now, of nothing less then living, and those that were clearer conscienced, and had before expected Quarter, now fell to refining upon themselves, in hopes still better to deserve it: So that here was I drawn in, and disposed of att the Caprice of these Impertinent thoughts (for to speake ingenuously I care not a Straw for either one or other of 'em, or what becomes of 'em) and for all what resistance my Matteriality could make, this troublesome immatteriality, as the distinction is that you taught me, gott the better, and I was forced to think whether I would or no: being thus att length forced to know and acknowledg the existence and much superiour force of an immatteriall part: So, finding it came upon me with such violence, I quitted hold, and lett myself be carried down in the midst of this immatteriall Stream,
― 667 ―
which mythinks I had much rather have called, this muddy one; if you would have lett one alone to ones naturall Epethites.
This here must Certainly maze you, if, as I cannot expect otherwise, You should have forgott the subject of the last discourse I had with you: therefore to recover you out of what confusion such a wild style as this may have putt you in, know the truth; that being Caught in an idle hour, and cutt of from the recours of Books, having onely this very Pen and Paper left me for my defence; I bethought myself of the Practice you have so often advised me to; and here being a very fair occasion offered, I resolved, to muster up my disorderly thoughts, and make all the Strength I Could for those Yesterday's notions that had fainted but att the apprehension of your siding against 'em, and that onely in your absence could come to something, where they might have liberty to gett to some head 'ere they were Crushed, and were not to be destroyed so still in their rise: but if after all, that was to be their fate, to perish under you; that I might have att least the honour of Yeilding with more resistance, and You of overcoming with greater opposition.
This is Enough to vindicate myself from what may appear shocking to any thing that relates to religion, by the side of the Argument I have chose to defend, which, I know, you would have me doe with Vigour: for as to my self; to make use of Monsieur Fontinell's words; Je respecte jusque aux delicatesses excessives que l'on a sur le fait de la Religion.†1
Thus farr in my letter I have lett you read without interrupting you: but, for the rest that follows, unless you are as Idle when you receive it, as I am now I write it; pray putt it up in your pockett, and doe not read it till you happen to be so; how long so ever it be till that time:.
So then, to our Argument. What ever was of matter you denyed to be any part of the Soul: and the onely part you justified to be immatteriall was Thought: Now what will thought prove when you doe not appropriate it to a body? What is it that thinks when no matteriall being does? What is Thought but the Ideas of naturall objects as they represent themselves to sensible Creatures? and if these Ideas doe not cease with the Sensibility of the Creature; why doe you attribute their originall to matter? Will you affirm that that which subsists without matter should have sprung from
― 668 ―
matter, and that that which sprung out of matter shall outlive it? Again, how is it that in distempers and obstructions in the order and motion of the matter of our bodyes, that the thinking faculty is by those obstructed: May there be a medium supposed, such a Liaison, compounded of matteriallity and immatteriallity to work these mutuall influences? or what hold els, shall plain matter have on that which has not any thing of its own Nature? Again, Does the thought fail ever as wee know the senses may? or doe wee think and not know it, feel and not know it, see and not know it? I would answer, wee doe not then feel, wee doe not then see: how then is it that wee still think: and think on you must: for you dare not allow of a suspension of the Exercise of thought for fear of destroying the onely relyance of its being.
Thus much in short: But lett us take away all matteriallity from the faculty of thinking, and all from the objects it is to work upon (for this must be, to suppose it compleatly independent from matter) and then give me an Idea of what this thought or Idea is to be. Or doe but remove a thing from us by the undiscovery of it to the sence or imagination of all living Creatures like us; Will you say an Idea shall simply rise from this real being? as thus: Before it was discovered that the Earth moved or that there were Antipodes, was there from this either thought or Idea for severall ages in the known parts of our world? Creatures dizzied have fancyed it to move, and by a wild inchoherence of rambling thought, men have been fancyed opposite as flyes on a table: but this makes no Idea of the existence of those things: for the very Ideas on which it must then be said to have been received themselves hinder the framing of such a one, and show it to be onely accidentall Clashing of Ideas that have no Just relation to one an other. In short, from a being hid from the Conceptions of all sensible Creatures (but such a one you cannott expect me to instance) there can no Idea or thought arise; for if it be inanimate, itt cannott have an Idea of its self: therefore as there is no Idea but from things substantiall; so there cannot be any from such but by the communication of them to the senses: and thus wee owe all to our sensibility: and by the measure this decreases, the other must.
Butt passing over all difficultyes, lett us suppose this independant being: Every different thought then, must be a different being: take care how you Confound it with a distinct seperate one: it must owe its duration to its self, and continue still the
― 669 ―
same thought, to continue the same being: for though in a thinking Engine the thoughts follow and drive out one an other; it cannott be supposed, that of its self thus independantly considered, one thought can pass its self into another: this would be a Metamorphosis: for it must as often as it alters Change its being and become a new one, since it derives not any being from any thing but its self: therefore when you shall have layed down such an imaginary being, there is no possibility afterwards of giving it one minutes duration.
But lett us see how by these immatterially independent beings wee are to define the Souls of Men when they have shook of matteriallity: Two thoughts that are the same when matter comes not in to distinguish, can be but one thought: for the distinction of every soul will then lye meerly on that of every thought: and if you tye the thought to nothing substantiall that thought which lives in a Million of distinct boddyes comes to be but one and the same being: so how the souls of these men doe all agree without any <demonstrable>†a distinction; and Yet differ; it requires finer immatteriality then mine to reconcile.
But to conclude with the best my Apprehension will afford me. I define thought as a Name given, not to the Power whereby animated boddyes are prepared and rendered capable of receiving the impressions of Ideas (for that Nature alone is to give an account of and how matter in some boddyes is animated and in others not) but to the Action, the Evident Workings of Exteriour objects by their Ideas on sensible Creatures, who receive them either by the immediate and forcible application of the Objects to the Senses; or More remotely and indirectly from the impressions they have left.
This depends on the naturall composition of the Brain or other essentiall parts, as it is courser or finer: for as in animated creatures, from those that are but in the first degree removed from vegitables to us that esteem our selves in the farthest, the senses multiply and grow in Vigour; So doe they, when arrived to a sufficient number and force, retain the Many Ideas they receive, and receive them afterwards by reflection: But here the imperfection of the remaining impressions, which the intervention of time has occasioned, or that originally may have been imperfect, and the Obscurity of a dubiouse Variety of these occurring representations; breed such alteration and Confusion, that there is often great difficulty
― 670 ―
and trouble ere a fixed Idea be framed in the mind: the last remaining being the subsequent Idea of the precedent ones, and formed from their concurrence: Those being Just, orderly, and full; the Generall, Comprehensive Idea that springs thence will be true, and the Nature of the thing decerted†1 in the Mind will appear as it is: Whereas if on the contrary they prove weak, deceitfull, confused, or imperfect; the Conclusive Ideas that are drawn from, and formed out of those will be defective, Corrupt, incertain, fals. Nothing is easyer then to trace home all the parts of the most puzzeling intrecate thought, and seperating every Idea, to find whence they arose and how they came thether, which when so mett make this Confusion or, if all be Clear, this Harmony, for which wee lay aside Matter, and will make a something els that demonstrably is Nothing, to be Itt, or the Cause of itt, or part of itt, —
Something to doe with it, that is: for I Protest, I know not how to define a thing that's unintelligable: My desire is to see where this immatteriallity putts in: Wee may Hear see, feel, etc: without the help of it: these Can leave their Ideas: and the impressions that according to the dulness or acuteness of the sence are received, by the same Vertue remain either in a Stronger or a Weaker degree: Now then, will it not be necessary that these remaining Ideas must often meet in that wee Call the Mind? and must it not happen often that where these impressions are in great numbers and livelyly retained, that on many occasions, two or three, or more occurr that are differently gathered of the same thing? So that a creature thus capable must waver in an uncertain beleif or apprehension of what concerns him: Now if this be thought, (as I am affraid it will be found but little more) it is so obviouse, that it would be impertinent to show it how this reighns amongst multitude of animalls whome wee can lett alone to their matteriallity: but from our Speech therefore I suppose immatteriallity will gett nothing: for if the motions these sounds express are matterially performed, I shall have nothing to defend but that noise and sound is not immatteriall.
In this I think I have not onely disproved the Existence of immatteriallity; but shown the necessary production of this that wee take for it: for certainly if Ideas are nothing els but such representations to the mind as are formed from the impressions of
― 671 ―
naturall objects upon the senses, and that the Vertue of retaining these bee allowed to the Mind without giving itt Immatteriallity; it must in the process of time gather up a numerouse Collection of these Ideas which will move in the Mind and lead in and follow one an other by their mutuall dependency; whilest the senses are not immediatly, in any manner affected, and the Exercise of them is onely in the Mind: as mechanically is demonstrated in the dreams of Us and other animals. How these Ideas are recalled into the mind either by the same objects whence they arose, or by the resemblance of some that but obliquely strike the sence, or as they are caught hold of by their near affinity to some Idea that was before in the Mind, and so fall in to the naturall series, which they too continue by bringing in their Companions or resemblances, and they theirs, and so on, till some innovating interruption happen from without; or a deficiency or obstruction within; is too Easy to need a larg Explanation and does as invisibly as the rest carry immatteriallity about it: of which I think I have said enough, and which, matterially speaking, I am sure, is Nothing, so that if your advise to me to exercize my Pen was about any thing and rather on what was slightest; If I have said all this about Nothing I think I have out done my instructions in doing greater: and should it be said I have made nothing of all this twill be so far from a Reproach to me, that, tis giving me the Bays I have fought for.†1 I long to see your Book to Enlighten me, and to know if you attempt to make something of nothing: I for my Part think I have honour enough if I make of it what it is: But in Expectation you will show me that something els in me, not matteriall, that I may have more by way of addition to Lay att your servise; I profess my self, now, as far as I can, (and till I know more of my self you will excuse me) as far, that is, as Matteriallity will Goe, Intirely Yours
A ASHLEY
Endorsed by Locke: L: Ashley Aug.89
― 672 ―
1170. Thomas Herbert, eighth earl of Pembroke, to Locke, 2/12 August [1689] (982, 1404)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 198-9. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Hague Aug: 12. S.N.
Sir
I had the satisfaction of receiving your letter, but of the number of your letters I shall never be satisfied, therfore pray let me heare from you as often as you can, all friends have the advantage of writing, but such whose Friendship with one an other is occasioned only by delighting in the same sensual pleasures, they can't take the satisfaction as others may whose very souls are fitted to unite, and I hope neither distance of Time or Place will be able to disunite you from
Your friend and servant
PEMBROKE

Sir
I can never enough acknowledge the oblidging opertunity you so kindly gave me to excuse my former neglect but you know tho I mean well I have but a very indiferent way of expressing it therefore I beceech you give me leave to deferr it till I am so happy to see you att Ivey church which I hope will be as soon as you can conveniently and I doubt not but you will pardon all that has unhappily pas'd amongst us. you know where much is forgiven you will have much love besides a great reward above. 1172. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 7 August 1689 (1163, 1178)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 256n. Printed in Ollion, pp. 188-9. Answers nos. 1158, 1163; answered by no. 1178.
(English)
Dorset Court 7 Aug.89
Vir Clarissime
Acceptis a Te duabus literis Cyprianum nostrum sine meis ad Te hinc abire pati non possum. Fructum illum benevolentiæ et amoris ex inchoatâ apud nos Tolerantiâ enasciturum una tecum spero, et brevi hoc credo fieret ut facile hominum mentes in mutuam charitatem coalescant†a nisi animi, aliquorum artificio, potius quam suâ jam sponte in diversum agerentur. Sed magna est veritas et prævalebit.†1 Nulla ego video istius de Tolerantiâ libelli apud bibliopolas nostros exemplaria, nescio an quia impeditiore jam navigatione non tam facile et libere quam olim ad nos <transferuntur>†b
― 674 ―
jam merces: Si prodeat Gallice unum ego libenter exemplar viderem. Spero te jam salutasse Legatum nostrum,†1 ei gratissimum fuisse tuum adventum certus scio, Nullos Episcopos juramentum præstitisse id omnino falsum esse. aliquos in sua sententia perseverare constat, aliquos mutare inter quos Dunelmensis†2 nuper juramentum præstitit. Sladum nostrum miror. Si huc transeat gaudebo tam bono vicino, sed videtur incertus animi. Librum Sancti Officii descriptum gaudeo spero brevi sub prælo futurum. Respublica literaria apud nos plane otiatur, omnes facti sumus politici, in hoc literarum justitio meus de Intellectu tractatus impellentibus temerè amicis sub prælo est, primum illius librum ego jam per Dominum Cyprianum ad Dominum Le Clerc transmisi.†3 Jam ad alteras tuas venio Hartsoekeri manu redditas. Gratum mihi facis quod aliquem ex amicis tuis mihi commendatum velis. raræ sunt in hoc orbis angulo occasiones quibus testari possim meum in Te tuosque animum. Plus quam tibi nemini debere possum, gratias certe habeo quam maximas, agere certe vellem. Si meâ vel operâ vel consilio opus habeat juvenis ille paratissimum me inveniet, promissi testis præsens, cum accessit Hartsoekerus, erat Cyprianus,
― 675 ―
præstiti officii erit ipse juvenis data occasione Omnes enim Tui mei sunt semperque erunt. Vale et me tui Amantissimum ut facis ama
JL
Uxorem tuam liberosque reliquosque amicos meos meo nomine salutes.
(Latin)
Dorset Court 7 Aug. 89
Distinguished Sir,
I have received two letters from you and cannot let our Cyprianus go from here without one of mine to you. I am one with you in hoping that that fruit of benevolence and love may be brought forth from the beginning of toleration that has been made with us, and I believe that it might have shortly come about that men's minds might easily be united in mutual charity, were it not that they were driven apart by the machinations of some people rather than now of their own accord. But truth is great and will prevail. I do not see any copies of that pamphlet on Toleration at our booksellers', possibly because the transport of wares to this country is not so easy and free as it was before, owing to the present interferences with navigation; if it comes out in [p. 674] French I should like to see a copy. I hope you have called on our ambassador†1 by now; I feel sure your visit will have been most welcome to him. It is certainly a mistake that no bishops have taken the oath of allegiance; it is known that some of them are persisting in their opinion, whilst others are changing their mind, among these the bishop of Durham,†2 who recently took the oath. I am wondering about our friend Sladus. If he comes over here I shall be glad of such a good neighbour, but it seems he has not made up his mind. I am glad to hear that the book of the Holy Office is transcribed and I hope that it will shortly be in the press. The commonwealth of learning here is taking a complete holiday; we have all become politicians. In this suspension of learning my own treatise on the Understanding is, owing to the hasty promptings of friends, now in the press; I have already sent the first book of it to Mr. Le Clerc by Mr. Cyprianus.†3 I come now to your other letter which was sent to me by Hartsoeker. You do me a kindness in wishing to recommend one of your friends to me; in this corner of the world I have few opportunities for giving proof of my feelings for you and yours. There is no one to whom I owe more than to you; I certainly feel the deepest gratitude, and I would as certainly wish to give expression to it. If this young man should have need of my help or advice he will find me most ready to give it; Cyprianus was a witness in person of my promise when Hartsoeker came to [p. 675] see me, and the young man himself will witness to its fulfilment as opportunity offers, for all that are yours are mine and always will be. Good-bye, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J L
Please remember me to your wife and children and to the rest of my friends.
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch by de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keijsars Gracht t'Amsterdam
1173. Mrs. Jane Stringer to Locke, 9 August [1689] (1171, 1192)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 105-6. Year from Locke's endorsement.
August the 9th
Sir
I cannot be satisfied to lett one post pass without returning you humble thanks for your transporting favour of the :3d: instant. if you could posibly have seen with what Joy I read those most oblidging expressions that gave me hopes not only of seeing you heare but allso with the same kindness friendship and charity you ever had for us, you would never suspect me wanting in the least degree of that true love honnour and esteem I Justly have for you. I bless god I have a hart full of gratitude and the most sincere desires to make all due acknowledgments for your exceeding great favours to me and mine which I dare beleeve I can never forgett but you know as well as I can tell you my great misfortune that I have neither tallent nor opertunity to make the expressions I ought tho I am sure if you could see my hart you would see somthing there that to one so generous as your self would supply all those defects. as for the occation of sending your picture (I will give you a faithfull account and hope you will not think me false tho you gave me such a caution:) Mrs Clark wrote to me for it and told me I
― 676 ―
must not ask questions but promised to return it safe again. I acquainted Mr Stringer with it and we both concluded imediately it was for your use and therefore with all chearfullness and readyness gott a frame made and with all posible care I had it well put up and by the next return of the carrier sent it to her, and if that designne had come imediately from your self it would have had the same effect only my delight and satisfaction had bin farr greater in doing it in obedience to your own commands, she must be my wittness that there was no other hessitation conditions or capitulation between us. but att her coming hither she acknowledged what we before apprehended and how earnest she was with you because of her promise to have the picture returned before she came down which both Mr Stringer and I was very much troubled to heare neither of us being willing to hasten your time or to hinder your useing it as long as you please. neither did we know the least of it nor did any thing in the least pass between us relating thereunto but what I have before acquainted you. and what discourse happed between you and her in that respect was only from her self out of extraordinary Caution because of her promise and therefore I beceech you be not Jealouss of the friendship and good intentions of your old acquaintance. you delight me much in seeming inclinable to like the place of Ivey church and country about it and untill you have other cause to suspect the owners of it I must beg your charrity not to be too severe upon them. your picture have had some experience of the place and them and I hope it hath not much reason to complain of Ill usage. when you have tryed, then you will be able to Judge whether the substance or shadow will be most wellcome. a picture can hardly be accepted for its own sake. I am of your mind that it is kindness and friendship oblidges which a picture is noe ways capable off and therefore all the good usage or concideration of a picture must be the never to be forgotten friendships and kindness of the friend it represents. Mr Stringer presents his humble serviss to you and bid me tell you that if you had any occation to try the hartyness of his affection you would find it is not the want of leggs could hinder him from crawling a thousand miles to doe you any reall serviss. I doubt this tedious epistle will quite tire you, but I hope you will most kindly prevent me troubling you with any more of this length for the future by a happy conversation without suspition or reserve as it was heretofore. I beleeve there is very much of truth in the Bishop Willkins beauty of
― 677 ―
providence†1 that sais there is noe cloud soe black but has its bright side if we can have but patience to waite for it I am sure it will appeare very splended to me when you come hither in the mean time I beg you will encourage me to hope I may be so happy. in compasion to you I will conclude
Sir
your most faithfull humble servant
J STRINGER

1174. Edward Clarke to Locke, 12 August 1689 (1167, 1313)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 6, f. 58. Printed in Rand, pp. 295-6.
Sutton-Court 12th. August 1689.
Deare Sir
My last of the 9th. from Wells being intended only to give you some Accompt of my Countrey-men's Behaviour at the Assises, I mentioned nothing therein relateing to your Private Affayres, But I write this to tell you that I mett Mr. Stratton in Wells the first day of the Assises,†2 and had a long Discourse with Him about your Businesse, and at last made an Appoyntment with Him to bee here Fryday night,†3 and to spend all Saturday in settling His Accompts, and getting in the Arreares of Rent due to you, etc: where I came accordingly, But instead of meeteing Him here, His extraordinary occasions carryed Him to Priddy-Fare,†4 which Hee hath since told mee Hee had perfectly forgott when Hee made the above mentioned appoyntment with mee: However I sent for your former Tennant Robert Harol, as thinkeing what remaines due from Him to bee the most desperate of any of the debts due to you in these parts, and have used my utmost indeavours to secure the remaineing part of it for you, wherein as in all other your Affayres here I shall more particularly informe you, when I can be soe happy as to see you next; I have this morning earnestly Pressed
― 678 ―
Mr. Stratton to the speedy performeance of severall things that I have directed Him in, which Hee promiseth shall bee done accordingly; I find there will bee some further Abatement on your Tenement at Beluton, But I sent for David Harol (the Present Tennant) and have done all that can bee with Him to keep up the value of it, and I was willing to have seen and settled Mr. Stratton's Accompts, but his Extraordinary Businesse (dureing my stay here) would not, as Hee sayes, permitt Him to doe it, but Hee will prepare it in a readinesse for your owne veiw and consideration when ever you shall please to come into this Countrey; This is all that I have to tell you at present from hence, more then that all your Old-Freinds and acquaintance in this Neighbourhood make verie Kind inquieryes after your Wellfare, and all give theire hearty services to you, as doth
Your most obleiged servant
EDW: CLARKE.

1175. George Walls to Locke, 20(?) August 1689 (1132, 1197)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 51-2. The upper margin of f. 51 (the letter) is damaged, and part of f. 52 (the cover) is torn away.
Hamburgh August 20†a . <16>89†b
Sir,
Havinge now beene with my masters <ve>rie†b neare an apprentiship†1 and out of the kingdome one whole kings reigne and parte of two others, I hope I shal not fall under your censure, if I thinke of my freedome and returninge into my owne countrie. In earnest (Sir) I am convinc'd that should I much longer pretende to keepe my hande to the plough in this hevie soyle, I should gall it to such a degree that twoulde be uncapable of anie worke hereafter; and tis come to this pointe that I must either lay down or sinke under my burthen. and to disguise nothinge from you, I have beene soe ill
― 679 ―
us'd by a faction of vitious rash men here in an indignitie offer'd me at the time of our annual Election; that I cannot with anie du regard to the dignitie of my function desire to live longer amongst um.†a And if ever I have the happines to see you, I doe not in the least question but to make it plaine that their proceedinge in reference to me has been highly unchristian consideringe both the time of their springinge their mine (when I was verie ill and under the dailie visits of my physitian) and the most dishonorable motives, all my friends here, and my own conscience tell me, they were acted by. When I entreted to know the resons of this brutish tretement (which wise men are redie to give, though masters neede not) I could obtaine no other answer but they were not oblig'd to give anie; but when they are agreed about them what they shal be, they may possibly be les reserv'd. I thought myselfe in dut<ie>†b oblig'd to give you this notice, before I quitted the place, which I designe to doe about 3 weeks hence. If there are anie of your commands to be obey'd here or in Holland, they will cheerfully be receiv'd by
Honour'd Sir
your most oblig'd humble servant
G: WALLS.

1178. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 6/16 September 1689 (1172, 1182)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 30-1. Answers no. 1172.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Literas tuas Cypriani manu mihi traditas lætus accepi. Ille nobis gratissima de statu tuo nuntiavit. Libelli illius de Tolerantia nulla hactenus in Anglia exstare exemplaria miror: Plura enim jam illuc ante aliquot hebdomadas missa bibliopola asserit; quare non dubito, quin jam apud bibliopolas vestrates reperiantur. Gallice hactenus non prodiit, nec an proditurus sit, scio; verum Belgice in officinis
― 682 ―
nostris prostat, et a pluribus maximo cum applausu legitur. Exspectarem quidem tam præstantis tractatus, decretorumque pacificorum, uberiorem fructum, nisi aliorum, qui suam rem agi putant, artificio, hominum a pace sua sponte non alienorum animi in diversum agerentur, quorum multi privatis suis commodis zelum pro gloria divina prætexunt. Strimesius gravem contra se expertus est adversarium, collegam suum Becmannum, qui Germanice stylum satis acriter contra eum strinxit. Defendit se Germanice Strimesius. Becmannus, ut eum fortius confutaret, judicia Academiarum, etiam Lutheranarum, undique conquisivit, quarum judiciis Strimesius ut Arminianus, imo Socinianus, condemnatus est: illisque munitus animosius in Strimesium insurrexit, eique plagii notam inurere voluit, quod in apologia sua plura ex Curcellæo descripserit, non tamen eum nominaverit. Res tandem ad supremum Senatum delata est, coram quo Becmannus ipsa academiarum judicia protulit, tantumque efficit, ut Strimesius omnia, tam dissertationis, quam illius apologiæ exemplaria supprimere coactus fuerit. Creditur Becmannus rem suam privatam agere, ne Strimesius Collegæ Grebenits, jam seni admodum, succedat, atque ita digniorem præ Becmanno stationem consequatur. Inde amarus ille pro religionis puritate zelus. Ita solent turbones propriæ ambitioni zelum pro
― 683 ―
gloria divina prætexere, et ne sua amittant, partes alere et factiones.†1 Ne ejusmodi hominum fraude inchoata apud vos Tolerantia sistatur, animitus precor. Legatum Angliæ†2 hactenus salutare non potui, quod doleo. Fui ego cum uxore Roterodami, inde Legati salutandi causa Hagam excurrere statueram: Verum eodem tempore Legatus Amstelodami fuit, eumque salutavit D.Clericus. Post reditum meum frater meus†3 Haga huc venit; interim feriæ nostræ elapsæ sunt. Statui tamen occasionem Legatum salutandi quærere, speroque brevi id futurum, ne honore, quem tua mihi conciliavit amicitia, culpâ meâ destituar. Literas accepi a D.Episcopo Sarisburiensi benevolentissimas,†4 in quibus plane eundem se, pacisque Ecclesiasticæ studiosissimum ostendit; damnat Episcoporum juramentum recusantium factum. Gaudeo Dunelmensem a sententia sua recessisse; illius exemplo fortasse et alii provocabuntur. Initium tui de Intellectu tractatus apud D.Clericum vidi: Utinam Latine prodeat! nam ex lectione libri in lingua mihi maximam partem
― 684 ―
ignota vix ullum possum sperare fructum, quem tamen ex illius epitome mihi maximum polliceor, si linguâ mihi notâ prodeat. Librum Sancti Officii jam relego, et apographum cum autographo accurate confero; verum quoniam ad id alterius etiam opera indigeo, illeque sæpe horis mihi commodissimis adesse non potest, paulo tardius procedit: Brevi tamen me ad finem libri perventurum spero. Verum Wetstenii frater,†1 qui nunc in Helvetiam abiit, edendi impetum omni studio sufflaminare conatur. Scripsit nuper Basilea, nobilem Anglum, nomine Waller,†2 volumen hoc Helvetiis obtulisse, ipsos autem modeste recusasse, quoniam tutius Batavis offerri posset: porro ipsos editionem dissuadere, et de distractione desperare, nisi historia†3 Inquisitionis illi præfixa totum volumen commendet: In Gallia vero jam ejusmodi historiam paratam esse.†4 Hic Wetstenius†5 aliquatenus hæret, incertus quid acturus. Ego interim sylvam mihi paro, unde Inquisitionis historia contexi possit. Verum plures mihi deësse libros comperio, unde aliquid lucis spero: Nollem enim, si quid scribam, minus accuratam historiam edi.
― 685 ―
Sladus noster post diuturnos errores tandem Brielam pervenit in Angliam trajecturus si incidat in jucundos comites. Fortasse ergo eum brevi videbis, cum literis meis jam ante tres menses scriptis.†1 Benevolentiam quam Hartsoekero exhibuisti mihi præstitam agnosco, semperque gratum me ac memorem ostendam. Ipse jam suis ad fratres literis ingentem tuam benevolentiam deprædicavit: ruri nunc degit, ut fœlicius linguam vestram addiscat, mox, ubi illam addidicit, Londinum reversurus. Soror ejus, quæ nunc in ædibus meis est, pro præstito fratri suo officio maximas Tibi gratias agit, Teque officiosissime salutat. Uxor D. de Wilde filia D. Venii natu major heri filiam peperit. Exspecto literas a D. Guenellon quas hisce includam.†2 Uxor liberique plurimam Tibi dicunt salutem. Vale Vir Amplissime, et, ut facis, ama
Tui Amantissimum
P. A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 16 Septembris
inline image
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I was glad to get your letter, which you sent to me by Cyprianus. He gave us very satisfactory news about yourself. I am surprised that no copies of that pamphlet on Toleration are so far to be had in England; the bookseller states that a number of them had already been sent thither some weeks ago; so I have no doubt that they are now to be found with your booksellers. The French translation has not appeared so far, nor do I know whether it will; but the Dutch is on sale in our shops and is being read by [p. 682] many people with great approval. I should indeed have expected that such an outstanding treatise and the pacific ordinances would have borne more abundant fruit; the truth is, however, that the minds of people who are not of themselves averse from peace are perverted by the devices of others who think it concerns them, many of them using zeal for the glory of God as a pretext for the advancement of their own interests. Strimesius has met with a formidable adversary, his colleague Becmann, who took up the pen against him virulently enough in German. Strimesius defended himself in the same language. Becmann, in order to confute him more decisively, collected the opinions of universities, including the Lutheran, from all parts, by whose verdict Strimesius was condemmed as an Arminian, indeed a Socinian; thus armed he attacked Strimesius with still greater animosity, seeking to brand him with plagiarism on the ground that in his Apology he had copied some remarks of Curcellaeus, but without naming him. The case was finally brought to the supreme senate, before which Becmann produced word for word the opinions of the universities, with such effect that Strimesius was compelled to suppress all copies as well of the dissertation as of the apology. Becmann is thought to be feathering his own nest, seeking, that is, to prevent Strimesius succeeding his colleague Grebenitz, who is now well on in years, and so securing a more honourable position than himself. Hence this bitter zeal for the purity of religion. Such is the way of mischief-makers, who pretend zeal for the glory of God as a screen for their private ambitions, [p. 683] and who encourage parties and factions in order not to lose what they themselves hold.†1 I heartily pray that toleration, now that it has made a beginning among you, may not be checked by the trickery of such persons. I have not so far been able to pay my respects to the English Ambassador,†2 for which I am sorry. I was at Rotterdam with my wife; I had determined to make the journey from there to The Hague in order to call on the ambassador but he was at that time in Amsterdam, where Mr. Le Clerc called on him. After my return my brother†3 came here from The Hague; meanwhile our holidays have run out. I am determined, however, to seek an opportunity of calling on the ambassador, and I hope it will be soon; for I should not wish to be deprived by any fault of my own of the honour which your friendship has put within my reach. I received a very kind letter from the bishop of Salisbury,†4 in which he clearly showed himself the same as ever and deeply concerned for peace in the Church; he condemns the action of those bishops who refuse the oath. I am glad that the bishop of Durham has reconsidered his opinion; perhaps others too will be moved by his example. I saw the beginning of your treatise on the Understanding at Mr. Le Clerc's; if only it would come out in Latin! for I can hardly hope to get any profit from reading a book in a language for the most part unknown to me; I [p. 684] promise myself a great deal, however, from the epitome of it, if it should appear in a language that I know. I am at present going over the book of the Holy Office again and carefully comparing the copy with the original; but I need the help of another man in this work, and since he is often unable to be with me at my most convenient hours, it proceeds rather slowly; I hope, however, that I shall soon reach the end of the book. But Wetstein's brother,†1 who has now gone to Switzerland, is trying his hardest to restrain my haste for publication. He wrote recently from Basle to say that an English nobleman of the name of Waller†2 had offered this book to the Swiss, but that they had discreetly refused it, on the ground that it might be safer to offer it to the Dutch; moreover, he said, they advised against publication and had little hope of a sale for it unless it were prefaced by an account†3 of the Inquisition which might recommend the book as a whole to readers; there was in fact already such a history available in France.†4 Wetstein†5 accordingly finds himself in a difficulty and is not sure how to proceed. I meanwhile am collecting material from which to put together such a history; but I find that I am in want of a number of books from which I hope to get some light on the matter; for I should not wish any published work of mine [p. 685] to be historically inaccurate. Our friend Sladus after protracted wanderings has at last reached the Brill, meaning to cross to England if he should fall in with pleasant company. Perhaps then you will see him soon together with a letter of mine, which was written three months ago.†1 The kindness you have shown to Hartsoeker I acknowledge as shown to myself, and I shall always remember it with gratitude. He himself in his letter to his brothers is full of praise for your very great kindness; he is now spending some time in the country in order to have a better chance of learning your language; after that, when he has mastered it, he means to return to London. His sister, who is now in my house, thanks you most heartily for your services to her brother and sends you her best respects. Mr. de Wilde's wife, the elder daughter of Mr. Veen, yesterday gave birth to a daughter. I am expecting a letter of Mr. Guenellon's to enclose with this of mine.†2 My wife and children send you their warmest greetings. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and keep me in your affections.
Your most affectionate
P. VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 16 September
1689

1179. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 6/16 September 1689 (1161, 1212)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 16-17.
Monsieur
Nous avons receu vostre agreable du 7 aoust avec la copie de la premiere partie de vostre ouvrage. je lay rendue d'abord a Monsieur le clerq qui l'a donné a un amis pour essayer de le traduire en latin.†1 comme cela sera tres utile pour le public je n'ay point voulu donner occasion en le retenant chez moy que cela fut delayé esperant de le lire apres. j'espere que vous aurez receu la boitte que nous vous avons envoyé ayant nouvelle que le vaisseau est arrivé a Londres. je nay point de nouvelle de Monsieur Charleton. depuis que Monsieur Daranda luy a rendu quelque Medailles dont je l'avois chargé, je vous supplie de luy faire mes compliments et de luy dire que je guette l'occasion de luy envoyer quelque chose de meilleur. Mon beau pere vous prie de nous de†a mander si vous cognoissez certain remede appellé terra hibernica†2 et a quoy elle est utile. Si on sen sert pour les flux de ventre. Monsieur Sladus part effectivement pour vos quartiers estant desja a la briel n'attendant que le vent pour partir. Nostre oncle arminius†3 apres quelques acces de fievre tierce continue est mort inopinement en defaillence dans l'acces. Monsieur Visscher se marie a une vielle de cinquante ans las et soulé des plaisirs de la vie. Ma seur de Wilde accoucha hier au soir d'une fille. et se porte bien pour l'estat ou elle est. jay receu la septmaine passée un pacquet de Monsieur furley. Je ne scay sil est encore a Londres. je payeray l'argent quil a deboursé ou il le commendera. autrement il pouroit se faire payer du tuteur de Monsieur thomas†4 qui demeure chez Monsieur pieter adriaensch, qui me doibt quarante florins pour un college†5 quil a frequenté chez moy cet hyver. Monsieur le clerq ma prié de vous saluer de sa part et quil se donn<era>†b l'honneur de vous escrire en bref. nous sommes icy presentement accablé d'une fievre Epidemique tierce
― 687 ―
et double tierce continue. dont la pluspart rechapent facilement apres des seignées iterees dans le commencement et l'usage de petits lavements, sans donner dans les purges qui en ont fait crever plusieurs. Ma femme vous presente ses tres humbles respects, et se porte mieux quelle navoit fait depuis longtemps. son fils†1 profite tousjours et j'espere quil sera bien tost en estat de vous escrire une lettre de remerciement sur tout ce que vous doibt. je ne vous mande point de nouvelles puisque estant toutes tres bonnes elles seront sans doubtes desja publiques chez vous. Toute la famille vous presente ses tres humbles respects et je suis comme je le doibs
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur

(English) Vir Clarissime
Consessâ inter nos aliquali indulgentiâ nondum tamen plane componitur animorum partiumque dissentio, etiamsi pacatius multo et modestius concessâ libertate se gesserint dissentientes quam expectaveram. De comprehensione jam aliquid sub incude est, ut proximo parlamenti consessui, quem brevi futurum credo, paratum offeratur.†1 quid hoc si obtineat effecturum sit nondum mihi perspectum est, nec eo modo pacem ecclesiasticam stabilitum iri sperare possum. dissentient semper inter se de religione homines et inter se lites bellumque agent partes nisi æquâ omnibus constitutâ libertate mutuæ charitatis vinculum quo omnes in unum corpus colligantur. Arma Schombergi†2 in Hibernia prospere satis promoventur. nec favente numine dubitatur successus. in Republicâ literariâ parum aut nihil agitur omnibus in politicam intentis. Quid
― 690 ―
prælum apud vos producit alicujus momenti scire cupio, sed magis quomodo Tu Tuique valetis. Expectamus hic jam quotidie reditum Comitis Pembrokiæ. Si hæ literæ satis maturè ad te perferrantur adeo ut optimæ Teæ libram integram vel dimidiam emere possis et Roterodamum ad famulum Furlei transmittere ante decessum Comitis Pembrokiæ, emas rogo. mihi inscribatur pixis. moneaturque famulus Furlei ut Pixidem illam summâ curâ Domino Barker Comitis secretario commendet. Optimam Team velim etiamsi constiterit libra quadraginta florenos. festinatione solum opus est ut sub tutelâ legati ad nos importetur, dubito enim an aliàs hoc permissum fuerit. Scio te hujus herbæ peritissimum Emptorem uti fuisti disertissimum Laudatorem. Vides qua libertate ego tuâ utor operâ, gratissimum mihi foret si potuero reddere vices, nec de meâ voluntate dubitare potes fac solum periculum. Vellem etiam ut una cum Tea ista Wetstenius mihi mittat Acta Eruditorum Anni 1687. Et duo Exemplaria eorundem actorum anni 1688.†1 Hæc tria exemplaria Actorum Erudit: incompacta, et alios libellos quos per†a dominum Le Clerc a Wetstenio quæsiverim, si Barkero nondum tradita sint, velim simul mittat cum Tea (si bonam inveneris
― 691 ―
veneris et sapidissimam) ad Furlei ædes ut cum supellectile Pembrokianâ transmittantur. Optimam tuam uxorem reliquosque tuos meosque meo nomine rogo salutes Vale et me ama

(Latin) Distinguished Sir,
The settlement of a certain measure of indulgence among us does not yet, however, result in a complete settlement of the differences between minds and parties, though with the granting of liberty those who differ from each other have been conducting themselves much more peaceably and moderately than I had expected. In the matter of comprehension there is already something on the anvil; the intention is that it should be submitted to the next session of parliament, which I believe will be soon.†1 What this measure is likely to effect, should it come into force, is not yet clear to me, nor can I feel any hope that ecclesiastical peace will be established in that way. Men will always differ on religious questions and rival parties will continue to quarrel and wage war on each other unless the establishment of equal liberty for all provides a bond of mutual charity by which all may be brought together into one body. Schomberg's†2 campaign in Ireland is going forward well enough, and if God wills there can be little doubt of its success. In the commonwealth of learning there is little or nothing going on, as everyone's [p. 690] attention is directed to politics. I desire to hear what the press is producing with you of any importance, but more to know how you and yours are. Here we expect the earl of Pembroke's return daily. If this letter should reach you in time to permit of your buying a whole or half-pound of the best tea and sending it to Furly's servant at Rotterdam before the earl's departure, please do so. The box should be addressed to me, and Furly's servant should be told to take particular care to entrust it to Mr. Barker, the earl's secretary. I should like the best tea, even if it should cost forty gulden a pound. The only thing is to be quick about it, so that it may be brought into this country under the ambassador's protection, as I doubt if this would otherwise be permitted. I know you are a most experienced buyer of this herb, just as you have been its most eloquent panegyrist. You see how freely I make use of your services; nothing would please me more than to be able to do as much for you, nor can you doubt my willingness; only try me! I should also be glad if along with that tea Wetstein would send me the Acta Eruditorum of the year 1687 and two copies of the same Acta of 1688,†1 these three copies of the Acta unbound, also the other pamphlets that I ordered from him through Mr. Le Clerc. If these have not yet been handed over to Barker, would he please send them together with the tea (if you [p. 691] have found a good and tasty kind) to Furly's house, so that they may be sent across with the earl's furniture. Please remember me to your wife and to the rest of your friends and mine. Good-bye, and love me
Your most affectionate JL
(Latin) The Epistola de Tolerantia has now been translated into English.†1 Please send me the French and Dutch translations, for many people here approve of what is advocated in it. All this at a rush and with too hurried a pen; but you will forgive me. I may be robbed of the necessary time for writing, but the spirit I write in can never change.
(Latin) Lord Dursley†2 is leaving this very day as successor to the earl of Pembroke; he will have another style at The Hague. He is also my friend and former pupil. As soon as he lands the earl will depart.
(Latin) I am surprised at the remissness of the booksellers, yours or ours. I cannot find the Epistola de Tolerantia and Strimesius's De Pace Ecclesiastica on sale anywhere here.

(English) Amplissime Vir
Meas 16 hujus mensis scriptas, cum inclusis D. Guenelloni, recte ad manus tuas pervenisse nullus dubito. Exinde 22°. ejusdem dië

Hagam D. Comitem Pembrokiæ videndi causa profectus sum: postridie aulam adii, Secretarium Barkerum conveni: Verum ob valetudinem D. Legati minus prosperam non nisi post triduum ad alloquium Excellentiæ suæ admitti potui. Interea amicitiam mecum contraxit Comiti in hac legatione a Sacris D. Barford,†1 vir sane eruditus ac humanissimus, qui me dië Lunæ, vid. 26 Septembris, ad Dominum suum introduxit. Benignissime exceptus fui, et licet valetudo vix ferre videretur serium sermonem, ultra horam tamen Dominus Comes mecum eruditissime disseruit, paucisque, sed significantissimis verbis, mihi explicuit subtilissimum suum conceptum, quo omnes disciplinas et artes ex Mathesi et principiis naturæ primis ac simplicissimis deducit.†2 Miror in Viro tanto, et tam illustri natalium splendore, tam assiduas et profundas meditationes, tam distinctas rerum ideas, et in ætate florente tam maturum, etiam de rebus intricatioribus ac perplexis, quæ senum, etiam in ista palæstra per omnem vitam exercitatorum ingenia fatigant, judicium, et sermonem adeo perspicuum et distinctum. Ego novo hoc beneficio denuo Tibi obstrictus sum, quod mihi ad tantum Virum aditum præparaveris, qui me et benignissime excepit,
― 694 ―
et humanissime dimisit, cujusque humanitatis et eruditionis nunquam obliviscar, dum spiritus hos reget artus.†1 Illud Tibi certo affirmare possim, nunquam, quousque mea fert memoria, huc appulisse Legatum a quocunque rege aut Republica cujus tam consentientibus omnium cujuscunque conditionis elogiis deprædicentur virtutes. Utinam egregium illud opus, quod jam magnam partem confecit, porro perficiat et in lucem edat!†2 Quantum exinde utilitatis totus quaquaversum patet orbis percipere posset, nemo rectius quam Tu novit. Tractatus tui de intellectu humano Verrini nostri frater natu minimus versionem Latinam inchoavit, et, teste D.Clerico, satis feliciter succedit: Itaque et illum Latine videbimus.†3 Negotium pacis Ecclesiæ spero proxima Parlamenti sessione feliciter perficiendum. Quid enim sperare nocet? Tolerantia, qua multorum animi pacatiores sunt redditi, eosdem porro disponet, ut æquas conditiones non respuant: æquas voco ejusmodi, quas Ecclesia Conformistarum, si non-Conformistarum loco esset, sibi offerri vellet: easdem itaque ut illa jam Non-Conformistis offerat, naturæ lex dictat. Et si tales offerantur conditiones, non dubitandum quin omnes, saltem quorum animus dissidia horret, Ecclesiâ
― 695 ―
adeo Christianâ comprehendi velint, et pacem respuentium numerus, utpote postulantium quod ipsi concessuri non essent, sensim sit imminuendus. Ego ad Rev. D.Episcopum Salisburiensem, qui de hoc argumento ad me scripsit, cujusque suffragium in hoc negotio valet, literas dedi, quibus illud paulo latius diduco. Dië martis†1 domum reversus gratissimas tuas accepi, pridie allatas; mox quæsivi Theam, si qua reperiri posset, præstantiorem, et, meo judicio, satis feliciter successit, nam et odore et sapore se mihi valde commendat. Est alterius generis Thea, multis maxime in deliciis, quam vulgo Cæsaream vocant,†2 foliis majoribus et laxioribus; verum eam Te non quærere, exinde collegi, quod ea Londini in officina Mrs. Ferguson venalis sit: ego hanc simul cum Thea ipsa cæsareâ bibi, ut quæ se mihi maxime probaret explorarem: Verum et odore et sapore mihi hæc præferenda videbatur: tum†a- et ingens est inter utriusque Theæ pretium discrimen: cæsareæ quippe libra valet 48 florenis nostratibus; hæc verum solummodo 28 florenis. An hæc generosa illa Thea sit, tam magnifice a Virgilio decantata,†1 Tu videris. (Latin) Excellent Sir,
My letter of the 16th of this month, with Dr. Guenellon's enclosed, has no doubt reached you safely. Shortly after that, on the 22nd, I set out for The [p. 693] Hague with the intention of seeing the earl of Pembroke; on the following day I called at his residence and met the secretary, Mr. Barker; but as the ambassador was somewhat unwell it was not till three days later that I was able to have speech with His Excellency. Meanwhile I made the friendly acquaintance of Mr. Barford,†1 chaplain to the earl on this embassy, a very scholarly and obliging man, who introduced me to his chief on Monday 26 September. I was most kindly received, and although his health seemed scarcely to admit of serious talk, nevertheless the earl conversed most learnedly with me for more than an hour; he explained to me, briefly but clearly, a very ingenious theory of his own, according to which he derives all sciences and arts from mathematics and from the first and simplest principles of nature.†2 I admire such diligent and deep reflection and such clarity of ideas in a man of his eminence and distinction of birth; and I am astonished that one who is still young should display such maturity of judgement, and that too in intricate and involved matters, over which older men, even those who have spent a lifetime in those particular studies, are wont to cudgel their brains; I am struck, too, by the lucidity and precision with which he expresses himself. I am indebted to you anew for the fresh benefit you have conferred on me in providing me with access to so great a man, who received me most graciously and dismissed me most courteously, [p. 694] and whose kindness and scholarship I shall never forget 'while breath shall rule this frame'.†1 Of this I can certainly assure you: never, so far as I can remember, has an envoy from any prince or state come hither whose high qualities have won such universal praise from people of all classes. May he in due course carry through and give to the light that admirable work which he has already in great part completed.†2 What great profit may result from it for the whole wide world no one knows better than yourself. Our friend Verrijn's youngest brother has begun a Latin translation of your treatise on the human understanding, and according to Mr. Le Clerc it is proceeding well; so we are to see that too in Latin.†3 I hope that the business of Church peace will be happily carried through in the next session of parliament. What harm is there in hoping? Toleration, which has made the minds of many people more inclined to peace, will in due course dispose them not to reject fair terms; and by fair I mean such as the Conformist Church, if it were in the place of the Nonconformists, would wish to have offered to itself; the law of nature therefore prescribes that it should now offer the same terms to them. And if such terms are offered there can be no doubt that all, at least those who have a horror of schism, will be willing to [p. 695] be embraced in so Christian a Church, and that the number of those who reject peace, as demanding what they would not themselves be prepared to concede, will gradually diminish. I have written on this matter in somewhat greater detail to the reverend the bishop of Salisbury, who had written to me on the same subject, and whose voice is of weight in this business. On returning home on Tuesday†1 I found your welcome letter, which had been delivered the previous day; I set out forthwith in search of a superior kind of tea, if such could be found anywhere, and in my own opinion I was quite successful, for I am thoroughly pleased with both its bouquet and its flavour. There is another kind of tea, greatly relished by many people, which is commonly called the Imperial,†2 with larger and looser leaves; but I gathered that you did not want that sort, as it is on sale in London at Mrs. Ferguson's shop. I drank some of the new kind at the same time as some Imperial, to see which I preferred; and in fact it seemed better to me both in bouquet and flavour. There is also a considerable difference between the prices of the two; a pound of the Imperial is valued at 48 of our gulden, but this other kind at only 28. The box costs 1 gulden 8 stivers. If the earl's departure had not been so hastened I would have waited until some ships which are expected here soon had come to port, in the hope that they might have brought us a more excellent kind of tea. But it is not certain when [p. 696] they will be here; and I found everything at The Hague so set for departure that they are only waiting for the ships which are to bring the earl's successor here. So I was obliged to hurry. Whether this is that excellent tea which Virgil celebrates so magnificently†1 I must leave you to judge. I went to Wetstein's shop, but was not able to see him, as his time is entirely taken up with managing the auction of Savouret's books,†2 the widow requiring his help; so I left word for an assistant to bring these Acta Eruditorum to my house. I did not mention your name; for it is all one whether they are put down to your account or mine; for they are sold at a fixed price, namely three gulden for each year's Acta, or 5 stivers for each monthly part.
(Latin) In the matter of learning there is nothing of great importance being done here at the moment, so far as I know; it seems that amid the clash of arms there is a lull in scholarship. Please look at the covers of the Acta Eruditorum; from them you will see that a notable work is still in the press.†3 I say this to refresh your memory of that work. I suppose copies of the Epistola de Tolerantia and of Strimesius's dissertation are now on sale in London; if they are not yet available I shall not cease to put pressure on Waesberge†4 until you write to tell me that they are on sale there. Here is a copy of the Dutch translation; [p. 697] the French is not yet printed, and I am not sure whether it is to be. We are all so far in excellent health, as are all Mr. Veen's family; there has only been the death of Mr. Arminius. As for Sladus, I do not know whether he has sailed for England or is still sticking somewhere in Holland. I am glad to learn that you have been appointed to a post of some kind, not too laborious, but honourable and sufficiently well paid; for its duties will not call you away from your studies to any extent.†1 I pray that you may fulfil those duties with honour, so long as it may please you to do so, and with the approbation of all good men. Our Visschertje†2 is betrothed; he is now teaching my daughter the art of painting; he sends you his greetings and wishes you the same condition, should you desire it. For my part I believe your wishes are very different from his. My wife and children, but especially my son, send you their warmest greetings. I pray that all may go well with you. Good-bye, best of men, and keep in your affections
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 30 September
1689

1185. Mrs. Elinor Hawkshaw to Locke, 23 September [1689] (1177, 1199)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, f. 167. Year from Locke's endorsement.
the 23d of September
dear Sir
I receve in every Letter new testimony of your kindnesse and freindship both to me and my sons, How poore doth an acknowledgment look, sinc tis all I can return you for your concern for me, tis but fitt I give you this account that by your Help I have sent my younger son to Oxford, for tho: I had not your mony which you lent me yett my Credit accommadated him for the Journey till it Came. the Elder waites for, Irelands Peac and I hope I shall not Long burthen my best of freinds, as I have found you, Good mr Lock write a pressing Letter to mr Cox at the Bell in Glocster, the post Calls and I must end but neve from being your
Obliged faithfull freind ELENOR HAWKSHAW

1187. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 27 September/7 October 1689 (1184, 1213)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 34-5. Apparently sent with no. 1184. Answered by no. 1213.
(English) Amplissime Vir
Cum intelligam Comitem Pembrokiensem nondum hac hebdomade discessurum, hasce prioribus meis adjungere consultum duxi. Denuo conveni Waesbergium; ait ille, se ante duos circiter menses centum exemplaria utriusque tractatus, Epistolæ vid: de Tolerantia, et dissertationis Strimesianæ, misisse Londinum ad bibliopolam Samuëlem Smith; itaque non dubitare, quin in illius officina nunc prostent; quoniam navis, quæ exemplaria illa hinc avexit, diu
― 700 ―
in Angliam appulit. Legi in novellis nostratibus, Magistrum Kidder electum esse Decanum Petroburgensem. Degit Londini quidam Richardus Kidder, vir eruditus, qui nuper ad me misit tractatum Anglicum a se editum, hoc titulo. A Demonstration of the Messias, anno 1684. Velim ex Te scire, an hic sit electus Decanus Petroburgensis.†1 Credidi literas D. Slado ad ipsum, inclusas puto literis ad D.Allix:†2 sed quoniam D.Sladus diu in patria nostra oberravit, alteras ad ipsum dedi, quas an jam acceperit ignoro. Jam mensis est, quod Brielam venerit Sladus, exinde nihil de ipso audivimus; quare jam tecum quin sit, vix dubitamus. Si D. Sladus D.Allix, aut D. Kidder videat, facile resciri poterit, an ipse sit decanus, et qua ratione literæ ad ipsum sint dirigendæ. Hoc enim valde molestum est, amicos efflagitare literas, et tamen non indicare aut locum domicilii, aut alia, quibus præcaveri possit ne literæ aberrent. D. Clericus, qui plurimum Te salvere jussit, monet, tractatus tui de Intellectu humano versionem pulchre procedere, monetque, ut, quæ deinceps impressa sunt, prima occasione mittas, ut dum sub prælo est tractatus versio ejus adornari possit. Ubi ad finem perducta
― 701 ―
erit, Tibi mittendam credo, ut relegas, et si quid non satis recte versum fuerit, aut mentem tuam non plene aut clare expresserit, emendes. Autumnus Medicorum messis est, quare hoc mense Collegium continuari nequit; aliis enim remediis quam Thea febres expugnandæ sunt, quæ ubi frequentiores sunt assiduam medicorum vigilantiam requirunt, et in magna hac civitate ipsis vix ullam concedunt requiem. Omnes Te quam amantissime salutant. Salutat Te uxor et liberi, imprimis ego
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH.
Amstelodami 7 Octobris
inline image
Veloci calamo.
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
As I understand that the earl of Pembroke does not yet sail this week I have thought it well to add these lines to my previous letter. I have seen Waesberge again; he says that he sent a hundred copies of both treatises, the Epistola de Tolerantia and Strimesius's dissertation, to the bookseller Samuel Smith in London about two months ago; he therefore feels sure that they are now on sale in Smith's shop, since the ship which carried them from here reached [p. 700] England some time ago. I read in our newspaper that a Mr. Kidder has been selected as dean of Peterborough. There is a certain Richard Kidder living in London, a scholarly man, who recently sent me a treatise in English published by himself with the title A Demonstration of the Messias, dated 1684. I should like to know from you whether it is he who has been selected as dean of Peterborough.†1 I entrusted Mr. Sladus with a letter to him, enclosed, I think, in one to Mr. Allix;†2 but as Mr. Sladus has been wandering about in our country for a long time I have written him another, which I do not know whether he has received by now. It is already a month since Sladus got to the Brill, after which we have heard nothing more of him; so we can hardly doubt that he is with you by now. If he sees Mr. Allix or Mr. Kidder he will easily ascertain whether that gentleman is the dean and how letters should be addressed to him. It is really most annoying that one's friends should keep asking for letters and yet give one no information either about their place of residence or other details which might help to prevent letters going astray. Mr. Le Clerc, who sends you his best wishes, tells me that the translation of your treatise on the Human Understanding is proceeding well; he also advises that you take the first opportunity to send him what is subsequently printed, so that the translation may be got ready whilst the treatise is in the press. When the translation is finished I think it should be [p. 701] sent to you, so that you may look over it and correct it if it is not sufficiently accurate in any respect, or if it has failed to express your meaning fully and clearly. Autumn is the doctor's harvest, so the Collegie cannot go on during this month; other remedies than tea are needed to combat the fevers; when these are more prevalent they require the constant vigilance of the doctors, allowing them hardly any rest in this big city. All here send you their most affectionate greetings, as do my wife and children, and especially myself,
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 7 October
1689
In haste
Address: For Doctor John Locke At London.

The Hurry of my departure and that which wee have been in since our Arrivall has hindred mee from acknowledging your Exceeding Civility to one who has had soe little the happynesse to deserve any thing from you, otherwise then by the Infinite Esteeme hee has allwaies had for your Extraordinary merit. 1192. Mrs. Jane Stringer to Locke, 5 [October 1689] (1173, 2829)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, ff. 107-8. Date: the letter answers a belated answer to no. 1173 of 9 August. Locke answered no. 1173 on 19 September: endorsement. The postmark for the present letter gives the month, and Locke's endorsement the year.
Sept: 5th:
Sir
I am very sory to find by your Last letter as well as your slow return. that you are so coldly disposed to a pure firm and lasting friendship. which I doubt not but you beleeve I was enough concernd for. tho I could but wish it in my power to give you any testimony of reall serviss. I hoped you had so much charity to beleeve me sincere and faithfull in my professions att least that I much desire to be soe. I confess a country peasant that makes Adress to a courtier is liable to be suspected of some mercinary designes but I hope I am not so much deceived in my self as to be one of that number tho I must own I am sencible of the advantage and pleasure of having you for my friend. if I can pretend to know my self att all (which I am told is a hard lesson to learn) my cheef
― 706 ―
motive was the remembrance of my obligations to you and the hopes I had that this might be an Easy healthy retireing place for you. but if you canot free your self from malincholly sordid apprehentions of us and be again possesed of that love and charity you had heretofore so as to bare with many failings and infirmitys. my hopes are deferred which Sollomon sais makes the hart sick. but if I can perswaid my self that I am of the number of those that all shall work for good to I am sure to be happy att my Journeys end tho many things hapen in the way which perhaps I should not choose. I doubt not but that sickness and all other afflictions may and ought to be improved to our advantage. those most Excellent treatisses (which you translated part of to such advantage for our church)†1 teaches the way so charmingly that I canot be without very good resollutions when I read them I owe so much of the happy ness of my life to them that I cannot express it. the treatise of mans weakness I am much pleased with because it sais tis posible that the best philosopher and wisest may have some failing.†2 I can asure you tis a consolation to the weak and Ignorant who might otherwise be too much dejected. I am very sorry you have any scruple remaining.†a you know I canot express my self fuller than I did.†b I humbly thank you for your great favour of enquiring so kindly affter our son†3 I can asure you he offten makes very honourable mention of you. about three dayes before I received your last I sent him a tooth pick (to cure his toothach) made of the wound wood†4 you recomended to Mrs Clark and sent him word it came from you as a remedy for that pain he answered imediatly if it came from you he was sure it would doe him good and according to the strength of his fancy and faith in you together with the vertue of the wood it gives him ease in a short time affter he uses it I have not
― 707 ―
seen him since but when I doe I shall delight him when he sees how you have honoured him with your kind remembrance he will be very proud of it I am sure for on all occations when his curiosity leads him to enquire into any dificultys that he canot be resolved he sais he is sure if Mr Lock were here he could give a good account of it thus he makes you amends as well as he can for giving him that title the Governour of Bexwells. Lord Ashly did us the honour to dine with us yesterday he seems worthy of all the praise you have or can give him I hope he will be blessd with a continuall increase of those admirable vertues that apear in him now. my thinks his discourse is very eddifying as well as delightfull sure if he gose on and improves as he has hitherto done there is all the reason that can be to hope he will be an extrordinary good and wise man Mr Stringer presents his humble servis and thanks to you and sais he shall not be wanting to doe him all faithfull serviss in his power. I fear you I think its high time to conclude
Sir
your oblidged and faithfull Servant
J STRINGER
if I had morgans witt I would not have sent you so dull a sermon

1195. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 11 October [1689] (1169, 1203)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 87-8. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Ivey Church Oct: the 11th:
Was not my Buisness in the Country brought to an End: What a surprising question, think Yee, was this to a Man that had heard almost this Month no other hardly, but; when will all his buisness in Town bee ended? or, what buisness has he there still? You did well to prevent me by following it immediatly with a wonder not; 'Twas spoke as if you had foreseen my disposition from such a distance of time as when you last saw me; or that you looked into me att the same time from the Place where you are. truly, since I am brought to my self; I beginn to reflect how very seasnably this Question came: if it had come but a little later, it might have been so far, for ought I know, from working the Effect that I find it has since, on mee; that not the Consideration of Who asked it would perhaps have wakened mee, or have made me sensible of what it meant; such a Lethergy was I falling into: But what are You, for heavens sake, that can in such a manner discover, and soe instantly and unaccountably Cure such a distemper? Convince others by your Writings that you know the Growth, the Motions and the distempers of the mind: I, for my Part, by this Experience shall stedfastly hold, that that part of man is better Known to You, then ever the Body has been to our Professours of Anotomy or Physick; or Els you must have some very strang and peculiar ascendant over mee: however it be, I Cannot choose but say as much as a morrall Poet did to one whome he owns such obligations to, as I have had to You:
Nescio quid certe est, quod me tibi temperat Astrum ...†1
for Certainly never was greater power in words: with one single Question to transform a Country Gentleman! and when I Consider too (as in this time that I was one of 'em I found) what tough, unplyable matter they are made of, and of how unalterable a shape
― 710 ―
and nature: 'tis but now to make a Courtier of mee and the Miracle is perfected; and it must be owned they Cease to Cease
All this while I should have told You how Mrs Stringer and I have been making the most of what You lett us have of you:
You have a better opinion of me then to think I would ask the sight of hers for the giving her the sight of mine: that had been unpardonable in a Man that had never been in France: but by way of return she would obleidge me with more varyety of what I take such pleasure in. But what Confusion doe you think I suffered when I found my self there, and Valued so much above my Worth? My Conscience began to accuse me of a Crime till then Unknown to me, and I Exclaimed att you within my self for having been able to Corrupt my long retained Humility with such poysenouse praises as my Ears were proof against till they Came through your mouth. Mythought it must have appeared like a premeditated device of mine to have boasted what my modesty should have made me kept within me though ever so full of it: and to see what Guilt is (for I will own to you I am tainted) after I had told Mrs Stringer that it was the Common practise of You Men of Witt to Choose allways the meanest subjects to Exercise your Witts upon, either in defending and Commending and all that, with more to that purpose to bring my self off; I was forced to <tell>†a her that I dared not say this to your Face and desired her not to inform against me for fear of drawing you down upon me with greater fury: and this I imagined would look but like an indirect cours towards the procuring to my self more praise; which would be Yett much wors then the divulging of what I had gott honestly and without Circumvention.
I would tell you of other of our entertainments here about you and some of a More seriouse Nature with Mr Stringer but for reasons you shall shortly know I would not Committ them but by word of Mouth.
He gives his Humble service to you as well as Mrs Stringer. My Time now Calls me and I think I need not say my Paper. Intirely Yours
A ASHLEY
Endorsed by Locke: L: Ashley 11 Oct. 89

1196. —— Passebon to Locke, 22 October 1689 (1232)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 192-3. I cannot identify the writer.
Monsieur,
Si javois suivy mon inclination, jaurois eu l'honneur de vous écrire souvent: mais jay pensé que le moindre de vos momens estant precieus je devois le menager, jusques a ce que j'eusse a vous informer du progrés que Mr Clarke auroit fait. J'ay laissé passer quelque temps avant que de faire usage de la Methode que vous avez jugée la plus propre a l'introduire dans le latin;†1 et depuis six semaines que je la luy fais pratiquer, il me satisfait assez sur l'oraison Dominicale, Le Symbole, Le Decalogue, et les quatre premiers Pseaumes, j'espere, Monsieur, qu'elle produira tout l'effet que vous vous en estes promis. Avant cela je luy ay fait prendre une legere teinture des Declinaisons, et des Conjugaisons. Pour Lecture françoise je luy fais voir le livre de Mr. de Condom,†2 et je ne laisse passer aucun trait d'Histoire propre a le former a la Geographie, sans le luy faire remarquer sur le Globe, ou sur les Cartes dont vous luy avez fait present. Il ne me paroit pas qu'il ayt fait un progrés bien sensible dans la langue françoise, cependant je puis dire, qu'il la parle presques toûjours, ne le perdant point de veüe, depuis le lever jusques au coucher. Et si j'en excepte le peu de temps que je donne a la lecture de l'Ecriture Sainte, tout le reste luy est entierement destiné. Ne trouveriez vous pas a propos, Monsieur, qu'apres l'avoir tenu quelque temps sur les Pseaumes, je luy fisse lire les fables de Phedre avec la traduction de Port-Royal.†3 Si cette proposition vous agrée, je vous supplie de dire a Monsieur son Pere de luy acheter ce livre, et quoyqu'il soit peu avancé dans l'Aritmetique, d'y joindre les Elemens des Mathematiques, imprimez chez Prâlard, et les nouveaux Elemens de Geometrie, imprimez chez Savreux,†4 suivant la note que vous m'en avez donnée un peu avant mon départ de Londres.
Monsieur et Madame Clarke ont toûjours beaucoup d'honnesteté pour moy, toutes les fois que vous m'avez fait l'honneur,
― 712 ―
Monsieur, de me donner des marques de vôtre souvenir dans vos lettres ils m'en ont informé. Je n'ay pas encore veu de maison mieux reglée que la leur. J'espere que vous me continüerez la faveur que vous m'avez déja faite de me donner vos bons avis pour l'éducation de Mr. leur fils, cependant je vous supplie d'estre bien persuadé que je ne manqueray jamais a la reconnoissance que je vous dois, et que je suis avec un attachement inviolable
Monsieur
Votre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
PASSEBON.
Permettez moy, Monsieur, de donner icy des marques de mes trés humbles respects a Madame Lockart,†1 et a Madame sa bonne amie.†2
A Chipley ce 22e Oct 89.
Je croy Madame La Comtesse de Southerland†3 en Ecosse, si d'avanture Elle est encore en Ville, ces Dames m'obligeront fort si Elles veulent bien luy faire un compliment fort soumis pour moy. Oserois-je bien vous prier, Monsieur, de vous souvenir du manuscrit.†4
Endorsed by Locke: Passebon 22 Oct.89 Answered 12 Dec.
