1197. George Walls to Locke, 26 October 1689 (1175, 1761)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 23, ff. 53-4, 54b. The postscript on f. 54b, which is a separate scrap of paper, apparently belongs to this letter.
Hamburgh Octob: 26th 1689
Deare Sir
You extremely oblig'd me in your kinde letter, for in truth; one of my gretest difficulties in comeinge to England was some apprehensions
― 713 ―
least you might be offended at my removeal. I could not contrive matters soe as to waite on my Lord of Pembroke into Englande, Mr Barfords letter that was to give me an account of the time of his goinge, lieing 12 daies on its way. so that I shall now uppon an earnest invitation from Sir William Colt†1 pas my Christmas at the courts of Zell Hannover and Wolfenbutel (places I have not yet seene), the motive inducinge me thereto beinge the givinge the H. Communion to the Dutches of Hannover†2 and the Envoy's familie. What care has beene taken for the mum†3 you desir'd will in some mesure appeare by the enclos'd from Bremen which came to my hands the day our convoy came on hither; so that there is some reson to feare I shal not be able to pay you the respect I design'd, till the next brewinge in February, which is alwaies accounted the best mum. then you shal not faile to be supply'd from Bremen; for Hamburgh yealds none worthy of such friends. If you shal plese to speake with anie of the merchant adventurers†4 of your acquaintance in London relatinge to me, and let them know that some considerable men in England may be apt to resent the treatment I have found; it might turne to my account in the manner of my discharge; for these gentlemen are capable of feare at this time, their trade beinge laid open; and a parliament sittinge is somewhat that they are redie to own is above um.†a †5 you may plese to know that I am elected till next midsomer, and though there was a conditi<on>†b in it; yet twas grounded on some feares of theirs which now take noe longer place; and therefore twill not by sober men be thought unresonable that my salarie should be continued to me till that time; I taking care that the companie be put to noe charge above that; and payinge the man that shal supply anie part of my absence to the utmost of his and their expectations. this I know you will kindly, and can discreetly manage. and there coulde not be the least difficultie in this; were it not for the passionat unresonable temper of one man here (mr Stratford); whose fierie way of acting
― 714 ―
had lately engag'd the two residencies†1 in differences that were like to ruine the companie; and will never let a minister live well here; that will live but christianly with tho<se>†a hee's ang<rie>†a with; and cannot favour his ill designes. If you plese to honour me with a <le>tter;†a twill finde me here till the beginning of Decemb: and be sent to me if it comes later. w<lb/> at†a favor you thinke fit to doe in order to <my>†a request must be done at your first leisure; because at Christmas matters will be determin'd. I pray thinke of some commands for
Honour'd Sir
your most oblig'd humble servant
G: WALLS.
be ples'd to accept of a couple of westphalia Hams which were verie good when they were put up for you; and I hope the longe expectation of the Convoy hath not prejudic'd. tis the earnest of your mum.
The bearer hereof hath serv'd a master here with great reputation; and I can engage without the least tincture of his principles, and if by your favor he may be recommended to the like station he hath quitted, you will most certainly have thanks for it, since he hath long approv'd here both his fidelitie, discretion, and sobrietie.†b

1200. Locke to J. G. GrÆvius, 5 November 1689 (1110, 1240)
Royal Library, Copenhagen, MS. Thott 1263-4°. Printed by C. Bastide in Revue internationale de l'enseignement, lv (January-June 1908), 389-91. Answers no. 1110; answered by no. 1240.

Londini 5 Nov. 89
(English) Vir Amplissime
Adeo notus est mihi tuus in me animus amoris et benevolentiæ plenus, ut diuturni silentii crimen quod in me ipso gravi censurâ condemno, te leni et benignâ facilitate condonaturum credere ausim. Multa sunt quæ me reversum in patriam impeditum et implicatum tenuerunt: Sed quicquid negotii sex vel septem annorum absentia, unâ cum novâ apud nos rerum facie mihi facessere poterat, nulla nec rei privatæ nec publicæ manus meas ad scribendum paratas tam diu detinuisset occupatio si Furlei decessus sæpe statutus et sæpe in alterum tempus rejectus non <fefellisset>†a <expectantem>.†b Cum enim plurimum meâ interest ut tibi non semper oblivionis vel negligentiæ nomine suspectus sim, hujusmodi nuntium desideravi cui ad Te darem literas, qui et certo traderet, et etiam mei in te affectus et amoris testis esse poterat. Nemo est Mi Grævi cui animum meum magis testatum cupere debeo quam Tibi. Qui humanitate, amicitia et omni officiorum genere peregrinum errantem et ignotum amplexus meritus es ut quicquid ego studio, cura, manu, votis, omni operâ assequi possim,†c id omne meritis tuis impendam. Id Tibi persuasissimum velim, Tua beneficia apud me, magnitudinis
― 718 ―
memoriam imo vero novitatis gratiam non perdidisse. Si quid inter homines æternum esse debeat id ego imprimis amicitiam credo. Ita igitur statuas apud Te, me quicquid a grato animo <proficisci>†a potest, eâdem mente, eâdemque voluntate jam post aliquot menses dicere quâ tibi valedicens dixissem, nec meam in te gratitudinem abolebit unquam vel imminuet longa dies.
(English) Præteritâ septimanâ Rex et Regina a civitate Londinensi convivio lautissimo summo cum omnium plausu et gaudio excepti.†1 Placuit invitantium animus, placuit prandii ornatus, copia, et ordo, Utraque simul adfuit domus parlamenti a civitate invitata. Hesterno die celebratur splendidissime Natalis regis in Aulâ Choreis, in Urbe sonitu campanarum, ignibus, et aliis gaudii publici testimoniis. Sladus noster huc ante duas vel tres septimanas appulit.†2 semel illum tantum vidi, postridie enim postquam ad me accessit rus profectus est nec dum post reditum vidi. Quando convenimus tui immemores non Erimus. Clarissimum vestrum Legatum Dikefeldium†3 aliquando in ædibus suis conveni, illum sæpius interpellare
― 719 ―
nec meæ erat modestiæ nec otii quanquam plurimi æstimo. Grevium nostrum†1 rogo ut meo nomine amicissime salutes. Champnei necessarios nuper conveni dixerunt mercatorem aliquem Amstelodamensem in mandatis habuisse ut solveret quicquid illius nomine uspiam Trajecti deberetur. Nescio an eâ curâ obtemperaverit ut Te non omiserit, De hac re a te Certiorem fieri cupio, etiamsi enim non sit magni ponderis tuum honorarium, graviter tamen animo meo insidet, et me commovet rei turpitudo. Dicas igitur rogo, nam mea res est et ego curabo. Si in scribendo tardus fueris te meam cunctationem et graviter ferre, et velle graviter ulcisci suspicabor. Me igitur certiorem fac ut <valeas>†a ut memineris nostri, impense efflagito. Iterum iterumque vale et ama ut facis
Tui amantissimum
J LOCKE
(English) Ita inscribendæ literæ tuæ
For Mr John Locke
in Dorset Court in Chanel row
Westminster.
(Latin) Excellent Sir,
I am so familiar with your affectionate and kindly feelings towards me that I dare to believe that you will be ready in your lenient and generous way to pardon the offence of having kept silence so long, for which I condemn myself in the strongest terms. I have been involved in many difficulties and perplexities since returning to my country; but whatever trouble my six or seven years' absence, together with the new aspect of affairs in England, may have caused me, yet no occupation with either private or public business would have kept me so long from writing when I was ready to do so, if Furly's departure, so often decided upon and so often put off to another time, had not belied my expectation. I am most seriously concerned not to be continually suspected by you of forgetfulness or negligence; so I wanted to secure the sort of messenger to whom I could entrust letters for you with the certainty of his delivering them, and one also who might bear witness to my regard and affection for you. There is no one, my dear Grævius, to whom I am more bound to desire that proof of my feelings should be given than to you. By the kindness and friendliness and good offices of every sort with which you welcomed a wandering stranger and foreigner you have deserved that all I can achieve by zeal and care, all my endeavours and all my wishes, should be devoted to the acknowledgement of those benefits. I would have you feel assured that the recollection of their [p. 718] magnitude, and indeed the charm of their unexpectedness, has in no way faded from my mind. If there is anything that should be eternal between men I believe that it is friendship above all. Be certain therefore that whatever can proceed from a grateful heart I now after some months express with the same mind and the same purpose as would have been mine on saying goodbye to you, and that my gratitude to you will never be obliterated or diminished by any lapse of time.
(Latin) Last week the King and Queen were entertained by the City of London at a sumptuous banquet, amid the acclamations and joy of all.†1 The spirit shown by the hosts was most gratifying, as was the equipment, abundance, and ordering of the feast. Both houses of parliament were present at the same time by the invitation of the City. Yesterday there was a splendid celebration of the king's birthday, with dancing at the court, ringing of bells in the city, bonfires, and other tokens of public rejoicing. Our friend Sladus landed here two or three weeks ago;†2 I have seen him only once, as he set off for the country the day after he called on me and I have not yet seen him since he returned. When we meet we shall not fail to remember you. I met your distinguished ambassador Dijkveld†3 on one occasion at his house, but modesty and lack of free time have prevented me from accosting [p. 719] him more frequently, though I hold him in the highest esteem. Please remember me most kindly to our friend de Greve.†1 I met Champneys's relations the other day; they said that some merchant in Amsterdam had been instructed to pay whatever was owing on his account anywhere in Utrecht. I do not know whether he carried out his instructions carefully enough not to omit you. This is what I want you to tell me about; though your fee may not amount to a large sum, still it is a great weight on my mind, and I am deeply affected by the disgrace of the thing. Please therefore let me know, as it is my affair and I will see to it. If you are slow in answering I shall suspect that you are annoyed with my own tardiness and wish to exact severe vengeance for it. Accordingly I beg you most earnestly to let me know how you are and that you have not forgotten me. Good-bye once again, and continue to love me
Your most affectionate
J LOCKE
(Latin) Your letters should be addressed
For Mr. John Locke
in Dorset Court in Chanel row
Westminster

1203. Anthony Ashley Cooper, styled Lord Ashley, later third earl of Shaftesbury, to Locke, 15 November [1689] (1195, 1412)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 7, ff. 89-90. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Ivy Church November the 15th
For att least four days more am I condemned to the Country. Since I am so unfortunate, thank Heavens I have with it so much Happiness att least, as to know my Doom: for that which has been wors then my banishment has been the Concealment of the time of its continuance:
It was not enough that I should be so much longer miserable in the Country then I expected; but, as my Ill fate would have it, I was still kept in ignorance of what did happen and in hopes of what did not; and this, with a continuall succession of dissappointments that with the greatest aggravation have rendered it more unsupportable. I would not have You think amiss of me on this occasion, or (which one of less refined notion,†2 or of a very undeserving opinion of mee might doe) imagine in mee, either a stubborn aversion to the Country, or a Giddy affection for the Town: I know you will reflect a little on the sence I may have of my own improvement, and on those small pretensions I have to the, Bon Goust,: but this will not be enough to justifie my so ill treating but one month or 2 of a life passed in the Country: I Could have spoke
― 722 ―
of it in gentler terms then I have here; If there were not more in the Case then all this.
I will not tell you how much I make you concerned in the considerations already mentioned, and consequently what hand you have had in all the abuses I have layed upon my Country: but I cannot help telling you that there was something in your reproaches, which though, by what I could discern, were no other then what I made every day to my self and my Ill fate; yett I found them of so much a sharper effect as to turn that which was before onely a tolerable pennance, into an incredible torment: But then when I thought nothing but of being in town sooner then my answer to your letter could have come there; and when my Concern was not Less to make You a speedy return, then to come immediatly to town my self; to find my self so deluded of both, from day to day; as to have lived to this time without either; I must leave you to Judg if it has been easy to mee. So that when I consider that I might have still gon on; and att last have come to you not onely late, but with the Guilt of having never so much as wrote my excuse in all that time; I begin to think my self not unhappy in this last stop of four days since it has been the means of taking of that weight from mee; and has sett mee in a Condition to think of seeing You without pain and to enjoy that without the allay of shame, which I so earnestly long for: I could have told you then; but I am more satisfied that I tell you now; how that it has been concerns of the last consequence to my family that have thus detained mee, accidents not unforseen by mee, or altogather unrevealed to You: but of which I desire to say no more here: and of any think els I think I need not since I depend upon the seeing you so soon. I would not have You wonder that when I write to you it is always from hence: for they can tell you here that I own my self (as indeed I am forced by Kindness) to be att home when here: onely I goe now and then for 4 or 5 days to St Giless†1 or abroad a Visiting: You may Judg then by what relation I have to the intrest of the family, if I am not bound to keep up fully a perfect correspondance between You, and all here: but having discovered certain interruptions which Mrs Stringer especially shows great concern for, I have declared to her I would take up the buisness and I must tell you I come to you with very advantageouse articles of
― 723 ―
accommodation on your side: for an other reason too you most own my Zeal in this to be very Just: for You were the person who cheifly minded of the regard I was to have for our freinds att Ivy Church; and who was ready had there been any such <occasion>†a to have undertaken that in my respect which by a reasnable retaliation I now doe in yours. no more now then that all present their service
You know how much I am
Dear Sir
Your sincere freind more obleidged and more Yett to be Obleidged to You then any body
A ASHLEY
Address: For Mr Lock att Mr's: Smithby'es In Dorsett Court In Channell Row Westminster
Postmark: NO 18
Endorsed by Locke: L: Ashley 15 Nov. 89
1204. William Stratton to Locke, 15 November 1689 (1129, 1208)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 41.
Sutton the 15th: nov: 1689
Dear Cosin
According to Mr: Clarks order I went to Pensford and did forbid the widdow Shatters Tenant of paying any more rent till you wear satisfied that Jonathan Floory weare liveing and I have weighted near three weakes to se whether the Widdow Cold have any satisfacktion from London, and doe perceive that shee hath none; but she saith That one Silke I think a pensford man said he was goeing to see about nine weaks sinc, if you are not throwly satisfied about his life or deth if you send your servant to my Cosin John Bonvill,†1 they may goe to floryes Wifes House whoe when I was In London formerly sould beare and then we had Information of him, and I think noe better way now if she be liveing and follow the same trade, theare is great neade that I should know with all speade, for the tenant that is In it by his Fathering Laws helpe for anything I know may buy it for they have beane desireous to know whether it
― 724 ―
be In your hand or noe and If I cannot satisfie then by the 28th: of this Instant they will provid another house it is the Custom as I perceive of St. Thomas Parish to provid a overseer for the poore by the house and the Widdow tells me the tenant doeth aske 3l: to serve the ofice this year for severall other resons its best to sell it the widdow and I by your order was very Like to deale few years sinc for 15l now I desire to know the Lowest price I must sell it at if the life be ded and I will Indever to make the most I can of it there is nothing goten by keeping it in hand for it hath stod without a Tenant sum time till of late; as for your other Concerns about pensford Tenants have a very hard matter to raise rent and theare must be sum abatements it was very bad about 3 or 4 years since but now it is wors Mr Clarke I suppose have before this time given you an accoun<t>†a how it is, Sledg is as far as I perceive honest and very Industreous and saith it is soe hard a matter to raise rent that he can keep but one suite of Cloths to his backe if I weare not fully satisfied about what he saith I would not troble you with loyns about It, and am very loath to let him goe, for I know not wheare to better him therfore if you leave it to my discretion I shall ackt as prudent as I can I was In sum hopes to have sene you this sumer but now am past hopes of seing you as yet I should be glad to see you to ballance accounts when ever you draw a bill I hope uppon sight or sudenly after to pay what is in my hands and doe hope that betwene this and 25th. Jany: next to have the most part of your rents in my hands my Wife presents her servis to you I take leave
your faithfull kinsman and Humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON
pray let me have an answer about the widdow Shatters conserns suddenly that I may know how to ackt in it

Postmark: NO 18.

1207. Dr. Mattheus Sladus to Locke, 24 [November?] 1689 (1210)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, ff. 112-13. Sladus's date, corresponding to 25 October, O.S., is almost certainly wrong. He came to London probably on 5 October: p. 728, n. 1. His movements after that are uncertain. Locke lent him a book on 29 October: Journal. If this is to be connected with the books sent to him by Locke, Sladus had gone to Colchester already. He returned to London probably on 13 November and left for Windsor and Oxford a few days later: nos. 1212, 1213. There is no sign of an earlier visit to Windsor, and the contents of the present letter link it with nos. 1210 and 1217, which are securely dated.
For the writer see no. 794.
(English) Amicissime et doctissime domine Locke,
Cum adhuc Windezorii hæream, ut videam et perlustrem bibliothecam Domini Vossii τοῦ μακαρίτου†1 et fortasse cum Dominis Bernardo†2 et Heydo,†3 præfecto bibliothecæ Bodleianæ, sim profecturus oxoniam (Qui ea de caussa quoque magno meo gaudio, ut excutiant bibliothecam, et fortasse emant, huc venerunt) non potui non illius rei te certiorem facere; itaque si quid sit quod mea interest scire, literas ad D. Vossium senatorem†4 mittere poteris. Habitat ac cum sorore†a in arce Windezorii, in eadem domo ubi Canonicus habitavit. Itaque aut Oxoniâ ad te scribet,†b aut,
― 728 ―
Windezorio redux, statim te compellabit, ut servitium suum tibi offerat,
M. SLADUS MD.
(English) Domini te salutant.
Vale. 4 Nov. st. n. Anno 1689. Windezorii.
Hanc chartulam inclusam mittes, si placet, ad hospitem meum Maquernes
(Latin) My dear and learned Mr. Locke,
I am still hanging on at Windsor in order to see and examine the library of the late Mr. Vossius,†1 and I shall perhaps set out for Oxford with Mr. Bernard†2 and Mr. Hyde,†3 who is the head of the Bodleian Library. They too have come here, to my great joy, for the purpose of examining the library and possibly buying it. So I could not help letting you know about that business. If therefore there is anything that it concerns me to know you can send a letter to Mr. Vossius, the councillor.†4 He is staying with his sister in Windsor Castle, in the same house that the canon lived in. Accordingly there will either [p. 728] write to you from Oxford or call on you to pay you his respects immediately on his return from Windsor
M. SLADUS M.D.
(Latin) The gentlemen I have mentioned send you their respects.
Goodbye. 4 Nov., New Style, 1689. At Windsor.
Please be good enough to send the enclosed paper to my host Maquernes.†1
Address: Jos. Maquernes†1 in de six sugarloves, in St. James-street. for Dominus Doctor Locke.

1208. William Stratton to Locke, 26 November 1689 (1204, 1246)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 19, f. 42.
Sutton the 26th: nov: 1689
Dear Cosin
I was In expecktation of A answear to my letter that I writ to you concerning the Widdow Shatters house but as yet have received noe letter but understand by the tenant that is in it that the widdow hath sent them word that the life is in being, the ocation of my writing at this time is about your teniment Att Belton, I was In hopes that David Horrall would have Continewed ther one
― 729 ―
year more but he was Resolved to leave it but uppon sum promises that I have made he will Continew one yeare more that is to seale the chese loft put sum paving in sum part of the Milke house and lay the barns floore and abate 40s for the next yeare of the rent that he now doeth Give as for abatements I would not but I promised him to give him back 20s of this years Rent and to give him 20s of the next years Rent as for the proposalls about mending those three things in the house it is soe bad that I Could not but consent to it and weare you presant to se hou it is you would have mutch more don I am sorry that I troble you with such loyns as thes but I know not how to help it, for as far as I can perceive tenants are every years wors able to pay theyr rent I am in great hopes If please the lord to preserve our lives that I shall see you next sumer In our Countery Mr Clarke I suppose have Given you an Account how it is to home pray present my Humble servs pray let me have a loyne from you whether you consent to what I have don one thing more he prest uppon me that I would give under my hand to discharg him of quartering souldiers which I shall not doe for he saith formerly the case was soe that the Charg of souldiers was soe great in one year as did amount to a years rent but I hope noe such thing now†1 the case is mutch more defecult to let tenements and rents mutch les but I hope god will mend it for it goeth very hard with many with us my Wife presents her humble servs to you I take leave
your Faithfull kinsman and Humble ser:
WILLIAM STRATTON
one thing I had forgotten to let you know that George Bonvill†2 is decesed and left a poore widdow and five small Children
Address: For Mr John Locke At Mrs: Smithsbys in Dorset Court in Chanell Row Westminster London
Postmark: DE 2
Endorsed by Locke: William Stratton 26 Nov 89 Answered 25 Jan.

1209. Mrs. Elinor Hawkshaw to Locke, 30 November [1689] (1205, 1211)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 171-2. Year from Locke's endorsement.
the 30 of November
dear Sir
Yours hath given me assureanc of your Care and kindness in that affare of mine, my Brother Flood writt to one mr Howard that in Case you did not apeere for me he should, but if it were not to great a trouble to you I should desire and wish none ells should receve what providence and our†a King orders for me†1 but you, doe as you think fitt, and as you have bin a Brother and a freind lett your Goodness continew so to my present Happyness my Ben troubles you, but when I know you have perfected†b my buissnes as your Concern assures me you are intent, I shall with sincerity and a Hart full of Acknowledgment owne my self
your Obliged freind
E H
Good mr Lock you did not a miss in what you did for me for I losst more then I mentioned to you
I an at the post office and in great Hast so that I cannot write at full, but pray take the matter into your Hand

B.L., MS. Locke c. 18, f. 114.
(English) Amicissime domine Locke,
Heri perveni Oxoniam, Vindsorâ decedens cum Dominis meis Bernardo et Heide, qui te salutant. Per octo et amplius dies hæsi
― 731 ―
Vidnsoræ, tum ut Dominum Vossium exspectarem et viderem M. S. Isaaci Vossii, τοῦ μακαρίτου. Sed cum iter hoc Oxoniense præter mentem mihi acciderit, et pecunia mea sit absumta, rogo ut quocumque modo mihi tres Guieneas, ut vocant, vel simile quid transmittas, mittes cum ad D. Bernardum, si placet; quamvis insigne domûs ubi deversor sit, Porcus cæruleus.†1 Vale, nam equus celes†a urget. Si a. alium scias modum, quo mihi succurrere possis, eadem mihi sedebit.
Vale amicissime, et me quod facis, ama.
Datum 1/11 Decembris
a tuo M. SLADO
ἐξ ἄκρου μυελοὖ ψυχῆς†2
(Latin) My dear friend Mr. Locke,
I reached Oxford yesterday, having left Windsor with my friends Mr. Bernard and Mr. Hyde, who send you their greetings. I hung on at Windsor [p. 731] for eight days and more to wait for Mr. Vossius and to see the late Isaac Vossius's manuscripts. But as I had to make this journey to Oxford unexpectedly, and as my money has run out, I beg you to find some way of sending me three guineas, as they call them, or something of the sort; you can send it (?) to Mr. Bernard, if you like, though the sign of the house I am putting up at is the Blue Pig.†1 Good-bye, as the post-horse is pressing. If, however, you know of any other way to assist me it will suit me equally well.
Good-bye, best of friends, and keep me in your affections.
Posted 1/11 December,
from M. SLADUS, who is yours
from the inmost marrow of his soul.†2
Address: Jos. Maquernes, in the Six sugarloves, in Sir James-street, for Doctor Locke Londonium
Postmark: DE 2
Endorsed by Locke: Sladus 1 Dec. 89

Bewmoriss the 2d (89)
Sir
The continewanc of your kindness gives you new troubles: and as you have bin a true freind since Irelands unhappyness and myne:
― 732 ―
so from the knowledg I have of it, I may hope for your farther concern in my afare, if our Good Kings bounty reach to me I have no freind but your self to authirese to act and receve: if so be you will take the trouble on you, the true form I understand not, but if you pleas to send one in your next to me I will signe it, or if I am so Happy to be in the number of the relieeved perhaps this which I send may sereve from a woman, I need excuse my self for my last ramblin Letter which intimated that my Brother Flod writt to one mr Howard to act if neither the Bishop of Killdare†1 nor you did appear for me, but I referr all to your goodness and freindship which hath obliged me to be whilst I am your
Sincere Freind
E. HAWKSHAW

1212. Dr. Pieter Guenellon to Locke, 2/12 December 1689 (1179, 1244)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 18-19.
Monsieur
Nous avons receu vostre agreable du 15 nov. et les remerciements que vous nous faitte valent cent fois le present. Ma femme vous
― 733 ―
demande tousjours le conte de ce que vous avez defroyé pour elle, et ne pretend vous escrire qu'apres que vous l'aurez envoyé. jay veu Monsieur le Clerq qui avoit desja receu vos cahiers.†1 jay salué Monsieur Limburgh et tous les amis du college de vostre part, et avons bien de la joye que monsieur Sladus soit recouvert, pourveu quil ne se perde pas une autre fois, comme on nous fait craindre.†2 enverité Monsieur cest donner une nouvelle atteinte à la foiblesse que j'ay eu de vouloir paroistre auteur, de quelques feuilles volantes que de men demander une copie.†3 il faudra pourtant vous obeir aveuglement puisque je suis convaincu que vous avez pour moy plus de charité qu'aucun. Je l'envoyeray quand Monsieur Cyprianus ou quelque autre amis passera vers vous. monsieur cyprianus espere de faire encore un voyage cet hyver, attiré sans doubte par les riches recompences de la Nation. Mon beau pere vous remercie de vostre obligeante lettre, il a esté malade et Monsieur Quina aussy a la fin d'une frequente practique, qui nous a fort occupe cet automme. on me presse de finir. le temps s'est ecoulé. je suis
Monsieur
Vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur
P GUENELLON
Amsterd. ce 12 dec. 1689.
Jay receu la lettre de monsieur charleton. la medaille quil me demande n'est encore qu'en idee mais un medailliste ma promit de la faire faire et si tost quelle paroistra j'en envoyeray une.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur J Locke a Londres
Endorsed by Locke: Dr Guenellon 12 Dec. 89 Answered 28 Jan.

1213. Locke to Philippus Van Limborch, 3 December [1689] (1187, 1215)
Amsterdam University Library, MS. R.K., Ba 258s. Printed in Ollion, pp. 191-3. Year from contents. Answers nos. 1184, 1187; answered by no. 1223.
(English)
London. 3 Dec
En tandem obæratus tuus respondet et agnoscit beneficia. Nosti me olim cunctatorem, nec ætate hoc vitium corrigitur, ignoscas moribus inveteratis, vel, si mavis, negotiorum quotidie nascentium importunæ occupationi, ut ut fit tibi persuasum velim me sive scribam sive taceam nunquam omittere ea de te et sentire et cogitare quæ tua in me officia et nostra mutua amicitia requirunt. Accepi Theam librosque quos tantâ curâ mihi parasti et misisti, gratiasque et ago et habeo, pretium horum si recte colligo est f 38-8, quod tibi rependendum inclusâ literâ cambii curavi, si commodum tibi fuerit hanc pecuniam Roterodami accipere, sin minus cum Furleio hic transigam ut aliquo modo curet tibi Amstelodami solvendam. Hodie ultimam tractatus mei de Intellectu humano schedam typis impressam esse spero, sic enim promiserunt typographi siqua fides isti hominum generi habenda sit,†1 utinam eâ scriptus esset linguâ ut tu de toto opere posses judicare. novi enim
― 735 ―
ingenium candorem et limatissimum judicium tuum. Si procedat apud vos versio Latina expectabo aliquando censuram tuam. Interim jacta est alea, et jam magnum æquor navigo. Gaudeo tibi placuisse legatum nostrum,†1 specie et splendore non dico, etiamsi illa non defuerint, sed eâ parte qua homines sumus mente et cogitatione. Hoc scio placuit ei valde quod tecum habuit colloquium et amplius scio placuisset si iterandi data fuisset occasio. Heri conveni Dominum Kiddar. literas Slado datas se accepisse a te fatetur et alias seriùs scriptas sed maturius allatas. Se brevi ad te scripturum dixit, quomodo inscribendæ ad te essent literæ indicavi. De Slado nostro quid dicam nescio semel tantum ex quo in Angliâ fuit illum vidi non illius nec meâ culpâ sed utriusque ut mihi videtur infortunio, nam quicquid incommodi illi eveniat mihi valde molestum erit, adfuit bis vel ter meo hospitio ego itidem illius sed semel tantum convenimus. paulo postquam me inviserat exiit ex urbe reversus meum adiit hospitium, et cum abfuerim per breve scriptum quod illic reliquit postulavit a me aliquos libros, quos postridie domum ejus misi ille enim aberat, post aliquot dies venit ad me Francus,†2 dixit ante aliquot dies decessisse Sladum ab
― 736 ―
hospitio nec dum rediisse, nec quo abierat scire quenpiam. addidit illum ex quo Londinum venerat ter lipothyma cedidisse plane exanimem. Terruit res, Quæsitum itur. Nusquam apparet nec vola nec vestigium. Ignotum alicubi interiisse certo credidi. Cum jam conclamatum esset, et vocatus Notarius publicus ut coram eo apperirentur sarcinæ, et rerum relictarum in hospitio iniretur ratio ipse Sladus apparet Colcestriâ reversus quo profectus est ad comedenda ostrea. Hæc mihi postridie vel perendie narravit Francus.†1 Salvum et sanum rediisse gaudeo. ipsum quamprimum invisere statuo, et hortari ut famulum sumat nec quoquam sine illo proficiscatur, nequid humanitus ex tam incommodo morbo ipsi accideret. Ille vero intra septimanam inopinate iterum decessit et quod mireris pedes hac tempestate Windsoriam contendit inde Oxonium profecturus. Maxime dolui quod plurimis impeditus negotiis ante decessum illum videre non potui, nec†a- ab eo tempore quicquam de eo auditum est.-†a†2 Francus ita de eo loquitur tanquam mente aliquo modo vacillaret, et hæc non valde sani esse hominis suspicari
― 737 ―
pronum est. Si ante diem Jovis†1 de eo certi nihil mihi allatum fuerit Oxonium scribam, ut illic quæratur et curetur. Hæc fusius ad Te scripsi, ut Dominum Hudde†2 unum ex Consulibus vestris certiorem de tota hac re facias, Francus enim dixit mihi nuper Illustrissimum Dominum Hudde rogare me ut Sladi nostri curam haberem. Hoc illius mandatum mihi valde a tanto viro honorificum duco, et rogo ut præfatis quæ a me ad tam illustrem virum conveniunt, dicere velis, nihil mihi acceptius esse quam illo impulsore excitari ad id ad quod mea voluntate et animo amicitiæ pleno sponte ferebar. Verum si ita res sit uti metuo, et aliquo modo vel levissime turbetur Sladi mens consilio opus erit et forsan aliqua authoritate ut eo deducatur res quo cupimus. rogas igitur oro Illustrissimum virum quid suadeat agendum et an non commodum forte erit si res ita postulet ut adeam Dominum Hop†3 concivem suum et Legatum hic ab Ordinibus, ut illius hortatu et monitu si opus fuerit ita temperemus Sladum nostrum ut illo autore ad id impellatur quod ex usu fuerit. Hæc tibi soli dico, nolim enim hujusmodi aliquem rumorem
― 738 ―
Amstelodami evulgari. Novi prudentiam tuam et scio te Illustrissimum consulem <vestrum>†a consulturum quid factu opus erit. Quamprimum redierit Sladus ipsum invisam et quo in statu sit videbo. Si non immutatum invenero curabo diligentissime ne iterum se negligat. Si obstinatum vel negligentem vel aliquo modo turbatum invenero, difficilior erit res, nosti enim hominem, et hortatore graviore opus erit. Hoc in casu Si Illustrissimus Dominus Hudde mihi author erit Clarissimum Dominum Hop vel quempiam alium adibo et de tota re consulam
(English) Dominum Clericum plurimum salvere jubeo. Secundum et tertium librum tractatus mei de intellectu mense ut memini septembri ad eum misi. Petrus Sunmans†1 Juvenis Roterodamensis Furlei familiæ notissimus secum abiens portavit. Quod restat brevi mittam, et si commodum ducat versionem ad me mittere siqua in parte a mente mea aberret corrigam. Finito uti causidici <nostri>†b loquuntur jam termino†2 expecto librorum impressorum catalogum†3 quem quamprimum accepero ad Dominum Clericum scribam.

(English) Tuos. Veeneos. Guenellonos omnes meo nomine quæso officiosissime salutes Vale et ut facis ama Tui amantissimum

(Latin)
London. 3 Dec.
Here at last is your debtor answering and acknowledging your kindnesses. You know me of old for a slowcoach, and this failing is not corrected by age. You must forgive habits that are now inveterate, or make allowances, if you prefer, for one continually harassed by matters of business that arise daily. However that may be, I would have you feel sure that whether I write or keep silence I never cease to have those feelings and thoughts about you that are demanded by all that you have done for me and by our mutual friendship. I have received the tea and the books which you took such trouble to procure and send to me, for which I give you my best thanks. The cost of these things, if I understand rightly, is fl. 38-8; I have arranged for this sum to be repaid to you by the enclosed letter of exchange, if you should find it convenient to get the money in Rotterdam; if not, I will arrange with Furly here to have it made payable to you by some means in Amsterdam. Today, as I hope, the last sheet of my treatise on the Human Understanding has been printed; that is what the printers promised, if any trust is to be put in that sort of people.†1 I wish it had been written in a language that might have enabled you to [p. 735] judge of the work as a whole; for I know the frankness of your nature and the fineness of your judgement. If the Latin translation is proceeding with you I shall expect some time to hear your criticisms. Meanwhile, the die is cast, and I am now embarked on the open sea. I am glad you were pleased with our ambassador;†1 I do not refer to outward appearance and splendour of state, though those things cannot have been wanting; I mean that part which makes us men, the mind and the power of thought. I know that the conversation he had with you gave him great pleasure, and that he would have been still better pleased if an opportunity of repeating it had been given him. Yesterday I met Mr. Kidder; he acknowledges having received the letter you sent him by Sladus and another which was written later but delivered earlier. He said that he would be writing to you shortly, and I told him how letters to you should be addressed. About our friend Sladus I do not know what to say; I have seen him only once since he has been in England, not through his fault or mine, but unluckily for us both, it seems to me; for if he meets with any trouble it will be most distressing to me. He called at my lodging two or three times, as I also did at his, but we met only once. He left town shortly after visiting me and on his return called at my lodging; as I was out, he left a short note there asking me for some books, which I sent the next day to his house, he being away. Some days afterwards Francke†2 came to see me and said that Sladus had left his lodging some days before [p. 736] and had not yet returned, nor did any one know where he had gone. He added that since Sladus's arrival in London he had three times fallen completely insensible in a fainting-fit. This was alarming, and a search was made for him. He was nowhere to be seen and not the slightest trace of him could be found. I believed for certain that he had perished in some place where no one knew him. When all hope had been given up, and when a notary public had been called in, in order to have Sladus's baggage opened in his presence and an inventory made of the articles left in his lodging, behold Sladus himself, just back from Colchester, where he had gone to eat oysters. I heard all this from Francke the next day or the day after.†1 I was happy to know that he had returned safe and sound, and I determined to go and see him as soon as possible and to urge him to engage a servant and not to set out for any destination without him, in case he should suffer some fatal accident as the result of such an unfortunate ailment. However, within the week he has once more departed unexpectedly and, which may well surprise you, is making at this time of year for Windsor on foot, and intends to go on from there to Oxford. I was extremely sorry that heavy pressure of business prevented me from seeing him before he left; nor has anything been heard of him since then.†2 Francke speaks of him as if he were somehow unsteady in his mind, and one may readily suspect that these are the actions of [p. 737] a man who is not altogether sane. If I hear nothing certain about him by Thursday†1 I shall write to Oxford to have him searched for and looked after there. I have told you all this at some length in order that you may inform Mr. Hudde,†2 one of your burgomasters, about this whole business; for Francke told me recently that His Honour Mr. Hudde was asking me to take care of our friend Sladus. I feel highly honoured by this charge as coming from such a great man; and I beg that you, after such prefatory expressions as should come from me to so distinguished a person, will be good enough to tell him that nothing is more welcome to me than to be urged by him to a course to which I was led by my own inclinations and in obedience to the dictates of friendship. If, however, it is as I fear and Sladus's mind is somehow deranged even in a very slight degree, we shall have to make plans and possibly use some authority to bring things to the position we desire. Please therefore ask His Honour what course he would advise, and whether perhaps it will not be well, should circumstances demand it, that I should approach Mr. Hop,†3 who is his fellow-citizen and an envoy here from the States, so that by his encouragement and advice we may if necessary control our friend Sladus sufficiently to induce him to do what is good for him at Hop's instance. This is for your ear alone, for I would not wish any rumour of this kind to get [p. 738] abroad in Amsterdam. I know your discretion, and am sure that you will consult your burgomaster about what should be done. As soon as Sladus returns I shall visit him and see what state he is in. If I find no change in him I will do my best to ensure that he does not repeat such thoughtless behaviour. If I find him obstinate or heedless or upset in any way things will be more difficult, for you know the man, and some adviser will be needed who can put greater pressure on him. In that case, if His Honour Mr. Hudde authorizes me to do so, I will call on the distinguished Mr. Hop or some other person and will consult him about the whole matter.
(Latin) Please remember me to Mr. Le Clerc. I sent him the second and third books of my treatise on the understanding in the month of September, so far as I remember; Peter Sunmans,†1 a young man from Rotterdam who is well known to Furly's family, took them with him when he left. I will send him the rest shortly, and if he thinks fit to send me the translation I will correct any passage in it that fails to represent my meaning. Now that the term, as our lawyers say, is over†2 I await the list of printed books;†3 I will write to Mr. Le Clerc as soon as I get it.
(Latin) [p. 739] Please remember me very kindly to your family and to all the Veens and Guenellons. Good-bye, and continue to love
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE
Address: Mijn Heer Mijn Heer Limborch bÿ de Remonstranse Kerck op de Keÿsars Graft t'Amsterdam
Noted by van Limborch beneath date: Accepta 23/13 Decemb.

1215. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 28 October/7 November and 3/13 December 1689 (1213, 1223)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 36-7. Probably enclosed with no. 1212: no. 1223. Answered by no. 1229.
(English) Vir Amplissime Amicorum Summe
Nullam ad Te scribendi occasionem prætermittere possum, licet nulla gravis scribendi materia se offerat, nisi hæc unica, quam Tibi non ingratam scio, omnes nos, omnesque Collegas, inter frequentes febres quibus tota Hollandia gravissime infestatur, rectissime valere: Deus spero nos porro ab iisdem immunes præservabit. Epistolas meas, Theam, et fasciculum librorum per Excellentissimum Legatum jam Tibi traditas nullus dubito. Post abitum Comitis Pembrokiensis, secretarius Domini Dorsleii†1 tuas ad D. Clericum misit, ex quibus intelligo, Te errore quodam petiisse bina exemplaria Actorum anni 1688. cum unum suffecisset. Si in tempore epistola hæc D.Clerico missa fuisset, potuisset error ille corrigi: Verum Secretarius, qui fortasse ignoravit festinandum esse, aliis impeditus non nisi post plures jam dies elapsos eam misit. Desideramus certiora de Tua valetudine cognoscere. Sladum nostrum jam vidisti; petiit a me commendatitias ad Rev. Episcopum Salisburiensem,
― 741 ―
quas homini amicissimo lubentissime misi, quamvis sciam tua commendatione instructum meâ neutiquam indigere. Habet literas meas ad D. Allix, cui aliæ ad D. Richardum Kidder inclusæ sunt: eas velim, ut tandem Londinum delatus, amicis meis exhibeat, ne a me audiat, tarde advenisse lentulum.†1 Librum de Inquisitione Tholosana totum jam perlegi, apographumque cum autographo accuratissime contuli, et Wetstenio obtuli: ille alia quaedam causatus moras nectit: nescio an chartæ caritas, an fratris dehortatio†2 eum tardiorem ad edendum reddat: an vero, argenti quod restat solutionem aliquamdiu differre cupiat, ideoque petierit, ut apographum apud me maneat. Quomodo hoc D. Furlæo placeat, ignoro. Causabitur fortasse ille, ita triennium illud, quod in contractu stipulatus est Wetstenius, posse in quadriennium extendi: verum incommodo illi aliquatenus occurri potest, si triennium illud inchoetur a dië, quo ipsi apographum obtuli. Posses, si nondum D. Furlæus Anglia exierit, hoc ipsi indicari. Velim etiam ipsi dare pecuniam, quæ hactenus in custodia meâ fuit: alienæ enim pecuniæ curâ me liberatum cupio. Si brevi huc redeat D. Furlæus, cum ipso
― 742 ―
omnia facillime transigere potero. Prodiit hic Richardi Simonis Historia Critica Versionum N. Testamenti,†1 qua multa lectu digna contineri credo; quæ enim sparsim apud alios inveniuntur, ille collegit. An omnium æquum se exhibeat judicem, valde dubito. Verum et nostrum est, ipsum cum judicio legere, quæ bona habet seligere; reliqua tanquam non scripta negligere. Ecquid placet in Anglia Clerici nostri historia Jansenismi decimo quarto Bibliothecæ Universalis tomo inserta?†2 Hic summo cum applausu legitur: Multa continet curiosa, et ex quibus exactior illius historia cognosci potest. An judicium illius liberum de Augustino, et de terminis in negotio prædestionis ab Augustino et Jansenistis adhiberi solitis, rigidioribus inter Calvinistas ullo modo placiturum sit, valde dubito. Sacrosancta ipsis est Augustini autoritas, et fortasse minus ægre ferunt Jacobi Apostoli, quam Divi Augustini ullatenus imminui autoritatem. Episcopius in scripto Belgico alicubi ait, Augustinum in juventute Manichaicis erroribus imbutum, fortasse illorum quasdam reliquias in disputatione contra Pelagium
― 743 ―
retinuisse. Id adeo indigne tulit Heidanus,†1 vix aliter, quam si esset convitium in ipsum Paulum Apostolum conjectum, cujus doctrina eadem est quæ Augustini. Dicit enim. 'An accusatio hæc eò solummodo respicit, quia ipse Manichæus fuit? Itaque eadem ratione accuset magnum nostrum Apostolum, quod post suam conversionem reliquias quasdam Pharisaismi retinuerit, quia Pharizæus et illius sectæ zelotes fuit. Si Episcopius hic quod sentit enuntiasset, non dubito quin eadem, et fortasse æquali jure, de Apostolo Paulo pronuntiare ausus fuisset.' Ecce quam inexpiabile crimen sit, aliquid de S. Augustino, quod Doctoribus illis ingratum est, enuntiare. Ubi affectus ejusmodi dominantur, tractatuum de pace Ecclesiæ vix ullum sperare possum fructum. Mitiora Anglorum ingenia spero, alias de pace inter partes dissidentes actum erit. Quamdiu humanæ autoritatis vinculis hominum conscientiæ constrictæ tenentur, frustra de pace laboramus. Unusquisque doctorum suorum placita pertinacissime defendet, et ne latum quidem unguem ab iis discedi patietur. Ita omnes Papatum, quem ore detestantur, animo fovent. Verum satis est. Ego omnia Tibi precor ex voto.
― 744 ―
DD. Venius et Guenellonus plurimam Tibi precantur salutem, uti et uxor mea liberique, omnesque precamur ut quam diutissime valeas.
Tui Amantissimus
PHILIPPUS A LIMBORCH

Amstelodami 13 Decembris

(Latin) Excellent Sir and best of friends,
I cannot lose any opportunity of writing to you, although there may be nothing of great importance to write about, unless it be this one thing, which I know you will be glad to hear, namely that all of us and all our Collegians are in excellent health, in spite of the widespread fevers now raging throughout Holland; I hope that God may continue to keep us free from them. No doubt my letters, the tea, and the parcel of books will have reached you by now through his excellency the ambassador. After the earl of Pembroke's departure Lord Dursley's secretary†1 sent your letter to Mr. Le Clerc; I understand from it that by some mistake you had asked for two copies of the Acta for the year 1688, whereas one would have been enough. If this letter had been sent to Mr. Le Clerc in time the mistake could have been corrected; but the secretary, who perhaps did not realize the need for haste, was busy with other things and did not send it until several days later. We desire definite news about your health. You have seen our friend Sladus by now; he asked me for a letter of introduction to the reverend [p. 741] the bishop of Salisbury, which I was very glad to send to such a good friend, though I am aware that being provided with your introduction he has no need of mine. He has a letter of mine for Mr. Allix, enclosed with which is another for Mr. Richard Kidder; I should like him to show these to my friends as proof that he has at last come to port in London, lest I should have to tell him that the laggard has arrived late.†1 I have now read right through the book of the Inquisition at Toulouse; I have carefully collated the copy with the original and have offered it to Wetstein; he is delaying the business for some other reasons; I do not know whether it is the dearness of paper or the discouragement he has received from his brother†2 that is making him slower to proceed with publication; it may be indeed that he desires to put off for a time the payment of the money still due, and that this is why he has asked that the copy may remain in my hands. I do not know how Mr. Furly may like this. Possibly he will complain that this may involve the extension to four years of the three agreed to by Wetstein in the contract; but that trouble can be met to some extent if the three years are made to begin from the day that I offered him the copy. You might point this out to Mr. Furly if he has not yet left England. I should also like to give him the money which has been in my keeping up to now; I desire to be relieved of the care of another person's money. If Mr. Furly returns here soon I shall [p. 742] be able to settle everything with him in person without difficulty. Richard Simon's Histoire critique des versions du Nouveau Testament has appeared here;†1 I believe there is much that is worth reading in it; he has collected material that is only to be found scattered in other writers. I doubt very much whether he shows a balanced judgement on all points. But it is our duty too to read him judiciously, choosing out the good to be found in him, and setting aside the rest as if it had never been written. What do they think in England of our friend Le Clerc's account of Jansenism, included in the fourteenth volume of the Bibliotbeque universelle?†2 It is meeting with great approval from readers in this country; there are many things of interest in it, and which enable one to obtain a more accurate knowledge of the history of the movement. Whether his freely expressed opinions on Augustine and on the terms customarily employed by Augustine and the Jansenists in the matter of predestination are likely to find any favour with the more rigid Calvinists is a matter of considerable doubt to me. Augustine's authority is sacrosanct to them, and one may guess that they are less put out by any disparagement of the Apostle James's authority than by any of St. Augustine's. Episcopius says somewhere in a Dutch work that Augustine, having been imbued in his youth with Manichaean errors, possibly retained some traces of these [p. 743] in his disputation against Pelagius. This offended Heidanus†1 almost as much as if it were a piece of abuse levelled at Paul the Apostle himself, whose doctrine is the same as Augustine's. He says: 'Does this accusation rest merely on the fact that Augustine was once a Manichee? By the same reasoning, then, let him accuse our great Apostle of having retained after his conversion certain vestiges of Pharisaism, because he had been a Pharisee and a fanatical member of that sect. If Episcopius had spoken out what was here in his mind, I have no doubt that he would have dared to make a similar pronouncement, and perhaps with equal justice, about the Apostle Paul.' You see what an unforgivable crime it is to utter a word about St. Augustine that displeases those doctors. Where such feelings hold sway I can hardly hope for any profit from treatises on Church peace. I hope that English tempers are milder, otherwise it will be all over with peace between the opposing parties. So long as men's consciences are shackled by human authority our labour for peace is in vain. Every one of the doctors will defend his particular tenets to the death and will not suffer departure from them by so much as a finger's breadth. So it is that they all cherish at heart the Popedom that they profess to detest. But enough of that. I pray that all may go happily with you. Messrs. Veen and [p. 744] Guenellon send you their warmest greetings, as do my wife and children, and we all pray for your lasting good health.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 7 November
1689
(Latin) Excellent Sir, you see the date of the above letter. Mr. Le Clerc took it from me and entrusted it to a bookseller who was hurrying to England and who was to deliver it to you;†1 he, however, had a similar experience to your servant's: after several days' tossing on the waves he at last returned to harbour here, not without considerable damage to his books through wetting with sea-water, and gave us back the letter. I now send it to you once more by the ordinary post, in the hope of overcoming your silence by writing frequently. My letter to Mr. Allix has now been delivered to him by Mr. Sladus, as he tells me in his own letter,†2 which I answered at some length about ten days ago; I hope my answer has not gone astray. I am glad that Mr. Sladus has returned to you and that there is an end of all the [p. 745] disquieting rumours about him. I have sent Mr. Allix, with Wetstein's consent, a brief account of the tenets and practices customary among the Albigenses as well as the Waldenses, which I hope has not been lost. I am, however, keeping it by me in a more studied form; for one cannot in a letter establish everything with supporting evidence or go into all details, unless the letter is to grow to the bulk of a pamphlet. I do not know whether he means to insert any points from my letter in his treatise on the Waldenses, which he has ready for publication.†1 I myself am soon going to write a preface, that is, a short account of the Holy Office, which may serve as a preface,†2 so that everything may be ready and Wetstein may not only make a start with the production but may be as quick as possible about it and finish it without delay. We hear nothing about the treatises on church peace in your country, so we cannot as yet promise ourselves any measure of success from them; so long as everyone continues to seek his own good and no one that of another, unless perhaps he desires to appropriate what belongs to that other, the work of peace will remain undone. All of us here are well. Mr. Veen had a rather serious illness, but he has now recovered. Mr. Quina, too, was in pain with the stone for some days; he is now better. But I expect Mr. Guenellon will write to you more fully about these matters. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and [p. 746] my very good friend, and show that you have not forgotten me by a letter, as long a one as you like.
Amsterdam 13 December
1689

Entre plusieurs obligations que je vous ai, Monsieur, l'honneur que vous me faites de me procurer la connoissance de vos Amis qui viennent en Hollande, n'est pas l'une des moindres. Barker.†2 J'ose vous prier de vous informer, sans qu'il paroisse que cela vienne de moi, si ces deux exemplaires ont été bien rendus; et s'ils l'ont été, comme je le crois, si la maniére dont j'ai traité cette Histoire est au goût d'une personne aussi éclairée que l'est cet illustre Comte. Je ne sais si je vous dois demander, Monsieur, vôtre propre jugement, parce qu'il m'est d'ordinaire si avantageux, que je commence à soupçonner que l'amitié dont vous m'honorez ne le corrompe un peu en ma faveur. Vôtre tres-humble et très obeïssant serviteur

1223. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 17/27 December 1689 (1215, 1229)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 38-9. Answers no. 1213; answered by no. 1229.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Gratissimas tuas diuque exspectatas 23 hujus mensis accepi. Interim meas D. Guenelloni inclusas literis†1 ad Te pervenisse, nullus dubito. Vides me quamvis ad Te scribendi occasionem avide arripere: si nimia loquacitate molestus sum, scito, me hac ratione ulcisci tuum silentium: nihil enim literis tuis gratius est, quæ quanto prolixiores, eo gratiores.†2 Nescio autem quid ætatem incuses, cum nullum contrahas senium, nec senectutis infirmitatibus graveris. Solent plerumque senes loquacitatis accusari: si vero exinde de ætate judicium fieri debeat, ego Te juvenem valde pronuntiare cogor, adeo exacte observas silentium. Dixerant mihi amici, munus Tibi obtigisse otiosum:†3 Gaudebam equidem, tum, quia nullum ex tali munere studiis tuis impedimentum, tum et crebriores ad nos literas sperabam: Verum nunc continuis occupationibus Te detineri scribis,
― 755 ―
quas sive muneris ratio, sive alia officia Tibi objiciunt, nos dulcissimo amicitiæ tuæ fructu destituimur. Interim si quid scriptu dignum hic acciderit, calamum cohibere non potero; et sicut Tui memor vivo, ita mei memoriam Tibi unquam excidere non patiar. Habes hic iterum loquacitatis meæ initium, quo pede si pergam, nec a tergo scripta epistola finem habebit.†1 Brevior ergo ero. Theam librosque Tibi traditos gaudeo: Theam spero placuisse. Melior hic non prostat, et sapor mihi maxime placebat. Non est, quod ita festines pretium mihi restituere. Ex postremis meis intellexeris jam partem pecuniæ Furleianæ in meis adhuc esse manibus. Si per Furleium mihi nummos illos annumerari velis, possem ex iis quos habeo illos mihi retinere, et literæ tuæ Cambii possent recipi a Furleio quando rationem commissæ mihi pecuniæ reddo: Vel si aliam malis rationem, mihi perinde est, totum id arbitrii tui facio. Gaudeo tractatui tuo de Intellectu humano ultimam esse impositam manum; doleo vero tantam mihi non esse linguæ Anglicanæ peritiam, ut eum bene intelligere queam: Ex compendio enim, quantum ex tam erudito et perspicuo tractatu utilitatis orbis percepturus sit, satis constat. Versionem ejus Latinam prodituram non dubito, quæ si a Te relegatur et corrigatur, etiam Te Latine loquentem aliquatenus
― 756 ―
habebimus. Quod non displicuerit Excellentissimo Comiti†1 alloquium meum, est quod mihi gratuler maximopere: Si alterum congressum sperare ausus fuissem, adhuc per diem unum aut alterum Hagæ substitissem. Chartas per juvenem Roterodamensem missas accepit D. Clericus, idque eum jam Tibi per literas significasse puto. D. Kidderi literas exspectabo: meas ad D. Allix recte perlatas spero; erant paulo prolixiores, variaque de Albigensibùs et Valdensibus iis erant inserta. Ut tandem ad Sladum nostrum veniam: Literas tuas prælegi Illustrissimo nostro Consuli D. Hudde; omnia quæ mihi scripsisti jam illi innotuerant: Commendat Tibi Sladum, aitque Te gratum sibi facturum officium, imo gratissimum, si pro prudentia tua eum cures, et modereris. Novit etiam ille ingenium illius; itaque prudenter curari debet, præsertim si ulla turbatæ mentis indicia adesse credantur. Minime tamen Tibi autor est, ut de ipso quicquam ad D. Hop referas: tum quia illi nulla est cum Slado familiaritas; tum etiam quia junior est, ac proinde nulla illius apud nostrum futura esset autoritas: quin imo si aliqua vellet uti autoritate, eam noster plane respueret; atque ita magis exasperaretur malum. Addebat D. Consul, D. Hop cum tota familia esse Londini:
― 757 ―
si quid ergo plenius ipsi de statu amici nostri innotescat, illud facile per totam ejus familiam posse disseminari: atque ita etiam huc transvolare. Quare commendat ut consilia tua de amico nostro cum illo non communices. Scripsit ipse Consul ad Sladum, monitaque ipsi salutaria suggessit, quæ alicujus apud ipsum spero fore autoritatis. Verum, quod doleo, rumor hic jam sparsus est, varia mentis sibi non constantis indicia in Slado deprehendi: quæcunque enim mihi scribis, jam indicata erant, etiam de itinere Windesoriano et Oxoniensi, quod solus absque comite hac anni tempestate pedibus conficere velle dicebatur: aliquis enim ipsi notus Londino huc reversus pluribus illud narravit. Quare si alia mentis bene sibi constantis indicia deprehendas, rogo ea scribas, ut sic sinistro isti rumori occurrere possim. Ego interim quod mihi scripsisti intra silentii arcana sancte asservabo. Etiam in nostra civitate habemus virum eximium, cui mens jam plane turbata est, Consulem videl. van Beuningen,†1 qui ad omnes literas mittit: omnes Christianos horrendæ accusat hæreseos et apostasiæ; omne ministerium
― 758 ―

abrogatum cupit, non tantum Ecclesiasticum, sed et civile: Judæos ad fidem Christi convertere vult: Nunc Apocalypsin explicat, novasque illius interpretationes excogitavit; scriptaque sua ad quosvis quaquaversum mittit: indignatur vero, a nemine se responsum obtinere, idque desperatæ impietatis indicium credit, cum omnes exitialium hæresium insimulet, nemoque illi respondere suamque causam defendere possit, quod ex silentio colligit, omnes tamen in cultibus suis hæreticis et apostaticis perseverent. Mira in illius ingenio mixtura est; varia legit, eaque nunc sine ullo ordine et delectu menti ipsius obversantur: Quasdam habet de officiis vitæ Christianæ periodus elegantissimas, succinctas, verbisque maxime emphaticis expressas; sed tot permixtas absurdis, ut omnis illarum usus pereat. Sermones ipsius plane sunt desultorii, et una hora de viginti ac pluribus materiis disserit, et quas jam reliquit subinde repetit, et abrumpit, sine ullo judicio ac methodo. Expertus loquor. Doleo sortem viri, summis in patria nostra honoribus, et ad Potentissimos Europæ reges legationibus magno cum honore functi. Verum hæc hactenus. Vides quam difficulter ac ægre desinam, cum ad Te scribo: Si nimiâ loquacitate molestus sum, crebrius ad Te scribendi occasionem suppedita, et brevior esse cogar. Venius,
― 759 ―
Guenellonus, omnesque amici plurimum Te salvere jubent. Imprimis autem salutem Tibi dicit uxor mea. Vale Amplissime Vir, ac memor semper vive
Tui
P. A LIMBORCH.

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
Your most welcome letter, which I had so long waited for, reached me on the 23rd of this month. Meanwhile you have no doubt received mine which was enclosed with Mr. Guenellon's.†1 You see how greedily I snatch at any opportunity of writing to you; if my excessive chatter is a nuisance to you, take notice that this is my way of having my revenge for your silence; for nothing gives me greater pleasure than letters from you; the longer they are the better I like them.†2 As for your age, I do not know why you should lay the blame on that, seeing that you show no signs of debility and are not weighed down by the infirmities of old age. Old men are usually accused of loquacity; but if one is to judge of age from that, I am compelled to pronounce you remarkably young, you are such a studious observer of silence. Friends had told me that the post you have obtained allowed you leisure;†3 I was glad of that, both because I hoped that such a post would not hinder your studies, and that you would write to us oftener; as it is, however, you say that you are continually occupied with affairs; whether such are imposed on you by [p. 755] the duties of your office or by other obligations, we at least are debarred from profiting by your friendship in the most delightful way. Meanwhile, if anything worth writing about happens here, I shall not be able to restrain my pen; just as you are always in my memory, so, I declare, I will never allow myself to drop out of yours. There you have me started once more on my chatter; if I go on at this rate the letter will never be finished, even if it is written on the back.†1 So I will be briefer. I am glad the tea and the books reached you safely; I hope the tea was to your liking. There is no better sort on sale here, and I was very pleased with its flavour. There is no need for you to hurry about paying me for it. You will have understood from my last that I still have some of Furly's money in my hands. If you would like to pay me the sum through Furly, I could then keep that amount for myself out of what I have of his, and Furly could accept your note of exchange when I give him my account of the money he entrusted to me; or if you should prefer to do it some other way, it makes no difference to me; I leave it entirely to you. I am glad to hear that your treatise on the Human Understanding is at last finished, though I regret that I have not enough knowledge of English to be able to understand it properly; for it is clear enough from the epitome what great advantage the world will derive from such a scholarly and lucid work. The Latin translation of it will no doubt appear; if this can be read over and corrected by yourself we shall even hear some sound of your voice in elegant Latin.†a [p. 756] That His Excellency the earl†1 was not displeased with my approach to him is a matter on which I much congratulate myself; if I had presumed to hope for a second meeting I would have stayed on at The Hague for another day or two. Mr. Le Clerc has received the papers you sent him by the hand of the young man from Rotterdam, as I expect he has already told you by letter. I shall await a letter from Mr. Kidder; my own to Mr. Allix I hope has reached him safely; it was a rather long one, with various things about the Albigenses and Waldenses in it. To come at last to our friend Sladus: I read your letter to our illustrious burgomaster Mr. Hudde; he was already acquainted with all that you told me in it; he recommends Sladus to your care, saying that he would be deeply, indeed most deeply obliged to you if you would in your wisdom see to him and control him. He too knows Sladus's temperament; he needs to be discreetly looked after, especially if there is reason to think that there are any signs of mental disturbance. He strongly advises you, however, not to say anything about Sladus to Mr. Hop; for one thing because he has no sort of intimacy with Sladus, also because he is a younger man, and would therefore not be likely to have any authority with our friend; indeed, if he tried to use any such authority our friend would flatly reject it, and so the trouble would be aggravated all the more. The burgomaster added that Mr. Hop was in London with his whole household; so that if he were to [p. 757] get any fuller information about our friend's condition this might easily be passed round his whole household, and so might even get across to this country. For this reason he recommends you not to communicate any of your plans for our friend to Mr. Hop. The burgomaster has written to Sladus himself and has given him some wholesome advice, which I hope will be of some weight with him. I am sorry to say, however, that there is already a rumour going about here that various signs of an unsettled mind are being observed in Sladus; all the things you mentioned to me in your letter had already been pointed out, even that journey to Windsor and Oxford, which, it was said, he wanted to make alone and unaccompanied on foot, and at this time of year; for some one who was known to him came back here from London and told a number of people about it. If, therefore, you should detect any other signs of better mental balance in him I beg you to let me know of them by letter, so that I can use them to counteract this disquieting talk. Meanwhile I will observe the most scrupulous silence about what you have told me. In our own city, too, we have a distinguished man whose mind is now manifestly deranged, I mean the burgomaster van Beuningen;†1 he writes letters to everyone, accusing all Christians of terrible heresy and apostasy; he desires the abolition of all government, not only in the Church but in the state as [p. 758] well; he wants to convert the Jews to the Christian faith. Just now he is explaining the Apocalypse; he has thought out some new interpretations of it and is sending his views in writing to anybody and everybody; what moves his wrath, however, is that he cannot get a reply from any one, which he takes for a sign of desperate ungodliness, seeing that though he is charging them all with mortal heresies not one of them is able to reply in defence of his own views, as he concludes from their silence; yet they all persist in their heretical and apostatical practices. There is a strange mixture in him; he has read widely, and the results of his reading now float before his mind indiscriminately and in no sort of order; he has some passages on the duties of the Christian life that are well and concisely worded and couched in very forcible language; but they are mixed up with so many absurdities that all their value is lost. His talk is utterly disconnected; in a single hour he discourses on twenty or more subjects; every now and then he returns to one he has already done with and drops it again, all without any judgement or method. I speak from experience. I grieve for the plight of a man who has enjoyed the highest honours in our country, and who has fulfilled with the greatest credit the duties of an envoy to the mightiest princes in Europe. But enough of this. You see how difficult and disagreeable I find it to leave off when I am writing to you; if I annoy you with my excessive loquacity you must give me occasion to write oftener, and I shall then have to be briefer. Veen, Guenellon, [p. 759] and all our friends send you their best wishes. My wife in particular sends you her greetings. Good-bye, excellent Sir, and ever keep in mind
<PS:"SO2">Your friend
P. VAN LIMBORCH.
Amsterdam 27 December
1689

1225. James Tyrrell to Locke, [c. 19] December [1689] (1015, 1226; see also no. 1027)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 71-2. Answer to a letter received on Wednesday, 18 December; written not later than 8 a.m. on 20 December; sent to Locke finally apparently on 22 December with no. 1227. The year from Locke's endorsement.
Oxford Decem:
Dear Sir
I have received your cold, and short letter in answere to which I am forced to write over and make much longer one I have had by me these 4; or 5 days; ever since your good Freind Dr: Sladus gave me notice of his intentions to returne to London, whose company as I have enjoyd here with a great deal of Freedome and satisfaction, so I hope he will tell you he hath not fared the worse for being your Freind: since besides his owne merits which may claime a great deal: I have not used him like a stranger upon your score: but in this letter which I have now before me; I let you know, that I was extreme glad to hear by him the good news of your health, and that without a cold this winter season; and in London; which I hope may be still continued to you, since (Ile assure you) it shall ever be of great concerne to me; (whatever unkind thoughts you may please to entertaine of me) for I thanke God I am not conscious to my self, of falling out with, or leaveing my Freinds upon small quarrells; or groundlesse suspicions, or think my self set loose from the bonds of Freindship, and gratitude, if a Person to whom I am obliged for many kindnesses declines my company, neglects to answere my letters; and in short lets me see by his constant coldnesse and reservednesse, that he has put me from the first rate of Freinds into the second or third of his ordinary acquaintance; how much truth there may be in this I leave it to his conscience to Judge who never answer'd his Freinds letter in 2, or three monthes, tho' he then intended to come for England, and might beleive that the notice of it would be welcome to him; yet could not communicate it because it was a publick secret. and therefore before you reprove me for not writeing; pray consider who writ last, and who hath made 20 visites without ever being repayed one. I doe not write this, that I stand upon such childish punctilios, or that I should thinke much to write 20 letters, or make as many visites without the least returne; if I did not see that these things are made occasions of unkindnesse from others; tho
― 762 ―
they are not so when done by your self; or that I were sure that such little slights were not signs of a decaying freindship; and which perhaps you may thinke too burdensome to you to†a- maintaine longer:-†a but for all this; I was so far from takeing notice of any of these things (tho I assure you they sate somewhat hard upon my mind) that in this letter, I had now writ to you, I had taken notice of no such thing: but as if I were altogether in fault had excused my long silence; hopeing you would take it for a sufficient reason that I writ not to you all the summer, since I knew not where to direct a letter to you. for you told me you thought you should goe to the Bathe in August; and should goe farther into the west till towards Michael masse; which whether you did or not is more then I can tell:†1 and indeed I had writ to you above a month since; but that I stayed for a latine booke of my Grandfathers which is newly come out de SS: in Lingua vernacula legendis.†2 which I hoped to have had to have sent with it: but that I could not hear from Dr: Parr where I might send for the Copyes he promised me out of those which the bookseller presented him with: but as soon as I can tell you where you may have one whether at Dr. Parrs booksellers: or Chiswells†3 (who prints it.) I will order one to be sent you; if you doe not call for it: I thought indeed when I first came up out of the northwest of England, where I had bin for near 3 monthes, to have come up to London the last Terme; but receiveing letters from my son; and from Sir William Colt who advised me to send him to the Academy of Wolfenboutel;†4 as he allso desired himself; presseing me allso for a present supply of money; since the half years pension is to be payed before hand; I was obliged to send him 2 bills of exchange for 40l: besides some cloathes; and more money I am to send him after Christmasse; which†b together with the great taxes; and ill payment of Tenants, makes me alter my mind as to my comeing up; and rather to chuse this place for cheapnesse as well as privacy; my Genius being neither suited. to get by bustleing nor scrambleing: If I can find here 2, or three ingenious men to passe the evening with sometimes it is company enough: I am
― 763 ―
about somewhat which perhaps may be usefull to the publick which you may see when it is done;†1 if you thinke it worth your while: thus haveing freely unburdened my heart to you, of what lay most heavy upon it; you may make what use of it you thinke good; either as a spur to quicken a decaying Freindship; or else to let it sinke into a bare civil acquaintance; for I hope wee shall not make a publick quarrell of it: but I call God to witnesse, that I never did, or sayd any thing on purpose or maliciously to your prejudice, or if I have not desired†a your Freindship with the utmost zeal: and If I have in any thing offended, pray let me know it; and if guilty I will beg pardon with all my heart; for Ile assure you nothing goes nearer my heart then the least slight; and unkindnesse from an old Freind: yet however I give you thankes for the onely gratefull part of your letter the kind offer of one of your bookes de Intellectu; which haveing already a great value for, from onely the rough draught still in my hands:†2 I have therefore so much the greater desire to reade it; now it is encreased with so many new notions. It came downe to oxford last weeke and many copyes are sold of it, and I hear it is well approved of by those who have began the readeing of it; for my part I have read no more then the Epistle and part of the preface: and for the rest wait for this much desired favour to
your most humble: and faithfull servant; (I dare not say
Freind because you doe not owne that title.)
J TYRRELL.

1226. James Tyrrell to Locke, 20 December [1689] (1225, 1227)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 73-4. For a copy see no. 1229 n. Year from Locke's endorsement. The time of writing is half an hour before or after noon. Apparently sent with no. 1227 on 22 December.
Oxford Dec: 20th: 1/2 of the clock
Dear Sir
I received yours on†b wednesday†b †3 and had writ a long letter in answere to it, by your good Freind Dr: Slade; which I hoped would have come to your hands as to morrow night, had it not bin for that, which disappoints all Mortal designes: the sudden death of the poor Doctor. of which I can onely give you this short account: that last night he supt very well, and I never heard him complaine of any illnesse: he tooke his leave of me; and went to his Lodging: this morneing he came to me againe presently after 8: to drinke a dish of chocolate before he went away in the Coach: I made it myself; dranke with him of it; and wee sate by the fire and talkt together till the Coach calld for him, I never saw him chearfuller; nor better since he came hither: I took my leave of him at the coach: little thinkeing I should never see him more alive: his last words to me were. Domine. gratias. pro tuis beneficiis, fere tibi debeo meum
― 765 ―
animum:†1 just as I was siting downe to dinner:†2 there came one from wheatley†3 to Dr: Bernard who brought word that the Doctor who went in the Coach dyed there: a little before he came to that Towne: the Fellow that came, is a barber that lets blood; and sayed he had let him blood but that he was stone dead before he could come to him: It is a sad accident; and that I am extremely troubled for, it; he was an honest, learned, and good humour'd man; and upon your account as well as his owne had he bin my Father I could not have used him with more kindnesse and respect: I have not time to write more the letter carrier being just ready to goe away, and I am just now goeing to Wheatley to give order for his being brought to Oxford, and buryed in the parish church where he dyed: I designe to have him opend before a Physitian to see what he dyed of and to have a certificate made of it for the satisfaction of his Freinds: Dr: Bernard and I will see him interred, as decently, and privately as wee can; and what it comes to you shall know; and I must leave it to you to see payed: who know his relations: whether in england or Holland I know, not; were I assured there was any of them in London. that would come downe; and take the trouble of his Funerall upon them; wee would let it alone till they came: however wee are resolved not to bury him (unlesse the body will not keep) untill twesday or wednesday night; wee know not whether: So that any one that will take the trouble to come downe may be here well enough by twesday 5 of the clock in the Coach: all the things shall be ready so that they shall be at no more trouble then to see the body layed in the ground: and to pay the charges. of the funeral; which however shall be done whether they come or not: He had but little Above 20s: about him to my knowledg which I hope I shall secure. I have no more but in much trouble, and hast rest
Your Freind; and humble servant.
J. TYRRELL.
