1227. James Tyrrell to Locke, 22 December [1689] (1226, 1228, 1236)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, f. 75. For a partial copy see no. 1229 n. Year from Locke's endorsement.
Oxford Decem 22th:
Dear Sir
These enclosed should have come to your hands last weeke; the lesser by the letter carrier on Saterday;†1 and the bigger by Dr: Slade:†2 If it pleased God not <to>†a have brought him to his Journeys <end>†a before he could reach London: therefore if you please before you proceed farther to reade this open†b letter†b (which the carrier being gone I was not able to send till to day) and you will see how frail a thing humane life is:—supposeing now you have read my first letter (which I could easyer send you as it is, then write over into this) all I can adde farther is; that wee have altered our resolutions as to the keeping of the body till twesday for some of his freinds to come to his funeral; since it is impossible now, unlesse he were embalmed: and therefore wee resolve to bury him this evening; and have invited near 20 Doctors of†c- Divinity and Physick-†c and Gentlemen of the University and Towne who had the happynesse to have any conversation with this good Doctor dureing the short time he stayed among us: wee bury him in St: Peters church yard,†3 where his Freinds may put a monument over him if they please: or remove him into the Church: but being to doe it out of other peoples purses wee have bin as frugal as wee could: I know not what the charge of it will come to yet; more then that small summe he had about him: but the next post I suppose Dr Bernard will send you an account of the whole of the funeral charges which I desire you to shew his Freinds in London because He; and I stand engaged for it, where it is due; and therefore wee desire it may be sent downe to him by bill or other wise as you shall thinke good: for wee have performed this last office for him with all the Decency; that wee could, avoydeing all unnecessary expence. yesterday in the afternoon as soon as the Corps was brought to Towne I orderd the head to be opend in the presence of Dr:
― 767 ―
Gibbons;†1 and divers other Physitians: who all agreed that he dyed of an Apoplexy; the vessels in the braine being more then ordinaryly distended with blood; and the Glandules in the small plexus Choroides being sweld to the bignesse: of a†a small fetche:†b †2 if he had not had the ill fortune to dye in the Coach where he had no help, he might have come to himself again by blooding: but when he came to Whetley the man tell me he tryed to bleed him but could not make him bleed, but it was in the Arme not in the Jugular: all the account I can give farther of his death (not speakeing as yet with the coach man my self) is that he walkt up Shotover Hill and when he came to the Top finding himself not well he tooke some Brandy at the cabbin on Top of the hill. after drinkeing which he fell worse; and so into the Agonyes of death so that before they reacht wheatley he was quite dead. I was never more surprised in my life then to hear it: that afternoon I went on purpose to wheatley: to give order about the striping and laying out of the body; and to secure his things: which together with his cloathes are all here; and shall be disposed of according to his Freinds orders: for they are safe lockt up at the Angel Inne:†3 onely my man who tooke some pains in the goeing to Wheatley; and seeing him coffind and brought to Towne, begs his cane and steel hilted if his freinds please to let him have it, if not it shall be sent up with the rest of his things: and bookes: which were very few; est enim valde curta supellex,†4 for so rich a man as I hear he is. So leaveing it to your discretion to mannage this affair: and expecting an answere from you to my letters I remaine
Your humble servant
J TYRRELL

[Tyrrell to Bernard:]
Reverend Sir
Being now to go out of Town, in haste, I hope you will excuse me from giving you any further trouble: Since I can only tell you that I have here sent you two Coppies of the Charges of the Doctors Funerals, one of which, I desire you would send by to morrow's Post, enclosed in a Letter, to Mr John Lock, at his lodgings at Mrs Smythbyes house in the new Court in Channel Row, and intreat him to speak to the Doctor's Friends in London to return down this 6 pounds four shilings for the Funeral Charges: And to let them know that if they doe not like his being buried in the Church yard; he shall be remov'd where they please. And likewise if they desire to have a Monument erected for him, That you and I will see it faithfully perform'd, according to what they please to allow for that purpose. If you receive the money before my return out of the Country, as I hope you will, I pray will you be pleas'd to discharge with it, all the Summs in this Note except it be those that are Cross'd, Mrs Parker†1 knows where the parties live to whom the money is to be paid, and I hope as soon as you have it you will be pleas'd to send to them, and what remains in your hands I desire you would Keep for my use, there being still more money due to me than the 01l.: 06s.: 06d found about him. So wishing you a happy restauration of your health, and that you may receive a Sp<eedy>†a Ans<w>er†a to this affaire I remain
Your most faithfull and humble servant
J TYRRELL
I have here sent you a Coppy of My Lord Primate late Treatise†2 in Sheets which were I to stay in Toun I would see bound but since I have not time, and do not know whither you do not desire to bind all your books alike, I have rather made bold to send it as it is than to presume to deprive you longer of it

Vir Amplissime
Gratissimas tuas 13o et 27o Decembris datas amore et benevolentiâ plenas recte accepi et tuum in me vel meâ negligentiâ immotum esse animum maxime gavisus sum. De cunctatione Wetstenii Furleium certiorem feci, qui propediem ad vos transiturus eam rem coram transiget. Interim editionem libri avide expecto. reliqua Clerici nostri scripta valde placeant. Salutes eum quæso meo nomine et gratias agas pro Epistola illius†1 cui proximâ septimanâ responsurus sum me hac vice impediit nimis funesta occasio. (Latin)
London 27 Dec 89
Excellent Sir,
I duly received your very welcome letters of 13 and 27 December, full as they are of affection and goodwill, and am most happy to know that your feelings towards me are unchanged even by my neglectfulness. I have told Furly about Wetstein's hesitation; he will be crossing to Holland shortly and will arrange the matter with him in person. Meanwhile I eagerly await the publication of the book. I feel sure that our friend Le Clerc's account of Jansenism will meet with approval from educated people in England, as his [p. 772] other writings are much appreciated. Please remember me to him and give him my thanks for his letter,†1 which I shall answer next week; I am prevented from doing so on this occasion by a very sad occurrence. It is only right that I should be anxious about the repayment of the money you have spent on my account; since, however, as you tell me, you have a certain amount of Furly's in your hands, please do whatever suits your convenience and as you may arrange it between you; it will be all the same to me so long as I get quit of that debt, at the same time giving you my best thanks.
(Latin) Ever since our friend Sladus left here for Oxford I had a foreboding of some trouble for him. Here at last is what the fates have willed. The enclosed letter to me from a friend at Oxford, a grandson of Ussher the great Archbishop of Armagh, will tell you the sad story of his death. Today, Furly, Francke, and I, in company with another Englishman and a notary public, visited his lodging in order to inspect whatever had been left there by him. Mr. Francke promised to write to His Honour Burgomaster Hudde tonight to let him know what was found there. The funeral was seen to by Mr. Bernard and Mr. Tyrrell, the archbishop's grandson. About 20 shillings of our money was found in Sladus's purse; in the box which he had left here in London there was nothing in gold or silver, though Francke told me he had [p. 773] seen him in possession of a considerable sum in gold. But since he did everything here without consulting his friends and saw me only once since he arrived in England, I do not know how one can set about an account of his money matters or where to make inquiries. He wrote to me when he was at Oxford to say he was short of money and to ask me to send him some, which I did, namely three and a half pounds sterling, that is, in your money about f.38 or f.39. The funeral expenses may, I think, be reckoned at about ten pounds sterling, or f.100; I hope this sum may be sent to us as quickly as possible, so that it may be repaid, with proper thanks, to those who have shown such kindness in undertaking that duty. This much in haste, as the post is just leaving; I will write to you soon more fully about these things. Meanwhile please give my respectful regards to the burgomaster and tell him how sorry I am to be relieved so soon of the charge he laid upon me. I send my best greeting to the Veens and Guenellons and to our Collegians. Goodbye and love me
Your most affectionate
J. LOCKE

1230. Mrs. Isabella Duke to Locke, 1 January 1690 (1168, 1263)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 8, ff. 41-2.
Otterton Jan: 1st. 89.
Dearest Sir
I have been now full three Months ballancing with my Selt which is the least disrespect to you, either omitting Writing to you wholly, or importuning you with repetitions of my Deep, and Gratfull Sense, of my Vast Obligations to you, which is the only Subject I can entertain you with from hence; and I cannot yet determin it; I have call'd in my Landlady's assistance too, and your Freind Mr Clarks, But neither of them will extricate me out of this great difficulty. permitt me then to Apply my self to you, the best of Freinds, since I know you have Goodness enough to help me in this Dilemna, or at least to pardon both my Silence and my Scribling; such kindness as your last expresses, will force even the Dumb to Speak; but when I reflect that I can say no more, But that I Love you, and that I Thank you; 'tis so poor a return to such Endearments, that I blush, and have not the Courage to send it; yet I have enough for my sex, on all other occasions. But, to Wast your pretious Time in reading what I have so often avow'd, and you have long since done me the Justice to believe, is to Trespass upon you, under the Colour of a Civillity; and to fail of that Great Respect with which I am, Dear Sir
Your most Obliged and Unalterable Freind and Servant
ISABELLA DUKE
My Master is your: most humble servant.
Address: These For Mr John Lock in London
Endorsed by Locke: I Duke 1 Jan 89/90

1232. —— Passebon to Locke, 7 January 1690 (1196, 1265)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 16, ff. 194-5.
Monsieur,
Le Pupille que vous m'avez fait l'honneur de me procurer, ne m'a pas donné lieu jusques a cette heure d'estre fort content de luy, pour toutes les peines, et tous les soins que j'en prens. Il n'a fait qu'un progrés mediocre en la langue Françoise, en l'écriture, et en l'Aritmetique: ce en quoy il me paroit avoir le plus profité, c'est
― 776 ―
en la lecture: car je conte pour rien, les dix Pseaumes françois et latins, ausquels il avoit appliqué depuis quelque temps une partie de son étude. Suivant le Conseil que vous me donnés, Monsieur, Je l'avanceray le plus que je pourrai en ma langue, et je l'exerceray en cette partie de la Grammaire qui regarde les declinaisons, et les conjugaisons: et pour la Geographie je la luy feray acquerir jusques au point que vous me marqués. Je ne vois pas qu'il soit necessaire de grossir sa biblioteque qu'a mesure de la necessité qu'il aura des livres. S'il estoit plus avancé en l'Aritmetique, Je vous prierois, Monsieur, de vous souvenir des Elemens des Mathematiques pour le temps du retour de Monsieur Son Pere.
Je savois bien, Monsieur, que vous prendriés quelque part au soin que je me donnerois de montrer le françois a vôtre petite maitresse, et que cela agréeroit a Monsieur son Pere et a Madame sa mere, il ne m'en falloit pas davantage pour l'en instruire avec plaisir, il n'estoit pas necessaire d'y joindre l'esperance de quelque benefice, puis que je n'en merite aucun. Je vous avoüe que Madame Clarke me surprit lors qu'elle me fit son present. Comme ma petite Ecoliere n'a rien plus a coeur que ce qui vous plait, Je vous supplie, Monsieur, de luy recommander par vos lettres de se bien appliquer aux leçons que je luy donne. Elle sait parfaitement bien son Catechisme en françois, et son frere dit qu'elle ne sait pas si exactement le mesme Catechisme en Anglois, Je feray en sorte qu'elle puisse savoir assez de François pour fournir a l'entretien, si elle vous voit dans quelques mois.
Lors que vous verrez Madame Lockard Je vous demande en grace, Monsieur, que vous l'assuriez de bien des respects pour moy, aussy bien que Madame sa Compagne†1 et que vous la priiez de faire mes soumissions tres respectueuses a Madame la Comtesse de Southerland, et de luy témoigner l'extreme part que je prends au rétablissement de sa santé. Ce que vous avez la bonté de me dire de ces Dames merite que je vous en remercie particulièrement. Je vous demande pardon d'abuser ainsi de vos faveurs; Je suis avec un tres profond respect,
Monsieur,
Vôtre tres humble et tres obeissant Serviteur
PASSEBON
A Chipley ce 7e Janvier 1690.

1233. Philippus Van Limborch to Locke, 10/20 January 1690 (1229, 1242)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 14, ff. 40-1. Answers no. 1229; answered by no. 1242.
(English) Vir Amplissime
Tandem literæ tuæ, 27 Decembris quidem scriptæ, non tamen ante diem 17 Januarii mihi redditæ, omnem nobis sollicitudinem, quam ex literis Franci de morte seu potius genere mortis Sladi conceperamus, exemerunt. Franci literæ, eodem dië quo tuæ scriptæ, integra hebdomade tuas anteverterunt, et generatim tantum D. Consuli Hudde subitum et inexspectatum Sladi obitum nuntiarunt, nulla omnino apoplexiæ, qua obiisse creditur, mentione facta: Et cum tuæ, quas ad me scriptas Francus indicabat, non comparerent, sinistri quid suspicati fuimus, quod vos sensim indicare consultum judicaveritis. D. Consul gratias Tibi per me agi voluit, quod eam amici sui curam habueris, testatusque est non semel, hoc tuum officium sibi esse gratissimum. Verum Francus errat, quod putet aureorum nummorum haud exiguum Slado fuisse numerum: Consanguinei ipsius unanimiter testantur, haud magnum aureorum nummorum numerum a Slado hinc in Angliam esse deportatum: habuisse ipsum literas cambii centum librarum Sterlingarum, quæ cum huc remissæ sint, inde colligunt, nihil pecuniæ avunculo suo ereptum, sed ipsum eâ, quam in crumena habuit, pecuniâ ad
― 778 ―
tolerandos quos in Anglia fecit sumptus, indiguisse. Misit Francus ad D. Consulem catalogum eorum, quæ in hospitio Sladi reperta sunt; Verum non sine admiratione in ea legit, mentionem fieri indusii, sanië quadam infecti, unde colligitur, eum incommodo aliquo in corpore suo laborasse. Non solent actuarii nostrates ejusmodi commentarios facere, sed nudum tantum rerum, quas inveniunt, scribere catalogum: Sed male D. Consulem habet, quod inimici Sladi inde eum calumniandi ansam arripere queant: itaque orat, ut mihi scribas, quali incommodo Sladus laborasse ex eâ sanië colligatur, an sint hæmorrhoides, vel simile quid; ut ita omnibus malevolis, qui publicum ejusmodi instrumentum inspicere possunt, si famam ejus traducere cupiant, os obstruatur. Jam præcedente hebdomade Sladi consanguinei literas cambii trecentarum librarum Sterlingarum in Angliam miserunt, ut omnes sumptus funebres, omniaque Sladi debita, solvantur: eas jam exhibitas nullus dubito, nisi forte trajectus tabellarii sævis hisce tempestatibus sit impeditus. Summas tibi consanguinei gratias agunt, easque DD. Doctoribus Oxoniensibus, quando sumptus ipsis restituuntur, per te agi cupiunt. Literas D. Doctoris Tyrrel, quæ obitus Sladi historiam continent, in gratiam D. Consulis et consanguineorum in linguam Belgicam verti curavi: illæ jam promiscue legi possunt a quibusvis,
― 779 ―
egregiumque Doctoris Tyrrel testimonium omnem sinistrum de Slado sparsum rumorem diluit; nam nulla mentis vacillantis indicia sunt, nisi inter ea ipsum iter Anglicanum, et clandestinas illas abitiones amicis inconsultis referamus. Verum hæc hactenus.

(Latin) Excellent Sir,
At last your letter, written on 27 December but not received by me until 17 January, has relieved us of all the anxiety we had begun to feel from Francke's letter about Sladus's death, or rather about the nature of it. His letter was written the same day as yours, but reached us a whole week ahead of it; it simply informed Mr. Burgomaster Hudde in general terms of Sladus's sudden and unexpected end; there was no mention whatever of apoplexy, which he is believed to have died of; and as the letter which Francke said you had written to me did not arrive we had begun to suspect that there was something unpleasant which you judged it prudent to break gradually to us. The burgomaster wishes to thank you through me for the care you have taken of his friend; he has assured me more than once how deeply grateful he is for this service of yours to himself. Francke is mistaken, however, in thinking that Sladus had a not inconsiderable sum in gold with him; Sladus's relations vouch one and all for the fact that he took no very large sum in gold from here to England; he had, they say, a letter of exchange for a hundred pounds sterling; as this letter has been sent back here, they conclude that no money can have been taken from their uncle, but that he must have needed what he had in his purse to defray [p. 778] his expenses in England. Francke sent the burgomaster a list of the articles which were found in Sladus's lodgings; on reading it, however, he was somewhat surprised at the mention of a shirt soiled with some kind of purulent discharge, from which it is inferred that Sladus was suffering from some bodily ailment. Notaries in our country are not accustomed to making such observations; they make only a bare list of the articles they find. But what troubles the burgomaster is the thought that Sladus's enemies may seize upon this as an excuse for defaming him; he therefore begs that you will write and tell me what indication the discharge gives of the kind of trouble that Sladus was suffering from, whether it was haemorrhoids or something like that; so that in this way any malicious persons who have the opportunity of inspecting a public document of this sort, if they desire to blacken his reputation, may have their mouths shut. Sladus's relations last week sent to England a letter of exchange for three hundred pounds sterling, for the payment of all funeral expenses and all Sladus's debts; no doubt this has come to hand by now, unless perhaps the passage of the post has been interfered with by these frightful storms. The relations send you their most sincere thanks, and they hope that you will convey the same to the Oxford doctors when their expenses are settled. I have had Dr. Tyrrell's letter containing the account of Sladus's death translated into Dutch for the benefit of the burgomaster and Sladus's relations; it can now be read by all and sundry, and Dr. [p. 779] Tyrrell's remarkable evidence puts an end to any adverse rumours that have been spread about Sladus; for there is nothing in it that points to any unsteadiness of mind, unless we are to count as such that journey of his in England and those occasions on which he slipped away without consulting his friends. So much for that.
(Latin) The publication of the book of the Holy Office is held up by the very high cost of paper; for this reason, glad as I should be to see it appear, I cannot hurry it on very much; nor can one hope for any fall in the price while this war continues, as all trade with France is strictly forbidden by law; this is what is keeping the work of the press at a standstill here and allowing so very few books to be printed. I hear that the earl of Pembroke is expected here once again;†1 I hope he will be successful in his business. When Furly comes here I will settle everything with him; it will also be most convenient for him to arrange matters with Wetstein himself. Psrzijphovius's works are now for the most part in print; there still remain some treatises on magistracy, which have been relegated to the end of the whole collection.†2 I had a letter from the dean of Salisbury,†3 in which he expresses his all too kind opinion of my disputation with Don Balthasar. I forbear to give you his actual words, [p. 780] as I should be unable to write them down without blushing. He approves of everything; very different from the Leipzigers.†1 Veen, Guenellon, and the rest of our Collegians, but most particularly my wife and children, join me in wishing you the best of health. Good-bye, excellent Sir.
Your most affectionate
PHILIPPUS VAN LIMBORCH
Amsterdam 20 January

1234. Jean Le Clerc to Locke, 11/21 January 1690 (1216, 1257)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 13, ff. 39-40. Printed in Bonno, Le Clerc, pp. 41-2.
A Amsterdam le 21 de Janvier 1690.
J'ai reçu, Monsieur, le billet, que vous m'avez fait l'honneur de m'écrire, le même ordinaire que M. de Limborch a reçu la rélation de la mort du pauvre M. Sladus. Depuis la Vente de sa Bibliotheque, on n'en pouvoit rien augurer de bon; car quand un homme, qui a pris plaisir toute sa vie à lire, est entiérement dégouté de ce plaisir, sans qu'il lui soit arrivé d'ailleurs de malheur, jam Proserpina caput ejus poscit; et eum mordet ab infernis Cerberus usque vadis.†2 Je vous suis
― 781 ―
obligé de l'offre que vous me faites de m'envoier le dernier Tome des Transactions Philosophiques, et je l'accepte, à condition que vous me chargerez de quelque commission semblable pour Amsterdam. J'ose encore vous prier d'y joindre les Catalogues of Books, depuis Michaelmas Term 1688, que j'ay, en cas qu'on les trouve.†1 Je prends cette liberté, dans la persuasion où je suis que vous en userez de même avec moi.
Lors que Mylord de Pembroke sera arrivé,†2 je lui envoierai le Jansenisme qu'il n'a pas reçu, quoi que je ne puisse comprendre comment, l'aiant porté moi même au batteau de la Haie, et l'aiant adressé à M. Barker. Je suis, Monsieur, Vôtre très-humble et très-obeïssant serviteur
J LE CLERC
Je n'attends qu'une occasion, pour vous envoier ce même livre, avec les Tomes XIV et XV de la Bibliotheque.†3 J'ai envoié le Jansenisme par la poste à Mr. l'Evêque de Salisbury, parce que l'on m'a assuré qu'il ne lui couteroit rien de port, étant membre du Parlement.†4 Si vous m'indiquiez quelque voie semblable, je pourrois m'en servir, pour vous le faire tenir plûtôt.
Address: A Monsieur Monsieur Locke A Londres.
Endorsed by Locke: Le Clerc 21 Jan 90 Answered 2 Feb.
1235. Nicolas Toinard to Locke, [c. 22 January/1 February 1690] (1231, 1293)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 21, ff. 176-7. The statement about the two 'adresses' and Ponton as agent shows that the letter is later than no. 1231. On 5 February, N.S., Eusèbe Renaudot wrote to Toinard, thanking him for his 'lettre du premier de ce mois, et les exemplaires de vos Dissertations': B.N., MS. N.Acq. fr. 563, ff. 136-7. The dissertations are probably the same as the quartos of this letter; if they are, the letter was probably written about the same time as that to Renaudot.

Aiant bezoin, monsieur, de me precautionner contre la prescription†5 dans l'honneur d'un souvenir qui m'est aussi precieux que la
― 782 ―
vôtre, je ne crains point de me servir pour l'interrompre, d'un moien qui vous sera onereux. c'est, monsieur, de vous envoier deux in 4° de ma façon,†1 dont je vous prie d'en donner un de ma part à l'Excellentissime et Illustrissime Lord Bishop of St Asaph.
J'ay un otre petit traité que l'on imprime De Annis Commodi,†2 qui sera plus agreable que ceque je vous envoie. Il sera fort court. car je n'entrepens que d'y faire voir une chose qui a choqué tous les Antiquaires à qui je l'ay communiquée, et je ne veux pas qu'ils aient dorenavant à soufler.
Je vous ay marqué deux adresses. mais la seconde est la plus seure A Monsieur Ponton Procureur du Roy de l'Amirauté.
A Calais
Ne savez vous point si l'on ne donnera rien de mr Vossius.†3 c'est un Auteur qu'avoit bien connu chez ele la Reine Christine,†4 car elle disoit de lui qu'il parloit de tout cequ'il ne savoit point, et ne disoit rien de cequ'il savoit. Il†a- savoit bien la Geographie anciene et le Grec des Septantes.-†a
La mort survenuë de mr Bigot, homme savantissime, et l'un de mes anciens amis depuis plus de quarente ans, m'engagera à faire un Admonitio De Cangianâ chronici Paschalis Editione. car si je n'etois plus, la posterité seroit bien tronpée touchant un Codex Holstenii, que cite incessament mr Du cange, et qui n'a jamais eté in Codicum naturâ. Il n'y avoit que mr Bigot et moy qui pussent en parler. cest une beveüe inexprimable. ce pretendu codex, estoit un exemplaire que j'ay sur ma table, dans lequel j'avois grifoné sur les marges tout cequi m'etoit venu dans la pensée. on me l'emprunta, et on le preta à mr Du cange, qui sachant que j'avois celui de Holstein, ou sont les Variæ Lectiones du Vatican, et ne connoissant point ma main, il la prit pour cele d'Holstein. cequi m'en revient, cest que c'est moy qui ait appellé Paschale, le Chronicon
― 783 ―
mal nommé Alexandrinum. Il y a plus d'une chose à dire la dessus.†1 A l'heure que je vous ecris, on fait pour moy une negociation à l'Escurial pour collationer un ou deux Manuscrits que l'on croit etre de cete chronique. J'ay eté trois fois dans ce Monastere Roial, mais je ne songeois pas alors à cela.
Hier le Triumvir me vint voir. nous parlames fort de vous à l'ordinere. Il vous salüe. Je l'entretins d'une double corection dans un passage de la Chron. Alexandr. page 632. de l'anciene edition.†2
Καὶ ἐν Σμύρνῃ — Ασίας, πρὸ δ' εἰδῶν Μαρτίων, ὅ έστι κατὰ Ασιανοὺς, μηνὶ ἓκτῳ ιβ. σαββάτου ὥρᾳ δεκάτῃ. cela est arivé Anno Ch. 251 lizez Ιουλίων, ὅ — μηνὶ αὐτῳ ιβ. σαββάτου
ante IV. Idus Julias, quod est secundùm Asiaticos, mense ipso, (die) duodecimâ, Sabbati horâ decimâ.
l'Auteur veut dire que le quatriême des Ides de Juillet, sont selon les Asiatiques le 12. du même mois, (de Juillet,) parceque les Asiatiques content ordine continuo à primâ die mensis, non autem retrogrado à Nonis Idibus vel Kalendis ut Romani. Il dit que c'est μηνὶ αὐτῷ, mense ipso sive eodem; parceque si ce quatriême jour etoit devant les Calendes ce ne seroit pas mense eodem, mais antecedenti. Dans tout le tems de l'Empire de Decius, qui est de plus de deux ans, (dont le commencement est entre le 17. Juin, ch. 249. car Philippe regnoit encore. Cod.Tit.35. L.i.†3 De revocandis Donationibus, et le 19. Octobre Decius lui avoit succedé. Ibid. Lib.iv. Tit.16.) vous ne trouverez point un 12. jour de Mars au [ ]†a c'est pourquoi j'ay mis Ιουλίον. Je†b- n'examineray pas ici ceque le Grand Usserius en a dit.-†b†4
Decius etoit mort avant la fin de l'année ch.151.†5 c'est depuis le mois de Juillet 149. jusques à ce tems la trois anneés de Puissance Tribuniciene, ut in nummis et lapidibus. mais c'est pleinement, et non de termino ad terminum, mais de die ad diem. Il y a par le
― 784 ―
premier moien deux années dans Galba, qui n'a eu que dix mois d'Empire. Le terminus cest 10. dies Decembris, quâ Tribuni Plebis ordinarii magistratum inibant. cujus interventu iterabatur Tribunicia Potestas Imperatorum. mais c'etoit selon la fantaisie des monetaires, et des graveurs d'Inscriptions. J'explique un nombre infini de medailles et d Inscriptions. Entr'otres les trois medailles de Trajan qui font tant de peine, et je les supose frapées entre le 10. et le dernier de Decembre de l'anneè 102.
Je vous communique ces choses pour en faire part à Mylord susdit, mais je vous prie de ne les pas publier, car cela fait une des plus belles parties de mon Traité (page 8. de cet in 4°) De Tribuniciâ—†1
Quand ma Dissertation sur les Anneès de Commode sera acheveé, je donneray ceque j'ay fait sur Lactance De Mortibus Persecutorum, qui ne sera pas gros, mais in 4°. J'y distingue les Interlocuteurs dans le Chapitre XVIII. ceque l'on n'a point fait encore. J'y ay fait une corection sur la fin. ex parte mutaverat. je lis ex fratre mutuaverat ominis causâ. c'est à dire que Diocletien avoit emprunté le nom de Maximianus (Herculius) son frere, consortio Imperii (ch. VIII. et in Thalmude,) pour le donner à Galerius Armentarius. La question est d'apuier mutuaverat pour mutuatus fuerat. J'ay St.Matth. V. <4>2.†a Priscien Lib. VIII.De verbo. Cæcilius dans Rob. Stephanus. Mutuationes pour Mutui acceptiones dans Ciceron. Trouvez moi ailleurs Mutuo pour Mutuor Δανείζομαι.†2
Si vous pouriez en atendant que le Josephe d'Oxfort†3 soit achevé, me procurer les variæ lectiones Greques et Latines des paidogonies†4 tant devant qu'apres le Deluge, vous me feriez bien plaisir. J'ay collationné les mss. du Roy sur ce point, et il est seur que Josephe a suivi le calcul de l'hebreu d'a present, par la et par d'otres argumens sans replique.
Outre la rectification de la fuite de st Joseph en Ægypte, et cele de son retour, j'en ay encore trouvé une belle, mais moins importante,
― 785 ―
des Paraboles du semeur, et de l'ivroie. Satoris et Zizaniorum. Vous orez le tout avec des caracterismes corigéz.

1236. James Tyrrell to Locke, 23 January [1690] (1227, 1228, 1239)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 76-7. Year from Locke's endorsement. The letter refers to no. 1225 and Locke's lost answer to it.
Oxford Jan: 23d:
Dear Sir
For so I will still make bold to call you, and so you must ever be to me, (tho you will not vouchsafe the same title): for I am not (as I told you in my first) so ungratefull; as to let smaller disobligations cancell greater benefites: but I hope you will not take it as a slight if I have not returned you a more speedy answere, since your last comeing to my hands, whilst I was in Buckinghamshire, and being there all the Christmasse in a perpetuall hurry of company; or removeing from one place to another; and allso since I came from thence haveing bin obliged to attend our Sessions,†1 I returned not hither againe to settle till the begining of this weeke: but as my answere required no great hast: so I desire you to beleive me when I assure you (as I doe now), that I did not write my former onely to vent my spleen: or to make you uneasy with so ill conversation; (which perhaps you might have to much reason not to be pleased with) but rather partly to let you see that if you had (as you supposed) sufficient cause to write me a cold, and unfreindly letter for so small an offence as neglecting to write to you: If such small punctilios might be any just cause of unkindnesse; I thought I had much more reason on my side to take exceptions. so that if I have vented my resentments a little too freely you may impute it to your first unkind letter; which forced me to Justifye my self, and to let you see that it was not my fault that our former freindship was not maintained with its usual warmth; since it was on your; and not on my side that I thought it first tooke cold; onely I am sorry that I
― 786 ―
could not well justifye my self without accuseing of you: since I supposed I could not by any better method convince you that you had no reason to take my not writeing ill; then to let you see your self was more guilty in the neglect of those outward ceremonyes of Freindship: and if Mr: T. hath at any time before put you upon so unpleaseing a taske as the†a justifyeing your self, it was not his fault, but that Gentlemans who writ him an unkind letter, blameing him for his silence, when he had commanded him not to write till he heard from him at his returne out of Germany:†1 this I grant produced a letter of the same kind with your last: in which you confest you had forgot that you ever writ such a letter; which Mr: T. took for a sufficient satisfaction; as he does now, when you have told him that you had forgot who writ. last: as for your other justifications, about not communicateing your comeing over, and not returneing visites. etc. as I have no desire to quarrel about such petty circumstances, so I take what you say as a sufficient excuse, especially since you assure me you have treated those other Freinds of yours; (who may expect more from you) after the same, manner; tho on the other side I hope you will pardon my ignorance if I before†b that†b expected wee should have conversed after the same rate wee used to doe 7; or 8 years agoe: but if you were to visite me it is more then I ever heard of: unlesse once about 5, or 6 a clock at night; at which hour had I come to have seen you: I beleive you would have thought that I onely calld by chance without expecting to find you at home: but since I find you doe not now observe such punctilios with your Freinds; I shall not expect them for the future: provided it be not taken ill, if I use the like Liberty: and therefore you need not endeavour to find a contradiction in what I writ; that I doe not stand upon such childish punctilios tho they sate somewhat heavy upon my mind: (which words whether they immediatly follow the former sentence I must leave to your ingenuity who repeat them) yet I thinke there will be no contradiction if you take into the sense that which I remember immediatly followd viz: provided I could be satisfyed it were done without any desire of being rid of a Freindship—etc.
and to which I may now adde another proviso: viz: that the Gentleman I write to, doe not fall into the
― 787 ―
same humane frailty; as I see he does, when he tells me that some offences taken in Towne lasted so long as to hinder me from remembering him in J.C.inline image †1 letter to Syl: and likewise from writeing to him my self, since if you please to examine your man he will tell you there was a very kind remembrance in it from Mr: T. by this good token; that the businesse of that postscript was to let Mr: L. know that if he desired to have his bookes or other things sent him up before Mr: T. went out of the Countrey his commands should be obeyd upon notice: and Mr: T. had writ that himself had He†a not seen you so lately; and besides was loath to lay a fresh obligation of writeing upon one of Mr: Ls: great businesse: if John C. writ any other letter but that, in which he did not remember my service it was done without my privity: and therefore I cannot answere for it: so that†b- I cannot-†b here forbear minding you of your owne good advice not to indulge needlesse Jealousyes and supitions towards your Freinds: as for what you likewise tell me that it is not your fashion to complaine (tho' sure the last accusation comes very neer it) for if it were you should not want matter of very serious concernement; since you are so reserved as not to discover it, I know not how either to Justify my self, or to aske your pardon.
but Ile assure you I will not fail to doe either the one or the other; whenever you please to discover that matter. for†c- I thinke;-†c I may challenge you (as you doe me) to tell what material acts of Freindship I have ever neglected, that were in my power; nay more what sins of commission I have done contrary to the strict rules of it. But to conclude and put an end to this dispute, (such kind of conversation being as little pleasant to me as it can be to you) I call God to witnesse that I write this as the former onely to create a better understanding for the future, which can be produced by no better means then by freely telling each other wherein wee thinke wee have trangressed the rules of Freindship; and since I appeal to no other Judg but your owne Conscience if that acquits you I doe: and if have bin mistaken in any thing that I layed to your charge I humbly beg your pardon; but if such kind of conversati<on>†d be uneasy to you, I will stifle my resentments for the future, rather then disturbe the quiet of one for one I have so entire a respect:
― 788 ―
onely remember that we all have our failings nor are those you have made your Freinds exempted from the common Fate of mankind: and therefore I shall leave this controversy to be ended by your owne good nature if you have any Freindship yet left for one you once called Freind: if not; that shall not make me lesse ready to expresse my self on all occasions (wherein I may be ever able to serve you)
your most reall; and faithfull Freind; and servant.
JT.
Endorsed by Locke: J: Tyrrell 23 Jan 89/90

1238. Benjamin Hawkshaw to Locke, 27 January 1690 (1214, 1310)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 11, ff. 157-8.
St. Johns Coll: Cam: January 27. 89.
Sir
I am Extreamly troubled that the Lancaster Waggener†4 should disappoint You and Impose on me who told me that he delivered it to the Maid, afterwards by som Examination finding he never delivered it, I thought fit to take it away from him and deliver it to this bearer 14 Shillings, Sir In my reply to Mr Sylvesters†5 letter I desired him to Inform me what it Cost and I should send it by the Next opportunity, Sir I am sorry things fell otherwise than I wished, who deserved so well at my hands, Pray Sir Pardon the many troubles I put you to, and I shall with all Respect subscribe my self
Your Most humble servant
BEN: HAWKSHAW.

1239. James Tyrrell to Locke, 27 January [1690] (1236, 1248)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 22, ff. 78-81; f. 80 is a scrap, presumably the part of a letter mentioned in the postscript. Year from Locke's note.
Jan: 27th:†a
Dear Sir
I received your last, yesterday, and am glad I can give Dr: Bernard an account; of the reason that hath retarded the returne of this small summe: for I feard the letter was miscarryed when wee were so long without hearing any thing from you about it; but now I am very well satisfyed with the cause of the delay and shall tell the partyes to whom the rest of the money is still due the reason of it: I know not whither there be any bill of Exchange among the Doctors papers, for receive<ing>†b yours late last night; I have not yet had time to goe to Dr: Bernards to examine them; if there be, his Freinds shall be sure to have it sent them by you: as for the summe it†c- was mistaken in the account-†c tho not much; for I had not then payed all the bills: but find now the whole charge to be seaven pounds seaven teen shillings according to this enclosed bill, which you may shew the partyes concerned.
But I am much obliged to you for your care of me, in not giveing the account till you had heard againe from me: since I alone stand engaged for the Coffin, wine, etc, which†d- are yet unpayd.-†d Dr: Bernard being sick and not able to stir abroad when the Body was buryed. as for the rings you mention you may doe as you please as to Dr: Bernard and my self tho wee doe not expect any such thing; and much lesse the Doctor who opend him who is an Italian Anatomist
― 791 ―
of great worth;†1 and lives now in the house with me, tho I am sorry the Thorax was not opend, as well as the Head; for I fancy the cause of his death might lye about the heart after all: if you send the money pray let it be now to me since I stand engaged to see all discharged; wee have since Dr: Bernards letter payed the Clarkes and parsons dues with the sale of his cloaths and a pair of silver buckles: which came to about 01:
I thanke you for your kind offer of your booke†2 which I pray send me by Oxford Waggon directed for me at one Mrs: Vigarss house over against the Theater: but pray let me know in a line or two by whom you send it: this enclosed was to have bin sent last post but stayd for the book to be bound which I have now sent you;†3 together with this enclosed by Bartlets waggon: I have no more at present but that I am your Freind; and humble servant
J TYRRELL.
I pray present my humble service to Mr: Clarke if in Towne; and Mr: Furley if in England.
This enclosed being part of a letter I lately received from a Freind of mine I thought fit to send it you: because you will thereby see the various reception your booke meets with in the world; according to the different temper of readers.
Mr: Pawleing hath a booke of your called the history of Salt Petre; written by Mr: B.†4 and allso the Patriarcha non Monarcha which I gave you if you thinke it worth while you may aske him for them: my service to him; and hope he hath got a place.†5 the rascall that kept your horse†6 has cheated both you; and me; of the case of pistolls; but if you give me authority under your hand to demand them of him I will doe it; or els threaten to arrest him if Syl: can prove the delivery of them, to him.
I have now lookt over all his papers which I send you (together with his Key; and Almanac) but can find no bill of exchange for any money: nor so much as aney account about any: He had no bookes but a Janua Linguarum which was sold with the Cloathes.

1240. J. G. GrÆvius to Locke, 27 January/6 February 1690 (1200, 1286)
B.L., MS. Locke c. 10, ff. 34-6. The last part of the letter ('Honorarii Champnei', etc.) is on a detached leaf; Locke's answer to the letter, no. 1286, shows that it belongs here. Answers no. 1200.
(English) Vir Nobilissime et Amplissime.
Si tu, vir gravissimus, gravissimis negotiis, quæ post tot annorum absentiam reducem exercent, occupatus culpam silentii deprecaris, quam ego rationem inibo culpam hanc diluendi, qui tuis, plenis amoris et officii, litteris tam diu responsum debeo? Nam cum ego,
― 794 ―
a quo tempore te vidi et cognovi, Te suspexerim et coluerim, tuasque virtutes ac ingenii dotes magni fecerim, acceptis litteris tuis magna laetitia perfundebar, et quod te tibi tuisque restitutum auspicato post tam longos errores significarent, et quod luculentissime testarentur, te non solum mei memorem vivere, sed et me amare, meaque caussa velle summopere, quo cave credas quicquam gratius mihi accidere potuisse. Statim igitur plenus tui, plenus gaudii me accingebam ad respondendum. Sed cum primo Frisicum iter intercessisset, postea nescio quae fatalis cunctatio, <dum>†a diem de die duco, meam scribendi voluntatem adhuc retardavit. Nunquam mihi magis infestus succensui quam ob hanc procrastinationem respondendi tibi. Si <patieris>†b confessione istius culpae satisfieri tibi, eam inposterum creberrimis officiis emendabo.
(English) Quid vero est, quod tu tantopere praedicas, quod tibi hic praestiti, aut per meam sortem praestare potui? Tenuia illa, quae nobiscum agenti navavi officia, num sine crimine barbarae cujusdam inhumanitatis poterant praetermitti? Nam qui te novit, et non deperit, ac non omni studii genere prosequitur, eum ego non dignum censeam, qui in hominibus praeditis moribus cultioribus, sed in inhospitalibus Scythis numeretur, tantae sunt tui ingenii suavitates, tanta
― 795 ―
vitae integritas, ne quid dicam de insigni eruditione, et salsa illa venustate, qua sermones tuos condire solebas. Utinam ea esset fortuna mihi, qua testatum facere possem, quantam mihi in te colendo constituerim pietatem, quantique te aestimem ac tuam amicitiam, profecto cognosceres neminem esse posse tui studiosiorem, licet longo annorum usu tibi sit conjunctissimus. Quod si potero aliquando ullo genere officii obsequiique consequi, omnia me consecutum esse putabo.
(English) Res vestras in dies laetiores facilioresque fieri gaudemus sane, et optamus ut tam firma sede collocentur, ut nullis res novas molientium artibus et machinis possint convelli et labefactari. Grande momentum videntur adferre ad hoc posse controversiae de ratione <regendi>†a ecclesiam, si possent componi et sopiri. Possent autem, si ab animis aequis, et nimio partium studio alienis ponderarentur. Sed, quae est multorum pertinacia in tuendis, quae semel imbiberunt, hac optare licet, sperare vix licet, quamvis sint, qui de concilio non nullorum Theologorum, quod Londini habetur,†1 utpote qui sint spectatae moderationis viri, laetiora promittant. Faxit deus
― 796 ―
ut viam inveniant in concordiam omnia reducendi. Vota quoque nuncupabimus pro itu et reditu Regis Wilhelmi. Iam enim fertur iter adornare in Scotiam†1 et Hiberniam, quod propter pericula varia, quibus id est obnoxium, nos habet sollicitos.
(English) Ab aliis accepi magna cum laetitia tuam disputationem de mente humana nunc typis describi non tantum lingua Anglica, sed et Latina, in quam sit translata. Nihil nobis longius est, quam ut tam pulchrum ingenii tui foetum videamus. Lutetiae sub proelis sudat Huetii opus de ratione et fide, cuius dissertationes contra Cartesianos vidisti credo.†2 Accipis hic parvum libellum docti Scoti Georgii Maukensei, qui modo hic prodiit.†3
(English) Sladum nostrum in avita patria obiisse pertulerunt ad nos amici. Equidem doleo me amisisse amicum doctum. Sed feralis annus superior mihi plures eripuit. Lugduni Batavorum Lemonium†4 et Ryckium,†5 in Gallia Emericum Bigotium, in Germania Marquardum Gudium, qui olim adolescens edidit in Parisiis genuinum

Hippolyti libellum de Antichristo.†1 Ingenio et judicio pollebat, et habebat bibliothecam tam editis, quam manu exaratis codicibus instructissimam. Vidi in illa multos patres Graecos antiquissimos, eosque ineditos, ut et non nullos Philosophos Platonicos, ac etymologicum ponderosum Photii.†2 Obiit in Holsatia, quae ei patria erat, Regi vero Daniae fuit a consiliis. Vale vir nobilissime, et me ama: ut vero te pergere in me amando intelligam, fac saepius a te litteras habeam, quod tamen fiat tuo commodo. Quam diu illis caruero, tam diu magno bono me carere credo. (English) Honorarii Champnei, necessarii vestri, pudet me te denuo meminisse. Tanti id non est. sed quia jubes, et imperas et quidem tam severe ac si amicitiae renunciaturus esses, nisi ego id facerem, imperanti obtemperandum est, ne ulla in re videar tibi refragari. Dimidia pars honorarii mihi est soluta, quindecim floreni. sed satis nummorum solutum est pro paucis horis, quas mecum exegit: Nam ceteras, quas mihi debebat impendere, suis impendit amicis. Si
― 798 ―
tamen nihil aequi a vobis obtinere potero, et vos omnino pertenditis quod mihi non debetur mittere, pro pecunia si mihi miseritis Kave vestri de scriptoribus ecclesiasticis librum in folio,†1 (nisi excedat ejus pretium quindecim libras Batavicas,)†2 quem vidi nuperius apud civem nostrum, sed qui in nostris tabernis haberi non potest, reponetur in meis forulis perpetuum monumentum vestri in me amoris.
(Latin) Illustrious and Excellent Sir,
If a man of your importance, occupied with the weighty affairs that claim your attention on your return after so many years' absence, sees fit to apologize for your silence, how am I to set about excusing that fault in myself, who have for so long been owing you a reply to your most affectionate and [p. 794] obliging letter? For ever since I saw you and came to know you I have looked up to and respected you and have set the highest value on your excellent qualities and gifts of intellect, so that I was overjoyed at receiving your letter, both because it told me that you were happily restored to yourself and your own people after your long wanderings and because it gave the clearest evidence that you not only keep me in mind but are fond of me and wish me all good, which, believe me, is the most welcome assurance that I could have. Accordingly with my mind full of you and full of joy I immediately made ready to reply. But there intervened first of all a journey to Friesland, and after that I was somehow beset by a fatal spirit of delay, which kept me dragging on from day to day and has up till now impeded my will to write. Never have I been more enraged with myself than for this procrastination in replying to you. If you can allow yourself to be satisfied with my confession of that fault I will make up for it in future by frequently doing my duty to you.
(Latin) But why do you make so much of what I did for you here, or what I was able to do for you in my position? Could such slight services as I rendered you whilst you were with us have been omitted without incurring the charge of a barbarous sort of inhumanity? for if any one knows you and fails to take you to his heart and to bestow every kind of attention on you, him I should consider unworthy to be numbered among civilized men, but rather to be numbered among inhospitable Scythians; such are the amenities of your [p. 795] nature and the probity of your conduct, to say nothing of your remarkable learning and the charming wit with which you were accustomed to season your conversation. I only wish I might be fortunate enough to be able to prove how firmly attention to you is fixed in my mind as a sacred duty and how highly I value you and your friendship; you would then realize that no one could be more devoted to you, even if he were united to you by long association. If I can ever achieve this by any kind of service or obedience to your wishes I shall think I have attained all that I could desire.
(Latin) We are very glad that the state of your country is becoming happier and easier from day to day, and we hope that it may be placed on such a firm footing that it cannot be shaken and overthrown by any arts or machinations of innovators. It might, it seems, greatly contribute to this end if the controversies on church government could be settled and laid to rest, as indeed they could be if the issues were weighed by fair minds uninfluenced by excessive party spirit. But such is the persistency of many people in holding to ideas they have once imbibed that one may wish for such a result but hardly hope for it, although there are some who promise happier things from the consultations of a number of divines which are being held in London,†1 they being men of known moderation. God grant that they may find a way [p. 796] of bringing about a general spirit of concord. We shall also pray for the safe journey and return of King William; for it is now said that he is preparing to set out for Scotland†1 and Ireland, which makes us anxious on account of the various dangers to which such an expedition is exposed.
(Latin) I have heard from others to my great joy that your treatise on the human understanding is now being printed not only in English but also in Latin, into which it has been translated. There is nothing we are so impatient for as the sight of such a fine offspring of your genius. Huet's work on reason and faith is being printed at Paris; I think you have seen his dissertations against the Cartesians.†2 I am sending you this small book by the Scottish scholar George Mackenzie, which recently appeared here.†3
(Latin) The news of our Sladus's death in his ancestral country has been brought to us by friends. I am sorry to have lost a scholarly friend. But the past year has been one of deaths and has robbed me of several. At Leyden there have been Lemonius†4 and Ryckius,†5 in France Emeric Bigot, and in Germany Marquard Gude, who formerly as a very young man published at Paris the genuine [p. 797] work of Hippolytus de Antichristo.†1 He had excellent talents and judgement and owned a library well equipped with printed as well as manuscript books. In it I saw many of the oldest Greek Fathers, and those unedited, as well as some Platonic philosophers and the ponderous Lexicon of Photius.†2 He died in Holstein, his native country; he was a counsellor to the king of Denmark. Good-bye, illustrious Sir, and love me; so that I may perceive that you continue to love me, see to it that I often hear from you, which must however be at your convenience. All the time that I am without your letters I feel that I am missing a great good. Good-bye again, my guiding star. Utrecht 6 February 1690.
(Latin) I am ashamed at your mentioning your connection Champneys's tuition fee once again. It is not of such importance. But since you bid and command me, and that as sternly as if you meant to renounce my friendship unless I comply, I must obey your orders, so as not to appear to thwart you in anything. Half the fee has been paid me, fifteen gulden; but that is payment enough for the few hours he spent with me; the rest, which he ought to have devoted to me, he devoted to his friends. However, if I cannot get you to see [p. 798] reason and you absolutely insist on sending me what is not due to me, send me, please, instead of money your countryman Cave's folio book De Scriptaribus Ecclesiasticis†1 (provided that it does not cost more than fifteen Dutch pounds),†2 which I saw the other day at a fellow-citizen's house, but which is not to be had in our bookshops; it shall be placed among my books as a perpetual memorial of your affection for me.
Endorsed by Locke: Grævius Feb 90 Answered 25 Apr.

Jan. 28. 1689. Oxon.
Honoured
Mr. Tyrrell hath sent the few things that the excellent doctor Slade left behind him, besides his cloathes, which were sold at a just rate for 29s. and 3d. You will find little or noe notice of any domestic concerne: but cheifly Greeke verses, which I admire at.
Mr. Tyrrell hath written at large to you by the Waggon of Bartlet that went hence yesterday: and the money due for the funerall, deductis deducendis,†3 comes to 4l. 18s. 3d. I cannot but lament that I lost so good and ingenious a freind in that sodaine surprize.
Our freinds at Christchurch are pretty well, especially the aged Doctor.†4
Honoured
I am your humble and obligd servant
E. BERNARD.

Index of Correspondents in this Volume
This index is by the numbers of the letters, italics being used as in the text to indicate letters not by Locke. A bracketed number is either for a letter between persons other than Locke, in which case it appears under the names of both writer (or writers) and person addressed, or for an item other than a letter. If there is correspondence in earlier or later volumes between Locke and a person in this index it is indicated by the citation of the next volume or volumes in which any of it occurs.
The citation immediately following a name is that of a biographical note on the person. For persons concerned with only one or two letters the citation is omitted sometimes if the biographical note occurs in the headnote and is insignificant.

Recurrent Designations other than Proper Names
These notes and the accompanying list are intended to enable readers to identify persons frequently mentioned in the letters in this volume by dignities, initials, nicknames, and similar designations. These designations are variable; a person may be indicated in several ways.
In the earlier part of the volume a group of friends is prominent: Sir Walter Yonge of Escot (Sir W, Sir Walter, Sir W Y); his sister Elizabeth Yonge, later Mrs. B. Beale (Locke's 'daughter Betty'); his sister Mrs. Isabella Duke (Sister D); and her husband Richard Duke of Otterton (Brother D, Mr D; called by Mrs. Duke 'my Master'; they have a daughter Betty). They are sometimes mentioned collectively as Locke's Spa or Devon or Tunbridge friends (the last includes John Freke). They were friends of Edward (Locke's 'friend Sumshire') and Mrs. Clarke, and the three estates, Chipley, Escot, and Otterton, are called collectively the Row; they were friends also of Dr. David Thomas and John Freke (J F or J Fr, Mr Fr). In letters written by Dr. Thomas, Clarke is sometimes E C; his children include Edward, called Master, and Elizabeth or Betty, Locke's 'mistress'.
Abbé, M.l': the Abbé François Gendron
Adrian (or A or Uncle A, etc.): Dr. David Thomas
Benjamin: Benjamin Furly
C (for Carmelin): Locke
C, J. (or John C, etc.): John Clerk (Tyrrell's servant)

†1 The Collegie. There is no satisfactory English equivalent for the word as used here. It applies to a group of persons (friends?) having a common interest and meeting from time to time (perhaps regularly) for discussion (or perhaps study) (the word club was current in this sense in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries but is now obsolete). Locke lists the members of the present group in his Journal, 22 May 1684, with the heading 'Nomina Collegarum Collegii privati Medici'. It appears to have had no connection with other groups of the kind. It was interested in general as well as medical subjects. All the members, apart from van Limborch, were physicians and all, apart from Locke, were probably Remonstrants. Besides van Limborch and Locke they were Guenellon, Veen, and Sladus; Abrahamus Quina (p. 412), Pieter Bernagie (p. 413), and Abrahamus Cyprianus (p. 651).
(A statement by Le Clerc in his account of Locke is clearly erroneous: Bibliotheque choisie, vi. 376. Dr. Dewhurst associates this group with a collegium privatum in which Gerard Blaes or Blasius (N.N.B.W.) was concerned: John Locke, p. 226 n.; I can find no link between the two.)
I am using the word Collegie for the present group, and Collegians for its members. The word college, French or English, is used for the Dutch word in another sense in nos. 1179, 1201, etc.

†4 Roman Catholic religion.
†5 Francis Osborne (no. 38), Historical Memoires, 1658, King James, § 14 (p. 41). Herb-John here is a tasteless herb of neutral qualities; coloquintida is extremely bitter and purgative: O.E.D.
†1 Sir Francis Wythens or Withens (D.N.B.), judge of the King's Bench, was dismissed on 22 April; Sir Richard Allibone (ibid.) was sworn a judge on 28 April: London Gazette, 25 April, 2 May. Wythens was probably hated by the Whigs and little liked by anyone else. There were other changes among the judges in April, but after them no more for some time.
†2 In July 1686 James II established a Commission for Ecclesiastical Affairs. It is arguable that he was within his rights, but it has generally been considered illegal. New commissions were appointed in January and October of this year. In February James ordered Dr. John Peachell, Master of Magdalene College, Cambridge, and vice-chancellor of the university (D.N.B.), to admit to the degree of M.A. Alban Francis, a Benedictine monk (ibid.), without his taking any oaths. The congregation of the university refused to obey the order, and Peachell and deputies of the senate were summoned to appear before the Ecclesiastical Commissioners in London. On 7 May the Commissioners deprived Peachell of the vice-chancellorship and suspended him ab officio et beneficio of his mastership: C. H. Cooper, Annals of Cambridge, 1842-1908, iii. 615-33.
†3 John Massey (D.N.B.), a recent convert, was installed dean on 29 December 1686: Wood, L. and T. iii. 201.
†4 For the building see ibid. iii. 232; see further p. 257.
†5 Obadiah Walker, Master of University College: D.N.B. Anthony Wood in February 1687 gives a list of about a dozen recent converts, men and women, including Walker and Massey: L. and T. iii. 214.
†6 In January 1687 Walker published through the University printer Two Discourses concerning the Adoration of Our Blessed Saviour in the Eucharist, by Abraham Woodhead (D.N.B.); some scholars obtaining the book sheet by sheet as it was printing, an answer by William Wake (the future archbishop of Canterbury; no. 835 n.) was published in February. Walker thereupon set up a press in his own lodgings in University College: Wood, L. and T. iii. 209; Athenæ, iii. 1161-4.
†1 A. Woodhead, Church Government. Part V: A Relation of the English Reformation, published in April: Wood, L. and T. iii. 217-18. The book by Nicholas Sanders is De Origine ac Progressu Schismatis Anglicani, first published in 1585: no. 506 n. The other writer is Jakob Gretser, S.J., 1562-1625, scholar and controversialist: A.D.B.
†2 Dr. Gilbert Burnet, Some Letters. Containing an Account of what seemed most Remarkable in Switzerland, Italy, &c., Amsterdam, 1686. 'My Lord, have you not seene Dr. Burnet's letters of his travells, of which many hundred copies are seized?': Sir C. Lyttelton to Lord Hatton, 29 March 1687, Hatton Correspondence, ii. 67; Clarke and Foxcroft, Burnet, p. 229. There is no satisfactory bibliography. L.L., nos. 527-8.
†3 Dr. Henry Clerke (D.N.B.), President of Magdalen, died on 24 March of this year. On 5 April the king ordered the vice-president and fellows to elect Anthony Farmer (ibid.), a man not qualified for the office of President according to the college statutes and of bad character; Farmer had ingratiated himself with Obadiah Walker by pretending to share his views, but apparently avoided conversion. The fellows petitioned against the king's mandate on 9 April, and on 15 April, the latest day allowed by the college statutes, elected as President John Hough, who had been chaplain to James Butler, duke of Ormonde, about 1678 (he was created D.D. on 22 June of this year; bishop of Oxford 1690; etc.; ibid.). On 21 April the king demanded an explanation of the fellows' conduct; they replied on 23 or 24 April: Magdalen College and King James II, ed. J. R. Bloxam (Oxford Historical Society, vol. vi, 1886; cited below as Bloxam), pp. 37-40. There are further narratives of the whole of the proceedings in Wood, L. and T. iii. 514-33.

†1 Pierre Bayle, 1647-1706: D.B.F.; E. Labrousse, Pierre Bayle, 1963-4. His health broke down in the spring through overwork; he was ill for about fifteen months: Labrousse, i. 190, 214, 215.

Quinquina and Cinchona (and see variant spellings). Goodall repeats his queries in no. 1002.

†1 Identifiable as the 'Liber Sententiarum Inquisitionis Tholosanæ', a manuscript recording the proceedings of the Inquisition at Toulouse from 1307 to 1323. Locke saw it, or a copy of it, at Montpellier in January 1677 and made notes and copied some passages from it: Journal, pp. 19-32, 34-5; B.L., MS. Locke c. 27, f. 48, dated on verso '77' and bearing a note, presumably added later, that the manuscript was 'now at Nismes' (further notes and extracts, ibid., ff. 32-47, belong perhaps to 1687-8 rather than to 1677). It may have belonged already at that time to the younger Sir William Waller (no. 353), whom Locke met and treated at Montpellier in November and December 1676: Journal. It probably belonged to Waller now; he left it with Furly as a pledge. Furly acquired it between 1695 and 1697: notices below. It was given in 1756 to the British Museum, where it is Add. MS. 4697. A late seventeenth-century manuscript copy in the Bibliothèque Nationale may be taken from the printed text rather than from the present or another, now lost, manuscript: British Museum Quarterly, xxxvi (1971-2), 84, 89. Another volume of reports is mentioned in no. 1473.
Furly and Locke tried at once to publish the manuscript. Van Limborch undertook the work; it appeared in 1692 with his Historia Inquisitionis prefixed to it: notices below.

†2 Evidently on account of the Abregé.
The separate printing has a title, Abregé d'un ouvrage intitulé Essai philosophique touchant l'entendement, with the imprint 'A Amsterdam ClϽ lϽC LXXXVIII'. It consists of the title-page, with a blank verso; the dedication to Pembroke, signed by Locke, occupying two pages; and the text, pp. 1-92.
The article in the Bibliotheque universelle (viii. 49-142; January-March 1688) is headed 'Extrait d'un Livre Anglois qui n'est pas encore publié, intitulé Essai Philosophique concernant l'Entendement, où l'on montre quelle est l'étenduë de nos connoissances certaines, & la maniere dont nous y parvenons. Communiqué par Monsieur Locke'.
The Abregé, apart from the four preliminary pages, is printed from the same typesetting as the 'Extrait', but with fresh page-headlines, pagination, and signatures (the imposition is the same throughout, A1 corresponding to C1, and p. 1 to p. 49). The upper part of the first page had to be changed for the 'Extrait', and at the end the 'Extrait' adds a paragraph (pp. 140-2) on Locke's thoughts about printing the Essay.

†1-1 In the Abregé Locke reduces the first book of the Essay to a paragraph; in it he tried to prove 'que nôtre Esprit est au commencement ce qu'on appelle tabula rasa; c'est à dire, sans idées et sans connoissance'. He then summarizes bk. II, ch. i, concluding 'Car n'y aiant dans l'Esprit aucune idée innée, ou naturelle, supposer l'esprit occupé par des idées, avant qu'il les ait reçuës de dehors, c'est supposer une chose contradictoire': pp. 1, 3. He does not use the phrase 'actual knowledge'. Lady Masham took it from Dr. Henry More's An Antidote against Atheism, and explains her meaning by shortening a passage there: 1. v (in A Collection of Several Philosophical Writings, 1662, p. 17).
†2-2 This appears to be compounded from passages in Cudworth's True Intellectual System, especially pp. 28-9, 47-9, and More, as in n. 1.

†1 This apparently relates to the pardon which Locke supposed Penn to be procuring for him: p. 307, etc. According to Lady Masham the pardon 'was actually offer'd him, but he would not accept of it as not owning that he needed it': letter to Le Clerc, 12 January 1705. There was a further consideration: if Locke were granted a pardon through any intermediary other than Pembroke, Pembroke might be offended; at the same time, should Penn offer to procure one for him, a refusal to accept the offer (or the pardon) might offend Penn. Tyrrell may have interfered less than Locke supposed; Locke was alarmed perhaps by Tyrrell's remarks about Penn's influence at court and the possibility of Locke's reinstatement at Christ Church: pp. 257, 311.

†1 Foecke Floris, fl. 1682-96, smith and Anabaptist (Mennonite) preacher, was compelled to leave Friesland in 1687 or early in 1688 on account of his supposed Socinian views. He moved to Oost-Zaandam near Haarlem, where he was attacked again, the Synod of North Holland (no. 1317 n.) appealing to the baljuw of Kennemerland, who threatened to imprison him unless he left the place. It was now that he appealed to William, who sheltered him from this and a later attack. He shared some of the Socinians' views, but was concerned with morals rather than with dogma, and was regarded as pious by Calvinists as well as by his friends: De Bie and Loosjes; see also Ollion, p. 180 n., and no. 1092.

Maurice Emmett probably after 1680 on the site of Dorset House. In the letter 'the ancient government ... in its originall constitution' is the imagined mixed or limited monarchy of pre-Stuart times.

†2 Her husband, William Popple, was born at Hull in 1638. His paternal grandfather was mayor of Hull in that year; his mother was a sister of Andrew Marvell. By 1661 he was in business in London. He married about 1664, his wife being Mary, daughter of Matthew Alured of Hull or Beverley and a niece of John Alured the regicide; she may have had a family connection with Lady Calverley. In 1670 he was settled with his family in Bordeaux, engaged probably in the wine trade. Mrs. Popple returned to England with their daughters in 1685. Popple and their son William were allowed to leave France for good in 1688 as a result of James II's representations to Louis XIV; Popple was perhaps indebted for this to Penn's influence with James. He had prospered as a merchant. Nothing is known about his livelihood from 1688 until 1696, when he was appointed secretary to the newly established Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations (the Board of Trade: nos. 1976, 2088, etc.). He resigned his secretaryship in 1707, when he was succeeded by his son William (no. 3169). He died in 1708; Mrs. Popple, in 1723. Their daughter Katherine married Maurice Ashley Cooper (no. 1449).
Popple was an earnest believer in Christian revelation, combining rationalism with some emotionalism, anti-clericalism, indifference as regards dogma, and ardour for freedom of conscience. He published in 1682 a French translation of Martin Clifford's A Treatise of Humane Reason (published in 1674; for Clifford see D.N.B.), probably writing the preface for it. An expanded English version of the preface was published in 1690 as A Discourse of Humane Reason (no. 1266). Popple's principal work was A Rational Catechism (1687), in which he links natural religion and Christian revelation (notice in Bibliotheque universelle, ix. 95-105). In 1688 he published Three Letters, in which he advocated the abolition of the penal laws and a new law for universal freedom of conscience, and later in the year A Letter to Mr. Penn, in which he advised Penn, who was suspected of being a Roman Catholic in disguise, to declare himself a Protestant; failing that, Penn would bring freedom of conscience into disrepute. In the summer of 1689 Popple translated into English Locke's Epistola de Tolerantia, adding a preface in which he wrote: 'Absolute Liberty, Just and True Liberty, Equal and Impartial Liberty, is the thing that we stand in need of.' This should be read in its context. Declarations of indulgence will only palliate, and acts of comprehension will increase, the evils that have risen from the partiality hitherto practised by the English government. What Popple asks for is equality of all churches, subject only to the secular requirements of the state, as opposed to concessions to dissidents by a dominating church; Locke's Epistola demonstrates 'the Equitableness and Practicableness' of this freedom.
Locke may have become acquainted with Popple at Bordeaux in 1677 or 1678; failing that, probably in the course of 1689; for a few years they were fairly close friends. Other friends or acquaintances of Popple's include Isaac Papin (nos. 890, 1317), who was tutor to his daughters for some time; Dr. L. Paul (no. 1449); Benjamin Furly; probably John Freke (Popple's will in 1698 was witnessed by a man of
― 624 ―
this name as well as by Paul); the members of the Dry Club (nos. 1567, 1608); above all, the third earl of Shaftesbury.
The principal authority is Caroline Robbins in William and Mary Quarterly, 3rd ser. xxiv (1967), 190-223; this is supplemented for his official career by I. K. Steele, Politics of Colonial policy ... 1696-1720, 1968. There are 31 letters from him to Locke below.

†1 Henry Booth, 1652-94; second Baron Delamer 1684; created earl of Warrington 1690: D.N.B. He and Monmouth were both Whigs and at this time commissioners of the Treasury; and hated one another.
